### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Morales v. People (Reckless Imprudence En Banc Resolution)
**Full Official Caption:** Francis O. Morales, Petitioner, vs. People of the Philippines, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 240337; Promulgated January 4, 2022; 919 Phil. 86; En Banc Resolution; Ponente: Associate Justice Rosmari D. Carandang.
**Voting Breakdown:** Gesmundo, C.J., Leonen, Hernando, Inting, Zalameda, M. Lopez, Gaerlan, Rosario, J. Lopez, Dimaampao, and Marquez, JJ., concurred. Perlas-Bernabe, J., filed a Concurring and Dissenting Opinion. Caguioa, J., filed a Separate Concurring Opinion. Lazaro-Javier, J., took no part due to prior participation in the Court of Appeals proceedings.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
Francis O. Morales (Petitioner / Accused): Driver and owner of the Mitsubishi Delica van (Plate No. XKZ-528) involved in a head-on vehicular collision.
People of the Philippines (Respondent): Represented by the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG), prosecuting the offense of criminal negligence.
Rico M. Mendoza (Private Complainant / Victim): Driver of the passenger jeepney (Plate No. CWR-138) who suffered physical injuries.
Leilani Mendoza, Myrna Cunanan, and Albert Vital (Private Complainants / Victims): Passengers aboard the passenger jeepney who sustained physical injuries.
Noel G. Garcia (Private Complainant / Vehicle Owner): Registered owner of the damaged Isuzu passenger jeepney.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 assailing the Court of Appeals (CA) Decision dated March 15, 2018, and Resolution dated June 22, 2018 (CA-G.R. CR No. 39341), which affirmed with modification the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Angeles City, Branch 56 conviction of petitioner for Reckless Imprudence Resulting in Damage to Property and Multiple Physical Injuries. The Supreme Court initially denied the petition in a Resolution dated September 21, 2020. This matter was resolved upon Petitioner's Motion for Reconsideration referred to the Court En Banc.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Article VIII (Judicial Department) → Section 4(3) (Mode of Sitting and Voting / Modification and Reversal of Doctrines En Banc).
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Criminal Law → Crimes Against Persons and Property / Quasi-Offenses → Article 365 in relation to Article 48 (Inapplicability of Complex Crimes to Criminal Negligence; Abandonment of **People v. De los Santos**).
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provision:**
**Article VIII, Section 4, Paragraph 3, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Cases or matters heard by a division shall be decided or resolved with the concurrence of a majority of the Members who actually took part in the deliberation on the issues in the case and voted thereon, and in no case without the concurrence of at least three of such Members. When the required number is not obtained, the case shall be decided **en banc**: **Provided**, that **no doctrine or principle of law laid down by the court in a decision rendered en banc or in division may be modified or reversed except by the court sitting en banc.**"
**Verbatim Statutory Provisions Interpreted:**
**Article 365, Paragraphs 1, 3, and 6, Revised Penal Code (as amended by R.A. No. 10951):**
"Art. 365. **Imprudence and negligence.** — Any person who, by reckless imprudence, shall commit any act which, had it been intentional, would constitute a grave felony, shall suffer the penalty of **arresto mayor** in its maximum period to **prisión correccional** in its medium period; if it would have constituted a less grave felony, the penalty of **arresto mayor** in its minimum and medium periods shall be imposed; **if it would have constituted a light felony, the penalty of arresto menor in its maximum period shall be imposed.**
...
**When the execution of the act covered by this article shall have only resulted in damage to the property of another, the offender shall be punished by a fine ranging from an amount equal to the value of said damages to three (3) times such value, but which shall in no case be less than Five thousand pesos (P5,000).**
...
**The provisions contained in this article shall not be applicable:**
**1. When the penalty provided for the offense is equal to or lower than those provided in the first two (2) paragraphs of this article, in which case the court shall impose the penalty next lower in degree than that which should be imposed in the period which they may deem proper to apply.**"
**Factual Trigger:**
At 3:00 a.m. on May 15, 2013, petitioner Morales recklessly overtook a vehicle along Sto. Rosario Street, encroached into the opposite lane, and struck an incoming passenger jeepney, causing slight physical injuries to four occupants and P150,000.00 in temperate damages to the jeepney. When the Court reviewed the lower courts' "complexing" of the resulting quasi-offense, it confronted an institutional constitutional impasse: the Second Division in **Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro** (2010) prohibited the complexing of quasi-crimes under Article 48, but the Court En Banc in **People v. De los Santos** (2001) had explicitly held that Article 48 applies to crimes through negligence.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**May 15, 2013 (Midnight to 3:00 a.m.):** After merrymaking with friends, petitioner Francis O. Morales and his 13-year-old son ate at a **gotohan** in Angeles City. At around 3:00 a.m., they drove home along Sto. Rosario Street bound for San Fernando City in Morales's Mitsubishi Delica van (Plate No. XKZ-528).
**May 15, 2013 (Approx. 3:00 a.m.):** Rico M. Mendoza was driving a passenger jeepney (Plate No. CWR-138, owned by Noel G. Garcia) along Sto. Rosario Street towards the Angeles City Market on the correct, rightful right lane. Passengers Leilani Mendoza, Myrna Cunanan, and Albert Vital were on board. Morales suddenly overtook the vehicle ahead of him on a dark, unlit road, swerving across the center line into the opposing lane and crashing into the front of the oncoming jeepney.
**Post-Collision Medical Treatment:** The victims were rushed for medical treatment. Rico Mendoza suffered a deep forehead laceration and cervical strain (2–3 days hospital confinement; P14,345.00 medical expenses). Leilani Mendoza sustained skin/soft tissue avulsion on her right forearm and a sprained ankle (3–5 days confinement; P34,763.50 expenses). Myrna Cunanan sustained multiple physical injuries (P3,045.00 expenses). Albert Vital incurred P2,895.80 in medical expenses. The jeepney was wrecked, with estimated repair costs of P350,000.00.
**June 5, 2013:** An Information was filed with the Municipal Trial Court in Cities (MTCC) of Angeles City charging Morales with Reckless Imprudence Resulting in Damage to Property and Multiple Physical Injuries. Morales pleaded not guilty.
**June 30, 2015:** The MTCC rendered a Decision finding Morales guilty beyond reasonable doubt, imposing an indeterminate sentence of one (1) month and twenty-one (21) days to two (2) months, and ordering payment of hospitalization expenses, lost income, moral damages, and P350,000.00 for the repair of the jeepney.
**August 25, 2015:** The MTCC denied Morales's Motion for Reconsideration.
**December 1, 2016:** The Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Angeles City, Branch 56, affirmed the MTCC Decision in its entirety, finding that Morales was speeding and had encroached into the inner lane occupied by the jeepney.
**March 15, 2018:** The Court of Appeals (CA) affirmed the conviction with modifications: it sentenced Morales to a straight penalty of two (2) months and one (1) day of **arresto mayor**; deleted the lost-income awards and substituted temperate damages of P8,000.00 to Spouses Mendoza and P2,000.00 to Myrna Cunanan; and deleted the P350,000.00 repair award for lack of receipt, substituting P150,000.00 in temperate damages to Noel Garcia.
**June 22, 2018:** The CA denied Morales's Motion for Reconsideration. Morales filed a Petition for Review on Certiorari (Rule 45) before the Supreme Court.
**September 21, 2020:** The Supreme Court (Third Division) issued a Resolution denying the petition for failure to show reversible error.
**Post-September 21, 2020:** Morales filed a Motion for Reconsideration. Because resolving the motion required formally abandoning the En Banc precedent of **People v. De los Santos** (2001) to validate the Division ruling in **Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro** (2010), the case was referred to the Court En Banc pursuant to Article VIII, Section 4(3) of the Constitution.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Francis O. Morales)
**Main Thesis:** The conviction should be reversed because the collision was caused by the negligence of jeepney driver Rico Mendoza, or alternatively, the penalty imposed under R.A. No. 10951 was retroactively unfavorable.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Hearsay Traffic Accident Report (TAR):** The CA erred in giving credence to the TAR, which was prepared without petitioner's presence while he was hospitalized and was made solely at the instance of private complainants.
2. **Last Clear Chance Doctrine:** The physical depression on the vehicles and the point of impact showed Rico steered directly into the Delica van. Since Rico admitted seeing the approaching van and failed to evade it, Rico had the last opportunity to avoid the collision.
3. **Failure to Prove Diligence and Speed:** The prosecution failed to establish the van's actual speed or that Rico was exercising due diligence.
4. **Unsubstantiated Temperate Damages:** The private complainants failed to establish pecuniary losses or earning capacity.
5. **Unfavorable Retroactivity of R.A. No. 10951:** The CA increased his penalty using R.A. No. 10951 (enacted in 2017) for an act committed in 2013, violating the non-retroactivity of penal laws unfavorable to the accused.
B. Respondent's Arguments (People of the Philippines through the OSG)
**Main Thesis:** The conviction and damages must be affirmed as all elements of reckless imprudence were proven beyond reasonable doubt.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Factual Concurrence:** The MTCC, RTC, and CA consistently found that Morales breached Section 41 of R.A. No. 4136 by overtaking on an unlit road at 3:00 a.m. without ensuring the oncoming lane was clear.
2. **Presumption of Negligence:** Under Article 2185 of the Civil Code, a driver violating a traffic regulation is presumed negligent. Morales encroached on the jeepney's lane and failed to rebut this presumption.
3. **Inapplicability of Last Clear Chance:** The doctrine cannot exonerate a defendant whose primary negligence caused the predicament; Rico was on his rightful lane.
4. **Soundness of Damages:** Temperate damages are authorized under Article 2224 of the Civil Code when pecuniary loss has been suffered but cannot be proven with certainty.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not a Supreme Court Division ruling (**Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro**) can reverse or modify an earlier En Banc doctrine (**People v. De los Santos**) applying Article 48 (complex crimes) to quasi-offenses under Article 365, in view of Article VIII, Section 4(3) of the 1987 Constitution.
2. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the first-level courts (MTCCs/MTCs) retain exclusive original jurisdiction over reckless imprudence resulting in damage to property and physical injuries irrespective of the imposable fine.
3. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not petitioner Morales was guilty beyond reasonable doubt of reckless imprudence under Article 365 of the Revised Penal Code, and whether the doctrine of last clear chance applies to absolve him.
4. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the third paragraph of Article 365 of the Revised Penal Code (imposing a fine for damage to property) applies when the reckless act also results in injuries to persons, and what the correct penalty is for reckless imprudence resulting in multiple slight physical injuries.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Mode of Sitting and Voting / Abandonment of Precedent En Banc
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** A Division cannot reverse an En Banc doctrine; consequently, the Supreme Court **sitting En Banc** must formally adopt the **Ivler** doctrine and **EXPRESSLY ABANDON** the En Banc ruling in **People v. De los Santos**.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **The Constitutional Constraint:** Under Article VIII, Section 4(3) of the 1987 Constitution, "no doctrine or principle of law laid down by the court in a decision rendered **en banc** or in division may be modified or reversed except by the court sitting **en banc**."
2. **The Jurisprudential Antinomy:** In the 2001 En Banc case of **People v. De los Santos**, the Court held that Article 48 of the RPC (complex crimes) applies to crimes committed through negligence, conceptualizing reckless imprudence not as an offense in itself, but as a mere modality or way of committing a crime. Conversely, in the 2010 Second Division case of **Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro**, the Court held that Article 48 is structurally incompatible with quasi-crimes; reckless imprudence is a distinct crime penalizing the mental attitude (**imprudencia punible**), and all resulting consequences must be prosecuted in a single charge without complexing.
3. **Institutional Defect of Ivler:** Because **Ivler** was decided by a Division, it lacked the constitutional power under Article VIII, Section 4(3) to overturn the En Banc precedent in **De los Santos**. As a result, subsequent post-**Ivler** decisions fell into disarray (some following **De los Santos** by complexing quasi-crimes, e.g., **Gonzaga**, **Senit**; others following **Ivler**, e.g., **Sevilla**, **Esteban**).
4. **Resolution En Banc:** To cure this constitutional and doctrinal irregularity, the Court En Banc convened, affirmed **Ivler** as sound law, and **formally abandoned People v. De los Santos**. Criminal negligence under Article 365 cannot be complexed under Article 48 because reckless imprudence is a distinct crime in itself, not a modality of committing intentional felonies.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Article VIII, Section 4(3) of the 1987 Constitution provides that 'no doctrine or principle of law laid down by the court in a decision rendered **en banc** or in division may be modified or reversed except by the court sitting **en banc**[.]' Thus, there is a need for the Court, sitting **En Banc**, to clarify whether it subscribes to the view pronounced in **Ivler**, thereby abandoning **De los Santos**."

"We rule that **Ivler** is a good law, notwithstanding the few stray cases that allowed the 'complexing' of the effects of a single quasi-offense. Forbidding the application of Article 48 of the RPC to quasi-offenses and their resultant acts/effects preserves the conceptual distinction between quasi-crimes and intentional felonies under the RPC. We thus declare that **De los Santos** is abandoned."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
A Division of the Supreme Court cannot overrule a doctrine laid down by the Court En Banc. While **Ivler** correctly explained that quasi-crimes cannot be complexed, it was only a Division ruling attempting to overrule the En Banc case of **De los Santos**. In this case, the Supreme Court En Banc stepped in, invoked its exclusive constitutional prerogative under Article VIII, Section 4(3), and officially struck down **De los Santos** while cementing **Ivler** as the definitive law of the land.
Issue 2: Jurisdiction of Trial Courts over Quasi-Crimes
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Under Batas Pambansa Blg. 129, as amended by Republic Act No. 7691, first-level courts (MeTCs, MTCs, MTCCs, MCTCs) have exclusive original jurisdiction over all offenses under Article 365, regardless of the amount of imposable fine.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Historical Jurisdiction Under Angeles and Villanueva:** Under earlier case law (**Angeles v. Jose**, **People v. Villanueva**), the imposable fine for damage to property under Article 365, paragraph 3 was factored into the penalty to determine jurisdiction. If the resulting fine exceeded the municipal court threshold, the Court of First Instance (now RTC) took jurisdiction.
2. **Statutory Amendment via R.A. No. 7691:** Under Section 32(2) of B.P. Blg. 129 as amended by R.A. No. 7691, first-level courts have exclusive original jurisdiction over offenses punishable with imprisonment not exceeding six (6) years, "irrespective of the amount of fine," with an express proviso granting them exclusive original jurisdiction in offenses involving damage to property through criminal negligence.
3. **Application to Article 365 Penalties:** The maximum basic penalty under Article 365 is **prisión correccional** in its medium and maximum periods (up to 6 years), which vests jurisdiction exclusively in the first-level courts.
4. **Sole Exception:** The only instance where the RTC acquires jurisdiction over an Article 365 offense is when the penalty is qualified under the second-to-last paragraph (failure to lend help on the spot to the injured party), which raises the penalty to **prisión mayor** minimum and medium (6 years and 1 day to 10 years). Here, Morales did not flee; hence, the MTCC had proper subject-matter jurisdiction.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Hence, the MeTCs, MTCs, MCTCs, and MTCCs have exclusive original jurisdiction over criminal negligence cases which results to damage to property, regardless of the imposable fine... BP 129 as amended by R.A. No. 7691, extended the jurisdiction of the first-level courts over criminal cases to include all offenses punishable with imprisonment not exceeding six (6) years irrespective of the amount of fine... Thus, the first-level courts have exclusive original jurisdiction over acts penalized under Article 365 of the RPC."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
The old rule that huge fines for property damage push a reckless imprudence case into the RTC is obsolete. Under R.A. No. 7691, MTCs and MTCCs have exclusive jurisdiction over quasi-crimes under Article 365 regardless of the fine, unless the driver fails to aid the victim on the spot, which elevates the penalty beyond six years and triggers RTC jurisdiction.
Issue 3: Guilt Beyond Reasonable Doubt and Inapplicability of Last Clear Chance
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Morales was proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt, and the last clear chance doctrine cannot apply because Morales's own reckless overtaking was the sole proximate cause of the collision.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Elements of Reckless Imprudence:** The prosecution established: (a) Morales executed an act (driving/overtaking); (b) the act was voluntary; (c) it was done without malice; (d) material damage and slight physical injuries resulted; and (e) there was an inexcusable lack of precaution.
2. **Statutory Violation & Legal Presumption:** Section 41 of R.A. No. 4136 forbids driving on the left side of the center line to pass unless it is clearly visible and free of oncoming traffic. Morales swerved into the opposing lane on an unlit road at 3:00 a.m. Under Article 2185 of the Civil Code, a driver violating a traffic regulation at the time of a mishap is presumed negligent. Morales failed to rebut this presumption.
3. **Inapplicability of Last Clear Chance:** The doctrine applies only where both parties are negligent, or where it is impossible to determine whose fault caused the incident. It cannot be invoked by an encroaching driver against a victim who was cruising lawfully in his rightful lane. Rico Mendoza had no duty to anticipate that Morales would suddenly emerge from the dark into his lane.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"[T]he last clear chance doctrine is inapplicable. The said doctrine presupposes that both parties are negligent but the negligent act of one is appreciably at a later point in time than that of the other, or where it is impossible to determine whose negligence or fault brought about the occurrence of the incident, the one who had the last clear opportunity to avoid the impending harm but failed to do so, is chargeable with the consequences arising therefrom. The documentary and testimonial evidence in this case show that petitioner was at fault."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
A reckless driver who overtakes on a dark curve and smashes into an oncoming car cannot blame the other driver for failing to swerve out of the way. The doctrine of last clear chance requires both parties to be negligent; here, only Morales was negligent, and his unlawful encroachment was the sole proximate cause of the crash.
Issue 4: Penalty Computation Under Article 365
**(a) Short Answer: PARTIALLY MERITORIOUS.** The lower courts erred in treating the crime as a complex crime and misclassified the injuries. Under the **Angeles-Ivler** framework, separate penalties must be imposed for each proven consequence: public censure for each count of slight physical injuries, and a separate fine of P150,000.00 for the damage to property.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Rejection of Complexing Formula:** The lower courts erred in failing to impose a separate fine for property damage, improperly assuming that Article 48 absorbed or combined the offenses. Under Article 365, each consequence is penalized separately.
2. **Classification of Injuries:** The CA misclassified slight physical injuries as a "less grave felony." Because the victims required medical attention/confinement for only 1 to 9 days (Rico 2–3 days; Leilani 3–5 days), the offense, if intentional, constitutes slight physical injuries under Article 266(1), which is a light felony penalized with **arresto menor**.
3. **Application of Article 365, Paragraph 6 (Penalty Reduction Rule):** Paragraph 1 of Article 365 penalizes reckless imprudence resulting in a light felony with **arresto menor** in its maximum period (21 to 30 days). However, Article 365, paragraph 6 dictates that if the penalty for the resulting offense, had it been intentional (**arresto menor**, 1 to 30 days), is equal to or lower than the penalty in paragraph 1, the court must impose the **penalty next lower in degree**. This preserves the fundamental penal distinction between intentional and negligent acts.
4. **Imposable Penalties:** The penalty next lower in degree to **arresto menor** is **public censure**. Since three persons (Rico, Leilani, Myrna) suffered slight physical injuries, Morales must suffer three penalties of public censure. Under paragraph 3 of Article 365 (following **Angeles** and **Ivler**), an independent criminal fine of P150,000.00 (equal to the temperate damage to the vehicle) is meted for the damage to property.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The underlying reason for this reduction in penalty is to preserve the difference between an act wilfully performed from one committed through negligence. Otherwise, a reckless or imprudent act would be punished with the same penalty imposable to an intentional act. Thus, the proper penalty for reckless imprudence resulting in slight physical injuries is public censure, this being the penalty next lower in degree to **arresto menor**."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
Because criminal negligence cannot be complexed, Morales had to be penalized separately for each resulting injury and for the property damage. Furthermore, the law will not punish an accidental or negligent act more harshly than an intentional one; therefore, under Article 365, paragraph 6, the penalty of **arresto menor** drops one degree to public censure for each victim, alongside a P150,000.00 fine for the wrecked jeepney.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → Article VIII: The Judicial Department → d. Mode of Sitting and Voting.
**Applied Lens:** Constitutional & Political Law Lens (En Banc Rule on Overturning Precedent).
Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Article VIII, Section 4[3]):
1. **A prior doctrine or principle of law exists:** Established in an En Banc or Division decision.
 Mapped to Case: People v. De los Santos, 407 Phil. 724 (2001), was an En Banc decision holding that Article 48 of the RPC applies to crimes through negligence.
2. **Subsequent modification or reversal is sought:** A later case attempts to change the legal doctrine.
 Mapped to Case: Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro**, 649 Phil. 478 (2010), sought to establish that Article 48 does not apply to quasi-crimes; however, **Ivler** was decided by the Second Division, rendering it constitutionally powerless to reverse **De los Santos.
3. **Action by the Court En Banc:** The Supreme Court must sit En Banc to effectuate the reversal or modification.
 Mapped to Case:** In **Morales v. People**, the Supreme Court sat En Banc specifically to cure the structural deficiency of **Ivler**, explicitly adopting **Ivler** and formally pronouncing the abandonment of **De los Santos.
Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):
**Article VIII, Section 4(3) Constitutional Prohibition:** "No doctrine or principle of law laid down by the court in a decision rendered **en banc** or in division may be modified or reversed except by the court sitting **en banc**."
**Quasi-offense as a distinct crime:** Reckless imprudence is an independent crime under Article 365, not a mere modality of committing felonies.
**Imprudencia Punible:** The criminalized mental attitude or condition behind the negligent act.
**Prohibition against complexing quasi-crimes:** Article 48 cannot be applied to Article 365 offenses.
**Penalty next lower in degree rule (Art. 365, par. 6):** Mandatory step-down in penalty to ensure negligent crimes are not punished more severely than intentional ones.
Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):
"Under Article VIII, Section 4(3) of the Constitution, only the Supreme Court sitting En Banc has the constitutional authority to modify or reverse a doctrine laid down En Banc or in Division. In **Morales v. People**, the En Banc exercised this specific institutional power to formally abandon the 2001 En Banc ruling in **People v. De los Santos** (which had erroneously applied the complex crime doctrine of Article 48 to quasi-crimes), thereby ratifying and elevating the 2010 Second Division ruling in **Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro** to definitive En Banc precedent."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
Separate Opinions Summary:
**Perlas-Bernabe, J. (Concurring and Dissenting):**
 Concurrence:** Fully concurred with upholding **Ivler**, abandoning **De los Santos, and confirming that quasi-crimes cannot be complexed under Article 48.
 Dissent: Dissented vigorously against the imposition of the P150,000.00 criminal fine under paragraph 3 of Article 365. She argued that paragraph 3 applies strictly and exclusively "[w]hen the execution of the act covered by this article shall have **only** resulted in damage to the property." Under the plain-meaning rule and the doctrine that penal laws are construed strictly against the State and liberally in favor of the accused, when property damage is accompanied by physical injuries, paragraph 3 does not apply. The accused should only pay civil damages for the property, not an additional criminal fine payable to the State.
**Caguioa, J. (Separate Concurring Opinion):**
** Fully supported the **ponencia** in abandoning **De los Santos** and upholding the **Angeles-Ivler rule that the fine under paragraph 3 is added to the penalties for personal injuries.
 Prosecutorial Warning: Emphasized that because quasi-crimes cannot be split or complexed, prosecutors must exercise utmost diligence to ensure **only one Information** is filed containing all casualties, injuries, and property damage resulting from the imprudent act. This prevents unscrupulous defense tactics—such as in **Ivler**—where an accused quickly pleads guilty to a minor charge (slight physical injuries) in one court to set up double jeopardy against the graver charge (homicide/damage to property) in another court.
Verbatim Fallo:
**WHEREFORE**, the motion is **DENIED**. Our Resolution dated September 21, 2020 is **AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION** in that:

(1) petitioner is found **GUILTY** beyond reasonable doubt of reckless imprudence resulting in multiple slight physical injuries and damage to property, and is sentenced to suffer the penalty of public censure for each of the resulting slight physical injuries committed to private complainants Rico Mendoza, Leilani Mendoza, and Myrna Cunanan, and to pay a fine in the amount of P150,000.00 as penalty for the resulting damage to property;

(2) petitioner is **ORDERED** to pay temperate damages in the amount of P8,000.00 to Spouses Rico and Leilani Mendoza and P2,000.00 to Myrna Cunanan;

(3) petitioner is **ORDERED** to pay Noel G. Garcia or his authorized representative temperate damages in the amount of P150,000.00;

(4) all monetary awards shall earn six percent (6%) interest **per annum** from the finality of this Resolution until fully paid.

**SO ORDERED.**
Plain-Language Outcome:
Petitioner Francis O. Morales's conviction was sustained, but his prison term was completely eliminated. The Supreme Court En Banc corrected the lower courts' errors by: (1) sentencing Morales to three separate penalties of public censure (one for each passenger who sustained slight physical injuries); (2) ordering him to pay a P150,000.00 criminal fine to the State for property damage; and (3) ordering him to pay temperate civil damages to the jeepney owner (P150,000.00) and the injured passengers (P10,000.00 total), with 6% legal interest.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Fortich v. Corona** (Resolution on Motion for Reconsideration / En Banc Referral)
**Full Official Caption:** Hon. Carlos O. Fortich, Provincial Governor of Bukidnon, Hon. Rey B. Baula, Municipal Mayor of Sumilao, Bukidnon, NQSR Management and Development Corporation, Petitioners, vs. Hon. Renato C. Corona, Deputy Executive Secretary, Hon. Ernesto D. Garilao, Secretary of the Department of Agrarian Reform, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 131457, August 19, 1999; 371 Phil. 672; Special Second Division; Ponente: Ynares-Santiago, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Promulgated by the Special Second Division. Melo, **J.**, filed a separate opinion. Puno, **J.**, concurred "in the result" (maintaining his original position that the case should go to the Court of Appeals for further proceedings). Mendoza, **J.**, concurred "in the result."
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Petitioners:**
**Hon. Carlos O. Fortich:** Provincial Governor of Bukidnon.
**Hon. Rey B. Baula:** Municipal Mayor of Sumilao, Bukidnon.
**NQSR Management and Development Corporation (NQSR):** Private corporate developer and landholder in Sumilao, Bukidnon.
**Respondents:**
**Hon. Renato C. Corona:** Deputy Executive Secretary, Office of the President (OP).
**Hon. Ernesto D. Garilao:** Secretary, Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR). Both represented by the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG).
**Intervenors (Movants):** Seasonal farmworkers claiming to be agrarian reform beneficiaries who were issued Certificates of Land Ownership Award (CLOAs) over the disputed Sumilao property under the OP's questioned "Win-Win" Resolution.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Before the Supreme Court Special Second Division are pending post-judgment incidents arising from an original Petition for Certiorari: (1) Intervenors' "Motion For Reconsideration With Motion To Refer The Matter To The Court En Banc" dated December 3, 1998; (2) Respondents' "Motion For Reconsideration Of The Resolution Dated November 17, 1998 And For Referral Of The Case To This Honorable Court En Banc (With Urgent Prayer For Issuance Of A Restraining Order)" dated December 2, 1998 (filed December 3, 1998); and (3) Intervenors' "Urgent Omnibus Motion For The Supreme Court Sitting En Banc To Annul The Second Division's Resolution Dated 27 January 1999 And Immediately Resolve The 28 May 1998 Motion For Reconsideration Filed By The Intervenors" dated March 2, 1999. Movants challenge the Court's Resolution of November 17, 1998, which denied reconsideration of the April 24, 1998 Decision by a 2–2 tie vote, and the Resolution of January 27, 1999, which noted without action intervenors' prior December 3, 1998 motion.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → The Judicial Department (Article VIII) → Supreme Court: Mode of Sitting and Voting / Division Voting Tie (Article VIII, Section 4[3])
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Civil Procedure → Prohibited Second Motions for Reconsideration (Rule 52, Section 2; Rule 56, Section 4) / Parties and Legal Standing to Intervene (Rule 19)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provision:**
**Article VIII, Section 4, Paragraph 3, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Cases or matters heard by a division shall be decided or resolved with the concurrence of a majority of the Members who actually took part in the deliberations on the issues in the case and voted thereon, and in no case without the concurrence of at least three of such Members. **When the required number is not obtained, the case shall be decided en banc: **Provided**, that no doctrine or principle of law laid down by the Court in a decision rendered **en banc** or in division may be modified or reversed except by the Court sitting **en banc."
**Factual Trigger:**
After the Supreme Court's Second Division unanimously nullified the Office of the President's "Win-Win" Resolution on April 24, 1998, respondents and intervenors filed motions for reconsideration. On November 17, 1998, the Division deadlocked 2–2 on the motions, causing the motions to be lost and the original decision to stand affirmed. Rather than accepting the outcome, respondents and intervenors demanded that the controversy be elevated to the Supreme Court **En Banc**, arguing that under Article VIII, Section 4(3), whenever a Division fails to muster three concurring votes on any pending incident, the entire case must automatically transfer to the **En Banc**.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**March 29, 1996:** The Office of the President (OP) renders a decision approving the conversion/reclassification of the disputed agricultural land in Sumilao, Bukidnon, owned/developed by NQSR Management and Development Corporation, to non-agricultural use. This OP Decision becomes final and executory after the reglementary period lapses without an appeal or motion for reconsideration being timely filed.
**November 7, 1997:** The Office of the President issues a "Win-Win" Resolution, substantially modifying its March 29, 1996 Decision by ordering the parceling of the Sumilao land between the developer and alleged agrarian beneficiaries.
**April 24, 1998:** The Supreme Court Second Division, by a unanimous vote of all five (5) members, renders a Decision granting the petition of Governor Fortich, Mayor Baula, and NQSR. The Court strikes down the OP's November 7, 1997 "Win-Win" Resolution as null and void on the ground that the March 29, 1996 OP Decision had long become final and executory. In the same Decision, the Court denies the seasonal farmworkers' motion for leave to intervene.
**May 28, 1998:** Intervenors file a Motion for Reconsideration of the April 24, 1998 Decision, praying for referral of the case to the Court **En Banc**. Respondents likewise file their own motion for reconsideration.
**November 17, 1998:** The Special Second Division resolves the separate motions for reconsideration. The members vote two-two (2–2). Justice Antonio M. Martinez pens an opinion stating that the issues presented are not of extraordinary import to merit the attention of the Court **En Banc** (citing **Province of Camarines Sur v. Court of Appeals**, establishing that local government units need not obtain DAR approval to reclassify lands). Because the movants failed to muster the required three concurring votes to overturn the April 24, 1998 Decision, the motions for reconsideration are deemed lost and the Decision stands affirmed.
**December 2–3, 1998:** Intervenors file a "Motion For Reconsideration With Motion To Refer The Matter To The Court En Banc" (December 3, 1998). On the same date, respondents, through the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG), file by registered mail a "Motion For Reconsideration Of The Resolution Dated November 17, 1998 And For Referral Of The Case To This Honorable Court En Banc (With Urgent Prayer For Issuance Of A Restraining Order)" accompanied by a Manifestation and Motion.
**January 27, 1999:** The Court issues a Resolution noting without action intervenors' December 3, 1998 motion, ruling that movants have no legal personality following the denial of intervention, that the motion is an impermissible second motion for reconsideration under Rule 52, Section 2 in relation to Rule 56, Section 4 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, and noting that respondents did not appear to have joined in the motion.
**March 2, 1999:** Intervenors file an "Urgent Omnibus Motion For The Supreme Court Sitting En Banc To Annul The Second Division's Resolution Dated 27 January 1999 And Immediately Resolve The 28 May 1998 Motion For Reconsideration Filed By The Intervenors."
**August 19, 1999:** The Supreme Court Special Second Division promulgates the present Resolution denying with finality all pending motions and prayers for referral to the Court **En Banc**.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondents' and Intervenors' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The 2–2 tie vote of the Special Second Division on November 17, 1998 did not validly resolve their motions for reconsideration; because the constitutional requirement of at least three concurring votes was not obtained, Article VIII, Section 4(3) of the 1987 Constitution mandates that the case be referred to and decided by the Court **En Banc**.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Constitutional Mandate for En Banc Referral:** Under Article VIII, Section 4(3), cases or matters heard by a division require the concurrence of at least three members. Where a 2–2 tie occurs, the required three votes are not met; hence, the incident must be transferred to the full Court sitting **en banc**.
2.  **Novelty / Issues of First Impression:** The issues submitted in their motions are of first impression, transcendental importance, and far-reaching consequence, necessitating full **En Banc** deliberation rather than summary disposal by a divided Division.
3.  **Substance Over Technicality:** The nullification of the "Win-Win" Resolution rested merely on a procedural technicality regarding the reglementary period of finality of the March 29, 1996 OP decision, which should yield to substantive social justice.
4.  **Standing of Intervenors:** Intervenors are real parties in interest because they are DAR-identified qualified agrarian beneficiaries and have already been issued Certificates of Land Ownership Award (CLOAs) over the property.
B. Petitioners' Arguments / Division Position
**Main Thesis:** The original April 24, 1998 Decision remains valid and affirmed; the tie vote in a motion for reconsideration merely results in the denial of the motion and does not transfer the decided case to the Court **En Banc**.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Reddendo Singula Singulis:** Article VIII, Section 4(3) distinguishes "cases" (which are "decided") from "matters" (which are "resolved"). Referral to the **En Banc** applies only when an undecided **case** ties; when a **motion for reconsideration** of an already decided case ties, the motion is simply lost.
2.  **Prohibited Second Motion for Reconsideration:** The new motions seek reconsideration of an order denying reconsideration, violating Section 2, Rule 52 in relation to Section 4, Rule 56 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, filed without leave of court.
3.  **Vested Rights and Finality:** The finality of the March 29, 1996 OP Decision is substantive, vesting rights in the petitioners and the community; the "Win-Win" Resolution was void **ab initio**.
4.  **Lack of Legal Interest:** Intervenors are seasonal farmworkers whose constitutional right is limited to a just share in the fruits, not land ownership, and their CLOAs derived from a void resolution.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the failure of a Supreme Court Division to obtain the required three (3) concurring votes when resolving a motion for reconsideration—resulting in a 2–2 tie vote—requires the referral of the case to the Court **En Banc** under Article VIII, Section 4, Paragraph 3 of the 1987 Constitution.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondents' and intervenors' motions for reconsideration of the November 17, 1998 Resolution are prohibited second motions for reconsideration under the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the "Win-Win" Resolution dated November 7, 1997 was validly set aside, or conversely, whether substantive justice warrants relaxing the rule on finality of the March 29, 1996 OP Decision.
4.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the seasonal farmworker-intervenors have the requisite legal personality and standing to intervene in the action.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Referral to En Banc upon Tie Vote on a Motion for Reconsideration
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not a 2–2 tie vote in a Division on a motion for reconsideration requires the case to be referred to the Court **En Banc** under Article VIII, Section 4(3)? **NO.** A tie vote on a motion for reconsideration in a Division does not leave the case undecided; the motion simply fails to muster the required majority and is lost, leaving the original decision affirmed without need for **En Banc** referral.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Textual and Syntactical Construction:** Under the rule of statutory construction **reddendo singula singulis** (referring each to each), the constitutional text in Article VIII, Section 4(3) deliberately distinguishes between "cases" and "matters." Cases are "decided," while matters (which include motions) are "resolved."
2.  **Application of the Second Sentence:** The second sentence of Section 4(3) states: **"When the required number is not obtained, the case shall be decided en banc."** The framers deliberately used the word **"case"** and omitted the word **"matter."**
3.  **Mechanism of Case vs. Motion:** When an original case heard by a Division fails to garner three votes to reach an initial judgment, there is no decision; thus, the **case** must be elevated to the **En Banc** to be disposed of. In sharp contrast, where a case has **already been decided** by the Division (here, unanimously by all 5 members on April 24, 1998), the judgment is extant. When a motion for reconsideration is filed, the burden is on the movant to secure at least three votes to overturn that judgment.
4.  **Legal Consequence of a Tie on Reconsideration:** If the voting on a motion for reconsideration deadlocks at 2–2, the movant fails to muster the necessary votes to modify or reverse the judgment. The motion is lost. The assailed decision is not reconsidered and remains affirmed.
5.  **Issues Not of Extraordinary Import:** The contention that the questions are novel or of first impression was directly refuted by the November 17, 1998 opinion citing **Province of Camarines Sur v. Court of Appeals**, which established that local government units have the authority to reclassify agricultural lands without DAR approval.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"A careful reading of the above constitutional provision, however, reveals the intention of the framers to draw a distinction between cases, on the one hand, and matters, on the other hand, such that cases are 'decided' while matters, which include motions, are 'resolved'. Otherwise put, the word 'decided' must refer to 'cases'; while the word 'resolved' must refer to 'matters', applying the rule of **reddendo singula singulis**."

"On the other hand, if a case has already been decided by the division and the losing party files a motion for reconsideration, the failure of the division to resolve the motion because of a tie in the voting does not leave the case undecided. There is still the decision which must stand in view of the failure of the members of the division to muster the necessary vote for its reconsideration. Quite plainly, if the voting results in a tie, the motion for reconsideration is lost. The assailed decision is not reconsidered and must therefore be deemed affirmed."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Article VIII, Section 4(3) only sends an unresolved **case** to the **En Banc** when the Division ties on the main decision. If the Division already rendered a valid decision and later ties 2–2 on a motion for reconsideration, the case is not left hanging—the motion simply fails because it did not obtain the three concurring votes needed to overturn the decision. Consequently, the tie denies the motion, the original decision stands affirmed, and referral to the **En Banc** is improper.
Issue 2: Propriety of the Second Motions for Reconsideration
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the pending motions constitute prohibited second motions for reconsideration under the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure? **YES.** The motions seek to reconsider the denial of an earlier motion for reconsideration, which is explicitly barred by procedural rules absent express prior leave of court and extraordinarily persuasive reasons.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Rule Prohibition:** Under Rule 56, Section 4, in relation to Rule 52, Section 2 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, second motions for reconsideration are prohibited.
2.  **Procedural Default:** While exceptional cases may allow a second motion for reconsideration where extraordinary and persuasive reasons exist, such motions must be filed with **express leave of court first obtained** (**Ortigas and Co. Ltd. Partnership v. Velasco**).
3.  **No Exceptional Justification:** Movants neither requested nor secured prior leave of court. Furthermore, stripping away the baseless demand for **En Banc** referral, their arguments were mere rehashes of grounds already passed upon and rejected in the November 17, 1998 Resolution.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The contention, therefore, that our Resolution of November 17, 1998 did not dispose of the earlier motions for reconsideration of the Decision dated April 24, 1998 is flawed. Consequently, the present motions for reconsideration necessarily partake of the nature of a second motion for reconsideration which, according to the clear and unambiguous language of Rule 56, Section 4, in relation to Rule 52, Section 2, of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, is prohibited."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Once a Division's tie vote denied the first motions for reconsideration, that incident was fully disposed of. Filing another round of motions without prior leave of court violated the strict procedural prohibition against second motions for reconsideration, especially since movants merely repeated previously rejected arguments.
Issue 3: Validity of the "Win-Win" Resolution and Finality of the OP Decision
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the OP "Win-Win" Resolution was void, and whether the Court disposed of the case on a mere technicality? **NO.** The "Win-Win" Resolution is void **ab initio** because the original March 29, 1996 OP Decision had attained finality, vesting immutable substantive rights in petitioners.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Inviolability of Final Judgments:** The OP's March 29, 1996 Decision had already become final and executory before the motion seeking its reconsideration was ever filed. An administrative agency loses jurisdiction to alter a final and executory decision.
2.  **Substantive Rights Protected:** The rule on finality of judgments is not an empty technicality; it protects substantive constitutional rights. As held in **Videogram Regulatory Board v. Court of Appeals**, just as a losing party has a right to appeal within the prescribed reglementary period, the winning party possesses a correlative substantive right to enjoy the finality and immutability of the resolution.
3.  **Vested Entitlements:** Finality vested property and development rights in the petitioners and the people of Bukidnon, rendering the subsequent "Win-Win" Resolution of November 7, 1997 void and legally nonexistent.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The crux of the controversy is the validity of the 'Win-Win' Resolution dated November 7, 1997. We maintain that the same is void and of no legal effect considering that the March 29, 1996 decision of the Office of the President had already become final and executory even prior to the filing of the motion for reconsideration which became the basis of the said 'Win-Win' Resolution... The issue in this case, therefore, is not a question of technicality but of substance and merit."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Finality of judgment is a substantive rule of law, not a mere technical trap. Because the March 29, 1996 OP decision became final and executory, the Office of the President had zero authority to issue the "Win-Win" Resolution, making that later resolution void from the beginning.
Issue 4: Legal Standing of Intervenors
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not seasonal farmworkers issued CLOAs have legal standing to intervene in this action? **NO.** Seasonal farmworkers have no constitutional right to own the land, and CLOAs originating from a void resolution confer no legal rights.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Constitutional Classification of Farmworkers:** Under Article XIII, Section 4 of the Constitution, only regular farmworkers are guaranteed the right to own the land. The rights of seasonal farmworkers are expressly limited to a just share in the fruits of the land.
2.  **Contingent Beneficiary Status:** The "Win-Win" Resolution itself conceded that qualified agrarian beneficiaries had yet to be meticulously determined by the DAR; thus, intervenors possessed no vested, definitive right.
3.  **Nullity of Derivative CLOAs:** The issuance of CLOAs to intervenors could not confer legal standing because their CLOAs sprouted entirely from the "Win-Win" Resolution, which is completely void. No legal rights emanate from a nullity.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Again as expressed in the opinion of Mr. Justice Martinez, intervenors, who are admittedly not regular but seasonal farmworkers, have no legal or actual and substantive interest over the subject land inasmuch as they have no right to own the land. Rather, their right is limited only to a just share of the fruits of the land... Likewise, the issuance of the CLOA's to them does not grant them the requisite standing in view of the nullity of the 'Win-Win' Resolution. No legal rights can emanate from a resolution that is null and void."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Intervenors are seasonal farmworkers who have no constitutional right to land ownership, only a right to a just share of the fruits. Furthermore, because their CLOAs were issued pursuant to a "Win-Win" Resolution that was completely void, those titles conferred no legal interest or standing to intervene.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Supreme Court: Mode of Sitting and Voting (**Article VIII, Section 4[3]**)
**Applied Lens:** Constitutional & Political Law
State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation
 State Power / Branch Exercised: Judicial Power (adjudicative authority of the Supreme Court sitting in Division to decide cases and resolve motions with finality).
 Constitutional Limitation Invoked:** Article VIII, Section 4(3) of the 1987 Constitution, which guarantees that no case or matter heard by a Division shall be decided or resolved without the concurrence of at least three members, and mandates referral to the Court **En Banc when the required vote is not obtained.
Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Division Voting vs. En Banc Transfer)
**Requisite 1: Unobtained Concurrence in a "Case"** — The requirement of referral to the Court **En Banc** triggers **only** when an unadjudicated **case** fails to obtain the majority vote of the participating Members (and at least 3 votes in Division).
 Application to Facts: **Absent.** The **case** had already been definitively decided on April 24, 1998 by a unanimous 5–0 vote of the Second Division.
**Requisite 2: Action on an Incidental "Matter" (Motion for Reconsideration)** — Motions are interlocutory "matters" requiring three votes to **overturn** a prior ruling.
 Application to Facts: **Present.** The incident at hand was merely a motion for reconsideration. The 2–2 tie meant the movants failed to obtain the three votes required to alter the judgment; hence, the motion was lost, and the original judgment remained affirmed.
Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words")
 Reddendo singula singulis (referring each to each; "cases" are decided, while "matters" are resolved).
 Motion is lost (the consequence of a tie vote on a motion for reconsideration).
 Prohibited second motion for reconsideration (Rule 52, Sec. 2; Rule 56, Sec. 4).
 Finality of judgment (creates substantive vested rights that cannot be disturbed on procedural pleas).
Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer)
"**Fortich v. Corona** is the leading authority on the application of the rule of **reddendo singula singulis** to Article VIII, Section 4(3) of the 1987 Constitution regarding Division voting. The Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional command requiring referral to the **En Banc** when the required three votes are not obtained applies exclusively to **cases** awaiting decision, not to incidental **matters** such as motions for reconsideration. Because the Second Division had already unanimously decided the case on the merits, the subsequent 2–2 tie vote on the motion for reconsideration simply meant that the movants failed to muster the required majority to reverse the ruling; thus, the motion was lost, the decision was deemed affirmed, and no referral to the **En Banc** was warranted."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Melo, J.:** Filed a Separate Opinion (referenced in the text; noting reservation/concurrence).
**Puno, J.:** Concurred "in the result," explicitly maintaining his original position that the case should be remanded to the Court of Appeals for further proceedings.
**Mendoza, J.:** Concurred "in the result."
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, based on the foregoing, the following incidents, namely: intervenors' 'Motion For Reconsideration With Motion To Refer The Matter To The Court En Banc,' dated December 3, 1998; respondents' 'Motion For Reconsideration Of The Resolution Dated November 17, 1998 And For Referral Of The Case To This Honorable Court En Banc (With Urgent Prayer For Issuance Of A Restraining Order),' dated December 2, 1998; and intervenors' 'Urgent Omnibus Motion For The Supreme Court Sitting En Banc To Annul The Second Division's Resolution Dated 27 January 1999 And Immediately Resolve The 28 May 1998 Motion For Reconsideration Filed By The Intervenors,' dated March 2, 1999; are all DENIED with FINALITY. No further motion, pleading, or paper will be entertained in this case.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Petitioners (Governor Fortich, Mayor Baula, and NQSR) prevailed completely. All motions for reconsideration and petitions to elevate the dispute to the Court **En Banc** filed by the Executive respondents and farmworker-intervenors were denied with finality, thereby cementing the permanent invalidation of the OP "Win-Win" Resolution and sustaining the finality of the March 29, 1996 land conversion decision.
