### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: In Re Gonzalez** (1988)
**Full Official Caption:** In Re First Indorsement from Honorable Raul M. Gonzalez Dated 16 March 1988 Requesting Honorable Justice Marcelo B. Fernan to Comment on an Anonymous Letter-Complaint (A.M. No. 88-4-5433)
**Citation & Metadata:** 243 Phil. 167; G.R. Administrative Matter No. 88-4-5433; April 15, 1988; **Per Curiam** En Banc (Concurring: Teehankee, **C.J.**, Yap, Narvasa, Melencio-Herrera, Cruz, Paras, Feliciano, Gancayco, Padilla, Bidin, Sarmiento, Cortes, and Griño-Aquino, **JJ.**; Fernan, **J.**, took no part; Gutierrez, Jr., **J.**, was on leave). No separate opinions filed.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Hon. Raul M. Gonzalez:** "Tanodbayan/Special Prosecutor" who issued the challenged 1st Indorsement requiring a sitting Supreme Court Justice to answer an anonymous administrative/disbarment complaint.
**Hon. Justice Marcelo B. Fernan:** Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines, the subject of the anonymous complaint and disbarment allegations, who referred the Indorsement to the Court **en banc**.
**Miguel Cuenco:** Former complainant in Administrative Case No. 3135 against Justice Fernan; sender of the telegram attached to the Indorsement urging the Tanodbayan to file responsive pleadings.
**"Concerned Employees of the Supreme Court":** Anonymous signatories of the letter-complaint dated December 14, 1987, requesting the Tanodbayan to intervene in the disbarment accusations against Justice Fernan.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Direct administrative referral. Associate Justice Marcelo B. Fernan formally referred to the Supreme Court **en banc** the 1st Indorsement dated March 16, 1988, issued by Tanodbayan/Special Prosecutor Raul M. Gonzalez, because it directly commanded an incumbent Justice to comment on an anonymous disbarment complaint within ten days, thereby raising profound constitutional questions of judicial independence and the exclusivity of the impeachment process.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department / Accountability of Public Officers → Tenure and Removal (Impeachment Exclusivity & Precondition)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Legal & Judicial Ethics → Disbarment & Disciplinary Jurisdiction → Immunity of Incumbent Constitutional Officers from Collateral Removal
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provisions:**
**Article XI, Section 2, 1987 Constitution:**
"Sec. 2. The President, the Vice-President, **the Members of the Supreme Court**, the Members of the Constitutional Commissions, and the Ombudsman **may be removed from office on impeachment for, and conviction of, culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, or betrayal of public trust.** All other public officers and employees may be removed from office as provided by law, **but not by impeachment.**"
**Article XI, Section 3, Paragraph 7, 1987 Constitution:**
"(7) **Judgment in cases of impeachment shall not extend further than removal from office and disqualification to hold any office under the Republic of the Philippines, but the party convicted shall nevertheless be liable and subject to prosecution, trial and punishment according to law.**"
**Article VIII, Section 7, Paragraph 1, 1987 Constitution:**
"Sec. 7. (1) No person shall be appointed Member of the Supreme Court or any lower collegiate court unless he is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines. **A Member of the Supreme Court must be at least forty years of age, and must have been for fifteen years or more a judge of a lower court or engaged in the practice of law in the Philippines.**"
**Historical Landmark Rule:**
**Historical Provision Cited: Article XIII, Section 2, 1973 Constitution:**
"Sec. 2. The President, the Members of the Supreme Court, and the Members of the Constitutional Commissions shall be removed from office on impeachment for, and conviction of, culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, other high crimes, or graft and corruption."
**Modern Provision Comparison:** The 1987 Constitution retained this framework in Article XI, Section 2, while adding the Vice-President and the Ombudsman to the list of impeachable officers, and introducing "betrayal of public trust" as an explicit ground. Both constitutions strictly restrict judgment in impeachment solely to removal and disqualification, deferring criminal and disciplinary liability until after removal.
**Factual Trigger:** Tanodbayan/Special Prosecutor Raul M. Gonzalez served a formal 1st Indorsement requiring sitting Supreme Court Associate Justice Marcelo B. Fernan to file a written comment within ten days on an anonymous letter-complaint and telegram asking the Tanodbayan to intervene in and act upon disbarment charges against the Justice.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**December 14, 1987:** An anonymous letter-complaint signed by "Concerned Employees of the Supreme Court" is addressed to Hon. Raul M. Gonzalez, calling attention to disbarment charges initiated by Miguel Cuenco against Associate Justice Marcelo B. Fernan and demanding that the Tanodbayan "do something about this."
**February 17, 1988:** The Supreme Court **en banc** issues a **per curiam** Resolution in Administrative Case No. 3135 (**Miguel Cuenco v. Honorable Marcelo B. Fernan**), dismissing Cuenco's disbarment charges against Justice Fernan for utter lack of merit. In the same resolution, the Court orders Cuenco to show cause why he should not be administratively sanctioned for bringing unfounded, serious accusations against an incumbent Justice, noting that disbarment during incumbency unconstitutionally circumvents the impeachment clause.
**February 29, 1988:** Cuenco files pleadings before the Supreme Court in Administrative Case No. 3135 asserting that Tanodbayan intervention is improper, yet simultaneously dispatches a telegram encouraging Gonzalez to file responsive pleadings before the Supreme Court **en banc** to accommodate the anonymous employees' petition.
**March 16, 1988:** Disregarding the constitutional mechanism for impeachable officers, Tanodbayan Raul M. Gonzalez issues the challenged "1st Indorsement" transmitting the anonymous letter-complaint and Cuenco's telegram directly to Justice Fernan, ordering him to submit his "comment within ten (10) days from receipt hereof."
**Justice Fernan’s Action (March 1988):** Rather than responding to the Tanodbayan, Justice Fernan refers the 1st Indorsement directly to the Supreme Court **en banc** to resolve the grave institutional and constitutional policy questions it created.
**March 30, 1988:** Having secured an extension from the Court, Cuenco files an omnibus pleading in Administrative Case No. 3135, which the Court treats as a Motion for Reconsideration of the February 17, 1988 dismissal.
**April 15, 1988:** The Supreme Court **en banc** issues two coordinated **per curiam** Resolutions:
1. Denying with finality Cuenco's Motion for Reconsideration in Administrative Case No. 3135; and
2. Promulgating the present Resolution in A.M. No. 88-4-5433, ruling that Gonzalez had no jurisdiction to entertain complaints or demand comments from incumbent Supreme Court Justices, and establishing that impeachable officers cannot face disbarment or criminal prosecution during their incumbency.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's / Indorsing Officer's Arguments (Tanodbayan Raul M. Gonzalez & Complainants)
**Main Thesis:** The Tanodbayan/Special Prosecutor possesses the authority to transmit complaints, even if anonymous, to an incumbent Supreme Court Justice and compel an answer or comment within ten days concerning alleged professional misconduct.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Anonymous Complainants: The Tanodbayan has the duty to intervene and take action when public complaints of misconduct or disbarrable offenses are leveled against high public officials, including Supreme Court Justices.
 Miguel Cuenco (via Telegram):** Encouraged the Tanodbayan to file responsive pleadings before the Supreme Court **en banc in response to the anonymous employees' petition, notwithstanding Cuenco's own pending pleadings before the Court.
B. Respondent's / The Court’s Stance (Justice Marcelo B. Fernan & Supreme Court En Banc)
**Main Thesis:** The Constitution exclusively prescribes impeachment as the sole mechanism to terminate the tenure of an incumbent Supreme Court Justice; disbarment or criminal prosecution cannot be initiated against such an officer during incumbency.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Constitutional Exclusivity: Article XI, Section 2 mandates that Supreme Court Members can only be removed from office through impeachment for specific constitutional offenses.
 Circumvention of Impeachment: Because membership in the Philippine Bar is an indispensable constitutional qualification for holding the office of Justice under Article VIII, Section 7(1), any disbarment proceeding during incumbency would result in indirect removal from judicial office, evading the impeachment process.
 Sequential Precondition:** Under Article XI, Section 3(7), criminal prosecution or administrative disbarment may only proceed **after the constitutional officer has been convicted in an impeachment trial and removed from office.
 Separation of Powers & Judicial Independence: Allowing prosecutors to entertain charges or demand explanations from sitting Justices exposes the Judiciary to harassment by disgruntled litigants, undermining institutional independence.
 Prosecutorial Duty:** Prosecutors and the Tanodbayan are bound to **motu proprio dismiss any criminal or disbarment complaints filed against incumbent impeachable officers.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not an incumbent Member of the Supreme Court may be subjected to disbarment proceedings, or to criminal prosecution for an offense carrying the penalty of removal from office, during his incumbency prior to being impeached and convicted.
2. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not a public prosecutor or the Tanodbayan/Special Prosecutor has the legal authority to entertain a disbarment or criminal complaint against an incumbent Supreme Court Justice and compel said Justice to comment thereon.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: May an incumbent Supreme Court Justice be subjected to disbarment or criminal prosecution prior to impeachment?
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Under the Constitution, an incumbent Supreme Court Justice may be removed solely by impeachment; disbarment or criminal prosecution cannot be entertained during incumbency because loss of Bar membership or a conviction carrying the penalty of removal unconstitutionally bypasses the impeachment process.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Constitutional Qualification vs. Method of Removal:** Article VIII, Section 7(1) of the 1987 Constitution requires that every Member of the Supreme Court must be a member of the Philippine Bar. Simultaneously, Article XI, Section 2 mandates that Members of the Court may be removed from office **only through the impeachment process.
 Proscription Against Collateral Removal: To disbar a sitting Justice would strip him of his mandatory constitutional qualification (membership in the Bar), effectively terminating his tenure and driving him out of office. Disbarment proceedings during incumbency are thus an unconstitutional circumvention of Article XI, Section 2.
 Scope and Sequential Nature of Impeachment Judgments:** Relying on **Lecaroz v. Sandiganbayan (1984) and Chief Justice Enrique Fernando’s constitutional commentaries, the Court emphasized that under Article XI, Section 3(7), judgment in impeachment extends solely to removal and perpetual disqualification. The provision dictates that "the party convicted shall nevertheless be liable and subject to prosecution, trial and punishment according to law."
 Impeachment as an Indispensable Condition Precedent:** The textual phrasing clearly establishes a sequence: an impeachable officer does not enjoy permanent personal immunity from criminal or ethical misbehavior, but a **fundamental procedural requirement must first occur. The official must first be removed from office via the constitutional route of impeachment. Only after his tenure is lawfully severed by impeachment conviction may he be haled before regular courts or the Supreme Court for disbarment or criminal liability.
 Application to Other Impeachable Officers: The Court explicitly ruled that the identical protection applies to all other constitutional officers who are required to be members of the Bar and are removable only by impeachment: the Ombudsman and his deputies (Art. XI, Sec. 8), the majority of the Commissioners of the Commission on Elections (Art. IX-C, Sec. 1[1]), and members of the Commission on Audit who are lawyers (Art. IX-D, Sec. 1[1]).
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"A public officer who under the Constitution is required to be a Member of the Philippine Bar as a qualification for the office held by him and who may be removed from office only by impeachment, cannot be charged with disbarment during the incumbency of such public officer. Further, such public officer, during his incumbency, cannot be charged criminally before the Sandiganbayan or any other court with any offence which carries with it the penalty of removal from office, or any penalty service of which would amount to removal from office."
"To grant a complaint for disbarment of a Member of the Court during the Member's incumbency, would in effect be to circumvent and hence to run afoul of the constitutional mandate that Members of the Court may be removed from office only by impeachment for and conviction of certain offenses listed in Article XI (2) of the Constitution."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
An incumbent Supreme Court Justice cannot be disbarred or criminally prosecuted while in office. Because the Constitution requires a Justice to be a lawyer, disbarring him would strip him of that required qualification and force his removal from the bench, bypassing the exclusive constitutional method of removal: impeachment. The Justice must first be impeached and convicted by Congress before any disbarment or criminal proceedings may legally proceed against him.
Issue 2: Does a prosecutor or the Tanodbayan have authority to entertain complaints or order an incumbent Justice to comment?
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** A fiscal, the Tanodbayan, or any other prosecuting officer lacks authority to entertain such charges and is legally mandated to dismiss them immediately and **motu proprio**.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Judicial Independence and Separation of Powers: The constitutional bar against prosecuting or disbarring an incumbent Justice is grounded upon the preservation of judicial independence. If prosecutors could entertain complaints or demand written explanations from Justices, dissatisfied litigants and lawyers would constantly utilize disciplinary complaints to harass members of the Court and influence judicial deliberations.
 Mandatory Immediate Dismissal: Because regular courts and administrative bodies lack subject-matter competence to remove an incumbent Justice collaterally, prosecuting authorities possess zero jurisdiction over such complaints.
 Proper Recourse: If any person has a legitimate, actionable grievance charging an incumbent Justice with an impeachable offense, the sole and exclusive remedy provided by the fundamental law is to initiate impeachment proceedings before the House of Representatives pursuant to Article XI, Section 3. Prosecuting officers must instantly reject and dismiss any attempt to circumvent this rule.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"The above rule rests on the fundamental principles of judicial independence and separation of powers. The rule is important because judicial independence is important. Without the protection of this rule, Members of the Supreme Court would be brought against them by unsuccessful litigants or their lawyers or by other parties who, for any number of reasons might seek to affect the exercise of judicial authority by the Court."
"It follows from the foregoing that a fiscal or other prosecuting officer should forthwith and motu proprio dismiss any charges brought against a Member of this Court. The remedy of a person with a legitimate grievance is to file impeachment proceedings."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Prosecutors, including the Tanodbayan, have no authority to process charges or order sitting Justices to file comments regarding disbarment or criminal accusations. Entertaining such complaints undermines judicial independence by allowing losing litigants to harass judges. Prosecutors must dismiss these complaints on their own motion (**motu proprio**), and anyone with a grievance must file an impeachment complaint in Congress instead.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Assigned Syllabus Topic: **j. Tenure and Removal** | Applied Lens: **Constitutional & Political Law**
**Constitutional & Political Law Mechanics:**
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 Exercised Power: Prosecutorial/Investigative power exercised by the Tanodbayan/Special Prosecutor under the executive/prosecutorial apparatus.
 Constitutional Limitation Invoked: Separation of Powers, Judicial Independence, and the Impeachment Exclusivity Clause under Article XI, Sections 2 and 3(7) of the 1987 Constitution, which restricts the removal of Supreme Court Justices strictly to conviction in an impeachment trial.
**Level of Scrutiny & Doctrinal Precondition Test:**
The Court applied an absolute categorical/jurisdictional bar. The mechanism is a **sequential condition precedent**:
1.  **Stage 1 (Exclusive Remedial Route):** Initiation, trial, and conviction via impeachment under Article XI, Section 3. Removal from office and disqualification are the sole initial consequences.
2.  **Stage 2 (Subsequent Liability):** Only **after** tenure is legally terminated via impeachment conviction may ordinary prosecutorial authority attach for criminal offenses or disbarment.
**Justiciability & Institutional Audit:**
 Lis Mota & Subject-Matter Jurisdiction: The Court intervened directly upon Justice Fernan's referral of the 1st Indorsement to prevent a structural breach of judicial independence. A prosecutor cannot exert coercive investigative processes (such as a 10-day directive to comment) upon an incumbent constitutional officer whose tenure is shielded by the impeachment clause.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
To determine whether a public officer is immune from disbarment or criminal prosecution during incumbency:
1.  **Impeachable Status:** The public officer must be among those removable exclusively by impeachment under Article XI, Section 2 (President, VP, SC Members, Constitutional Commissioners, Ombudsman). **[Present: Associate Justice Fernan is an incumbent SC Member].**
2.  **Mandatory Bar Qualification:** The office held requires membership in the Philippine Bar as an explicit constitutional qualification under Article VIII, Section 7(1) or related clauses. **[Present: SC Justices must be Bar members].**
3.  **Nature of the Penalty:** The charge (disbarment or crime) carries the penalty of loss of Bar standing or removal from public office, which would destroy the constitutional qualification and force a forfeiture of the seat. **[Present: Disbarment revokes law license, thereby collaterally stripping the Justice of judicial qualification].**
**Result:** The proceeding cannot prosper during incumbency and must be dismissed **motu proprio**.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Impeachment as sole method of removal
 Circumvention of the constitutional mandate
 Collateral removal from office
 Judicial independence and separation of powers
 Motu proprio dismissal
 Condition precedent / Sequential liability
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
**In Re Gonzalez** is placed under "Tenure and Removal" because it defines the strict exclusivity of impeachment as the sole constitutional vehicle for terminating the tenure of a sitting Supreme Court Justice. The Court held that because Bar membership is an ongoing constitutional qualification for the bench, subjecting an incumbent Justice to disbarment or criminal prosecution amounts to an unconstitutional collateral removal that violates judicial independence. Consequently, prosecutors must **motu proprio** dismiss such charges, as ordinary legal liability can only be enforced **after** the officer has been impeached and convicted.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed. (All concurring Justices signed the **per curiam** resolution; Justice Marcelo B. Fernan took no part; Justice Hugo E. Gutierrez, Jr. was on leave).
**Verbatim/Near-Verbatim Fallo:**
"The Clerk of Court is hereby DIRECTED to serve a copy of this Resolution upon Hon. Raul M. Gonzales and Mr. Miguel Cuenco."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court formally rebuffed Tanodbayan Raul M. Gonzalez, establishing as a binding constitutional rule that neither he nor any other prosecutor has the authority to entertain disbarment or criminal charges against an incumbent Supreme Court Justice. The 1st Indorsement was rendered legally ineffective, leaving impeachment before Congress as the sole legal avenue for anyone seeking to remove or sanction a sitting Justice.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Republic v. Sereno** (The Quo Warranto Case against Chief Justice Sereno)
**Full Official Caption:** Republic of the Philippines, represented by Solicitor General Jose C. Calida, Petitioner, **v.** Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno, Respondent
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 237428; Promulgated May 11, 2018; En Banc; Ponente: Associate Justice Noel Gimenez Tijam.
**Voting Breakdown:** 8–6 to GRANT the Petition.
**Majority (8):** Tijam (**ponente**), Leonardo-De Castro (concurring), Bersamin (concurring), Peralta (separate concurring), Jardeleza (concurring via certified vote), Martires (concurring in result with separate opinion), A. Reyes, Jr. (concurring), Gesmundo (concurring).
**Dissenting / Concurring in Part (6):** Carpio (dissenting), Velasco, Jr. (concurring and dissenting), Del Castillo (dissenting), Perlas-Bernabe (separate opinion/dissenting on quo warranto), Leonen (dissenting), Caguioa (dissenting).
**No Part (1):** Sereno (**respondent / Chief Justice**).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Petitioner:** Republic of the Philippines, represented by Solicitor General Jose C. Calida, asserting the State's prerogative to oust an alleged usurper from public office.
**Respondent:** Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno, incumbent Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines, whose title and qualifications were challenged.
**Judicial and Bar Council (JBC):** The constitutional screening body tasked with vetting nominees for judicial posts, which short-listed Sereno in 2012.
**House Committee on Justice:** The legislative committee that conducted probable cause hearings on the impeachment complaint against Sereno filed by Atty. Larry Gadon.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Original Petition for the Issuance of the Extraordinary Writ of **Quo Warranto** filed by the Republic under Rule 66 of the Rules of Court in relation to Section 5(1), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution, directly seeking to declare void the appointment of respondent as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court and to oust and exclude her therefrom.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Article XI (Accountability of Public Officers) → Tenure and Removal of Impeachable Officers **vis-à-vis** Quo Warranto under Rule 66
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Article VIII (Judicial Department) → Section 7(3) (Qualifications of the Judiciary: Proven Competence, Integrity, Probity, and Independence) & Supervisory Power over the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provisions:**
**Article XI, Section 2, 1987 Constitution:**
"Section 2. The President, the Vice-President, the Members of the Supreme Court, the Members of the Constitutional Commissions, and the Ombudsman **may be removed from office on impeachment** for, and conviction of, culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, or betrayal of public trust. All other public officers and employees may be removed from office as provided by law, but not by impeachment."
**Article VIII, Section 7(3), 1987 Constitution:**
"A Member of the Judiciary must be a person of **proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence**."
**Article XI, Section 17, 1987 Constitution:**
"A public officer or employee shall, **upon assumption of office and as often thereafter as may be required by law, submit a declaration under oath of his assets, liabilities, and net worth**. In the case of the President, the Vice-President, the Members of the Cabinet, the Congress, the Supreme Court, the Constitutional Commissions and other constitutional offices, and officers of the armed forces with general or flag rank, the declaration shall be disclosed to the public in the manner provided by law."
**Section 1, Rule 66, Rules of Court (Quo Warranto):**
"Section 1. **Action by Government against individuals.** — An action for the usurpation of a public office, position or franchise may be commenced by a verified petition brought in the name of the Republic of the Philippines against:
(a) **A person who usurps, intrudes into, or unlawfully holds or exercises a public office**, position or franchise;
(b) A public officer who does or suffers an act which, by the provision of law, constitutes a ground for the forfeiture of his office; or
(c) An association which acts as a corporation within the Philippines without being legally incorporated or without lawful authority so to act."
**Section 11, Rule 66, Rules of Court:**
"Section 11. **Limitations.** — Nothing contained in this Rule shall be construed to authorize an action against a public officer or employee for his ouster from office **unless the same be commenced within one (1) year after the cause of such ouster, or the right of the petitioner to hold such office or position, arose**; nor to authorize an action for damages in accordance with the provisions of the next preceding section unless the same be commenced within one (1) year after the entry of the judgment establishing the petitioner's right to the office in question."
**Factual Trigger:**
During the 2017–2018 House Committee on Justice hearings regarding an impeachment complaint filed by Atty. Larry Gadon, official certifications from the University of the Philippines (UP) and the Office of the Ombudsman revealed that respondent failed to file her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs) for multiple years during her 20-year tenure as a UP College of Law professor, and failed to submit at least ten (10) consecutive SALNs required by the JBC for the 2012 Chief Justice vacancy. Relying on these discoveries, the Republic, through Solicitor General Jose C. Calida, instituted a **quo warranto** petition directly before the Supreme Court to nullify her 2012 appointment on the ground that she lacked the constitutional qualification of "proven integrity" from the very beginning.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**November 1986 – June 1, 2006:** Respondent served as a faculty member at the UP College of Law—initially as temporary faculty (1986–1991), then as permanent regular faculty until her resignation on June 1, 2006. She was paid a regular monthly salary by UP. During this 20-year period, she took several official leaves of absence: June 1, 2000–May 31, 2002; November 1, 2003–May 31, 2004; June 1, 2004–October 31, 2004; November 1, 2004–February 10, 2005; February 11, 2005–October 31, 2005; and November 15, 2005–May 31, 2006.
**October 2003 – 2009:** Concurrent with her academic post (until 2006) and thereafter until 2009, respondent was engaged as legal counsel for the Republic in two international arbitrations (**PIATCO v. Republic** and **Fraport AG v. Republic**), receiving fees amounting to over P30 million. The UP Human Resources Development Office (HRDO) certified that there was no record in her 201 file of any written permission to engage in limited practice of profession.
**1986 – 2006 SALN Track Record:** Out of her 20 years in UP, official records showed that respondent only filed eleven (11) SALNs: 1985, 1989, 1990, 1991, 1993, 1994, 1995, 1996, 1997, 1998, and 2002. No SALNs were on file with UP HRDO or the Office of the Ombudsman for 1986, 1987, 1988, 1992, 1999, 2000, 2001, 2003, 2004, 2005, and 2006. She filed no exit SALN upon resigning on June 1, 2006.
**July 2010:** Respondent applied for the vacant position of Associate Justice of the Supreme Court. In support thereof, she submitted a SALN for 2006 signed only on July 27, 2010, bearing no stamp receipt from UP HRDO.
**August 16, 2010:** President Benigno C. Aquino III appointed respondent as Associate Justice of the Supreme Court, and she took her oath of office.
**June 4 – 5, 2012:** Following the impeachment of Chief Justice Renato C. Corona, the JBC En Banc opened nominations for the Chief Justice post. The JBC resolved that applicants from government must submit "all previous SALNs (up to 31 December 2011)" and execute a bank secrecy waiver. The published announcement expressly warned that applicants with incomplete documentary requirements would not be interviewed or considered for nomination.
**June 25, 2012:** The JBC En Banc resolved to exempt incumbent Supreme Court Justices from clearances, requiring them only to submit SALNs, bank waivers, medical certificates, lab results, and PDS.
**July 2, 2012:** Respondent accepted nominations for Chief Justice, submitting only three (3) SALNs: 2009, 2010, and 2011.
**July 20, 2012:** The JBC held a Special En Banc meeting to examine candidate compliance. The Executive Officer reported that respondent had not submitted her SALNs for a period of ten (10) years (from 1986 to 2006). The Council extended the submission deadline to July 23, 2012, delegating to its Executive Committee (Execom) the determination of substantial compliance (which had unofficially settled on requiring at least the previous 10 years of SALNs, i.e., 2001–2011).
**July 23, 2012:** Respondent transmitted a letter to the JBC stating that she was a full-time private practitioner between 2006 and 2010; that because most of her academic records were more than 15 years old, it was "reasonable to consider it infeasible to retrieve all of those files"; and that UP had issued her a clearance dated September 19, 2011, which should serve as assurance that she complied with all requirements.
**July 24 – 27, 2012:** Despite submitting only three SALNs and without the JBC En Banc or Execom ever formally deliberating on her July 23, 2012 letter, the JBC Secretariat annotated on candidate matrices that respondent had "COMPLETE REQUIREMENTS." Respondent was interviewed on July 27, 2012.
**August 13, 2012:** The JBC transmitted an 8-person shortlist to the President, which included respondent alongside Justices Carpio, Abad, Brion, Jardeleza, Leonardo-De Castro, and candidates Zamora and Villanueva.
**August 24, 2012:** President Aquino III appointed respondent as the 24th Chief Justice of the Supreme Court.
**August 30, 2017:** Atty. Larry Gadon filed an impeachment complaint against respondent before the House Committee on Justice, alleging culpable violation of the Constitution, corruption, and failure to declare truthful assets in her SALNs.
**February 7 – 27, 2018:** During House committee hearings, JBC officials and Supreme Court Justices testified that respondent had missing SALNs and that the JBC En Banc was never apprised of, nor did it deliberate upon, her July 23, 2012 explanatory letter. Certifications from UP HRDO and the Ombudsman established the non-existence of her SALNs for multiple years.
**February 21, 2018:** Atty. Eligio Mallari wrote to the Solicitor General requesting the initiation of a **quo warranto** proceeding against respondent.
**March 5, 2018:** The Republic, through Solicitor General Calida, filed the instant Petition for **Quo Warranto** directly with the Supreme Court.
**April 10, 2018:** The Supreme Court heard the case in Oral Arguments at Baguio City, where respondent appeared personally and was interpellated by her colleagues.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Republic / OSG)
**Main Thesis:** Respondent is ineligible to hold the office of Chief Justice because her repeated, chronic failure to file her mandatory SALNs while a UP professor and her failure to submit the required SALNs to the JBC prove that she lacked the constitutional qualification of "proven integrity" at the time of her appointment, rendering the appointment void **ab initio**.
**Availability of Quo Warranto against Impeachable Officers:** Impeachment and **quo warranto** are distinct remedies that can proceed simultaneously. Impeachment tests the public officer's **fitness to remain** in office based on serious offenses committed during incumbency; **quo warranto** questions the **legality of the title and appointment ab initio** based on pre-existing disqualifications. The text "may be removed" in Article XI, Section 2 is permissive, not exclusive.
**Prescription / Timeliness:** The one-year prescriptive period under Section 11, Rule 66 does not run against the State under the ancient maxim **nullum tempus occurrit regi** (no time runs against the king/State). Alternatively, if the period applies, it is reckoned from the **discovery** of the fraud/cause of ouster, which occurred only during the 2017–2018 House committee hearings.
**Non-applicability of Presumption of Regularity:** Regularity attaches only to official duties attached to a public post; the filing of personal SALNs is an individual obligation. Even if presumed, the certifications of the Ombudsman and UP HRDO completely rebutted the presumption.
**Lack of Proven Integrity:** Integrity requires strict adherence to constitutional and legal mandates. Violations of R.A. 3019 and R.A. 6713 are **mala prohibita**, rendering good faith or lack of criminal intent immaterial. Her July 23, 2012 letter to the JBC was dishonest because she concealed that she did not file 11 SALNs, instead misleading the Council by claiming the records were merely "infeasible to retrieve."
B. Respondent's Arguments (Chief Justice Sereno)
**Main Thesis:** The Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction to unseat an incumbent Chief Justice via **quo warranto**. Impeachment under Section 2, Article XI of the 1987 Constitution is the constitutionally mandated, single, and exclusive vehicle for removing an impeachable officer, preserving judicial independence from executive harassment.
**Exclusivity of Impeachment & Separation of Powers:** The word "may" in Section 2, Article XI qualifies the penalty of removal from office, not the mode. Allowing the Solicitor General to file **quo warranto** enables the Executive to bypass Congress's sole power of impeachment and administrative oversight.
**Prescription:** The petition is time-barred under Section 11, Rule 66, which requires actions to be filed within one (1) year after the cause of ouster arose (August 2012, upon appointment), not from its discovery.
**Political Question & JBC Discretion:** Determining whether an applicant possesses "proven integrity" is a subjective assessment textually committed to the sound discretion of the JBC and the President, constituting a political question outside the scope of judicial review, absent a direct petition alleging grave abuse of discretion.
**Factual Compliance & The Doblada Doctrine:** Respondent insisted she filed all her SALNs, invoking **Concerned Taxpayer v. Doblada, Jr.**, which held that the mere absence of a record in an office repository does not prove non-filing. Eleven SALNs were located, establishing a pattern of filing.
**Legal Exemptions:** She had no duty to file SALNs during periods she was on official leave of absence without pay, as she earned no government compensation and fell under the exemption for those serving without compensation.
**Spurious Connections to Integrity:** The submission of SALNs was merely an administrative documentary requirement of the JBC, not a constitutional qualification. Non-filing does not equal lack of integrity absent proof of corruption or ill-gotten wealth.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[Procedural / Preliminary Issue]** Whether the Associate Justices who testified before the House Committee on Justice or participated in Oral Arguments are legally mandated to inhibit themselves from hearing and deciding the petition.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to take cognizance of a petition for **quo warranto** under Rule 66 to oust an incumbent Chief Justice who is an impeachable officer, concurrent with ongoing impeachment proceedings.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether the petition for **quo warranto** is barred by the one-year statute of limitations under Section 11, Rule 66 of the Rules of Court.
4.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether the determination of a judicial candidate's qualifications and "proven integrity" by the JBC is a political question immune from the Supreme Court's supervisory and judicial power.
5.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether respondent failed to file her mandatory SALNs as required by the Constitution and law, and whether such failure, together with her non-submission of SALNs to the JBC, impairs her "proven integrity" and voids her nomination and appointment **ab initio**.
6.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether the subsequent nomination by the JBC and appointment by the President cured respondent's ineligibility, clothing her with **de jure** title.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Motion for Disqualification / Inhibition of the Six Associate Justices
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether the six challenged Associate Justices are legally mandated to recuse themselves due to actual bias. **NO.** Testifying under compulsion of legislative subpoena with En Banc authorization does not constitute disqualifying bias.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Standard for Voluntary Inhibition:** Imputations of partiality must be substantiated by clear and convincing evidence of extrinsic bias, malice, or corrupt purpose. Opinions formed during judicial or official inquiries do not establish personal bias.
2.  **Nature of Legislative Appearance:** The Justices testified before the House Committee on Justice pursuant to official En Banc clearance to shed light on administrative processes within their personal knowledge; they deliberately refused to pronounce conclusions on whether respondent's acts constituted impeachable offenses.
3.  **Mechanics of Collegial Recusal:** Under **Jurado & Co. v. Hongkong Bank**, a challenge to a judge’s competence is determined by the challenged judge and the Court sitting collegially. A party cannot be permitted to paralyze the High Court by moving to disqualify a majority of its members.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Absent strong and compelling evidence establishing actual bias and partiality on the part of the Justices whose recusal was sought, respondent's motions for inhibition must perforce fail. Mere conjectures and speculations cannot justify the inhibition of a Judge or Justice from a judicial matter."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** An appearance before a congressional committee under legal subpoena and En Banc clearance does not prove actual bias. A justice cannot be compelled to inhibit based on speculative assertions, and the Court will not permit a litigant to incapacitate the collegial body by selectively targeting its members.
Issue 2: Supreme Court Jurisdiction over Quo Warranto against an Impeachable Officer
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether an impeachable officer, like the Chief Justice, can be ousted via **quo warranto**. **YES.** Impeachment and **quo warranto** address fundamentally different causes of action, grounds, and legal remedies; impeachment targets misbehavior in office to forfeit **de jure** title, while **quo warranto** strips away a usurper's color of title to an office she never legally acquired.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Textual Construction of Section 2, Article XI:** The Constitution provides that impeachable officials "**may** be removed from office on impeachment." The term "may" is permissive and directory; it does not establish impeachment as an exclusive, all-encompassing mechanism to the exclusion of direct judicial inquiry into title.
2.  **Dichotomy of Remedies:** Impeachment is a political process conducted by the Legislature to vindicate the violation of the public trust and penalize official misconduct committed **during tenure**. **Quo warranto** is a judicial proceeding under Section 5(1), Article VIII of the Constitution and Rule 66 to determine whether an appointee possessed the requisite constitutional qualifications **at the inception** of appointment.
3.  **Reductio ad Absurdum of Exclusivity:** Adopting respondent’s view would mean that if an individual who is a foreign citizen or a fake bar member is mistakenly appointed Chief Justice, the Republic would be entirely powerless to oust the usurper unless they happen to commit an impeachable offense. The law cannot tolerate an absurdity where an unqualified impostor remains untouchable.
4.  **Precedents on Parallel Remedies:** The 2010 PET Rules expressly allow **quo warranto** against an elected President or Vice-President on grounds of ineligibility. Similarly, **Estrada v. Desierto** entertained **quo warranto** to resolve title to the Presidency. The remedies do not clash; they proceed upon different tracks.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"While impeachment concerns actions that make the officer unfit to continue exercising his or her office, **quo warranto** involves matters that render him or her ineligible to hold the position to begin with. ... It is not legally possible to impeach or remove a person from an office that he/she, in the first place, does not and cannot legally hold or occupy."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Impeachment strips a legal officer of legitimate title because of malfeasance in office; **quo warranto** establishes that the appointee never had legitimate title to begin with due to ineligibility at the starting line. Therefore, an ineligible person occupying an impeachable post is not immune from **quo warranto**.
Issue 3: Prescription under Section 11, Rule 66
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether the **quo warranto** petition is barred by the one-year prescriptive period. **NO.** Prescription does not run against the sovereign State when asserting a public right to protect the integrity of government office; alternatively, the period is reckoned only from the discovery of the fraud/cause of ouster.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Maxim Nullum Tempus Occurrit Regi:** The one-year prescriptive period in Section 11, Rule 66 is designed to penalize private individuals asserting private claims to an office to avoid dual payroll burdens on the government. Under **Agcaoili v. Suguitan** and Civil Code Article 1108(4), statutes of limitation do not apply to the State when it sues in its sovereign capacity to enforce a public right and end a continuing usurpation.
2.  **Discovery Rule & Concealment Exception:** Under **Cristobal v. Melchor**, prescription will not bar the government where delay was induced by the officer’s own acts. Respondent obscured her missing SALNs by offering vague explanations to the JBC (stating records were "infeasible to retrieve") rather than admitting non-filing. The State only discovered the disqualification during the 2017–2018 House committee hearings.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"As a general principle it may be stated that ordinary statutes of limitation, civil or penal, have no application to **quo warranto** proceeding brought to enforce a public right. ... Indeed, when the government is the real party in interest, and is proceeding mainly to assert its rights, there can be no defense on the ground of laches or prescription."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Time does not run against the State when it acts to unseat an unauthorized official holding a public office. Because respondent concealed her failure to file her SALNs by misrepresenting to the JBC that the documents were simply old and hard to retrieve, the one-year period could only begin to run from the actual discovery of her non-filing during the House hearings.
Issue 4: Political Question Doctrine and Supervisory Power over the JBC
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether the vetting of qualifications and nomination by the JBC is a political question beyond judicial review. **NO.** The JBC is an office placed under the express constitutional supervision of the Supreme Court, and whether a candidate possesses the minimum constitutional qualifications is an objective, justiciable question of law.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Supervisory Jurisdiction:** Article VIII, Section 8(1) vests the Supreme Court with administrative supervision over the JBC. Supervision includes ensuring that the JBC adheres to the Constitution and its own procedural rules (**Jardeleza v. Sereno**).
2.  **Absence of Political Question Indicators:** Under **Baker v. Carr**, a political question involves policy commitments entrusted to elective branches. Evaluating compliance with objective minimum qualifications prescribed by Section 7, Article VIII (citizenship, age, experience, and integrity) is a purely legal inquiry, not an unbridled discretionary policy choice.
3.  **Discretion is Subordinate to Law:** The JBC's discretion only applies to selecting among candidates who are **qualified**. It cannot waive, dilute, or bargain away mandatory constitutional and statutory qualifications.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The JBC's exercise of discretion is not automatically equivalent to an exercise of policy decision as to place, in wholesale, the JBC process beyond the scope of the Court's supervisory and corrective powers. ... The question of whether or not a nominee possesses the requisite qualifications is determined based on facts and therefore does not depend on, nor call for, the exercise of discretion on the part of the nominating body."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Supreme Court is constitutionally tasked with supervising the JBC to guarantee it abides by the Constitution. Checking whether an applicant meets the minimum qualifications for the bench is a question of law, not a political question, and the JBC possesses zero authority to waive constitutional prerequisites.
Issue 5: Respondent’s Failure to File SALNs and Its Effect on "Proven Integrity"
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether respondent chronically failed to file her SALNs and whether this failure voids her appointment for lack of "proven integrity." **YES.** Respondent repeatedly violated the Constitution and anti-graft statutes by failing to file eleven SALNs and submitting only three to the JBC, which demonstrates dishonesty and negates the constitutional qualification of proven integrity.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Constitutional and Statutory Mandate:** Article XI, Section 17 of the Constitution, Section 7 of R.A. 3019, and Section 8 of R.A. 6713 impose an absolute, mandatory duty on all public officers to file sworn SALNs. These laws are **mala prohibita**; failure to comply is a penal offense where criminal intent is immaterial.
2.  **Factual Finding of Non-Filing:** The Republic met its burden of proof by presenting official certifications from the UP HRDO and the Ombudsman demonstrating that respondent had no SALNs on file for 11 years (1986–1988, 1992, 1999–2001, 2003–2006). The burden of evidence shifted to respondent to produce proof of filing, which she failed to do.
3.  **Inapplicability of the Doblada Doctrine: Concerned Taxpayer v. Doblada, Jr.** does not apply. In **Doblada**, the respondent presented a transmittal letter proving the repository received his SALN; here, respondent presented no transmittal records, while the Ombudsman issued a categorical negative certification that no SALNs existed.
4.  **Rejection of the "Leave Without Pay" Exemption:** Section 8 of R.A. 6713 only exempts those serving in an honorary capacity, casuals, and manual laborers. Government employees on official leave remain public officers subject to the SALN law. Her receipt of income between leaves and her concurrent private arbitrations during her tenure dismantled this defense.
5.  **Integrity Deficit:** "Proven integrity" under Article VIII, Section 7(3) is an indispensable, continuing qualification. Repeated, chronic evasion of a constitutional duty, coupled with deceitful letters claiming records were "infeasible to retrieve" when they were never filed, constitutes grave dishonesty, permanently disqualifying her from the bench.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Failure to file the SALN is clearly a violation of the law. The offense is penal in character and is a clear breach of the ethical standards set for public officials and employees. It disregards the requirement of transparency as a deterrent to graft and corruption. For these reasons, a public official who has failed to comply with the requirement of filing the SALN cannot be said to be of proven integrity and the Court may consider him/her disqualified from holding public office."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Filing a SALN is not a trivial bureaucratic checkbox; it is a mandatory constitutional safeguard against corruption. Failing to file SALNs for 11 years while serving at UP, and lying about their retrieveability to the JBC, betrays a lack of probity and uprightness that fundamentally strips an aspirant of the constitutional qualification of "proven integrity."
Issue 6: Effect of Subsequent JBC Nomination and Presidential Appointment
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether the JBC shortlist and the President's appointment cured respondent's ineligibility. **NO.** A void act produces no legal effect; neither the JBC nor the President has the legal power to validate a candidacy that is disqualified under the Constitution.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Qualifications Must Be Possessed at Inception:** An appointee must possess all qualifications before nomination and maintain them continuously throughout tenure. One who lacks the constitutional qualification of proven integrity is ineligible **ab initio**.
2.  **Limits of Appointing Discretion:** Under **Luego v. Civil Service Commission**, executive discretion to appoint is absolute **only if** the appointee possesses all qualifications required by law. If the appointee is disqualified, the appointment is void and cannot be insulated by executive choice.
3.  **De Facto Officer Status:** Because the appointment was void, respondent was never a **de jure** Chief Justice. She occupied the position under a mere color of title, making her a **de facto** officer whose tenure is subject to direct ouster by the State via **quo warranto**.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"As the qualification of proven integrity goes into the barest standards set forth under the Constitution to qualify as a Member of the Court, the subsequent nomination and appointment to the position will not qualify an otherwise excluded candidate. In other words, the inclusion of respondent in the shortlist of nominees submitted to the President cannot override the minimum Constitutional qualifications."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Neither JBC nomination nor Presidential appointment can transform an ineligible person into an eligible judge. Because Chief Justice Sereno never possessed the required proven integrity, her appointment was void from day one, leaving her as a mere **de facto** officer holding color of title.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Topic: j. Tenure and Removal | Applied Lens: Constitutional & Political Law Lens
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 Governmental Act / Power Exercised:** The Republic exercised the State's sovereign power via the Solicitor General to file a direct judicial inquiry (**Quo Warranto under Rule 66) to expel an unlawful occupant from high office.
 Constitutional Limitation Invoked:** Article XI, Section 2 (Impeachment clause as an institutional shield protecting high officials and judicial independence) and Article VIII (Separation of Powers / Security of Tenure during good behavior until age 70). The Court held that the Impeachment Clause limits only the mode of removing **de jure officers for official misconduct, and does not limit the Court's judicial power to determine whether title to the office ever legally vested.
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
 Standard Applied:** Pure Statutory and Constitutional Interpretation / Substantial Compliance Review. The Court examined whether respondent met the objective, non-waivable constitutional criteria for appointment under Article VIII, Section 7(3). The Court applied an absolute liability standard (**malum prohibitum) regarding the legal duty to file SALNs under R.A. 3019 and R.A. 6713, holding that good faith is immaterial to the objective fact of non-compliance.
**Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit:**
 Actual Case or Controversy: Present; a real legal dispute existed between the State claiming usurpation of sovereign functions and an occupant claiming legitimate tenure.
 Locus Standi: Confirmed; under Rule 66, Section 1, the Solicitor General possesses exclusive standing on behalf of the Republic to challenge usurpation of public office. (Private intervenors, lacking claim of title, were denied standing).
 Transcendental Importance: Invoked to resolve the threshold issue of judicial title at the apex court.
 Political Question Doctrine: Explicitly rejected; determining compliance with statutory and constitutional qualifications is an exercise of judicial power, not a political question committed to coordinate branches.
 Lis Mota:** The constitutionality of respondent's appointment was the absolute **lis mota of the proceedings.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Quo Warranto (By what authority)
 De Jure** Officer vs. **De Facto Officer
 Nullum tempus occurrit regi (No time runs against the king/State)
 Proven Integrity (Article VIII, Section 7[3])
 Malum Prohibitum
 Sub Judice Rule
Color of Title / Usurper
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"Under the topic of Tenure and Removal, **Republic v. Sereno** establishes that the constitutional provision stating impeachable officers 'may be removed from office on impeachment' (Art. XI, Sec. 2) is non-exclusive and does not foreclose a **quo warranto** action under Rule 66. The Supreme Court ruled that while impeachment addresses offenses committed **during** incumbency to forfeit a valid title, **quo warranto** directly tests whether the appointee was eligible **at the time of appointment**. Because respondent failed to file her mandatory SALNs for 11 years as a UP professor and failed to submit them to the JBC, she lacked the constitutional qualification of 'proven integrity' under Article VIII, Section 7(3), rendering her appointment void **ab initio** and subject to judicial ouster as a **de facto** officer."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Carpio, J. (Dissenting):** Argued vigorously that an incumbent Member of the Supreme Court can be removed from office **only by impeachment** by the Senate. Quo warranto against an impeachable officer unconstitutionally eviscerates judicial independence, subverts checks and balances, and bypasses the exclusive constitutional forum of the Senate Impeachment Court. He noted, however, that respondent's failure to file SALNs constituted non-feasance punishable under anti-graft laws through impeachment.
**Velasco, Jr., J. (Concurring and Dissenting):** Concurred that the Court has jurisdiction to entertain **quo warranto** to determine eligibility at inception, but dissented on the finding of ineligibility, arguing the Republic failed to conclusively establish that respondent did not file her UP SALNs, given the unreliability of repository files.
**Leonardo-De Castro, J. (Concurring):** Emphasized that respondent systematically deceived the JBC by withholding information on her non-filing, undermining the integrity test required of every judicial applicant.
**Peralta, J. (Separate Concurring):** Clarified his role as former Acting JBC Chair, stressing that the JBC En Banc was deliberately bypassed and kept in the dark regarding respondent's missing SALNs and her July 23, 2012 letter.
**Bersamin, J. (Concurring):** Underscored that the Supreme Court's supervisory power over the JBC permits it to nullify nominations that blatantly disregard mandatory constitutional qualifications.
**Leonen, J. (Dissenting):** Denounced the decision as a legal monstrosity and a fatal blow to judicial independence, stating that **quo warranto** was weaponized by the Executive through the Solicitor General to purge a sitting Chief Justice, completely stripping the Senate of its constitutional role as the sole impeachment tribunal.
**Caguioa, J. (Dissenting):** Maintained that the Constitution intentionally created an arduous, single mechanism—impeachment—to remove high judicial officers. Creating an exception through **quo warranto** places a sword of Damocles over every judge's head, held by the Executive branch.
**Perlas-Bernabe, J. (Separate Opinion / Dissenting on Quo Warranto):** Voted to dismiss the petition, opining that the Constitution sets impeachment as the exclusive vehicle to remove sitting Supreme Court Justices, preserving the institutional architecture of checks and balances.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"**WHEREFORE**, the Petition for **Quo Warranto** is **GRANTED**. Respondent Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno is found **DISQUALIFIED** from and is hereby adjudged **GUILTY of UNLAWFULLY HOLDING and EXERCISING the OFFICE OF THE CHIEF JUSTICE**. Accordingly, Respondent Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno is **OUSTED** and **EXCLUDED** therefrom.

The position of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court is declared vacant and the Judicial and Bar Council is directed to commence the application and nomination process.

This Decision is immediately executory without need of further action from the Court.

Respondent Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno is ordered to **SHOW CAUSE** within ten (10) days from receipt hereof why she should not be sanctioned for violating the Code of Professional Responsibility and the Code of Judicial Conduct for transgressing the **sub judice** rule and for casting aspersions and ill motives to the Members of the Supreme Court.

**SO ORDERED.**"
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court granted the Republic’s petition, nullifying Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno's appointment as Chief Justice of the Philippines on the ground that she lacked the constitutional qualification of "proven integrity" due to her failure to file her mandatory SALNs. She was immediately ousted and excluded from office, the post of Chief Justice was declared vacant, and the JBC was directed to open a new selection process.
