### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: In Re: Save the Supreme Court (Mijares v. Abolition of JDF)**
**Full Official Caption:** In the Matter of: Save the Supreme Court Judicial Independence and Fiscal Autonomy Movement vs. Abolition of Judiciary Development Fund (JDF) and Reduction of Fiscal Autonomy (UDK-15143)
**Citation & Metadata:** UDK-15143; 751 Phil. 30; Promulgated January 21, 2015; En Banc Resolution; Ponente: Associate Justice Marvic M.V.F. Leonen. Voting Breakdown: Unanimous; Sereno, C.J., Carpio, Velasco, Jr., Leonardo-De Castro, Peralta, Bersamin, Del Castillo, Villarama, Jr., Perez, Mendoza, Reyes, Perlas-Bernabe, and Jardeleza, JJ., concurred; Brion, J., was on official leave.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Rolly Mijares:** Petitioner; self-described Filipino citizen, concerned taxpayer, and crusader for the rule of law representing the "Save the Supreme Court Judicial Independence and Fiscal Autonomy Movement."
**House of Representatives / 16th Congress of the Philippines (specifically Rep. Rodolfo Fariñas and Rep. Niel Tupas, Jr.):** The legislative department whose members introduced House Bill Nos. 4690 and 4738 seeking to repeal Presidential Decree No. 1949 and abolish the Judiciary Development Fund (JDF).
**President Benigno Simeon C. Aquino III:** President of the Republic of the Philippines whose televised speech criticizing the Supreme Court’s rulings on executive spending served as part of the alleged threat against judicial independence.
**The Supreme Court of the Philippines:** Respondent institution against which the petition for mandamus was directed, praying that it actively assert its fiscal autonomy and revoke congressional actions.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Original Letter-Petition for Mandamus with Manifestation filed directly before the Supreme Court by Rolly Mijares on August 27, 2014, docketed as an unnumbered case (UDK-15143), seeking to compel the Supreme Court to invoke and enforce its constitutional fiscal autonomy against pending congressional bills that proposed to abolish the Judiciary Development Fund (JDF) and replace it with a national treasury-remitted "Judiciary Support Fund."
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Fiscal Autonomy (Art. VIII, Sec. 3)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Judicial Review → Requisites (Actual Case or Controversy, Ripeness, Locus Standi) → Special Civil Actions → Mandamus (Rule 65)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article VIII, Section 3, 1987 Constitution of the Republic of the Philippines:**
"Section 3. **The Judiciary shall enjoy fiscal autonomy. Appropriations for the Judiciary may not be reduced by the legislature below the amount appropriated for the previous year and, after approval, shall be automatically and regularly released.**"
**Article VIII, Section 1, 1987 Constitution of the Republic of the Philippines:**
"Section 1. The judicial power shall be vested in one Supreme Court and in such lower courts as may be established by law.
Judicial power includes the duty of the courts of justice to **settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable**, and to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government."
**Rule 65, Section 3, 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure:**
"SEC. 3. **Petition for mandamus.** — When any tribunal, corporation, board, officer or person **unlawfully neglects the performance of an act which the law specifically enjoins as a duty resulting from an office, trust, or station**, or unlawfully excludes another from the use and enjoyment of a right or office to which such other is entitled, and there is no other plain, speedy and adequate remedy in the ordinary course of law, the person aggrieved thereby may file a verified petition in the proper court, alleging the facts with certainty and praying that judgment be rendered commanding the respondent, immediately or at some other time to be specified by the court, to do the act required to be done to protect the rights of the petitioner, and to pay the damages sustained by the petitioner by reason of the wrongful acts of the respondent."
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):** Following Supreme Court decisions striking down the Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF) and portions of the Disbursement Acceleration Program (DAP), two House Representatives filed bills proposing to repeal Presidential Decree No. 1949, abolish the Judiciary Development Fund (JDF), and require all judicial collections to be remitted to the National Treasury under legislative control; in response, petitioner filed a petition for mandamus asking the Supreme Court to proactively strike down these pending legislative bills and defend its fiscal autonomy.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**November 19, 2013:** The Supreme Court promulgates **Belgica v. Ochoa** (G.R. No. 208566), declaring the legislative Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF) unconstitutional.
**July 1, 2014:** The Supreme Court promulgates **Araullo v. Aquino** (G.R. No. 209287), declaring specific executive acts and practices under the Disbursement Acceleration Program (DAP) unconstitutional.
**First week of July 2014:** Ilocos Norte Representative Rodolfo Fariñas files House Bill No. 4690, proposing to require the Supreme Court to remit its Judiciary Development Fund (JDF) collections to the National Treasury.
**July 14, 2014:** Iloilo Representative Niel Tupas, Jr. files House Bill No. 4738, titled "The Act Creating the Judicial Support Fund (JSF) under the National Treasury, repealing for the purpose Presidential Decree No. 1949."
**July 14, 2014:** President Benigno Simeon C. Aquino III delivers a televised national address criticizing the Supreme Court's DAP decision, stating that the executive used mechanisms similar to past judicial practices, warning against two equal branches going head-to-head, and urging the Court to review and reconsider its ruling.
**August 27, 2014:** Petitioner Rolly Mijares, styling himself as a concerned citizen and taxpayer under the "Save the Supreme Court Judicial Independence and Fiscal Autonomy Movement," sends a letter captioned **"Petition for Mandamus with Manifestation to invoke the Judicial Independence and Fiscal Autonomy as mandated under the Constitution"** addressed to the Chief Justice and Associate Justices of the Supreme Court.
**August 27, 2014 / Case Intake:** The letter-petition is referred to the Clerk of Court En Banc for appropriate action and officially docketed as UDK-15143.
**September 9, 2014:** The Judicial Department presents its statistical data during congressional hearings on its proposed 2015 national budget, highlighting persistent deficits in trial court Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE) and hall of justice funding.
**January 21, 2015:** The Supreme Court En Banc resolves to dismiss the petition outright for failure to present a justiciable case or controversy, lack of legal standing, and the non-availability of mandamus against legislative processes.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Rolly Mijares)
**Main Thesis:** The Supreme Court must issue a writ of mandamus compelling itself to exercise its judicial power, protect its constitutional fiscal autonomy, and strike down the hostile congressional attempts to abolish the Judiciary Development Fund (JDF).
**Specific Contentions:**
 Grave Abuse of Discretion and Usurpation: Congress committed grave abuse of discretion and a blatant usurpation of the Supreme Court's judicial independence and fiscal autonomy by moving to abolish the JDF via House Bill Nos. 4690 and 4738.
 Legislative Hostility:** Members of Congress acted in an arbitrary and despotic manner out of personal hostility following the Supreme Court's rulings declaring the PDAF (**Belgica**) and DAP (**Araullo) unconstitutional.
 Wreckers of the Law: Members of Congress acted as "wreckers of the law" by attempting to clip the powers of the High Tribunal and committing a "blunder of monumental proportions" in seeking to reduce the judiciary's 2015 budgetary allocations.
 Direct Remedial Prayer: The Court must exercise its powers to "REVOKE/ABROGATE and EXPUNGE whatever irreconcilable contravention of existing laws affecting the judicial independence and fiscal autonomy as mandated under the Constitution to better serve public interest and general welfare of the people."
B. Respondent's Arguments (The Government / Legislative / Institutional Counterpart)
 Note on Record:** Not expressly stated in the decision. The Court resolved the letter-petition **motu proprio upon referral without requiring formal comments from the named legislative proponents or the Office of the Solicitor General.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the letter-petition presents an actual, justiciable case or controversy ripe for judicial determination.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not petitioner Rolly Mijares possesses legal standing (**locus standi**) or satisfies the criteria for matters of transcendental importance to challenge proposed legislative bills.
3.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not a writ of mandamus lies to compel the Supreme Court to preventively intervene against proposed legislative bills and declare the abolition of the Judiciary Development Fund (JDF) violative of judicial fiscal autonomy.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Existence of an Actual Case or Controversy
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the letter-petition presents an actual, justiciable case or controversy ripe for judicial determination.
**NO.** A proposed legislative bill is not a law, creates no enforceable rights or duties, and cannot be judicially reviewed prior to its formal enactment.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Constitutional Limitation of Judicial Power:** Under Article VIII, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution, judicial power is confined to settling actual controversies involving rights legally demandable and enforceable, and determining grave abuse of discretion. Courts cannot render advisory opinions upon conjectural, anticipatory, or theoretical questions (**Information Technology Foundation of the Phils. v. COMELEC).
 Proposed Bills Lack Legal Effect:** Applying **Montesclaros v. COMELEC**, the Court reaffirmed that a proposed bill is not a law. It creates no rights, imposes no duties, and inflicts no direct constitutional injury. Because a bill produces no legal effect until passed into law, the Court has no jurisdiction to adjudicate its constitutionality **in vacuo.
 Separation of Powers Protects the Legislative Mill: Under the principle of separation of powers, the internal processes of Congress—including the introduction of bills by legislators, committee deliberations, bicameral reconciliation, and voting—are immune from judicial restraint. The judiciary must await the final enactment of a statute before exercising judicial review; to intervene while the bill is pending would shatter the constitutional balance among coordinate branches.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Petitioners' prayer to prevent Congress from enacting into law a proposed bill lowering the membership age in the SK does not present an actual justiciable controversy. A proposed bill is not subject to judicial review because it is not a law. A proposed bill creates no right and imposes no duty legally enforceable by the Court. A proposed bill, having no legal effect, violates no constitutional right or duty. The Court has no power to declare a proposed bill constitutional or unconstitutional because that would be in the nature of rendering an advisory opinion on a proposed act of Congress. The power of judicial review cannot be exercised **in vacuo**." **(Quoting Montesclaros v. COMELEC)**
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Supreme Court cannot review or invalidate a mere bill pending in Congress because a bill has no force of law and hurts nobody yet. Judicial review cannot operate in a vacuum or offer advisory opinions on what Congress **might** pass. Until a bill actually survives the entire legislative mill and is signed into law, any constitutional attack on it is purely speculative and premature.
Issue 2: Legal Standing (**Locus Standi**) and Transcendental Importance
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not petitioner Rolly Mijares possesses legal standing or qualifies under the transcendental importance exception.
**NO.** Petitioner failed to demonstrate any direct, personal injury resulting from pending bills, and the speculative nature of an unpassed bill prevents invocation of the transcendental importance doctrine.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Failure Under the Direct Injury Test:** Pursuant to Section 2, Rule 3 of the Rules of Court and **David v. Macapagal-Arroyo**, a party must be a real party-in-interest who has sustained or is in immediate danger of sustaining a direct personal injury (**People v. Vera). Suing as a "concerned citizen" or "taxpayer" is insufficient where the assailed acts consist merely of unacted legislative bills that, even if enacted, would directly govern the Judiciary rather than individual taxpayers.
 Absence of Francisco Determinants:** The procedural relaxation of standing for issues of transcendental importance (**Biraogo v. Philippine Truth Commission**) requires meeting the three determinants formulated by Justice Feliciano in **Francisco v. House of Representatives: (1) the character of the funds or assets involved; (2) the presence of a clear disregard of a constitutional or statutory prohibition; and (3) the absence of any other party with a more direct and specific interest.
 No Imminent Threat to Rights:** Citing the separate opinion in **Imbong v. Ochoa, transcendental importance cannot be invoked on abstract and speculative pleadings. Because the passage of House Bill Nos. 4690 and 4738 remained contingent and hypothetical, there was no imminent, grave, or irreparable injury that justified dispensing with jurisdictional standing rules.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Petitioner has not shown that he has sustained or will sustain a direct injury if the proposed bill is passed into law. While his concern for judicial independence is laudable, it does not, by itself, clothe him with the requisite standing to question the constitutionality of a proposed bill that may only affect the judiciary."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** An ordinary citizen cannot run to the Supreme Court simply because he dislikes a bill filed in Congress. Under the direct injury test, the petitioner must prove that he personally suffered or will suffer real harm from an official act. Because the bills were unpassed and solely affected judicial funding mechanisms, petitioner had no personal stake, and the Court will not relax the rules on transcendental importance based on pure guesswork about whether a bill will ever become law.
Issue 3: Propriety of the Writ of Mandamus and the Fiscal Autonomy Framework
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not a writ of mandamus lies to compel the Supreme Court to preventively intervene against proposed legislative bills and declare the abolition of the Judiciary Development Fund (JDF) violative of judicial fiscal autonomy.
**NO.** Mandamus lies solely to compel the performance of a non-discretionary, ministerial duty resulting from an office, trust, or station, not to force an adjudicative body to prematurely exercise judicial review where no justiciable controversy exists.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Ministerial vs. Discretionary Acts:** Under Rule 65, Section 3, mandamus is an extraordinary remedy available only when a respondent tribunal or officer unlawfully neglects a specifically enjoined ministerial duty (**Special People, Inc. Foundation v. Canda). It never lies to dictate the exercise of judgment or compel an official to act in the absence of an enforceable legal right.
 Mandamus Cannot Compel Premature Judicial Review: The Supreme Court has no ministerial duty to issue premature declarations or to lobby against another coordinate branch. Since there was no ripe case or controversy, the Court could not be legally compelled to exercise judicial review.
 Doctrinal Reality of Fiscal Autonomy (Art. VIII, Sec. 3):** In its **Final Note**, the Court underscored that Article VIII, Section 3 of the Constitution explicitly guarantees that the Judiciary enjoys fiscal autonomy—prohibiting the legislature from reducing judicial appropriations below the amount of the previous year and requiring automatic and regular fund releases (**Bengzon v. Drilon).
 Institutional Vulnerability: The Court observed the harsh reality that the Judiciary remains the weakest branch: it has neither the power of the sword nor the purse, receiving less than 1% of the national budget annually (0.82% in 2014, with trial courts receiving a meager average of ~₱46,000 monthly MOOE, contrasted with the House of Representatives Batasan compound's ~₱282.2 million monthly MOOE). While the JDF (created under P.D. 1949) serves as an essential lifeline to augment trial court operations, repair dilapidated halls of justice, and subsidize personnel compensation, the Court cannot preserve this fund through unauthorized political lobbying or unconstitutional pre-enforcement judicial decrees.
 Proper Recourse is Political: Because courts operate purely on legal analysis rather than political releases or lobbying, a citizen seeking to defend judicial fiscal autonomy against pending legislation must channel his advocacy to the halls of Congress where legislative discretion is actively debated.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The Judiciary, the Constitutional Commissions, and the Ombudsman must have the independence and flexibility needed in the discharge of their constitutional duties. The imposition of restrictions and constraints on the manner the independent constitutional offices allocate and utilize the funds appropriated for their operations is anathema to fiscal autonomy and violative not only of the express mandate of the Constitution but especially as regards the Supreme Court, of the independence and separation of powers upon which the entire fabric of our constitutional system is based." **(Quoting Bengzon v. Drilon)**

"Courts are not constitutionally built to do political lobbying. By constitutional design, it is a co-equal department to the Congress and the Executive. By temperament, our arguments are legal, not political... It seems that we have no champions when it comes to ensuring the material basis for fiscal autonomy or judicial independence."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Mandamus can only be used to force an official to carry out a purely automatic, non-discretionary legal duty. It cannot be used to order the Supreme Court to preemptively strike down bills that are still being debated in Congress, because the Court has no duty—and in fact lacks constitutional authority—to rule on proposed laws. Although the Court agreed that the Judiciary's fiscal autonomy under Article VIII, Section 3 is constantly strained by shoestring budgetary allocations (less than 1% of the national budget), the proper remedy for a concerned citizen is to lobby his representatives in Congress, not to ask the Court to commit a constitutional overreach.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Fiscal Autonomy (Article VIII, Section 3)
**Applied Lens:** Constitutional & Political Law (Separation of Powers, Justiciability, and Institutional Independence)
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 Branch Power Exercised: Congressional legislative power (the power to initiate, deliberate, and introduce bills under Article VI) and the power of the purse.
 Constitutional Limitation Invoked: Judicial Fiscal Autonomy (Article VIII, Section 3) and Separation of Powers, which shield the Judiciary's internal budgetary management and prohibit the reduction of judicial appropriations below the prior year's level.
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
 Threshold Justiciability Review: The Court applied the strict **Four Invariable Requisites of Judicial Review** (**Actual Case or Controversy, Locus Standi, Earliest Opportunity, and Lis Mota**).
 Ripeness / Non-Interference Doctrine: The Court enforced the categorical rule that legislative procedures within Congress are non-justiciable prior to statutory enactment, barring any pre-enforcement scrutiny of proposed bills.
**Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit:**
 Actual Case or Controversy: **Absent.** A proposed bill creates no rights, imposes no duties, and has no legal effect. The issue is purely conjectural and non-ripe.
 Locus Standi: **Absent.** Petitioner failed the "direct injury test" (**People v. Vera**). He had no specific, personal, or substantial interest injured by unpassed bills.
 Transcendental Importance: **Rejected.** None of the **Francisco** determinants were present; speculative fears of what a bill might do cannot bypass the requirement of an imminent, grave injury to fundamental rights.
 Lis Mota: **Not reached**, because the non-satisfaction of threshold requisites precluded any constitutional determination on the merits.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Fiscal Autonomy - Art. VIII, Sec. 3):**
1.  **Legislative Floor:** Appropriations for the Judiciary may not be reduced by the legislature below the amount appropriated for the previous year. **(Examined by the Court as a core constitutional limitation).**
2.  **Automatic and Regular Release:** Approved appropriations must be automatically and regularly released without executive or legislative withholding.
3.  **Budgetary Flexibility & Self-Administration:** The Judiciary retains absolute independence in allocating and utilizing funds appropriated for its operations without external operational constraints (**Bengzon v. Drilon**).
**Application to Trigger Facts:** The Court recognized that while the Judiciary Development Fund (P.D. 1949) is vital to mitigating the chronic underfunding of trial courts (which receive less than 1% of the GAA), the threat posed by House Bill Nos. 4690 and 4738 remained contingent. Thus, the constitutional guarantee cannot be weaponized defensively against unpassed bills.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Fiscal Autonomy (Art. VIII, Sec. 3)
 Power of Judicial Review cannot be exercised in vacuo
 Proposed bill is not a law
 Direct Injury Test
 Transcendental Importance Determinants
 Separation of Powers and System of Checks and Balances
 Ministerial Duty vs. Discretionary Function
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
**In Re: Save the Supreme Court** falls under Fiscal Autonomy because it explores whether the Court can proactively defend its special funds (the Judiciary Development Fund) from being abolished by Congress. The Supreme Court dismissed the mandamus petition, ruling that an unpassed legislative bill is not a law and presents no justiciable case or controversy. Although Article VIII, Section 3 strictly protects the Judiciary's fiscal autonomy by forbidding budget reductions below the previous year's allocation and ensuring independent fund management (**Bengzon v. Drilon**), courts cannot violate the separation of powers by pre-emptively enjoining the legislative mill; the proper recourse to protect the Judiciary's budget from pending bills is legislative lobbying, not premature constitutional litigation.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed. (Associate Justice Arturo D. Brion was on official leave; all other participating Justices concurred fully with the Resolution penned by Justice Leonen).
**Verbatim Fallo:**
**"WHEREFORE, the petition is DISMISSED.**
**SO ORDERED."**
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The petition for mandamus was dismissed outright. The Supreme Court declined to intervene against Congress or declare the pending bills unconstitutional, leaving House Bill Nos. 4690 and 4738 within the legislative mill and instructing the petitioner that his crusade to protect judicial fiscal autonomy must be pursued through congressional lobbying rather than court litigation.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** CHR Employees’ Association v. CHR (Resolution)
**Full Official Caption:** Commission on Human Rights Employees' Association (CHREA), Represented by its President, Marcial A. Sanchez, Jr., Petitioner, vs. Commission on Human Rights, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 155336; July 21, 2006; 528 Phil. 658; Chico-Nazario, **J.**; Special Second Division; Concurring: Puno (**Chairman**), Austria-Martinez, Callejo, Sr., and Tinga, **JJ.** No separate opinions filed.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Petitioner:** Commission on Human Rights Employees' Association (CHREA), the legitimate collective negotiating representative of the rank-and-file employees of the Commission on Human Rights, represented by its President, Marcial A. Sanchez, Jr.
**Respondent:** Commission on Human Rights (CHR), an independent constitutional office created under Article XIII, Section 17 of the 1987 Constitution, acting through its Chairperson and Commissioners.
**Intervening Administrative Bodies:**
 Department of Budget and Management (DBM): Headed by Secretary Benjamin Diokno; the executive agency mandated by law to administer the compensation and position classification system under Republic Act No. 6758.
 Civil Service Commission (CSC): Constitutional commission composed of the CSC-National Capital Region (CSC-NCR) Office and the CSC-Central Office.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** This resolution arose from a **Motion for Reconsideration** filed by the CHR challenging the Supreme Court’s Division Decision dated November 25, 2004. In that underlying Decision, the Court granted CHREA’s Rule 45 Petition for Review on Certiorari, reversed the Court of Appeals (CA) Decision dated November 29, 2001 and Resolution dated September 11, 2002 (CA-G.R. SP No. 59678), reinstated the CSC-NCR ruling of March 29, 1999, and disallowed CHR Resolutions Nos. A98-047, A98-055, and A98-062 for lack of DBM approval.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Judicial Department & Independent Constitutional Bodies → Fiscal Autonomy (Scope, Extent, and Limitations)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Administrative Law → Position Classification and Compensation Scheme → Compensation Standardization Law (R.A. No. 6758) & Role of the DBM
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional & Statutory Provisions:**
**Article XIII, Section 17, 1987 Constitution:**
Sec. 17. (1) There is hereby created an independent office called the Commission on Human Rights.
x x x x
(4) **The approved annual appropriations of the Commission shall be automatically and regularly released.**
**Article VIII, Section 3, 1987 Constitution (Judiciary):**
Sec. 3. **The Judiciary shall enjoy fiscal autonomy.** Appropriations for the Judiciary may not be reduced by the legislature below the amount appropriated for the previous year and, after approval, **shall be automatically and regularly released.**
**Article IX, Part A, Section 5, 1987 Constitution (Constitutional Commissions):**
Sec. 5. **The Commission shall enjoy fiscal autonomy. Their approved annual appropriations shall be automatically and regularly released.**
**Article XI, Section 14, 1987 Constitution (Office of the Ombudsman):**
Sec. 14. **The Office of the Ombudsman shall enjoy fiscal autonomy. Its approved annual appropriations shall be automatically and regularly released.**
**Republic Act No. 8522 (General Appropriations Act of 1998), Article XXXIII (Special Provisions Applicable to All Constitutional Offices Enjoying Fiscal Autonomy):**
Organizational Structure. Any provision of law to the contrary notwithstanding and within the limits of their respective appropriations as authorized in this Act, the Constitutional Commissions and Offices enjoying fiscal autonomy are authorized to formulate and implement the organizational structures of their respective offices, to fix and determine the salaries, allowances, and other benefits of their personnel, and whenever public interest so requires, make adjustments in the personal services itemization including, but not limited to, the transfer of item or creation of new positions in their respective offices: PROVIDED, That officers and employees whose positions are affected by such reorganization or adjustments shall be granted retirement gratuities and separation pay in accordance with existing laws, which shall be payable from any unexpended balance of, or savings in the appropriations of their respective offices: **PROVIDED, FURTHER, That the implementation hereof shall be in accordance with salary rates, allowances and other benefits authorized under compensation standardization laws.**

Use of Savings. The Constitutional Commissions and Offices enjoying fiscal autonomy are hereby authorized to use savings in their respective appropriations for: (a) printing and/or publication of decisions, resolutions, and training information materials; (b) repair, maintenance and improvement of central and regional offices, facilities and equipment; (c) purchase of books, journals, periodicals and equipment; (d) necessary expenses for the employment of temporary, contractual and casual employees; (e) payment of extraordinary and miscellaneous expenses, commutable representation and transportation allowances, and fringe benefits for their officials and employees as may be authorized by law; and (f) other official purposes, subject to accounting and auditing rules and regulations.
**Book VI, Chapter 1, Section 1(9), Executive Order No. 292 (Administrative Code of 1987):**
SEC. 1. Constitutional Policies on the Budget. — x x x
(9) Fiscal autonomy shall be enjoyed by the Judiciary, Constitutional Commissions, Office of the Ombudsman, Local Government and Commission on Human Rights.
**Factual Trigger:**
Invoking fiscal autonomy under R.A. No. 8522 (the 1998 GAA) and its membership in the Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy Group (CFAG), the CHR unilaterally passed internal resolutions upgrading, reclassifying, and creating plantilla positions and collapsing vacancies to fund salary increases. When DBM Secretary Benjamin Diokno disapproved the scheme for violating R.A. No. 6758 (the Compensation Standardization Law) and GAA restrictions on creating unauthorized key units, the CHR insisted that its fiscal autonomy insulated it from DBM oversight, prompting CHREA's legal challenge.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**February 14, 1998:** Congress enacts Republic Act No. 8522 (General Appropriations Act FY 1998), containing "Special Provisions Applicable to All Constitutional Offices Enjoying Fiscal Autonomy" under Article XXXIII, authorizing fiscally autonomous bodies to formulate organizational structures, fix compensation, adjust items, and utilize savings, provided implementation complies with compensation standardization laws.
**July 24, 1998:** The Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy Group (CFAG), with CHR Chairperson Aurora P. Navarette-Reciña signing as an active member, adopts CFAG Joint Resolution No. 49, defining fiscal autonomy as broad independence from outside control regarding financial matters, encompassing budget preparation, fund utilization, use of savings, and disposition of receipts.
**September 4, 1998:** Relying on the 1998 GAA special provisions and CFAG membership, the CHR promulgates Resolution No. A98-047, approving an upgrading and reclassification scheme effective Calendar Year 1998 funded by savings from Personal Services, proposing 10 new plantilla items (including one Director IV, SG-28; four Security Officer II, SG-15; and five Process Servers, SG-5).
**October 19, 1998:** The CHR passes Resolution No. A98-055, raising the salary grades of selected positions and authorizing further augmentation from Personal Services savings.
**November 17, 1998:** The CHR enacts Resolution No. A98-062, "collapsing" vacant positions (one Attorney III, four Attorney IV, one Chemist III, three Special Investigator I, one Clerk III, and one Accounting Clerk II) to fund the upgraded staffing scheme.
**January 20, 1999:** DBM Secretary Benjamin Diokno formally denies CHR's request for approval of the staffing modification. The DBM rules that: (1) elevating field units and divisions to regional offices/bureaus (upgrading 12 Attorney VI, SG-26 to Director IV, SG-28, and three Director III, SG-27 to Director IV, SG-28) changes contextual rank from support to substantive without actual functional shifts; (2) Section 78 of the 1998 GAA General Provisions bars creating organizational units (Finance Management Office and Public Affairs Office) or key positions without statutory or presidential authority; and (3) CFAG membership does not exempt agencies from the DBM's sole power under R.A. No. 6758 to administer the unified position classification system.
**March 29, 1999:** Prompted by the DBM’s denial, the CSC-NCR issues a Memorandum recommending to the CSC-Central Office the rejection of all appointments issued pursuant to the CHR upgrading scheme.
**December 16, 1999:** Denying the request of rank-and-file employees represented by CHREA, the CSC-Central Office issues Resolution No. 99-2800, reversing the CSC-NCR's recommendation and upholding the validity of the CHR reclassification scheme.
**June 9, 2000:** The CSC-Central Office issues Resolution No. 001354 denying CHREA's Motion for Reconsideration.
**November 29, 2001:** The Court of Appeals, in CA-G.R. SP No. 59678, dismisses CHREA's petition and affirms the CSC-Central Office, ruling that the upgrading and reclassification fall within the CHR's constitutional fiscal autonomy. The CA subsequently denies reconsideration on September 11, 2002.
**November 25, 2004:** The Supreme Court (Division) promulgates its Decision granting CHREA’s petition, setting aside the CA rulings, reinstating the CSC-NCR ruling of March 29, 1999, and disallowing CHR Resolutions Nos. A98-047, A98-055, and A98-062 for lack of DBM approval. The Court holds that CHR is not a constitutional commission and possesses no legal basis for fiscal autonomy.
**Post-Promulgation Phase:** The CHR files a Motion for Reconsideration praying that the Court reverse its holding that CHR lacks fiscal autonomy; CHREA files an Opposition.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondent CHR's Arguments (Motion for Reconsideration)
**Main Thesis:** The CHR is an independent constitutional body vested with fiscal autonomy under Article XIII, Section 17(4) of the 1987 Constitution, the 1998 GAA, and the Administrative Code of 1987; consequently, its unilateral reorganization, position upgrading, and collapsing of items do not require prior DBM evaluation or approval.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Constitutional Intent on Fiscal Autonomy:** While Article XIII, Section 17(4) omits the opening phrase **"The Commission shall enjoy fiscal autonomy"** and only mandates that appropriations be automatically and regularly released, the omission was intended as an editorial elimination of surplusage. As explained by Commissioner Hilario G. Davide, Jr. during the Constitutional Commission (ConCom) deliberations, the automatic and regular release of funds **is** the very essence of fiscal autonomy.
2.  **Statutory Recognition in the Administrative Code of 1987:** Book VI, Chapter 1, Section 1(9) of E.O. No. 292 explicitly lists the CHR alongside the Judiciary, Constitutional Commissions, Ombudsman, and LGUs as entities enjoying fiscal autonomy.
3.  **Application of the 1998 GAA Special Provisions:** Under Article XXXIII of R.A. No. 8522, offices enjoying fiscal autonomy are legally authorized to formulate organizational structures, create new positions, and utilize Personal Services savings to fund reorganizations.
4.  **CFAG Membership & Executive Concessions:** The CHR is an acknowledged member of the Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy Group (CFAG) and should enjoy parity with other constitutional entities, consistent with Presidential Administrative Order No. 137 conferring equivalent benefits.
B. Petitioner CHREA's Arguments (Opposition)
**Main Thesis:** The Supreme Court's November 25, 2004 Decision must be maintained. The CHR lacks broad constitutional fiscal autonomy, and even if it enjoyed an aspect of fiscal autonomy, it remains subordinate to the Salary Standardization Law administered exclusively by the DBM.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Strict Separation of Constitutional Commissions:** The CHR is created under Article XIII (Social Justice and Human Rights), not Article IX (Constitutional Commissions). It cannot claim the systemic, structural prerogatives of the CSC, COMELEC, or COA.
2.  **Mandatory Submission to R.A. No. 6758:** The DBM is the sole executive agency tasked by law with administering the Unified Position Classification and Compensation System. No government agency, even one enjoying fiscal autonomy, can bypass DBM authorization to create offices or reclassify positions in contravention of national standards.
3.  **Affirmance of CSC-NCR and DBM:** The CSC-NCR correctly recognized that appointments premised on disapproved, unstandardized reclassifications are legally defective and must be rejected.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) is invested with full constitutional fiscal autonomy under the 1987 Constitution and the Administrative Code of 1987.
2.  **[Secondary Statutory / Administrative Issue]** Whether or not the approval of the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) is a mandatory condition precedent for the implementation of the CHR's position upgrading, reclassification, creation, and collapsing scheme under the Compensation Standardization Law (R.A. No. 6758) and the General Appropriations Act.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Whether or not the CHR enjoys full constitutional fiscal autonomy.
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The CHR does not possess broad, full-scale fiscal autonomy; under both the 1987 Constitution and the Administrative Code of 1987, it enjoys only a **limited** fiscal autonomy restricted exclusively to the automatic and regular release of its approved annual appropriations.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Strict Constitutional Text Analysis:** The 1987 Constitution explicitly guarantees fiscal autonomy using a two-sentence formula to only three classes of institutions: the Judiciary (Art. VIII, Sec. 3), the Constitutional Commissions (Art. IX-A, Sec. 5), and the Office of the Ombudsman (Art. XI, Sec. 14). Each provision explicitly dictates that the entity **"shall enjoy fiscal autonomy"** followed by the rule of automatic and regular release. By contrast, the CHR’s creation under Article XIII, Section 17(4) entirely omits the affirmative clause granting fiscal autonomy, retaining **only** the operational mandate: **"The approved annual appropriations of the Commission shall be automatically and regularly released."**
2.  **ConCom Intent and Surplusage Myth:** A comprehensive reading of the 1986 Constitutional Commission records shows that Commissioner Davide's remark on "surplusage" did not mean full fiscal autonomy was implicitly granted. Rather, the ConCom determined that **"the autonomy actually intended is the automatic release of these appropriations."** When Commissioner Guingona inquired whether the CHR would have budgetary prioritization like education, Commissioner Bengzon clarified: **"It only refers to the release which should be automatic and regular."** The ConCom consciously withheld full-spectrum fiscal powers from an investigative, recommendatory body.
3.  **The Bengzon v. Drilon Benchmark:** Full fiscal autonomy contemplates **"a guarantee of full flexibility to allocate and utilize their resources with the wisdom and dispatch that their needs require,"** encompassing the power to levy fees, adjust compensation scales, and direct fund utilization without outside control. In **Bengzon v. Drilon**, the **En Banc** recognized this extensive independence only for the Judiciary, CSC, COA, COMELEC, and Ombudsman. The CHR was conspicuously omitted.
4.  **CFAG Estoppel:** CFAG Joint Resolution No. 49 (signed by the CHR Chairperson) itself declared that fiscal autonomy **"does not mean mere automatic and regular release"** but encompasses budget preparation, fund flexibility, and use of savings. The CHR cannot contradict its own signed joint resolution by arguing that automatic release equates to complete fiscal autonomy.
5.  **Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius:** The express textual enumeration of entities granted broad fiscal autonomy implies the exclusion of all others.
6.  **Reconciling the Administrative Code:** Book VI, Section 1(9) of E.O. No. 292, listing the CHR as enjoying fiscal autonomy, is merely a general budgetary policy statement that must be reconciled with Book V, Section 6, which specifically labels the CHR's section as "Annual Appropriations" rather than "Fiscal Autonomy," and confines it to automatic release. General provisions cannot expand a limited constitutional grant.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Consequently, this Court concludes that the 1987 Constitution extends to respondent a certain degree of fiscal autonomy through the privilege of having its approved annual appropriations released automatically and regularly. However, it withholds from respondent fiscal autonomy, in its broad or extensive sense, as granted to the Judiciary, constitutional commissions, and the Office of the Ombudsman. Operative herein is the rule of statutory construction, **expressio unius est exclusio alterius**..." (528 Phil. 658, 672)
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The CHR is an independent office, but it is not a Chapter IX Constitutional Commission or a co-equal branch. The framers intentionally gave the CHR only the protection of having its budget automatically released to prevent executive strangulation, while denying it the broad fiscal autonomy (budget preparation, item creation, and absolute internal spending discretion) granted to the Courts, the Ombudsman, and the Constitutional Commissions.
Issue 2: Whether or not the implementation of CHR’s staffing reclassification scheme is subject to prior DBM approval.
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Regardless of the degree of fiscal autonomy enjoyed, any reclassification, upgrading, or organizational modification in the CHR must strictly conform to the Compensation Standardization Law (R.A. No. 6758) and requires prior DBM approval.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Universality of the Salary Standardization Law:** Even constitutional entities clothed with broad, express fiscal autonomy (such as the Judiciary) are not exempt from R.A. No. 6758. The 1998 GAA special provisions themselves explicitly subject fiscally autonomous offices to the condition that **"the implementation hereof shall be in accordance with salary rates, allowances and other benefits authorized under compensation standardization laws."** If the Judiciary must submit its reclassification and allowance schemes to DBM parameters (as reflected in R.A. No. 9227 and Joint Circular 2004-1), the CHR cannot assert superior immunity.
2.  **Exclusive DBM Jurisdiction:** Congress delegated the administration of the unified position classification system strictly to the DBM. Bypassing DBM oversight imperils the core public policy of R.A. No. 6758—"providing equal pay for substantially equal work."
3.  **Violation of GAA General Provisions:** Under Section 78 of the 1998 GAA General Provisions, no new organizational units or key position modifications may be authorized without a statutory mandate or presidential directive. The CHR attempted to unilaterally elevate divisions into services/bureaus and reclassify field Attorney VI (SG-26) items into Director IV (SG-28) positions without changing substantive duties, and sought to establish new units (Finance Management Office and Public Affairs Office) without legal foundation.
4.  **Binding Weight of Administrative Expertise:** Courts accord great respect and deference to the specialized technical judgment of administrative bodies like the DBM on national budgetary standards, and will not disturb the Budget Secretary’s findings absent grave abuse of discretion.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Being a member of the fiscal autonomy group does not vest the agency with the authority to reclassify, upgrade, and create positions without approval of the DBM. While the members of the Group are authorized to formulate and implement the organizational structures of their respective offices and determine the compensation of their personnel, such authority is not absolute and must be exercised within the parameters of the Unified Position Classification and Compensation System established under RA 6758... If the judiciary, a co-equal branch of government, which was expressly granted by the Constitution with fiscal autonomy, is required to conform to the Salary Standardization Law and is subject to the scrutiny of the DBM, sagaciously, the respondent cannot be deemed to enjoy a better position than the Judiciary." (528 Phil. 658, 674-675)
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Fiscal autonomy is not a blank check to ignore the Salary Standardization Law. Because Congress vested the DBM with the exclusive authority to maintain uniformity across government salary grades, every agency—even the Supreme Court—must operate within DBM-administered classification rules. Therefore, the CHR’s unilateral internal resolutions creating and upgrading plantilla positions without DBM evaluation are legally void.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → k. Fiscal autonomy
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
To claim **Broad Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy** (as enunciated in **Bengzon v. Drilon**), an entity must satisfy two constitutional criteria:
1.  **Express Constitutional Designation:** The organic text must positively enact the command clause: **"The [Entity] shall enjoy fiscal autonomy."**
 Applied to CHR: **ABSENT.** Found only in Art. VIII, Sec. 3 (Judiciary), Art. IX-A, Sec. 5 (Constitutional Commissions), and Art. XI, Sec. 14 (Ombudsman). Omitted in Art. XIII, Sec. 17(4).
2.  **Full Operational Flexibility:** The agency must possess independent legal power to formulate budget policies, use savings without collateral legislative restrictions, levy fees, and establish compensation outside ordinary executive oversight.
 Applied to CHR: **ABSENT.** CHR is restricted to **Limited Fiscal Autonomy**, extending solely to the automatic and regular disbursement of approved funds.
3.  Exemption from Compensation Standardization (Salary Standardization Law):
 Applied to CHR: **ABSENT ACROSS ALL BRANCHES.** Even broad fiscal autonomy does not exempt an agency from R.A. No. 6758 or DBM classification standards.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Fiscal Autonomy (Broad vs. Limited): Full flexibility of resource allocation vs. mere automatic/regular release of appropriations.
 Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius: The express mention of one thing implies the exclusion of others.
 Automatic and Regular Release: The narrow financial guarantee designed to prevent the Executive from withholding approved congressional appropriations.
 Surplusage: The rejected defense argument that the express grant of fiscal autonomy was omitted from the Constitution merely because it was repetitive of automatic release.
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 Executive Power Exercised: The DBM Secretary's statutory power to enforce uniform classification and compensation standards under R.A. No. 6758 and the GAA.
 Structural Check Invoked: Independent institutional status under Article XIII, Section 17; asserted fiscal autonomy; and CFAG membership.
 Judicial Ruling: Executive control over position classification and budgetary execution prevails where the Constitution provides only limited fiscal autonomy (automatic release), keeping the entity bound to statutory compensation systems.
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
 Statutory and Constitutional Harmonization:** The Court scrutinized the organic text alongside the ConCom records, applying statutory construction (**expressio unius est exclusio alterius and holistic harmonious construction) to demarcate the precise boundaries of fiscal autonomy.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"Professor, this case falls under **Fiscal Autonomy** because it defines the boundary between **broad** fiscal autonomy and **limited** fiscal autonomy. The Supreme Court held that the CHR possesses only limited fiscal autonomy, meaning it is strictly entitled to the automatic and regular release of its approved appropriations, but lacks the broad flexibility to independently reorganize, upgrade, or create plantilla items. Furthermore, the Court established that even bodies with fiscal autonomy—including the Judiciary—remain subject to the Salary Standardization Law, making DBM approval a mandatory condition precedent to implementing any reclassification scheme."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:** No separate opinions filed.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the Motion for Reconsideration is PARTIALLY GRANTED. The assailed decision of this Court dated 25 November 2004 is hereby MODIFIED, declaring the respondent CHR as a constitutional body enjoying limited fiscal autonomy, in the sense that it is entitled to the automatic and regular release of its approved annual appropriations; nonetheless, it is still required to conform to the Salary Standardization Law. Accordingly, its entire reclassification scheme remains subject to the approval of the DBM. No pronouncement as to costs.
SO ORDERED." (528 Phil. 658, 676)
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The CHR’s Motion for Reconsideration was partially granted only to clarify its constitutional classification: the Court modified its earlier Decision by recognizing that the CHR enjoys **limited** fiscal autonomy (the automatic and regular release of funds). However, the substantive outcome remained unchanged—the CHREA prevailed, the CHR’s unilateral position reclassifications remained disallowed, and the requirement of prior DBM approval was reaffirmed in full.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Bengzon v. Drilon (The Judicial Fiscal Autonomy and Retirement Pension Veto Case)
**Full Official Caption:** Cesar Bengzon, Querube Makalintal, Lino M. Patajo, Jose Leuterio, et al., Petitioners, vs. Hon. Franklin N. Drilon, in his capacity as Executive Secretary, Hon. Guillermo Carague, in his capacity as Secretary of Department of Budget and Management, and Hon. Rosalinda Cajucom, in her capacity as National Treasurer, Respondents; consolidated with A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA, Request of Retired Justices Manuel P. Barcelona, Juan P. Enriquez, Juan O. Reyes, Jr. and Guardson R. Lood for Readjustment of their Monthly Pension.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 103524 / A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA; April 15, 1992; 208 SCRA 133; En Banc; Gutierrez, Jr., **J.** Voting: Narvasa, **C.J.**, Melencio-Herrera, Cruz, Paras, Feliciano, Padilla, Bidin, Griño-Aquino, Medialdea, Regalado, Davide, Jr., Romero, and Nocon, **JJ.**, concur; Bellosillo, **J.**, on leave.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Cesar Bengzon, Querube Makalintal, Lino M. Patajo, Jose Leuterio, Manuel P. Barcelona, Juan P. Enriquez, Juan O. Reyes, Jr., Guardson R. Lood, et al. (Petitioners):** Retired Chief Justices and Associate Justices of the Supreme Court and Court of Appeals claiming adjusted monthly retirement pensions.
**Hon. Franklin N. Drilon (Respondent):** Executive Secretary, sued in his official capacity as head of the Executive office implementing budget vetoes.
**Hon. Guillermo Carague (Respondent):** Secretary of the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), responsible for executing appropriations, allotments, and fund releases.
**Hon. Rosalinda Cajucom (Respondent):** National Treasurer of the Philippines, charged with the custody and disbursement of public funds.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petitioners filed an original petition for **certiorari** and prohibition directly with the Supreme Court challenging the constitutionality of the President's veto of specific lines and provisions in the General Appropriations Act (GAA) for Fiscal Year 1992 (House Bill No. 34925 / Republic Act No. 7180) relating to the payment of adjusted pensions to retired Justices. This was consolidated with Administrative Matter No. 91-8-225-CA, wherein the Court had previously resolved on November 28, 1991 to adjust the pensions of retired Court of Appeals Justices pursuant to Republic Act No. 1797.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Fiscal Autonomy (Article VIII, Section 3)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Constitutional Law I → The Legislative Department → Executive Approval and Item-Veto Power (Article VI, Section 27[2]) → Augmentation from Savings (Article VI, Section 25[5])
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provision(s):**
**Article VIII, Section 3, 1987 Constitution of the Philippines:**
"Sec. 3. **The Judiciary shall enjoy fiscal autonomy. Appropriations for the Judiciary may not be reduced by the legislature below the amount appropriated for the previous year and, after approval, shall be automatically and regularly released.**"
**Article VI, Section 27(2), 1987 Constitution of the Philippines:**
"Sec. 27. (2) **The President shall have the power to veto any particular item or items in an appropriation, revenue, or tariff bill, but the veto shall not affect the item or items to which he does not object.**"
**Article VI, Section 25(5), 1987 Constitution of the Philippines:**
"Sec. 25. (5) **No law shall be passed authorizing any transfer of appropriations; however, the President, the President of the Senate, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and the heads of Constitutional Commissions may, by law, be authorized to augment any item in the general appropriations law for their respective offices from savings in other items of their respective appropriations.**"
**Factual Trigger:**
President Corazon C. Aquino exercised her line-item veto power on January 15, 1992 to strike down specific special provisions and lines in the 1992 General Appropriations Act (HB 34925) that authorized the Chief Justice and the Presiding Justice of the Court of Appeals to use operational savings to augment funds for paying adjusted retirement pensions to retired appellate Justices under Republic Act No. 1797 and the Supreme Court’s Resolution in A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**June 20, 1953:** Congress enacts Republic Act No. 910, establishing retirement pensions for Justices of the Supreme Court and Court of Appeals who render at least 20 years of government service (at least partly in the judiciary) and reach age 70 or resign due to incapacity.
**June 21, 1957:** Congress approves Republic Act No. 1797, inserting Section 3-A into RA 910, providing an automatic readjustment feature: whenever the salary of an active Justice is increased or decreased, such change shall automatically apply to the pension of retired Justices.
**November 12, 1974:** President Ferdinand E. Marcos promulgates Presidential Decree No. 578 on Armed Forces Loyalty Day, extending the automatic readjustment benefits of RA 1797 to members of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP).
**January 25, 1975:** President Marcos issues Presidential Decree No. 644, purporting to repeal Section 3-A of RA 1797, RA 3595, and PD 578, abolishing the automatic salary-linked pension adjustment for retired Justices, Constitutional Commissioners, and the military. The decree bears the notation "NOT FOR PUBLICATION."
**June 11, 1978 – September 10, 1979:** Under Presidential Decree No. 1638 and Presidential Decree No. 1909, President Marcos restores the automatic pension readjustment privileges for tens of thousands of retired military officers and enlisted men, but omits restoring the privilege for retired Justices.
**1990:** Congress passes House Bill No. 16297 and Senate Bill No. 740 to reenact RA 1797 and RA 3595, under the erroneous belief that PD 644 had validly repealed them. The explanatory note highlights that former Chief Justices and Justices are receiving meager monthly pensions (e.g., ₱3,333.33 and ₱2,666.66) eroded by inflation.
**July 11, 1990:** President Corazon C. Aquino vetoes HB 16297, asserting it undermines the standardization of compensation under the Salary Standardization Law (RA 6758) and grants preferential treatment to a select group of officials.
**April 22, 1991:** Retired Court of Appeals Justices Manuel P. Barcelona, Juan P. Enriquez, Juan O. Reyes, Jr., and Guardson R. Lood submit a letter-petition (docketed as A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA) to the Supreme Court requesting readjustment of their monthly pensions under RA 1797. They prove through the National Printing Office that PD 644 was unpublished until an unannounced, back-dated April 4, 1977 Supplement to the Official Gazette was released on September 5, 1983, rendering PD 644 void under **Tañada v. Tuvera**.
**November 28, 1991:** The Supreme Court En Banc issues a Resolution in A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA granting the retired Justices' request. The Court rules definitively that PD 644 never became law for lack of valid publication, meaning RA 1797 was never repealed and remains effective law.
**December 1991:** In the General Appropriations Bill for FY 1992 (HB 34925), Congress includes specific appropriations, operational savings augmentation provisions, and funding authorizations under the Judiciary budget and General Fund Adjustments to implement the adjusted pensions mandated by RA 1797 and A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA.
**January 15, 1992:** President Aquino signs the 1992 General Appropriations Act but issues a Veto Message expressly striking down:
1. Special Provision 1 (underlined clause on savings augmentation) and Special Provision 4 (entirety) of the Supreme Court and Lower Courts budget;
2. Special Provision 1 (underlined clause on savings augmentation) and Special Provision 2 (entirety) of the Court of Appeals budget; and
3. Special Provision 1.3 (underlined phrase mentioning A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA) of the General Fund Adjustments. The President argues that Congress circumvented her 1990 veto of HB 16297.
**February 14, 1992:** The Supreme Court resolves to consolidate A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA with the newly filed petition for **certiorari** (G.R. No. 103524) initiated by retired Chief Justices Cesar Bengzon and Querube Makalintal, et al.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments:
**Main Thesis:** The President’s veto of the special provisions in the 1992 GAA is unconstitutional and void because it is not an item veto, violates separation of powers, infringes on judicial fiscal autonomy, and deprives retired Justices of vested statutory rights.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Improper Item Veto:** The President did not veto an "item" (an indivisible sum of money appropriated for a stated purpose), but rather chopped up provisions, methods, and conditions regarding fund utilization and savings augmentation.
2.  **Violation of Separation of Powers:** The Executive cannot use the veto power to overrule or set aside the final and executory judgment of the Supreme Court in A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA, nor can the Executive unilaterally repeal RA 1797, which has been in force since 1957.
3.  **Infringement on Fiscal Autonomy:** Under Article VIII, Section 3 and Article VI, Section 25(5), the Chief Justice has the constitutional prerogative to use savings to augment deficits within the Judiciary. Denying this power subjects the Judiciary to unlawful Executive micromanagement and control by the DBM.
4.  **Impairment of Vested Rights:** Having rendered long service to the State and retired under the provisions of RA 910/RA 1797, the retired Justices possess a vested property right to their adjusted pensions that cannot be arbitrarily withdrawn.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Office of the Solicitor General):
**Main Thesis:** The Presidential veto of the questioned portions of the 1992 GAA was a valid exercise of the constitutional line-item veto power designed to prevent the subversion of national salary standardization policies.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Valid Exercise of Item Veto:** The Executive possessed the power to excise the specific legislative authorizations because they effectively nullified the President's prior July 11, 1990 veto of HB 16297.
2.  **Protection of Salary Standardization:** The provisions violate the policy of the Compensation and Position Classification Act of 1989 (RA 6758) by granting preferential, distinct pension privileges to a select group of officials over ordinary civil servants.
3.  **Misuse of Public Funds for Private Persons:** Paying adjusted pensions to retired Justices amounts to taxing citizens to bestow funds on favored private individuals who no longer render public service, which the OSG argued constitutes "robbery... done under the forms of law" citing **Citizen's Savings and Loan Association v. Topeka**.
4.  **DBM Administrative Control:** The DBM's oversight, work-and-financial plans, and allotment releases over constitutional bodies are legitimate exercises of executive administration over the expenditure of national funds.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the Executive's veto of the subject special provisions in the General Appropriations Act of 1992 constitutes a valid item veto under Section 27(2), Article VI of the Constitution.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Presidential veto impairs the constitutional guarantee of fiscal autonomy granted to the Judiciary under Article VIII, Section 3 and the Chief Justice's authority to augment appropriations from savings under Article VI, Section 25(5) of the Constitution.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the Executive veto violates the doctrine of separation of powers by attempting to repeal Republic Act No. 1797 and reverse a final and executory judgment of the Supreme Court.
4.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not retired Justices have a vested right to the automatic readjustment of their pensions under Republic Act No. 1797.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Validity of the Line-Item Veto
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the Executive's veto was a valid exercise of the item-veto power under Section 27(2), Article VI of the Constitution?
**NO.** The veto was unconstitutional because it excised mere **provisions** and conditions rather than severable, indivisible **items** of appropriation, effectively attempting to edit legislation.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Rule on Executive Veto:** Under the Constitution, the Executive must generally veto a bill in its entirety or approve it. The President cannot act as an editor crossing out specific lines or paragraphs. The sole exception is in appropriation, revenue, or tariff bills under Article VI, Section 27(2), which permits an "item veto" to avoid legislative riders.
2.  **Definition of "Item" vs. "Provision":** An **item** refers to an indivisible sum of money dedicated to a stated purpose; it is a specific appropriation of money. A **provision**, on the other hand, is a general rule, method, condition, or limitation placed by Congress upon fund utilization.
3.  **Application to the Vetoed Measures:** The President did not veto the indivisible appropriations themselves (such as the ₱500,000,000.00 General Fund Adjustment or the general lump-sum appropriations for the Judiciary). Instead, the President unconstitutionally chopped up the sections, vetoing only the **provisions** detailing how savings could be transferred by the Chief Justice or how obligations recognized by court decisions could be drawn. The augmentation mechanism is a provision granting authority, not a specific appropriation of money.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The terms **item** and **provision** in budgetary legislation and practice are concededly different. An **item** in a bill refers to the particulars, the details, the distinct and severable parts... of the bill... It is an indivisible sum of money dedicated to a stated purpose... The power to disapprove any item or items in an appropriate bill does not grant the authority to veto a part of an item and to approve the remaining portion of the same item."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The President cannot pick up a pen and cross out particular sentences or operational guidelines in a budget bill while leaving the money intact. The line-item veto only applies to distinct, specific sums of money allocated for a singular purpose. By striking down the guidelines authorizing the Chief Justice to use savings for pension adjustments without vetoing the overall appropriation, the President acted as an unconstitutional editor of congressional legislation.
Issue 2: Impairment of Fiscal Autonomy and Augmentation Power
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the Presidential veto impairs the constitutional guarantee of fiscal autonomy of the Judiciary and the Chief Justice's power to augment appropriations from savings?
**YES.** By dictating how judicial appropriations and internal savings should be utilized, the Executive encroached upon the Judiciary's constitutionally protected fiscal autonomy and negated the Chief Justice's constitutional augmentation authority under Article VI, Section 25(5).
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **The Concept of Fiscal Autonomy:** Under Article VIII, Section 3, the Judiciary is guaranteed fiscal autonomy, which contemplates full flexibility to allocate and utilize resources with wisdom and dispatch according to its own needs, completely free from outside control or executive micromanagement.
2.  **DBM's Unconstitutional Practices:** The Court observed that the DBM has historically undermined fiscal autonomy by severely pruning judicial proposals, altering budgets without notice, requiring the Judiciary to defend altered proposals before Congress, and imposing tight bureaucratic controls (such as Monthly Allotments, Notices of Cash Allocation, and Work and Financial Plans) that force the Chief Justice to make "pilgrimages to DBM for additional funds."
3.  **Augmentation from Savings:** Under Article VI, Section 25(5) and **Gonzales v. Macaraig**, the Chief Justice is explicitly empowered by the Constitution to augment any item in the Judiciary’s appropriations from operational savings. The vetoed provisions in the 1992 GAA merely confirmed this constitutional power. By vetoing the clause allowing the Chief Justice to use savings to pay pension adjustments, the President unconstitutionally withheld the Chief Justice’s authority to manage the internal funds of the co-equal Judicial department.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Fiscal autonomy means freedom from outside control... The imposition of restrictions and constraints on the manner the independent constitutional offices allocate and utilize the funds appropriated for their operations is anathema to fiscal autonomy and violative not only of the express mandate of the Constitution but especially as regards the Supreme Court, of the independence and separation of powers upon which the entire fabric of our constitutional system is based... The veto impairs the power of the Chief Justice to augment other items in the Judiciary's appropriation, in contravention of the constitutional provision on 'fiscal autonomy.'"
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Fiscal autonomy gives the Supreme Court total independence to spend its congressionally approved budget without executive interference. Once Congress passes the Judiciary's budget, the Executive (via the President or DBM) cannot dictate which judicial programs get funded or prevent the Chief Justice from moving operational savings from one item to cover shortages in another. The President's veto directly trampled on this constitutional independence.
Issue 3: Violation of Separation of Powers (Repeal of Laws and Reversal of SC Decisions)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the Presidential veto violated separation of powers by attempting to set aside a final judgment of the Supreme Court and repeal Republic Act No. 1797?
**YES.** The President possesses no constitutional authority to overrule an executory decision of the Supreme Court or to repeal a substantive statute enacted by Congress decades earlier through the expedient of an appropriations veto.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Invalidity of PD 644:** Under **Tañada v. Tuvera**, unpublished presidential decrees have no binding legal effect. Presidential Decree No. 644 (which purported to repeal RA 1797) was intentionally hidden as a secret decree marked "NOT FOR PUBLICATION" and was only published in a back-dated Gazette in 1983 in bad faith. PD 644 never became law.
2.  **Subsistence of RA 1797:** Because PD 644 was void **ab initio**, Section 3-A of RA 1797 was never repealed. It has remained continuous, valid, and subsisting law since 1957. Funds necessary to pay statutory retirement pensions are deemed automatically appropriated.
3.  **Finality of A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA:** In its Resolution of November 28, 1991, the Supreme Court definitively adjudicated that RA 1797 remains effective and ordered the payment of adjusted pensions. This was a binding judicial decision.
4.  **Limits of Executive Power:** Under the separation of powers, the Executive cannot act as a court of review to set aside an executory judgment of the Supreme Court. Nor can the President use the veto power in 1992 to repeal a 1957 statute. Vetoing the budget provisions that recognized these rights was an ultra vires arrogation of judicial and legislative authority.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"We need no lengthy justifications or citations of authorities to declare that no President may veto the provisions of a law enacted thirty-five (35) years before his or her term of office. Neither may the President set aside or reverse a final and executory judgment of this Court through the exercise of the veto power... The Executive has no authority to set aside and overrule a decision of the Supreme Court."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The President only enforces the law; the Supreme Court interprets it. The Court conclusively ruled in A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA that PD 644 was void for lack of publication and that RA 1797 is alive and kicking. The President cannot use a line-item veto in an annual budget to circumvent or nullify that final judicial decision, nor can she use it to repeal a 35-year-old law passed by Congress.
Issue 4: Vested Rights of Retirees
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not retired Justices have a vested property right to their adjusted retirement pensions under Republic Act No. 1797?
**YES.** Once a Justice satisfies all statutory prerequisites for retirement, the right to the retirement pension becomes vested and cannot be revoked, diminished, or impaired by the State.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Nature of Pension Rights:** A public retirement pension is founded on long service rendered to the State. When a judicial officer meets all legal conditions under RA 910/1797 (20 years of service, reaching age 70 or disability), the pension transforms from an expectancy into a vested property right protected by due process.
2.  **Constitutional Rationale for Judicial Protections:** Judicial pensions are not arbitrary privileges; they form part of the constitutional fabric safeguarding judicial independence (alongside non-diminution of salary, security of tenure until age 70, impeachment protection, and fiscal autonomy). An independent judiciary cannot exist if judges fear poverty in their old age after rendering public service.
3.  **Refutation of the OSG's "Robbery" Contention:** The OSG’s argument—that giving pensions to retired judges who lead private lives is "robbery under the forms of law" based on the 1874 US case **Loan Association v. Topeka**—was severely rebuked by the Court. The OSG misquoted the case title, misinterpreted an irrelevant municipal bond case, and ignored modern social justice principles. Liberal construction must always favor the retiree.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Where a judge has complied with the statutory prerequisite for retirement with pay, his right to retire and draw salary becomes vested and may not, thereafter, be revoked or impaired... All that the retirees ask is to be given the benefits granted by law. To characterize them as engaging in 'robbery' is intemperate, abrasive, and disrespectful more so because the argument is unfounded."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
When Justices retire after decades of dedicated service, their pension is not a charitable handout—it is a vested property right guaranteed by law to preserve judicial independence. The government cannot arbitrarily refuse to pay these adjusted benefits once the statutory retirement requirements have been met.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Fiscal Autonomy (Article VIII, Section 3)
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy):**
1.  **Full Flexibility in Resource Allocation:** The Judiciary possesses exclusive authority to allocate and utilize its financial resources without outside administrative interference. (Trigger: DBM attempted to dictate spending priorities and scrutinize court expenditures).
2.  **Non-Diminution of Budget:** The Legislature cannot reduce appropriations for the Judiciary below the amount appropriated for the previous year. (Acknowledged as a core structural bar).
3.  **Automatic and Regular Release:** Upon approval of the GAA, funds appropriated for the Judiciary must be released automatically and regularly, without requiring the Court to request allotments or submit to DBM cash allocation ceilings. (Trigger: DBM forced the Court to submit monthly allotment requests and work plans).
4.  **Constitutional Augmentation from Savings:** The Chief Justice possesses the explicit constitutional prerogative under Art. VI, Sec. 25(5) to use operational savings to augment any deficiency in any item within the Judiciary's budget. (Trigger: President vetoed the Chief Justice's authority to use savings for pension adjustments).
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Fiscal Autonomy (guarantee of full flexibility to allocate and utilize resources free from outside control)
 Item Veto vs. Provision Veto (an item is an indivisible sum of money for a specified purpose, not a general provision or condition)
 Executive Overreaching / Encroachment (transgression of separation of powers)
 Vested Right (property right accrued upon fulfillment of statutory retirement criteria)
 Automatic and Regular Release (constitutional mandate precluding executive withholding or conditioning of funds)
 Ultra Vires Veto (veto striking down a prior substantive statute or a final judicial judgment)
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
**Bengzon v. Drilon** is the landmark case defining Judicial Fiscal Autonomy under Article VIII, Section 3. The Court held that fiscal autonomy guarantees the Judiciary complete freedom from outside executive control and DBM micromanagement, specifically securing the Chief Justice's constitutional power under Article VI, Section 25(5) to augment deficiencies in the Court's appropriations using operational savings. The President's veto of the GAA provisions authorizing the payment of adjusted judicial pensions was declared void because the Executive cannot use the line-item veto to excise budget conditions/provisions, repeal substantive existing laws (RA 1797), or overturn a final and executory Supreme Court judgment.
**Subject-Specific Directive (Constitutional & Political Law Lens):**
 State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation: The Executive exercised its line-item veto power under Article VI, Section 27(2). This was checked by Article VIII, Section 3 (Judicial Fiscal Autonomy), Article VI, Section 25(5) (Augmentation from Savings), and the overarching doctrine of Separation of Powers.
 Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test: The Court applied the **Constitutional Boundary / Separation of Powers Test** (**Angara v. Electoral Commission**), determining whether the Executive acted **ultra vires** by encroaching upon the exclusive domain of the Judiciary and Legislature.
 Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit:
 Actual Case or Controversy: Present; the President's veto directly halted the administrative release of appropriated funds for judicial pensions.
 Locus Standi: Petitioners are retired Justices directly denied their statutory pension adjustments; they have direct personal and substantial injury.
 Ripeness & Lis Mota: Fully ripe; the GAA of 1992 was already signed with the veto in effect, creating an immediate impediment to the implementation of A.M. No. 91-8-225-CA.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed. (All participating Justices concurred fully with the **ponencia** of Gutierrez, Jr., **J.**; Bellosillo, **J.**, was on leave).
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is hereby GRANTED. The questioned veto is SET ASIDE as illegal and unconstitutional. The vetoed provisions of the 1992 Appropriations Act are declared valid and subsisting. The respondents are ordered to automatically and regularly release pursuant to the grant of fiscal autonomy the funds appropriated for the subject pensions as well as the other appropriations for the Judiciary. The resolution in Administrative Matter No. 91-8-225-CA dated November 28, 1991 is likewise ordered to be implemented as promulgated.

SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The retired Justices won completely. The Supreme Court struck down the Presidential veto as unconstitutional and declared the vetoed budget provisions valid and operational. The Executive Secretary, the DBM, and the National Treasurer were ordered to immediately, regularly, and automatically release all funds appropriated for the Judiciary and implement the adjusted pension payments under RA 1797.
