### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: In Re: Cunanan (The Bar Flunkers’ Case)**
**Full Official Caption:** In the Matter of the Petitions for Admission to the Bar of Unsuccessful Candidates of 1946 to 1953; Albino Cunanan et al., Petitioners
**Citation & Metadata:** 94 Phil. 534; En Banc Resolution Promulgated March 18, 1954; Ponente: Diokno, J.
**Voting Breakdown:** Concurring with the main opinion: Bengzon, Montemayor, Jugo, Labrador, Pablo, Padilla, and Reyes, JJ. (Justice Labrador filed an additional concurring/dissenting opinion voting to strike down the entire Act; Chief Justice Paras filed a separate concurring/dissenting opinion voting to uphold the Act in its entirety; two Justices did not take part in voting).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Albino Cunanan et al.:** Petitioners; unsuccessful postwar Philippine Bar candidates (examinations from 1946 to 1953) seeking admission to the Bar under Republic Act No. 972 or via motions for grade reconsideration.
**Juan R. Liwag:** Solicitor General of the Philippines, appearing as amicus curiae/respondent contesting the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 972.
**Congress of the Philippines:** Legislative body that enacted Republic Act No. 972 over the known objections of the Supreme Court.
**Jose M. Aruego, M. H. de Joya, Miguel R. Cornejo, Antonio Enrile Inton, E. Voltaire Garcia, Vicente J. Francisco, Vicente Pelaez, and Buenaventura Evangelista:** Counsel and amici curiae advocating for petitioners and defending the validity of Republic Act No. 972.
**U.P. Women Lawyers’ Circle, Arturo A. Alafriz, Enrique M. Fernando, Vicente Abad Santos, Carlos A. Barrios, Vicente del Rosario, Juan de Blancaflor, Mamerto V. Gonzales, and Roman Ozaeta:** Bar organizations, counsel, and amici curiae arguing against the validity of Republic Act No. 972.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Original ex parte mass and individual petitions filed directly before the Supreme Court by unsuccessful postwar Bar examinees praying for admission to the Bar and permission to take the lawyer's oath pursuant to Republic Act No. 972, joined with pending and resolved motions for grade reconsideration. Entertaining grave doubts regarding the law's validity, the Supreme Court set the petitions for hearing exclusively on the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 972.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Judicial Department → Rule-Making Power of the Supreme Court → Admission to the Practice of Law and Regulation Thereof
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Separation of Powers & Bill of Rights → Equal Protection Clause (Class Legislation) & One-Title-One-Subject Rule
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Historical Constitutional Basis (1935 Philippine Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 13):**
"Sec. 13. **The Supreme Court shall have the power to promulgate rules concerning pleading, practice, and procedure in all courts, and the admission to the practice of law.** Said rules shall be uniform for all courts of the same grade and shall not diminish, increase, or modify substantive rights. The existing laws on pleading, practice, and procedure are hereby repealed as statutes, and are declared Rules of Courts, subject to the power of the Supreme Court to alter and modify the same. **The Congress shall have the power to repeal, alter, or supplement the rules concerning pleading, practice, and procedure, and the admission to the practice of law in the Philippines.**"
**Corresponding Modern Provision (1987 Philippine Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 5, Para. 5):**
"Sec. 5. The Supreme Court shall have the following powers:
...
(5) **Promulgate rules concerning the protection and enforcement of constitutional rights, pleading, practice, and procedure in all courts, the admission to the practice of law, the Integrated Bar, and legal assistance to the underprivileged.** Such rules shall provide a simplified and inexpensive procedure for the speedy disposition of cases, shall be uniform for all courts of the same grade, and shall not diminish, increase, or modify substantive rights. **Rules of procedure of special courts and quasi-judicial bodies shall remain effective unless disapproved by the Supreme Court.**"
**(Note: The 1987 Constitution deleted the congressional power to repeal, alter, or supplement the procedural and admission rules of the Supreme Court, making the judicial rule-making authority plenary and exclusive).**
**Title & Substantive Sections of Republic Act No. 972:**
**AN ACT TO FIX THE PASSING MARKS FOR BAR EXAMINATIONS FROM NINETEEN HUNDRED AND FORTY-SIX UP TO AND INCLUDING NINETEEN HUNDRED AND FIFTY-FIVE.**
**SECTION 1.** Notwithstanding the provisions of section fourteen, Rule numbered one hundred twenty-seven of the Rules of Court, **any bar candidate who obtained a general average of seventy per cent in any bar examinations after July fourth, nineteen hundred and forty-six up to the August nineteen hundred and fifty-one bar examinations; seventy-one per cent in the nineteen hundred and fifty-two bar examinations; seventy-two per cent in the nineteen hundred and fifty-three bar examinations; seventy-three per cent in the nineteen hundred and fifty-four bar examinations; seventy-four per cent in the nineteen hundred and fifty-five bar examinations without a candidate obtaining a grade below fifty per cent in any subject, shall be allowed to take and subscribe the corresponding oath of office as member of the Philippine Bar**: Provided, however, That for the purpose of this Act, any exact one-half or more of a fraction, shall be considered as one and included as part of the next whole number.
**SEC. 2. Any bar candidate who obtained a grade of seventy-five per cent in any subject in any bar examination after July fourth, nineteen hundred and forty-six shall be deemed to have passed in such subject or subjects and such grade or grades shall be included in computing the passing general average that said candidate may obtain in any subsequent examinations that he may take.**
**SEC. 3.** This Act shall take effect upon its approval.
**(Enacted on June 21, 1953, without Executive approval).**
**Factual Trigger:**
Following World War II, the Supreme Court exercised administrative discretion to lower the general Bar passing marks (normally 75% per Rule 127) for certain examination years (1946 to 1949). Unsuccessful candidates whose grades were not reconsidered agitated in Congress, prompting the passage of Republic Act No. 972 (the "Bar Flunkers' Act of 1953"). The statute retroactively lowered passing grades to as low as 69.5% for the 1946–1955 examinations and allowed candidates to permanently credit passed individual subjects indefinitely. Hundreds of flunked candidates immediately petitioned the Supreme Court to mandate their admission and oath-taking under the statute.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**August 1946 – August 1953:** The Supreme Court conducts annual Bar Examinations under Rule 127, Section 14 of the Rules of Court (which sets the passing threshold at a 75% general average without falling below 50% in any subject). Due to post-war adjustments and perceived variations in exam difficulty, the Court exercises its discretion to admit examinees with lower passing marks:
 August & November 1946: Passing grade lowered to 72%;
 1947: Passing grade lowered to 69%;
 1948: Passing grade lowered to 70%;
 1949: Passing grade lowered to 74%;
 1950 to 1953: The Court maintains the 75% passing rule, but exercises discretion by rounding up grades of 74% to 75%. Candidates scoring below these discretionary adjustments are formally rejected and their individual motions for reconsideration are denied.
**May 3, 1951:** Responding to agitation by unsuccessful examinees who claimed unfair discrimination, Congress passes Senate Bill No. 12, seeking to retroactively lower the Bar passing grade to 70% effective July 4, 1946, and to establish an installment/subject-crediting system.
**June 5, 1951:** Upon request of the President for comment, seven Justices of the Supreme Court submit written objections, observing that retroactive lowering of passing marks revokes final judicial resolutions and forces the Court to accept unqualified individuals as court officers.
**June 16, 1951:** President Elpidio Quirino vetoes Senate Bill No. 12, citing class legislation, unconstitutional revocation of final Supreme Court resolutions, and dangerous precedent for other state-regulated professions. Congress does not override the veto.
**1953 (Election Year):** Senator Pablo Angeles David sponsors Senate Bill No. 371, reintroducing the vetoed measure with sliding passing grades (70% to 74%) from 1946 to 1955 and permanent single-subject passing credits. Congress approves the bill.
**June 21, 1953:** The President allows Senate Bill No. 371 to lapse into law without executive signature, becoming Republic Act No. 972.
**Post-June 21, 1953:** Numerous unsuccessful examinees (totaling 604 petitioners, representing a broader group of 1,094 flunked candidates) file mass and individual petitions before the Supreme Court demanding automatic admission to the Philippine Bar and administration of the lawyer's oath under RA 972. Other candidates with pending motions for grade revision invoke RA 972 as an alternative basis for relief.
**July 6 & 11, 1953:** The Supreme Court resolves individual motions for grade reconsideration on their merits without reference to the Act, finding no justification to alter any grades. Doubting the validity of RA 972, the Court sets the matter for oral argument solely on the constitutionality of the statute and invites leading bar associations and jurists as amici curiae.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments (and Amici Curiae supporting the Law)
**Main Thesis:** Republic Act No. 972 is a valid exercise of congressional power under Article VIII, Section 13 of the 1935 Constitution to alter, repeal, and supplement the Rules of Court concerning admission to the Bar; it operates as a valid, benign curative statute.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Express Constitutional Authority: Article VIII, Section 13 explicitly grants Congress concurrent power to repeal, alter, or supplement rules promulgated by the Supreme Court concerning pleading, practice, procedure, and admission to the Bar.
 Nature of Bar Admission: The admission to the Bar is not an exclusive judicial function. The Legislature possesses incidental police power to prescribe qualifications and minimum conditions for the practice of law to protect the public interest.
 Curative Legislation: RA 972 is a legitimate curative statute designed to cure the Court’s arbitrary fluctuations in passing grades (from 69% to 74% between 1946 and 1951) and eliminate unfair discrimination against examinees who took identical or harder exams under severe post-war handicaps (e.g., destroyed libraries, lack of textbooks, post-liberation trauma).
 Valid Classification: The classification of candidates by specific years (1946–1955) is reasonable and germane to the post-war emergency conditions, which are temporary and will normalize by 1956. Pre-war examinees were omitted because pre-war records were destroyed during the war and pre-war conditions were normal.
 Title Sufficiency: The title of the Act broadly encompasses the fixation of passing marks, and the crediting of individual subjects under Section 2 is directly related to computing the general average passing mark.
 Lack of Finality in Bar Adjudications: Supreme Court resolutions denying admission or motions for reconsideration are administrative/regulatory, not final judgments in adversary litigation; hence, no vested private rights are impaired.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Solicitor General, Bar Associations, and Opposing Amici Curiae)
**Main Thesis:** Republic Act No. 972 is an unconstitutional legislative encroachment upon the inherent and primary judicial power of the Supreme Court to admit attorneys to the Bar, constitutes arbitrary class legislation, and violates the constitutional one-subject-one-title mandate.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Inherent Judicial Prerogative: Admission to the Bar has been an exclusively judicial function for more than six centuries in Anglo-American jurisprudence. An attorney is an officer of the court. The power to admit, suspend, disbar, and reinstate belongs inherently and primarily to the judiciary.
 Limits of Congressional Rule-Making: The constitutional power of Congress to "repeal, alter, or supplement" procedural and admission rules is prospective and limited to enacting general norms or minimum standards. It does not empower Congress to act as an examining board, exercise adjudicative discretion, or directly license specific, determinate individuals.
 Legislative Usurpation of Adjudication (Judgment by Statute): By retroactively declaring flunked examinees to have passed and ordering their admission en masse, RA 972 is not a rule of law, but a legislative judgment revoking final Supreme Court resolutions that previously denied admission to those exact candidates.
 Arbitrary Class Legislation: The law violates equal protection. Classifying unsuccessful candidates by sliding percentage brackets year by year (1946–1955) while excluding pre-war candidates and future candidates rests on artificial, non-germane distinctions.
 Public Interest and Injury to the Profession: Enacting a law to lower standards so that confessedly unprepared individuals (over 1,000 flunkers) may practice law poses a grave danger to society, which entrusts life, liberty, honor, and property to attorneys.
 Defective Title: Section 2 of RA 972 introduces a permanent installment/subject-crediting system of indefinite duration, whereas the title strictly limits the Act to fixing passing marks from 1946 to 1955.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Republic Act No. 972 constitutes an unconstitutional legislative encroachment upon the primary and inherent power of the Supreme Court to regulate admission to the practice of law and admit attorneys-at-law.
2.  **[Secondary Issue]** Whether or not Republic Act No. 972 operates as an unconstitutional legislative revocation or reversal of final judicial resolutions/judgments promulgated by the Supreme Court.
3.  **[Secondary Issue]** Whether or not Republic Act No. 972 violates the Equal Protection Clause as arbitrary class legislation.
4.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not Section 2 of Republic Act No. 972 violates the constitutional requirement that a bill shall embrace only one subject which must be expressed in its title.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Legislative Encroachment on Judicial Admission Power
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Republic Act No. 972 encroaches upon the primary, traditional, and inherent constitutional responsibility of the Supreme Court to determine who possesses the requisite qualifications to be admitted to the practice of law.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Six Centuries of Judicial Tradition: The admission, suspension, disbarment, and reinstatement of attorneys have been an exclusively judicial responsibility for over 600 years in Anglo-Saxon jurisprudence, from which the Philippine judicial system is derived. An attorney is an officer and attaché of the court, not a public civil officer.
 Nature of the Admission Function: Admission to the Bar requires: (1) previously established rules and principles, (2) concrete facts affecting determinate individuals, and (3) a judicial determination of whether those facts satisfy the rules. This process is the quintessential exercise of judicial power, requiring ultimate judicial discretion.
 Harmonization of Powers under Art. VIII, Sec. 13: The 1935 Constitution did not grant Congress and the Supreme Court equal or identical responsibilities over Bar admissions. The primary authority resides in the Court. Congress holds merely a concurrent authority to "repeal, alter, or supplement" the general rules.
 General Norms vs. Individual Licensing:** The legislature may examine existing rules and legislate minimum, prospective qualifications to protect the public interest. However, these legislative standards serve only as **minimum conditions beyond which the Court may require higher standards. Congress cannot substitute itself for the Court, dispense with judicial discretion, or directly license determinate individuals whom the Court has found lacking in legal learning and ability.
 Subversion of Public Interest: The declared intent of RA 972 was to admit candidates despite inadequate preparation due to wartime disruption. The Court observed that legal materials were widely available after the war. Passing over 1,000 inadequately prepared candidates into a profession charged with safeguarding life, liberty, and property constitutes a serious societal hazard.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"In the judicial system from which ours has been evolved, the admission, suspension, disbarment and reinstatement of attorneys at law in the practice of the profession and their supervision have been indisputably a judicial function and responsibility. Because of this attribute, its continuous and zealous possession and exercise by the judicial power have been demonstrated during more than six centuries, which certainly 'constitutes the most solid of titles.'"
"Congress may repeal, alter and supplement the rules promulgated by this Court, but the authority and responsibility over the admission, suspension, disbarment and reinstatement of attorneys at law and their supervision remain vested in the Supreme Court. The power to repeal, alter and supplement the rules does not signify nor permit that Congress substitute or take the place of this Tribunal in the exercise of its primary power on the matter. The Constitution does not say nor mean that Congress may admit, suspend, disbar or reinstate directly attorneys at law, or a determinate group of individuals to the practice of law."
**(d) Recitation-Ready Explanation:**
Under the 1935 Constitution, the power to repeal, alter, or supplement rules allows Congress to establish prospective minimum standards for the Bar, but the ultimate power to admit individuals as officers of the court remains exclusively judicial. Congress cannot usurp judicial discretion by enacting a statute that directly admits flunked examinees to the practice of law.
Issue 2: Legislative Usurpation via Revocation of Final Judicial Judgments
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** By retroactively ordering the mass admission of examinees whose petitions for admission and motions for grade reconsideration were previously heard and denied, Republic Act No. 972 acts as a legislative judgment setting aside final judicial action.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Nature of Legislative vs. Judicial Action: Legislation establishes general rules governing future or subsequent transactions. Adjudication determines rights, duties, and qualifications based on past transactions and existing facts.
 Act Operates as a Judgment: In declaring that examinees who obtained 70% from 1946 to 1952 are admitted to the Bar, RA 972 is not an act of rule-making; it is a legislative decree that revokes the prior resolutions promulgated by the Supreme Court denying admission to those specific individuals.
 Curative Theory Rejected: Proponents argued RA 972 was a curative statute intended to remedy the Court's shifting passing grades. The Court countered that Congress was not curing defective rules, but attempting to cure what it perceived as the Court's "defect of judgment" or "lack of will." Only the Supreme Court possesses the constitutional authority to modify or reconsider its own final resolutions.
 Suspension, Not Amendment: By enacting RA 972, Congress did not amend general procedural rules; it suspended the existing rules in order to substitute its own will for the judgment of the Court over past cases.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"In decreeing that bar candidates who obtained in the bar examinations of 1946 to 1952, a general average of 70 per cent without falling below 50 per cent in any subject, be admitted in mass to the practice of law, the disputed law is not a legislation; it is a judgment — a judgment revoking those promulgated by this Court during the aforecited year affecting the bar candidates concerned; and although this Court certainly can revoke these judgments even now, for justifiable reasons, it is no less certain that only this Court, and not the legislative nor executive department, that may be so."
**(d) Recitation-Ready Explanation:**
Congress cannot act as a court of appeals over the Supreme Court. When the Court graded the 1946–1952 examinations and denied the examinees' motions for reconsideration, those resolutions became final judicial determinations. Congress invaded the judicial sphere by enacting a retroactive statute that nullified those final orders and declared the examinees qualified.
Issue 3: Equal Protection and Class Legislation
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Republic Act No. 972 is unconstitutional class legislation because its arbitrary classification of unsuccessful candidates by specific years and sliding grades rests on no substantial distinction germane to the law's purpose.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Requisites of Valid Classification: A legislative classification must: (1) rest on substantial distinctions; (2) be germane to the purpose of the law; (3) not be limited to existing conditions only; and (4) apply equally to all members of the same class.
 Arbitrary Brackets: RA 972 creates arbitrary, sliding passing scores for specific calendar cohorts: 70% (1946–1951), 71% (1952), 72% (1953), 73% (1954), and 74% (1955). There is no reasonable factual basis for treating an examinee scoring 70% in 1951 differently from an examinee scoring 70% in 1952 or 1953.
 Arbitrary Exclusions: The statute completely excludes unsuccessful examinees who took the Bar in 1945, 1944, or pre-war years under identical hardships. The excuse that the Court lost its pre-war records cannot justify granting exclusive privileges to post-war cohorts while denying them to earlier examinees who could prove their grades through secondary evidence.
 Special Privilege: The statute singles out a closed group of unsuccessful examinees to confer a special legislative favor—admission to an elite profession without satisfying standard qualifications.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Republic Act No. 972 is a class legislation. There is no actual nor reasonable basis to classify unsuccessful bar candidates by years nor to exclude those of other years... The proviso is for the sole purpose of bestowing privileges upon certain defined persons."
**(d) Recitation-Ready Explanation:**
The law creates arbitrary privileges by lowering passing marks only for examinees of specific years (1946–1955) using an unjustified sliding scale, while excluding those who failed before 1946. Because legal fitness cannot be determined by an arbitrary calendar cutoff, the law constitutes unconstitutional class legislation.
Issue 4: Defective Title and Subject-Matter Inseparability
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Section 2 of Republic Act No. 972 introduces a permanent, indefinite installment examination system that is not expressed in the title of the Act, rendering Section 2 void, which in turn infects the validity of the whole statute.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Constitutional Mandate (1935 Const., Art. VI, Sec. 21[1]): "No bill which may be enacted into law shall embrace more than one subject which shall be expressed in its title."
 Variance Between Title and Text:** The title of RA 972 is explicitly restricted: **"An Act to Fix the Passing Marks for Bar Examinations from Nineteen Hundred and Forty-Six up to and Including Nineteen Hundred and Fifty-Five." The title promises a temporary, 10-year fix for passing marks.
 Permanent Subject-Crediting Scheme:** In contrast, Section 2 provides that any candidate scoring 75% in any individual subject in any examination after July 4, 1946, shall permanently pass that subject and may credit it toward subsequent examinations **indefinitely. This creates a permanent "installment plan" for the Bar, unlimited in time.
 Grave Policy Flaw: The Court observed that laws and jurisprudence change rapidly. An examinee who passes a subject in 1946 and completes the remaining subjects decades later will be licensed despite being completely ignorant of modern legal developments.
 Inseparability: Because Section 2 is an integral incentive inextricably linked with the legislative compromise in Section 1, its constitutional defect affects the statute as a whole.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"While this law according to its title will have temporary effect only from 1946 to 1955, the text of article 2 establishes a permanent system for an indefinite time. This is contrary to Section 21(1), article VI of the Constitution, which vitiates and annuls article 2 completely; and because it is inseparable from article 1, it is obvious that its nullity affects the entire law."
**(d) Recitation-Ready Explanation:**
The title of RA 972 states that it only fixes passing marks temporarily from 1946 to 1955. However, Section 2 creates a permanent, indefinite system allowing examinees to pass the Bar "on installment" by crediting individual subjects forever. Because this permanent reform is completely hidden from the title, it violates the one-subject-one-title rule.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → Judicial Department → Admission to the Practice of Law and Regulation Thereof
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 Exercised Power: Congressional Legislative Power under Art. VI, Sec. 1 in conjunction with the concurrent rule-amending power under Art. VIII, Sec. 13 (1935 Constitution).
 Constitutional Checks Invoked: Judicial Independence & Separation of Powers (inherent judicial power over court officers); Equal Protection of the Laws (Art. III, Sec. 1); One-Subject-One-Title Mandate (Art. VI, Sec. 21[1]).
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
 Separation of Powers / Rule-Making Test: The Court applied the **Doctrine of Inherent Judicial Powers** and the **Minimum Standards Doctrine**. Under this framework, congressional power over practice and admission is strictly **regulatory, general, and prospective**. Legislative enactments regarding qualifications serve only as **minimum thresholds** that limit the pool available for admission; they cannot compel the judiciary to admit candidates whom the Court deems unqualified.
 Equal Protection Test: Traditional **Rational Basis Review for Valid Classification**. The Court held the classification failed because the temporal distinctions (1946–1951 vs. 1952 vs. 1953–1955) lacked any real or substantial difference related to legal aptitude or the public interest.
**Justiciability & Threshold Audit:**
 Actual Case or Controversy: Satisfied via original petitions for admission filed by candidates asserting statutory rights under RA 972, opposed by the Solicitor General and amicus bar associations representing the public interest.
 Locus Standi: The examinees possessed direct personal interests in seeking admission; the Court permitted broad amicus curiae participation given the transcendental importance of maintaining the integrity of the Bar and the administration of justice.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Valid Exercise of Congressional Power over Bar Admission under 1935 Const.):**
1.  **Nature of Action:** Must repeal, alter, or supplement general rules, NOT decide individual cases or directly admit persons. **(Failed: RA 972 admitted determinate individuals en masse).**
2.  **Temporal Scope:** Must be prospective to govern future conduct, NOT retroactive. **(Failed: RA 972 revoked past judicial resolutions).**
3.  **Standard:** Must prescribe minimum public interest standards to elevate the profession, NOT force the Court to lower standards and admit unqualified persons. **(Failed: RA 972 forced admission of candidates with failing marks).**
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Officer of the court** / **Attaché of the courts
 Judgment by legislation (legislative usurpation of adjudication)
 Most solid of titles (600 years of judicial possession of admission power)
 Installment plan (criticizing individual subject crediting)
 Minimum standards (legislative qualifications limit the class, but do not exhaust the court's power to require more)
 Class legislation
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
**In Re: Cunanan** is the seminal Philippine case delineating the boundary between legislative power and judicial authority over the Bar. The Supreme Court held that while Congress under the 1935 Constitution could amend procedural rules to set **minimum prospective qualifications**, the ultimate power to admit attorneys belongs exclusively to the Court as an inherent judicial function. RA 972 was declared unconstitutional because it operated as a legislative judgment retroactively admitting flunkers, lowering professional standards against public interest, creating arbitrary class legislation, and concealing a permanent subject-crediting scheme under a misleading, temporary title.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Labrador, J. (Concurring and Dissenting):** Voted to declare Republic Act No. 972 **unconstitutional in toto**. He emphasized that the power to determine whether an examinee made the passing grade is strictly judicial and involves non-delegable discretion. Forcing the Court to pass candidates in 1953, 1954, and 1955 with sliding lower marks is an unconstitutional legislative directive that undermines judicial independence and constitutes arbitrary discrimination.
**Paras, C.J. (Concurring and Dissenting):** Voted to declare Republic Act No. 972 **constitutional in its entirety**. He reasoned that under Art. VIII, Sec. 13, Congress and the Supreme Court possess concurrent power over Bar admissions. Bar admission proceedings are administrative rather than adversary litigation, so resolutions denying admission do not constitute untouchable final judgments. Because the Court itself had repeatedly lowered passing marks between 1946 and 1948, Congress acted reasonably within its curative power to eliminate discrimination against postwar candidates.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"Upon mature deliberation by this Court... we, the eight members of the Court who subscribe to this decision have voted and resolved, and have decided for the Court, and under the authority of the same:

1. That (a) the portion of article 1 of Republic Act No. 972 referring to the examinations of 1946 to 1952, and (b) all of article 2 of said law are unconstitutional and, therefore, void and without force and effect.

2. That, for lack of unanimity in the eight Justices, that part of article 1 which refers to the examinations subsequent to the approval of the law, that is from 1953 to 1955 inclusive, is valid and shall continue to be in force, in conformity with section 10, article VII of the Constitution.

Consequently, (1) all the above-mentioned petitions of the candidates who failed in the examinations of 1946 to 1952 inclusive are denied, and (2) all candidates who in the examinations of 1953 obtained a general average of 71.5 per cent or more, without having a grade below 50 per cent in any subject, are considered as having passed, whether they have filed petitions for admission or not. After this decision has become final, they shall be permitted to take and subscribe the corresponding oath of office as members of the Bar on the date or dates that the Chief Justice may set. So ordered."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court struck down the retroactive portion of RA 972 (covering the 1946–1952 Bar examinations) and the entire subject-crediting scheme (Section 2) as unconstitutional, denying the admission petitions of all pre-1953 flunkers. However, because the Court lacked the required two-thirds majority (eight votes) to strike down the prospective portion, Section 1 remained operative for the 1953–1955 examinations, allowing examinees from the 1953 Bar who scored at least 71.5% (with no subject below 50%) to be admitted to the Bar.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: In Re: Social Media Posts of Edgar S. Dizon**
**Full Official Caption:** IN RE: SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS OF EDGAR S. DIZON (Bar Matter No. 4734)
**Citation & Metadata:** B.M. No. 4734; July 15, 2026; **En Banc**; **Per Curiam**.
**Voting Breakdown:** Gesmundo, **C.J.**, Caguioa, Hernando, Lazaro-Javier, Inting, Zalameda, Gaerlan, Rosario, Dimaampao, Marquez, Kho, Jr., Singh, and Villanueva, **JJ.**, concurred. Leonen, **SAJ.**, filed a Separate Concurring Opinion. Lopez, **J.**, was on leave.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Edgar S. Dizon ("Teacher Edgar") [Respondent]:** 2016 Arellano School of Law graduate who passed the 2016 Bar Examinations but whose oath-taking was withheld due to pending murder cases; creator and administrator of the Facebook accounts/pages **Bar Law for Dummies Training Program** and **Tsidkenu Dizon**, through which he conducted commercial coaching for repeat bar examinees.
**Office of the 2023 Bar Chair [Supervising Authority]:** The Supreme Court entity tasked with the administration, technical execution, and integrity of the 2023 digitalized Bar Examinations.
**Office of the Bar Confidant (OBC) [Recommending Arm]:** The administrative office of the Supreme Court that evaluated Dizon’s viral social media posts and recommended the issuance of a show-cause order for indirect contempt.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
This is an original, summary administrative disciplinary and indirect contempt proceeding initiated **motu proprio** by the Supreme Court **En Banc** pursuant to a Show Cause Resolution dated October 24, 2023, following an investigation and recommendation submitted by the Office of the Bar Confidant regarding Dizon's public social media publications concerning the checking of the 2023 Bar Examinations.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Constitutional Law → The Judicial Department → Exclusive Constitutional Power to Regulate Admission to the Practice of Law (1987 Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 5[5]) → Supervision over Bar Examinations and Inherent Contempt Power
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Legal Ethics & Remedial Law → Rule 71 (Contempt) → Section 3(c), (d), and (e) (Indirect Contempt: Unlawful Interference, Degrading the Administration of Justice, and Unauthorized Practice of Law)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article VIII, Section 5, Paragraph 5, 1987 Constitution:**
"SECTION 5. The Supreme Court shall have the following powers:
. . .
(5) **Promulgate rules concerning the protection and enforcement of constitutional rights, pleading, practice, and procedure in all courts, the admission to the practice of law, the Integrated Bar, and legal assistance to the underprivileged.** Such rules shall provide a simplified and inexpensive procedure for the speedy disposition of cases, shall be uniform for all courts of the same grade, and shall not diminish, increase, or modify substantive rights. Rules of procedure of special courts and quasi-judicial bodies shall remain effective unless disapproved by the Supreme Court."
**Rule 71, Section 3(c), (d), and (e), Rules of Court:**
"SEC. 3. **Indirect contempt to be punished after charge and hearing.** — After a charge in writing has been filed, and opportunity given to the respondent to comment thereon within such period as may be fixed by the court and to be heard by himself[/herself] or counsel, a person guilty of any of the following acts may be punished for indirect contempt:
. . .
(c) **Any abuse of or any unlawful interference with the processes or proceedings of a court** not constituting direct contempt under section 1 of this Rule;
(d) **Any improper conduct tending, directly or indirectly, to impede, obstruct, or degrade the administration of justice;**
(e) **Assuming to be an attorney or an officer of a court, and acting as such without authority;**
. . .
But nothing in this section shall be so construed as to prevent the court from issuing process to bring the respondent into court, or from holding him in custody pending such proceedings."
**Sections 2 (para. 3) and 17 (para. 4), A.M. No. 24-10-05-SC (2025 Proposed Amendments to Rule 138 of the Rules of Court):**
Section 2, paragraph 3 / Section 17, paragraph 3:
"**In the Supreme Court's assessment and sole discretion**, considering the gravity of the claim or offense charged, any prior cases filed against the applicant, **and similar reasons**, the Supreme Court may defer the oath-taking of the concerned applicant, **or impose any other preventive measures, as warranted.**"

Section 17, paragraph 4:
"In any case, any false or inaccurate information, concealment or failure to disclose, or misrepresentation on the part of an applicant shall be a ground for either the denial of the application, disqualification from taking the examinations, **or delisting from the list of passers**, depending on the stage of discovery, and without prejudice to other disciplinary sanctions that the Supreme Court may impose."
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):**
On September 21, 2023, during the final preparation phase of the digitalized 2023 Bar Examinations, Edgar S. Dizon published a post on his Facebook pages stating that examinees must start answers with "YES or NO" because **"Yan ang unang hahanapin ng AI Checking to sort out the correct answers."** The post went viral, sparking panic and confusion among examinees, disrupting bar operations by forcing the Court to divert personnel and resources to trace the leak, coordinate with the NBI, and issue a public clarification, culminating in Dizon demanding a 24-hour public apology from the Court and an audience for a photograph with the Bar Chair.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**2016:** Edgar S. Dizon graduates from Arellano School of Law and successfully passes the 2016 Philippine Bar Examinations. His oath-taking is deferred by the Supreme Court due to pending murder charges filed against him.
**Post-2016 to Mid-2023:** Despite not being admitted to the Philippine Bar, Dizon establishes the **Bar Law for Dummies Training Program**, authoring extensive bar review materials across all bar subjects, conducting topical lectures, and coaching examinees who have failed the bar exam more than three times.
**September 21, 2023:** In the final stages of preparations for the 2023 Bar Examinations, Dizon publishes a viral advisory on his Facebook accounts (**Bar Law for Dummies Training Program** and **Tsidkenu Dizon**) instructing examinees: **"ALWAYS START WITH YES or NO Yan ang unang hahanapin ng AI Checking to sort out the correct answers."** The post spreads rapidly, creating anxiety among examinees.
**September 23, 2023:** The Office of the 2023 Bar Chair issues an official Advisory condemning the social media posts as false, baseless, and defamatory, reiterating that the examinations are manually evaluated by four human examiners per subject and that the Court has engaged the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) to probe the administrator behind the posts.
**Post-September 23, 2023:** Dizon refuses to take down the posts. Instead, he grants a media interview threatening the Supreme Court with legal action and demanding an official public apology within 24 hours. Concurrently, Dizon sends multiple emails to the Judiciary Public Assistance Section asserting that the Court's Advisory destroyed his life without hearing his side, insisting that the Court issue a statement rectifying the advisory, and requesting a photo opportunity with the 2023 Bar Chair because **"idol ko po kayo."**
**October 24, 2023:** Upon the evaluation and recommendation of the Office of the Bar Confidant, the Supreme Court **En Banc** issues a Show Cause Resolution ordering Dizon to explain within five working days why he should not be cited for indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(c), (d), and (e) of the Rules of Court.
**March 14, 2024:** Dizon submits his Explanation admitting account ownership and authoring the post, but denying that he claimed artificial intelligence would execute the checking; he further denies engaging in the illegal practice of law by framing his coaching as mere pedagogical guidance on answering techniques.
**July 15, 2026:** The Supreme Court **En Banc** promulgates its **Per Curiam** Decision finding Dizon guilty of indirect contempt, fining him PHP 30,000.00, ordering him delisted from the roll of successful bar examinees, and warning him against the unauthorized practice of law.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondent Edgar S. Dizon’s Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Dizon did not commit indirect contempt or unlawfully interfere with the Bar Examinations, because his post was merely pedagogical coaching advice that was misconstrued; nor did he engage in the illegal practice of law, as his coaching activities merely applied the art of teaching without rendering legal advice on actual cases.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Absence of Misinformation Regarding AI:** He insists he used the phrase "TO HELP" in his posts and never categorically asserted that artificial intelligence would replace human examiners in sorting, checking, or grading the exam answers.
2.  **Pedagogical Nature of Bar Coaching (Non-Practice of Law):** As a holder of a Master’s Degree in Education, he merely identifies learning gaps and coaches examinees on structural presentation and logical drafting styles. He explicitly instructs students to call him "Teacher Edgar" and never "Attorney."
3.  **Absence of Legal Representation on Actual Controversies:** Under paragraph 6(b) of his Explanation, he argued that as a teacher, he does not give legal opinions on actual cases, but merely discusses answers to past bar questions and utilizes his non-wasted legal knowledge to help repeaters pass.
4.  **Chilling Effect and Procedural Injustice:** The Court's public Advisory condemned him without due process (**"Hindi man lang nakuha ang side ko bago nailagay sa Advisory yung pangalan ko"**), causing him severe personal and emotional devastation.
B. The Supreme Court's / Bar Confidant's Findings & Indictments
**Main Thesis:** Dizon’s viral falsehoods directly disrupted the administration of the 2023 Bar Examinations, cast aspersion on the integrity of the judicial admission process, and demonstrated the unauthorized practice of law, compounded by insolent post-incident conduct.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Unlawful Interference with Judicial Process (Rule 71, Sec. 3[c], [d]):** Announcing that AI would check the bar examinations caused panic among examinees and forced the Court to scramble and redirect lean administrative personnel and time toward crisis containment and coordination with law enforcement.
2.  **Res Ipsa Loquitur Rebuttal:** Dizon’s own literal text (**"Yan ang unang hahanapin ng AI Checking to sort out the correct answers"**) refutes his claim that he did not state AI would do the sorting and checking.
3.  **Illegal Practice of Law (Rule 71, Sec. 3[e]):** Coaching bar examinees, lecturing on substantive law doctrines, and authoring bar review summation notes and syllabi-based questions across all bar subjects constitute the practice of law under **Cayetano v. Monsod**. Dizon is a non-lawyer whose admission remains suspended due to pending murder charges.
4.  **Lack of Remorse and Audacity:** Demanding a public apology within 24 hours under threat of suit, refusing to delete the contumacious posts, and trivializing the Court's processes by demanding a photograph with the Bar Chair demonstrate unfitness for membership in the bar.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Edgar S. Dizon is guilty of indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(c) and (d) of the Rules of Court for publishing false claims that the 2023 Bar Examinations would be checked and sorted using artificial intelligence.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Edgar S. Dizon engaged in the unauthorized practice of law, constituting indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(e) of the Rules of Court, by authoring comprehensive bar review materials and conducting substantive coaching classes for bar reviewees.
3.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Supreme Court possesses the constitutional authority to impose the administrative sanction of delisting an applicant from the roll of successful bar examinees on grounds of contumacious conduct and unauthorized practice of law prior to oath-taking.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Liability for Indirect Contempt via Interference with Bar Examinations
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did Dizon’s viral social media post claiming that the 2023 Bar Examinations would be sorted and checked by artificial intelligence constitute indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(c) and (d)?
**YES.** The unauthorized publication of fabricated examination mechanics severely disrupted court administration, eroded public trust in the admission process, and caused acute panic among examinees during a critical phase of judicial operations.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Supervisory Primacy over Bar Admissions:** Pursuant to Article VIII of the Constitution and established doctrine in **In re: Parazo**, the Supreme Court holds plenary, exclusive responsibility over the admission of members to the bar. Because the Court demands high standards of honesty and fair dealing, any insinuation of irregularity or procedural anomaly in the Bar Examinations is imbued with paramount public interest.
2.  **Physical Reality of Examination Evaluation:** Under Bar rules and guidelines (Section 12, A.M. No. 24-10-05-SC), the Committee of Bar Examiners consists of real "warm bodies"—a Supreme Court Justice as Chairperson and expert members of the Philippine Bar. They are not powered, sorted, or guided by artificial intelligence.
3.  **Rejection of the "To Help" Defense via Res Ipsa Loquitur:** Dizon’s claim that he merely indicated AI would "help" is contradicted by the face of his post: **"ALWAYS START WITH YES or NO Yan ang unang hahanapin ng AI Checking to sort out the correct answers."** Under the principle of **res ipsa loquitur**, the text clearly told examinees that an AI system was deployed to sort and evaluate responses.
4.  **Tangible Disruption to the Administration of Justice:** Contempt does not require physical obstruction of a courtroom. Dizon’s posts forced the Office of the 2023 Bar Chair to divert its limited personnel away from execution details to investigate the source, coordinate with the NBI, issue emergency advisories, and handle public panic. This conduct directly impeded, obstructed, and degraded the administration of justice.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"Clearly, Dizon unlawfully interfered in the conduct of the 2023 Bar Examinations, a court-sanctioned activity, by peddling false information and causing alarm and panic among the examinees. His irresponsible and baseless post that the AI will do the sorting and checking undermined the integrity not only of the bar examinations but likewise of the 'Supreme Court itself which has the overall supervision and control over the examinations.'"

"This is **res ipsa logitur**. Dizon clearly and categorically mentioned that the AI will do the checking and sorting of the examinees' answers."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The Supreme Court found Dizon in indirect contempt because his social media posts falsely claimed that AI would grade the 2023 Bar Examinations. This was not harmless advice; it panicked examinees right before exam week and forced the Court to divert personnel to trace the leak, coordinate with law enforcement, and issue emergency clarifications. Because the bar exam is an official judicial proceeding under the Court's exclusive constitutional authority, manufacturing false procedures that erode faith in the grading system directly obstructs the administration of justice.
Issue 2: Unauthorized Practice of Law by a Non-Admitted Bar Passer
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did Dizon engage in the unauthorized practice of law under Rule 71, Section 3(e) by operating his **Bar Law for Dummies Training Program** and authoring specialized legal review modules?
**YES.** Providing instructional bar coaching, analyzing past bar questions, and authoring substantive review outlines for compensation or institutionalized training necessitate the continuous application of legal knowledge and constitute the practice of law, which is forbidden to non-lawyers.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Doctrinal Scope of the Practice of Law:** Under **Cayetano v. Monsod**, the practice of law is not limited to appearing in court or representing clients in litigation. It encompasses "any activity, in or out of court, which requires the application of law, legal procedure, knowledge, training and experience."
2.  **Legal Knowledge Applied in Bar Coaching:** Dizon’s defense that he was merely executing pedagogical techniques as a Master of Education is unavailing. Teaching bar reviewees how to resolve legal problems requires substantive legal analysis.
3.  **Admission against Interest in Pleadings:** In paragraph 6(b) of his own Explanation, Dizon explicitly conceded: **"I only discuss the answers in the past bar questions as part of my coaching job"** and stated **"na hindi [niya] inaksaya ang [kanyang] knowledge of law and skills in coaching and teaching."**
4.  **Substantive Authorship of Legal Compendiums:** Dizon authored over twenty-two comprehensive subject-matter modules (including **BLD Persons and Family Relations**, **Topical Bar Questions and Answers in Remedial Law**, **Summation Pre-Week Notes**, and lectures on affirmative defenses). Preparing specialized legal syntheses necessitates the application of trained legal intellect, which Dizon had no legal authority to practice given that his oath-taking was held in abeyance.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"'Practice of law means any activity, in or out of court, which requires the application of law, legal procedure, knowledge, training and experience.' . . . Discussing past bar examination answers definitely requires an application of legal knowledge. Interestingly, Dizon himself admitted 'na hindi [niya] inaksaya ang [kanyang] knowledge of law and skills in coaching and teaching.'"

"The preparation of all these materials required the application of legal knowledge. Thus, there can be no conclusion other than that Dizon illegally engaged in the practice of law. Thus, for engaging in the unauthorized practice of law, Dizon is similarly guilty of indirect contempt."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Passing the bar exam does not make someone a lawyer; oath-taking and signing the Roll of Attorneys are mandatory prerequisites. Because Dizon never took the lawyer's oath due to pending murder charges, he remained a non-lawyer. Teaching repeaters how to answer bar exams and authoring pre-week reviewers require the active interpretation and application of legal principles, which falls squarely within the definition of the practice of law under **Cayetano v. Monsod**. Doing so without being admitted to the bar is an unauthorized practice of law punishable as indirect contempt.
Issue 3: Constitutional Power to Delist an Examinee Prior to Oath-Taking
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does the Supreme Court have the authority to delist Dizon from the list of successful bar examinees as a preventive and administrative sanction?
**YES.** The practice of law is a privilege subject to the continuing fitness of the applicant; the Supreme Court possesses plenary, sole discretion under its constitutional mandate and procedural rules to purge unfit candidates from the roll of bar passers before they take the oath.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **The Court as Exclusive Gatekeeper:** The practice of law is not a vested constitutional property right, but a distinct privilege reserved exclusively for individuals demonstrating unyielding compliance with academic, intellectual, and moral/character standards.
2.  **Preventive Authority under Amended Rule 138:** Pursuant to A.M. No. 24-10-05-SC (Sections 2 and 17 of the Proposed Amendments to Rule 138), the Supreme Court exercises sole discretion, based on the gravity of an offense or related circumstances, to defer oath-taking or impose any other preventive measures, explicitly including "delisting from the list of passers."
3.  **Compounded Defiance and Moral Unfitness:** Dizon's ongoing exclusion from the bar originated from pending murder cases. Rather than proving moral rehabilitation, he displayed profound insolence by threatening the Court with legal action on television, demanding a 24-hour public apology, refusing to retract his false posts, and treating solemn proceedings as a novelty by requesting a photo opportunity with the Bar Chair. This conduct establishes complete unfitness to join the legal fraternity.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Jurisprudence is settled that the Court is the gatekeeper to the bar. The practice of law is a privilege and not a vested right. Thus, only those applicants who complied with all the academic and character requirements are allowed to join the legal fraternity. The Court has the sole discretion to assess the fitness of the applicants and to impose preventive measures, as warranted, to prevent those who are unqualified from becoming members of the bar."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The Supreme Court is the sole gatekeeper to the legal profession. Because passing the written examination confers only an inchoate privilege, the Court retains total authority to withdraw that privilege at any point prior to the administration of the oath if the candidate demonstrates moral unfitness. Dizon's combination of spreading disruptive falsehoods, practicing law unlawfully, and petulantly demanding an apology from the Court proved he lacked the character demanded of a lawyer, justifying his summary delisting from the list of bar passers.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I / Legal Ethics → 3) Admission to the Practice of Law and Regulation thereof.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
1.  State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:
 Power Exercised: The Supreme Court’s exclusive constitutional prerogative to regulate admission to the bar (Art. VIII, Sec. 5[5], 1987 Constitution) paired with its inherent judicial contempt power to defend the integrity of its proceedings.
 Right Invoked Against It: Freedom of Speech and Expression (Art. III, Sec. 4) raised implicitly by Dizon’s defense of fair teaching commentary.
2.  The Dual Pre-Conditions to Membership in the Bar:
 Requisite 1: Academic & Written Examination Competence. (Met by Dizon in 2016).
 Requisite 2: Continuing Moral Character & Judicial Authorization (Oath & Roll Signing). (Failed). The Court reiterated that passing the written test yields only an expectancy; character must remain unsullied until the actual oath-taking.
3.  Elements of Indirect Contempt via Obstruction & Usurpation (Rule 71, Sec. 3):
 Interference/Degradation (Sec. 3[c], [d]):** Unlawful external acts calculated to impede, embarrass, or disrupt court-supervised processes. (**Proven: Dissemination of false AI-checking claims that threw the 2023 Bar Examinations into operational turmoil).
 Usurpation of Legal Authority (Sec. 3[e]):** Engaging in legal custom, advice, or instruction without admission to the Roll of Attorneys. (**Proven: Authoring pre-week notes, charging for substantive bar prep, and explaining legal applications to repeaters).
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Gatekeeper to the Bar (Supreme Court's exclusive plenary control over admission).
 Privilege, Not a Vested Right (Legal status of bar membership).
 Practice of Law** (**Cayetano v. Monsod formulation: any activity requiring legal training, knowledge, and experience).
 Res Ipsa Loquitur (The post spoke for itself to establish contumacious intent).
 Delisting from the List of Passers (Preventive administrative forfeiture of examination success).
 Clear and Present Danger / Incitement Test (Addressed by SAJ Leonen regarding speech directed at court integrity).
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
**In Re: Dizon** falls squarely under the regulation of admission to the bar because it defines the boundary between passing the bar exam and actually being admitted to practice. The Supreme Court held that passing the bar does not confer a vested right to practice law or teach substantive law review courses, both of which require admission to the roll. When an unadmitted passer spreads viral falsehoods that disrupt ongoing bar examinations and brazenly threatens the Court, the Court may exercise its exclusive constitutional gatekeeping power under Article VIII, Section 5(5) to cite the individual for indirect contempt, fine him, and administratively delist him from the roll of bar passers.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**SAJ. Leonen (Separate Concurring Opinion):** Concurred fully in the conviction, but analyzed the constitutional intersection between the inherent power of contempt and the Article III, Section 4 guarantee of Free Speech. Applying the **Clear and Present Danger Test** (**Cabansag v. Fernandez**), the **Incitement Test** (**Brandenburg v. Ohio** / **Re: Badoy**), and J.L. Austin's linguistic Speech-Act framework (locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts), Justice Leonen emphasized that speech must be evaluated as an intentional act situated in context. Dizon's posts were not protected criticism; they were deliberate falsehoods designed to exploit examinees' anxieties for online clout and panic, creating a clear, imminent danger to the administration of justice. He underscored that penalties must educate and enforce digital responsibility, not merely punish.
**Verbatim/Near-Verbatim Fallo:**
"FOR THESE REASONS, Edgar S. Dizon is found GUILTY of indirect contempt and is directed to PAY a FINE of PHP 30,000.00. The Office of the Bar Confidant is DIRECTED to DELIST Edgar S. Dizon from the list of bar passers and to make a report thereon to the Court within five days from notice. Dizon is WARNED from further engaging in the unauthorized practice of law.

SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Edgar S. Dizon was found guilty of indirect contempt of court, ordered to pay a fine of PHP 30,000.00, and warned to cease practicing law. More severely, the Supreme Court stripped him of his successful 2016 examination standing by ordering the Office of the Bar Confidant to permanently delist him from the roster of bar passers, effectively barring him from ever taking the lawyer's oath based on that examination.
