### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** De La Llana v. Alba
**Full Official Caption:** Gualberto J. De La Llana, Presiding Judge, Branch II of the City Court of Olongapo, Estanislao L. Cesa, Jr., Fidela Y. Vargas, Benjamin C. Escolango, Juanito C. Atienza, Manuel Reyes Rosapapan, Jr., Virgilio E. Acierto, and Porfirio Aguillon Aguila, Petitioners, v. Manuel Alba, Minister of Budget, Francisco Tantuico, Chairman, Commission on Audit, and Ricardo Puno, Minister of Justice, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 57883; March 12, 1982; 198 Phil. 1; Ponente: Fernando, **C.J.**; En Banc.
- Voting Breakdown: Fernando, **C.J.**, penned the opinion, joined by Makasiar and Escolin, **JJ.**; Concepcion, Jr., **J.**, concurred in the result; Fernandez, **J.**, concurred with a qualification regarding consultation; Barredo, Aquino, Guerrero, De Castro, and Melencio-Herrera, **JJ.**, filed separate concurring opinions; Abad Santos and Plana, **JJ.**, filed separate concurring and dissenting opinions; Teehankee, **J.**, filed a dissenting opinion.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
- **Gualberto J. De La Llana:** Presiding Judge, Branch II of the City Court of Olongapo, representing incumbent lower court judges facing separation upon court abolition.
- **Estanislao L. Cesa, Jr., Fidela Y. Vargas, Benjamin C. Escolango, Juanito C. Atienza, Manuel Reyes Rosapapan, Jr., Virgilio E. Acierto, and Porfirio Aguillon Aguila:** Members of the Philippine Bar and taxpayers co-petitioning against the statute.
- **Manuel Alba:** Minister of the Budget, charged with funding organizational changes and administering appropriations under the challenged Act.
- **Francisco Tantuico:** Chairman of the Commission on Audit, tasked with auditing expenditures and compensation under the reorganization.
- **Ricardo Puno:** Minister of Justice, responsible for administrative matters, sponsorship of Cabinet Bill No. 42, and implementation measures under the Executive branch.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Original petition filed before the Supreme Court, captioned as a Petition for Declaratory Relief and/or Prohibition (treated by the Court solely as a Petition for Prohibition under Rule 65), directly challenging the constitutionality of **Batas Pambansa Blg. 129** (**The Judiciary Reorganization Act of 1980**) and seeking to enjoin respondents from enforcing or implementing its provisions.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Tenure and Removal of Judges
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Separation of Powers → Non-Delegation of Legislative Power
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provisions:**
- **Article X, Section 1, 1973 Constitution (Historical Basis Decided Upon):**
"The Judicial power shall be vested in one Supreme Court and in such **inferior courts as may be established by law**."
**(Modern Counterpart: Article VIII, Section 1, 1987 Constitution).**
- **Article X, Section 7, 1973 Constitution (Historical Basis Decided Upon):**
"The Members of the Supreme Court and **judges of inferior courts shall hold office during good behavior until they reach the age of seventy years or become incapacitated to discharge the duties of their office.** The Supreme Court shall have the power to discipline judges of inferior courts and, **by a vote of at least eight Members, order their dismissal**."
(Modern Counterpart: Article VIII, Section 11, 1987 Constitution: "The Members of the Supreme Court and judges of lower courts shall **hold office during good behavior until they reach the age of seventy years or become incapacitated to discharge the duties of their office.** The Supreme Court **en banc** shall have the power to discipline judges of lower courts, or **order their dismissal by a vote of a majority of the Members who actually took part in the deliberations** on the issues in the case and voted thereon.")
- **Article X, Section 6, 1973 Constitution (Historical Basis Decided Upon):**
"The Supreme Court shall have **administrative supervision over all courts and the personnel thereof**."
**(Modern Counterpart: Article VIII, Section 6, 1987 Constitution).**
- **Batas Pambansa Blg. 129, Section 44 (Challenged Statutory Trigger):**
"SEC. 44. **Transitory provisions.** — The provisions of this Act shall be immediately carried out in accordance with an Executive Order to be issued by the President. The Court of Appeals, the Courts of First Instance, the Circuit Criminal Courts, the Juvenile and Domestic Relations Courts, the Courts of Agrarian Relations, the City Courts, the Municipal Courts, and the Municipal Circuit Courts shall continue to function as presently constituted and organized, until the completion of the reorganization provided in this Act as declared by the President. **Upon such declaration, the said courts shall be deemed automatically abolished and the incumbents thereof shall cease to hold office.** The cases pending in the old Courts shall be transferred to the appropriate Courts constituted pursuant to this Act, together with the pertinent functions, records, equipment, property and the necessary personnel..."
**Factual Trigger:** The enactment and impending implementation of Batas Pambansa Blg. 129, whose Section 44 decreed the mass abolition of all inferior courts below the Supreme Court (except the Sandiganbayan and Court of Tax Appeals), terminating the incumbency of 1,180 sitting judges without individual disciplinary hearings or findings of bad behavior.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**June 16, 1901:** Act No. 136 (**The Judiciary Act of 1901**) is enacted, establishing the original judicial hierarchy of the Philippines under American administration.
**June 17, 1948:** Republic Act No. 296 (**The Judiciary Act of 1948**) is approved, standardizing regular inferior courts: Court of Appeals, Courts of First Instance (CFIs), Municipal Courts, and Justice of the Peace Courts.
**January 17, 1973:** The 1973 Philippine Constitution takes effect, lodging administrative supervision over all lower courts and the exclusive power to discipline/dismiss inferior court judges in the Supreme Court, while authorizing the legislature to establish inferior courts.
**August 7, 1980:** President Ferdinand E. Marcos issues Executive Order No. 611, creating the Presidential Committee on Judicial Reorganization (chaired by Chief Justice Enrique Fernando and co-chaired by Justice Minister Ricardo Puno; joined by Justices Ramon Aquino and Ameurfina Melencio-Herrera) to formulate plans for restructuring lower courts.
**September 5, 1980:** Executive Order No. 619-A amends the committee's mandate, directing it to submit reorganization plans within 70 days covering all lower courts except the Sandiganbayan.
**October 17, 1980:** The Committee on Judicial Reorganization submits its formal Report and "Proposed Guidelines for Judicial Reorganization" to the President, addressing severe docket congestion and the need for procedural modernization.
**Late 1980 – Early 1981:** Cabinet Bill No. 42 is introduced in the Batasang Pambansa based largely on the Committee's report. Public hearings, bench-bar dialogues, and committee reports yield extensive legislative debates spanning 590 pages in the Batasan records.
**August 10, 1981:** The Batasang Pambansa approves Cabinet Bill No. 42 on Third Reading.
**August 14, 1981:** President Marcos signs Cabinet Bill No. 42 into law as **Batas Pambansa Blg. 129** (**The Judiciary Reorganization Act of 1980**). It restructures inferior courts into the Intermediate Appellate Court, Regional Trial Courts, Metropolitan Trial Courts, Municipal Trial Courts, and Municipal Circuit Trial Courts. Section 44 provides that upon presidential declaration of completion of reorganization, the old courts are automatically abolished and incumbents cease to hold office.
**Late August 1981:** Judge Gualberto J. De La Llana and seven practicing lawyers file an original action before the Supreme Court seeking to nullify B.P. Blg. 129 for violating judicial independence, security of tenure, and the non-delegation doctrine.
**September 8, 1981:** At the start of oral arguments, petitioners move to disqualify Chief Justice Fernando and Associate Justices Aquino and Melencio-Herrera due to their prior service on the Presidential Committee on Judicial Reorganization. The Court denies the motion in open court, ruling their participation was purely academic and preliminary.
**October 8–13, 1981:** The Solicitor General files a Supplemental Answer defending the law as a valid legislative reorganization enacted in good faith; petitioners file their Reply.
**October 15, 1981:** The Supreme Court hears oral arguments from the parties and various **amici curiae** (including bar associations, Dean Irene Cortes, and former senators). The case is submitted for decision.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments
- **Main Thesis:** Batas Pambansa Blg. 129 is unconstitutional because its mass abolition of all inferior courts legislates incumbent judges out of office, violating their constitutionally guaranteed security of tenure, stripping the Supreme Court of its exclusive constitutional prerogative to discipline and dismiss judges, and effecting an unlawful delegation of legislative authority to the Executive.
- **Specific Contentions:**
1. **Security of Tenure Collision:** Under Art. X, Sec. 7 of the 1973 Constitution, judges hold office during good behavior until age 70 or incapacitation. Section 44 of B.P. Blg. 129 abruptly terminates their incumbency en masse without any showing of misbehavior or due process.
2. **Infringement on Supreme Court Powers:** The 1973 Constitution exclusively lodged administrative supervision (Art. X, Sec. 6) and disciplinary/dismissal authority (Art. X, Sec. 7) over lower court judges in the Supreme Court. The mass legislative ouster under Section 44 bypasses this judicial mechanism.
3. **Lack of Good Faith / Arbitrariness:** The abolition of the courts is a disguised purge or pretext to eliminate judges without administrative charges, lacking good faith and constituting arbitrary action.
4. **Undue Delegation of Legislative Power:** Section 41 impermissibly delegates to the President unbridled authority to fix judicial compensation and allowances, and Section 44 gives him unchecked discretion to determine the completion date of reorganization without a definite statutory time frame.
5. **Cosmetic Structural Changes:** The "new courts" are merely the "old courts" renamed and rearranged, transferring identical cases, personnel, and records; therefore, the offices are not genuinely abolished.
B. Respondents' Arguments
- **Main Thesis:** Batas Pambansa Blg. 129 is a valid, good-faith exercise of the plenary legislative power of the Batasang Pambansa under Art. X, Sec. 1 to establish, organize, reorganize, and abolish inferior statutory courts, which power is co-extensive and superior to any personal tenure rights in abolished offices.
- **Specific Contentions:**
1. **Lack of Standing & Justiciability:** The petition is improper and premature; declaratory relief cannot be brought originally in the Supreme Court; prohibition is improper because no jurisdictional usurpation occurred; Judge De La Llana has sustained no direct injury since he has not been separated, and lawyer-petitioners possess only generalized grievances.
2. **Abolition vs. Removal:** There is a settled legal distinction between removal from an existing office and termination caused by the abolition of the office itself. When an office is legally abolished in good faith, it ceases to exist; without an office, there can be no tenure.
3. **Presumption and Existence of Good Faith:** The law was enacted after comprehensive study by a joint committee, exhaustive public hearings, and 590 pages of parliamentary debate to cure catastrophic docket congestion and modernize the judicial system, completely disproving bad faith.
4. **Valid Standards for Delegation:** Section 41 contains sufficient statutory standards for fixing compensation by expressly referencing LOI No. 93, P.D. No. 985, and P.D. No. 1597. Sections 43 and 44 contain explicit time frames (30 days for staffing pattern) tethered to the President's duty of faithful execution.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not petitioners (a sitting city judge and seven practicing lawyers/taxpayers) possess legal standing (**locus standi**) to assail the constitutionality of Batas Pambansa Blg. 129.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the abolition of existing inferior courts under Section 44 of Batas Pambansa Blg. 129 violates the security of tenure guaranteed to judges under Article X, Section 7 of the 1973 Constitution.
3. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the enactment of Batas Pambansa Blg. 129 was attended by arbitrariness and lack of good faith.
4. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not Section 41 and Section 44 of Batas Pambansa Blg. 129 constitute an undue delegation of legislative power to the President regarding judicial compensation and the implementation time frame.
5. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the Chief Justice and two Associate Justices were disqualified from participating in the adjudication due to their previous membership in the Presidential Committee on Judicial Reorganization.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Legal Standing of Petitioners
- **Short Answer: YES.** Both the judicial petitioner and the lawyer-taxpayer petitioners possess standing to maintain the suit.
- **Step-by-Step Ratio:** Under **People v. Vera**, a party impugning a statute must show a personal and substantial interest resulting in direct injury. Judge De La Llana, as an incumbent presiding judge of an inferior court explicitly marked for abolition under Section 44, faces direct and imminent separation from office. As to the remaining petitioners who are members of the Bar and taxpayers, their standing is sustained under the liberal doctrine recognized in **Aquino, Jr. v. COMELEC** and **Pascual v. Secretary of Public Works**. Bar members are officers of the court with a vital stake in the administration of justice and public constitutionalism. The old restrictive barrier of **Mellon v. Frothingham** has given way to broader taxpayer standing to contest sweeping institutional changes.
- **Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"As far as Judge de la Llana is concerned, he certainly falls within the principle set forth in Justice Laurel’s opinion in **People v. Vera**... 'The unchallenged rule is that the person who impugns the validity of a statute must have a personal and substantial interest in the case such that he has sustained, or will sustain, direct injury as a result of its enforcement.' The other petitioners as members of the bar and officers of the court cannot be considered as devoid of 'any personal and substantial interest' on the matter... Moreover, petitioners have convincingly shown that in their capacity as taxpayers, their standing to sue has been amply demonstrated."
- **Recitation-Ready Explanation:** The Supreme Court held that Judge De La Llana faced direct loss of his judicial post upon the abolition of his court, satisfying the direct-injury requirement. The practicing lawyers had standing both as officers of the court directly affected by judicial restructuring and as taxpayers challenging the expenditure of funds under an allegedly unconstitutional statute.
Issue 2: Validity of Court Abolition vis-à-vis Security of Judicial Tenure
- **Short Answer: NO.** The abolition of inferior courts does not violate the constitutional security of tenure of judges, as tenure attaches to the office, and when the office is abolished in good faith, tenure is necessarily extinguished.
- **Step-by-Step Ratio:**
1. **Constitutional Text & Competence:** Article X, Section 1 expressly grants the legislature the power to establish inferior courts, which inherently includes the plenary power to alter, reorganize, and abolish them.
2. **Distinction Between Removal and Abolition:** A sharp legal distinction exists between "removal from office" and "abolition of office." Removal presupposes that the office subsists while the occupant is ousted; abolition extinguishes the office itself. Where there is no office, there is no occupant and no tenure. Security of tenure protects a judge from arbitrary ouster while the court exists, but does not guarantee the immortality of statutory courts.
3. **Harmonization of Provisions:** The legislative power to reorganize courts (Art. X, Sec. 1) and the judicial tenure guarantee (Art. X, Sec. 7) must be harmonized. Tenure cannot operate as an insurmountable roadblock against institutional progress or structural judicial reforms.
4. **Supreme Court Dismissal Power:** The Court's exclusive constitutional authority to discipline and dismiss judges (Art. X, Sec. 7) applies strictly to disciplinary removals from continuing offices. It does not inhibit legitimate legislative abolition.
5. **Constitutional Construction to Preserve Validity:** To ensure the Act remains free from any unconstitutional taint regarding the removal power, the Executive should consult the Supreme Court and give its views fullest consideration in screening incumbents for reappointment, ensuring worthy judges continue their service without real interruption.
- **Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Removal is, of course, to be distinguished from termination by virtue of the abolition of the office. There can be no tenure to a non-existent office. After the abolition, there is in law no occupant. In case of removal, there is an office with an occupant who would thereby lose his position. It is in that sense that from the standpoint of strict law, the question of any impairment of security of tenure does not arise."
- **Recitation-Ready Explanation:** Security of tenure protects a judge from being unlawfully removed from an existing court, but it does not prevent the legislature from abolishing the court itself in a bona fide reorganization. When the office is abolished, tenure over that office terminates by operation of law because an incumbent cannot hold a non-existent position.
Issue 3: Good Faith vs. Arbitrariness in Enacting B.P. Blg. 129
- **Short Answer: NO.** B.P. Blg. 129 was not tainted by arbitrariness; it was enacted in manifest good faith to resolve an urgent public crisis.
- **Step-by-Step Ratio:** Under established jurisprudence (**Cruz v. Primicias, Jr.**, **Zandueta v. De la Costa**), the abolition of an office is fully valid if done in good faith, but invalid if used as a pretext or cloak to oust specific incumbents for political or illicit reasons. Here, good faith was comprehensively demonstrated by the extensive preparatory history: the creation of a specialized Presidential Committee on Judicial Reorganization under Executive Orders Nos. 611 and 619-A; a meticulous Report documenting the crushing docket backlog (over 400,000 pending cases) and societal development needs; and exhaustive legislative deliberations in the Batasang Pambansa spanning 590 transcript pages alongside nationwide dialogues with the Bench and Bar. Petitioners failed to present an iota of evidence proving improper motive or bad faith.
- **Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Nothing is better settled in our law than that the abolition of an office within the competence of a legitimate body if done in good faith suffers from no infirmity... As well-settled as the rule that the abolition of an office does not amount to an illegal removal of its incumbent is the principle that, in order to be valid, the abolition must be made in good faith... What appears undoubted and undeniable is the good faith that characterized its enactment from its inception to the affixing of the Presidential signature."
- **Recitation-Ready Explanation:** An abolition of office is lawful if executed in good faith and unconstitutional only if used as a fraudulent guise to bypass civil service or judicial protections to target individuals. Because the legislative records showed years of study and hundreds of pages of debate aimed at solving docket paralysis, good faith was firmly established, defeating petitioners' claims.
Issue 4: Delegation of Legislative Power (Compensation and Time Frame)
- **Short Answer: NO.** Sections 41 and 44 do not constitute an undue delegation of legislative power because they provide sufficient statutory standards and mandatory directives.
- **Step-by-Step Ratio:**
1. **Completeness and Sufficient Standard Tests:** Under **Edu v. Ericta**, a statute survives delegation challenges if it lays down fundamental policy and provides a standard (express or implied) to map out executive execution.
2. **Section 41 (Compensation):** It does not grant arbitrary discretion to the President; it specifically requires that salaries and allowances be authorized "along the guidelines set forth in Letter of Implementation No. 93 pursuant to Presidential Decree No. 985, as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1597." The standard is thus express and detailed.
3. **Section 44 (Reorganization Time Frame):** The absence of a rigid completion calendar is not a fatal defect. Section 43 strictly requires the Supreme Court to submit a staffing pattern within 30 days of the Act's effectivity, and Section 44 directs that its provisions be "immediately carried out" by Executive Order. The President is constitutionally bound to take care that the laws be faithfully executed, precluding indefinite delay.
- **Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The questioned provision reads as follows: 'Intermediate Appellate Justices, Regional Trial Judges, and Municipal Circuit Trial Judges shall receive such compensation and allowances as may be authorized by the President along the guidelines set forth in Letter of Implementation No. 93 pursuant to Presidential Decree No. 985, as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1597.' The existence of a standard is thus clear... The standard may be either express or implied. If the former, the non-delegation objection is easily met."
- **Recitation-Ready Explanation:** There was no unlawful delegation because the legislature expressly tied judicial compensation to established salary guidelines under specific presidential decrees, providing an adequate statutory standard. Furthermore, the directive that the law be carried out "immediately" based on a staffing pattern submitted within 30 days provided an operative framework governed by the President's constitutional duty of faithful execution.
Issue 5: Disqualification of the Chief Justice and Associate Justices
- **Short Answer: NO.** The participation of the Justices in the preliminary reorganization committee did not disqualify them from sitting in judgment.
- **Step-by-Step Ratio:** The members of the Court appointed to the Presidential Committee on Judicial Reorganization acted strictly within the realm of academic and scholarly study to formulate reform options, which has historically been part of the judiciary's consultative role in law reform (dating back to the 1901 Judiciary Act and pre-war practices). The Justices neither drafted Cabinet Bill No. 42 nor participated in the legislative debates of the Batasang Pambansa. Since the 1973 Constitution specifically transferred administrative supervision of lower courts to the Supreme Court, the Court possesses direct institutional knowledge of judicial inefficiencies, making participation in reform studies natural and permissible.
- **Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"It was made clear then and there that not one of the three members of the Court had any hand in the framing or in the discussion of Batas Pambansa Blg. 129. They were not consulted. They did not testify. The challenged legislation is entirely the product of the efforts of the legislative body. Their work was limited, as set forth in the Executive Order, to submitting alternative plans for reorganization. That is more in the nature of scholarly studies."
- **Recitation-Ready Explanation:** The Supreme Court denied the motion to disqualify because the Justices merely conducted preparatory policy studies and provided reform options. They had no hand in authoring or debating the actual statute in the legislature, meaning they maintained the necessary judicial objectivity to resolve its constitutionality.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Assigned Syllabus Topic: d. Tenure | Applied Lens: Constitutional & Political Law
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Abolition of Office vs. Security of Tenure):**
1. **Plenary Legislative Competence:** The legislative body must possess the express constitutional power to establish, alter, or abolish the office (Art. X, Sec. 1).
- **Applied:** Batasang Pambansa has plenary power over all statutory/inferior courts.
2. **Good Faith in Enactment (The Bona Fide Test):** The abolition must be genuine, motivated by public welfare, organizational efficiency, or economy, and not designed as a personal purge or pretext to circumvent tenure.
- **Applied:** Massive backlog, demographic changes, and 590 pages of debate proved bona fide institutional reform.
3. **Substantial Structural Change:** The reorganization must effect an actual institutional alteration, rather than a colorable or cosmetic renaming of identical positions to swap personnel.
- **Applied:** The law eliminated concurrent jurisdictions, created regional trial networks, specialized divisions, and expanded appellate fact-finding powers.
4. **Legal Extinction of Office:** The legal office itself must cease to exist, dissolving any incumbent rights attached thereto.
- **Applied:** Section 44 expressly declared old courts automatically abolished; without an office, there is no tenure.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
- **Abolition vs. Removal:** Removal assumes an existing office whose occupant is ousted; abolition extinguishes the office, leaving no post to which tenure can attach.
- **Good Faith (Bona Fide Reorganization):** The indispensable prerequisite validating legislative abolition of public offices.
- **There can be no tenure to a non-existent office:** Axiomatic constitutional principle reconciling Art. X, Sec. 1 with Art. X, Sec. 7.
- **Completeness and Sufficient Standard Tests:** Dual criteria governing constitutional delegations of legislative power.
- **Public office is a public trust:** Constitutional baseline (Art. XIII, Sec. 1) barring any private vested property rights in judicial office.
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
- **Governmental Power Exercised:** Legislative power of judicial reorganization and statutory abolition under Art. X, Sec. 1, combined with the Executive power of appointment.
- **Constitutional Limitations Invoked:** Judicial Security of Tenure (Art. X, Sec. 7); the Supreme Court's exclusive power to discipline and dismiss judges (Art. X, Sec. 7); and the Non-Delegation of Legislative Power.
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:** Presumption of Constitutionality and the **Bona Fide** (Good Faith) Test in statutory office abolition, requiring clear and convincing proof of bad faith or palpable constitutional repugnancy before an act of a coordinate branch will be struck down.
**Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit:**
- **Actual Case or Controversy:** Sustained by the majority due to the imminent enforcement of Section 44 terminating lower court incumbency (though disputed as premature by Concurring Justices Aquino and De Castro).
- **Locus Standi:** Confirmed for Judge De La Llana under the **People v. Vera** direct injury test, and for co-petitioners as members of the Bar and taxpayers under **Aquino v. COMELEC**.
- **Lis Mota:** The constitutionality of B.P. Blg. 129 was directly dispositive of whether respondents could be enjoined from implementing the judicial reorganization.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
In **De La Llana v. Alba**, the Supreme Court established that the constitutional guarantee of security of judicial tenure protects judges from arbitrary removal only while their offices exist; it does not restrict the plenary power of the legislature to abolish inferior courts through a bona fide judicial reorganization. Because Batas Pambansa Blg. 129 was enacted in evident good faith to address nationwide docket congestion and implement structural institutional reforms, the statutory abolition of the old inferior courts was valid. Consequently, the termination of the incumbents' tenure was an unavoidable legal consequence of the extinction of their offices, not an unconstitutional removal.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
- **Barredo, J. (Concurring):** Emphasized that tenure ends when an office dies (**dura lex, sed lex**). He stressed the reality of judicial corruption and docket paralysis, asserting that drastic societal ills justify extraordinary legislative remedies (**"Grandes males, grandes remedios"**).
- **Aquino, J. (Concurring in Result):** Argued the petition should have been dismissed outright for lack of jurisdiction over declaratory relief, prematurity, lack of a justiciable controversy, and lack of personality on the part of the lawyer-petitioners.
- **Guerrero, J. (Concurring):** Approached the issue via sociological jurisprudence and functional utility. Cited alarming statistics of 450,000 clogged cases and 322 judges administratively charged to prove the compelling necessity and good faith of the reorganization.
- **De Castro, J. (Concurring):** Maintained that the legislative power to create and abolish courts is plenary and continuing, under the rule that no irrepealable laws may be passed. Judicial tenure takes a secondary position to the state's police power to provide a functional judicial system (**"Salus populi est suprema lex"**). Found the petition premature.
- **Melencio-Herrera, J. (Concurring):** Distinguished "tenure of courts" from "tenure of judges." Judges are entailed to their courts, but courts are not entailed to their judges. Outlined the profound structural reforms in B.P. Blg. 129 proving it was not a cosmetic change. Rejected requiring the President to submit judicial names in the staffing pattern as an infringement on executive appointment power.
- **Ericta, J. (Concurring):** Reaffirmed that security of tenure cannot be invoked against the good-faith abolition of an office, which is an established legislative prerogative.
- **Abad Santos, J. (Concurring & Dissenting):** Concurred that the law is constitutional, but dissented from the majority's suggestion that the Executive must consult the Supreme Court in appointing new judges, calling it an unconstitutional invasion of the President's exclusive appointing domain.
- **Plana, J. (Concurring & Dissenting):** Concurred in upholding the law's good faith, but dissented from requiring presidential consultation with the Court. Noted that the 1973 Constitution fused executive and legislative powers, significantly eroding the traditional rigid non-delegation doctrine.
- **Teehankee, J. (Dissenting):** Championed the Bengzon majority rationale in **Ocampo v. Secretary of Justice** (1955). Argued that an express constitutional guarantee of tenure must override implied legislative authority to abolish courts. Contended that the 1973 Constitution deliberately ruled out legislative ousters by granting the Supreme Court exclusive power to discipline and dismiss judges. Maintained that B.P. Blg. 129 effected a mere cosmetic restructuring/renaming, and that incumbent judges were constitutionally entitled to be carried over into the corresponding replacement courts unless removed for cause after due process.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the unconstitutionality of Batas Pambansa Blg. 129 not having been shown, this petition is dismissed. No costs."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court dismissed the petition and upheld the constitutionality of Batas Pambansa Blg. 129 in its entirety. The challenged mass reorganization and abolition of all inferior courts took full legal effect, allowing the Executive to proceed with implementing the new judicial structure and appointing judges to the newly created courts.

digest:
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Chavez v. Judicial and Bar Council (Resolution on Motion for Reconsideration)
**Full Official Caption:** Francisco I. Chavez, Petitioner, vs. Judicial and Bar Council, Sen. Francis Joseph G. Escudero, and Rep. Niel C. Tupas, Jr., Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 202242; April 16, 2013; 709 Phil. 478; En Banc; Ponente: Mendoza, J.
- **Voting Breakdown:** Carpio, Leonardo-De Castro, Peralta, Bersamin, Villarama, Jr., Perez, Reyes, and Perlas-Bernabe, JJ., concur; Sereno, C.J., took no part (JBC Chairperson); Velasco, Jr., J., took no part (participation in JC); Brion, J., took no part; Del Castillo, J., joined the dissent of Abad, J.; Abad, J., filed a Dissenting Opinion; Leonen, J., filed a Dissenting Opinion.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
- **Francisco I. Chavez:** Former Solicitor General of the Philippines; nominee for the position of Chief Justice of the Supreme Court following the removal of Renato C. Corona; Petitioner.
- **Judicial and Bar Council (JBC):** The constitutionally created body tasked with recommending nominees for judicial vacancies; Respondent.
- **Sen. Francis Joseph G. Escudero:** Member of the Senate of the Philippines and Chairman of the Senate Committee on Justice and Human Rights; sitting ex officio representative in the JBC; Respondent.
- **Rep. Niel C. Tupas, Jr.:** Member of the House of Representatives of the Philippines and Chairman of the House Committee on Justice; sitting ex officio representative in the JBC; Respondent.
- **Office of the Solicitor General (OSG):** Legal counsel representing Respondents Sen. Escudero and Rep. Tupas, Jr.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Motion for Reconsideration filed by the Office of the Solicitor General on behalf of Respondents Sen. Escudero and Rep. Tupas, Jr., seeking to overturn the Supreme Court En Banc's Decision dated July 17, 2012, which declared the numerical composition of the JBC unconstitutional and ordered it reconstituted so that only one member of Congress sits as a representative in its proceedings.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Article VIII (Judicial Department) → Section 8: The Judicial and Bar Council (Composition & Representation)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Judicial Review → Doctrine of Operative Fact; Principles of Constitutional Construction (**Verba Legis**, **Casus Omissus**, Separation of Powers).
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provision:**
**Article VIII, Section 8, Paragraph 1, 1987 Constitution of the Republic of the Philippines:**
"Section 8. (1) A Judicial and Bar Council is hereby created under the supervision of the Supreme Court composed of the Chief Justice as **ex officio** Chairman, the Secretary of Justice, and **a representative of the Congress** as **ex officio** Members, a representative of the Integrated Bar, a professor of law, a retired Member of the Supreme Court, and a representative of the private sector."
**Historical Landmark Rule:**
Under the **1899 Malolos Constitution (Art. 80, Title X)**, the Chief Justice and Solicitor-General were chosen by the National Assembly in concurrence with the President and Secretaries. Under the **1935 Constitution (Art. VIII, Sec. 5)**, judicial appointments were made by the President with the consent of the Commission on Appointments. Under the **1973 Constitution (Art. X, Sec. 4)**, the appointment power was vested exclusively in the President without need for legislative confirmation. The **1987 Constitution** deliberately eliminated legislative confirmation through the Commission on Appointments and instituted the JBC under Art. VIII, Sec. 8(1) to insulate appointments from political partisanship.
**Factual Trigger:**
Following the removal of Chief Justice Renato C. Corona on May 29, 2012, the JBC commenced proceedings to nominate a successor. Petitioner Francisco I. Chavez was nominated, but challenged the constitutionality of the JBC's ongoing composition—in which both a Senator and a House Representative sat simultaneously as **ex officio** members, each casting one full vote—arguing it violated the express textual limitation of Article VIII, Section 8(1) restricting Congress to "a representative."
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1987:** The 1987 Constitution is ratified. Section 8(1), Article VIII creates the Judicial and Bar Council, providing that it be composed of the Chief Justice as **ex officio** Chairman, the Secretary of Justice, and "a representative of the Congress" as **ex officio** members, alongside four regular members (a representative of the Integrated Bar, a professor of law, a retired Supreme Court Justice, and a private sector representative). Congress designates one representative, alternating between the Senate and the House of Representatives by rotation.
**1994:** The seven-member numerical balance is altered. An eighth member is introduced as the Senate and the House of Representatives begin sending two representatives to sit simultaneously, with each wielding one-half (1/2) vote.
**January 12, 2000 / May 30, 2001:** The JBC En Banc substantially changes this arrangement. It abandons the half-vote system and decides to grant each congressional representative (one from the Senate and one from the House) one full vote, effectively raising total voting members to eight.
**March 14, 2007:** Associate Justice Leonardo A. Quisumbing submits an opinion as JBC Consultant to the Chief Justice, concluding that two congressional votes violate the Constitution, run counter to the intended seven-member framework, and create the risk of deadlocks.
**March 27, 2007:** Representative Simeon A. Datumanong submits a formal position paper arguing that Congress is entitled strictly to one representative under the unambiguous terms of Section 8(1), Article VIII, and that double representation negates the equality of the three co-equal branches.
**Undated:** Secretary of Justice Agnes VST Devanadera submits a position paper affirming that the text explicitly restricts Congress to a single individual representative, and that eight members exceeds the constitutional blueprint.
**May 29, 2012:** Chief Justice Renato C. Corona is removed from office by impeachment, creating a vacancy in the Supreme Court. The JBC initiates nominations; Francisco I. Chavez is nominated as a candidate.
**July 17, 2012:** The Supreme Court renders its Decision in G.R. No. 202242, granting Chavez’s petition. It declares the JBC’s eight-member composition unconstitutional, commands the JBC to reconstitute itself with only one congressional representative, and orders the ruling immediately executory.
**July 24–31, 2012:** The OSG, on behalf of Sen. Escudero and Rep. Tupas, Jr., files a Motion for Reconsideration. The Senate passes Resolutions Nos. 111, 112, 113, and 114 urging deferral of nominations, reiterating the propriety of two representatives with full votes, requesting oral arguments, and authorizing Sen. Joker P. Arroyo to argue. On July 31, 2012, the Court sets the motion for oral argument.
**August 2, 2012:** The Supreme Court hears the parties in oral argument.
**August 3, 2012:** The Supreme Court issues a Resolution directing the parties to submit memoranda within ten days, and suspends the immediately executory nature of the July 17, 2012 dispositive portion pending review.
**April 16, 2013:** The Supreme Court promulgates its En Banc Resolution denying Respondents' Motion for Reconsideration and lifting the suspension on immediate execution.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondents' Arguments (Motion for Reconsideration via OSG)
- **Main Thesis:** Article VIII, Section 8(1) must be interpreted to allow two representatives from Congress—one Senator and one Representative—each exercising one full vote, because the legislature is bicameral.
- **Specific Contentions:**
1. **Absurdity in Bicameral Context:** Restricting Congress to one representative leads to an absurdity because a Senator cannot represent the House, and a House Member cannot represent the Senate. Each chamber has distinct constituencies, rules, organizations, and mandates.
2. **Plain Oversight Theory:** The use of the singular phrasing "a representative of the Congress" was sheer inadvertence and plain oversight by the Constitutional Commission. When the Framers shifted the legislative structure from unicameralism to bicameralism, they adjusted other provisions but inadvertently omitted modifying Section 8(1).
3. **No Danger of Partisanship:** Allowing two congressional members does not subvert the Framers' intent to insulate the JBC from partisan politics, as the Executive already exerts substantial influence over the regular members through appointment.
4. **Even-Numbered Deadlock Refuted:** The Court's premise that the JBC requires an odd seven-member framework to break ties is flawed. The JBC shortlists multiple candidates based on pluralities; it does not render binary yes/no determinations requiring a tie-breaking vote.
5. **Acquiescence / Long-Standing Practice:** The practice of having two representatives dates back years and was never questioned, demonstrating constitutional acceptance.
B. Petitioner's Arguments (Chavez Opposition & Memorandum)
- **Main Thesis:** The plain language of the Constitution is absolute; Section 8(1), Article VIII deliberately restricts Congress to only one seat and one vote in the JBC.
- **Specific Contentions:**
1. **Verba Legis:** The text clearly uses the singular indefinite article "a" ("a representative of the Congress"). Where the text is clear, there is no room for interpretation.
2. **Refutation of Oversight:** The Framers adjusted multiple other constitutional provisions when adopting bicameralism (e.g., presidential election tie-breakers, Vice-President vacancy confirmations, revocation of martial law). Their decision not to alter Section 8(1) demonstrates deliberate intent.
3. **Equal Branch Representation:** The three branches participate **ex officio** in the JBC as equal institutional departments. Congress interacts with the JBC not in its legislative capacity, but in an institutional check-and-balance function. Giving Congress two seats and two votes distorts inter-branch parity by giving the legislature twice the quantitative influence of the Executive and the Judiciary.
4. **Prohibition of Vote-Splitting:** A single representative is entitled to one full vote; dividing a vote into halves or duplicating it violates constitutional commands.
5. **Inapplicability of Estoppel:** Past unconstitutional practices, no matter how habitual or established, cannot ripen into constitutional validity under estoppel or laches.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the singular phrase "a representative of the Congress" in Section 8(1), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution permits both the Senate and the House of Representatives to seat one member each in the Judicial and Bar Council.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the failure of the 1986 Constitutional Commission to adjust Section 8(1), Article VIII upon shifting from a unicameral to a bicameral legislature constitutes a "plain oversight" that warrants judicial correction.
3. **[Secondary Substantive Issue]** Whether or not the lone congressional representative in the JBC may split their vote into one-half (1/2) each between two members of Congress.
4. **[Secondary Substantive Issue]** Whether or not long-standing practice and lack of prior challenge estop the petitioner or insulate the unconstitutional composition of the JBC from judicial nullification.
5. **[Secondary Substantive Issue]** Whether or not the declaration of unconstitutionality invalidates all prior official acts and recommendations performed by the JBC while operating with an eight-member composition.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Proper Number of Congressional Representatives in the JBC
- **(a) Short Answer: NO.** Section 8(1), Article VIII permits only one representative from Congress to sit in the JBC.
- **(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Textualism and Verba Legis:** The Constitution is the supreme direct act of the sovereign people. In interpreting it, the Court presumes the Framers meant what they said. The deliberate selection of the singular word "a" in "a representative of the Congress" demonstrates that the legislature is entitled to exactly one seat.
2. **Inter-Branch Parity in Non-Legislative Functions:** The JBC is an independent body created under judicial supervision to recommend nominees to the President. The three branches participate through **ex officio** representatives: the Chief Justice (Judicial), the Secretary of Justice (Executive), and "a representative of the Congress" (Legislative). The JBC totals seven members. In non-legislative bodies where the legislature interacts externally with co-equal branches, Congress participates as one single branch. Conferring two seats on Congress gives it two votes against one for the Executive and one for the Judiciary, subverting inter-branch equality.
3. **Constricted Representation is Not Absurd:** While the two Houses operate separately in lawmaking, appropriation, treaties, and impeachment, no internal bicameral interplay is required inside the JBC. Any member of Congress chosen to sit acts as a representative of the **entire** Congress. While this authority is constricted, it is entirely constitutional.
- **(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"The unmistakeable tenor of Article VIII, Section 8(1) was to treat each **ex-officio** member as representing one co-equal branch of government... The representatives of the Senate and the House of Representatives act as such for one branch and should not have any more quantitative influence as the other branches in the exercise of prerogatives evenly bestowed upon the three."
- **(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:** The Constitution expressly limits legislative representation in the JBC to "a representative." Because the JBC's role is non-legislative, Congress sits not as two independent chambers representing localized or national constituencies, but as a single co-equal department alongside the Executive and Judiciary; giving it two seats and two votes unconstitutionally tilts inter-branch equality.
Issue 2: Plain Oversight and Judicial Activism
- **(a) Short Answer: NO.** The omission of dual representation was not an oversight, and the Court has no power to amend the Constitution under the guise of interpretation.
- **(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Systematic Constitutional Adaptation:** The Framers demonstrated that they knew how to adapt constitutional text when switching from unicameralism to bicameralism. In multiple provisions (e.g., Art. VII, Sec. 4 [breaking presidential election ties], Art. VII, Sec. 9 [confirming Vice-Presidential vacancies], and Art. VII, Sec. 18 [revoking/extending martial law]), the text was expressly adjusted to state "both Houses of the Congress, voting separately" or "voting jointly." The absence of any such modification in Article VIII, Section 8(1) demonstrates that the singular representation was intentional.
2. **Casus Omissus Pro Omisso Habendus Est:** Under the canon of **casus omissus**, a matter omitted is held to have been intentionally omitted. Even if the omission arose from lack of foresight, courts cannot supply what they imagine the Framers would have enacted, as that constitutes improper judicial legislation.
3. **Rejection of Exuberant Activism:** The Court declined respondents' plea for judicial activism to solve practical bicameral difficulties. Judicial activism must not cross into "judicial exuberance" or constitutional alteration.
- **(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"Pursuant to this, 'the Court cannot under its power of interpretation supply the omission even though the omission may have resulted from inadvertence or because the case in question was not foreseen or contemplated.' 'The Court cannot supply what it thinks the legislature would have supplied had its attention been called to the omission, as that would be judicial legislation.'"
- **(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:** The Court cannot invoke "oversight" to rewrite the Constitution. When the Framers restored the bicameral legislature, they consciously updated multiple provisions but chose to leave the JBC composition at one congressional representative; under **casus omissus**, the judiciary cannot supply an omitted seat without impermissibly amending the Charter.
Issue 3: Validity of Vote-Splitting Schemes
- **(a) Short Answer: NO.** Dividing a single vote into two half-votes between two members of Congress is unconstitutional.
- **(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Prohibition of Indirect Evasion:** The lone representative of Congress authorized by the Constitution carries one full vote. What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.
2. **Preservation of Constitutional Symmetry:** Allowing two legislators to sit simultaneously while splitting a vote disrupts normal voting order and circumvents the textual cap. The Constitution contemplates single, individual representatives across each designated category.
- **(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"From this score stems the conclusion that the lone representative of Congress is entitled to one full vote. This pronouncement effectively disallows the scheme of splitting the said vote into half (1/2), between two representatives of Congress. Not only can this unsanctioned practice cause disorder in the voting process, it is clearly against the essence of what the Constitution authorized."
- **(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:** The Constitution designates a single representative with one whole vote. Splitting a vote into halves to allow both chambers to sit simultaneously is an impermissible circumvention of the text that compromises the integrity and order of JBC voting proceedings.
Issue 4: Estoppel and Long-Standing Practice
- **(a) Short Answer: NO.** Unconstitutional government acts cannot acquire legitimacy through passage of time, frequent practice, or official acquiescence.
- **(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Primacy of the Fundamental Law:** An act that infringes the Constitution is void **ab initio**.
2. **Inapplicability of Laches and Estoppel:** Past toleration or acquiescence by the government, the JBC, or citizens does not cure constitutional defects. Frequency and notoriety of an invalid practice cannot generate legal authority.
- **(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Well-settled is the rule that acts done in violation of the Constitution no matter how frequent, usual or notorious cannot develop or gain acceptance under the doctrine of estoppel or laches, because once an act is considered as an infringement of the Constitution it is void from the very beginning and cannot be the source of any power or authority."
- **(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:** The fact that the JBC allowed two members of Congress to sit and vote since 1994 without challenge does not create a prescriptive right; unconstitutional practices can never be legitimized by estoppel or lapse of time.
Issue 5: Validity of Past Actions Under the Doctrine of Operative Fact
- **(a) Short Answer: YES.** Under the doctrine of operative fact, all previous official proceedings, nominations, and shortlists issued by the JBC prior to the finality of this declaration of unconstitutionality remain completely valid.
- **(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Exception to Void Ab Initio Principle:** While unconstitutional acts generally confer no rights and create no offices, equity and fair play mandate exceptions when undoing past reliance would result in massive disruption and injustice.
2. **Preservation of Judicial Nominations:** Prior reliance on the invalidly composed JBC was an operative historical fact. Invalidating past JBC actions would throw into legal limbo hundreds of judicial appointments, impairing judicial stability and imposing an undue burden on the public.
- **(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"The doctrine of operative fact, as an exception to the general rule, only applies as a matter of equity and fair play. It nullifies the effects of an unconstitutional law by recognizing that the existence of a statute prior to a determination of unconstitutionality is an operative fact and may have consequences which cannot always be ignored. The past cannot always be erased by a new judicial declaration."
- **(d) Recit-Ready Explanation:** The Court invoked the doctrine of operative fact as a matter of equity to ensure that its ruling operates prospectively. All prior JBC nominations and judicial appointments made under the unconstitutional eight-member setup remain fully valid to prevent systemic chaos.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | 4. The Judicial and Bar Council | Constitutional & Political Law Lens
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
- **Governmental Act:** Congress' exercise of structural representation by sending two delegates (one Senator and one Representative) wielding two full votes in the JBC; and the JBC En Banc’s internal administrative resolutions altering its numerical composition from seven to eight members.
- **Constitutional Limitation:** Article VIII, Section 8(1) of the 1987 Constitution, restricting congressional membership to "a representative," maintaining inter-branch parity among the three co-equal departments, and enforcing the doctrine of separation of powers.
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
- **Strict Textual Construction (Verba Legis):** Applied when constitutional language is unambiguous. The word "a" commands a singular numerical ceiling.
- **Casus Omissus Canon:** A matter omitted must be treated as intentionally omitted; courts cannot supply perceived legislative omissions under the banner of interpretation.
- **Anti-Usurpation / Restraint Test:** The Court refused "judicial exuberance" or rewriting constitutional provisions under the guise of resolving bicameral anomalies.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (JBC Composition Analysis):**
- **1. Supervised Entity:** Created under the direct supervision of the Supreme Court. **(Met)**
- **2. Total Number Contemplated:** Seven (7) members total. **(Violated: expanded to 8)**
- **3. Ex-Officio Branch Representation:**
- Judiciary: Chief Justice as **ex officio** Chairman (1 seat, 1 vote). **(Met)**
- Executive: Secretary of Justice (1 seat, 1 vote). **(Met)**
- Legislative: "a representative of the Congress" (1 seat, 1 vote). **(Violated: 2 seats, 2 votes occupied by Senate and House chairs simultaneously)**
- **4. Regular Members:** Four (4) regular members representing the Integrated Bar, legal academia, retired Supreme Court Justices, and the private sector, all subject to Commission on Appointments confirmation. **(Met)**
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
- **Ex officio** representation
- **Verba legis**
- **Casus omissus**
- Inter-branch equality / Co-equal branches
- Doctrine of operative fact
- Judicial exuberance vs. Judicial activism
- Void **ab initio**
**Justiciability & Threshold Audit:**
- **Locus Standi & Actual Controversy:** Petitioner Chavez possessed standing as a citizen, taxpayer, and direct nominee for the vacancy of Chief Justice affected by the composition of the screening council.
- **Estoppel against Constitutional Challenges:** Rejected. Past unconstitutional practices, regardless of how routine or notorious, cannot ripen into legality.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
This case is the leading authority on the composition of the Judicial and Bar Council under Article VIII, Section 8(1). The Supreme Court held that Congress is entitled strictly to **one representative** and **one full vote**, rejecting the bicameral argument of "plain oversight" because the text unambiguously uses the singular article "a." Giving Congress two seats distorts inter-branch parity by giving the legislature double the quantitative influence of the Executive and Judiciary in the JBC; however, under the **doctrine of operative fact**, all prior official acts and shortlists generated by the unconstitutionally constituted eight-member council remain completely valid.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
- **Abad, J., Dissenting:** Argued that the Motion for Reconsideration should be granted. Insisted that insisting on a single representative ignores the constitutional reality of a bicameral legislature where neither House can represent the other. Pointed out that JBC representation is explicitly defined as **ex officio**, which by Senate and House rules attaches automatically to the Justice Committee Chair of each chamber; therefore, adhering to a literal reading denies real **ex officio** representation to Congress. Concluded each chamber is constitutionally entitled to one full vote, as splitting votes renders legislators "second class members."
- **Leonen, J., Dissenting:** Argued that the Constitution must be interpreted as an integrated whole (**ut magis valeat quam pereat**) rather than by hyper-focusing on the single preposition "a." Under the Charter's design, Congress exists strictly as a bicameral body; a Senator reports only to the Senate and represents a national constituency, while a Representative reports to the House and represents local/party-list constituencies. Neither can represent the other or the whole Congress. Emphasized that the Constitutional Commission records show the JBC seven-member model was discussed while the Commission was still assuming a unicameral assembly, and the Failure to adjust Section 8(1) after the 23–22 vote restoring bicameralism was a clear mechanical oversight. Argued that the JBC does not make binary decisions requiring an odd-numbered tie-breaker since it produces shortlists based on pluralities, and having eight members violates no constitutional objective.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
**"WHEREFORE**, the Motion for Reconsideration filed by respondents is hereby **DENIED**. The suspension of the effects of the second paragraph of the dispositive portion of the July 17, 2012 Decision of the Court, which reads, 'This disposition is immediately executory,' is hereby **LIFTED**."
### "SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court firmly maintained its July 17, 2012 ruling: Petitioner Francisco I. Chavez prevailed, while Respondents Sen. Escudero, Rep. Tupas, and the OSG lost. The practice of having two members of Congress sit simultaneously with full votes in the JBC was conclusively reaffirmed as unconstitutional, the immediate enforceability of the reconstitution order was reinstated, and Congress was required to designate only one member to sit and vote in the JBC.
