### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Fortich v. Corona** (Resolution on Motion for Reconsideration / En Banc Referral)
**Full Official Caption:** Hon. Carlos O. Fortich, Provincial Governor of Bukidnon, Hon. Rey B. Baula, Municipal Mayor of Sumilao, Bukidnon, NQSR Management and Development Corporation, Petitioners, vs. Hon. Renato C. Corona, Deputy Executive Secretary, Hon. Ernesto D. Garilao, Secretary of the Department of Agrarian Reform, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 131457, August 19, 1999; 371 Phil. 672; Special Second Division; Ponente: Ynares-Santiago, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Promulgated by the Special Second Division. Melo, **J.**, filed a separate opinion. Puno, **J.**, concurred "in the result" (maintaining his original position that the case should go to the Court of Appeals for further proceedings). Mendoza, **J.**, concurred "in the result."
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Petitioners:**
**Hon. Carlos O. Fortich:** Provincial Governor of Bukidnon.
**Hon. Rey B. Baula:** Municipal Mayor of Sumilao, Bukidnon.
**NQSR Management and Development Corporation (NQSR):** Private corporate developer and landholder in Sumilao, Bukidnon.
**Respondents:**
**Hon. Renato C. Corona:** Deputy Executive Secretary, Office of the President (OP).
**Hon. Ernesto D. Garilao:** Secretary, Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR). Both represented by the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG).
**Intervenors (Movants):** Seasonal farmworkers claiming to be agrarian reform beneficiaries who were issued Certificates of Land Ownership Award (CLOAs) over the disputed Sumilao property under the OP's questioned "Win-Win" Resolution.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Before the Supreme Court Special Second Division are pending post-judgment incidents arising from an original Petition for Certiorari: (1) Intervenors' "Motion For Reconsideration With Motion To Refer The Matter To The Court En Banc" dated December 3, 1998; (2) Respondents' "Motion For Reconsideration Of The Resolution Dated November 17, 1998 And For Referral Of The Case To This Honorable Court En Banc (With Urgent Prayer For Issuance Of A Restraining Order)" dated December 2, 1998 (filed December 3, 1998); and (3) Intervenors' "Urgent Omnibus Motion For The Supreme Court Sitting En Banc To Annul The Second Division's Resolution Dated 27 January 1999 And Immediately Resolve The 28 May 1998 Motion For Reconsideration Filed By The Intervenors" dated March 2, 1999. Movants challenge the Court's Resolution of November 17, 1998, which denied reconsideration of the April 24, 1998 Decision by a 2–2 tie vote, and the Resolution of January 27, 1999, which noted without action intervenors' prior December 3, 1998 motion.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → The Judicial Department (Article VIII) → Supreme Court: Mode of Sitting and Voting / Division Voting Tie (Article VIII, Section 4[3])
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Civil Procedure → Prohibited Second Motions for Reconsideration (Rule 52, Section 2; Rule 56, Section 4) / Parties and Legal Standing to Intervene (Rule 19)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provision:**
**Article VIII, Section 4, Paragraph 3, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Cases or matters heard by a division shall be decided or resolved with the concurrence of a majority of the Members who actually took part in the deliberations on the issues in the case and voted thereon, and in no case without the concurrence of at least three of such Members. **When the required number is not obtained, the case shall be decided en banc: **Provided**, that no doctrine or principle of law laid down by the Court in a decision rendered **en banc** or in division may be modified or reversed except by the Court sitting **en banc."
**Factual Trigger:**
After the Supreme Court's Second Division unanimously nullified the Office of the President's "Win-Win" Resolution on April 24, 1998, respondents and intervenors filed motions for reconsideration. On November 17, 1998, the Division deadlocked 2–2 on the motions, causing the motions to be lost and the original decision to stand affirmed. Rather than accepting the outcome, respondents and intervenors demanded that the controversy be elevated to the Supreme Court **En Banc**, arguing that under Article VIII, Section 4(3), whenever a Division fails to muster three concurring votes on any pending incident, the entire case must automatically transfer to the **En Banc**.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**March 29, 1996:** The Office of the President (OP) renders a decision approving the conversion/reclassification of the disputed agricultural land in Sumilao, Bukidnon, owned/developed by NQSR Management and Development Corporation, to non-agricultural use. This OP Decision becomes final and executory after the reglementary period lapses without an appeal or motion for reconsideration being timely filed.
**November 7, 1997:** The Office of the President issues a "Win-Win" Resolution, substantially modifying its March 29, 1996 Decision by ordering the parceling of the Sumilao land between the developer and alleged agrarian beneficiaries.
**April 24, 1998:** The Supreme Court Second Division, by a unanimous vote of all five (5) members, renders a Decision granting the petition of Governor Fortich, Mayor Baula, and NQSR. The Court strikes down the OP's November 7, 1997 "Win-Win" Resolution as null and void on the ground that the March 29, 1996 OP Decision had long become final and executory. In the same Decision, the Court denies the seasonal farmworkers' motion for leave to intervene.
**May 28, 1998:** Intervenors file a Motion for Reconsideration of the April 24, 1998 Decision, praying for referral of the case to the Court **En Banc**. Respondents likewise file their own motion for reconsideration.
**November 17, 1998:** The Special Second Division resolves the separate motions for reconsideration. The members vote two-two (2–2). Justice Antonio M. Martinez pens an opinion stating that the issues presented are not of extraordinary import to merit the attention of the Court **En Banc** (citing **Province of Camarines Sur v. Court of Appeals**, establishing that local government units need not obtain DAR approval to reclassify lands). Because the movants failed to muster the required three concurring votes to overturn the April 24, 1998 Decision, the motions for reconsideration are deemed lost and the Decision stands affirmed.
**December 2–3, 1998:** Intervenors file a "Motion For Reconsideration With Motion To Refer The Matter To The Court En Banc" (December 3, 1998). On the same date, respondents, through the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG), file by registered mail a "Motion For Reconsideration Of The Resolution Dated November 17, 1998 And For Referral Of The Case To This Honorable Court En Banc (With Urgent Prayer For Issuance Of A Restraining Order)" accompanied by a Manifestation and Motion.
**January 27, 1999:** The Court issues a Resolution noting without action intervenors' December 3, 1998 motion, ruling that movants have no legal personality following the denial of intervention, that the motion is an impermissible second motion for reconsideration under Rule 52, Section 2 in relation to Rule 56, Section 4 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, and noting that respondents did not appear to have joined in the motion.
**March 2, 1999:** Intervenors file an "Urgent Omnibus Motion For The Supreme Court Sitting En Banc To Annul The Second Division's Resolution Dated 27 January 1999 And Immediately Resolve The 28 May 1998 Motion For Reconsideration Filed By The Intervenors."
**August 19, 1999:** The Supreme Court Special Second Division promulgates the present Resolution denying with finality all pending motions and prayers for referral to the Court **En Banc**.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondents' and Intervenors' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The 2–2 tie vote of the Special Second Division on November 17, 1998 did not validly resolve their motions for reconsideration; because the constitutional requirement of at least three concurring votes was not obtained, Article VIII, Section 4(3) of the 1987 Constitution mandates that the case be referred to and decided by the Court **En Banc**.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Constitutional Mandate for En Banc Referral:** Under Article VIII, Section 4(3), cases or matters heard by a division require the concurrence of at least three members. Where a 2–2 tie occurs, the required three votes are not met; hence, the incident must be transferred to the full Court sitting **en banc**.
2.  **Novelty / Issues of First Impression:** The issues submitted in their motions are of first impression, transcendental importance, and far-reaching consequence, necessitating full **En Banc** deliberation rather than summary disposal by a divided Division.
3.  **Substance Over Technicality:** The nullification of the "Win-Win" Resolution rested merely on a procedural technicality regarding the reglementary period of finality of the March 29, 1996 OP decision, which should yield to substantive social justice.
4.  **Standing of Intervenors:** Intervenors are real parties in interest because they are DAR-identified qualified agrarian beneficiaries and have already been issued Certificates of Land Ownership Award (CLOAs) over the property.
B. Petitioners' Arguments / Division Position
**Main Thesis:** The original April 24, 1998 Decision remains valid and affirmed; the tie vote in a motion for reconsideration merely results in the denial of the motion and does not transfer the decided case to the Court **En Banc**.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Reddendo Singula Singulis:** Article VIII, Section 4(3) distinguishes "cases" (which are "decided") from "matters" (which are "resolved"). Referral to the **En Banc** applies only when an undecided **case** ties; when a **motion for reconsideration** of an already decided case ties, the motion is simply lost.
2.  **Prohibited Second Motion for Reconsideration:** The new motions seek reconsideration of an order denying reconsideration, violating Section 2, Rule 52 in relation to Section 4, Rule 56 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, filed without leave of court.
3.  **Vested Rights and Finality:** The finality of the March 29, 1996 OP Decision is substantive, vesting rights in the petitioners and the community; the "Win-Win" Resolution was void **ab initio**.
4.  **Lack of Legal Interest:** Intervenors are seasonal farmworkers whose constitutional right is limited to a just share in the fruits, not land ownership, and their CLOAs derived from a void resolution.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the failure of a Supreme Court Division to obtain the required three (3) concurring votes when resolving a motion for reconsideration—resulting in a 2–2 tie vote—requires the referral of the case to the Court **En Banc** under Article VIII, Section 4, Paragraph 3 of the 1987 Constitution.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondents' and intervenors' motions for reconsideration of the November 17, 1998 Resolution are prohibited second motions for reconsideration under the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the "Win-Win" Resolution dated November 7, 1997 was validly set aside, or conversely, whether substantive justice warrants relaxing the rule on finality of the March 29, 1996 OP Decision.
4.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the seasonal farmworker-intervenors have the requisite legal personality and standing to intervene in the action.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Referral to En Banc upon Tie Vote on a Motion for Reconsideration
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not a 2–2 tie vote in a Division on a motion for reconsideration requires the case to be referred to the Court **En Banc** under Article VIII, Section 4(3)? **NO.** A tie vote on a motion for reconsideration in a Division does not leave the case undecided; the motion simply fails to muster the required majority and is lost, leaving the original decision affirmed without need for **En Banc** referral.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Textual and Syntactical Construction:** Under the rule of statutory construction **reddendo singula singulis** (referring each to each), the constitutional text in Article VIII, Section 4(3) deliberately distinguishes between "cases" and "matters." Cases are "decided," while matters (which include motions) are "resolved."
2.  **Application of the Second Sentence:** The second sentence of Section 4(3) states: **"When the required number is not obtained, the case shall be decided en banc."** The framers deliberately used the word **"case"** and omitted the word **"matter."**
3.  **Mechanism of Case vs. Motion:** When an original case heard by a Division fails to garner three votes to reach an initial judgment, there is no decision; thus, the **case** must be elevated to the **En Banc** to be disposed of. In sharp contrast, where a case has **already been decided** by the Division (here, unanimously by all 5 members on April 24, 1998), the judgment is extant. When a motion for reconsideration is filed, the burden is on the movant to secure at least three votes to overturn that judgment.
4.  **Legal Consequence of a Tie on Reconsideration:** If the voting on a motion for reconsideration deadlocks at 2–2, the movant fails to muster the necessary votes to modify or reverse the judgment. The motion is lost. The assailed decision is not reconsidered and remains affirmed.
5.  **Issues Not of Extraordinary Import:** The contention that the questions are novel or of first impression was directly refuted by the November 17, 1998 opinion citing **Province of Camarines Sur v. Court of Appeals**, which established that local government units have the authority to reclassify agricultural lands without DAR approval.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"A careful reading of the above constitutional provision, however, reveals the intention of the framers to draw a distinction between cases, on the one hand, and matters, on the other hand, such that cases are 'decided' while matters, which include motions, are 'resolved'. Otherwise put, the word 'decided' must refer to 'cases'; while the word 'resolved' must refer to 'matters', applying the rule of **reddendo singula singulis**."

"On the other hand, if a case has already been decided by the division and the losing party files a motion for reconsideration, the failure of the division to resolve the motion because of a tie in the voting does not leave the case undecided. There is still the decision which must stand in view of the failure of the members of the division to muster the necessary vote for its reconsideration. Quite plainly, if the voting results in a tie, the motion for reconsideration is lost. The assailed decision is not reconsidered and must therefore be deemed affirmed."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Article VIII, Section 4(3) only sends an unresolved **case** to the **En Banc** when the Division ties on the main decision. If the Division already rendered a valid decision and later ties 2–2 on a motion for reconsideration, the case is not left hanging—the motion simply fails because it did not obtain the three concurring votes needed to overturn the decision. Consequently, the tie denies the motion, the original decision stands affirmed, and referral to the **En Banc** is improper.
Issue 2: Propriety of the Second Motions for Reconsideration
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the pending motions constitute prohibited second motions for reconsideration under the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure? **YES.** The motions seek to reconsider the denial of an earlier motion for reconsideration, which is explicitly barred by procedural rules absent express prior leave of court and extraordinarily persuasive reasons.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Rule Prohibition:** Under Rule 56, Section 4, in relation to Rule 52, Section 2 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, second motions for reconsideration are prohibited.
2.  **Procedural Default:** While exceptional cases may allow a second motion for reconsideration where extraordinary and persuasive reasons exist, such motions must be filed with **express leave of court first obtained** (**Ortigas and Co. Ltd. Partnership v. Velasco**).
3.  **No Exceptional Justification:** Movants neither requested nor secured prior leave of court. Furthermore, stripping away the baseless demand for **En Banc** referral, their arguments were mere rehashes of grounds already passed upon and rejected in the November 17, 1998 Resolution.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The contention, therefore, that our Resolution of November 17, 1998 did not dispose of the earlier motions for reconsideration of the Decision dated April 24, 1998 is flawed. Consequently, the present motions for reconsideration necessarily partake of the nature of a second motion for reconsideration which, according to the clear and unambiguous language of Rule 56, Section 4, in relation to Rule 52, Section 2, of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, is prohibited."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Once a Division's tie vote denied the first motions for reconsideration, that incident was fully disposed of. Filing another round of motions without prior leave of court violated the strict procedural prohibition against second motions for reconsideration, especially since movants merely repeated previously rejected arguments.
Issue 3: Validity of the "Win-Win" Resolution and Finality of the OP Decision
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the OP "Win-Win" Resolution was void, and whether the Court disposed of the case on a mere technicality? **NO.** The "Win-Win" Resolution is void **ab initio** because the original March 29, 1996 OP Decision had attained finality, vesting immutable substantive rights in petitioners.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Inviolability of Final Judgments:** The OP's March 29, 1996 Decision had already become final and executory before the motion seeking its reconsideration was ever filed. An administrative agency loses jurisdiction to alter a final and executory decision.
2.  **Substantive Rights Protected:** The rule on finality of judgments is not an empty technicality; it protects substantive constitutional rights. As held in **Videogram Regulatory Board v. Court of Appeals**, just as a losing party has a right to appeal within the prescribed reglementary period, the winning party possesses a correlative substantive right to enjoy the finality and immutability of the resolution.
3.  **Vested Entitlements:** Finality vested property and development rights in the petitioners and the people of Bukidnon, rendering the subsequent "Win-Win" Resolution of November 7, 1997 void and legally nonexistent.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The crux of the controversy is the validity of the 'Win-Win' Resolution dated November 7, 1997. We maintain that the same is void and of no legal effect considering that the March 29, 1996 decision of the Office of the President had already become final and executory even prior to the filing of the motion for reconsideration which became the basis of the said 'Win-Win' Resolution... The issue in this case, therefore, is not a question of technicality but of substance and merit."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Finality of judgment is a substantive rule of law, not a mere technical trap. Because the March 29, 1996 OP decision became final and executory, the Office of the President had zero authority to issue the "Win-Win" Resolution, making that later resolution void from the beginning.
Issue 4: Legal Standing of Intervenors
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not seasonal farmworkers issued CLOAs have legal standing to intervene in this action? **NO.** Seasonal farmworkers have no constitutional right to own the land, and CLOAs originating from a void resolution confer no legal rights.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Constitutional Classification of Farmworkers:** Under Article XIII, Section 4 of the Constitution, only regular farmworkers are guaranteed the right to own the land. The rights of seasonal farmworkers are expressly limited to a just share in the fruits of the land.
2.  **Contingent Beneficiary Status:** The "Win-Win" Resolution itself conceded that qualified agrarian beneficiaries had yet to be meticulously determined by the DAR; thus, intervenors possessed no vested, definitive right.
3.  **Nullity of Derivative CLOAs:** The issuance of CLOAs to intervenors could not confer legal standing because their CLOAs sprouted entirely from the "Win-Win" Resolution, which is completely void. No legal rights emanate from a nullity.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Again as expressed in the opinion of Mr. Justice Martinez, intervenors, who are admittedly not regular but seasonal farmworkers, have no legal or actual and substantive interest over the subject land inasmuch as they have no right to own the land. Rather, their right is limited only to a just share of the fruits of the land... Likewise, the issuance of the CLOA's to them does not grant them the requisite standing in view of the nullity of the 'Win-Win' Resolution. No legal rights can emanate from a resolution that is null and void."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Intervenors are seasonal farmworkers who have no constitutional right to land ownership, only a right to a just share of the fruits. Furthermore, because their CLOAs were issued pursuant to a "Win-Win" Resolution that was completely void, those titles conferred no legal interest or standing to intervene.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Supreme Court: Mode of Sitting and Voting (**Article VIII, Section 4[3]**)
**Applied Lens:** Constitutional & Political Law
State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation
 State Power / Branch Exercised: Judicial Power (adjudicative authority of the Supreme Court sitting in Division to decide cases and resolve motions with finality).
 Constitutional Limitation Invoked:** Article VIII, Section 4(3) of the 1987 Constitution, which guarantees that no case or matter heard by a Division shall be decided or resolved without the concurrence of at least three members, and mandates referral to the Court **En Banc when the required vote is not obtained.
Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Division Voting vs. En Banc Transfer)
**Requisite 1: Unobtained Concurrence in a "Case"** — The requirement of referral to the Court **En Banc** triggers **only** when an unadjudicated **case** fails to obtain the majority vote of the participating Members (and at least 3 votes in Division).
 Application to Facts: **Absent.** The **case** had already been definitively decided on April 24, 1998 by a unanimous 5–0 vote of the Second Division.
**Requisite 2: Action on an Incidental "Matter" (Motion for Reconsideration)** — Motions are interlocutory "matters" requiring three votes to **overturn** a prior ruling.
 Application to Facts: **Present.** The incident at hand was merely a motion for reconsideration. The 2–2 tie meant the movants failed to obtain the three votes required to alter the judgment; hence, the motion was lost, and the original judgment remained affirmed.
Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words")
 Reddendo singula singulis (referring each to each; "cases" are decided, while "matters" are resolved).
 Motion is lost (the consequence of a tie vote on a motion for reconsideration).
 Prohibited second motion for reconsideration (Rule 52, Sec. 2; Rule 56, Sec. 4).
 Finality of judgment (creates substantive vested rights that cannot be disturbed on procedural pleas).
Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer)
"**Fortich v. Corona** is the leading authority on the application of the rule of **reddendo singula singulis** to Article VIII, Section 4(3) of the 1987 Constitution regarding Division voting. The Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional command requiring referral to the **En Banc** when the required three votes are not obtained applies exclusively to **cases** awaiting decision, not to incidental **matters** such as motions for reconsideration. Because the Second Division had already unanimously decided the case on the merits, the subsequent 2–2 tie vote on the motion for reconsideration simply meant that the movants failed to muster the required majority to reverse the ruling; thus, the motion was lost, the decision was deemed affirmed, and no referral to the **En Banc** was warranted."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Melo, J.:** Filed a Separate Opinion (referenced in the text; noting reservation/concurrence).
**Puno, J.:** Concurred "in the result," explicitly maintaining his original position that the case should be remanded to the Court of Appeals for further proceedings.
**Mendoza, J.:** Concurred "in the result."
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, based on the foregoing, the following incidents, namely: intervenors' 'Motion For Reconsideration With Motion To Refer The Matter To The Court En Banc,' dated December 3, 1998; respondents' 'Motion For Reconsideration Of The Resolution Dated November 17, 1998 And For Referral Of The Case To This Honorable Court En Banc (With Urgent Prayer For Issuance Of A Restraining Order),' dated December 2, 1998; and intervenors' 'Urgent Omnibus Motion For The Supreme Court Sitting En Banc To Annul The Second Division's Resolution Dated 27 January 1999 And Immediately Resolve The 28 May 1998 Motion For Reconsideration Filed By The Intervenors,' dated March 2, 1999; are all DENIED with FINALITY. No further motion, pleading, or paper will be entertained in this case.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Petitioners (Governor Fortich, Mayor Baula, and NQSR) prevailed completely. All motions for reconsideration and petitions to elevate the dispute to the Court **En Banc** filed by the Executive respondents and farmworker-intervenors were denied with finality, thereby cementing the permanent invalidation of the OP "Win-Win" Resolution and sustaining the finality of the March 29, 1996 land conversion decision.

Garcia-Codilla v. Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp., Ltd.
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Garcia-Codilla v. Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp., Ltd.
**Full Official Caption:** Governor Gwendolyn Garcia-Codilla, Petitioner, vs. Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp., Ltd., Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 255252, Promulgated December 4, 2023, 949 Phil. 730; Second Division; Ponente: Kho, Jr., J.; Concurred in by Leonen, SAJ. (Chairperson), Lazaro-Javier, M. Lopez, and J. Lopez, JJ. (Unanimous).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Governor Gwendolyn Garcia-Codilla (Garcia):** Petitioner; judgment obligor; individual doing business under the registered sole proprietorship names "GGC Enterprises" and "GGC Shipping" (GGC); former member of the House of Representatives and Governor.
**Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp., Ltd. (HSBC):** Respondent; commercial banking corporation; judgment creditor and issuer of the irrevocable commercial letter of credit.
**Sam Whan Phils. Trading Co. Ltd. (Sam Trading):** Seller/beneficiary under the documentary credit line from whom Garcia purchased a light cargo transit barge.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court assailing the June 30, 2020 Decision and January 7, 2021 Resolution of the Court of Appeals (CA) in CA-G.R. SP No. 159953. The CA had affirmed the September 17, 2018 and January 3, 2019 Orders of the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Makati City, Branch 57, which denied Garcia’s Urgent Motion to Quash the Alias Writ of Execution in Civil Case No. 00-863.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Article VIII (The Judicial Department) → Section 14 (Constitutional Requirement for Factual and Legal Bases of Decisions)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Civil Procedure → Rule 39 (Execution of Judgments; Writs and Alias Writs of Execution; Doctrine of Immutability of Final Judgments)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
Article VIII, Section 14, 1987 Constitution:
"SECTION 14. No **decision** shall be rendered by any court without expressing therein clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based.

No petition for review or motion for reconsideration of a decision of the court shall be refused due course or denied without stating the legal basis therefor."
Rule 39, Section 8, Rules of Court:
"SECTION 8. **Issuance, form and contents of a writ of execution.** — The writ of execution shall: (1) issue in the name of the Republic of the Philippines from the court which granted the motion; (2) state the name of the court, the case number and title, the dispositive part of the subject judgment or order; and (3) require the sheriff or other proper officer to whom it is directed to enforce the writ according to its terms, in the manner hereinafter provided:
(a) If the execution be against the property of the judgment obligor, to satisfy the judgment, with interest, out of the real or personal property of such judgment obligor;
(b) If it be against real or personal property in the hands of personal representatives, heirs, devisees, legatees, tenants, or trustees of the judgment obligor, to satisfy the judgment, with interest, out of such property;
(c) If it be for the sale of real or personal property to sell such property describing it, and apply the proceeds in conformity with the judgment, the material parts of which shall be recited in the writ of execution;
(d) If it be for the delivery of the possession of real or personal property, to deliver the possession of the same, describing it, to the party entitled thereto, and to satisfy any costs, damages, rents, or profits covered by the judgment out of the personal property of the person against whom it was rendered, and if sufficient personal property cannot be found, then out of the real property; and
(e) In all cases, the writ of execution shall specifically state the amount of the interest, costs, damages, rents, or profits due as of the date of the issuance of the writ, aside from the principal obligation under the judgment. For this purpose, the motion for execution shall specify the amounts of the foregoing reliefs sought by the movant."
**Factual Trigger:** After a monetary judgment ordering Garcia to pay HSBC attained finality, HSBC obtained an **ex parte** Alias Writ of Execution because the initial writ had lapsed unsatisfied. Garcia moved to quash the alias writ, arguing that it violated Article VIII, Section 14 of the Constitution for failing to state on its face the facts and law upon which it was based, and that issuing it without notice and hearing violated her right to procedural due process.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**November 19, 1996:** HSBC opens Documentary Credit Line No. DPCCEB960015 for USD 900,000.00 in favor of Sam Trading to finance the purchase of a light cargo transit barge by GGC, a registered sole proprietorship owned by Garcia. Under the irrevocable credit, HSBC agrees to pay Sam Trading in five semi-annual installments of USD 180,000.00 each from October 15, 1997 through October 15, 1999. Garcia secures the facility with a Real Estate Mortgage over two parcels of land, an October 15, 1997 Trust Receipt over the barge, and a General Surety Agreement Relating to Goods.
**Subsequent Defaults & Attachments:** Garcia and GGC default on reimbursing HSBC. HSBC terminates Garcia's USD 200,000.00 dollar time deposit to apply against the arrears and demands physical delivery of the barge, which goes unheeded. HSBC continues paying the installment obligations to Sam Trading under the irrevocable letter of credit.
**March 31, 2000:** Garcia’s unpaid balance reaches USD 720,000.00 principal plus USD 103,522.91 in accrued interest.
**July 17, 2000:** HSBC files a Complaint for sum of money with prayer for preliminary attachment against Garcia and her husband before Branch 57, RTC of Makati City (Civil Case No. 00-863). The RTC issues the writ of preliminary attachment and subsequently declares Garcia and her husband in default for failing to file a responsive pleading.
**December 21, 2001:** The RTC renders a default judgment ordering Garcia and her husband to pay HSBC: (1) USD 890,347.92 or its Philippine peso equivalent as actual damages; (2) PHP 1,000,000.00 as moral and exemplary damages; and (3) PHP 960,765.48 as costs of suit.
**October 17, 2006:** On appeal (CA-G.R. CV No. 75861), the CA affirms liability but modifies damages: reduces actual damages to USD 700,000.00; deletes moral and exemplary damages; reduces costs to PHP 650,503.90; and imposes 12% legal interest reckoned from November 17, 1998 until full payment.
**August 22, 2012:** The Supreme Court Third Division (G.R. No. 177734) denies Garcia's Petition for Review on Certiorari via Minute Resolution, further modifying the award: costs of suit are reduced to PHP 404,560.50, and the starting point for the 12% legal interest is re-anchored to July 17, 2000 (complaint filing date) due to insufficient proof of the earlier demand letter.
**February 25, 2013:** The Supreme Court denies Garcia's motion for reconsideration with finality. The judgment is entered in the Book of Entries of Judgment.
**September 20, 2013:** Pursuant to an RTC order granting HSBC's execution motion, the RTC issues a Writ of Execution commanding the sheriff to satisfy the judgment debt of USD 1,877,148.50 (inclusive of legal interest) and PHP 404,560.50 in costs. Three court sheriffs attempt personal service on Garcia at the Batasan Pambansa Complex. Following two unsuccessful attempts where staff claim lack of authorization, the sheriffs effect substituted service on the third attempt by leaving copies with her Protocol Officer and Head of Operations.
**February 22, 2018:** HSBC files an Urgent Ex-Parte Motion for the Issuance of an Alias Writ of Execution, as the original writ remained unsatisfied.
**February 23, 2018:** The RTC grants the motion and issues an Alias Writ of Execution directing the collection of USD 2,825,636.79 (inclusive of accumulated legal interest) and suit costs.
**June 13, 2018:** Garcia files an Urgent Motion to Quash the Alias Writ of Execution, claiming it violated procedural due process because HSBC's motion was not set for hearing.
**September 17, 2018 & January 3, 2019:** The RTC issues Orders denying Garcia's motion to quash and her subsequent motion for reconsideration.
**June 30, 2020:** The CA dismisses Garcia’s Rule 65 petition (CA-G.R. SP No. 159953), holding that Article VIII, Section 14 applies only to decisions on the merits and not execution writs; that alias writ issuance on a final judgment is ministerial; and that service at the Batasan office was valid.
**January 7, 2021:** The CA denies Garcia’s motion for reconsideration.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Gwendolyn Garcia-Codilla)
**Main Thesis:** The Alias Writ of Execution is void for failing to comply with constitutional content requirements and for having been issued **ex parte** in violation of procedural due process.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Constitutional Infraction:** Under Article VIII, Section 14 of the 1987 Constitution, the Alias Writ must clearly and distinctly express the facts and law upon which it is based.
2. **Defective Service:** Service was void because the debt belonged to GGC, a sole proprietorship with registered offices in Ormoc and Cebu, not the Batasan. Furthermore, Rule 13, Section 7 rules on personal service of pleadings are mandatory and were violated.
3. **Lack of Notice and Hearing:** The motion for an alias writ is a litigious motion. Because HSBC filed it **ex parte** without a notice of hearing, it was a mere scrap of paper. Garcia was denied due process to challenge the calculation of the accumulated interest.
B. Respondent's Arguments (HSBC)
**Main Thesis:** The issuance of an alias writ of execution on an immutable final judgment is a non-litigious, ministerial act governed strictly by Rule 39, rendering constitutional content mandates and notice-of-hearing rules inapplicable.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Scope of Article VIII, Section 14:** The constitutional mandate applies exclusively to decisions and resolutions on the merits resolving controversies, not to interlocutory enforcement processes or writs of execution.
2. **Personality of Sole Proprietorship:** GGC has no separate juridical personality independent of Garcia. Service upon her office at the Batasan with responsible persons in charge complied with procedural rules.
3. **Ministerial Nature of Execution:** Execution of an entered, final, and executory judgment is an absolute matter of right. Motions for writs and alias writs of execution do not require advance notice or hearings, as the debtor's defenses on the merits are precluded by the doctrine of immutability.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the constitutional requirement under Article VIII, Section 14 of the 1987 Constitution—mandating that decisions state clearly and distinctly the facts and law on which they are based—applies to a writ or alias writ of execution.
2. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not an **ex parte** motion for the issuance of an alias writ of execution is a litigious motion requiring prior notice and hearing under the due process clause.
3. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the service of the Writ of Execution and Notice of Demand to Pay at the judgment debtor's legislative office, rather than her sole proprietorship's registered business addresses, was procedurally defective under Rule 13 of the Rules of Court.
4. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the legal interest rate awarded in a 2012 final and executory judgment (12% per annum) may be reduced to 6% per annum pursuant to BSP Monetary Board Circular No. 799, Series of 2013.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Applicability of Article VIII, Section 14 to Writs of Execution
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does Article VIII, Section 14 apply to writs or alias writs of execution? **NO.** Writs of execution are ministerial enforcement orders, not decisions or judgments on the merits.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
The form and content of writs of execution are governed by Rule 39, Section 8 of the Rules of Court, which requires: (1) issuance in the name of the Republic; (2) designation of the court, case number, title, and the dispositive portion of the subject judgment; and (3) a direction to the sheriff to satisfy the judgment out of property. Nothing in Rule 39, Section 8 demands that the court specify the facts and law upon which the writ is based.
Textually, Article VIII, Section 14 of the 1987 Constitution explicitly restricts its command to a "decision" or an order resolving a "petition for review or motion for reconsideration of a decision."
A writ of execution is an enforcement order issued after a judgment attains finality. It does not adjudicate rights or resolve the underlying merits of a dispute; it merely executes what was already resolved.
The factual and legal bases are already set forth in the underlying decision being enforced. Requiring them within the writ would be entirely redundant.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"A writ of execution is an order issued by the court upon motion once a judgment becomes final and executory. A writ of execution is not a decision or judgment. It is issued to enforce the terms of a final and executory decision or judgment. The facts and law on which the writ of execution is based should already be clearly set forth in the decision or judgment which it is enforcing."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Article VIII, Section 14 of the Constitution applies only to decisions resolving the merits of a lawsuit. A writ of execution is merely an administrative tool designed to carry out a final judgment; because it decides nothing new, it does not need to re-state the factual and legal background.
Issue 2: Due Process and Hearing Requirements for an Alias Writ of Execution
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Is a motion for an alias writ of execution a litigious motion requiring notice and hearing? **NO.** Execution of a final and executory judgment is a matter of right, making the issuance of an alias writ a ministerial duty that requires no advance notice or hearing.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Once a judgment becomes final and executory, the prevailing party is entitled to execution as a matter of right, and the court has the ministerial duty to issue the writ.
Settled jurisprudence establishes that motions for execution do not need to be served on the adverse party or set for hearing. The absence of advance notice does not violate due process because the obligor has already had her day in court.
Since an original writ of execution does not require a hearing, an alias writ—which merely reiterates the original writ that lapsed unsatisfied through no fault of the creditor—likewise does not require notice or hearing. It is not a litigious motion.
The debtor’s remedy is a motion to quash, which is strictly limited to exceptional grounds (e.g., change in situation making execution inequitable, controversy never submitted to court, improvident issuance, satisfaction of debt, or lack of authority). Garcia failed to prove any of these grounds and did not establish any specific mathematical error in the interest computation.
Entertaining dilatory challenges against ministerial writs violates the doctrine of immutability and unalterability of final judgments.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"When a prevailing party files a motion for execution of a final and executory judgment, it is not mandatory for such party to serve a copy of the motion to the adverse party and to set it for hearing. The absence of such advance notice to the judgment debtor does not constitute an infringement of due process... Since a motion for a writ of execution need not be set for hearing, it also follows that a motion for an alias writ of execution likewise does not need to be set for a hearing."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Once a decision is final, execution is a matter of right. A motion for an alias writ is non-litigious; setting it for hearing would merely invite dilatory tactics to stall the enforcement of an immutable judgment.
Issue 3: Validity of Service of the Writ of Execution
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Was the service of the writ improper because it was served at the Batasan rather than GGC's business addresses, or because it did not comply with Rule 13? **NO.** A sole proprietorship has no legal personality separate from its owner, and Rule 39—not Rule 13—governs the enforcement of execution writs.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
GGC is a sole proprietorship. Under Philippine law, a sole proprietorship does not possess an independent juridical personality distinct from its proprietor; Garcia and GGC are legally identical.
Garcia's invocation of Rule 13 is misplaced. Rule 13 governs the filing and service of pleadings, motions, and court papers. Writs of execution are governed by Rule 39, which dictates how writs are enforced against property and does not impose Rule 13 service formalities.
The record shows that the sheriffs attempted personal service twice at Garcia's official legislative office, and on the third attempt properly left copies with persons of suitable age and discretion having charge thereof (her Protocol Officer and Head of Operations). Garcia had actual knowledge of the writ.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Rule 39 enumerates only the manner by which the execution of a judgment may be enforced and does not provide strict requisites for a writ of execution's service. Significantly, the CA found that Garcia had been aware of the demand to pay and the Writ of Execution; she only claims—wrongly—that the Writ of Execution, Notice of Demand to Pay, and Alias Writ of Execution should have been served in accordance with Rule 13 of the Rules of Court."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Garcia cannot hide behind her trade name because a sole proprietorship has no separate personality from its individual owner. Furthermore, Rule 13 applies to pleadings, not to sheriffs enforcing execution writs under Rule 39.
Issue 4: Modification of Final Legal Interest Rates under BSP Circular No. 799
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Can the 12% legal interest rate fixed in a 2012 judgment be modified to 6% under BSP Circular No. 799? **NO.** Because the judgment became final and executory on February 25, 2013, before the circular took effect on June 30, 2013, the doctrine of immutability of judgments bars any modification.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
BSP-MB Circular No. 799, Series of 2013, lowered the legal interest rate from 12% to 6% per annum effective June 30, 2013.
However, the Supreme Court's Minute Resolution setting the interest rate at 12% per annum attained finality and was entered on February 25, 2013.
Under the doctrine of immutability of judgments, once a judgment attains finality, it becomes unalterable in all respects, even to correct perceived legal or factual errors, and even if applied to interest rate adjustments.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"However, since the Minute Resolution dated August 22, 2012 became final and executory on February 25, 2013, it can no longer be modified even as to the legal interest rate."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** A final and executory decision is carved in stone. Because the judgment became final months before the BSP circular took effect, the awarded 12% interest rate can never be altered.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I / Legal Method → Decisions and Resolutions - Factual and Legal Bases (Article VIII, Section 14)
**Constitutional & Political Law Mechanics:**
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:** Judicial Power (specifically the trial court’s enforcement power to execute final judgments) versus the procedural due process constraints and structural drafting mandates under Article VIII, Section 14 (requiring clear factual and legal expressions in decisions).
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny:** Standard of Grave Abuse of Discretion under Rule 65 (acted without or in excess of jurisdiction, or with whimsical, arbitrary, or capricious exercise of judgment).
**Constitutional Test Applied:** Textual and Functional Delimitation of "Decision." The Court interpreted "decision" strictly: Article VIII, Section 14 applies only to adjudications on the merits that resolve substantive controversies. It does not apply to interlocutory, ancillary, or enforcement orders (such as writs or alias writs of execution), whose factual and legal predicates are already settled in the underlying, immutable final judgment.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
**Constitutional Mandate of Art. VIII, Sec. 14 Requisites:**
1. Applicable Instrument: Must be a **Decision** on the merits, or an order/resolution resolving a **Petition for Review** or **Motion for Reconsideration of a decision**. (Trigger applied: A writ of execution fails this requisite—it is an enforcement order, not a decision).
2. Content Requirement: Must state clearly and distinctly the facts and law upon which it is based. (Trigger applied: Satisfied by the original final judgment; inapplicable to the secondary ministerial writ).
**Exceptions Allowing Quashal of an Alias Writ of Execution:**
1. Change in situation of parties making execution inequitable. (Absent)
2. Controversy never submitted to the judgment of the court. (Absent)
3. Writ improvidently issued, defective in substance, issued against the wrong party, or debt fully paid. (Absent)
4. Writ issued without authority. (Absent)
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Decision on the merits
 Ministerial duty
 Matter of right
 Non-litigious motion
 Immutability and unalterability of final judgments
 Sole proprietorship (lack of separate juridical personality)
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
This case falls under Article VIII, Section 14 because Garcia attempted to invalidate an Alias Writ of Execution by arguing that it failed to state the facts and the law on which it was based. The Supreme Court rejected this argument, ruling that the constitutional mandate applies strictly to "decisions" and resolutions on the merits. A writ of execution is an enforcement order issued as a ministerial duty pursuant to a final, immutable judgment; its legal and factual bases are already embedded in the judgment it executes, making Article VIII, Section 14 inapplicable to execution writs.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:** No separate opinions filed.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"ACCORDINGLY, the petition is DENIED. The Decision dated June 30, 2020 and the Resolution dated January 7, 2021 of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 159953 are hereby AFFIRMED. This case is hereby REMANDED to Branch 57, Regional Trial Court of Makati City for immediate execution of the Minute Resolution dated August 22, 2012 of the Supreme Court in G.R. No. 177734, which affirmed with modification the Decision dated October 17, 2006 of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. CV No. 75861.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court ruled in favor of HSBC and denied Garcia’s petition. The CA Decision and RTC Orders sustaining the Alias Writ of Execution were affirmed, and the case was remanded to the Makati RTC for immediate execution of the multi-million dollar judgment debt at the immutable 12% legal interest rate.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Yao v. Court of Appeals
**Full Official Caption:** George Yao, Petitioner, vs. Hon. Court of Appeals, and The People of the Philippines, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 132428; October 24, 2000; 398 Phil. 86 (2000); First Division; Davide, Jr., C.J. (**Ponente**); Puno, Pardo, and Ynares-Santiago, JJ., concurring; Kapunan, J., on leave.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
George Yao: Petitioner; President and General Manager of Tradeway Commercial Corporation (TCC), criminally charged and convicted of Unfair Competition.
Alfredo Roxas: Member of the Board of Directors of TCC; co-accused who was acquitted by the trial court.
Tradeway Commercial Corporation (TCC): Commercial enterprise whose Caloocan City warehouse was raided, yielding counterfeit General Electric (GE) fluorescent lamp starters.
Philippine Electrical Manufacturing Company (PEMCO): Private complainant; sole local subsidiary of GE-USA, represented by Castillo Laman Tan & Pantaleon Law Offices.
People of the Philippines: Public respondent; prosecuting sovereign represented by the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) and the Caloocan City Prosecutor.
Court of Appeals (CA): Public respondent appellate tribunal (Eleventh Division) that dismissed Yao’s appeal and directed execution.
** Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Caloocan City, Branch 121 (Presiding Judge Adoracion G. Angeles): Appellate court that rendered a one-page decision affirming **in toto Yao's conviction.
Metropolitan Trial Court (MeTC) of Caloocan City, Branch 52 (Presiding Judge Delfina Hernandez Santiago): Trial court of origin that convicted Yao of unfair competition.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on **Certiorari** under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court assailing the CA Resolution dated April 25, 1995 (dismissing Yao’s appeal and remanding the records to the MeTC for execution) and Resolution dated January 26, 1998 (denying his Urgent Motion to Set Aside Entry of Judgment).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Judicial Department (Article VIII) → Decisions and Resolutions — Factual and Legal Bases (Section 14)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Criminal Procedure / Civil Procedure → Mode of Appeal & Liberal Relaxation of Procedural Rules
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article VIII, Section 14, 1987 Constitution:**
"SECTION 14. **No decision shall be rendered by any court without expressing therein clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based.**

No petition for review or motion for reconsideration of a decision of the court shall be refused due course or denied without stating the legal basis therefor."
**Section 40, Batas Pambansa Blg. 129 (The Judiciary Reorganization Act of 1980):**
"Sec. 40. **Form of decision in appealed cases.** — **Every decision or final resolution of a court in appealed cases shall clearly and distinctly state the findings of fact and the conclusions of law on which it is based which may be contained in the decision or final resolution itself, or adopted by reference from those set forth in the decision, order or resolution appealed from.**"
**Factual Trigger:** After petitioner was convicted by the MeTC of unfair competition, the RTC on appeal affirmed his conviction via a hollow, one-page decision that merely copied the MeTC’s dispositive portion and declared without elaboration that it found "no cogent reason to disturb the findings"; thereafter, petitioner mistakenly filed an ordinary Notice of Appeal instead of a Petition for Review to the CA, causing the CA to treat the RTC decision as final and executory.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**June 1990:** PEMCO notices an influx of GE lamp starters in the local market despite having imported or manufactured none since 1983. PEMCO commissions Gardsmarks, Inc. to run a market survey; its investigator, Martin Remandaman, finds 30 retail establishments selling GE starters, all tracing their supply to TCC. Remandaman buys 50 counterfeit starters directly from TCC.
**October 10, 1990 (Search and Seizure):** Armed with a search warrant issued by MeTC Caloocan Branch 49, authorities raid TCC’s Caloocan City warehouse, seizing eight boxes containing 15,630 counterfeit GE fluorescent lamp starters.
**Subsequent Indictment:** An Information for unfair competition under Article 189(1) of the Revised Penal Code is filed before MeTC Caloocan Branch 52 against George Yao (President and General Manager of TCC) and Alfredo Roxas (Director), docketed as Criminal Case No. C-155713.
**Trial Phase:** Prosecution presents trademark specialist testimony and PEMCO officials showing genuine GE starters feature stenciled silk-screen printing, a drumlike glowbulb, and an M&M-shaped capacitor (.006) priced at P7.00 wholesale, whereas TCC’s products had sticker jackets, improper capacitors, and sold at P1.60. Yao testifies as the sole defense witness, admitting overall managerial control and purchase approvals, but denying knowledge that the units delivered by suppliers were counterfeit.
**October 20, 1993:** MeTC renders a 13-page decision acquitting Roxas (prosecution failed to prove corporate directorship at seizure) but convicting Yao as principal, sentencing him to 4 months and 21 days of **arresto mayor** to 1 year and 5 months of **prision correccional**, plus P20,000 consequential damages and P20,000 attorney’s fees.
**March 7, 1994:** MeTC denies Yao’s Motion for Reconsideration.
**May 24, 1994:** The appeal is docketed as Criminal Case No. C-47255(94) before RTC Caloocan Branch 121. Presiding Judge Adoracion G. Angeles orders both parties to submit memoranda.
**July 4, 1994:** Yao files his Appeal Memorandum.
**July 27, 1994:** Without awaiting the prosecution’s memorandum (filed later on August 20, 1994), Judge Angeles issues a one-page Decision affirming the MeTC **in toto**, simply quoting the MeTC **fallo** and stating: **"After going over the evidence on record, the Court finds no cogent reason to disturb the findings of the Metropolitan Trial Court."**
**August 16, 1994:** Yao receives the RTC decision.
**August 30, 1994:** Yao files a Motion for Reconsideration before the RTC (14 days of his 15-day appeal period used).
**September 28, 1994:** RTC issues an order denying the motion for reconsideration for being devoid of merit.
**October 3, 1994:** Yao receives the RTC denial order, leaving him exactly one (1) day to appeal.
**October 4, 1994:** Yao files a Notice of Appeal by registered mail addressed to the CA (an erroneous mode under Rule 42, which requires a Petition for Review).
**October 28, 1994:** CA receives the transmitted records from the RTC Branch Clerk of Court; the case is docketed as CA-G.R. CR No. 16893.
**February 28, 1995:** Acting on Yao’s motion for extension, the CA grants him an extension until March 12, 1995, to file his Appellant’s Brief. Yao files the brief on March 2, 1995.
**March 24, 1995:** The City Prosecutor files a Manifestation asserting the appeal period lapsed on October 4, 1994, because Yao resorted to a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review.
**April 25, 1995:** The CA issues a Resolution declaring the RTC decision final and executory due to the wrongful and belated appeal, ordering the remand of the records to the MeTC for execution.
**May 26, 1995:** CA issues an Entry of Judgment.
**Subsequent Interlocutory Filings:** Yao files an Urgent Motion to Set Aside Entry of Judgment, arguing that the April 25, 1995 Resolution did not formally dismiss the appeal and that procedural defects were cured.
**January 26, 1998:** The CA denies Yao's Urgent Motion, ruling that the April 25, 1995 Resolution had in effect dismissed the appeal.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (George Yao)
**Main Thesis:** The CA’s Entry of Judgment was legally defective, procedural lapses were cured, and he was denied substantive due process when his conviction was upheld without an adjudication on the merits.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **No Formal Judgment Dismissing Appeal:** Under Section 1, Rule 11 of the Revised Internal Rules of the Court of Appeals, entry of judgment is premature because the CA Resolution of April 25, 1995, did not explicitly dismiss the appeal.
2. **Defects Cured by Appellate Action:** Any procedural defect in the appeal was cured when the RTC transmitted the records and the CA actively took cognizance, ordered the filing of an appellant's brief, and granted an extension of time.
3. **Equity Over Technicalities:** The invocation of a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review was a harmless procedural misstep; the Court should relax technical rules because none of the elements of unfair competition were proven, and strict adherence sacrifices substantial justice.
B. Respondent's Arguments (People of the Philippines / OSG)
**Main Thesis:** The petition is devoid of merit because Yao failed to perfect his appeal in the manner and time prescribed by law, rendering the RTC conviction final, executory, and beyond appellate jurisdiction.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Wrong Mode of Appeal Fatal:** The RTC was acting in its appellate capacity; pursuant to Section 1, Rule 42 of the Rules of Court, the exclusive mode of appeal was a Petition for Review. Yao filed a Notice of Appeal.
2. **Lapse of Reglementary Period:** When Yao received the denial of his motion for reconsideration on October 3, 1994, he had only one day left. By filing the wrong pleading on October 4, 1994, he failed to file the proper petition within the statutory period, divesting the CA of jurisdiction.
3. **Unambiguous Resolution:** While the April 25, 1995 CA Resolution did not state the word "dismissed" in the body, its declaration of finality and order to remand for execution operated as an effective and irrevocable dismissal of the appeal.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the petitioner perfected his appeal to the Court of Appeals when he filed a Notice of Appeal instead of a Petition for Review within the remaining reglementary period.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the one-page decision of the Regional Trial Court affirming **in toto** the MeTC conviction complies with the mandate of Section 14, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution requiring courts to state clearly and distinctly the factual and legal bases of their decisions.
3. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the procedural lapse committed by petitioner in choosing the wrong mode of appeal must yield to the demands of substantial justice in order to set aside the void RTC judgment.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Validity and Timeliness of the Mode of Appeal
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did Yao properly perfect his appeal to the Court of Appeals? **NO.** Yao availed himself of the wrong mode of appeal by filing an ordinary Notice of Appeal instead of a Petition for Review under Rule 42 within the remaining reglementary period.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Appeal is not a natural right or an inherent component of due process; it is a purely statutory privilege that must be exercised strictly within the conditions set by law.
Perfecting an appeal within the prescribed reglementary period and via the mandatory mode is both mandatory and jurisdictional. Non-compliance extinguishes appellate jurisdiction and leaves the judgment final.
Yao had 15 days from August 16, 1994, to appeal. His motion for reconsideration filed on August 30, 1994 (14 days elapsed), tolled the period. Upon receiving the denial on October 3, 1994, he had only one day left—October 4, 1994. By filing a notice of appeal rather than a petition for review, Yao lost the right to appeal under established procedural rules.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The right to appeal is not a constitutional, natural or inherent right. It is a statutory privilege of statutory origin and, therefore, available only if granted or provided by statute. Since the right to appeal is not a natural right nor a part of due process, it may be exercised only in the manner and in accordance with the provisions of law."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** An appeal from an RTC decision rendered in its appellate jurisdiction can only be elevated to the CA through a Rule 42 Petition for Review. Yao mistakenly filed an ordinary Notice of Appeal with only one day left in his appeal period, which fundamentally failed to toll or perfect an appeal.
Issue 2: Constitutional Validity of the RTC's One-Page Decision
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does the one-page decision of the RTC pass constitutional muster under Section 14, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution? **NO.** The RTC decision is an absolute nullity because it failed to state any facts or law upon which it was based, reducing judicial review to an empty formality.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Section 14, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution explicitly forbids any court from rendering a decision without expressing therein clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based. This is reinforced by Section 40 of B.P. Blg. 129 and procedural rules.
** While "memorandum decisions" are sanctioned for appellate courts under B.P. Blg. 129 to foster judicial efficiency, they must rigorously meet the conditions laid down in **Francisco v. Permskul:
1. The decision cannot incorporate findings of fact and conclusions of law only by "remote reference"; it must embody them directly in an annex attached to and made an indispensable part of the decision.
2. The decision being adopted must itself comply with Section 14, Article VIII.
3. Memorandum decisions must be sparingly used and confined to simple litigations where facts are largely undisputed and no complex doctrinal issues exist.
The RTC judgment did not even qualify as a memorandum decision. It merely copied the dispositive portion of the MeTC ruling and concluded, without a single factual summary or legal analysis, that there was no cogent reason to disturb the MeTC findings.
** The constitutional mandate is designed to ensure that the judge decides through legal reasoning rather than **ipse dixit. A decision devoid of factual and legal bases violates due process because it deprives the losing party of the ability to pinpoint judicial errors for meaningful appeal.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"Tested against these standards, we find that the RTC decision at bar miserably failed to meet them and, therefore, fell short of the constitutional injunction. The RTC decision is brief indeed, but it is starkly hallow, otiosely written, vacuous in its content and trite in its form. It achieved nothing and attempted at nothing, not even at a simple summation of facts which could easily be done. Its inadequacy speaks for itself."

"The parties to a litigation should be informed of how it was decided, with an explanation of the factual and legal reasons that led to the conclusions of the court. The court cannot simply say that judgment is rendered in favor of X and against Y and just leave it at that without any justification whatsoever for its action. The losing party is entitled to know why he lost... It is, thus, a safeguard against the impetuosity of the judge, preventing him from deciding **ipse dixit**."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** A court cannot simply copy-paste the dispositive portion of a lower court decision and declare that it finds no reason to disturb it. Section 14, Article VIII requires judges to explain how and why they decided, preventing arbitrary **ipse dixit** rulings and preserving the litigant’s due process right to know the precise grounds of conviction.
Issue 3: Substantial Justice vs. Procedural Technicality
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Can the Supreme Court relax technical rules on the wrong mode of appeal to strike down the constitutionally deficient RTC decision? **YES.** Where an appealed decision is a constitutional nullity, procedural rules of the most mandatory character must yield to prevent manifest injustice and the denial of due process.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
** While Yao resorted to the wrong mode of appeal, the judgment being appealed from was void **ab initio for direct disobedience to the fundamental law.
A void judgment produces no legal effects and can never attain finality.
Although the CA cannot strictly be faulted for enforcing procedural rules regarding appeals, the Supreme Court, in the exercise of equity and its primary duty to uphold the Constitution, may relax procedural rules where manifest injustice would otherwise result, particularly in a criminal case where an individual’s liberty is jeopardized.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"In the interest of substantial justice, procedural rules of the most mandatory character in terms of compliance, may be relaxed. In other words, if strict adherence to the letter of the law would result in absurdity and manifest injustice or where the merit of a party's cause is apparent and outweighs consideration of non-compliance with certain formal requirements, procedural rules should definitely be liberally construed."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Even though Yao committed a fatal error by using a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review, the Supreme Court excused the lapse because the RTC’s one-page decision was completely void under the Constitution. A void decision cannot become final and executory, especially when a person's liberty is at stake.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → Judicial Department → Decisions and Resolutions — Factual and Legal Bases (Article VIII, Section 14).
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (The Francisco v. Permskul Memorandum Decision Test):**
1. **Form of Incorporation:** Findings of fact and conclusions of law cannot be incorporated by remote reference; they must be embodied in a statement directly attached as an annex and made an indispensable part of the decision.
→ **Applied to Facts:** FAILED. The RTC did not attach the MeTC decision as an annex nor did it reproduce the facts; it only copied the MeTC dispositive portion (**fallo**).
2. **Validity of Underlying Decision:** The decision being adopted must itself comply with Article VIII, Section 14.
→ **Applied to Facts:** While the MeTC decision contained findings, mere unattached adoption cannot cure an unconstitutional appellate decision.
3. **Threshold of Litigation:** Must be sparingly used only in simple litigations (e.g., ordinary collection cases) where the facts are largely undisputed and no complex doctrinal complications exist.
→ **Applied to Facts:** FAILED. This was a criminal prosecution for unfair competition involving technical intellectual property distinctions and disputed corporate knowledge.
4. **Direct Meeting of Issues:** The appellate decision must directly confront the assignments of error raised on appeal.
→ **Applied to Facts:** FAILED. The RTC decision failed to resolve or even mention a single issue raised in Yao’s appeal memorandum.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Ipse dixit (deciding purely by bare assertion without supporting reason).
 Memorandum Decision (a summary appellate decision adopting the findings/conclusions of the lower court).
 Clear and distinct statement of facts and law (the constitutional minimum for valid judicial adjudication).
 Remote reference (impermissible indirect adoption of another court’s findings without attaching them).
 Substantial justice over procedural technicality (the equitable doctrine relaxing strict adherence to rules of appeal to correct a void judgment).
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"In **Yao v. Court of Appeals**, the Supreme Court nullified a one-page RTC appellate decision that affirmed a criminal conviction for unfair competition by merely quoting the trial court's **fallo** and stating there was 'no cogent reason to disturb' the findings. The Court ruled that such a vacuous decision violates Section 14, Article VIII of the Constitution, which requires all courts to state clearly and distinctly the facts and law on which decisions are based. Furthermore, the decision failed to qualify as a valid memorandum decision under the **Francisco v. Permskul** doctrine because it did not annex the lower court's findings nor resolve the assigned errors. Even though the accused committed a fatal procedural error by filing a notice of appeal instead of a petition for review, the Court relaxed the rules because a void judgment can never become final."
**Constitutional & Political Law Lens Focus:**
 State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation: The Judicial power to convict and deprive an individual of liberty (Section 1, Article VIII) was exercised in contravention of the structural and procedural due process check embodied in Section 14, Article VIII (the requirement of reasoned decisions).
 Level of Judicial Scrutiny: Absolute invalidation. Failure to articulate factual and legal bases renders the judgment a constitutional nullity; expediency and brevity can never substitute for substance.
 Justiciability & Review Audit: The Court bypassed the procedural barrier of an unperfected appeal (jurisdictional finality) by invoking substantial justice to review and strike down an unconstitutional, void act of a trial court.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, in view of all the foregoing, the petition in this case is GRANTED. The questioned 25 April 1995 resolution of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. No. 16893 is hereby SET ASIDE and the 27 July 1994 decision of the Regional Trial Court, Branch 121 of Kalookan City rendered in its appellate jurisdiction is NULLIFIED. The records are hereby remanded to said Regional Trial Court for further proceedings and for the rendition of judgment in accordance with the mandate of Section 14, Article VIII of the Constitution.

No costs.

SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** George Yao prevailed. The Supreme Court set aside the Court of Appeals’ dismissal and declared the RTC’s one-page decision completely void for violating the Constitution; the case was remanded to the RTC to prepare a proper, reasoned judgment containing full factual findings and legal conclusions.
