### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Eizmendi v. Fernandez (Resolution on Motion for Reconsideration)
**Full Official Caption:** Francisco C. Eizmendi, Jr., Jose S. Tayag, Jr., Joaquin L. San Agustin, Eduardo V. Francisco, Edmidio V. Ramos, Jr., Albert G. Blancaflor, Rey Nathaniel C. Ifurung, Manuel H. Acosta, Jr., and Valle Verde Country Club, Inc., Petitioners, v. Teodorico P. Fernandez, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 215280; November 27, 2019; 866 Phil. 638; Special Third Division; Peralta, C.J. (**Ponente**); Leonen and J. Reyes, Jr., JJ., concurring; A. Reyes, Jr., J., dissenting; Gesmundo, J., on wellness leave.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Francisco C. Eizmendi, Jr., Jose S. Tayag, Jr., Joaquin L. San Agustin, Eduardo V. Francisco, Edmidio V. Ramos, Jr., Albert G. Blancaflor, Rey Nathaniel C. Ifurung, and Manuel H. Acosta, Jr. (Individual Petitioners):** Claimed newly elected members of the Board of Directors (BOD) of Valle Verde Country Club, Inc. (VVCCI) following the contested February 23, 2013 annual meeting.
**Valle Verde Country Club, Inc. (VVCCI) (Corporate Petitioner):** A non-stock sports and recreational club corporation whose leadership and board actions are disputed.
**Teodorico P. Fernandez (Respondent):** Member of VVCCI suspended for six months by the Individual Petitioners; plaintiff in the underlying intra-corporate complaint assailing the BOD's authority and his suspension.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Resolution resolving Respondent Fernandez's **Motion for Reconsideration** dated October 29, 2018, seeking to set aside the Supreme Court's Decision dated September 5, 2018.
The September 5, 2018 Decision granted Petitioners' Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45, reversed and set aside the Court of Appeals' (CA) Decision (June 30, 2014) and Resolution (October 24, 2014) in CA-G.R. SP No. 134704, and reinstated the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Pasig City, Branch 158 Order (January 28, 2014) in Commercial Case No. 13-202, which disallowed evidence concerning the February 23, 2013 BOD elections.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law / Remedial Law → Effects of Decisions and Resolutions → Stare Decisis / Precedential Effect of Minute Resolutions vs. Signed Decisions
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Special Proceedings / Commercial Law → Interim Rules of Procedure Governing Intra-Corporate Controversies (A.M. No. 01-2-04-SC) → Election Contests (Rule 6, Sections 2, 3, & 4)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article VIII, Section 4(3), 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Cases or matters heard by a division shall be decided or resolved with the concurrence of a majority of the Members who actually took part in the deliberations on the issues in the case and voted thereon, and in no case without the concurrence of at least three of such Members. When the required number is not obtained, the case shall be decided **en banc**: **Provided**, that **no doctrine or principle of law laid down by the court in a decision rendered en banc or in division may be modified or reversed except by the court sitting en banc.**"
**Article VIII, Section 14, Paragraph 1, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"**No decision shall be rendered by any court without expressing therein clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based.**"
**Section 6(c), Rule 13, Internal Rules of the Supreme Court (A.M. No. 10-4-20-SC):**
"By **unsigned resolution**, the Court disposes of the case on the merits, but its ruling is essentially meaningful only to the parties; has no significant doctrinal value; or is minimal interest to the law profession, the academe, or the public."
**Section 2, Rule 6, Interim Rules of Procedure for Intra-Corporate Controversies (A.M. No. 01-2-04-SC):**
"**Definition.** — An election contest refers to **any controversy or dispute involving title or claim to any elective office in a stock or non-stock corporation, the validation of proxies, the manner and validity of elections, and the qualifications of candidates, including the proclamation of winners**, to the office of director, trustee or other officer directly elected by the stockholders in a close corporation or by members of a non-stock corporation where the articles of incorporation or by-laws so provide."
**Section 3, Rule 6, Interim Rules of Procedure for Intra-Corporate Controversies (A.M. No. 01-2-04-SC):**
"**Complaint.** — In addition to the requirements in section 4, Rule 2 of these Rules, the complaint in an election contest must state the following: (1) The case was filed **within fifteen (15) days from the date of the election** if the by-laws of the corporation do not provide for a procedure for resolution of the controversy, or within fifteen (15) days from the resolution of the controversy by the corporation as provided in its by-laws; and (2) The complainant has exhausted all administrative remedies provided in the by-laws."
**Factual Trigger:**
Following a disputed annual meeting on February 23, 2013 where the hold-over board declared a lack of quorum but the Individual Petitioners proceeded to declare a quorum and elect themselves as directors, the newly installed board suspended Respondent Fernandez from VVCCI for six months on October 18, 2013. On November 28, 2013—nine months after the election—Fernandez filed a complaint to nullify his suspension and the underlying corporate acts by challenging the board’s legitimate authority, prompting the RTC to bar any evidence questioning the election because the 15-day reglementary period for election contests had expired.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**February 23, 2013:** VVCCI convenes its scheduled annual membership meeting through its hold-over BOD. The hold-over board adjourns the meeting for lack of quorum. Immediately after adjournment, the Individual Petitioners (Eizmendi, Jr. et al.) take over the proceedings, determine quorum using 1,500 membership certificates as the base, declare the presence of a quorum (alleging 790 or 793 members present in person or by proxy), and elect themselves as the new BOD of VVCCI.
**October 14, 2013:** In G.R. No. 209120 (**Valle Verde Country Club, Inc., represented by its hold-over Board of Directors, etc. v. Francisco C. Eizmendi, Jr., et al.**), the Supreme Court issues an unsigned/minute resolution dismissing VVCCI's petition and holding that an action assailing the February 23, 2013 election based on lack of quorum and proxy validity constitutes an "election contest" under Section 2, Rule 6 of the Interim Rules.
**October 18, 2013:** The newly constituted BOD under the Individual Petitioners passes a resolution finding Respondent Fernandez guilty of less serious violations of the club's by-laws and penalizing him with a six-month suspension from VVCCI.
**November 28, 2013:** Fernandez files a Complaint for Invalidation of Corporate Acts and Resolutions with Application for Writ of Preliminary Injunction against the Individual Petitioners before the RTC of Pasig City, Branch 158 (Commercial Case No. 13-202), praying to nullify the February 23, 2013 meeting, invalidate subsequent board resolutions (specifically his suspension), and enjoin the board from acting.
**January 28, 2014:** During the injunction hearing, the RTC rules that Fernandez’s challenge against the legitimacy of the BOD composition is an election contest filed beyond the mandatory 15-day period under the Interim Rules. The RTC issues an Order disallowing the presentation of any evidence relating to the conduct and validity of the February 23, 2013 elections, limiting the trial solely to whether the six-month suspension complied with due process.
**June 30, 2014:** The CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 134704) reverses the RTC, ruling that Fernandez’s complaint is not an election contest but an ordinary intra-corporate action questioning the authority of the directors, thus making evidence of the election admissible.
**October 24, 2014:** The CA denies Petitioners’ Motion for Reconsideration.
**September 5, 2018:** The Supreme Court (Third Division) renders a Decision granting Petitioners' Rule 45 petition, reversing the CA, and reinstating the RTC Order of January 28, 2014. The Court applies the ruling in the October 14, 2013 **Valle Verde** Resolution, holding that Fernandez's challenge to the election constitutes an election contest barred by the 15-day prescriptive period.
**October 29, 2018:** Fernandez files the present Motion for Reconsideration assailing the September 5, 2018 Decision.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondent Fernandez's Arguments (Movant)
**Main Thesis:** The Court erred in applying **stare decisis** to his complaint; the October 14, 2013 Resolution in G.R. No. 209120 (**Valle Verde**) is an unsigned minute resolution that has no binding precedential or doctrinal value upon non-parties, and his complaint is an action to invalidate unauthorized corporate acts, not an election contest.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Lack of Doctrinal Precedent: Under Section 6(c), Rule 13 of the Internal Rules of the Supreme Court, unsigned minute resolutions are meaningful only to the immediate parties and carry no significant doctrinal value.
 Obiter Dictum:** The legal disquisitions in **Valle Verde** regarding what constitutes an "election contest" were mere **obiter dicta** and cannot bind subsequent litigation under the doctrine of **stare decisis.
 Inapplicability of Statutory Construction Maxim: The maxim "what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly" applies only when there is an explicit constitutional or statutory prohibition; it cannot be extended to procedural rules of court, such as a 15-day prescriptive period.
 Non-Applicability of 15-Day Period: The 15-day limitation under Section 3, Rule 6 of the Interim Rules cannot bind him because he was not a candidate in the February 23, 2013 election and had no cause of action until his suspension on October 18, 2013.
 Disregard of Prayer: The prayer of a complaint cannot create a cause of action and should be disregarded when determining the true nature of an action.
B. Petitioners' Arguments (Eizmendi, Jr. et al. & VVCCI)
**Main Thesis:** The complaint is a disguised election contest barred by the strict 15-day limitation of the Interim Rules, and the RTC correctly excluded evidence attacking the election.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Prescription of Election Challenge: Fernandez is a member of VVCCI; any challenge to the election of the board of directors had to be mounted within 15 days from February 23, 2013.
 Prevention of Collateral Attacks: Allowing a disciplined member to collaterally assail board authority months later by attacking the underlying election would open the floodgates to continuous disruption of corporate leadership.
 Harmonious Application of Procedural Rules: Rules of court have the force and effect of law; procedural rules setting strict periods must be enforced to ensure speedy intra-corporate adjudication.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the unsigned/minute Resolution in G.R. No. 209120 (**Valle Verde**) constitutes a binding precedent that governs the characterization of Fernandez's complaint under the doctrine of **stare decisis**.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the disquisitions in the **Valle Verde** Resolution defining an "election contest" constitute mere **obiter dicta**.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the statutory construction principle "what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly" applies to the interpretation of procedural rules, specifically the 15-day reglementary period for election contests under the Interim Rules.
4.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not a non-candidate member who sustained injury months after an election is exempted from the 15-day prescriptive period for filing an election contest under Rule 6 of the Interim Rules.
5.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the relief prayed for in the complaint must be considered in determining the true nature of the action and the court's jurisdiction.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Precedential Effect of the Unsigned "Valle Verde" Resolution
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** While ordinary minute resolutions do not create binding judicial precedent for third parties, an unsigned resolution that clearly and distinctly states the factual and legal grounds directly resolving a substantive issue of law creates a binding precedent on that specific legal characterization.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 General Rule on Minute Resolutions:** As reiterated in **Philippine Health Care Providers, Inc. v. CIR** and **Deutsche Bank AG Manila Branch v. CIR**, an unsigned minute resolution dismisses a petition on the merits, rendering the challenged decision final and operating as **res judicata** between the same parties on the same subject matter and issues. If different parties or different subject matters are involved, a typical minute resolution does not establish a binding precedent under **stare decisis, because it generally lacks constitutional exposition of facts and law, is signed only by the Clerk of Court, and is unpublished in the Philippine Reports.
 The Exception/Distinction in This Case:** The October 14, 2013 **Valle Verde Resolution was not a bare dismissal for failure to comply with formal or substantive procedural requirements. Rather, it set forth "clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based."
 Judicial Authority: Even though signed by the Division Clerk of Court, the resolution was promulgated under the explicit authority of the Justices who deliberated on the case. It directly determined the legal threshold under Section 2, Rule 6 of the Interim Rules, establishing that when a complaint’s averments and prayers assert that an election was unlawfully held due to lack of quorum and proxy invalidity, the dispute is an election contest. Hence, it operates as a binding legal standard for characterization of identical factual triggers.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Even if **Valle Verde** is an unsigned resolution, it still creates a binding precedent to the extent that the Court pointed out in the assailed Decision, **i.e.**, if the allegations and prayers in the complaint raise issues of validation of proxies, and the manner and validity of elections, such as the nullification of the election was unlawfully conducted due to lack of quorum, then such complaint falls under the definition of 'election contest' under the Interim Rules. This is because **Valle Verde** stated clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based, and it is not just a mere dismissal of a petition for failure to comply with formal and substantive requirements."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
A minute resolution usually does not set a universal precedent because it merely disposes of a case between specific parties without explaining the law. However, where an unsigned resolution actually contains a full legal analysis setting out clear facts and substantive statutory applications—as the Court did in the 2013 **Valle Verde** case—it carries authoritative legal weight. The Court held that it is bound to treat an identical challenge involving the same meeting and the same election in the exact same legal manner.
Issue 2: Whether the Pronouncements in "Valle Verde" Were Obiter Dicta
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The legal disquisitions were not **obiter dicta** because they directly addressed and adjudicated the core substantive question raised by the petitioner in that case.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Definition of Obiter Dictum:** Citing **Land Bank of the Philippines v. Suntay**, an **obiter dictum is an incidental or collateral opinion expressed by a court upon a point not directly before it or not necessary to the determination of the cause, made without full consideration or argument.
 Direct Adjudication:** In **Valle Verde, VVCCI specifically argued that its petition was not an election contest because the annual meeting was adjourned and no valid election occurred. The Court directly evaluated this argument against Section 2, Rule 6 of the Interim Rules and expressly held that asserting an election was void for lack of quorum directly places the validity and manner of the election in issue.
Because resolving that question was the central holding necessary to determine whether VVCCI’s complaint was viable, the pronouncement was an essential judicial determination, not an incidental remark.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"**Valle Verde** directly resolved the substantive issue raised by VVCCI as to whether its complaint is an election contest... The determination of the validity of the proxies and of the manner and validity of elections is necessary in adjudicating whether the respondents are the lawful directors and officers of Valle Verde... Valle Verde's assertion that there was no election is merely an effect of the declaration of the nullity of the election if the current petition would be found meritorious."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
A statement is only **obiter dictum** if it is an unnecessary, passing remark that has nothing to do with the judgment. In **Valle Verde**, the petitioner squarely asked the Court whether an action to stop persons claiming to be directors after an adjourned meeting was an "election contest." The Court had to answer that exact question to decide the case; therefore, its answer was a binding ratio decidendi.
Issue 3: Application of the Maxim "What Cannot Be Done Directly Cannot Be Done Indirectly" to Procedural Rules
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Rules of procedure promulgated under constitutional authority have the force and effect of law; statutory construction doctrines apply equally to procedural rules to prevent the circumvention of mandatory deadlines.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Force of Law:** Under Section 5(5), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution, the Supreme Court has the power to promulgate rules of pleading, practice, and procedure. Established jurisprudence (**Shioji v. Harvey) confirms that rules of court have the force and effect of law.
 Harmonious Construction:** As pronounced in **Blay v. Baña, general canons of statutory construction apply when interpreting procedural rules.
 Circumvention Prohibited: The Interim Rules impose a strict 15-day prescriptive period for election contests to quickly remove uncertainty surrounding corporate management. Allowing a party to challenge the validity of an election months or years later under the guise of an action to nullify board resolutions would permit an indirect circumvention of the 15-day bar, violating the core principle that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"To disallow the application of such principle would defeat the purpose of the Interim Rules which is meant to expedite the resolution of intra-corporate cases, and would sanction the circumvention of said rules. As stressed in the Court's Decision, the 15-day reglementary period to file an election contest under the Interim Rules aims to hasten the submission and resolution of corporate election controversies, so that the state of uncertainty in the corporate leadership is settled."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
Rules of Court promulgated by the Supreme Court carry the same weight as statutes. The Interim Rules require corporate election disputes to be filed within 15 days so corporations are not paralyzed by constant leadership doubts. A litigant cannot be allowed to bypass this strict 15-day rule by simply labeling his lawsuit as an "action to invalidate corporate acts" when the real substance of his claim requires proving that the board was never validly elected.
Issue 4: Application of the 15-Day Prescriptive Period to Non-Candidates
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The 15-day prescriptive period under Section 3, Rule 6 applies universally to any person questioning an election; the rule makes no distinction between candidates and non-candidates.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Objective Criteria:** Section 2 and Section 3 of Rule 6 determine an "election contest" solely by the **subject matter of the controversy (title to office, validation of proxies, validity and manner of election, qualifications), not by the status of the complainant.
 Member Status: Fernandez was a member of VVCCI at the time of the February 23, 2013 election. His right to assail the election accrued from the date the election was conducted.
 Policy Hazard: Creating an exception for non-candidates who are later disciplined would destabilize corporate governance. Any member subjected to corporate discipline could revive expired election challenges anytime by simply asserting that the disciplining board lacked legitimate authority due to an invalid election held months or years prior.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The definition of an election contest is clear; it hardly distinguishes whether the complainant is a participant in the election or not, and it is determined only by the nature of the controversy or dispute involved... Fernandez is a member of VVCCI, and the time to question their election is within 15 days from the election; to allow him to belatedly question their authority as members of the board would open the floodgate to any member who will be disciplined by petitioners or to question their act by questioning the validity of their election anytime."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
The 15-day deadline to challenge a corporate election applies to all members, not just those who ran for office. If the Court allowed members to wait until they were disciplined by the board to challenge the original election, the 15-day prescriptive rule would become meaningless, and no corporate board’s authority would ever be definitively settled.
Issue 5: Significance of the Prayer in Determining the Cause of Action
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The prayer for relief is an integral part of the body of the pleading under Rule 7 of the Rules of Court and must be considered alongside factual allegations to ascertain the true nature of the action and court jurisdiction.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Composition of Pleading: Under Section 2, Rule 7 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, the body of a pleading explicitly includes the relief prayed for.
 Jurisdictional Standard:** Citing **Spouses Trayvilla v. Sejas**, subject-matter jurisdiction and the nature of an action are governed by the relevant allegations in the complaint, the law in force, and the **character of the relief sought.
 Precedent on Election Contests:** In **Yujuico v. Quiambao, the Court directly relied on the relief sought in the complaint (nullification of an election conducted at an improper venue) to conclude that the action was an election contest governed by the Interim Rules. Because Fernandez's prayer expressly sought to nullify the February 23, 2013 annual membership meeting and board elections, the prayer itself confirmed that the action was partly an election contest.
 RTC Dismissal Valid: The RTC committed no grave abuse of discretion under Section 4, Rule 6 and Section 3, Rule 1 of the Interim Rules when it barred evidence on the election, as the election contest cause of action was barred on its face by prescription.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Section 2, Rule 7 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure provides that the body of the pleading sets forth its designation, the allegations of the party's claims or defenses, the relief prayed for, and the date of the pleading. Considering that the prayer in a complaint is a 'relief,' which is part of the body of such pleading, the prayer in Fernandez's complaint cannot be simply ignored in deciding his case."
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:**
A court cannot ignore what a plaintiff explicitly asks for in the prayer of his complaint. Under the Rules of Court, the relief prayed for is part of the pleading and defines the nature of the lawsuit. Because Fernandez specifically prayed for the nullification of the election meeting, his complaint was undeniably an election contest, and the trial court correctly dismissed that portion of the case as time-barred.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I / Remedial Law | Effects of Decisions and Resolutions (Precedential Value of Minute/Unsigned Resolutions vs. Full Signed Decisions; **Stare Decisis**)
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
1.  Standard Minute Resolution (Non-Precedential):
Signed only by the Clerk of Court.
No statement of facts or legal disquisition (falls outside Section 14, Article VIII, Constitution).
Not published in the Philippine Reports.
 Legal Effect:** Operates as **res judicata **only** between identical parties, subject matter, and causes of action. Holds **no stare decisis** effect for third parties.
2.  Substantive Unsigned Resolution (Precedential Exception under Eizmendi):
Issued under the authority of the deliberating Justices.
Expresses "clearly and distinctly the facts and the law on which it is based."
Directly adjudicates and disposes of a substantive question of law (not dismissed on mere technical defects).
 Legal Effect: Operates as a **binding precedent** (**stare decisis**) on the specific legal issue resolved, even against subsequent actions involving different non-parties.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Minute Resolution / Unsigned Resolution
 Stare Decisis et non quieta movere
 Res Judicata
 Obiter Dictum** vs. **Ratio Decidendi
 Rule-Making Power of the Supreme Court (Sec. 5[5], Art. VIII)
 "What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly"
 Election Contest (Sec. 2, Rule 6, Interim Rules)
 15-Day Reglementary Period
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
Under the topic **Effects of Decisions and Resolutions**, **Eizmendi v. Fernandez** clarifies the exception to the rule that minute resolutions lack precedential value under **stare decisis**. While typical minute resolutions bind only the immediate parties as **res judicata**, an unsigned resolution that clearly and distinctly sets forth the factual and legal grounds resolving a substantive issue of law establishes a binding judicial precedent. Applying this, the Court held that its prior unsigned resolution in **Valle Verde** definitively established that any complaint assailing the validity of an election for lack of quorum is an "election contest"; thus, Fernandez’s subsequent complaint questioning the same election was barred by the mandatory 15-day prescriptive period.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Dissenting Opinion of Associate Justice Andres B. Reyes, Jr.:**
 Core Divergence: Voted to grant the Motion for Reconsideration, set aside the September 5, 2018 Decision, and reinstate the CA Decision.
 Reasoning:** Argued that a holistic reading of Fernandez’s complaint reveals its true nature as an action assailing the inherent validity of a corporate meeting for lack of quorum under Section 50 in relation to Section 52 of the Corporation Code, which is legally distinct from an "election contest" under Rule 6 of the Interim Rules (citing **Bernas v. Cinco** and **Lim v. Moldex Land). The prayer to invalidate the board is merely incidental to declaring the meeting void. Treating any challenge to a meeting as an election contest forces litigants into an impossible 15-day prescriptive window and sets a dangerous precedent. The RTC should have received evidence regarding the lack of quorum.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"**WHEREFORE**, the Motion for Reconsideration dated October 29, 2018 is **DENIED** for lack of merit.

**SO ORDERED.**"
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Respondent Fernandez’s Motion for Reconsideration was denied with finality, meaning Petitioners won. The Supreme Court upheld its September 5, 2018 Decision, keeping in force the RTC Order that completely barred Fernandez from introducing any evidence attacking the February 23, 2013 board elections; Fernandez's remaining trial in Commercial Case No. 13-202 was restricted purely to whether his six-month suspension violated due process.

digest:
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** CHR Employees’ Association v. CHR (Resolution)
**Full Official Caption:** Commission on Human Rights Employees' Association (CHREA), Represented by its President, Marcial A. Sanchez, Jr., Petitioner, vs. Commission on Human Rights, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 155336; July 21, 2006; 528 Phil. 658; Chico-Nazario, **J.**; Special Second Division; Concurring: Puno (**Chairman**), Austria-Martinez, Callejo, Sr., and Tinga, **JJ.** No separate opinions filed.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Petitioner:** Commission on Human Rights Employees' Association (CHREA), the legitimate collective negotiating representative of the rank-and-file employees of the Commission on Human Rights, represented by its President, Marcial A. Sanchez, Jr.
**Respondent:** Commission on Human Rights (CHR), an independent constitutional office created under Article XIII, Section 17 of the 1987 Constitution, acting through its Chairperson and Commissioners.
**Intervening Administrative Bodies:**
 Department of Budget and Management (DBM): Headed by Secretary Benjamin Diokno; the executive agency mandated by law to administer the compensation and position classification system under Republic Act No. 6758.
 Civil Service Commission (CSC): Constitutional commission composed of the CSC-National Capital Region (CSC-NCR) Office and the CSC-Central Office.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** This resolution arose from a **Motion for Reconsideration** filed by the CHR challenging the Supreme Court’s Division Decision dated November 25, 2004. In that underlying Decision, the Court granted CHREA’s Rule 45 Petition for Review on Certiorari, reversed the Court of Appeals (CA) Decision dated November 29, 2001 and Resolution dated September 11, 2002 (CA-G.R. SP No. 59678), reinstated the CSC-NCR ruling of March 29, 1999, and disallowed CHR Resolutions Nos. A98-047, A98-055, and A98-062 for lack of DBM approval.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Judicial Department & Independent Constitutional Bodies → Fiscal Autonomy (Scope, Extent, and Limitations)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Administrative Law → Position Classification and Compensation Scheme → Compensation Standardization Law (R.A. No. 6758) & Role of the DBM
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional & Statutory Provisions:**
**Article XIII, Section 17, 1987 Constitution:**
Sec. 17. (1) There is hereby created an independent office called the Commission on Human Rights.
x x x x
(4) **The approved annual appropriations of the Commission shall be automatically and regularly released.**
**Article VIII, Section 3, 1987 Constitution (Judiciary):**
Sec. 3. **The Judiciary shall enjoy fiscal autonomy.** Appropriations for the Judiciary may not be reduced by the legislature below the amount appropriated for the previous year and, after approval, **shall be automatically and regularly released.**
**Article IX, Part A, Section 5, 1987 Constitution (Constitutional Commissions):**
Sec. 5. **The Commission shall enjoy fiscal autonomy. Their approved annual appropriations shall be automatically and regularly released.**
**Article XI, Section 14, 1987 Constitution (Office of the Ombudsman):**
Sec. 14. **The Office of the Ombudsman shall enjoy fiscal autonomy. Its approved annual appropriations shall be automatically and regularly released.**
**Republic Act No. 8522 (General Appropriations Act of 1998), Article XXXIII (Special Provisions Applicable to All Constitutional Offices Enjoying Fiscal Autonomy):**
Organizational Structure. Any provision of law to the contrary notwithstanding and within the limits of their respective appropriations as authorized in this Act, the Constitutional Commissions and Offices enjoying fiscal autonomy are authorized to formulate and implement the organizational structures of their respective offices, to fix and determine the salaries, allowances, and other benefits of their personnel, and whenever public interest so requires, make adjustments in the personal services itemization including, but not limited to, the transfer of item or creation of new positions in their respective offices: PROVIDED, That officers and employees whose positions are affected by such reorganization or adjustments shall be granted retirement gratuities and separation pay in accordance with existing laws, which shall be payable from any unexpended balance of, or savings in the appropriations of their respective offices: **PROVIDED, FURTHER, That the implementation hereof shall be in accordance with salary rates, allowances and other benefits authorized under compensation standardization laws.**

Use of Savings. The Constitutional Commissions and Offices enjoying fiscal autonomy are hereby authorized to use savings in their respective appropriations for: (a) printing and/or publication of decisions, resolutions, and training information materials; (b) repair, maintenance and improvement of central and regional offices, facilities and equipment; (c) purchase of books, journals, periodicals and equipment; (d) necessary expenses for the employment of temporary, contractual and casual employees; (e) payment of extraordinary and miscellaneous expenses, commutable representation and transportation allowances, and fringe benefits for their officials and employees as may be authorized by law; and (f) other official purposes, subject to accounting and auditing rules and regulations.
**Book VI, Chapter 1, Section 1(9), Executive Order No. 292 (Administrative Code of 1987):**
SEC. 1. Constitutional Policies on the Budget. — x x x
(9) Fiscal autonomy shall be enjoyed by the Judiciary, Constitutional Commissions, Office of the Ombudsman, Local Government and Commission on Human Rights.
**Factual Trigger:**
Invoking fiscal autonomy under R.A. No. 8522 (the 1998 GAA) and its membership in the Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy Group (CFAG), the CHR unilaterally passed internal resolutions upgrading, reclassifying, and creating plantilla positions and collapsing vacancies to fund salary increases. When DBM Secretary Benjamin Diokno disapproved the scheme for violating R.A. No. 6758 (the Compensation Standardization Law) and GAA restrictions on creating unauthorized key units, the CHR insisted that its fiscal autonomy insulated it from DBM oversight, prompting CHREA's legal challenge.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**February 14, 1998:** Congress enacts Republic Act No. 8522 (General Appropriations Act FY 1998), containing "Special Provisions Applicable to All Constitutional Offices Enjoying Fiscal Autonomy" under Article XXXIII, authorizing fiscally autonomous bodies to formulate organizational structures, fix compensation, adjust items, and utilize savings, provided implementation complies with compensation standardization laws.
**July 24, 1998:** The Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy Group (CFAG), with CHR Chairperson Aurora P. Navarette-Reciña signing as an active member, adopts CFAG Joint Resolution No. 49, defining fiscal autonomy as broad independence from outside control regarding financial matters, encompassing budget preparation, fund utilization, use of savings, and disposition of receipts.
**September 4, 1998:** Relying on the 1998 GAA special provisions and CFAG membership, the CHR promulgates Resolution No. A98-047, approving an upgrading and reclassification scheme effective Calendar Year 1998 funded by savings from Personal Services, proposing 10 new plantilla items (including one Director IV, SG-28; four Security Officer II, SG-15; and five Process Servers, SG-5).
**October 19, 1998:** The CHR passes Resolution No. A98-055, raising the salary grades of selected positions and authorizing further augmentation from Personal Services savings.
**November 17, 1998:** The CHR enacts Resolution No. A98-062, "collapsing" vacant positions (one Attorney III, four Attorney IV, one Chemist III, three Special Investigator I, one Clerk III, and one Accounting Clerk II) to fund the upgraded staffing scheme.
**January 20, 1999:** DBM Secretary Benjamin Diokno formally denies CHR's request for approval of the staffing modification. The DBM rules that: (1) elevating field units and divisions to regional offices/bureaus (upgrading 12 Attorney VI, SG-26 to Director IV, SG-28, and three Director III, SG-27 to Director IV, SG-28) changes contextual rank from support to substantive without actual functional shifts; (2) Section 78 of the 1998 GAA General Provisions bars creating organizational units (Finance Management Office and Public Affairs Office) or key positions without statutory or presidential authority; and (3) CFAG membership does not exempt agencies from the DBM's sole power under R.A. No. 6758 to administer the unified position classification system.
**March 29, 1999:** Prompted by the DBM’s denial, the CSC-NCR issues a Memorandum recommending to the CSC-Central Office the rejection of all appointments issued pursuant to the CHR upgrading scheme.
**December 16, 1999:** Denying the request of rank-and-file employees represented by CHREA, the CSC-Central Office issues Resolution No. 99-2800, reversing the CSC-NCR's recommendation and upholding the validity of the CHR reclassification scheme.
**June 9, 2000:** The CSC-Central Office issues Resolution No. 001354 denying CHREA's Motion for Reconsideration.
**November 29, 2001:** The Court of Appeals, in CA-G.R. SP No. 59678, dismisses CHREA's petition and affirms the CSC-Central Office, ruling that the upgrading and reclassification fall within the CHR's constitutional fiscal autonomy. The CA subsequently denies reconsideration on September 11, 2002.
**November 25, 2004:** The Supreme Court (Division) promulgates its Decision granting CHREA’s petition, setting aside the CA rulings, reinstating the CSC-NCR ruling of March 29, 1999, and disallowing CHR Resolutions Nos. A98-047, A98-055, and A98-062 for lack of DBM approval. The Court holds that CHR is not a constitutional commission and possesses no legal basis for fiscal autonomy.
**Post-Promulgation Phase:** The CHR files a Motion for Reconsideration praying that the Court reverse its holding that CHR lacks fiscal autonomy; CHREA files an Opposition.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondent CHR's Arguments (Motion for Reconsideration)
**Main Thesis:** The CHR is an independent constitutional body vested with fiscal autonomy under Article XIII, Section 17(4) of the 1987 Constitution, the 1998 GAA, and the Administrative Code of 1987; consequently, its unilateral reorganization, position upgrading, and collapsing of items do not require prior DBM evaluation or approval.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Constitutional Intent on Fiscal Autonomy:** While Article XIII, Section 17(4) omits the opening phrase **"The Commission shall enjoy fiscal autonomy"** and only mandates that appropriations be automatically and regularly released, the omission was intended as an editorial elimination of surplusage. As explained by Commissioner Hilario G. Davide, Jr. during the Constitutional Commission (ConCom) deliberations, the automatic and regular release of funds **is** the very essence of fiscal autonomy.
2.  **Statutory Recognition in the Administrative Code of 1987:** Book VI, Chapter 1, Section 1(9) of E.O. No. 292 explicitly lists the CHR alongside the Judiciary, Constitutional Commissions, Ombudsman, and LGUs as entities enjoying fiscal autonomy.
3.  **Application of the 1998 GAA Special Provisions:** Under Article XXXIII of R.A. No. 8522, offices enjoying fiscal autonomy are legally authorized to formulate organizational structures, create new positions, and utilize Personal Services savings to fund reorganizations.
4.  **CFAG Membership & Executive Concessions:** The CHR is an acknowledged member of the Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy Group (CFAG) and should enjoy parity with other constitutional entities, consistent with Presidential Administrative Order No. 137 conferring equivalent benefits.
B. Petitioner CHREA's Arguments (Opposition)
**Main Thesis:** The Supreme Court's November 25, 2004 Decision must be maintained. The CHR lacks broad constitutional fiscal autonomy, and even if it enjoyed an aspect of fiscal autonomy, it remains subordinate to the Salary Standardization Law administered exclusively by the DBM.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Strict Separation of Constitutional Commissions:** The CHR is created under Article XIII (Social Justice and Human Rights), not Article IX (Constitutional Commissions). It cannot claim the systemic, structural prerogatives of the CSC, COMELEC, or COA.
2.  **Mandatory Submission to R.A. No. 6758:** The DBM is the sole executive agency tasked by law with administering the Unified Position Classification and Compensation System. No government agency, even one enjoying fiscal autonomy, can bypass DBM authorization to create offices or reclassify positions in contravention of national standards.
3.  **Affirmance of CSC-NCR and DBM:** The CSC-NCR correctly recognized that appointments premised on disapproved, unstandardized reclassifications are legally defective and must be rejected.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) is invested with full constitutional fiscal autonomy under the 1987 Constitution and the Administrative Code of 1987.
2.  **[Secondary Statutory / Administrative Issue]** Whether or not the approval of the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) is a mandatory condition precedent for the implementation of the CHR's position upgrading, reclassification, creation, and collapsing scheme under the Compensation Standardization Law (R.A. No. 6758) and the General Appropriations Act.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Whether or not the CHR enjoys full constitutional fiscal autonomy.
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The CHR does not possess broad, full-scale fiscal autonomy; under both the 1987 Constitution and the Administrative Code of 1987, it enjoys only a **limited** fiscal autonomy restricted exclusively to the automatic and regular release of its approved annual appropriations.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Strict Constitutional Text Analysis:** The 1987 Constitution explicitly guarantees fiscal autonomy using a two-sentence formula to only three classes of institutions: the Judiciary (Art. VIII, Sec. 3), the Constitutional Commissions (Art. IX-A, Sec. 5), and the Office of the Ombudsman (Art. XI, Sec. 14). Each provision explicitly dictates that the entity **"shall enjoy fiscal autonomy"** followed by the rule of automatic and regular release. By contrast, the CHR’s creation under Article XIII, Section 17(4) entirely omits the affirmative clause granting fiscal autonomy, retaining **only** the operational mandate: **"The approved annual appropriations of the Commission shall be automatically and regularly released."**
2.  **ConCom Intent and Surplusage Myth:** A comprehensive reading of the 1986 Constitutional Commission records shows that Commissioner Davide's remark on "surplusage" did not mean full fiscal autonomy was implicitly granted. Rather, the ConCom determined that **"the autonomy actually intended is the automatic release of these appropriations."** When Commissioner Guingona inquired whether the CHR would have budgetary prioritization like education, Commissioner Bengzon clarified: **"It only refers to the release which should be automatic and regular."** The ConCom consciously withheld full-spectrum fiscal powers from an investigative, recommendatory body.
3.  **The Bengzon v. Drilon Benchmark:** Full fiscal autonomy contemplates **"a guarantee of full flexibility to allocate and utilize their resources with the wisdom and dispatch that their needs require,"** encompassing the power to levy fees, adjust compensation scales, and direct fund utilization without outside control. In **Bengzon v. Drilon**, the **En Banc** recognized this extensive independence only for the Judiciary, CSC, COA, COMELEC, and Ombudsman. The CHR was conspicuously omitted.
4.  **CFAG Estoppel:** CFAG Joint Resolution No. 49 (signed by the CHR Chairperson) itself declared that fiscal autonomy **"does not mean mere automatic and regular release"** but encompasses budget preparation, fund flexibility, and use of savings. The CHR cannot contradict its own signed joint resolution by arguing that automatic release equates to complete fiscal autonomy.
5.  **Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius:** The express textual enumeration of entities granted broad fiscal autonomy implies the exclusion of all others.
6.  **Reconciling the Administrative Code:** Book VI, Section 1(9) of E.O. No. 292, listing the CHR as enjoying fiscal autonomy, is merely a general budgetary policy statement that must be reconciled with Book V, Section 6, which specifically labels the CHR's section as "Annual Appropriations" rather than "Fiscal Autonomy," and confines it to automatic release. General provisions cannot expand a limited constitutional grant.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Consequently, this Court concludes that the 1987 Constitution extends to respondent a certain degree of fiscal autonomy through the privilege of having its approved annual appropriations released automatically and regularly. However, it withholds from respondent fiscal autonomy, in its broad or extensive sense, as granted to the Judiciary, constitutional commissions, and the Office of the Ombudsman. Operative herein is the rule of statutory construction, **expressio unius est exclusio alterius**..." (528 Phil. 658, 672)
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The CHR is an independent office, but it is not a Chapter IX Constitutional Commission or a co-equal branch. The framers intentionally gave the CHR only the protection of having its budget automatically released to prevent executive strangulation, while denying it the broad fiscal autonomy (budget preparation, item creation, and absolute internal spending discretion) granted to the Courts, the Ombudsman, and the Constitutional Commissions.
Issue 2: Whether or not the implementation of CHR’s staffing reclassification scheme is subject to prior DBM approval.
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Regardless of the degree of fiscal autonomy enjoyed, any reclassification, upgrading, or organizational modification in the CHR must strictly conform to the Compensation Standardization Law (R.A. No. 6758) and requires prior DBM approval.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Universality of the Salary Standardization Law:** Even constitutional entities clothed with broad, express fiscal autonomy (such as the Judiciary) are not exempt from R.A. No. 6758. The 1998 GAA special provisions themselves explicitly subject fiscally autonomous offices to the condition that **"the implementation hereof shall be in accordance with salary rates, allowances and other benefits authorized under compensation standardization laws."** If the Judiciary must submit its reclassification and allowance schemes to DBM parameters (as reflected in R.A. No. 9227 and Joint Circular 2004-1), the CHR cannot assert superior immunity.
2.  **Exclusive DBM Jurisdiction:** Congress delegated the administration of the unified position classification system strictly to the DBM. Bypassing DBM oversight imperils the core public policy of R.A. No. 6758—"providing equal pay for substantially equal work."
3.  **Violation of GAA General Provisions:** Under Section 78 of the 1998 GAA General Provisions, no new organizational units or key position modifications may be authorized without a statutory mandate or presidential directive. The CHR attempted to unilaterally elevate divisions into services/bureaus and reclassify field Attorney VI (SG-26) items into Director IV (SG-28) positions without changing substantive duties, and sought to establish new units (Finance Management Office and Public Affairs Office) without legal foundation.
4.  **Binding Weight of Administrative Expertise:** Courts accord great respect and deference to the specialized technical judgment of administrative bodies like the DBM on national budgetary standards, and will not disturb the Budget Secretary’s findings absent grave abuse of discretion.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Being a member of the fiscal autonomy group does not vest the agency with the authority to reclassify, upgrade, and create positions without approval of the DBM. While the members of the Group are authorized to formulate and implement the organizational structures of their respective offices and determine the compensation of their personnel, such authority is not absolute and must be exercised within the parameters of the Unified Position Classification and Compensation System established under RA 6758... If the judiciary, a co-equal branch of government, which was expressly granted by the Constitution with fiscal autonomy, is required to conform to the Salary Standardization Law and is subject to the scrutiny of the DBM, sagaciously, the respondent cannot be deemed to enjoy a better position than the Judiciary." (528 Phil. 658, 674-675)
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Fiscal autonomy is not a blank check to ignore the Salary Standardization Law. Because Congress vested the DBM with the exclusive authority to maintain uniformity across government salary grades, every agency—even the Supreme Court—must operate within DBM-administered classification rules. Therefore, the CHR’s unilateral internal resolutions creating and upgrading plantilla positions without DBM evaluation are legally void.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → k. Fiscal autonomy
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
To claim **Broad Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy** (as enunciated in **Bengzon v. Drilon**), an entity must satisfy two constitutional criteria:
1.  **Express Constitutional Designation:** The organic text must positively enact the command clause: **"The [Entity] shall enjoy fiscal autonomy."**
 Applied to CHR: **ABSENT.** Found only in Art. VIII, Sec. 3 (Judiciary), Art. IX-A, Sec. 5 (Constitutional Commissions), and Art. XI, Sec. 14 (Ombudsman). Omitted in Art. XIII, Sec. 17(4).
2.  **Full Operational Flexibility:** The agency must possess independent legal power to formulate budget policies, use savings without collateral legislative restrictions, levy fees, and establish compensation outside ordinary executive oversight.
 Applied to CHR: **ABSENT.** CHR is restricted to **Limited Fiscal Autonomy**, extending solely to the automatic and regular disbursement of approved funds.
3.  Exemption from Compensation Standardization (Salary Standardization Law):
 Applied to CHR: **ABSENT ACROSS ALL BRANCHES.** Even broad fiscal autonomy does not exempt an agency from R.A. No. 6758 or DBM classification standards.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Fiscal Autonomy (Broad vs. Limited): Full flexibility of resource allocation vs. mere automatic/regular release of appropriations.
 Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius: The express mention of one thing implies the exclusion of others.
 Automatic and Regular Release: The narrow financial guarantee designed to prevent the Executive from withholding approved congressional appropriations.
 Surplusage: The rejected defense argument that the express grant of fiscal autonomy was omitted from the Constitution merely because it was repetitive of automatic release.
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 Executive Power Exercised: The DBM Secretary's statutory power to enforce uniform classification and compensation standards under R.A. No. 6758 and the GAA.
 Structural Check Invoked: Independent institutional status under Article XIII, Section 17; asserted fiscal autonomy; and CFAG membership.
 Judicial Ruling: Executive control over position classification and budgetary execution prevails where the Constitution provides only limited fiscal autonomy (automatic release), keeping the entity bound to statutory compensation systems.
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
 Statutory and Constitutional Harmonization:** The Court scrutinized the organic text alongside the ConCom records, applying statutory construction (**expressio unius est exclusio alterius and holistic harmonious construction) to demarcate the precise boundaries of fiscal autonomy.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"Professor, this case falls under **Fiscal Autonomy** because it defines the boundary between **broad** fiscal autonomy and **limited** fiscal autonomy. The Supreme Court held that the CHR possesses only limited fiscal autonomy, meaning it is strictly entitled to the automatic and regular release of its approved appropriations, but lacks the broad flexibility to independently reorganize, upgrade, or create plantilla items. Furthermore, the Court established that even bodies with fiscal autonomy—including the Judiciary—remain subject to the Salary Standardization Law, making DBM approval a mandatory condition precedent to implementing any reclassification scheme."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:** No separate opinions filed.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the Motion for Reconsideration is PARTIALLY GRANTED. The assailed decision of this Court dated 25 November 2004 is hereby MODIFIED, declaring the respondent CHR as a constitutional body enjoying limited fiscal autonomy, in the sense that it is entitled to the automatic and regular release of its approved annual appropriations; nonetheless, it is still required to conform to the Salary Standardization Law. Accordingly, its entire reclassification scheme remains subject to the approval of the DBM. No pronouncement as to costs.
SO ORDERED." (528 Phil. 658, 676)
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The CHR’s Motion for Reconsideration was partially granted only to clarify its constitutional classification: the Court modified its earlier Decision by recognizing that the CHR enjoys **limited** fiscal autonomy (the automatic and regular release of funds). However, the substantive outcome remained unchanged—the CHREA prevailed, the CHR’s unilateral position reclassifications remained disallowed, and the requirement of prior DBM approval was reaffirmed in full.
