### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Estipona v. Lobrigo
**Full Official Caption:** Salvador Estipona, Jr. y Asuela, Petitioner, vs. Hon. Frank E. Lobrigo, Presiding Judge of the Regional Trial Court, Branch 3, Legazpi City, Albay, and People of the Philippines, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 226679; Promulgated August 15, 2017; 816 Phil. 789; En Banc; Ponente: Peralta, J.; Concurring: Sereno, C.J., Carpio, Velasco, Jr., Leonardo-De Castro, Bersamin, Del Castillo, Perlas-Bernabe, Leonen (with Separate Concurring Opinion), Jardeleza, Martires, Tijam, A. Reyes, Jr., and Gesmundo, JJ.; On Leave: Caguioa, J.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
Salvador A. Estipona, Jr. (Petitioner): Accused in Criminal Case No. 13586 for illegal drug possession under Section 11, Article II, R.A. No. 9165.
Hon. Frank E. Lobrigo (Respondent Judge): Presiding Judge, Regional Trial Court (RTC), Branch 3, Legazpi City, Albay, who denied the plea-bargaining motion.
People of the Philippines (Respondent): Represented by the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG), prosecuting the criminal charge.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition under Rule 65 with an urgent prayer for a Temporary Restraining Order and/or Writ of Preliminary Injunction, directly challenging the Orders dated July 12, 2016 and July 26, 2016 issued by the RTC of Legazpi City, Branch 3, which denied petitioner's Motion to Allow the Accused to Enter into a Plea Bargaining Agreement on the ground that Section 23 of Republic Act (R.A.) No. 9165 prohibits plea bargaining in all drug cases.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Criminal Procedure → Rule 116 (Arraignment and Plea) & Rule 118 (Pre-Trial) → Plea Bargaining / Rule-Making Power of the Supreme Court
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Article VIII (Judicial Department) → Section 5(5) (Rule-Making Power) → Separation of Powers
**Full Text of Governing Provisions:**
**Section 5(5), Article VIII, 1987 Constitution of the Philippines:**
"Sec. 5. The Supreme Court shall have the following powers:
...
(5) **Promulgate rules concerning the protection and enforcement of constitutional rights, pleading, practice, and procedure in all courts**, the admission to the practice of law, the Integrated Bar, and legal assistance to the underprivileged. Such rules shall provide a simplified and inexpensive procedure for the speedy disposition of cases, shall be uniform for all courts of the same grade, and **shall not diminish, increase, or modify substantive rights**. Rules of procedure of special courts and quasi-judicial bodies shall remain effective unless disapproved by the Supreme Court."
**Section 23, Republic Act No. 9165 (Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002):**
"SEC. 23. **Plea-Bargaining Provision.** — **Any person charged under any provision of this Act regardless of the imposable penalty shall not be allowed to avail of the provision on plea-bargaining.**"
**Rule 116, Section 2, 2000 Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure:**
"SEC. 2. **Plea of guilty to a lesser offense.** — At arraignment, the accused, with the consent of the offended party and the prosecutor, may be allowed by the trial court to plead guilty to a lesser offense which is necessarily included in the offense charged. After arraignment but before trial, the accused may still be allowed to plead guilty to said lesser offense after withdrawing his plea of not guilty. No amendment of the complaint or information is necessary."
**Rule 118, Section 1(a), 2000 Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure:**
"SEC. 1. **Pre-trial; mandatory in criminal cases.** — In all criminal cases cognizable by the Sandiganbayan, Regional Trial Court, Metropolitan Trial Court, Municipal Trial Court in Cities, Municipal Trial Court and Municipal Circuit Trial Court, the court shall, after arraignment and within thirty (30) days from the date the court acquires jurisdiction over the person of the accused, unless a shorter period is provided for in special laws or circulars of the Supreme Court, order a pre-trial conference to consider the following:
(a) plea bargaining;
..."
**Historical Landmark Rule:**
 Under the 1935 Constitution (Art. VIII, Sec. 13):** The Court’s power to promulgate rules of pleading, practice, and procedure was co-existent with legislative authority, providing that: **"The Congress shall have the power to repeal, alter or supplement the rules concerning pleading, practice and procedure, and the admission to the practice of law in the Philippines."
 Under the 1973 Constitution (Art. X, Sec. 5[5]): The Batasang Pambansa retained the concurrent power to "repeal, alter, or supplement" procedural rules.
 Modern Text (1987 Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 5[5]): The Framers deliberately deleted all textual references granting Congress concurrent power to alter, repeal, or supplement rules of procedure, thereby making the Supreme Court's rule-making authority **sole and exclusive**.
**Factual Trigger:** Salvador Estipona, Jr., charged with possession of 0.084 gram of **shabu** under Section 11 of R.A. No. 9165, moved to withdraw his not-guilty plea and enter a plea of guilty to Section 12 (possession of drug paraphernalia) to avail of rehabilitation. The trial court denied the motion on the ground that Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165 completely bars plea bargaining in all drug offenses.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**March 21, 2016:** Salvador A. Estipona, Jr. is arrested in Legazpi City, Albay, for possessing one heat-sealed transparent plastic sachet containing 0.084 gram of white crystalline substance testing positive for methamphetamine hydrochloride (**shabu**).
**Undated:** Estipona is charged before the Regional Trial Court of Legazpi City, Branch 3, docketed as Criminal Case No. 13586, for violation of Section 11, Article II of R.A. No. 9165 (Possession of Dangerous Drugs).
**June 15, 2016:** Estipona files a **Motion to Allow the Accused to Enter into a Plea Bargaining Agreement**, praying to withdraw his not-guilty plea and plead guilty to Section 12, Article II of R.A. No. 9165 (Possession of Equipment, Instrument, Apparatus and Other Paraphernalia for Dangerous Drugs) with a penalty of rehabilitation, asserting he is a first-time offender caught with a minimal quantity. He attacks Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165 as an unconstitutional encroachment on the Supreme Court's rule-making authority.
**June 27, 2016:** The prosecution files a Comment/Opposition moving to deny the motion based on Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165, arguing it was within congressional prerogative to bar plea bargaining for specified crimes.
**June 29, 2016:** The prosecution files an amended Comment/Opposition manifesting that while it is open to plea bargaining to serve the statutory intent of rehabilitation, it is constrained to reject the proposal due to the express statutory prohibition in Section 23.
**July 12, 2016:** Respondent Judge Frank E. Lobrigo issues an Order denying Estipona's motion. The judge notes the merit of the constitutional challenge regarding encroachment upon judicial rule-making, but declines to declare Section 23 unconstitutional out of "becoming modesty" and the potential ramifications on pending drug prosecutions.
**July 26, 2016:** The RTC issues an Order denying Estipona’s Motion for Reconsideration.
**September 2016:** Estipona files a Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition directly with the Supreme Court challenging the constitutionality of Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165 and the RTC Orders.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Salvador Estipona, Jr.)
**Main Thesis:** Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165 is unconstitutional because it violates the Equal Protection Clause, usurps the Supreme Court’s exclusive constitutional power to promulgate rules of procedure, and violates the separation of powers.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Equal Protection Violation:** Section 23 unreasonably discriminates against drug offenders by denying them the statutory benefits of plea bargaining granted to accused persons in other crimes with equal or graver penalties.
2. **Infringement of Judicial Rule-Making:** Plea bargaining is strictly a rule of procedure governed by Rule 116, Section 2 and Rule 118, Section 1 of the Rules of Court; Congress unconstitutionally encroached upon the Supreme Court’s sole prerogative under Section 5(5), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution when it prohibited plea bargaining via statute.
3. **Frustration of Legislative Purpose:** The absolute ban undermines the rehabilitative intendment expressed in Section 2, paragraph 3 of R.A. No. 9165.
4. **Grave Abuse of Discretion:** The RTC committed grave abuse of discretion by refusing to strike down Section 23 despite recognizing its constitutional infirmity.
B. Respondent's Arguments (People of the Philippines via OSG)
**Main Thesis:** The petition is procedurally fatal and Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165 is a valid exercise of legislative power over substantive criminal law.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Procedural Defects:** Congress was not impleaded as an indispensable party; the constitutionality cannot be assailed collaterally; and the proper remedy was declaratory relief before the RTC or a petition for certiorari before the CA/RTC.
2. **Requisites of Judicial Review Unmet:** Petitioner lacks locus standi as he suffered no direct injury (plea bargaining not being a right); there is no actual controversy; and the constitutional issue is not the **lis mota** of the criminal prosecution.
3. **Substantive Prerogative:** The determination of penalties and the availability of plea bargaining is a matter of legislative policy within the police power of Congress to curb the drug epidemic.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the procedural objections raised by the OSG (failure to implead Congress, direct recourse, locus standi, lack of actual controversy, and **lis mota**) preclude the Supreme Court from exercising its power of judicial review.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165, which prohibits plea bargaining in all drug cases, is unconstitutional for encroaching upon the exclusive constitutional rule-making power of the Supreme Court under Section 5(5), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution.
3. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165 violates the Equal Protection Clause of the 1987 Constitution.
4. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondent Judge Frank E. Lobrigo committed grave abuse of discretion in denying petitioner's motion to enter into a plea-bargaining agreement.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Propriety of Judicial Review Over Procedural Defects
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Procedural barriers take a backseat when an issue of transcendental and monumental importance regarding the national drug problem and institutional judicial independence is presented.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio:**
1. **Power to Suspend Rules:** The Court possesses the inherent constitutional authority to relax or suspend the application of procedural rules where strict adherence would frustrate substantial justice.
2. **Transcendental Importance:** The drug menace has assumed epidemic and harrowing proportions, affecting public welfare, the administration of criminal justice, and the fundamental rights of thousands of accused persons.
3. **Final Arbiter Role:** Novel questions of first impression with far-reaching consequences demand definitive guidance from the highest court, warranting the brush-aside of alleged technical infirmities (e.g., failure to implead Congress, hierarchy of courts).
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"When public interest requires, the Court may brush aside procedural rules in order to resolve a constitutional issue. ... [T]he Court is invested with the power to suspend the application of the rules of procedure as a necessary complement of its power to promulgate the same."
**(d) Recitation Explanation:** The Supreme Court bypassed traditional procedural barriers like court hierarchy and joinder of parties because the constitutional clash between an act of Congress and the Court's judicial authority directly affected thousands of pending drug cases nationwide. Substantive justice and the need for clear guidance overrode procedural technicalities.
Issue 2: Encroachment on Exclusive Rule-Making Power
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165 is unconstitutional as plea bargaining is an adjective rule of procedure falling exclusively within the Supreme Court's constitutional domain under Section 5(5), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio:**
1. **Evolution to Exclusive Power:** Under the 1935 and 1973 Constitutions, Congress shared concurrent authority with the Supreme Court to repeal, alter, or supplement procedural rules. The 1987 Constitution deliberately deleted this legislative check, cementing procedural rule-making as the sole, exclusive domain of the Supreme Court.
2. **Substantive vs. Procedural Test:** A substantive law creates, defines, and regulates rights; a procedural (adjective) law prescribes the method of enforcing rights or obtaining redress. If a rule merely operates as a means of implementing an existing right or regulates the judicial process, it is procedural.
3. **Nature of Plea Bargaining:** Plea bargaining confers no substantive constitutional right upon an accused to demand a lesser penalty; rather, it is a procedural mechanism designed to facilitate prompt, inexpensive, and mutually satisfactory disposition of criminal cases. Because it creates no vested substantive right, regulating or prohibiting it is procedural.
4. **Unconstitutional Incursion:** Since plea bargaining is incorporated into the Rules of Court (Rule 116 and Rule 118) pursuant to judicial authority, Congress cannot statutorily suspend or prohibit its application without violating the doctrine of separation of powers.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The power to promulgate rules of pleading, practice and procedure is now Our exclusive domain and no longer shared with the Executive and Legislative departments. ... The separation of powers among the three co-equal branches of our government has erected an impregnable wall that keeps the power to promulgate rules of pleading, practice and procedure within the sole province of this Court."
**(d) Recitation Explanation:** Under the 1987 Constitution, Congress lost all power to alter court rules. Because plea bargaining is a procedural tool designed for case administration rather than a substantive right, Congress invaded the judiciary's exclusive constitutional domain when it barred plea bargaining via statute in Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165.
Issue 3: Violation of Equal Protection Clause
**(a) Short Answer: UNRESOLVED / DEFERRED.** The Court refrained from ruling on the equal protection challenge to avoid preempting future policy determinations regarding plea bargaining parameters.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio:**
1. **Judicial Restraint:** The declaration that Section 23 unconstitutionally encroached upon judicial rule-making fully resolved the petition (**lis mota** satisfied).
2. **Pending Policy Considerations:** The Court reserved determination on the classification of drug offenders versus other offenders until it formally considered adopting the prohibition or a modified scheme through its own administrative rules.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"At this point, We shall not resolve the issue of whether Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165 is contrary to the constitutional right to equal protection of the law in order not to preempt any future discussion by the Court on the policy considerations behind Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165."
**(d) Recitation Explanation:** The Court found it unnecessary to resolve whether Section 23 violated the Equal Protection Clause because the statute was already void for violating the exclusive rule-making clause. Addressing equal protection prematurely would bind the Court's internal rule-making policy discussions.
Issue 4: Grave Abuse of Discretion by the Trial Judge
**(a) Short Answer: PARTIALLY MERITORIOUS.** While the RTC judge correctly observed "becoming modesty," his refusal to apply the Rules of Court on plea bargaining must be set aside due to the unconstitutionality of Section 23.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio:**
1. **Becoming Modesty Recognized:** The trial court declined to declare Section 23 unconstitutional citing judicial modesty regarding sensitive penal laws with broad ramifications.
2. **Supervening Nullity:** While lower courts possess constitutional jurisdiction to resolve constitutional issues, Section 23's invalidity requires the trial court to now proceed under Rule 116, Section 2 and Rule 118, Section 1(a).
3. **Discretionary Conditions:** Plea bargaining remains subject to the consent of the prosecutor and the trial judge's evaluation of the prosecution's evidence.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The plea is further addressed to the sound discretion of the trial court, which **may** allow the accused to plead guilty to a lesser offense which is necessarily included in the offense charged. The word **may** denotes an exercise of discretion upon the trial court on whether to allow the accused to make such plea."
**(d) Recitation Explanation:** The trial judge acted cautiously under existing doctrine, but because Section 23 is void, his blanket denial can no longer stand. The case must proceed to pre-trial where the judge can exercise judicial discretion on whether to approve a plea bargain based on prosecutorial consent and the evidence.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I / Remedial Law | Topic: Pleading and Procedure (Rule-Making Power of the Judiciary)
Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist
**Exclusive Rule-Making Power (Art. VIII, Sec. 5[5], 1987 Constitution):**
1. **Enactment of Rules:** Relates to protection and enforcement of constitutional rights, pleading, practice, and procedure in all courts, admission to the bar, integrated bar, and legal assistance. (Proven: Plea bargaining operates under Rules 116 and 118).
2. **Uniformity and Speed:** Provides a simplified, inexpensive procedure for the speedy disposition of cases. (Proven: Plea bargaining avoids trial congestion and accelerates rehabilitation).
3. **Limitation on Substantive Rights:** Rules must **not** diminish, increase, or modify substantive rights. (Proven: Plea bargaining does not create or take away vested substantive rights; it merely regulates the manner of enforcing penal liabilities).
4. **Absence of Legislative Concurrence:** 1987 Constitution removed congressional authority to repeal, alter, or supplement court rules. (Proven: Section 23 sought to modify procedural rules without constitutional authority).
Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words")
 Adjective Law vs. Substantive Law
 Exclusive Domain / Impregnable Wall
 Becoming Modesty
 Mutuality of Advantage
 Condition Precedent (Prosecutorial & Court Consent)
 Lis Mota
Remedial Law & Evidence Lens
**Procedural Remedy & Jurisdiction Audit:** Direct recourse via Rule 65 (Certiorari and Prohibition) to the Supreme Court was exceptionally permitted despite bypassing the hierarchy of courts and failing to implead Congress. The issue posed a pure question of law touching upon the constitutional independence and exclusive rule-making power of the Court.
**Evidentiary & Quantum of Proof Analysis:** Plea bargaining after arraignment is not a matter of right. Where an offer to plead to a lesser offense is made, the trial court's acceptance depends strictly on the **evidence on record**. If the prosecution has rested or completed bail hearings, the change of plea is impermissible if the evidence of guilt for the higher crime is sufficient; the trial court must issue a reasoned order disclosing the relative strength or weakness of the prosecution's evidence.
Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer)
This case sits squarely under Pleading and Procedure because it establishes that plea bargaining is an adjective, procedural mechanism rather than a substantive right. In **Estipona**, the Supreme Court held that the 1987 Constitution intentionally eliminated the power of Congress to repeal, alter, or supplement court rules; consequently, Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165—which prohibited plea bargaining in drug cases—is unconstitutional for encroaching upon the exclusive rule-making authority of the Supreme Court under Section 5(5), Article VIII.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Leonen, J. (Concurring):** Emphasized that plea bargaining is not an absolute right of the accused but a consensual, discretionary process requiring the express agreement of the prosecution and approval of the court. He underscored that Section 23 encroached upon judicial power by tying the hands of trial courts, and agreed that declaring it unconstitutional restored judicial discretion without creating an entitlement to an automatic bargain.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition for certiorari and prohibition is GRANTED. Section 23 of Republic Act No. 9165 is declared unconstitutional for being contrary to the rule-making authority of the Supreme Court under Section 5(5), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Salvador Estipona, Jr. prevailed. Section 23 of R.A. No. 9165 was struck down as unconstitutional, clearing the way for trial courts nationwide to entertain plea-bargaining proposals in dangerous drugs cases pursuant to the Rules of Criminal Procedure.

digest:
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Re: Draft DOJ-NPS Rules on Preliminary Investigations and Inquest Proceedings
**Full Official Caption:** Re: Draft Department of Justice-National Prosecution Service's [DOJ-NPS] Rules on Preliminary Investigations and Inquest Proceedings
**Citation & Metadata:** A.M. No. 24-02-09-SC; May 28, 2024; 955 Phil. 15; En Banc; Zalameda, **J.** (Voting: Unanimous; Gesmundo, **C.J.**, Leonen, **SAJ.**, Caguioa, Hernando, Lazaro-Javier, Inting, M. Lopez, Gaerlan, Rosario, J. Lopez, Dimaampao, Marquez, Kho, Jr., and Singh, **JJ.**, concur; No separate opinions filed).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
** Supreme Court of the Philippines (**En Banc) – The constitutional organ vested with exclusive rule-making authority over pleading, practice, and procedure in all courts.
Sub-Committee on the Revision of the Rules of Criminal Procedure (Sub-Committee) – Chaired by Associate Justice Rodil V. Zalameda, tasked with revising Rule 112 of the Rules of Court.
Department of Justice (DOJ) / National Prosecution Service (NPS) – Executive department led by Secretary of Justice; represented in discussions by Undersecretary Raul T. Vasquez; drafted executive rules governing executive preliminary investigations and inquest proceedings.
Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo – Chief Justice of the Philippines; initiated transmittal of Court comments and proposed the formal recognition of DOJ's executive rule-making power and the corresponding repeal of inconsistent provisions in Rule 112.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
This administrative matter originated internally upon transmittal by a DOJ member of the draft Department Circular containing the proposed **Rules on Preliminary Investigations and Inquest Proceedings in the National Prosecution Service** (DOJ-NPS Rules) to the Court's Sub-Committee on the Revision of the Rules of Criminal Procedure. The Court resolved **en banc** whether to recognize the DOJ's authority to promulgate executive rules on preliminary investigations and inquest proceedings, and whether to repeal the corresponding provisions in Rule 112 of the 2000 Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Rule-Making Power (Article VIII, Section 5[5]) → Pleading, Practice, and Procedure vs. Executive Investigatory Powers
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Remedial Law → Criminal Procedure → Preliminary Investigation (Rule 112) → Executive Nature of Preliminary Investigation
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provision:**
**Article VIII, Section 5, Paragraph 5, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"The Supreme Court shall have the following powers:
xxx
(5) **Promulgate rules concerning the protection and enforcement of constitutional rights, pleading, practice, and procedure in all courts**, the admission to the practice of law, the Integrated Bar, and legal assistance to the underprivileged. Such rules shall provide a simplified and inexpensive procedure for the speedy disposition of cases, shall be uniform for all courts of the same grade, and shall not diminish, increase, or modify substantive rights. Rules of procedure of special courts and quasi-judicial bodies shall remain effective unless disapproved by the Supreme Court."
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):**
The Department of Justice drafted its own administrative rules governing preliminary investigations and inquest proceedings (the 2024 DOJ-NPS Rules). Because preliminary investigation had historically been codified under Rule 112 of the Rules of Court, the DOJ sought alignment with the Judiciary, triggering the Supreme Court to evaluate whether public prosecutors possess independent authority to formulate their own investigatory rules and whether the Court must proactively repeal the inconsistent provisions of Rule 112 to eliminate legal friction.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**October 2023:** The Supreme Court Sub-Committee on the Revision of the Rules of Criminal Procedure (chaired by Justice Zalameda, with Justice J. Lopez as Vice-Chairperson, and Justices Marquez, Kho, Jr., and Singh as members) received a draft copy of the proposed DOJ Circular on the **Rules on Preliminary Investigations and Inquest Proceedings in the National Prosecution Service** (DOJ-NPS Rules) from a DOJ member serving on the Sub-Committee.
**October 27, 2023:** Because the Court's own rules on Preliminary Investigation under Rule 112 were simultaneously slated for revision under the Proposed Rules on Criminal Procedure, Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo transmitted the internal comments of the members of the **Banc** to DOJ Undersecretary Raul T. Vasquez for consideration to ensure administrative harmony.
**January 22, 2024:** DOJ Undersecretary Vasquez sent a letter to Chief Justice Gesmundo attaching the final version of the DOJ-NPS Rules and highlighting the Court's comments and suggestions that the DOJ incorporated into its regulatory framework.
**February 7, 2024:** Chief Justice Gesmundo addressed a formal letter to the members of the **Banc** urging the Court to formally recognize the authority of the DOJ to promulgate the DOJ-NPS Rules. He emphasized that under established jurisprudence, the conduct of a preliminary investigation is an executive, not a judicial, function; he further advised that this recognition would necessitate the repeal of inconsistent provisions under Rule 112 of the 2000 Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure.
**Historical Trajectory Traced by the Court:**
**1940 & 1964 Rules of Court:** Preliminary investigation (or preliminary examination) was defined as an inquiry conducted by an authorized judge or officer to determine reasonable grounds to issue an arrest warrant and hold the accused for trial. Authority was shared among justices of the peace, municipal judges, city fiscals, and municipal mayors (and provincial fiscals under the 1964 Rules).
**Judiciary Act of 1948 (R.A. No. 296, as amended by R.A. No. 3828) & Judiciary Reorganization Act of 1980 (B.P. Blg. 129):** First-level judges (justices of the peace, judges of Municipal Courts, and later MTC/MCTC judges) were legislatively authorized to conduct preliminary investigations for offenses cognizable by the Courts of First Instance / Regional Trial Courts.
**Executive Authority Enactments:** R.A. No. 732, R.A. No. 5180 (as amended by P.D. Nos. 77 and 911), and R.A. No. 10071 (**Prosecution Service Act of 2010**) conferred primary executive authority upon fiscals and state prosecutors to conduct preliminary investigations and file criminal informations.
**1985 & 2000 Revised Rules on Criminal Procedure:** Retained shared authority among judges and prosecutors to conduct preliminary investigations for offenses penalized by at least 4 years, 2 months, and 1 day.
**August 30, 2005 Amendment (A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC):** The Supreme Court amended Rule 112 by officially stripping first-level court judges (MTC/MCTC) of the authority to conduct preliminary investigations, shifting investigatory proceedings exclusively to public prosecutors and other legally designated officers.
**May 28, 2024:** The Supreme Court **En Banc** promulgated the subject Resolution in A.M. No. 24-02-09-SC, recognizing the DOJ's authority to promulgate its rules and ordering the conditional repeal of inconsistent provisions of Rule 112 upon the official promulgation of the 2024 DOJ-NPS Rules.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
**(Note: As an internal administrative matter between the Supreme Court and the Department of Justice regarding judicial and executive rule-making spheres, the positions are framed through the internal transmittals and official recommendations).**
A. Sub-Committee / Chief Justice's Proposition:
**Main Thesis:** The Judiciary should formally recognize the independent power of the DOJ to promulgate its own preliminary investigation and inquest rules and purge conflicting provisions from Rule 112 of the Rules of Court.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Executive Nature of the Proceeding:** Long-standing jurisprudence (**Salta v. Court of Appeals**, **People v. Navarro**) settles that conducting preliminary investigations and determining probable cause to charge a defendant in court is purely an executive and prosecutorial function, not a judicial one.
2. **Policy of Judicial Non-Interference:** Under **Chan v. Secretary of Justice**, courts defer to executive findings of probable cause and adhere to non-interference in prosecutorial investigations absent grave abuse of discretion.
3. **Elimination of Procedural Friction:** The coexistence of Rule 112 and separate DOJ rules causes jurisdictional confusion. Conflicting sections of Rule 112 must be repealed to clear any obstacle to the DOJ's implementation of its administrative circular.
B. Jurisdictional & Institutional Considerations of the Court:
**Main Thesis:** While executive rule-making over preliminary investigations is conceded, the Court retains absolute, non-delegable authority over court procedure under Article VIII, Section 5(5) of the Constitution; thus, the DOJ-NPS Rules cannot **ipso facto** amend the Rules of Court without judicial action.
**Specific Contentions:**
1. **Exclusivity of Supreme Court Rule-Making:** Pursuant to **Estipona v. Lobrigo**, the power to promulgate, amend, or repeal rules of pleading, practice, and procedure resides exclusively within the Supreme Court and cannot be altered by executive circulars.
2. **Judicial Repeal Requirement:** Because an executive department cannot amend the Rules of Court, the Supreme Court itself must expressly repeal the inconsistent provisions of Rule 112 to take effect once the DOJ promulgates its rules.
3. **Reservation of Inherent Judicial Rule-Making:** The repeal of inconsistent provisions in Rule 112 is without prejudice to the Supreme Court enacting its own revised criminal procedure rule governing the threshold entry of preliminary investigations into the judicial docket (e.g., definitions, judicial determination of probable cause for warrant issuance, and non-DOJ investigatory bodies like the Ombudsman and COMELEC).
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Procedural / Substantive Boundary Issue]:** Whether or not the Department of Justice possesses the legal and administrative authority to promulgate its own operational rules governing preliminary investigations and inquest proceedings in the National Prosecution Service.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]:** Whether or not the promulgation of the DOJ-NPS Rules automatically repeals inconsistent provisions in Rule 112 of the Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure, or whether such repeal requires an affirmative act of the Supreme Court pursuant to its constitutional rule-making power.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Authority of the DOJ to Promulgate its Own Rules on Preliminary Investigation
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
Whether or not the Department of Justice possesses the authority to promulgate its own operational rules on preliminary investigations and inquest proceedings. **YES.** Preliminary investigation is an executive function belonging exclusively to the prosecutorial arm of the government, vesting the DOJ with administrative autonomy to regulate its conduct.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **Evolution to Executive Exclusivity:** While preliminary investigation was historically shared between municipal judges and fiscals under the 1940 and 1964 Rules of Court, the Judiciary Act of 1948, and B.P. Blg. 129, the paradigm shifted toward exclusivity. In 2005 (via A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC), the Court amended Rule 112 to eliminate first-level court judges from the list of officers authorized to conduct preliminary investigations.
2. **Preliminary Investigation is Non-Judicial:** Settled jurisprudence establishes that the inquiry to ascertain whether there is reasonable ground to believe a crime was committed and that the respondent is probably guilty is not a judicial function. As held in **Salta v. Court of Appeals** and **People v. Navarro**, directing and controlling the investigation and indictment is part of the prosecution's mandate as an executive agency.
3. **Adherence to Non-Interference:** Courts maintain a policy of non-interference in the prosecutor's exercise of discretion during preliminary investigation, intervening only upon a clear showing of grave abuse of discretion (**Chan v. Secretary of Justice**). Trial courts cannot order an assistant prosecutor to conduct an investigation over superior objections because doing so impermissibly meddles in executive and administrative functions. Consequently, the DOJ has the inherent administrative power to prescribe procedural rules for its prosecutors.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"A preliminary investigation is intended to protect the accused from the inconvenience, expense, and burden of defending himself in a formal trial until the reasonable probability of his guilt has first been ascertained in a fairly summary proceeding by a competent officer. It is also intended to protect the State from having to conduct useless and expensive trials. xxx **The preliminary investigation proper is, therefore, not a judicial function. It is a part of the prosecution's job, a function of the executive.**" **(Quoting Salta v. Court of Appeals)**

"Considering the nature of preliminary investigations, and the Court's policy on non-interference in the conduct thereof, the Court resolves to recognize the authority of the DOJ to promulgate its own rules on preliminary investigation. Indeed, **it is within the DOJ's prerogative to direct and control the conduct of preliminary investigations, and the Court will not interfere with the same so long as it not tainted with grave abuse of discretion.**"
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The Supreme Court recognized that public prosecutors are executive officials whose fundamental job is to evaluate whether a suspect should be criminally charged. Because preliminary investigation is an executive, prosecutorial duty rather than a judicial trial function, the Department of Justice has full authority to enact internal procedural guidelines governing how state prosecutors conduct inquiries and inquests without needing the Judiciary to micromanage them.
Issue 2: Exclusivity of Judicial Rule-Making and Repeal of Rule 112
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
Whether or not the promulgation of the DOJ-NPS Rules **ipso facto** repeals the provisions of Rule 112 of the Rules of Court. **NO.** Under the 1987 Constitution, the power to promulgate, amend, or repeal rules of pleading, practice, and procedure resides exclusively within the Supreme Court; therefore, executive rules cannot automatically repeal court rules, requiring the Supreme Court to formally decree the repeal of conflicting provisions in Rule 112.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1. **The Estipona Constitutional Doctrine:** Under Article VIII, Section 5(5) of the 1987 Constitution, as expounded in **Estipona v. Lobrigo**, the authority to promulgate rules of pleading, practice, and procedure is no longer shared with the Executive or Legislative departments. The power belongs to the Supreme Court's exclusive domain.
2. **Executive Rules Cannot Annul Rules of Court:** Because the Court alone asserts the constitutional discretion to amend, modify, or strike down procedural rules, the promulgation of the DOJ-NPS Rules cannot **ipso facto** repeal Rule 112 of the 2000 Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure.
3. **Judicial Repeal and Harmonization:** To remove procedural obstacles and prevent irreconcilable conflicts between the old judicial rules and the new executive circular, the Supreme Court directly decreed that upon the DOJ's official promulgation of the 2024 DOJ-NPS Rules, the inconsistent provisions of Rule 112 are deemed repealed.
4. **Retention of Judicial Rule-Making Regarding Preliminary Investigations:** This repeal does not bar the Supreme Court from enacting a newly configured Rule 112. The Court noted that other independent constitutional bodies (such as the Office of the Ombudsman and the Commission on Elections) conduct preliminary investigations outside DOJ jurisdiction, and courts still retain the independent constitutional responsibility to judicially evaluate probable cause for the issuance of warrants of arrest.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Further, to obviate any obstacle in the DOJ's implementation of the DOJ-NPS Rules, the Court resolves to repeal the provisions of Rule 112 of the 2000 Rules that are inconsistent therewith. **It must be stressed that the promulgation of the DOJ-NPS Rules would not ipso facto repeal Rule 112 of the 2000 Rules.**

In **Estipona v. Hon. Lobrigo**, the Court held that **the power to promulgate rules of pleading, practice, and procedure is now within its exclusive domain and no longer shared with the Executive and Legislative departments**, and that the Court could assert its discretion to amend, repeal, or even establish new rules of procedure, to the exclusion of these branches of government.

Thus, **it is settled that only the Court could repeal Rule 112 of the 2000 Rules.**"
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Even though preliminary investigation is an executive function, the Department of Justice does not possess the power to amend or repeal the Rules of Court. Under the Constitution, the Supreme Court has exclusive rule-making authority over legal procedures. Consequently, to give legal room for the DOJ rules to take effect without procedural collisions, the Supreme Court exercised its own exclusive power by proactively declaring that inconsistent portions of Rule 112 will be deemed repealed the moment the DOJ officially promulgates its new rules.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I / Remedial Law | Topic: 2) Pleading and Procedure (Article VIII, Section 5[5], 1987 Constitution; Criminal Procedure).
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
 Executive vs. Judicial Function Test:
1. **Executive Preliminary Investigation:** The determination of whether there is sufficient ground to engender a well-founded belief that a crime has been committed and the respondent is probably guilty and should be held for trial (prosecutorial probable cause to indict). Vested in the Executive (DOJ/NPS, Ombudsman, COMELEC).
2. **Judicial Preliminary Investigation / Examination:** The personal determination by a judge of the existence of probable cause for the purpose of issuing a warrant of arrest or search warrant under Article III, Section 2 of the Constitution. Vested exclusively in the Judiciary.
 Validity of Rule Repeal Checklist:
1. **Promulgation Source:** Must emanate directly from the Supreme Court **En Banc** under Article VIII, Section 5(5).
2. **Condition Precedent:** Formal promulgation of the 2024 DOJ-NPS Rules by the Executive department.
3. **Scope of Repeal:** Strictly limited to "pertinent provisions inconsistent therewith," preserving judicial jurisdiction over cases filed in court and non-DOJ investigatory proceedings.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Executive Function: Preliminary investigation proper is part of the prosecution's mandate, not a judicial function.
 Policy of Non-Interference:** Courts will not micromanage or interfere with prosecutorial probable-cause determinations absent **grave abuse of discretion.
 Ipso Facto: The principle that an executive administrative issuance cannot automatically or by itself repeal an existing Supreme Court rule of procedure.
 Exclusive Rule-Making Domain:** The constitutional doctrine (**Estipona) that the 1987 Constitution stripped the Executive and Legislative branches of shared power over rules of pleading, practice, and procedure.
**Subject-Specific Directive (Remedial Law Lens):**
 Procedural Vehicle & Jurisdiction Audit:** The matter came before the Court as an Administrative Matter (**A.M.), invoking the Court’s plenary administrative and constitutional rule-making power. The Court reaffirmed that municipal and first-level judges have had zero jurisdiction to conduct preliminary investigations since the 2005 amendments (A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC).
 Quantum of Proof Analysis:** The Resolution tracks the evidentiary threshold of preliminary investigations: from historical **prima facie evidence (under early codes) to evidence engendering a "well-founded belief" as to the fact of the commission of a crime and respondent’s probable guilt. The Court underscored that this prosecutorial determination of probable cause is distinct from the judge's personal determination of probable cause required to issue an arrest warrant under Circular No. 12-87.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
In **A.M. No. 24-02-09-SC**, the Supreme Court resolved the jurisdictional overlap between Rule 112 of the Rules of Court and the DOJ's new rules on preliminary investigation. The Court held that conducting a preliminary investigation is an executive, prosecutorial function, thereby recognizing the DOJ's authority to promulgate its 2024 DOJ-NPS Rules. However, applying the **Estipona** doctrine, the Court held that executive circulars cannot **ipso facto** repeal the Rules of Court because rule-making is exclusively judicial; hence, the Supreme Court itself expressly decreed the repeal of inconsistent provisions of Rule 112, effective upon the DOJ's formal promulgation of its rules.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed. The resolution was adopted unanimously by all fourteen participating Justices of the **En Banc**.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"**FOR THESE REASONS**, the Court hereby **RECOGNIZES the AUTHORITY** of the Department of Justice to promulgate its 2024 DOJ-National Prosecution Service Rules on Preliminary Investigations and Inquest Proceedings (2024 DOJ-NPS Rules).

Thereafter, and once the 2024 DOJ-NPS Rules are promulgated by the DOJ, the pertinent provisions of Rule 112 of the 2000 Revised Rules on Criminal Procedure, as amended, inconsistent therewith are deemed **REPEALED**. This shall be without prejudice to the Court's promulgation of its own rules of procedure, of a new rule touching upon preliminary investigation, consistent with the 2024 DOJ-NPS Rules.

Let a copy of the 2024 DOJ-NPS Rules be endorsed to the Sub-Committee on the Revision of the Rules of Criminal Procedure for its guidance and appropriate action.

**SO ORDERED.**"
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court upheld the power of the Department of Justice to draft and enforce its own internal rules governing preliminary investigations and inquest proceedings. Simultaneously, the Court ordered that all provisions in Rule 112 of the Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure that conflict with the new DOJ rules are officially deemed repealed once the DOJ promulgates them, while reserving the Supreme Court's constitutional prerogative to issue a streamlined, revised Rule 112 for the courts.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: In Re: Social Media Posts of Edgar S. Dizon**
**Full Official Caption:** IN RE: SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS OF EDGAR S. DIZON (Bar Matter No. 4734)
**Citation & Metadata:** B.M. No. 4734; July 15, 2026; **En Banc**; **Per Curiam**.
**Voting Breakdown:** Gesmundo, **C.J.**, Caguioa, Hernando, Lazaro-Javier, Inting, Zalameda, Gaerlan, Rosario, Dimaampao, Marquez, Kho, Jr., Singh, and Villanueva, **JJ.**, concurred. Leonen, **SAJ.**, filed a Separate Concurring Opinion. Lopez, **J.**, was on leave.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Edgar S. Dizon ("Teacher Edgar") [Respondent]:** 2016 Arellano School of Law graduate who passed the 2016 Bar Examinations but whose oath-taking was withheld due to pending murder cases; creator and administrator of the Facebook accounts/pages **Bar Law for Dummies Training Program** and **Tsidkenu Dizon**, through which he conducted commercial coaching for repeat bar examinees.
**Office of the 2023 Bar Chair [Supervising Authority]:** The Supreme Court entity tasked with the administration, technical execution, and integrity of the 2023 digitalized Bar Examinations.
**Office of the Bar Confidant (OBC) [Recommending Arm]:** The administrative office of the Supreme Court that evaluated Dizon’s viral social media posts and recommended the issuance of a show-cause order for indirect contempt.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
This is an original, summary administrative disciplinary and indirect contempt proceeding initiated **motu proprio** by the Supreme Court **En Banc** pursuant to a Show Cause Resolution dated October 24, 2023, following an investigation and recommendation submitted by the Office of the Bar Confidant regarding Dizon's public social media publications concerning the checking of the 2023 Bar Examinations.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Constitutional Law → The Judicial Department → Exclusive Constitutional Power to Regulate Admission to the Practice of Law (1987 Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 5[5]) → Supervision over Bar Examinations and Inherent Contempt Power
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Legal Ethics & Remedial Law → Rule 71 (Contempt) → Section 3(c), (d), and (e) (Indirect Contempt: Unlawful Interference, Degrading the Administration of Justice, and Unauthorized Practice of Law)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article VIII, Section 5, Paragraph 5, 1987 Constitution:**
"SECTION 5. The Supreme Court shall have the following powers:
. . .
(5) **Promulgate rules concerning the protection and enforcement of constitutional rights, pleading, practice, and procedure in all courts, the admission to the practice of law, the Integrated Bar, and legal assistance to the underprivileged.** Such rules shall provide a simplified and inexpensive procedure for the speedy disposition of cases, shall be uniform for all courts of the same grade, and shall not diminish, increase, or modify substantive rights. Rules of procedure of special courts and quasi-judicial bodies shall remain effective unless disapproved by the Supreme Court."
**Rule 71, Section 3(c), (d), and (e), Rules of Court:**
"SEC. 3. **Indirect contempt to be punished after charge and hearing.** — After a charge in writing has been filed, and opportunity given to the respondent to comment thereon within such period as may be fixed by the court and to be heard by himself[/herself] or counsel, a person guilty of any of the following acts may be punished for indirect contempt:
. . .
(c) **Any abuse of or any unlawful interference with the processes or proceedings of a court** not constituting direct contempt under section 1 of this Rule;
(d) **Any improper conduct tending, directly or indirectly, to impede, obstruct, or degrade the administration of justice;**
(e) **Assuming to be an attorney or an officer of a court, and acting as such without authority;**
. . .
But nothing in this section shall be so construed as to prevent the court from issuing process to bring the respondent into court, or from holding him in custody pending such proceedings."
**Sections 2 (para. 3) and 17 (para. 4), A.M. No. 24-10-05-SC (2025 Proposed Amendments to Rule 138 of the Rules of Court):**
Section 2, paragraph 3 / Section 17, paragraph 3:
"**In the Supreme Court's assessment and sole discretion**, considering the gravity of the claim or offense charged, any prior cases filed against the applicant, **and similar reasons**, the Supreme Court may defer the oath-taking of the concerned applicant, **or impose any other preventive measures, as warranted.**"

Section 17, paragraph 4:
"In any case, any false or inaccurate information, concealment or failure to disclose, or misrepresentation on the part of an applicant shall be a ground for either the denial of the application, disqualification from taking the examinations, **or delisting from the list of passers**, depending on the stage of discovery, and without prejudice to other disciplinary sanctions that the Supreme Court may impose."
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):**
On September 21, 2023, during the final preparation phase of the digitalized 2023 Bar Examinations, Edgar S. Dizon published a post on his Facebook pages stating that examinees must start answers with "YES or NO" because **"Yan ang unang hahanapin ng AI Checking to sort out the correct answers."** The post went viral, sparking panic and confusion among examinees, disrupting bar operations by forcing the Court to divert personnel and resources to trace the leak, coordinate with the NBI, and issue a public clarification, culminating in Dizon demanding a 24-hour public apology from the Court and an audience for a photograph with the Bar Chair.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**2016:** Edgar S. Dizon graduates from Arellano School of Law and successfully passes the 2016 Philippine Bar Examinations. His oath-taking is deferred by the Supreme Court due to pending murder charges filed against him.
**Post-2016 to Mid-2023:** Despite not being admitted to the Philippine Bar, Dizon establishes the **Bar Law for Dummies Training Program**, authoring extensive bar review materials across all bar subjects, conducting topical lectures, and coaching examinees who have failed the bar exam more than three times.
**September 21, 2023:** In the final stages of preparations for the 2023 Bar Examinations, Dizon publishes a viral advisory on his Facebook accounts (**Bar Law for Dummies Training Program** and **Tsidkenu Dizon**) instructing examinees: **"ALWAYS START WITH YES or NO Yan ang unang hahanapin ng AI Checking to sort out the correct answers."** The post spreads rapidly, creating anxiety among examinees.
**September 23, 2023:** The Office of the 2023 Bar Chair issues an official Advisory condemning the social media posts as false, baseless, and defamatory, reiterating that the examinations are manually evaluated by four human examiners per subject and that the Court has engaged the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) to probe the administrator behind the posts.
**Post-September 23, 2023:** Dizon refuses to take down the posts. Instead, he grants a media interview threatening the Supreme Court with legal action and demanding an official public apology within 24 hours. Concurrently, Dizon sends multiple emails to the Judiciary Public Assistance Section asserting that the Court's Advisory destroyed his life without hearing his side, insisting that the Court issue a statement rectifying the advisory, and requesting a photo opportunity with the 2023 Bar Chair because **"idol ko po kayo."**
**October 24, 2023:** Upon the evaluation and recommendation of the Office of the Bar Confidant, the Supreme Court **En Banc** issues a Show Cause Resolution ordering Dizon to explain within five working days why he should not be cited for indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(c), (d), and (e) of the Rules of Court.
**March 14, 2024:** Dizon submits his Explanation admitting account ownership and authoring the post, but denying that he claimed artificial intelligence would execute the checking; he further denies engaging in the illegal practice of law by framing his coaching as mere pedagogical guidance on answering techniques.
**July 15, 2026:** The Supreme Court **En Banc** promulgates its **Per Curiam** Decision finding Dizon guilty of indirect contempt, fining him PHP 30,000.00, ordering him delisted from the roll of successful bar examinees, and warning him against the unauthorized practice of law.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondent Edgar S. Dizon’s Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Dizon did not commit indirect contempt or unlawfully interfere with the Bar Examinations, because his post was merely pedagogical coaching advice that was misconstrued; nor did he engage in the illegal practice of law, as his coaching activities merely applied the art of teaching without rendering legal advice on actual cases.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Absence of Misinformation Regarding AI:** He insists he used the phrase "TO HELP" in his posts and never categorically asserted that artificial intelligence would replace human examiners in sorting, checking, or grading the exam answers.
2.  **Pedagogical Nature of Bar Coaching (Non-Practice of Law):** As a holder of a Master’s Degree in Education, he merely identifies learning gaps and coaches examinees on structural presentation and logical drafting styles. He explicitly instructs students to call him "Teacher Edgar" and never "Attorney."
3.  **Absence of Legal Representation on Actual Controversies:** Under paragraph 6(b) of his Explanation, he argued that as a teacher, he does not give legal opinions on actual cases, but merely discusses answers to past bar questions and utilizes his non-wasted legal knowledge to help repeaters pass.
4.  **Chilling Effect and Procedural Injustice:** The Court's public Advisory condemned him without due process (**"Hindi man lang nakuha ang side ko bago nailagay sa Advisory yung pangalan ko"**), causing him severe personal and emotional devastation.
B. The Supreme Court's / Bar Confidant's Findings & Indictments
**Main Thesis:** Dizon’s viral falsehoods directly disrupted the administration of the 2023 Bar Examinations, cast aspersion on the integrity of the judicial admission process, and demonstrated the unauthorized practice of law, compounded by insolent post-incident conduct.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Unlawful Interference with Judicial Process (Rule 71, Sec. 3[c], [d]):** Announcing that AI would check the bar examinations caused panic among examinees and forced the Court to scramble and redirect lean administrative personnel and time toward crisis containment and coordination with law enforcement.
2.  **Res Ipsa Loquitur Rebuttal:** Dizon’s own literal text (**"Yan ang unang hahanapin ng AI Checking to sort out the correct answers"**) refutes his claim that he did not state AI would do the sorting and checking.
3.  **Illegal Practice of Law (Rule 71, Sec. 3[e]):** Coaching bar examinees, lecturing on substantive law doctrines, and authoring bar review summation notes and syllabi-based questions across all bar subjects constitute the practice of law under **Cayetano v. Monsod**. Dizon is a non-lawyer whose admission remains suspended due to pending murder charges.
4.  **Lack of Remorse and Audacity:** Demanding a public apology within 24 hours under threat of suit, refusing to delete the contumacious posts, and trivializing the Court's processes by demanding a photograph with the Bar Chair demonstrate unfitness for membership in the bar.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Edgar S. Dizon is guilty of indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(c) and (d) of the Rules of Court for publishing false claims that the 2023 Bar Examinations would be checked and sorted using artificial intelligence.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Edgar S. Dizon engaged in the unauthorized practice of law, constituting indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(e) of the Rules of Court, by authoring comprehensive bar review materials and conducting substantive coaching classes for bar reviewees.
3.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Supreme Court possesses the constitutional authority to impose the administrative sanction of delisting an applicant from the roll of successful bar examinees on grounds of contumacious conduct and unauthorized practice of law prior to oath-taking.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Liability for Indirect Contempt via Interference with Bar Examinations
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did Dizon’s viral social media post claiming that the 2023 Bar Examinations would be sorted and checked by artificial intelligence constitute indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(c) and (d)?
**YES.** The unauthorized publication of fabricated examination mechanics severely disrupted court administration, eroded public trust in the admission process, and caused acute panic among examinees during a critical phase of judicial operations.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Supervisory Primacy over Bar Admissions:** Pursuant to Article VIII of the Constitution and established doctrine in **In re: Parazo**, the Supreme Court holds plenary, exclusive responsibility over the admission of members to the bar. Because the Court demands high standards of honesty and fair dealing, any insinuation of irregularity or procedural anomaly in the Bar Examinations is imbued with paramount public interest.
2.  **Physical Reality of Examination Evaluation:** Under Bar rules and guidelines (Section 12, A.M. No. 24-10-05-SC), the Committee of Bar Examiners consists of real "warm bodies"—a Supreme Court Justice as Chairperson and expert members of the Philippine Bar. They are not powered, sorted, or guided by artificial intelligence.
3.  **Rejection of the "To Help" Defense via Res Ipsa Loquitur:** Dizon’s claim that he merely indicated AI would "help" is contradicted by the face of his post: **"ALWAYS START WITH YES or NO Yan ang unang hahanapin ng AI Checking to sort out the correct answers."** Under the principle of **res ipsa loquitur**, the text clearly told examinees that an AI system was deployed to sort and evaluate responses.
4.  **Tangible Disruption to the Administration of Justice:** Contempt does not require physical obstruction of a courtroom. Dizon’s posts forced the Office of the 2023 Bar Chair to divert its limited personnel away from execution details to investigate the source, coordinate with the NBI, issue emergency advisories, and handle public panic. This conduct directly impeded, obstructed, and degraded the administration of justice.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"Clearly, Dizon unlawfully interfered in the conduct of the 2023 Bar Examinations, a court-sanctioned activity, by peddling false information and causing alarm and panic among the examinees. His irresponsible and baseless post that the AI will do the sorting and checking undermined the integrity not only of the bar examinations but likewise of the 'Supreme Court itself which has the overall supervision and control over the examinations.'"

"This is **res ipsa logitur**. Dizon clearly and categorically mentioned that the AI will do the checking and sorting of the examinees' answers."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The Supreme Court found Dizon in indirect contempt because his social media posts falsely claimed that AI would grade the 2023 Bar Examinations. This was not harmless advice; it panicked examinees right before exam week and forced the Court to divert personnel to trace the leak, coordinate with law enforcement, and issue emergency clarifications. Because the bar exam is an official judicial proceeding under the Court's exclusive constitutional authority, manufacturing false procedures that erode faith in the grading system directly obstructs the administration of justice.
Issue 2: Unauthorized Practice of Law by a Non-Admitted Bar Passer
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did Dizon engage in the unauthorized practice of law under Rule 71, Section 3(e) by operating his **Bar Law for Dummies Training Program** and authoring specialized legal review modules?
**YES.** Providing instructional bar coaching, analyzing past bar questions, and authoring substantive review outlines for compensation or institutionalized training necessitate the continuous application of legal knowledge and constitute the practice of law, which is forbidden to non-lawyers.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Doctrinal Scope of the Practice of Law:** Under **Cayetano v. Monsod**, the practice of law is not limited to appearing in court or representing clients in litigation. It encompasses "any activity, in or out of court, which requires the application of law, legal procedure, knowledge, training and experience."
2.  **Legal Knowledge Applied in Bar Coaching:** Dizon’s defense that he was merely executing pedagogical techniques as a Master of Education is unavailing. Teaching bar reviewees how to resolve legal problems requires substantive legal analysis.
3.  **Admission against Interest in Pleadings:** In paragraph 6(b) of his own Explanation, Dizon explicitly conceded: **"I only discuss the answers in the past bar questions as part of my coaching job"** and stated **"na hindi [niya] inaksaya ang [kanyang] knowledge of law and skills in coaching and teaching."**
4.  **Substantive Authorship of Legal Compendiums:** Dizon authored over twenty-two comprehensive subject-matter modules (including **BLD Persons and Family Relations**, **Topical Bar Questions and Answers in Remedial Law**, **Summation Pre-Week Notes**, and lectures on affirmative defenses). Preparing specialized legal syntheses necessitates the application of trained legal intellect, which Dizon had no legal authority to practice given that his oath-taking was held in abeyance.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"'Practice of law means any activity, in or out of court, which requires the application of law, legal procedure, knowledge, training and experience.' . . . Discussing past bar examination answers definitely requires an application of legal knowledge. Interestingly, Dizon himself admitted 'na hindi [niya] inaksaya ang [kanyang] knowledge of law and skills in coaching and teaching.'"

"The preparation of all these materials required the application of legal knowledge. Thus, there can be no conclusion other than that Dizon illegally engaged in the practice of law. Thus, for engaging in the unauthorized practice of law, Dizon is similarly guilty of indirect contempt."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Passing the bar exam does not make someone a lawyer; oath-taking and signing the Roll of Attorneys are mandatory prerequisites. Because Dizon never took the lawyer's oath due to pending murder charges, he remained a non-lawyer. Teaching repeaters how to answer bar exams and authoring pre-week reviewers require the active interpretation and application of legal principles, which falls squarely within the definition of the practice of law under **Cayetano v. Monsod**. Doing so without being admitted to the bar is an unauthorized practice of law punishable as indirect contempt.
Issue 3: Constitutional Power to Delist an Examinee Prior to Oath-Taking
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does the Supreme Court have the authority to delist Dizon from the list of successful bar examinees as a preventive and administrative sanction?
**YES.** The practice of law is a privilege subject to the continuing fitness of the applicant; the Supreme Court possesses plenary, sole discretion under its constitutional mandate and procedural rules to purge unfit candidates from the roll of bar passers before they take the oath.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **The Court as Exclusive Gatekeeper:** The practice of law is not a vested constitutional property right, but a distinct privilege reserved exclusively for individuals demonstrating unyielding compliance with academic, intellectual, and moral/character standards.
2.  **Preventive Authority under Amended Rule 138:** Pursuant to A.M. No. 24-10-05-SC (Sections 2 and 17 of the Proposed Amendments to Rule 138), the Supreme Court exercises sole discretion, based on the gravity of an offense or related circumstances, to defer oath-taking or impose any other preventive measures, explicitly including "delisting from the list of passers."
3.  **Compounded Defiance and Moral Unfitness:** Dizon's ongoing exclusion from the bar originated from pending murder cases. Rather than proving moral rehabilitation, he displayed profound insolence by threatening the Court with legal action on television, demanding a 24-hour public apology, refusing to retract his false posts, and treating solemn proceedings as a novelty by requesting a photo opportunity with the Bar Chair. This conduct establishes complete unfitness to join the legal fraternity.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Jurisprudence is settled that the Court is the gatekeeper to the bar. The practice of law is a privilege and not a vested right. Thus, only those applicants who complied with all the academic and character requirements are allowed to join the legal fraternity. The Court has the sole discretion to assess the fitness of the applicants and to impose preventive measures, as warranted, to prevent those who are unqualified from becoming members of the bar."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The Supreme Court is the sole gatekeeper to the legal profession. Because passing the written examination confers only an inchoate privilege, the Court retains total authority to withdraw that privilege at any point prior to the administration of the oath if the candidate demonstrates moral unfitness. Dizon's combination of spreading disruptive falsehoods, practicing law unlawfully, and petulantly demanding an apology from the Court proved he lacked the character demanded of a lawyer, justifying his summary delisting from the list of bar passers.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I / Legal Ethics → 3) Admission to the Practice of Law and Regulation thereof.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist:**
1.  State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:
 Power Exercised: The Supreme Court’s exclusive constitutional prerogative to regulate admission to the bar (Art. VIII, Sec. 5[5], 1987 Constitution) paired with its inherent judicial contempt power to defend the integrity of its proceedings.
 Right Invoked Against It: Freedom of Speech and Expression (Art. III, Sec. 4) raised implicitly by Dizon’s defense of fair teaching commentary.
2.  The Dual Pre-Conditions to Membership in the Bar:
 Requisite 1: Academic & Written Examination Competence. (Met by Dizon in 2016).
 Requisite 2: Continuing Moral Character & Judicial Authorization (Oath & Roll Signing). (Failed). The Court reiterated that passing the written test yields only an expectancy; character must remain unsullied until the actual oath-taking.
3.  Elements of Indirect Contempt via Obstruction & Usurpation (Rule 71, Sec. 3):
 Interference/Degradation (Sec. 3[c], [d]):** Unlawful external acts calculated to impede, embarrass, or disrupt court-supervised processes. (**Proven: Dissemination of false AI-checking claims that threw the 2023 Bar Examinations into operational turmoil).
 Usurpation of Legal Authority (Sec. 3[e]):** Engaging in legal custom, advice, or instruction without admission to the Roll of Attorneys. (**Proven: Authoring pre-week notes, charging for substantive bar prep, and explaining legal applications to repeaters).
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Gatekeeper to the Bar (Supreme Court's exclusive plenary control over admission).
 Privilege, Not a Vested Right (Legal status of bar membership).
 Practice of Law** (**Cayetano v. Monsod formulation: any activity requiring legal training, knowledge, and experience).
 Res Ipsa Loquitur (The post spoke for itself to establish contumacious intent).
 Delisting from the List of Passers (Preventive administrative forfeiture of examination success).
 Clear and Present Danger / Incitement Test (Addressed by SAJ Leonen regarding speech directed at court integrity).
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
**In Re: Dizon** falls squarely under the regulation of admission to the bar because it defines the boundary between passing the bar exam and actually being admitted to practice. The Supreme Court held that passing the bar does not confer a vested right to practice law or teach substantive law review courses, both of which require admission to the roll. When an unadmitted passer spreads viral falsehoods that disrupt ongoing bar examinations and brazenly threatens the Court, the Court may exercise its exclusive constitutional gatekeeping power under Article VIII, Section 5(5) to cite the individual for indirect contempt, fine him, and administratively delist him from the roll of bar passers.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**SAJ. Leonen (Separate Concurring Opinion):** Concurred fully in the conviction, but analyzed the constitutional intersection between the inherent power of contempt and the Article III, Section 4 guarantee of Free Speech. Applying the **Clear and Present Danger Test** (**Cabansag v. Fernandez**), the **Incitement Test** (**Brandenburg v. Ohio** / **Re: Badoy**), and J.L. Austin's linguistic Speech-Act framework (locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts), Justice Leonen emphasized that speech must be evaluated as an intentional act situated in context. Dizon's posts were not protected criticism; they were deliberate falsehoods designed to exploit examinees' anxieties for online clout and panic, creating a clear, imminent danger to the administration of justice. He underscored that penalties must educate and enforce digital responsibility, not merely punish.
**Verbatim/Near-Verbatim Fallo:**
"FOR THESE REASONS, Edgar S. Dizon is found GUILTY of indirect contempt and is directed to PAY a FINE of PHP 30,000.00. The Office of the Bar Confidant is DIRECTED to DELIST Edgar S. Dizon from the list of bar passers and to make a report thereon to the Court within five days from notice. Dizon is WARNED from further engaging in the unauthorized practice of law.

SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Edgar S. Dizon was found guilty of indirect contempt of court, ordered to pay a fine of PHP 30,000.00, and warned to cease practicing law. More severely, the Supreme Court stripped him of his successful 2016 examination standing by ordering the Office of the Bar Confidant to permanently delist him from the roster of bar passers, effectively barring him from ever taking the lawyer's oath based on that examination.
