digest:
### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Re: Disturbing Social Media Posts of Lawyers/Law Professors (2023)
**Full Official Caption:** Re: Disturbing Social Media Posts of Lawyers/Law Professors (Atty. Noel V. Antay, Jr., Atty. Ernesto A. Tabujara III, Atty. Israel P. Calderon, Atty. Morgan Rosales Nicanor, and Atty. Joseph Marion Peña Navarrete)
**Citation & Metadata:** A.M. No. 21-06-20-SC; April 11, 2023; 939 Phil. 475; **Per Curiam**; En Banc (Concurring Opinion by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Mario Victor F. Leonen; all other participating Justices concurred).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**The Supreme Court of the Philippines (Motu Proprio Disciplinary Body):** Initiated the administrative investigation against the erring lawyers.
**Atty. Noel V. Antay, Jr. (Respondent Lawyer / Facebook Account "SP Leon Yatna"):** Practicing lawyer who initiated the offensive Facebook thread narrating his prosecution of an LGBTQIA+ individual and characterizing the presiding judge.
**Atty. Ernesto A. Tabujara III (Respondent Lawyer / Law Professor / Radio Host):** Practicing lawyer, law professor, and online page moderator who made disparaging remarks regarding the sexual orientation, mental health, and integrity of Taguig City judges.
**Atty. Israel P. Calderon (Respondent Lawyer / Law Professor / Facebook Account "Denden Calderon"):** Law professor and lawyer who posted demeaning, sexually charged conjectures regarding the convict's motives.
**Atty. Morgan Rosales Nicanor (Respondent Lawyer / Law Professor):** Law professor and lawyer of over a decade who joined and affirmed the derogatory repartee.
**Atty. Joseph Marion Peña Navarrete (Respondent Lawyer / Prosecutor):** Lawyer/prosecutor who joined the exchange by bringing up a demeaning past incident involving a male client admiring Atty. Nicanor.
**Office of the Bar Confidant (OBC):** Investigating arm of the Supreme Court tasked with evaluating the compliance and explanations of the respondents.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** This administrative matter originated directly within the Supreme Court **motu proprio** via a Show Cause Resolution dated June 29, 2021, requiring the respondent lawyers to explain circulating screenshots of their Facebook comment thread. It was referred to the OBC for investigation, report, and recommendation, which recommended admonition. The matter is before the Supreme Court **En Banc** for final disciplinary adjudication.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Legal Ethics & Judicial Ethics → Regulation of the Practice of Law → Duties of Lawyers to the Dignity of the Profession and Respect for Courts (Online Decorum & SOGIESC Discrimination)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Bill of Rights → Right to Privacy (Reasonable Expectation of Privacy in Social Media) & Freedom of Expression
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Code of Professional Responsibility (CPR), Rule 7.03:**
"Rule 7.03 - A lawyer shall not engage in conduct that adversely reflects on his fitness to practice law, nor shall he whether in public or private life, behave in a scandalous manner to the discredit of the legal profession."
**Code of Professional Responsibility (CPR), Rule 8.01:**
"Rule 8.01 - A lawyer shall not, in his professional dealings, use language which is abusive, offensive or otherwise improper."
**Code of Professional Responsibility (CPR), Canon 11:**
"CANON 11 - A LAWYER SHALL OBSERVE AND MAINTAIN THE RESPECT DUE TO THE COURTS AND TO JUDICIAL OFFICERS AND SHOULD INSIST ON SIMILAR CONDUCT BY OTHERS."
**1987 Philippine Constitution, Article II, Section 11:**
"Section 11. The State values the dignity of every human person and guarantees full respect for human rights."
**Rules of Court, Rule 138, Section 20(b):**
"Sec. 20. **Duties of attorneys.** — It is the duty of an attorney: x x x (b) To observe and maintain the respect due to the courts of justice and judicial officers; x x x"
**Factual Trigger:** Atty. Noel V. Antay, Jr. posted a thread on Facebook boasting about prosecuting a member of the LGBTQIA+ community and describing the judge who came to his defense as "somewhat effeminate." This elicited an online exchange among five lawyers and law professors featuring homophobic slurs, demeaning sexual insinuations, and sweeping accusations that Taguig City judges on the first floor are "bakla at mga corrupt" and on the second floor "may sira sa ulo."
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**Prior to June 2021:** Atty. Antay, Jr. posted on Facebook under the handle "SP Leon Yatna": **"Just prosecuted and helped convict a member of the LGBTA community for large scale estafa. The new convict then began cussing at me accusing me of being a bigot. A first for me. =) The judge (who is somewhat effeminate) comes to my defense and warns the felon to behave. All in a day's work. =) =) =)"**
**Contemporaneous Comment Thread:** Atty. Tabujara III commented, asking: **"Sino yung bakla na judge sa Taguig sa MTC sa first floor? Naka eye liner and eye shadow pag nag hehearing. Ang taray pa!"** Atty. Antay, Jr. responded that the judge had been promoted to the RTC. Atty. Tabujara III then wrote: **"The joke among lawyers is that sa Taguig sa 2nd floor puro may sira sa ulo mga judge, sa baba bakla at mga corrupt."** Atty. Antay, Jr. replied: **"No comment, Boss Ticky. May mga kaso pa ako doon eh. =) =) =)"**
**Contemporaneous Comment Thread:** Atty. Calderon chimed in: **"Baka type ka."** When Atty. Antay, Jr. replied, **"Bad ka, Prof.,"** Atty. Calderon added: **"malay mo. Nakita n'ya intelligence mo given na good looks eh na convict mo pa s'ya. Tapos syempre di ka mapapasakamay n'ya kaya ayon imbyerna I. Charot haha."**
**Contemporaneous Comment Thread:** Atty. Nicanor joined: **"SP Leon Yatna oo tama. feel ko type ka bossing. hehehe."** Atty. Tabujara III added: **"Dapat kinurot mo! Charot!"** Atty. Navarrete then brought up an earlier incident at the Ombudsman involving Atty. Nicanor's male client, noting: **"Ang natatandaan ko lang is malagkit tingin kay papa, este Prof. Morgan,"** to which Atty. Antay, Jr. responded: **"Matikas kasi si Prof. Morgan eh, Habulin. =)"**
**June 29, 2021:** The Supreme Court **En Banc**, having taken notice of the circulating screenshots, issued a **motu proprio** Show Cause Resolution requiring all five lawyers to explain why no administrative charges should be filed against them.
**October 6, 2021:** Atty. Nicanor filed his Explanation, expressing apologies for a lapse in judgment and lack of discernment, stating his comment was playful banter made in jest.
**October 7, 2021:** Atty. Navarrete filed his Explanation, apologizing for an insensitive joke, claiming an upbringing surrounded by LGBTQIA+ friends and relatives, and asserting he never intended to degrade anyone.
**October 25, 2021:** Atty. Antay, Jr. filed his Compliance, professing remorse and shame, but invoking his right to privacy by claiming his Facebook profile was "locked" and unviewable to outsiders, while arguing his terms ("effeminate", "member of the LGBT community") were merely descriptive and not disparaging.
**November 7, 2021:** Atty. Tabujara III filed his Comment, claiming 30 years of ethical practice, denying bigotry, submitting affidavits from LGBTQIA+ clients and radio show guests to show allyship, and offering a conditional apology (**"If I have hurt anyone, I am sorry..."**).
**June 21, 2022:** The Court referred the administrative matter to the Office of the Bar Confidant (OBC) for investigation, report, and recommendation.
**July 26, 2022:** The Court resolved that Atty. Calderon was deemed served with court processes.
**August 31, 2022:** The OBC submitted its Report and Recommendation, finding the comments degrading to the Judiciary and the LGBTQIA+ community, but recommending mere **admonition** in view of the lawyers' apologies, remorse, and lack of ill intent.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondent Lawyers' Arguments
**Atty. Noel V. Antay, Jr.:**
 Main Thesis: He has remorse and profound shame, but his locked privacy settings shielded him, and his words lacked discriminatory intent.
 Specific Contentions:
1.  **Right to Privacy:** His Facebook account is locked; external access was impossible without a breach. He had a reasonable expectation of privacy in what was intended as a private post.
2.  **Descriptive, Not Pejorative:** Stating "member of the LGBT community" was purely descriptive. Using "effeminate" was intended solely to describe a non-antagonistic, calm judicial demeanor, not to mock the magistrate.
3.  **Mitigation:** He tried to end the thread by saying "Bad ka" and never intended to undermine the Judiciary or discriminate against LGBTQIA+ persons.
**Atty. Ernesto A. Tabujara III:**
 Main Thesis: The posts were banter made in good faith; he is not a bigot, has championed LGBTQIA+ individuals, and made no direct attacks.
 Specific Contentions:
1.  **History and Practice:** He has practiced for over 30 years without disciplinary infractions and has served as an IBP officer.
2.  **Allyship:** He has LGBTQIA+ friends, clients, and radio show guests (submitting supporting affidavits from Lexter Victorio and Ma. Nidzhen Salanguit-Angeles).
3.  **Absence of Malice:** The remarks were merely jokes passed among lawyers; he offered an apology if anyone took offense, maintaining nobody is 100% perfect.
**Atty. Israel P. Calderon:**
 Main Thesis & Specific Contentions: Not expressly stated in the decision (failed to file a separate responsive pleading; deemed served by the Court on July 26, 2022).
**Atty. Morgan Rosales Nicanor:**
 Main Thesis: His lone comment was playful banter made in jest without malice.
 Specific Contentions:
1.  He contributed only a single remark (**"feel ko type ka bossing"**), teasing a fellow commenter.
2.  He had over a decade of unblemished legal practice and sincerely apologized for his lapse in judgment and lack of discernment.
**Atty. Joseph Marion Peña Navarrete:**
 Main Thesis: His comments were a playful recollection of a past event without reference to sexual orientation or intent to disparage.
 Specific Contentions:
1.  He attended an all-boys school, grew up with LGBTQIA+ friends/relatives, and has close LGBTQIA+ friends who are godparents to his children.
2.  His comment merely recalled an event at the Ombudsman without specifying the sex or gender identity of the client; it was harmless teasing of Atty. Nicanor.
B. Investigating Arm (Office of the Bar Confidant - OBC) Position
 Main Thesis: The conduct violated decorum and dignity, but mitigating factors warrant only admonition.
 Specific Contentions: The comments degraded both the Judiciary and the LGBTQIA+ community. However, considering respondents apologized, expressed remorse, pleaded for mercy, and claimed no deliberate intent to disrespect the courts, a penalty of admonition is sufficient.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the respondent lawyers can validly invoke their constitutional right to privacy to shield themselves from administrative liability for their online social media exchanges.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Attys. Antay, Jr., Tabujara III, Calderon, Nicanor, and Navarrete violated Rule 7.03 of the Code of Professional Responsibility (CPR), as well as related ethical mandates regarding respectful language and respect due to the courts, through their homophobic and derogatory comments on Facebook.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Invocation of the Right to Privacy as an Administrative Shield
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** A lawyer’s right to privacy in social media activities is limited and cannot serve as a shield against administrative discipline, particularly where no reasonable expectation of privacy exists on Facebook.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Limited Application to Online Conduct:** Reaffirming **Belo-Henares v. Atty. Guevarra, the Court emphasized that a lawyer’s right to privacy has limited application to social media activities.
 The Two-Part Expectation Test: In privacy law, the test requires determining (1) whether by conduct, the person exhibited an expectation of privacy, and (2) whether that expectation is one that society recognizes as reasonable.
 Structural Porosity of Social Media: Even if privacy settings are set to "Friends" or an account is alleged to be "locked," there is no reasonable expectation of privacy in Facebook posts. Digital content can be easily screenshotted, downloaded, shared, or tagged to outsiders by one's own connections or through a leak ("a rat amidst them").
 Failure of Proof: Atty. Antay, Jr.'s claim that his account was locked was a bare allegation, which does not constitute proof. The undeniable reality that the screenshots circulated publicly completely negates any objective claim of privacy.
 Transformation to Public Forum: The Court ruled that once private conversations leak into public view, they are treated as public discourse—as if uttered during a formal court proceeding.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"[R]estricting the privacy of one's Facebook posts to 'Friends' does not guarantee absolute protection from the prying eyes of another user who does not belong to one's circle of friends. ... Under the circumstances, therefore, respondent's claim of violation of right to privacy is negated."

"It is not a defense that the discriminatory language was uttered in what was seemingly intended to be private exchanges among the macho men. The fact that their exchanges became public trumps whatever intention they may have had to keep their communications private. Seekers of righteousness cannot seek cover under a pledge of anonymity when their actions are brought to light for everyone's scrutiny."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** You cannot hide behind Facebook's privacy settings to escape disbarment or disciplinary sanction. The Supreme Court applies the reasonable expectation of privacy test: because social media posts can easily be screenshot, forwarded, or shared by "friends," society does not recognize an absolute expectation of privacy on Facebook, even on locked profiles. Once your unethical comments leak into the open, the Court treats them as if you shouted them inside an open courtroom.
Issue 2: Violation of Rule 7.03 of the Code of Professional Responsibility (CPR)
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** All five respondents violated Rule 7.03 of the CPR by engaging in improper, scandalous, and homophobic conduct that devalues LGBTQIA+ individuals and degrades the integrity of the Judiciary, with Atty. Tabujara III incurring heavier liability for reckless, wanton, and unapologetic attacks on the bench.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 High Social Responsibility in Public and Private Life: Under Rule 7.03 of the CPR, a lawyer must not engage in conduct that adversely reflects on fitness to practice law, nor behave scandalously in public or private life. Disciplinary authority reaches lawyers even in purely private conduct if their acts show a want of probity or good moral character.
 Constitutional and International Mandate of Non-Discrimination:** Relying on **Ang Ladlad LGBT Party v. COMELEC**, **CBEAI v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas**, and **Falcis v. Civil Registrar General, the Court underscored that the Philippine legal framework is anchored on human dignity, non-discrimination, and equality under international instruments (UDHR, ICCPR, CEDAW) and domestic laws (Article II, Section 11 of the Constitution; Safe Spaces Act / R.A. No. 11313). Lawyers are bound by their oath to uphold these laws and must respect the constitutional right of LGBTQIA+ persons to express their identity.
 Individual Liability of Respondents:
 Atty. Antay, Jr.: Initiated the thread with homophobic undertones, gratuitously focusing on the convict's sexual orientation and describing the judge as "effeminate," exhibiting clear gender bias.
 Atty. Calderon & Atty. Nicanor: Perpetuated harmful and degrading stereotypes by insinuating that the criminal litigant's outrage stemmed from frustrated sexual longing ("mapapasakamay", "type ka") toward Atty. Antay, Jr. Atty. Nicanor expressly validated this offensive framing.
 Atty. Navarrete: Sustained the improper theme by recounting a demeaning narrative about a male client casting an admiring ("malagkit") gaze at Atty. Nicanor at the Ombudsman.
 Atty. Tabujara III (Severe Infraction): Singled out a Taguig judge's gender expression (eyeliner/eyeshadow), attacked the mental stability of the second-floor judges ("sira sa ulo"), and explicitly equated homosexual judges with corrupt judges ("sa baba bakla at mga corrupt"). This directly assaulted public confidence in the administration of justice, violating Canon 11 and Rule 8.01.
 Penalties Adjusted: The Court rejected the OBC's recommendation of mere admonition. Admonition and warnings are not penalties. The gravity of homophobic stereotyping requires a **Reprimand** for Attys. Antay, Jr., Calderon, Nicanor, and Navarrete.
 Heavier Penalty for Tabujara III:** Atty. Tabujara III showed no remorse, issued an insincere conditional apology (**"If I have hurt anyone..."**), weaponized alleged allyship as an excuse, and breached his heightened duty as a law professor ("molder of minds of soon-to-be lawyers" under **Re: Co Untian). Due to the multiplier effect of social media, the Court imposed a **Fine of PHP 25,000.00**.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Rule 7.03 - A lawyer shall not engage in conduct that adversely reflects on his fitness to practice law, nor shall he whether in public or private life, behave in a scandalous manner to the discredit of the legal profession."

"Additionally, he made sweeping statements about the mental state of Taguig judges, thus, implying they are unfit to perform their duties. Worse, Atty. Tabujara III lumped the allegedly homosexual judges with the allegedly corrupt ones, thereby implying that homosexual judges have the same degree of immorality as those of corrupt judges. Undoubtedly, such sweeping, baseless and homophobic statements perpetuate the stereotype of homosexuality as a moral flaw and abomination that must be quashed."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Lawyers are keepers of public faith who must maintain dignity in both public and private spaces. Using homophobic tropes, mocking gender expressions, and stereotyping LGBTQIA+ persons violates Rule 7.03 of the CPR, as lawyers are bound to uphold constitutional guarantees of human dignity and international equality standards. Atty. Tabujara received a PHP 25,000 fine instead of a reprimand because he compounded homophobic insults with malicious attacks on the mental health and honesty of the Taguig judiciary, gave an insincere conditional apology, and failed in his elevated duty as a law professor.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I / Legal Ethics → Admission to the Practice of Law and Regulation Thereof (Disciplinary Authority of the Supreme Court over Members of the Bar).
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Application to Regulation of Practice of Law):**
1.  **Jurisdictional Reach over Private Conduct:** Does Supreme Court disciplinary authority extend to private life? **YES.** Misconduct need not occur in the courtroom or during professional representation; any act revealing a lack of good moral character or fitness to practice falls within the Court's regulatory power under Rule 7.03.
2.  The Reasonable Expectation of Privacy Test:
 Subjective Prong: Did the lawyer exhibit an expectation of privacy? **FAILED.** Claiming an account is "locked" is a bare allegation without proof, and sending messages to a multi-member comment thread negates confidentiality.
 Objective Prong: Does society recognize the expectation as reasonable? **FAILED.** Due to the architecture of social media (features allowing friends to screenshot, share, and tag), there is no reasonable expectation of privacy on Facebook.
3.  **Gender-Fair Language & Anti-Discrimination Compliance:** Lawyers must conform their conduct to the constitutional principle of human dignity (Art. II, Sec. 11), international treaties (ICCPR, CEDAW), and the Safe Spaces Act (R.A. No. 11313). Using homophobic tropes ("bakla," "effeminate," demeaning sexual banter) constitutes punishable misconduct.
4.  **Respect Due to the Judiciary (Canon 11 & Rule 8.01):** Lawyers may not circulate sweeping, scandalous accusations questioning the mental fitness or integrity of the bench without proof.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Rule 7.03 / Fitness to practice law
 Reasonable expectation of privacy (Two-part test)
 Informational privacy in cyberspace
 Gender-fair language
 Homophobic slurs / SOGIESC (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Expression, and Sex Characteristics)
 Molder of minds of soon-to-be lawyers (heightened ethical standard for law professors)
 Conditional apology** (**"If I have hurt anyone..." — rejected as lack of genuine remorse)
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
Under its constitutional power to regulate the Bar and discipline lawyers for conduct occurring even in their private lives, the Supreme Court ruled in **Re: Disturbing Social Media Posts** that lawyers have no reasonable expectation of privacy in their Facebook exchanges because of the open, shareable nature of social media platforms. The Court held five lawyers and law professors administratively liable under Rule 7.03 of the CPR for engaging in an online thread filled with homophobic tropes and demeaning sexual insinuations, emphasizing that lawyers have a positive constitutional and statutory duty to respect human dignity, practice non-discrimination, and uphold the integrity of the Judiciary.
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 Power Exercised: The Supreme Court’s plenary administrative and disciplinary authority to regulate the practice of law and enforce moral fitness (1987 Constitution, Art. VIII, Sec. 5[5]).
 Constitutional Protections Invoked: Right to Privacy (Art. III, Sec. 2 / Informational Privacy) and Freedom of Expression (Art. III, Sec. 4), weighed against the State's interest in regulating Bar integrity and protecting human dignity (Art. II, Sec. 11).
 Level of Scrutiny / Judicial Review Audit:** Applied the two-part **Reasonable Expectation of Privacy test. The Court held that lawyers who post online fail the objective prong because the technological architecture of social media platforms enables external dissemination, terminating any reasonable privacy claim and exposing the speech to professional disciplinary scrutiny.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Senior Associate Justice Marvic Mario Victor F. Leonen (Concurring Opinion):** Fully concurred in the penalties. He expounded deeply on the constitutional concepts of **Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Expression, and Sex Characteristics (SOGIESC)**, tracing their definitions from **Falcis v. Civil Registrar General**. SAJ Leonen emphasized that Article II, Section 11 of the Constitution (human dignity) inherently commands respect for SOGIESC. He highlighted that all human beings—not just LGBTQIA+ individuals—possess a SOGIESC, but marginalized groups face persistent systemic violence and discrimination. He stressed that lawyers hold an elevated duty under their oath to affirm the right of LGBTQIA+ persons to exist with equal human dignity; using homophobic language reduces an entire class to "subhuman" status and can never be excused as "macho" locker-room humor.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"ACCORDINGLY, the Court RESOLVES to:

1) REPRIMAND Atty. Morgan Rosales Nicanor, Atty. Joseph Marion Peña Navarrete, Atty. Noel V. Antay, Jr. and Atty. Israel P. Calderon for violation of Rule 7.03 of the Code of Professional Responsibility, with STERN WARNING that a repetition of the same or similar offense will be dealt with more severely; and

2) IMPOSE A FINE in the amount of PHP 25,000.00 on Atty. Ernesto A. Tabujara III for violation of Rule 7.03 of the Code of Professional Responsibility, with STERN WARNING that a repetition of the same or similar offense will be dealt with more severely.

Let a copy of this Decision be attached to the respective personal records of Atty. Morgan Rosales Nicanor, Atty. Joseph Marion Peña Navarrete, Atty. Noel V. Antay, Jr., Atty. Israel P. Calderon, and Atty. Ernesto A. Tabujara III in the Office of the Bar Confidant.

Too, furnish a copy of this Decision to the Integrated Bar of the Philippines for its information and guidance; and the Office of the Court Administrator for dissemination to all courts of the Philippines.

SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court rejected the OBC's lenient recommendation of mere admonition. Attys. Antay, Jr., Calderon, Nicanor, and Navarrete were formally **reprimanded** with stern warnings, while Atty. Tabujara III was **fined PHP 25,000.00** with a stern warning. The ruling establishes that lawyers cannot use social media privacy settings as a defense to escape sanctions for online homophobic slurs and attacks on the integrity of the Judiciary.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Funa v. Villar
**Full Official Caption:** Dennis A. B. Funa, Petitioner, v. The Chairman, Commission on Audit, Reynaldo A. Villar, Respondent
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 192791; April 24, 2012; 686 Phil. 571; En Banc; Ponente: Velasco, Jr., J.
**Voting Breakdown:** Concurred in by Corona, C.J., Leonardo-De Castro, Brion, Peralta, Bersamin, Del Castillo, Abad, Villarama, Jr., Perez, Sereno, Reyes, and Perlas-Bernabe, JJ. Carpio, J., filed a Concurring and Dissenting Opinion. Mendoza, J., filed a Separate Concurring and Dissenting Opinion.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Dennis A. B. Funa:** Petitioner; citizen and taxpayer challenging the legality of the Commission on Audit (COA) leadership appointment.
**Reynaldo A. Villar:** Respondent; appointed COA Commissioner in 2004 for a 7-year term, designated Acting Chairman in February 2008, and subsequently appointed and confirmed as COA Chairman in 2008.
**Guillermo N. Carague:** Predecessor COA Chairman who served a full 7-year constitutional term from February 2, 2001 to February 2, 2008.
**Evelyn R. San Buenaventura:** Appointed COA Commissioner on January 5, 2010 to serve the unexpired term of Villar as Commissioner ending February 2, 2011.
**Ma. Gracia Pulido-Tan:** Appointed COA Chairman by President Benigno S. Aquino III following Villar’s resignation/stepping down.
**Office of the Solicitor General (OSG):** Statutory counsel defending the validity of Villar’s appointment up to February 2, 2011 while questioning the procedural vehicle of the petition.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Original Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition under Rule 65 of the Rules of Court filed directly with the Supreme Court, assailing the constitutionality of President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo's appointment of Reynaldo A. Villar as COA Chairman and seeking an injunction and declaration of nullity.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Constitutional Commissions → Commission on Audit (COA) / Common Provisions → Terms of Office, Rotational Staggering, and Prohibition Against Reappointment
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Special Civil Actions → Judicial Review (Locus Standi, Mootness Exceptions, Certiorari under Expanded Jurisdiction)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provision(s):**
**Article IX(D), Section 1(2), 1987 Constitution:**
"(2) The Chairman and Commissioners shall be appointed by the President with the consent of the Commission on Appointments for a term of seven years without reappointment. Of those first appointed, the Chairman shall hold office for seven years, one commissioner for five years, and the other commissioner for three years, without reappointment. Appointment to any vacancy shall be only for the unexpired portion of the term of the predecessor. In no case shall any member be appointed or designated in a temporary or acting capacity."
**Historical Landmark Rule:**
Under the **1935 Constitution (Article XI, Section 1 / Article X, Section 1 as amended)**, the phrasing read:
"There shall be an independent Commission on Elections composed of a Chairman and two other members to be appointed by the President with the consent of the Commission on Appointments, who shall hold office for a term of nine years and **may not be reappointed**. Of the Members of the Commission first appointed, one shall hold office for nine years, another for six years and the third for three years."
In contrast, the **1987 Constitution** inserted the phrase **"without reappointment" twice** into Section 1(2) of Article IX, covering both regular seven-year appointees and the initial staggered appointees, and added an explicit restriction that **"[a]ppointment to any vacancy shall be only for the unexpired portion of the term of the predecessor"** and **"[i]n no case shall any member be appointed or designated in a temporary or acting capacity."**
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):**
Upon the expiration of the full 7-year term of COA Chairman Guillermo Carague on February 2, 2008, sitting COA Commissioner Reynaldo Villar—who was midway through his own 7-year term as Commissioner (expiring February 2, 2011)—was designated Acting Chairman and subsequently appointed by President Arroyo as COA Chairman. Villar claimed he was entitled to a brand new 7-year term as Chairman ending in 2015, while his appointment paper and the executive branch considered his term to expire on February 2, 2011 (coinciding with the expiration of his original term as Commissioner), triggering a direct constitutional challenge by petitioner Funa.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**February 15, 2001:** President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo appoints Guillermo N. Carague as Chairman of the Commission on Audit (COA) for a constitutional term of seven (7) years, commencing February 2, 2001 and expiring February 2, 2008.
**February 7, 2004:** President Macapagal-Arroyo appoints Reynaldo A. Villar as the third member (Commissioner) of the COA for a 7-year term starting February 2, 2004 and expiring February 2, 2011.
**February 2, 2008:** Chairman Carague's 7-year term officially expires, creating a regular vacancy in the COA chairmanship.
**February 4, 2008 to April 14, 2008:** Villar, while serving in his fourth year as COA Commissioner, is designated by President Macapagal-Arroyo as Acting Chairman of the COA.
**April 18, 2008:** President Macapagal-Arroyo nominates and appoints Villar as permanent Chairman of the COA, with his appointment paper expressly stating that he is to serve until the expiration of the original term of his office as COA Commissioner, or until February 2, 2011.
**June 11, 2008:** The Commission on Appointments confirms Villar’s appointment as COA Chairman. Villar, however, asserts that his appointment entitles him to a fresh 7-year term running until February 2, 2015.
**January 5, 2010:** Evelyn R. San Buenaventura is appointed by President Macapagal-Arroyo as COA Commissioner to serve the unexpired term vacated by Villar as Commissioner, explicitly designated to end on February 2, 2011.
**July 26, 2010:** Dennis A. B. Funa files the instant Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition under Rule 65 before the Supreme Court, challenging the constitutionality of Villar’s appointment as Chairman.
**February 22, 2011:** While the petition is pending, Villar addresses a formal letter to President Benigno S. Aquino III expressing his intention to step down from the COA chairmanship upon the appointment and qualification of his replacement.
**June 10, 2011:** President Aquino appoints Ma. Gracia Pulido-Tan as COA Chairman (for a term expiring February 2, 2015) and Heidi Mendoza as Commissioner (for a term expiring February 2, 2018). Villar formally vacates the office of COA Chairman, leading respondents to claim the petition has become moot and academic.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Dennis A. B. Funa)
**Main Thesis:** The appointment of an incumbent Commissioner as Chairman of the COA constitutes an unconstitutional "reappointment" prohibited under Section 1(2), Article IX(D) of the 1987 Constitution, rendering Villar's appointment void **ab initio**.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Prohibition on Any Reappointment:** Section 1(2), Article IX(D) prohibits any and all forms of reappointment within the Commission. A second appointment, whether to the same office (Commissioner) or to an upgraded office (Chairman), requires a brand-new presidential appointment and Commission on Appointments confirmation, which constitutes a prohibited reappointment under **Matibag v. Benipayo**.
**Safeguard of Independence:** Citing Justice J.B.L. Reyes' dissent in **Visarra v. Miraflor**, the constitutional prohibition exists to insulate Commissioners from the "carrot and stick" of executive patronage. If sitting Commissioners may be promoted to Chairman, they will forfeit their independence to curry favor with the appointing authority.
**Constitutional Impossibility of Term Length:** Villar could not be appointed to a full 7-year term because that would exceed the 7-year constitutional aggregate limit, nor could he be appointed to a shortened term because the President has no power to alter or split the constitutionally fixed 7-year term attached to a vacancy resulting from the expiration of a predecessor's full term.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Reynaldo A. Villar and OSG)
**Main Thesis:** The petition is procedurally barred due to lack of standing, improper remedy, and mootness; substantively, Villar's appointment as Chairman was valid, with Villar asserting entitlement to a full 7-year term up to 2015, and the OSG arguing the appointment was valid up to February 2, 2011.
**Specific Contentions (Procedural):**
**Lack of Locus Standi:** Funa suffered no direct, personal, and material injury from the appointment and lacks standing as a citizen or taxpayer.
**Improper Remedy:** The OSG contended that Funa should have filed a petition for Declaratory Relief under Rule 63 or Quo Warranto under Rule 66, not a petition for Certiorari and Prohibition under Rule 65.
**Mootness:** Villar’s resignation and the supervening appointment and assumption of Ma. Gracia Pulido-Tan as COA Chairman rendered the case entirely moot and non-justiciable.
**Specific Contentions (Substantive):**
**Villar's Theory (Fresh 7-Year Term):** A promotional appointment to Chairman is an appointment to a distinct and separate constitutional office. Because Carague completed his full term, the vacancy was for a full 7-year cycle, granting Villar a term running from 2008 to 2015.
**OSG's Theory (Unexpired Term Validation):** The appointment of Villar was valid for the period ending February 2, 2011, as indicated on his appointment papers, preserving the aggregate 7-year ceiling by allowing him to serve out his remaining years.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the supervening resignation of Reynaldo A. Villar and the appointment of Ma. Gracia Pulido-Tan as COA Chairman rendered the constitutional challenge moot and academic, thereby precluding judicial review.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not petitioner Dennis A. B. Funa possesses legal standing (**locus standi**) to challenge the appointment of the COA Chairman, and whether Certiorari under Rule 65 is the appropriate procedural remedy.
3.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Section 1(2), Article IX(D) of the 1987 Constitution per se prohibits the promotional appointment or upgrading of an incumbent COA Commissioner to the position of COA Chairman.
4.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the appointment of Reynaldo A. Villar as COA Chairman—issued for a term of less than seven (7) years to succeed a Chairman whose full term had expired—is constitutionally valid.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Mootness and Exceptions to Judicial Review
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not supervening events rendered the petition moot and academic, barring adjudication.
**NO.** While technically moot due to Villar vacating the office and Tan's appointment, the Court retained jurisdiction under established exceptions because the controversy involves grave constitutional violations, issues of paramount public interest, the need for controlling principles to guide the bench and bar, and matters capable of repetition yet evading review.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
A case is moot when its purpose is stale or supervening events negate any practical legal relief. Generally, courts do not decide moot cases.
**   Under **David v. Macapagal-Arroyo, the Court recognizes four exceptions: (1) a grave violation of the Constitution; (2) situations of exceptional character and paramount public interest; (3) the need to formulate controlling principles to guide the bench, bar, and public; and (4) cases capable of repetition yet evading review.
**   All four exceptions apply here. The rotational appointment plan and term limitations of Constitutional Commissions directly impact governance. If not definitively settled, future administrations will encounter the identical dilemma when promoting or appointing members to constitutional vacancies. Citing **Javier v. Pacificador, justice demands acting for guidance and future restraint even when the immediate dispute has evaporated.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The 'moot and academic' principle is not a magical formula that can automatically dissuade the courts in resolving a case. Courts will decide cases, otherwise moot and academic, if: first, there is a grave violation of the Constitution, second, the exceptional character of the situation and the paramount public interest is involved, third, when constitutional issue raised requires formulation of controlling principles to guide the bench, the bar, and the public, and fourth, the case is capable of repetition yet evading review."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Even though Villar stepped down and a new COA Chairman was installed, the Supreme Court refused to dismiss the case. The Court held that when an executive appointment involves grave constitutional questions and risks disrupting the leadership cycle of Constitutional Commissions in future administrations, the case falls squarely under the exceptions to mootness as a matter of exceptional public importance capable of repetition yet evading review.
Issue 2: Locus Standi and Propriety of Rule 65 Certiorari
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not petitioner Funa has legal standing and properly invoked Rule 65 Certiorari.
**YES.** Procedural standing requirements are relaxed in cases of transcendental importance, and Certiorari under Rule 65 is appropriate under the Supreme Court's expanded constitutional duty to correct grave abuse of discretion.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
 Locus standi requires a personal and material interest resulting in direct injury. However, procedural technicalities yield where issues of transcendental importance and far-reaching constitutional implications are presented by concerned citizens.
**   Under **David, concerned citizens are accorded standing when constitutional issues of transcendental significance must be settled early.
Regarding the OSG's challenge to Rule 65, the 1987 Constitution under Article VIII, Section 1 expanded judicial review. Certiorari lies not only to correct lack or excess of jurisdiction in judicial or quasi-judicial acts, but also to determine whether any branch or instrumentality of government committed grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction. The claim that the President exercised appointing power in direct violation of constitutional term limits constitutes an allegation of grave abuse of discretion remediable by Certiorari.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"For under the expanded concept of judicial review under the 1987 Constitution, the corrective hand of certiorari may be invoked not only 'to settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable,' but also 'to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the government.'"
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Funa has standing as a concerned citizen because determining the constitutional legality of the COA Chairman's term is of transcendental importance to the nation. Certiorari under Rule 65 is the correct remedy because petitioner alleges that the President acted with grave abuse of discretion by overriding explicit constitutional limits on appointments.
Issue 3: Permissibility of Promotional Appointments from Commissioner to Chairman
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not Section 1(2), Article IX(D) of the 1987 Constitution categorically bars an incumbent Commissioner from being promoted to Chairman.
**NO.** The constitutional ban on "reappointment" applies strictly to a second appointment to one and the same office; it does not prohibit a promotional appointment to a different office (Commissioner to Chairman), provided the appointee has not served a full 7-year term, does not exceed an aggregate of 7 years in the Commission, and the promotional appointment fills an unexpired term resulting from death, resignation, disability, or impeachment.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**   Applying the **verba legis** rule, the Constitution states that members shall be appointed for a term of seven years without reappointment. In legal contemplation, "reappointment" refers to a second appointment to **one and the same office** after ceasing to occupy it. A promotion from Commissioner to Chairman is an appointment to a **different office, not a reappointment.
The records and debates of the 1986 Constitutional Commission (specifically exchanges between Commissioners Felicitas Aquino, Christian Monsod, and Vicente Foz) prove that the Framers expressly contemplated and allowed the "upgrading of position" from Commissioner to Chairman.
The Framers explicitly intended that promotional appointments are valid provided that: (1) the appointee in no case serves an aggregate period of more than seven (7) years; and (2) the appointee serves only the unexpired portion of the predecessor's term pursuant to the third sentence of Section 1(2). As Commissioner Foz stated, an appointee accepting an upgrade takes it at his own risk of shortening his overall tenure.
**   The Court expressly abandoned the contrary **obiter dictum** in **Matibag v. Benipayo (specifically its "fourth situation"), clarifying that a promotional appointment from Commissioner to Chairman is constitutionally permissible under the defined parameters.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The phrase 'upgrading of position' found in the underscored portion unmistakably shows that Sec. 1(2), Art. IX(D) of the 1987 Constitution, for all its caveat against reappointment, does not per se preclude, in any and all cases, the promotional appointment or upgrade of a commissioner to chairman, subject to this proviso: the appointee's tenure in office does not exceed 7 years in all. Indeed, such appointment does not contextually come within the restricting phrase 'without reappointment' twice written in that section."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The Constitution does not ban promotions within the Commission. "Reappointment" strictly means being appointed twice to the identical post. Moving from Commissioner to Chairman is a new appointment to a distinct office. The Framers allowed this promotion as long as the official's total combined service does not exceed 7 years and the promotion only fills an unexpired term.
Issue 4: Constitutionality of Villar's Appointment as COA Chairman
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not Villar’s promotional appointment as COA Chairman was constitutionally valid.
**NO, IT IS UNCONSTITUTIONAL.** When a vacancy in the chairmanship occurs because the predecessor's full 7-year term has expired, the Constitution mandatorily commands that the appointment be for a fixed 7-year term. Because Villar had already served 4 years as Commissioner, he could not be given a 7-year term without breaching the 7-year aggregate ceiling; conversely, the President had no power to give him a truncated 3-year term, because the appointing power cannot split or alter a constitutionally fixed term.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**   The Constitution mandates two, and only two, types of appointments to Constitutional Commissions: (1) a full 7-year appointment when the vacancy arises from the **expiration of a predecessor's term**; or (2) an appointment for the **unexpired portion when the vacancy arises mid-term due to death, resignation, disability, or impeachment.
**   Former Chairman Carague served his full 7-year term expiring on February 2, 2008. Therefore, there was **no unexpired portion to fill. The vacancy created was for a brand-new, fixed 7-year term.
Where the Constitution fixes the term of an office, the appointing authority has no discretion to specify a shorter or longer term. The President cannot split terms or alter the constitutional duration.
Villar's promotional appointment was caught in an insurmountable constitutional dilemma:
President Arroyo could not appoint him to a full 7-year term (to 2015) because his aggregate service in COA would then reach 11 years, directly violating the 7-year maximum ceiling and destroying the rotational cycle.
President Arroyo could not appoint him to a shortened 3-year term (to 2011) because Carague's term had expired, legally requiring a 7-year term, and the President has no constitutional power to invent a 3-year term to accommodate an incumbent's remaining years.
**   Furthermore, truncating Villar’s term to expire on February 2, 2011 caused two vacancies to occur simultaneously (his post and that of Commissioner San Buenaventura), violating the constitutional rotational system (**Republic v. Imperial**, **Gaminde v. COA) which requires that only one vacancy occur every two years to prevent a single President from dominating the Commission.
**   Additionally, Villar's prior designation as "Acting Chairman" from February to April 2008 violated the absolute prohibition in Section 1(2): **"In no case shall any member be appointed or designated in a temporary or acting capacity."
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Where the Constitution or, for that matter, a statute, has fixed the term of office of a public official, the appointing authority is without authority to specify in the appointment a term shorter or longer than what the law provides. If the vacancy calls for a full seven-year appointment, the President is without discretion to extend a promotional appointment for more or for less than seven (7) years. There is no in between. He or she cannot split terms. It is not within the power of the appointing authority to override the positive provision of the Constitution which dictates that the term of office of members of constitutional bodies shall be seven (7) years."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Villar's appointment was impossible under the Constitution. Carague completed his full 7-year term, so his successor **had** to be appointed for a mandatory 7-year term. Villar could not receive that 7-year term because he had already served 4 years as Commissioner and the law forbids anyone from serving more than 7 years total. But President Arroyo also could not legally give him a 3-year term, because the President cannot chop up constitutionally fixed terms. Because neither a 7-year nor a 3-year appointment was lawful, Villar was constitutionally ineligible to succeed Carague.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | The Constitutional Commissions - Common Provisions
**Applied Lens:** Constitutional & Political Law
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
**Governmental Power Exercised:** Executive Appointing Power of the President (Article VII, Section 16).
**Constitutional Limitations Invoked:**
1.  Fixed 7-Year Term Limit and Rotational Staggering Rule (Article IX-D, Section 1(2)).
2.  Prohibition against Reappointment (Article IX-D, Section 1(2)).
3.  Limitation of Vacancy Appointments to the Unexpired Portion (Article IX-D, Section 1(2)).
4.  Absolute Prohibition against Temporary or Acting Designations (Article IX-D, Section 1(2)).
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
**Expanded Judicial Review / Grave Abuse of Discretion Test:** The Court evaluated whether the President acted arbitrarily, despotically, or in gross evasion of positive constitutional commands by modifying a fixed constitutional term of office and ignoring the structural mechanics of the rotational plan.
**Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit:**
**Actual Case or Controversy:** Satisfied initially; although rendered moot by Villar's resignation and Tan's appointment, reviewed under the four **David** exceptions.
**Locus Standi:** Relaxed under the "Transcendental Importance" doctrine for non-traditional suitors (concerned citizen/taxpayer).
**Ripeness & Mootness:** Mootness bypassed due to grave constitutional infraction, paramount public interest, necessity of controlling principles, and capability of repetition yet evading review.
**Lis Mota:** The constitutionality of the promotional appointment and term calculation was the very heart of the controversy.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Valid Appointment to Constitutional Commissions):**
1.  **Fixed Staggered Term:** Must be for a full seven (7) years if succeeding a member whose term expired. (Violated: Villar was given 3 years).
2.  **Unexpired Portion Limitation:** A term of less than 7 years is valid **only** if filling an unexpired vacancy created by death, resignation, disability, or impeachment. (Violated: Carague did not vacate mid-term; his term expired).
3.  **Aggregate 7-Year Ceiling:** In no case may any member serve in any capacity (Commissioner, Chairman, or combination) for more than 7 aggregate years. (Villar claimed 11 years; appointment paper attempted an unlawful 3-year split).
4.  **No Temporary/Acting Capacity:** Absolute proscription against acting designations. (Violated: Villar was designated Acting Chairman from Feb to April 2008).
5.  **Rotational Preservation:** Appointments must preserve the 2-year interval cycle. (Violated: Villar's appointment caused two terms to expire simultaneously on Feb 2, 2011).
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Verba legis non est recedendum (plain-meaning rule)
 Rotational plan / Staggered terms
 Lines of succession
 Unexpired portion of the term
 Aggregate 7-year service limitation
 Prohibition on reappointment vs. Promotional appointment
 Temporary or acting capacity proscription
 Transcendental importance
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
In **Funa v. Villar**, the Supreme Court ruled that while an incumbent Commissioner may legally receive a promotional appointment to Chairman, such promotion is valid **only** if the vacancy occurred by death, resignation, disability, or impeachment, and only for the unexpired portion, provided total service does not exceed 7 years. Where the Chairman's vacancy occurs because their 7-year term naturally **expired** (as with Carague), the Constitution mandates a fresh 7-year appointment. Because an incumbent Commissioner who has already served several years cannot receive a new 7-year term without exceeding the 7-year aggregate ceiling, and because the President has zero constitutional authority to shorten or split terms, an incumbent Commissioner is constitutionally ineligible to succeed a Chairman whose full term has expired.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Carpio, J. (Concurring and Dissenting):** Concurs that Villar's appointment as Chairman (and acting Chairman) was unconstitutional, but strongly dissents from the majority's doctrine that promotional appointments are ever allowed. Justice Carpio asserts that the Framers intentionally inserted the words "without reappointment" **twice** in Section 1(2) specifically to overturn the 1963 **Visarra v. Miraflor** ruling and prohibit "any reappointment of any kind," including promotional appointments from Commissioner to Chairman. Promoting a Commissioner requires a second appointment, second confirmation, and second oath to a higher office, offering an executive "carrot" that destroys commission independence. Furthermore, designating Villar Acting Chairman was a blatant violation of the explicit constitutional ban on temporary appointments.
**Mendoza, J. (Separate Concurring and Dissenting):** Concurs with the majority that promotional appointments from Commissioner to Chairman are constitutional and not prohibited reappointments. However, he dissents from the holding that an incumbent Commissioner can only be promoted when a vacancy arises from death, resignation, disability, or impeachment. He argues that nothing in the Constitution bars promoting a Commissioner when the Chairman's term **expires**, provided the promoted Commissioner serves only their own remaining years up to the 7-year aggregate limit (meaning Villar's appointment up to February 2, 2011 was valid).
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is PARTLY GRANTED. The appointment of then Commissioner Reynaldo A. Villar to the position of Chairman of the Commission on Audit to replace Guillermo N. Carague, whose term of office as such chairman has expired, is hereby declared UNCONSTITUTIONAL for violation of Sec. 1(2), Art. IX(D) of the Constitution.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Dennis Funa prevailed in part. The Supreme Court declared Reynaldo Villar’s appointment as Chairman of the Commission on Audit unconstitutional. The Court established binding doctrine that while promotional upgrades are permitted to fill mid-term unexpired vacancies (up to an aggregate of 7 years), an incumbent Commissioner cannot be appointed to succeed a Chairman whose term fully expired, as the President cannot lawfully truncate the constitutionally mandated 7-year term.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** CHREA v. Commission on Human Rights (Resolution)
**Full Official Caption:** Commission on Human Rights Employees' Association (CHREA), represented by its President, Marcial A. Sanchez, Jr., Petitioner, vs. Commission on Human Rights, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 155336; July 21, 2006; 528 Phil. 658; Special Second Division; Chico-Nazario, **J.** (Ponente); Concurring: Puno (**Chairman**), Austria-Martinez, Callejo, Sr., and Tinga, **JJ.** No separate opinions filed.
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Petitioner:** Commission on Human Rights Employees' Association (CHREA), the recognized labor organization representing the rank-and-file personnel of the Commission on Human Rights, represented by its President Marcial A. Sanchez, Jr.
**Respondent:** Commission on Human Rights (CHR), an independent constitutional office created pursuant to Section 17, Article XIII of the 1987 Constitution, represented by its then Chairperson Aurora P. Navarette-Reciña and Commissioners Nasser A. Marohomsalic, Mercedes V. Contreras, Vicente P. Sibulo, and Jorge R. Coquia.
**Key Intervening Agencies / Officials:** Department of Budget and Management (DBM), headed by Secretary Benjamin Diokno; Civil Service Commission-National Capital Region (CSC-NCR); Civil Service Commission-Central Office (CSC-CO).
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** This resolution resolves the **Motion for Reconsideration** filed by respondent CHR challenging the Supreme Court Second Division's **Decision dated November 25, 2004**. The 2004 Decision granted CHREA's Petition for Review under Rule 45, reversing the Court of Appeals (CA) Decision dated November 29, 2001 and Resolution dated September 11, 2002 (CA-G.R. SP No. 59678), reinstating the CSC-NCR Memorandum dated March 29, 1999, and disallowing CHR Resolutions Nos. A98-047, A98-055, and A98-062 for lack of DBM approval.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law → Constitutional Commissions → Common Provisions → Fiscal Autonomy (Scope, Extent, and Limitations)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Administrative Law → Civil Service & Compensation Standardization → DBM Regulatory Authority over Plantilla Reclassifications (R.A. No. 6758)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional Provisions:**
**Article IX, Part A, Section 5, 1987 Constitution (Common Provisions on Constitutional Commissions):**
"Sec. 5. **The Commission shall enjoy fiscal autonomy.** Their approved annual appropriations shall be **automatically and regularly released**."
**Article XIII, Section 17(1) & (4), 1987 Constitution (Commission on Human Rights):**
"Sec. 17. (1) There is hereby created an independent office called the Commission on Human Rights.
x x x x
(4) The approved annual appropriations of the Commission shall be **automatically and regularly released**."
**Article VIII, Section 3, 1987 Constitution (The Judiciary):**
"Sec. 3. The Judiciary shall enjoy fiscal autonomy. Appropriations for the Judiciary may not be reduced by the legislature below the amount appropriated for the previous year and, after approval, shall be automatically and regularly released."
**Article XI, Section 14, 1987 Constitution (Office of the Ombudsman):**
"Sec. 14. The Office of the Ombudsman shall enjoy fiscal autonomy. Its approved annual appropriations shall be automatically and regularly released."
**Factual Trigger:** The CHR promulgated internal resolutions (Nos. A98-047, A98-055, and A98-062) upgrading, reclassifying, and creating organizational units and key positions by collapsing vacant items and utilizing savings, invoking full "fiscal autonomy" under the 1998 General Appropriations Act (GAA) and membership in the Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy Group (CFAG). When DBM Secretary Benjamin Diokno denied approval because the restructuring violated the Salary Standardization Law (R.A. No. 6758) by elevating field units from divisions to regional offices/services without statutory basis, CHR asserted that its constitutional fiscal autonomy exempted it from DBM oversight.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**February 14, 1998:** Congress enacts Republic Act No. 8522 (General Appropriations Act of 1998), which includes **Special Provisions Applicable to All Constitutional Offices Enjoying Fiscal Autonomy**, authorizing fiscally autonomous entities to formulate/implement organizational structures, fix salaries/allowances, adjust personal services itemizations, and use savings, provided implementation complies with compensation standardization laws.
**July 24, 1998:** The Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy Group (CFAG)—with CHR participating as a member—passes and approves CFAG Joint Resolution No. 49, adopting internal rules implementing the special provisions of R.A. No. 8522.
**September 4, 1998:** Citing the 1998 GAA special provisions and CFAG Joint Resolution No. 49, the CHR promulgates Resolution No. A98-047, approving an upgrading and reclassification scheme supported by savings from Personal Services, proposing ten additional plantilla positions (one Director IV [SG-28] for the Caraga Regional Office, four Security Officer II [SG-15], and five Process Servers [SG-5]).
**October 19, 1998:** CHR issues Resolution No. A98-055, upgrading the salary grades of selected positions in the Commission, funded by augmenting savings from Personal Services.
**November 17, 1998:** CHR issues Resolution No. A98-062, "collapsing" vacant plantilla positions (one Attorney III, four Attorney IV, one Chemist III, three Special Investigator I, one Clerk III, and one Accounting Clerk II) to provide funding for the staffing modifications.
**January 20, 1999:** DBM Secretary Benjamin Diokno formally denies CHR's request for approval of the staffing modification and upgrading scheme. The DBM justifies the denial on grounds that: (1) the proposal elevates field units from divisions to services/regional offices without statutory basis; (2) under Section 78 of the 1998 GAA General Provisions, no organizational unit or changes in key positions shall be authorized unless provided by law or directed by the President; (3) under R.A. No. 6758, the DBM possesses sole authority to administer the unified compensation and position classification system; and (4) membership in CFAG does not confer absolute authority to upgrade or create positions without DBM approval.
**March 29, 1999:** In view of the DBM denial, the Civil Service Commission-National Capital Region (CSC-NCR) issues a memorandum recommending to the CSC-Central Office that the subject appointments under the CHR upgrading scheme be rejected.
**November 1999 – December 16, 1999:** Petitioner CHREA, representing rank-and-file employees, petitions the CSC-Central Office to uphold the CSC-NCR recommendation, arguing that the DBM alone holds statutory authority to approve reclassifications. On December 16, 1999, the CSC-Central Office issues Resolution No. 99-2800 reversing the CSC-NCR, thereby validating CHR's upgrading scheme under the theory of fiscal autonomy.
**June 9, 2000:** The CSC-Central Office denies CHREA's Motion for Reconsideration via Resolution No. 001354.
**November 29, 2001:** The Court of Appeals (Special Seventh Division), in CA-G.R. SP No. 59678, dismisses CHREA's petition for review and affirms the CSC-Central Office resolutions, holding that CHR possessed fiscal autonomy to implement the reorganization.
**September 11, 2002:** The Court of Appeals denies CHREA's Motion for Reconsideration.
**November 25, 2004:** The Supreme Court (Second Division) promulgates its Decision granting CHREA's Rule 45 petition, reversing the CA and CSC-Central Office, reinstating the CSC-NCR ruling of March 29, 1999, and expressly disallowing CHR Resolutions Nos. A98-047, A98-055, and A98-062 for lack of DBM approval.
**July 21, 2006:** The Supreme Court (Special Second Division) promulgates the subject Resolution on CHR's Motion for Reconsideration, modifying the ratio to clarify that CHR enjoys **limited** fiscal autonomy (the right to automatic and regular release of appropriations), but firmly reaffirming the disallowance of the staffing scheme absent DBM approval.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Respondent CHR's Arguments (Motion for Reconsideration)
**Main Thesis:** The CHR is a constitutional office invested with full fiscal autonomy under the Constitution, the Administrative Code of 1987, and the 1998 GAA; therefore, its staffing restructuring, position reclassification, and personal services augmentations are valid internal corporate acts exempt from DBM prior approval.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Constitutional Intent of Article XIII, Section 17(4):** Then-Commissioner Hilario G. Davide, Jr. remarked during Constitutional Commission deliberations that deleting the explicit clause "The Commission shall enjoy fiscal autonomy" was done purely because it was "surplusage," since the autonomy intended was embodied in the automatic release clause.
2.  **Statutory Charter in the Administrative Code of 1987:** Book VI, Chapter 1, Section 1(9) of Executive Order No. 292 explicitly lists the CHR alongside the Judiciary, Constitutional Commissions, Ombudsman, and LGUs as entities enjoying fiscal autonomy.
3.  **Application of GAA Special Provisions:** The Special Provisions of R.A. No. 8522 (1998 GAA) applicable to Constitutional Offices enjoying Fiscal Autonomy explicitly authorized the formulation of organizational structures, position itemization adjustments, and use of savings.
4.  **CFAG Membership:** As an active signatory and member of the Constitutional Fiscal Autonomy Group under CFAG Joint Resolution No. 49, CHR holds the prerogative to implement staffing adjustments using operational savings.
5.  **Equal Treatment:** The Executive and Legislature recognized CHR's parity with constitutional commissions through presidential directives and budgetary provisions.
B. Petitioner CHREA's Arguments (Opposition to Motion for Reconsideration)
**Main Thesis:** The DBM is the sole executive agency tasked by law to administer the unified position classification and compensation system; CHR does not possess broad fiscal autonomy and cannot bypass DBM approval under the guise of internal reorganizations.
**Specific Contentions:**
1.  **Exclusive Constitutional Grants:** The 1987 Constitution intentionally confined broad fiscal autonomy to the Judiciary (Art. VIII, Sec. 3), the Constitutional Commissions under Article IX (CSC, COMELEC, COA), and the Ombudsman (Art. XI, Sec. 14).
2.  **Textual Omission in Article XIII:** Unlike Article IX-A, Section 5, Section 17(4) of Article XIII deliberately deleted the declaration of fiscal autonomy, leaving only the guarantee of automatic release of appropriations.
3.  **Supremacy of the Salary Standardization Law (R.A. No. 6758):** Even assuming **arguendo** that CHR enjoys fiscal autonomy, any organizational restructuring and compensation adjustment must strictly adhere to R.A. No. 6758 as administered by the DBM.
4.  **Prohibition on Creating Key Offices:** Under Section 78 of the 1998 GAA General Provisions, agencies cannot elevate divisions to regional bureaus or services without legislative authorization or executive presidential direction.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) is invested by the 1987 Constitution and the Administrative Code of 1987 with broad and extensive fiscal autonomy identical to that enjoyed by the Constitutional Commissions under Article IX, the Judiciary, and the Ombudsman.
2.  **[Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the prior evaluation and approval of the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) is a mandatory condition precedent for the validity and implementation of CHR's staffing modification, position reclassification, upgrading, and collapsing scheme under the Salary Standardization Law (R.A. No. 6758) and the 1998 GAA.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Extent of CHR's Constitutional and Statutory Fiscal Autonomy
**(a) Short Answer: NO (PARTIALLY MERITORIOUS as to limited autonomy).** The CHR is not a constitutional commission under Article IX and does not enjoy broad, full fiscal autonomy; it enjoys only **limited** fiscal autonomy consisting exclusively of the automatic and regular release of its approved annual appropriations.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Structural Placement under the 1987 Constitution:** Article IX unambiguously identifies only three Constitutional Commissions: the Civil Service Commission, Commission on Elections, and Commission on Audit. The CHR was created under Article XIII (Social Justice and Human Rights), Section 17, as an "independent office." It cannot claim the common provisions of Article IX.
2.  **Textual Disparity across Constitutional Grants:** In granting fiscal autonomy to the Judiciary (Art. VIII, Sec. 3), the Constitutional Commissions (Art. IX-A, Sec. 5), and the Ombudsman (Art. XI, Sec. 14), the Constitution adopted a uniform two-sentence formula: (1) an express declaration that the entity "shall enjoy fiscal autonomy"; and (2) a mandate that its approved appropriations "shall be automatically and regularly released." In sharp contrast, Article XIII, Section 17(4) deliberately omits the first sentence and retains only the second.
3.  **ConCom Deliberations Re-examined:** While Commissioner Davide remarked that the first sentence was surplusage, the record reveals his precise reasoning: "the autonomy **actually intended** is the automatic release of these appropriations." Further exchanges between Commissioners Bengzon and Guingona settled that the text "means what it says and it is clear" and "only refers to the release which should be automatic and regular," rejecting any broader operational fiscal prerogatives that would tie the hands of the political branches in budgetary priorities.
4.  **Doctrinal Definition in Bengzon v. Drilon:** Under **Bengzon v. Drilon** (G.R. No. 103524, April 15, 1992), true fiscal autonomy means "full flexibility to allocate and utilize their resources with the wisdom and dispatch that their needs require," including fixing compensation rates, collecting fees, and absolute freedom from outside control. **Bengzon** explicitly listed only the Judiciary, CSC, COA, COMELEC, and the Ombudsman as possessing this plenary autonomy; the CHR was omitted.
5.  **Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius:** The explicit constitutional grant of plenary fiscal autonomy to specified bodies implies the intentional exclusion of the CHR from the broad genus.
6.  **Harmonization of the Administrative Code of 1987:** While Section 1(9), Chapter 1, Book VI refers generally to CHR enjoying fiscal autonomy under budgetary policies, it is a mere restatement of constitutional policy and cannot confer rights greater than the Constitution. Under rules of statutory construction, this general provision in Book VI must be qualified and restricted by Book V, Title II, Subtitle A, Section 6, which specifically headings the CHR provision as "Annual Appropriations" (not "Fiscal Autonomy") and confines CHR solely to the automatic release of approved appropriations.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quotes:**
"Therefore, after reviewing the deliberations of the ConCom on Article XIII, Section 17(4), of the 1987 Constitution, in its entirety, not just bits and pieces thereof, this Court is convinced that the ConCom had intended to grant to the respondent the privilege of having its approved annual appropriations automatically and regularly released, but nothing more. While it may be conceded that the automatic and regular release of approved annual appropriations is an aspect of fiscal autonomy, it is just one of many others."

"Consequently, this Court concludes that the 1987 Constitution extends to respondent a certain degree of fiscal autonomy through the privilege of having its approved annual appropriations released automatically and regularly. However, it withholds from respondent fiscal autonomy, in its broad or extensive sense, as granted to the Judiciary, constitutional commissions, and the Office of the Ombudsman."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The CHR is an independent constitutional office, but it is not an Article IX Constitutional Commission. The framers intentionally gave full fiscal autonomy (complete spending, structuring, and budgeting independence) only to the Judiciary, the three Article IX Commissions, and the Ombudsman. For the CHR, the framers deliberately struck out the broad phrase "shall enjoy fiscal autonomy" and preserved only the guarantee that once Congress approves its budget, that money must be automatically released without executive withholding.
Issue 2: Requirement of DBM Approval for CHR Personnel Upgrading and Restructuring
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The approval of the DBM is an indispensable condition precedent to the validity of any reclassification, upgrading, creation, or collapsing of plantilla positions within the CHR.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Inapplicability of GAA Special Provisions:** Because CHR does not enjoy broad fiscal autonomy, it cannot invoke the **Special Provisions Applicable to All Constitutional Offices Enjoying Fiscal Autonomy** under R.A. No. 8522 to unilaterally reorganize and establish positions.
2.  **Subjection of All Autonomous Bodies to the Salary Standardization Law (R.A. No. 6758):** Even assuming **arguendo** that CHR possessed full fiscal autonomy, such autonomy is never absolute. Even the Judiciary—a coordinate constitutional branch with full fiscal autonomy—must strictly comply with R.A. No. 6758. If the Judiciary cannot reorganize beyond the limits of compensation standardization laws and must coordinate with the DBM (as demonstrated in R.A. No. 9227 and Joint Circular No. 2004-1), the CHR cannot assert superior immunity.
3.  **Exclusive Statutory Authority of the DBM:** Under Section 2 of R.A. No. 6758, Congress designated the DBM as the sole administrative agency mandated to establish and enforce a unified compensation and position classification system. DBM's authority forms an integral component of the constitutional system of checks and balances.
4.  **Lack of Substantive Legal Justification:** The DBM correctly found that CHR's proposed restructuring ran afoul of Section 78 of the 1998 GAA General Provisions ("no organizational unit or changes in key positions shall be authorized unless provided by law or directed by the President"). The CHR attempted to convert divisions into full regional services/bureaus and upgrade Attorney VI (SG-26) to Director IV (SG-28) without any statutory enactment creating such regional offices or altering substantive duties.
5.  **Judicial Deference to Administrative Expertise:** The DBM is the specialized agency charged with technical oversight of public expenditures and civil service compensation. Its findings that CHR's modifications changed nomenclature from support to substantive without real changes in functions command judicial respect under **Energy Regulatory Board v. Court of Appeals**.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Being a member of the fiscal autonomy group does not vest the agency with the authority to reclassify, upgrade, and create positions without approval of the DBM. While the members of the Group are authorized to formulate and implement the organizational structures of their respective offices and determine the compensation of their personnel, such authority is not absolute and must be exercised within the parameters of the Unified Position Classification and Compensation System established under RA 6758 more popularly known as the Compensation Standardization Law."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Even if an agency has fiscal autonomy, that autonomy does not place it above the Salary Standardization Law. The DBM is the government's official gatekeeper tasked by Congress to administer position classifications and equal-pay standards. Because CHR upgraded its field attorneys to directors and created new corporate units without statutory authority, its internal resolutions were completely invalid without DBM's approval.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | The Constitutional Commissions - Common Provisions (Fiscal Autonomy)
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (The Two Types of Fiscal Autonomy):**
| Component Element | Plenary Fiscal Autonomy (Judiciary, CSC, COMELEC, COA, Ombudsman) | Limited Fiscal Autonomy (Commission on Human Rights) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Constitutional Basis** | Art. VIII, Sec. 3; Art. IX-A, Sec. 5; Art. XI, Sec. 14. | Art. XIII, Sec. 17(4). |
| **Express Textual Phrase** | Contains: **"shall enjoy fiscal autonomy" AND "automatically and regularly released."** | Contains: **ONLY "automatically and regularly released."** |
| **Appropriations Protection** | Budget cannot be reduced below previous year's level (Judiciary); automatic release. | Automatic and regular release of approved amounts only. |
| **Fund Flexibility & Internal Control** | Full flexibility to allocate/utilize resources; levy/collect authorized fees; utilize savings; exempt from pre-audit (**Bengzon v. Drilon**). | **None.** No independent power to alter structures or reallocate outside DBM and GAA parameters. |
| **Salary Standardization Law Compliance** | Required to adhere to R.A. No. 6758 framework, but possesses structural itemization powers. | Strictly subordinate to R.A. No. 6758 and requires mandatory prior DBM approval. |
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Fiscal Autonomy in the Broad Sense** vs. **Limited Fiscal Autonomy
 Automatic and Regular Release
 Surplusage Doctrine (Davide Formulation Refuted)
 Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius
 Unified Position Classification and Compensation System (R.A. No. 6758)
 Checks and Balances in Public Expenditures
**Constitutional & Political Law Operational Metrics:**
 State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation: CHR exercised asserted autonomous corporate power to unilaterally reorganize and reallocate savings; the Court enforced the Executive's statutory control through the DBM (under R.A. No. 6758 and Section 78 of the GAA) as a valid legislative restriction and check.
 Level of Judicial Scrutiny: Plain-meaning structural construction supplemented by Constitutional Commission intent analysis (debates of Commissioners Davide, Bengzon, Guingona, Monsod, and De Castro).
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
"In this Resolution, the Supreme Court held that the CHR is not an Article IX Constitutional Commission and does not enjoy broad fiscal autonomy. The phrase 'fiscal autonomy' was deliberately omitted from Section 17(4), Article XIII of the Constitution, leaving the CHR with only **limited** fiscal autonomy—meaning solely the automatic and regular release of its approved appropriations. Consequently, the CHR cannot invoke the GAA's special organizational provisions for fiscally autonomous bodies, cannot collapse items or upgrade positions on its own, and remains strictly subject to the Salary Standardization Law and the mandatory prior approval of the DBM."
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed. (All concurring: Puno, **J.** [**Chairman**], Austria-Martinez, Callejo, Sr., and Tinga, **JJ.**).
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the Motion for Reconsideration is PARTIALLY GRANTED. The assailed decision of this Court dated 25 November 2004 is hereby MODIFIED, declaring the respondent CHR as a constitutional body enjoying **limited** fiscal autonomy, in the sense that it is entitled to the automatic and regular release of its approved annual appropriations; nonetheless, it is still required to conform to the Salary Standardization Law. Accordingly, its entire reclassification scheme remains subject to the approval of the DBM. No pronouncement as to costs.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The CHR lost its plea to implement its upgrading and reclassification scheme. The Supreme Court partially granted the Motion for Reconsideration only to formally clarify that the CHR possesses **limited** fiscal autonomy (the right to the automatic release of its funds), but firmly sustained its original disposition disallowing CHR Resolutions Nos. A98-047, A98-055, and A98-062 because any restructuring of positions requires mandatory prior evaluation and approval by the DBM.
