### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title:** Manila Electric Company v. Pasay Transportation Company
**Full Official Caption:** Manila Electric Company, Petitioner, v. Pasay Transportation Company, Inc., E.B. Gutierrez, Raymundo Transportation Co., and J. Ampil, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 37878; November 25, 1932; 57 Phil. 600; Ponente: Malcolm, J.; En Banc (Concurred in by Avanceña, C.J., Street, Villamor, Ostrand, Villa-Real, Abad Santos, Hull, Vickers, Imperial, and Butte, JJ.; no separate opinions).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Petitioner:** Manila Electric Company (Meralco), a public utility corporation operating an electric railway and bridge system under a franchise.
**Respondents:** Pasay Transportation Company, Inc., E.B. Gutierrez, Raymundo Transportation Co., and J. Ampil, competing public utility transportation operators who sought or were subject to terms regarding the use of Meralco's Pasig bridge.
**Interested Government Official:** The Attorney-General of the Philippine Islands (notified by court order; disclaimed interest).
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Original Petition filed directly before the Supreme Court of the Philippine Islands requesting its members, sitting as a statutory board of arbitrators pursuant to Section 11 of Act No. 1446, to fix the terms and compensation for respondents' use of petitioner's Pasig bridge.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Safeguards of Judicial Independence / Non-Judicial Work
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Administrative Law & Separation of Powers → Principle of Separation of Powers → Incompatibility of Administrative/Non-Judicial Functions with Judicial Office
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Section 11, Act No. 1446:**
"Whenever any franchise or right of way is granted to any other person or corporation, now or hereafter in existence, over portions of the lines and tracks of the grantee herein, the terms on which said other person or corporation shall use such right of way, and the compensation to be paid to the grantee herein by such other person or corporation for said use, shall be **fixed by the members of the Supreme Court, sitting as a board of arbitrators, the decision of a majority of whom shall be final**."
**Section 26, Philippine Organic Act of 1916 (Jones Law / Act of Congress of August 29, 1916) [Historical Basis]:**
"That the Supreme Court and the Courts of First Instance of the Philippine Islands shall possess and **exercise jurisdiction as heretofore provided and such additional jurisdiction as shall hereafter be prescribed by law**... The Chief Justice and associate justices of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate of the United States."
**Section 12, Article VIII, 1987 Philippine Constitution [Modern Counterpart]:**
"The Members of the Supreme Court and of other courts established by law **shall not be designated to any agency performing quasi-judicial or administrative functions.**"
**Factual Trigger:** Manila Electric Company filed a petition directly invoking Section 11 of its statutory franchise (Act No. 1446), demanding that the individual Justices of the Supreme Court sit as an extrajudicial "board of arbitrators" to determine the compensation and contractual terms payable by other transportation operators for crossing its Pasig bridge.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1906 (Enactment of Franchise):** The Philippine Commission enacted Act No. 1446, granting Charles M. Swift (predecessor-in-interest of petitioner Manila Electric Company) a franchise to construct, maintain, and operate an electric railway and electric light, heat, and power system extending from Manila eastward to Pasig, Rizal. Under Section 11 of the Act, disputes regarding compensation and terms for third parties using the grantee's right of way and tracks were designated to be arbitrated and conclusively resolved by the members of the Supreme Court sitting as a board of arbitrators.
**Date Unstated (Prior to November 1932):** Disputes arose between Manila Electric Company and several independent public transportation operators (Pasay Transportation Co., E.B. Gutierrez, Raymundo Transportation Co., and J. Ampil) concerning the terms, conditions, and tolls/compensation for the latter's vehicular use of petitioner’s Pasig bridge.
**1932 (Filing of Petition):** Manila Electric Company filed an original petition with the Supreme Court, petitioning its members to convene as a board of arbitrators pursuant to Section 11 of Act No. 1446 to fix the contested terms and compensation.
**1932 (Procedural Directives):** The Supreme Court ordered petitioner to serve copies of the petition upon the Attorney-General and all affected transportation companies. The Attorney-General formally entered an appearance disclaiming any governmental interest in the proceedings. The respondent public utility operators filed written oppositions challenging the validity of the proceeding.
**1932 (Hearing & Submission):** Following an oral hearing, the parties submitted written memoranda on the preliminary threshold question regarding the validity of Section 11 of Act No. 1446 and the legal right of the members of the Supreme Court to sit as an extrajudicial arbitral tribunal.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Manila Electric Company)
**Main Thesis:** The members of the Supreme Court possess lawful authority and are statutorily required under Section 11 of Act No. 1446 to sit as a board of arbitrators to fix the terms and compensation for the use of the Pasig bridge.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Statutory Mandate: Section 11 of Act No. 1446 expressly confers this arbitral duty upon the members of the Court, making the decision of the majority final and binding.
 Permissible Delegation:** Citing **Tallassee Falls Mfg. Co. v. Commissioner’s Court (158 Ala. 263), petitioner argued that authorizing a court or its members to regulate rates or fix bridge tolls does not constitute an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power.
B. Respondents' Arguments (Pasay Transportation Company, Inc., et al.)
**Main Thesis:** The petition must be dismissed because Section 11 of Act No. 1446 is invalid and the Justices of the Supreme Court cannot constitutionally or lawfully act as a private board of arbitrators.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Ouster of Judicial Jurisdiction: The statutory clause making the majority award of the arbitrators final violates public policy and articles 1820 and 1821 of the Civil Code by stripping non-signatory public utilities of their fundamental right of recourse to courts of law for judicial determination of property rights.
 Incompatible Extrajudicial Functions: Members of the Supreme Court cannot be compelled or authorized to perform non-judicial, administrative, or private arbitral duties.
### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the members of the Supreme Court may lawfully sit as a board of arbitrators pursuant to Section 11 of Act No. 1446 to resolve private or administrative compensation disputes.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not Section 11 of Act No. 1446 is legally void for improperly ousting the courts of jurisdiction by making the arbitral award of the Justices final and unappealable against third parties.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Legal Right of Supreme Court Members to Act as a Board of Arbitrators
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the members of the Supreme Court may lawfully sit as a board of arbitrators pursuant to Section 11 of Act No. 1446.
**NO.** Under the doctrine of separation of powers and the Organic Act, the Supreme Court and its individual members may exercise **strictly judicial power and judicial power only**, and cannot be tasked with administrative, non-judicial, or arbitral duties.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Strict Sphere of Judicial Power:** Under the tripartite system established by the Organic Act, the Supreme Court forms one coordinate branch. It is confined strictly to exercising powers expressly or impliedly conferred by organic law. It cannot be required or permitted to perform any duty or assume any trust unconnected with administering judicial functions.
2.  **Entity vs. Individual Members:** Section 26 of the Organic Act confers "jurisdiction" on the Supreme Court as an organic, corporate entity acting as a court of law. It does not confer jurisdiction upon individual Justices sitting extrajudicially as an administrative or arbitral panel. A board of arbitrators is not a "court" in any legal sense.
3.  The Jurisdictional Dilemma:
**   If the Justices act **judicially as arbitrators, the statutory finality clause is an anomaly that impermissibly ousts courts of jurisdiction. If subject to judicial review, it produces the absurd spectacle of the Supreme Court as a court reviewing the decisions of its own individual members sitting as arbitrators.
**   If the Justices act **administratively or quasi-judicially, they are performing non-judicial work that members of the highest court cannot lawfully assume under the Organic Act.
4.  **Inherent Inefficacy of Non-Judicial Awards:** Citing Chief Justice Taney in **Gordon v. United States**, the Court emphasized that judicial power inherently requires the authority to render enforceable judgments with execution. Non-judicial duties that yield mere advisory or extrajudicial determinations degrade the constitutional standing of the judiciary.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The Supreme Court of the Philippine Islands represents one of the three divisions of power in our government. It is judicial power and judicial power only which is exercised by the Supreme Court. Just as the Supreme Court, as the guardian of constitutional rights, should not sanction usurpations by any other department of the government, so should it as strictly confine its own sphere of influence to the powers expressly or by implication conferred on it by the Organic Act. The Supreme Court and its members should not and cannot be required to exercise any power or to perform any trust or to assume any duty not pertaining to or connected with the administering of judicial functions." (57 Phil. 600, 605)
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Supreme Court is constitutionally restricted to exercising purely judicial functions. The legislature cannot designate the Court's members to serve as an extrajudicial board of arbitrators to fix franchise rates, because doing so forces judicial officers to perform non-judicial, administrative work, which violates the separation of powers.
Issue 2: Validity of Final Arbitration Clauses Ousting Court Jurisdiction
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not Section 11 of Act No. 1446 is legally void for attempting to oust courts of jurisdiction by making the arbitral award final against third parties.
**YES.** A statutory franchise clause making an extrajudicial arbitral award final and conclusive against non-signatory third parties illegally ousts the courts of their jurisdiction and is contrary to public policy.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Contractual Nature of Arbitration:** Submission to arbitration is grounded on contract (Articles 1820 and 1821, Civil Code). While voluntary arbitrations are favored, private parties cannot contractually oust courts of their established jurisdiction (**Wahl v. Donaldson, Sims & Co.**; **Puentebella v. Negros Coal Co.**).
2.  **Deprivation of Judicial Recourse:** Act No. 1446 is a franchise contract between the government and Meralco's predecessor. Making the board's decision completely "final" forces independent public utility operators—who never agreed to the franchise—into compulsory arbitration while stripping them of all recourse to courts of law for judicial determination of their rights.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Here, however, whatever else may be said in extenuation, it remains true that the decision of the board of arbitrators is made final, which if literally enforced would leave a public utility, not a party to the contract authorized by Act No. 1446, without recourse to the courts for a judicial determination of the question in dispute." (57 Phil. 600, 603–604)
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** A statute cannot force third parties into binding arbitration while declaring the award unappealable and final, because completely shutting the courthouse doors against litigants deprives them of judicial protection and violates public policy.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I → The Judicial Department → Safeguards of Judicial Independence / Prohibition on Non-Judicial Work.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (Judicial vs. Non-Judicial Power):**
 Exercise of Exclusively Judicial Power: The Court must act only on justiciable controversies affecting legal rights, rendering enforceable judgments. (Failed: Arbitrating franchise toll terms is administrative rate-fixing, not the exercise of judicial power).
 Institutional Action as a Court:** Constitutional jurisdiction is conferred upon the Supreme Court **as an entity, not upon its individual members dispersed into non-judicial committees or boards. (Failed: Section 11 conferred powers on individual members acting as a board).
 Integrity of the Appellate Hierarchy: A statute cannot create a structure where Supreme Court Justices render decisions in lower/arbitral capacities that might subsequently be reviewed by the Court itself.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"): Judicial power and judicial power only**; **Board of arbitrators is not a court**; **Ouster of jurisdiction**; **Separation of powers**; **Organic Act**; **Non-judicial functions**.
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer): Meralco v. Pasay Transportation Co.** is the foundational Philippine precedent prohibiting the legislature from assigning non-judicial work to members of the judiciary. When Meralco petitioned the Justices to fix bridge tolls pursuant to Section 11 of Act No. 1446, the Supreme Court declined, ruling that under the separation of powers, Justices can exercise "judicial power and judicial power only." They cannot sit as an administrative board of arbitrators, an anomaly that laid the jurisprudential groundwork for what is now explicitly codified in Article VIII, Section 12 of the 1987 Constitution.
**Subject-Specific Directive (Constitutional & Political Law Lens):**
 State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation: Legislative power (franchise enactment under Act No. 1446) collided with the Principle of Separation of Powers and the Judicial Department's institutional independence under Section 26 of the Jones Law.
 Doctrinal Scrutiny: Structural check via the doctrine of separation of powers and judicial incompatibility.
 Justiciability Audit: The petition presented an institutional, structural threshold challenge: the Supreme Court as a court was petitioned to authorize its own members to act in a non-judicial capacity. The Court resolved this threshold question by declaring the statutory designation unconstitutional and declining to act.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
No separate opinions filed. (Avanceña, C.J., Street, Villamor, Ostrand, Villa-Real, Abad Santos, Hull, Vickers, Imperial, and Butte, JJ., concurred fully with the **ponencia** of Malcolm, J.).
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"Conforming the decision to the basic question at issue, the Supreme Court holds that section 11 of Act No. 1446 contravenes the maxims which guide the operation of a democratic government constitutionally established, and that it would be improper and illegal for the members of the Supreme Court, sitting as a board of arbitrators, the decision of a majority of whom shall be final, to act on the petition of the Manila Electric Company. As a result, the members of the Supreme Court decline to proceed further in the matter."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of respondents' oppositions and declared Section 11 of Act No. 1446 unconstitutional and void. The members of the Supreme Court formally refused to sit as a board of arbitrators and dismissed the proceedings.

### 1. Case Header, Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Concise Recognizable Title: Buenafe v. COMELEC** (The 2022 Marcos Disqualification Cases)
**Full Official Caption:** Fr. Christian B. Buenafe, Fides M. Lim, Ma. Edeliza P. Hernandez, Celia Lagman Sevilla, Roland C. Vibal, and Josephine Lascano, Petitioners, vs. Commission on Elections, Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos, Jr., The Senate of the Philippines, represented by the Senate President, The House of Representatives, represented by the Speaker of the House of Representatives, Respondents (G.R. No. 260374); Bonifacio Parabuac Ilagan, Saturnino Cunanan Ocampo, Maria Carolina Pagaduan Araullo, Trinidad Gerilla Repuno, Joanna Kintanar Cariño, Elisa Tita Perez Lubi, Liza Largoza Maza, Danilo Mallari Dela Fuente, Carmencita Mendoza Florentino, Doroteo Cubacub Abaya, Jr., Erlinda Nable Senturias, Sr. Arabella Cammagay Balingao, Sr. Cherry M. Ibardolaza, CSSJB, Sr. Susan Santos Esmile, SFIC, Homar Rubert Roca Distajo, Polynne Espineda Dira, James Carwyn Candila, and Jonas Angelo Lopena Abadilla, Petitioners, vs. Commission on Elections, Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos, Jr., The Senate of the Philippines, represented by the Senate President, The House of Representatives, represented by the Speaker of the House of Representatives, Respondents (G.R. No. 260426).
**Citation & Metadata:** 924 Phil. 201; G.R. Nos. 260374 & 260426, June 28, 2022; En Banc; Ponente: Zalameda, J. Voting Breakdown: Unanimous dismissal (13-0 participating). Concurring: Gesmundo, C.J., Hernando, Rosario, and Marquez, JJ. Separate Concurring Opinions filed by: Leonen, SAJ.; Caguioa, J. (on official leave but left his vote); Lazaro-Javier, J.; M. Lopez, J.; Gaerlan, J.; J. Lopez, J.; Dimaampao, J.; and Singh, J. Took No Part: Inting, J. (due to sister Commissioner Socorro B. Inting's participation in COMELEC) and Kho, Jr., J. (due to prior participation as COMELEC Commissioner).
**Key Parties & Roles (The Cast):**
**Fr. Christian B. Buenafe, et al. (G.R. No. 260374 Petitioners):** Registered voters, civic leaders, and human rights advocates representing organizations such as TFDP, KAPATID, MAG, FIND, PAHRA, and BALAY. Petitioners in the Section 78 Petition to Cancel/Deny Due Course to Marcos, Jr.'s Certificate of Candidacy (COC).
**Bonifacio Parabuac Ilagan, et al. (G.R. No. 260426 Petitioners):** Martial law victims, rights advocates, and registered voters. Petitioners in the Section 12 Petition for Disqualification against Marcos, Jr.
**Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos, Jr. (Private Respondent):** Proclaimed President-elect of the Philippines following the May 9, 2022 National Elections; former Vice-Governor and Governor of Ilocos Norte (1982–1986); convicted by the Court of Appeals (CA) in 1997 for non-filing of Income Tax Returns (ITRs) for taxable years 1982–1985.
**Commission on Elections (COMELEC) (Public Respondent):** The constitutional electoral commission whose Second Division, Former First Division, and En Banc resolutions dismissed petitioners' cancellation and disqualification suits.
**The Senate of the Philippines & House of Representatives (Public Respondents):** Legislative bodies that convened jointly on May 24, 2022 as the National Board of Canvassers (NBOC) and proclaimed Marcos, Jr. on May 25, 2022.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Consolidated Petitions for Certiorari with Urgent Prayers for Temporary Restraining Order (TRO) and/or Preliminary Injunction filed under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 of the Rules of Court, assailing: (1) COMELEC Second Division Resolution dated January 17, 2022 and COMELEC En Banc Resolution dated May 10, 2022 in SPA No. 21-156 (DC); and (2) COMELEC Former First Division Resolution dated February 10, 2022 and COMELEC En Banc Resolution dated May 10, 2022 in SPA No. 21-212 (DC).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision & Factual Trigger
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Constitutional Law I → Executive Department → Section 4, Article VII (Presidential Electoral Tribunal Jurisdiction vs. Supreme Court Certiorari Review)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Election Law → Batas Pambansa Blg. 881 (Omnibus Election Code) → Section 78 in relation to Section 74 (Denial/Cancellation of COC for False Material Representation) vs. Section 12 (Disqualification for Conviction of Crime Involving Moral Turpitude or Penalty Exceeding 18 Months)
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional & Statutory Provisions:**
**Article VII, Section 4, Paragraph 7, 1987 Constitution:**
"The **Supreme Court, sitting en banc, shall be the sole judge of all contests relating to the election, returns, and qualifications of the President or Vice-President**, and may promulgate its rules for the purpose."
**Article VII, Section 2, 1987 Constitution:**
"No person may be elected President unless he is a **natural-born citizen of the Philippines, a registered voter, able to read and write, at least forty years of age on the day of the election, and a resident of the Philippines for at least ten years immediately preceding such election**."
**Section 78, Omnibus Election Code (Batas Pambansa Blg. 881):**
"Sec. 78. **Petition to deny due course to or cancel a certificate of candidacy.** — A verified petition seeking to deny due course or to cancel a certificate of candidacy may be filed by the person **exclusively on the ground that any material representation contained therein as required under Section 74 hereof is false**. The petition may be filed at any time not later than twenty-five days from the time of the filing of the certificate of candidacy and shall be decided, after due notice and hearing, not later than fifteen days before the election."
**Section 12, Omnibus Election Code (Batas Pambansa Blg. 881):**
"Sec. 12. **Disqualifications.** — Any person who has been declared by competent authority insane or incompetent, or **has been sentenced by final judgment for subversion, insurrection, rebellion or for any offense for which he has been sentenced to a penalty of more than eighteen months or for a crime involving moral turpitude, shall be disqualified to be a candidate and to hold any office**, unless he has been given plenary pardon or granted amnesty.
These disqualifications to be a candidate herein provided shall be deemed removed upon the declaration by competent authority that said insanity or incompetence had been removed or **after the expiration of a period of five years from his service of sentence**, unless within the same period he again becomes disqualified."
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):** When Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. filed his COC for President on October 6, 2021, he declared under oath in Item 11 that he was "eligible for the office I seek to be elected to" and checked "No" in Box 22 asking whether he had ever been found liable for any offense carrying the accessory penalty of perpetual disqualification to hold public office by a final and executory judgment. Petitioners immediately initiated administrative actions before the COMELEC, asserting that these declarations were fraudulent and that Marcos, Jr. was perpetually disqualified and ineligible to run under the Tax Code and Section 12 of the OEC by virtue of a 1997 Court of Appeals conviction for failure to file ITRs from 1982 to 1985.
### 3. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**November 3, 1982 – March 31, 1986:** Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. serves as Vice-Governor, and later Governor, of the Province of Ilocos Norte.
**February 25, 1986:** The Marcos family leaves the Philippines for Hawaii following the EDSA People Power Revolution.
**June 27, 1990:** A Special Tax Audit Team created by Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) Commissioner Jose U. Ong investigates the tax liabilities of the late President Ferdinand E. Marcos, his immediate family, and associates.
**July 25, 1991:** BIR Commissioner Ong files a letter-complaint with the Department of Justice against Marcos, Jr., leading to the filing of eight criminal informations before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC), Branch 105: Criminal Cases Nos. Q-91-24391, Q-92-29212, Q-92-29213, and Q-92-29217 (failure to file ITRs for 1982, 1983, 1984, and 1985 under the 1977 NIRC); and Q-91-24390, Q-92-29214, Q-92-29215, and Q-92-29216 (failure to pay deficiency income taxes for 1982 to 1985).
**July 27, 1995:** The QC RTC, Branch 105 convicts Marcos, Jr. on all eight counts. For failure to file ITRs, it sentences him to six months imprisonment and a P2,000 fine each for 1982, 1983, and 1984; and three years imprisonment and a P30,000 fine for 1985. For failure to pay taxes, it sentences him to identical prison terms and fines, and orders payment of taxes due with penalties, interest, and surcharges.
**October 31, 1997:** The Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. CR No. 18569, penned by Paras, J.) modifies the RTC judgment. The CA **acquits** Marcos, Jr. of non-payment of deficiency taxes (Sections 50/73, 1977 NIRC) due to lack of prior notice from the BIR, but finds him **guilty** of failure to file ITRs (Section 45, 1977 NIRC) for taxable years 1982 to 1985. The CA **completely deletes the prison terms**, sentencing him solely to pay a fine of P2,000 each for 1982, 1983, and 1984, and P30,000 for 1985, plus deficiency taxes and interest. The CA **fallo** does not mention perpetual disqualification.
**August 8, 2001:** The Supreme Court grants Marcos, Jr.'s urgent motion to withdraw his motion for extension of time to file a petition for review (G.R. No. 148434).
**August 31, 2001:** Entry of Judgment is recorded by the Supreme Court, rendering the 1997 CA Decision final and executory. (The CA had entered judgment on November 10, 1997).
**December 27, 2001:** Marcos, Jr. pays the BIR deficiency taxes and fines amounting to P67,137.27 via Landbank Official Receipt using BIR Form 0605.
**October 6, 2021:** Marcos, Jr. files his COC for President in the May 9, 2022 National Elections, ticking "No" to Box 22 and affirming his eligibility in Item 11.
**November 2, 2021:** Petitioners Buenafe, et al. file a Petition to Deny Due Course to or Cancel Marcos, Jr.'s COC under Section 78 in relation to Section 74 of the OEC (SPA No. 21-156 [DC]).
**November 20, 2021:** Petitioners Ilagan, et al. file a Petition for Disqualification against Marcos, Jr. under Section 12 of the OEC (SPA No. 21-212 [DC]).
**December 2, 2021:** The QC RTC Branch 105 issues a certification stating there is no record on file of compliance or payment/satisfaction of the 1995 RTC or 1997 CA decisions.
**January 17, 2022:** The COMELEC Second Division denies the Buenafe Petition for lack of merit, finding no false material representation, no moral turpitude, and no perpetual disqualification in the CA **fallo**.
**February 10, 2022:** The COMELEC Former First Division dismisses the Ilagan Petition, ruling that failure to file an ITR does not involve moral turpitude, that Marcos, Jr. was not sentenced to more than 18 months imprisonment, and that perpetual disqualification was not imposed.
**May 9, 2022:** The National Elections take place. Marcos, Jr. garners 31,629,783 votes (58.77% of votes cast).
**May 10, 2022:** The COMELEC En Banc issues twin resolutions denying the Motions for Partial Reconsideration in SPA No. 21-156 (DC) and SPA No. 21-212 (DC).
**May 18, 2022:** Petitioners Buenafe, et al. (G.R. No. 260374) and Ilagan, et al. (G.R. No. 260426) file their respective Rule 65 Petitions for Certiorari with prayers for TRO before the Supreme Court.
**May 25, 2022:** Congress, sitting as the National Board of Canvassers, proclaims Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr. as the duly elected President of the Republic of the Philippines.
**June 28, 2022:** The Supreme Court En Banc promulgates its decision dismissing the consolidated petitions.
### 4. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments
1. Fr. Christian B. Buenafe, et al. (G.R. No. 260374):
**Main Thesis:** Marcos, Jr.'s COC must be cancelled under Section 78 of the OEC because he deliberately made false material representations regarding his eligibility and his non-liability for an offense carrying perpetual disqualification.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Automatic Imposition by Operation of Law:** Section 286(c) of the 1977 NIRC (as amended by P.D. 1994, effective January 1, 1986) mandates that any public officer convicted of any crime penalized under the NIRC **shall** be dismissed from service and **perpetually disqualified** from holding public office, voting, and participating in elections. Under **Jalosjos, Jr. v. COMELEC**, perpetual disqualification is an ineligibility that attaches automatically upon conviction by operation of law and is deemed written into the final judgment, even if omitted from the CA **fallo.
 Status as Public Officer: Marcos, Jr. was Governor of Ilocos Norte throughout 1982 to 1985 and up to March 31, 1986. His failure to file his 1985 return fell due on March 18, 1986, while he was still a public officer.
 Deliberate Intent to Deceive: Having actively litigated his criminal tax cases through the RTC, CA, and Supreme Court, Marcos, Jr. knew of his conviction and perpetual disqualification, making his representations in Item 11 and Box 22 of his COC intentional falsehoods designed to mislead the electorate.
 Improper Procedural Dismissal: The COMELEC Second Division erred in holding that the petition combined prohibited grounds for disqualification under its procedural rules.
2. Bonifacio Parabuac Ilagan, et al. (G.R. No. 260426):
**Main Thesis:** Marcos, Jr. must be disqualified under Section 12 of the OEC because he was convicted by final judgment of a crime involving moral turpitude and sentenced (or legally mandated to be sentenced) to more than 18 months imprisonment.
**Specific Contentions:**
 Moral Turpitude:** Willful failure to file ITRs for four consecutive years (1982–1985) while serving as Vice-Governor and Governor is an intentional, repeated, and unlawful breach of a public officer’s civic duty, constituting moral depravity, tax evasion, and a crime involving moral turpitude under **Zari v. Flores.
 Void CA Judgment:** The 1997 CA Decision deleting the prison sentence and imposing only fines is void **ab initio** because it violated Section 286(c) of P.D. 1994, which made mandatory the imposition of the **maximum penalty (both fine and imprisonment) upon public officers. A void judgment cannot attain finality.
 Non-Service of Sentence: The RTC Branch 105 certification proves Marcos, Jr. never paid the fines or served the sentence; hence, the disqualification under Section 12 remains active.
 Stray Votes & Second Placer Doctrine: Marcos, Jr.'s votes should be treated as stray, and the qualified presidential candidate garnering the second highest number of votes should be proclaimed.

1. Private Respondent Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr.:

 Non-Imposition of Perpetual Disqualification:** Perpetual disqualification under Section 286(c) of P.D. 1994 is a principal penalty, not an automatic accessory penalty under the Revised Penal Code (RPC). Because it was omitted from the CA **fallo**, the doctrine of immutability of final judgments bars reading it into the sentence. **Jalosjos, Jr. applies solely to RPC felonies carrying accessory penalties under Article 73.
 No Moral Turpitude:** Under **Republic v. Marcos II (2009), the mere omission to file an ITR is not a crime involving moral turpitude because fraud and willfulness to evade taxes are not elements of the offense.

### 5. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Supreme Court has jurisdiction under Rule 65 to determine the validity of the COMELEC's pre-election resolutions regarding the qualifications of a proclaimed winning presidential candidate, or whether exclusive jurisdiction has transferred to the Presidential Electoral Tribunal (PET).
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the consolidated petitions were rendered moot and academic by the conduct of the May 9, 2022 National Elections and the subsequent proclamation of respondent Marcos, Jr. by Congress sitting as the National Board of Canvassers.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the COMELEC committed grave abuse of discretion in holding that the Buenafe Section 78 Petition was subject to summary dismissal for impermissibly combining grounds for disqualification and cancellation of COC.
4.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondent Marcos, Jr.'s representations in his COC (that he is eligible for President and has not been convicted of an offense carrying perpetual disqualification) are material representations under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code.
5.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the accessory penalty of perpetual disqualification from public office was automatically imposed by operation of law upon respondent Marcos, Jr.'s conviction for failure to file ITRs under the 1977 NIRC, as amended by P.D. 1994, despite its omission from the dispositive portion of the final 1997 Court of Appeals Decision.
6.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the 1997 Court of Appeals Decision is void for deleting the penalty of imprisonment and imposing solely a fine, thereby precluding it from attaining finality.
7.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondent Marcos, Jr.'s conviction for failure to file income tax returns constitutes a conviction of a crime involving moral turpitude under Section 12 of the Omnibus Election Code.
8.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondent Marcos, Jr. committed false material representations under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code with deliberate intent to deceive the electorate, justifying the cancellation of his COC.
### 6. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: PET Jurisdiction vs. Supreme Court Certiorari Review
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the Supreme Court has jurisdiction under Rule 65 to determine the validity of the COMELEC's pre-election resolutions, or whether exclusive jurisdiction has transferred to the Presidential Electoral Tribunal.
**YES.** The Supreme Court retains certiorari jurisdiction to review COMELEC En Banc resolutions assailed under Rules 64 and 65 prior to the proclaimed President-elect’s oath-taking and assumption of office at noon on June 30; the conditions precedent for the exercise of PET jurisdiction were not met.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Constitutional Grant and Textual Parallelism:** Section 4, Paragraph 7, Article VII of the 1987 Constitution constitutes the Supreme Court En Banc as the "sole judge of all contests relating to the election, returns, and qualifications of the President or Vice-President." This language parallels Section 17, Article VI governing the Senate Electoral Tribunal (SET) and House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal (HRET).
2.  **The Reyes Tripartite Trigger Point:** In **Reyes v. COMELEC** (2013), the Court established that an electoral tribunal's jurisdiction as "sole judge" is activated only upon the concurrence of three requisites: (1) a valid proclamation; (2) a proper oath; and (3) assumption of office. Applying this doctrine to the presidency, a candidate does not become the "President" until noon of June 30 next following the election (Section 4, Article VII).
3.  **Absence of Assumption and Actual Contest:** Prior to noon of June 30, 2022, respondent Marcos, Jr., though proclaimed, had not yet taken his oath or assumed office. Furthermore, no formal election protest or **quo warranto** petition had been initiated before the PET under the 2010 PET Rules.
4.  **PET is Not a Separate Court:** Citing **Macalintal v. PET** (2010) and **Lopez v. Roxas** (1966), the Court clarified that the PET is an institution independent of the three political branches, but not separate from the Supreme Court. Concurring with specialized court analogies, the Court held that Section 4, Article VII confers an additional original jurisdiction upon the Court En Banc and does not divest or diminish its constitutional power of judicial review under Section 1, Article VIII and Rule 64 to review pre-proclamation COMELEC actions.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Applying the ruling in **Reyes** to the present petitions, this Court, sitting **En Banc**, can only take cognizance of an election contest if the following requisites concur: (a) a petition is filed before it; and (b) the petition is filed against a Presidential or Vice-Presidential candidate who has been validly proclaimed, properly taken his or her oath, and assumed office. These conditions are not present here. ... By the same token, the PET is not a separate and distinct entity from the Supreme Court, albeit it has functions peculiar only to the Tribunal. ... Section 4, Article VII of the 1987 Constitution therefore should not be considered as a limitation on the jurisdiction of the Court over the pending petitions."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The Supreme Court retains full jurisdiction under Rule 65 to review COMELEC decisions on pre-election candidate eligibility up until the winning candidate actually takes the oath and assumes office on June 30. The Presidential Electoral Tribunal’s exclusive jurisdiction applies only to post-assumption election contests (protests and **quo warranto**) filed against an incumbent President who has satisfied all three **Reyes** elements: proclamation, oath, and assumption.
Issue 2: Mootness by Election and Proclamation
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the consolidated petitions were rendered moot and academic by the completion of the May 9, 2022 National Elections and the proclamation of Marcos, Jr.
**NO.** The receipt of the highest number of votes and subsequent proclamation do not moot a direct challenge to a candidate’s legal eligibility and qualifications to hold public office.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Nature of Mootness:** A case is moot only when supervening events terminate the legal controversy so completely that the court can grant no practical relief.
2.  **Qualifications Cannot Be Waived by Popular Vote:** While popular sovereignty is the bedrock of a democratic republic, an overwhelming mandate (even 31.6 million votes or 58.77%) cannot override mandatory statutory or constitutional disqualifications. A candidate must possess all qualifications and none of the disqualifications.
3.  **Quizon v. COMELEC Distinguished:** Precedents like **Quizon v. COMELEC**—holding that election rules are mandatory before election but directory after to give effect to the will of the people—apply strictly to innocuous, formal, or technical defects in the COC (such as improper verification or notarization), never to substantive ineligibility or statutory disqualifications.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The issues raised in both the Buenafe and Ilagan Petitions – whether respondent Marcos, Jr. is guilty of material misrepresentation of his eligibility and whether he suffers any of the grounds for disqualification – are not rendered moot by his receipt of the highest number of votes or by his subsequent proclamation. ... We cannot stress enough that the qualification of the candidate is not waived by his or her subsequent election to the office."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Winning an election by tens of millions of votes does not cure a candidate's legal ineligibility. The Supreme Court's duty to determine whether a candidate is disqualified under the law remains a live, justiciable controversy that is never mooted by a proclamation.
Issue 3: Propriety of COMELEC’s Procedural Summary Dismissal Ground
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the COMELEC gravely abused its discretion in treating the Buenafe Petition as subject to summary dismissal for commingling Section 78 cancellation grounds with Section 12 disqualification grounds.
**NO.** The issue is moot and non-prejudicial because the COMELEC Second Division and En Banc expressly relaxed technical rules and fully adjudicated the petitions on their substantive merits.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Rule 23 Restrictions:** Section 1, Rule 23 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure (as amended by Resolution No. 9523) provides that a Section 78 petition combining grounds for disqualification or other separate remedies shall be summarily dismissed.
2.  **Actual Adjudication on the Merits:** The COMELEC Second Division explicitly waived this procedural defect in its January 17, 2022 Resolution "in the interest of justice and of paramount importance" and resolved the controversy on its merits.
3.  **Interchangeability of Overlapping Grounds:** Under **Chua v. COMELEC** (2016) and **Fermin v. COMELEC** (2008), while Section 78 (cancellation) and Section 12/68 (disqualification) are distinct remedies with different grounds, timeframes, and substitution consequences, a petitioner may properly invoke a statutory ground for disqualification in a Section 78 cancellation petition if the candidate falsely certified in their COC under Section 74 that they are "eligible" for the office.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"However, these arguments are neither decisive of, nor relevant to, the present controversy. The COMELEC did not dismiss the petition on the ground of violating Section 1, Rule 23 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure. Instead, it proceeded to rule on the substantive issues raised and denied the petition for lack of merit."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Whether the Buenafe petitioners mixed up cancellation and disqualification grounds in their initial pleading is irrelevant because the COMELEC waived the procedural error and ruled on the substantive merits anyway. Moreover, an ineligibility can be raised in a Section 78 petition because declaring that one is "eligible" when legally disqualified is a false representation.
Issue 4: Materiality of perpetual Disqualification Declarations in COC
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not Marcos, Jr.'s representations regarding eligibility and perpetual disqualification in his COC are "material" under Section 78 of the OEC.
**YES.** Representations concerning perpetual disqualification and overall legal eligibility are material facts because they directly affect the candidate's legal capacity to run for, be elected to, and hold public office.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Test of Materiality:** Under **Salcedo II v. COMELEC** (1999) and **Villafuerte v. COMELEC** (2014), a representation is material under Section 78 if it refers to the qualifications and eligibility for the elective office sought, rather than innocuous mistakes.
2.  **Eligibility Defined:** In **Aratea v. COMELEC** (2012) and **Jalosjos, Jr. v. COMELEC** (2012), "eligibility" under Section 74 encompasses having all the qualifications and none of the ineligibilities. Perpetual disqualification is an ineligibility that completely deprives a person of the capacity to hold public office.
3.  **Non-Exclusivity of Article VII, Section 2:** The Court rejected Marcos, Jr.'s contention that presidential eligibility is exclusively limited to the text of Section 2, Article VII of the 1987 Constitution. Statutes such as the Omnibus Election Code lawfully establish general ineligibilities and disqualifications (e.g., Section 12, OEC; Section 69 nuisance candidate provisions) that apply to presidential aspirants.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Perpetual disqualification is an ineligibility. Necessarily, therefore, it directly affects one's eligibility to run for office. Equally established is that the enumeration of qualifications in the 1987 Constitution, as reiterated in Section 63 of the OEC, is not exclusive. Other pertinent laws lay down requirements for qualification and eligibility to run for and hold elective office. These considerations are sufficient to meet the requirement of materiality under Section 78 of the OEC."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Statements in a COC affirming eligibility or denying perpetual disqualification are legally "material" because suffering from perpetual disqualification bars anyone from holding public office. The qualifications listed in the Constitution are not a closed list that insulates presidential candidates from general statutory disqualifications.
Issue 5: Automatic Imposition of Perpetual Disqualification under the Tax Code
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the accessory penalty of perpetual disqualification was automatically imposed upon Marcos, Jr. by operation of law under the 1977 NIRC (as amended by P.D. 1994) despite being omitted from the Court of Appeals **fallo**.
**NO.** Perpetual disqualification under Section 286(c) of the 1977 NIRC is not an automatic accessory penalty; it must be expressly decreed in the dispositive portion of the judgment of conviction, and under the doctrine of immutability of final judgments, courts cannot retroactively read omitted penalties into an immutable sentence.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Temporal Applicability of P.D. 1994:** Non-filing of ITRs for taxable years 1982, 1983, and 1984 was governed by Section 73 of the 1977 NIRC, which carried only a fine of up to P2,000, imprisonment of up to six months, or both. Perpetual disqualification was only introduced on November 5, 1985 via P.D. 1994, which took effect on January 1, 1986. Applying P.D. 1994 to 1982–1984 returns would violate the constitutional ban on **ex post facto** laws.
2.  **Public Officer Status for 1985 Return:** The 1985 ITR fell due on March 18, 1986. However, Marcos, Jr. and his family were ousted and flown into exile on February 25, 1986, thereby ceasing to be an incumbent public officer before the deadline expired.
3.  **Special Penal Law vs. Revised Penal Code System:** The Court distinguished **Jalosjos, Jr. v. COMELEC** and **People v. Silvallana**. Under Article 73 of the RPC, accessory penalties automatically attach to principal penalties (Articles 40–45) by legislative presumption. Under the landmark doctrine of **People v. Simon** (1994), RPC rules on penalties do not apply suppletorily to special penal laws where the statutory penalties bear no relation to the RPC scale.
4.  **Textual Structure of Section 286(c):** Section 286(c) uses the word "automatically" exclusively for the revocation of a certified public accountant's license ("his certificate... shall, upon conviction, be **automatically** revoked"). In contrast, it does not use "automatically" for perpetual disqualification of public officers.
5.  **Immutability of Judgments and Dispositive Portion:** The CA **fallo** of October 31, 1997 sentenced Marcos, Jr. purely to fines and deficiency taxes, without decreeing imprisonment or perpetual disqualification. Execution adheres strictly to the **fallo**. Under **Estarija v. People** (2009), even if a court erroneously fails to impose a mandatory penalty, once the judgment becomes final and executory, it is immutable and cannot be amended by any court. Under **in dubiis reus est absolvendus**, all doubts must be resolved in favor of the accused.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Here, petitioners Ilagan et al.'s theory that perpetual disqualification was automatically imposed with the mere fact of conviction finds basis from jurisprudence **involving disqualifications under the RPC**. Respondent Marcos, Jr.'s conviction, on the other hand, is for the non-filing of income tax return **under the 1977 NIRC**. Whereas the RPC contained a system of penalties categorized between principal or accessory penalties, as well as an express presumption in regard to the imposition of certain penalties upon the mere fact of conviction, the 1977 NIRC did not. ... This Court thus holds that, unless explicitly provided for in the **fallo**, the penalty of disqualification from public office under Section 286(c) is not deemed automatically imposed on a public officer or employee found to have violated the provisions of the 1977 NIRC."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The automatic imposition of accessory penalties applies only to crimes under the Revised Penal Code, which contains an explicit rule (Article 73) deeming accessory penalties written into the verdict. The Tax Code has no such provision. Because the Court of Appeals did not expressly write perpetual disqualification into the dispositive portion of its 1997 conviction, and that decision became final in 2001, the doctrine of immutability of judgments prohibits any court from retroactively adding that penalty today.
Issue 6: Validity of the 1997 Court of Appeals Decision
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the 1997 Court of Appeals Decision is void for deleting the RTC's prison sentence and imposing solely fines.
**NO.** The CA Decision is completely valid because the applicable tax laws granted the appellate court full judicial discretion to impose a fine, imprisonment, or both.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Disjunctive Penalties in Governing Law:** For 1982–1984, Section 73 of the 1977 NIRC punished non-filing with "a fine of not more than two thousand pesos or by imprisonment for not more than six months, or both." For 1985, Section 288 (as amended by P.D. 1994) penalized non-filing with a fine "or" imprisonment "or both."
2.  **Judicial Discretion:** The word "or" is disjunctive. The CA possessed lawful authority to impose fines alone without imprisonment.
3.  **Prospective Effect of R.A. 8424:** It was only with the enactment of the 1997 NIRC (Republic Act No. 8424) in 1998 that Section 255 made the imposition of **both** fine and imprisonment mandatory. Imposing R.A. 8424 retroactively on 1982–1985 acts would violate the constitutional prohibition against **ex post facto** laws.
4.  **Lack of Standing for Private Parties:** In criminal cases, only the State through the OSG can assail an erroneous criminal sentence; private complainants or third-party voters lack standing to seek the invalidation or increase of a final criminal sentence.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Clearly the CA had the discretion to impose the penalty of a fine **or** imprisonment **or** both, upon respondent Marcos, Jr. The CA's Decision imposing only the penalty of a fine is valid. Consequently, respondent Marcos, Jr. cannot be disqualified on the ground that he was sentenced by final judgment to a penalty of more than eighteen months under Section 12 of the OEC."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The 1997 Court of Appeals decision was not void because the tax laws in force from 1982 to 1985 gave judges the option to impose a fine, prison, or both. The CA legally chose to impose only fines. The mandatory requirement to impose both prison and fines did not exist until 1998, and retroactive application of that requirement would be unconstitutional.
Issue 7: Moral Turpitude in Failure to File ITRs
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not the failure to file an income tax return constitutes a crime involving moral turpitude under Section 12 of the OEC.
**NO.** The mere failure to file an income tax return is an omission that does not involve moral turpitude because it lacks the elements of fraud, deceit, and willful tax evasion.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Definition and Roots:** Tracing the doctrine from U.S. immigration jurisprudence (**Jordan v. De George**) through early Philippine rulings (**In Re Basa**, **Tak Ng**, **Zari v. Flores**), moral turpitude refers to acts inherently base, vile, or depraved, contrary to justice, honesty, modesty, or good morals (**mala in se**), not acts prohibited merely by statute (**mala prohibita**).
2.  **Tax Evasion vs. Mere Failure to File:** In **Zari v. Flores**, tax evasion was held to involve moral turpitude because it requires actual, intentional fraud, deceit, and an evil mind to escape taxes. In contrast, under **CIR v. Toda** and Section 248 of the NIRC, the law treats simple "failure to file a return" (25% penalty) separately from "willful neglect or fraudulent return" (50% fraud penalty).
3.  **Direct Precedent in Republic v. Marcos II (2009):** In **Republic v. Marcos II** (2009)—which evaluated the exact same 1997 CA conviction against Marcos, Jr. to determine his fitness to be an estate executor—the Supreme Court specifically ruled that failure to file an ITR is not a crime involving moral turpitude because mere omission completes the offense regardless of fraudulent intent. Under **stare decisis**, this holding governs.
4.  **Clarification on Decriminalization & Withholding:** The Court clarified that the TRAIN Law (R.A. 10963) and BIR regulations on substituted filing (Section 51-A) did not fully decriminalize non-filing for all taxpayers, but established that pure compensation earners whose taxes were fully withheld are excused from filing. In Marcos, Jr.'s case, local government certifications established that taxes had been withheld by the provincial government, further negating any fraudulent design to cheat the public treasury.
5.  **Satisfaction of Fines:** Marcos, Jr. presented BIR Form 0605 and a Landbank receipt dated December 27, 2001 showing payment of P67,137.27 covering the fines and deficiency taxes, which the COMELEC correctly credited. Non-payment of fines is not a ground for disqualification under Section 12 of the OEC.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"The 'failure to file an income tax return' is not a crime involving moral turpitude as the mere omission is already a violation regardless of the fraudulent intent or willfulness of the individual. ... Thus, this Court holds that even if the conviction of respondent Marcos II is affirmed, the same not being a crime involving moral turpitude cannot serve as a ground for his disqualification. ... Significantly, **Republic v. Marcos II** involved the same Decision in CA-G.R. CR No. 18569 and considered the same act of non-filing of income tax returns at issue in the present Petitions."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Not every crime involves moral turpitude. Moral turpitude requires fraud, dishonesty, or baseness. While actively evading taxes through false records is a crime of moral turpitude, simply failing to file an annual income tax return—especially when compensation taxes were already withheld at source—is a mere statutory omission (**malum prohibitum**). The Supreme Court already settled this exact issue regarding Marcos, Jr. in 2009.
Issue 8: Absence of Intent to Deceive under Section 78
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Whether or not respondent Marcos, Jr. deliberately intended to deceive the electorate when certifying his eligibility in his COC, justifying its cancellation.
**NO.** The cancellation of a COC under Section 78 requires not only a false representation of a material fact, but also proof of a deliberate, malicious intent to deceive the electorate, which was utterly lacking.
**(b) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
1.  **Twin Requirements of Section 78:** Under **Salcedo II** and **Mitra v. COMELEC**, to cancel a COC, two elements must concur: (1) a false representation of a material fact; and (2) a deliberate intent to mislead, misinform, or hide a fact from the electorate regarding one’s qualifications.
2.  **No Falsehood Committed:** Because Marcos, Jr. was never sentenced to perpetual disqualification by the CA and was not convicted of a crime involving moral turpitude or sentenced to over 18 months prison, his affirmative declaration of eligibility was not false.
3.  **Subjective Good Faith:** Marcos, Jr. had reasonable, valid, and legitimate grounds based on the text of the final 1997 CA Decision—which omitted perpetual disqualification and imprisonment—and this Court's 2009 ruling in **Republic v. Marcos II**, to believe he was fully eligible. He previously ran unhindered for Governor, Representative, and Senator. There was no showing of malicious deception.
**(c) Golden Verbatim Quote:**
"Notably, not every false representation warrants the denial of due course to or cancellation of a COC. It must be shown that the false representation pertained to material information and was made with an 'intention to deceive the electorate as to one's qualifications for public office.' ... Respondent Marcos, Jr. had no intention to mislead, misinform, and deceive the electorate."
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Canceling a certificate of candidacy requires clear proof of a deliberate, fraudulent scheme to lie to the voters about one's qualifications. Because Marcos, Jr. relied on a final Court of Appeals decision that sentenced him only to a fine, as well as a 2009 Supreme Court ruling clearing him of moral turpitude, he acted in good faith and had no fraudulent intent to deceive the electorate.
### 6.5. Subject-Specific Doctrinal & Recitation Spotlight
**Assigned Course & Syllabus Focus:** Constitutional Law I | Topic: m. Presidential Electoral Tribunal | Applied Lens: Constitutional & Political Law Lens
**State Power vs. Constitutional Limitation:**
 State Power Asserted: Exercise of the Supreme Court’s expanded judicial power (Article VIII, Section 1) via certiorari review (Rule 64/65) over the COMELEC's constitutional authority to administer election laws (Article IX-C, Section 2), set alongside the legislative power of Congress acting as the National Board of Canvassers (Article VII, Section 4) to canvass and proclaim the President-elect.
 Constitutional Allocation Invoked:** The exclusive grant to the "Supreme Court, sitting **en banc, as the sole judge of all contests relating to the election, returns, and qualifications of the President or Vice-President" (Article VII, Section 4, Paragraph 7) invoked by respondents as a jurisdictional bar divesting the Court of certiorari jurisdiction.
**Level of Judicial Scrutiny / Doctrinal Test:**
 Standard of Review: Grave Abuse of Discretion standard under Rule 64, Section 2 in relation to Rule 65, Section 1. To overturn the COMELEC, petitioners must establish capricious, whimsical, arbitrary, or despotic exercise of judgment equivalent to lack of jurisdiction. Findings of fact by the COMELEC supported by substantial evidence are final and non-reviewable.
 Penal Construction:** Strict construction of penal statutes and disqualifications against the State and liberal construction in favor of the accused (**in dubio pro reo and rule of lenity).
**Justiciability & Judicial Review Audit:**
 Actual Case or Controversy: Present. The qualifications of a presidential candidate present an active, justiciable controversy concerning fundamental democratic governance that survives the counting of votes.
 Locus Standi: Sustained for petitioners as registered voters and aggrieved parties before the COMELEC entitled to seek certiorari review under Rule 64, Section 2. Marcos, Jr. did not challenge petitioners' standing below.
 Mootness Exception:** Overruled COMELEC's mootness defense. Even with 31.6 million votes and proclamation, popular election cannot waive mandatory legal qualifications. (Reaffirms **Tecson** and **Poe-Llamanzares).
 Lis Mota: Resolved strictly on statutory construction of the 1977 NIRC and Omnibus Election Code, preserving the finality of the 1997 CA Decision.
**Doctrinal Requisites / Elements Checklist (PET Jurisdiction vs. Supreme Court Review):**
To transfer jurisdiction over a winning candidate's qualifications from the Supreme Court / COMELEC to the Electoral Tribunals (SET, HRET, or PET), there must be a concurrence of three requisites:
1.  [x] Valid proclamation by the canvassing board;
2.  [ ] Proper oath of office;
3.  [ ] Assumption of office (term commencing at noon on June 30).
**Application:** Because Marcos, Jr. had not yet assumed office at noon on June 30, 2022, and no election protest or **quo warranto** petition had been filed under the 2010 PET Rules, the PET had not acquired jurisdiction, and the Supreme Court En Banc properly retained jurisdiction under Rule 65.
**Subject-Specific Terms of Art ("Magic Words"):**
 Sole judge of all contests (Article VII, Section 4, Para. 7)
 Contest (Post-election challenge initiated after proclamation, oath, and assumption)
 Independent but not separate (Structure of the PET within the Supreme Court En Banc)
 Reyes Tripartite Requisites (Proclamation, Oath, Assumption)
 Immutability of final judgments
 In dubiis reus est absolvendus (All doubts resolved in favor of the accused)
 Mala prohibita vs. Mala in se
 Moral turpitude (Baseness, vileness, depravity)
**Cold-Call Synthesis (The 30-Second Recit Answer):**
Under Section 4, Article VII of the Constitution, the Supreme Court En Banc acting as the Presidential Electoral Tribunal (PET) does not automatically oust the Supreme Court's Rule 65 certiorari jurisdiction over pre-election COMELEC qualification rulings the moment a candidate is proclaimed. Applying the **Reyes** doctrine, PET jurisdiction over "election contests" is triggered only after the winning candidate concurs in three acts: valid proclamation, taking of oath, and actual assumption of office at noon on June 30. Prior to noon of June 30, the Supreme Court En Banc retains full constitutional authority to decide whether the candidate is disqualified under Section 12 or committed false material representation under Section 78 of the Omnibus Election Code. On the merits, the Court held that Marcos, Jr. was never perpetually disqualified because that penalty was omitted from the final 1997 Court of Appeals **fallo**, and failure to file an ITR is a mere statutory omission (**malum prohibitum**) that does not constitute a crime involving moral turpitude.
### 7. Separate Opinions & Overall Verdict (Fallo)
**Separate Opinions Summary:**
**Leonen, SAJ. (Concurring):** Emphasized that presidential qualifications under Article VII, Section 2 are intentionally sparse and cannot be expanded by statute or judicial interpretation. Confirmed that the PET only takes cognizance of post-election contests against an official who has assumed office. Failure to file an ITR by an employee whose taxes were withheld does not involve moral turpitude. Severely admonished the COMELEC for its unmitigated delay in resolving the petitions only **after** the May 9 elections.
**Caguioa, J. (Concurring):** Clarified that the Court and the PET are one and the same body; thus, the Court does not "lose" jurisdiction upon oath and assumption, but rather the procedural vehicle changes (re-docketing as a PET case under the 2010 PET Rules, akin to **Gonzales v. GJH Land**). Maintained that perpetual disqualification is an ineligibility under Section 74, but Marcos, Jr.'s representation was not maliciously false because it was omitted from the CA **fallo**. Emphasized that whether a crime involves moral turpitude must be determined strictly from the statutory nature and elements of the offense, not through a dangerous post-conviction inquiry into the offender's "totality of circumstances."
**Lazaro-Javier, J. (Concurring):** Stressed popular sovereignty: in applying election laws, it is better to err in favor of the voters' obvious choice than in complex legalisms. Non-filing of ITRs was decriminalized for pure compensation earners via substituted filing. Retroactively reading perpetual disqualification into a final 25-year-old judgment violates the **ex post facto** clause. Marcos, Jr. could not have filed his 1985 return in March 1986 due to legal impossibility caused by exile (**Marcos v. Manglapus**).
**M. Lopez, J. (Concurring):** Re-examined **Jalosjos, Jr.**, urging that Section 78 cancellation grounds should not be conflated with Section 12/68 disqualification grounds. Section 286(c) of P.D. 1994 did not apply because Marcos, Jr. ceased to be a public officer when his 1985 return became due.
**Gaerlan, J. (Concurring):** Traced the 200-year history of moral turpitude from American common law (**Brooker v. Coffin**, **Jordan v. De George**) to Philippine jurisprudence. Established that tax crimes require fraud and deceit to involve moral turpitude. Simple non-filing of an ITR under Section 45 of the 1977 NIRC is an omission lacking fraud, as affirmed in **Republic v. Marcos II** (2009).
**J. Lopez, J. (Concurring):** Emphasized that PET jurisdiction begins only upon assumption of office at noon on June 30 under **Reyes**. Perpetual disqualification under Section 286(c) of the 1977 NIRC is a principal penalty, not an accessory penalty; hence, its absence in the CA **fallo** means it was never imposed.
**Dimaampao, J. (Concurring):** Explained that non-filing of an ITR may morph into tax evasion only when attended by willfulness. However, Marcos, Jr. was an employee of the provincial government, which acted as withholding agent; thus, the omission was not a willful scheme to evade taxes.
**Singh, J. (Concurring):** Affirmed the Court’s constitutional duty of judicial review under Article VIII, Section 1. Strongly defended the doctrine of immutability of final judgments, emphasizing that an alleged erroneous penalty does not make a judgment void.
**Inting and Kho, Jr., JJ.:** Took no part.
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, in view of the foregoing, the Petitions in G.R. Nos. 260374 and 260426 are hereby DISMISSED. The Resolutions of the Commission on Elections in SPA No. 21-156 (DC) dated 17 January 2022 and 10 May 2022, and in SPA No. 21-212 (DC) dated 10 February 2022 and 10 May 2022 are hereby AFFIRMED.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court unanimously dismissed all petitions challenging Ferdinand Marcos, Jr.'s presidential candidacy. The Court affirmed the COMELEC rulings, declaring that Marcos, Jr. is fully qualified to serve as President of the Philippines, that his Certificate of Candidacy is valid and contains no false material representation, that he was never perpetually disqualified from public office, and that his 1997 conviction for failure to file income tax returns did not involve moral turpitude. Marcos, Jr.'s proclamation as President was upheld in all respects.
