digest:
### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Short Recognizable Title: Maxey v. Court of Appeals**
**Full Official Caption:** Margaret Maxey assisted by Santiago Magbanua; Florence Maxey assisted by Ofrecinio Santos; and Lucille Maxey, **Petitioners**, v. The Honorable Court of Appeals and The Spouses Beato C. Macayra and Alacopue Monday, **Respondents**.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. L-45870, May 11, 1984 (129 SCRA 187)
**Ponente:** Gutierrez, Jr., **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** First Division: Teehankee (**Chairman**), Escolin, Relova, and De la Fuente, **JJ.**, concur; Melencio-Herrera, **J.**, took no part; Plana, **J.**, reserved his vote.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Civil Law → Persons and Family Relations → Property Relations of Informal Unions / Co-ownership → Retroactivity and Household Contribution (Article 144, Civil Code)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Civil Law → Transitional Provisions / Statutory Construction → Vested Rights and Retroactive Operation of New Rights (Articles 2252 and 2253, Civil Code)
Full Text of Governing Provisions
**Article 144, Civil Code of the Philippines (Republic Act No. 386):**
"When a man and a woman live together as husband and wife, but they are not married, or their marriage is void from the beginning, **the property acquired by either or both of them through their work or industry or their wages and salaries shall be governed by the rules on co-ownership.**"
**(Modern Codal Note: Superseded by Articles 147 and 148 of the Family Code of the Philippines [Executive Order No. 209]. Under Art. 147, care and maintenance of the family and household is expressly deemed a contribution to the acquisition of common property).**
**Article 2252, Civil Code of the Philippines (Republic Act No. 386):**
"Changes made and new provisions and rules laid down by this Code which may **prejudice or impair vested or acquired rights** in accordance with the old legislation shall have **no retroactive effect**."
**Article 2253, Civil Code of the Philippines (Republic Act No. 386):**
"The Civil Code of 1889 and other previous laws shall govern rights originated, under their said acts, from acts done or events which took place under their regime, even though this Code may regulate them in a different manner, or may not recognize them. But **if a right should be declared for the first time in this Code, it shall be effective at once, even though the act or event which gives rise thereto may have been done or may have occurred under the prior legislation, provided said new right does not prejudice or impair any vested or acquired right, of the same origin.**"
Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provisions
**General Rule / Provision Triggered:** Under Article 144, co-ownership attaches to properties acquired during cohabitation without a valid marriage through the work or industry of **either or both** parties. Under Article 2253, newly declared statutory rights apply retroactively to past acts, provided no **vested or acquired rights** are impaired.
**Sub-Rules & Tests Clarified:**
1.  **Expansion of "Work or Industry" to Domestic Labors:** The statutory phrase "work or industry" and the requirement of "real contribution" (**Yaptinchay v. Torres**) are not confined to direct monetary, business, or cash-earning activities. They embrace household administration, child-rearing, husbanding scarce family resources, and freeing the working partner from domestic burdens.
2.  **Presumption of Equal Share ("Either or Both"):** Even if only the man works outside the home for wages, property acquired during cohabitation belongs to both partners in equal (fifty-fifty) shares.
3.  **Retroactive Application Without Impairment of Vested Rights:** A right is **vested** only when fixed, established, and no longer open to doubt or controversy. An alleged exclusive title of the cohabiting man prior to the 1950 Civil Code was not vested because it was burdened by the woman's concurrent equitable right established under prior jurisprudence (informal civil partnerships).
**Factual Trigger:** Melbourne Maxey acquired parcels of land in 1911 and 1912 while cohabiting with Regina Morales and raising their children. In 1953, long after Regina's death (following their 1919 church wedding), Melbourne's second wife sold the entirety of the parcels under a power of attorney, disregarding the co-ownership rights inherited by Regina's children.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
Key Parties & Roles
**Melbourne Maxey:** Member of the 1899 American occupation forces; held government positions (teacher, school supervisor, provincial treasurer, deputy governor, school superintendent). Cohabited with Regina Morales from 1903 until their church marriage in 1919.
**Regina Morales (Maxey):** Common-law partner of Melbourne from 1903; mother of his six children; legally married Melbourne on February 16, 1919; died later in 1919.
**Petitioners (Margaret Maxey, Florence Maxey, Lucille Maxey):** Legitimate children of Melbourne and Regina; sued to annul the 1953 sale and recover their mother's 1/2 share.
**Julia Pamatluan Maxey:** Second wife of Melbourne; acted as his attorney-in-fact in 1953 to execute the sale of the disputed lands.
**Respondents (Spouses Beato C. Macayra and Alacopue Monday):** Buyers who purchased the disputed lands in 1953 and possessed them continuously thereafter.
Procedural Posture
**January 26, 1962:** Petitioners filed a complaint before the Court of First Instance (CFI) of Davao for annulment of sale documents, recovery of possession, and damages against the Macayra spouses.
**CFI Davao Ruling:** Rendered judgment for Petitioners. Applied Article 144 of the Civil Code, declared the 1953 deeds of sale null and void, ordered respondents to return the lands, pay annual rentals (₱1,000/year from 1953 plus legal interest), ₱500 actual damages, and ₱3,000 attorney's fees.
**Court of Appeals (CA) Ruling:** Reversed the CFI. Set aside the trial court's decision, declared the 1953 deeds of sale valid, and pronounced the Macayra spouses absolute owners on grounds that the properties were the exclusive acquisitions of Melbourne and that Article 144 could not apply retroactively.
**Supreme Court Review:** Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 filed by petitioners challenging the CA decision.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1899:** Melbourne Maxey arrives in the Philippines as part of the American occupation forces.
**1903:** Melbourne Maxey and Regina Morales begin living together as husband and wife in Baganga, Davao. The children claim a union was celebrated "in the military fashion." John Carlos Maxey is born that same year.
**Subsequent Years:** The couple conceives six children: John Carlos, Lucille, Margaret, Florence, Fred, and George. Except for George, all children are born prior to the property acquisitions.
**1911–1912:** Melbourne acquires the disputed parcels of land in Davao (Exhibits 4-a and 5-1). During this period, he holds positions as teacher, provincial treasurer, deputy governor, and school supervisor. Regina stays at home, managing the household and caring for the children, with no separate personal estate, salary, or independent business.
**February 16, 1919:** Melbourne and Regina legitimize their union through a formal church wedding ceremony.
**Later in 1919:** Regina Morales passes away.
**Intervening Years:** Melbourne remarries Julia Pamatluan Maxey.
**1953:** Melbourne, through Julia Pamatluan Maxey acting as his attorney-in-fact, sells the disputed parcels of land to the Spouses Beato C. Macayra and Alacopue Monday for ₱1,300.00. The Macayra spouses immediately take open, continuous possession.
**1961:** The Maxey children discover the 1953 sale of the disputed lands.
**January 26, 1962:** Petitioners file an action in the CFI of Davao to annul the sale and recover possession, asserting that the properties were conjugal/common properties of Melbourne and Regina.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The 1953 sales are void as to their mother's one-half undivided share because the lands formed part of their parents' common co-ownership; Melbourne had no legal right to convey the whole estate without the knowledge and consent of Regina's heirs.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Validity of Initial Marriage:** Melbourne and Regina were validly married as early as 1903 "in the military fashion," making the parcels acquired in 1911–1912 fully conjugal.
**Co-ownership Under Joint Efforts:** Even if the formal marriage occurred only in 1919, the properties were acquired through joint effort and industry under Article 144 of the Civil Code.
**Broad Definition of "Joint Efforts":** The CA erred in restricting "joint efforts" to direct financial/monetary contributions. A woman's domestic labors, running the household, and rearing children are valuable contributions under Philippine customs and tradition that legally establish co-ownership.
B. Respondents' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The properties belonged exclusively to Melbourne Maxey; the 1953 sale conveyed complete and absolute title to the Macayra spouses as purchasers in good faith and for value.
**Specific Contentions:**
**No Legal Marriage in 1903:** The alleged "military fashion" marriage was non-existent and unrecognized by Philippine law; the parties were married only on February 16, 1919.
**Sole Financial Acquisition:** Melbourne was gainfully employed in high-paying provincial and educational positions, generating the funds to purchase the lands.
**No Monetary Contribution by Common-Law Wife:** Testimony of Regina's sister-in-law (Juana Morales) established that Regina had no separate property, business, or income. Citing **Aznar v. Garcia**, respondent spouses argued that in the absence of clear monetary contribution ("pesos and centavos"), no co-ownership can arise.
**Non-Retroactivity of Article 144:** Article 144 of the 1950 Civil Code cannot apply retroactively to 1911–1912 acquisitions because doing so would impair Melbourne's vested rights under the prior Civil Code of 1889.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues
1.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether the Court of Appeals erred in finding that Melbourne Maxey and Regina Morales were legally married only in 1919, rejecting the claim of a 1903 "military fashion" marriage.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not a purported marriage performed "in the military fashion" in 1903 is legally valid under the marriage laws then in force.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Article 144 of the Civil Code applies retroactively to property acquired in 1911–1912 by a man and woman cohabiting without marriage.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Does the retroactive application of Article 144 violate the rule against impairing vested rights under Article 2252 and Article 2253 of the Civil Code?
3.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether the phrase "work or industry" and the requirement of "joint efforts" under Article 144 of the Civil Code necessitate actual monetary contribution, or if a woman's domestic contribution as a homemaker and mother qualifies.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not the domestic services, household management, and child-rearing of a common-law wife constitute "work or industry" sufficient to vest in her a 1/2 co-ownership interest in properties acquired by the partner during cohabitation.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Validity of the 1903 "Military Fashion" Marriage
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did the lower courts err in finding that the parties were married only in 1919 and not in 1903? **NO.** Philippine law in force in 1903 did not recognize marriages celebrated "in the military fashion."
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"Since Act No. 3613 was approved on December 4, 1929 and took effect six months thereafter, it could not have applied to a relationship commenced in 1903 and legitimized in 1919 through a marriage performed according to law. The marriage law in 1903 was General Order No. 70. There is no provision in General Order No. 68 as amended nor in Act No. 3613 which would recognize as an exception to the general rule on valid marriages, a so called 'military fashion' ceremony or arrangement."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Applicable Law at the Time:** In 1903, marriage was governed by General Order No. 68 (as amended by General Order No. 70).
**Lack of Statutory Basis:** Neither General Order No. 68 nor subsequent marriage statutes (like Act No. 3613, which was enacted much later in 1929) contained exceptions recognizing a "military fashion" marriage as legally binding.
**Binding Nature of Factual Findings:** Both the trial court and the CA determined that the legal marriage occurred on February 16, 1919 in church. Finding evidentiary support in the record, the Supreme Court refused to disturb this factual finding.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** A "military fashion" marriage had no legal status under the marriage laws in force in 1903. Melbourne and Regina were legally married only when they had a formal church wedding in 1919; thus, during the 1911 and 1912 land acquisitions, they were legally regarded as an unmarried cohabiting couple.
Issue 2: Retroactivity of Article 144 and Impairment of Vested Rights
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does Article 144 apply retroactively to acquisitions made in 1911–1912 without impairing vested rights? **YES.** Article 144 applies retroactively because Melbourne never acquired an undisputed, exclusive "vested right" over the properties to the exclusion of Regina's recognized equitable share.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"A vested right is defined by this Court as property which has become fixed and established, and is no longer open to doubt or controversy; an immediately fixed right of present or future enjoyment as distinguished from an expectant or contingent right... This cannot be said of the 'exclusive' right of Melbourne Maxey over the properties in question when the present Civil Code became effective for standing against it was the concurrent right of Regina Morales or her heirs to a share thereof."
"With the enactment of the new Civil Code, Article 144 codified the law established through judicial precedents but with the modification that the property governed by the rules on co-ownership may be acquired by **either or both of them** through their work or industry. Even if it is only the man who works, the property acquired during the man and wife relationship belongs through a fifty-fifty sharing to the two of them."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Pre-Civil Code Jurisprudence Already Protected Informal Unions:** Even prior to August 30, 1950, decisions such as **Aznar v. Garcia**, **Flores v. RFC**, **Marata v. Dionio**, and **Lesaca v. Lesaca** established that an informal civil partnership forms between a man and woman living together, granting each an equal share in properties acquired through their joint effort.
**Statutory Retroactivity Mandate (Arts. 2252 & 2253):** Newly declared rights apply immediately to prior acts/events if dictated by justice and public policy, provided they do not infringe upon vested rights.
**No Vested Right Impaired:** For a right to be "vested," it must be fixed, certain, and not open to doubt or controversy. Melbourne's claim was never exclusively absolute or uncontested because Regina held a concurrent, equitable co-ownership right from the inception of the union under prevailing jurisprudence.
**Timing of the Sale:** The properties were sold in 1953, well after the new Civil Code took full effect; hence, the buyer acquired only what the seller had the legal capacity to convey under the prevailing law.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** The Civil Code's co-ownership rules for common-law couples apply retroactively here because Melbourne never had an absolute, uncontested title to the properties. Even under old court decisions, an informal partnership existed between cohabiting couples; therefore, giving Regina her 1/2 share under Article 144 takes away no "vested right" from Melbourne.
Issue 3: Expansion of "Work or Industry" and "Joint Efforts" to Domestic Services
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does "work or industry" under Article 144 require proof of direct monetary investment or income? **NO.** Household management, childcare, and performing the customary duties of a homemaker qualify as "work or industry" and "real contribution," creating an equal co-ownership.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"This new article in the Civil Code recognizes that it would be unjust and abnormal if a woman who is a wife in all aspects of the relationship except for the requirement of a valid marriage must abandon her home and children, neglect her traditional household duties, and go out to earn a living or engage in business before the rules on co-ownership would apply."
"The 'real contribution' to the acquisition of property mentioned in **Yaptinchay vs. Torres** (28 SCRA 489) must include not only the earnings of a woman from a profession, occupation, or business but also her contribution to the family's material and spiritual goods through caring for the children, administering the household, husbanding scarce resources, freeing her husband from household tasks, and otherwise performing the traditional duties of a housewife."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Rejection of the Narrow "Monetary Contribution" Rule:** The Court rejected the CA's position that "joint efforts" rigidly demands proof of financial or "peso-and-centavo" contributions from the woman.
**Legislative Intent of "Either or Both":** Article 144 expressly uses the phrase "either or both of them through their work or industry." This modification ensures that even if only the husband earns outside income, the domestic work of the wife produces an equal 50–50 co-ownership.
**Societal Reality & Gender Roles:** The law is premised on Filipino customary roles where the woman serves as family purse-holder and household administrator, directly freeing the man to focus on generating external income.
**Status of the Disputed Properties:** Because Regina substantially contributed through running the household and caring for their six children, the properties acquired in 1911–1912 belonged to both Melbourne and Regina in equal common shares. Upon her death in 1919, her 1/2 undivided share descended to her heirs. Melbourne had no power to sell her 1/2 interest in 1953.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** A woman does not need to bring cash or hold an outside job for the properties acquired during cohabitation to be jointly owned. By maintaining the home, raising six children, and managing family resources, she frees her partner to work outside; her domestic efforts constitute genuine "work or industry" entitling her to an equal half of the acquired assets.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions are discussed in the text of the decision. (Melencio-Herrera, **J.**, took no part; Plana, **J.**, reserved his vote).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
Verbatim Fallo
"WHEREFORE, the petition for review on certiorari is hereby granted. The judgment of the Court of Appeals is reversed and set aside insofar as one-half of the disputed properties are concerned. The private respondents are ordered to return one-half of said properties to the heirs of Regina Morales. No costs.
SO ORDERED."
Plain-Language Outcome
Petitioners prevailed in part. The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals and held that the disputed lands were co-owned by Melbourne Maxey and Regina Morales. Because Melbourne could validly sell only his own 1/2 share in 1953, the sale was invalid with respect to Regina's 1/2 share. The Macayra spouses were ordered to return one-half of the properties to Regina's heirs (on equitable grounds, the Court deemed the return of ₱650 [half the purchase price] offset by the buyers' past possession and use without paying rentals).

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Gono-Javier v. Court of Appeals**
**Full Official Caption:** Sotenia Gono-Javier, Teburcio Gono, Anunciacion G. Javier, Germana G. Gulay, Lucio Gono, Ramon Gono, Alfredo Gono and Manuel Gono, Petitioners, vs. The Hon. Court of Appeals, Restituta Casocot, Fermin Casocot, Alicia Yonson, Adriano Casocot, Carlos Monte De Ramos, Regina Duglas and Nonito Marave, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:**
G.R. No. 111994
Date of Promulgation: December 29, 1994
### 239 SCRA 593
Ponente: Vitug, **J.**
Voting Breakdown: Third Division; Bidin, Romero, and Melo, **JJ.**, concur; Feliciano, **J.**, on leave.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Law / Paternity and Filiation → Illegitimate Children / Recognition → Posthumous Recognition and Lifetime Requirement
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Procedure → Dismissal of Actions → Dismissal for Failure to Prosecute → Res Judicata / Adjudication on the Merits
**Full Text of Governing Statutory / Procedural Provisions:**
**Article 278, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 278. Recognition shall be made in the record of birth, a will, a statement before a court of record, or **in any authentic writing**."
**Article 281, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 281. **A child who is of age cannot be recognized without his consent.**
When the recognition of a minor does not take place in a record of birth or in a will, judicial approval shall be necessary.
A minor can in any case impugn the recognition within four years following the attainment of his majority."
**Article 285, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 285. **The action for the recognition of natural children may be brought only during the lifetime of the presumed parents, except in the following cases:**
(1) If the father or mother died during the minority of the child, in which case the latter may file the action before the expiration of four years from the attainment of his majority;
(2) If after the death of the father or of the mother a document should appear of which nothing had been heard and in which either or both parents recognize the child.
In this case, the action must be commenced within four years from the finding of the document."
**Modern Equivalent Provisions (Family Code of the Philippines):**
**Art. 172.** "The filiation of legitimate children is established by any of the following:
(1) The record of birth appeared in the civil register or a final judgment; or
(2) An admission of legitimate filiation in a public document or a private handwritten instrument and signed by the parent concerned.
In the absence of the foregoing evidence, the filiation shall be proved by:
(1) The open and continuous possession of the status of a legitimate child; or
(2) Any other means allowed by the Rules of Court and special laws." **(Applied to illegitimate children under Art. 175).**
**Art. 175, par. 2:** "The action must be brought within the same period specified in Article 173, except when the action is based on the second paragraph of Article 172, in which case the action may be brought during the lifetime of the alleged parent."
**Section 3, Rule 17, Revised Rules of Court (1964):**
"Sec. 3. **Failure to prosecute.** — If plaintiff fails to appear at the time of the trial, or to prosecute his action for an unreasonable length of time, or to comply with these rules or any order of the court, the action may be dismissed upon motion of the defendant or upon the court’s own motion. **This dismissal shall have the effect of an adjudication upon the merits, unless otherwise provided by court.**"
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Rule on Voluntary Recognition:** Under Article 278, voluntary acknowledgment in an authentic writing is a completed, consummated act that requires no judicial declaration to be operative.
**The Bilateral Lifetime Requirement Test:** Voluntary acknowledgment can legally be effected **only during the lifetime of both the acknowledging parent and the acknowledged illegitimate child**. A deceased adult child cannot be voluntarily recognized posthumously because Article 281 requires the child's consent.
**Involuntary vs. Voluntary Recognition Standards:** Possession of status does not itself constitute an acknowledgment; it merely provides a ground to compel judicial recognition under Article 285.
**Procedural Effect of Dismissal for Failure to Prosecute:** An unconditional dismissal of a complaint for failure to prosecute under Rule 17, Section 3 is with prejudice and constitutes an adjudication on the merits (**res judicata**).
**Factual Trigger:** Juan Casocot executed a deed of donation in 1954 in favor of Eugenia Gonzales, referring to her as the surviving spouse of his son Catalino Gono had with his common-law wife. However, Catalino had already died in 1942 or 1943—over eleven years before the writing was executed—rendering the posthumous acknowledgment legally impossible.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Juan Casocot:** Original registered owner of five parcels of land; died in 1964; alleged natural grandfather of petitioners.
**Catalino Gono:** Alleged natural son of Juan Casocot; died in 1942 or 1943.
**Eugenia Gonzales:** Surviving spouse/widow of Catalino Gono; donee of one parcel in a 1954 deed of donation.
**Petitioners (Sotenia Gono-Javier, Teburcio Gono, Anunciacion G. Javier, et al.):** Children of deceased Catalino Gono claiming ownership over Juan Casocot's lands via intestate succession and tax delinquency repurchase.
**Restituta and Fermin Casocot:** Niece and nephew of Juan Casocot; purchasers of the disputed parcels under a 1960 notarized Deed of Sale.
**Other Private Respondents (Alicia Yonson, Adriano Casocot, Carlos Monte de Ramos, Regina Duglas, Nonito Marave):** Relatives and subsequent transferees/purchasers of portions of the disputed land.
**Atty. Noli G. Cortel:** Notary public who notarized Juan Casocot’s 1960 Deed of Sale to Restituta and Fermin Casocot.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 assailing the Court of Appeals Decision which reversed the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Butuan City and dismissed petitioners' complaint for recovery of ownership and possession.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**Pre-1942:** Juan Casocot owned five parcels of land in Nasipit, Agusan, covered by Tax Declaration (T.D.) Nos. 2667, 3227, 1209, 738, and 2666.
**1942 or 1943:** Catalino Gono, father of petitioners and alleged illegitimate son of Juan Casocot, died.
**March 29, 1954:** Juan Casocot executed a notarized Deed of Donation conveying the parcel covered by T.D. No. 738 to Eugenia Gonzales (Catalino's widow), stating therein that the donee was **"the surviving spouse of my son had with my common law wife."**
**May 28, 1956:** The provincial government levied the properties for real property tax delinquency.
**June 5 & 20, 1956:** Petitioner Anunciacion Gono-Javier was issued a Certificate of Repurchase of Real Property after Sale by the provincial government.
**February 2, 1959:** Juan Casocot redeemed the properties by making partial payments of the delinquent taxes for the period covering May 29, 1956 to February 2, 1959.
**February 3, 1959:** A prepared Final Bill of Sale to Anunciacion was left unsigned and unexecuted by the Provincial Treasurer because Juan Casocot had repurchased the lands. Anunciacion Gono-Javier was refunded the sum of ₱850.00 via a municipal voucher signed and received by her.
**April 19, 1960:** Juan Casocot (then in his 80s) executed a notarized Deed of Sale conveying the four remaining parcels (T.D. Nos. 2667, 3227, 1209, and 2666) to respondents Restituta Casocot and Fermin Casocot. Atty. Noli G. Cortel translated the document into Visayan; Juan voluntarily signed it in full possession of his faculties. TCT No. RT-349 was later issued for the parcel under T.D. No. 1209.
**Circa 1964:** Juan Casocot died.
**August 10, 1965:** In Civil Case No. 896 (**Juan Casocot v. Restituta Casocot and Fermin Casocot**), the Court of First Instance of Agusan unconditionally dismissed Juan Casocot’s complaint to annul the 1960 Deed of Sale for failure to prosecute. No appeal was taken, and the order became final.
**February 13, 1978:** Petitioners filed an action before the RTC of Butuan City against private respondents to recover ownership and possession of the five parcels, claiming implied trust, intestate succession as grandchildren, and tax repurchase.
**Trial Court Judgment:** The Butuan City RTC ruled for petitioners, holding the 1960 Deed of Sale simulated/void, ruling Catalino was recognized via the 1954 donation, upholding the tax auction sale to Anunciacion, and nullifying respondents' titles.
**Court of Appeals Judgment:** The Court of Appeals reversed the RTC and dismissed petitioners' complaint, holding that: (1) recognition could not occur after Catalino’s death without his consent; (2) Anunciacion was fully refunded and Juan Casocot repurchased the land; (3) the 1960 Deed of Sale was authentic; and (4) the 1965 dismissal in Civil Case No. 896 was **res judicata**.
**Petition for Review:** Petitioners appealed the CA decision to the Supreme Court.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Petitioners are the rightful owners of the disputed parcels by virtue of intestate succession as the children of Juan Casocot's recognized natural child (Catalino Gono), and alternatively, through Anunciacion's tax delinquency purchase.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Sufficiency of Recognition:** Juan Casocot’s statement in the 1954 Deed of Donation that Eugenia Gonzales was the "surviving spouse of my son" is a sufficient, authentic voluntary recognition under Article 278.
**Tax Purchase Title:** The property was validly acquired by Anunciacion Gono-Javier at a tax delinquency public auction sale in 1956.
**Simulation of Sale:** The April 19, 1960 Deed of Sale to Restituta and Fermin Casocot was simulated and void because Juan Casocot was already in his 80s and would not have parted with valuable real estate.
**Absence of Res Judicata:** The dismissal of Civil Case No. 896 cannot bar the present suit because Juan Casocot was not served notice of the July 24, 1965 hearing, rendering the dismissal void.
B. Respondent's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Petitioners have no successional rights because Catalino Gono was never legally recognized; moreover, respondents hold valid title derived from the notarized 1960 sale, and the claim is barred by prescription and **res judicata**.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Lack of Recognition:** Catalino Gono was never recognized in a record of birth or a will; an independent action for recognition was required.
**No Posthumous Recognition:** A child cannot be voluntarily recognized after his death, especially when the child was of age and could not give consent.
**Refund of Tax Redemption:** Anunciacion Gono-Javier was fully refunded the ₱850.00 she paid, and Juan Casocot himself repurchased the lands; the final bill of sale was never executed.
**Validity of 1960 Sale:** The deed of sale was notarized and executed while Juan Casocot was in full possession of his mental faculties, as attested by the notary public.
**Res Judicata and Prescription:** Civil Case No. 896 dismissed the challenge to the sale with finality, and private respondents have possessed the lands in good faith and for value for over 17 years.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the statement made by Juan Casocot in the 1954 Deed of Donation constituted a valid voluntary recognition of Catalino Gono as his natural child under Article 278, notwithstanding that Catalino had died over a decade prior to the execution of the deed.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether the appellate court gravely erred in reversing the trial court's decision holding that Catalino Gono was the acknowledged natural child of Juan Casocot and that the declaration in the deed of donation was sufficient recognition.
2. **[Secondary Substantive Issue]** Whether or not petitioners acquired lawful ownership of the disputed lands by virtue of the tax delinquency repurchase certificate issued to Anunciacion Gono-Javier.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether the appellate court gravely erred in reversing the trial court's decision holding that the land belonged to petitioners by virtue of the tax auction purchase.
3. **[Secondary Substantive Issue]** Whether or not the April 19, 1960 notarized Deed of Sale executed by Juan Casocot in favor of Restituta and Fermin Casocot was simulated and void.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether the appellate court gravely erred in reversing the trial court's decision holding that the sale between Juan Casocot and private respondents was simulated and void.
4. **[Secondary Procedural Issue]** Whether or not the dismissal of Civil Case No. 896 for failure to prosecute barred petitioners' action to nullify the 1960 Deed of Sale under the principle of **res judicata**.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether the appellate court gravely erred in ruling that the action for recovery of possession and ownership is barred by the dismissal of the complaint for nullification of the Deed of Sale in Civil Case No. 896.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Validity of Posthumous Voluntary Recognition
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** A voluntary acknowledgment of an illegitimate child under Article 278 cannot be legally effected after the child has already died.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"The provisions of the Civil Code on acknowledgment would readily indicate that voluntary acknowledgment can legally be effected only during the lifetime of both the acknowledging parent and the acknowledged illegitimate child."
"When that voluntary recognition is so timely made, as above, an action for its judicial declaration can survive the death of either or both parties... The reason for this latter rule is that the due recognition of an illegitimate child in a record of birth, a will, a statement before a court of record, or in any authentic writing (Art. 278, Civil Code) is, in itself, a consummated act of acknowledgment of the child, and no further court action is required... albeit not prohibited, to yet have it declared as such."
"Parenthetically, where a claim for recognition is predicated on other evidence merely tending to prove paternity, i.e., outside of a record of birth, a will, a statement before a court of record or an authentic writing, judicial action within the applicate statute of limitations is essential in order to establish the child's acknowledgment. Thus, the mere possession of status of a child, contrary to the assertion in passing of petitioners, does not itself constitute an acknowledgment; it is only a ground for the child to compel, by judicial action, recognition by his assumed parent."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Applicable Law & the Incidental Recognition Rule:** The 1954 Deed of Donation was governed by Article 278 of the New Civil Code. Juan Casocot’s statement describing Eugenia Gonzales as the "surviving spouse of my son had with my common law wife" was an authentic public document that would have qualified as an express or incidental recognition of Catalino Gono.
**The Timing Defect (Lapse of Life):** Voluntary recognition cannot be made posthumously. Catalino Gono died in 1942 or 1943. Juan Casocot executed the donation on March 29, 1954—eleven years after Catalino's death.
**Interplay with Article 281:** Under Article 281 of the Civil Code, an illegitimate child of legal age cannot be recognized without his consent. Because Catalino was already dead when the deed was executed, it was legally impossible for him to give his required consent.
**Possession of Status Distinct from Acknowledgment:** The Court rejected petitioners' passing reliance on possession of status. Possession of status is merely a ground to compel judicial recognition under Article 285 (which must be brought within prescribed periods during the parent's lifetime), not a self-executing acknowledgment.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):** While an authentic public document can prove recognition, the parent and the child must both be alive at the time the voluntary acknowledgment is made. Because Catalino had been dead for 11 years before Juan signed the 1954 deed of donation, and could not give his required consent as an adult, the recognition was invalid and conferred no hereditary rights on his children.
Issue 2: Ownership Claim via Delinquency Repurchase
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** Anunciacion Gono-Javier did not acquire ownership because she was fully refunded her payment and the land was repurchased by Juan Casocot himself.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Petitioners, in their second and third assignment of errors, would want us to reverse the Court of Appeals in finding: (a) that while petitioner Anunciacion Gono-Javier was issued a Certificate of Repurchase (Exh. 'N') on 20 June 1956, she was, however, fully refunded for the price paid and actual redemption was, in truth, made by Juan Casocot and (b) that the deed of sale executed by Juan Casocot, duly notarized, was validly executed. These factual findings by the appellate court, having been amply explained and substantiated by it, should not further be disturbed."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Factual Negation of Title:** Although a Certificate of Repurchase was issued to Anunciacion on June 20, 1956, she was refunded her ₱850.00 payment on February 3, 1959 via a municipal voucher.
**Redemption by Original Owner:** The redemption was actually consummated by Juan Casocot himself, who made payments covering delinquent taxes from May 29, 1956 to February 2, 1959.
**Failure of Final Conveyance:** The Final Bill of Sale was never signed or executed by the Agusan Provincial Treasurer, leaving petitioners with no tax auction title.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):** Petitioners could not claim ownership through the tax auction because the municipal government refunded Anunciacion her money and the true owner, Juan Casocot, personally redeemed the property before any final deed was executed.
Issue 3: Validity of the 1960 Deed of Sale
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** The 1960 Deed of Sale was valid and not simulated.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"...a public document, which is executed with all the solemnities of the law, should not be set aside on such slender grounds as those cited by the trial court."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Rebuttal of Old Age Presumption:** The RTC erroneously assumed the sale was simulated solely because Juan Casocot was in his 80s and the land was valuable. Advanced age alone does not negate contractual capacity or prove lack of intent to sell.
**Presumption of Regularity in Notarized Instruments:** The deed was duly notarized. The notary public, Atty. Cortel, affirmatively testified that Juan was mentally sound, physically capable, had the document translated and explained to him in the Visayan dialect, and signed it voluntarily.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):** A notarized deed of sale carries a presumption of regularity that cannot be overturned simply because the seller was in his eighties. The notary public testified that Juan was of sound mind and voluntarily signed the document after it was translated into his dialect.
Issue 4: Res Judicata Effect of Dismissal for Failure to Prosecute
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: YES.** The unconditional dismissal of Juan Casocot’s 1965 annulment complaint for failure to prosecute was an adjudication on the merits that barred subsequent litigation on the deed's validity.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Suffice it to say that an unconditional dismissal of an action for failure to prosecute under Section 3, Rule 17, of the Rules of Court is with prejudice and has the effect of an adjudication on the merits..."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Procedural Rule Applied:** Under Section 3, Rule 17 of the Rules of Court, an unconditional dismissal for failure to prosecute operates as an adjudication on the merits unless the dismissal order explicitly states that it is without prejudice.
**Finality of Prior Order:** Civil Case No. 896 (**Juan Casocot v. Restituta Casocot and Fermin Casocot**) was unconditionally dismissed on August 10, 1965, and no appeal was taken.
**Lack of Jurisdiction to Reopen Final Dismissal:** The RTC had no authority to reopen or disregard that dismissal in a collateral proceeding based on an alleged lack of notice to Juan Casocot for the July 24, 1965 hearing. The final dismissal is **res judicata**.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):** When Juan Casocot’s lawsuit to annul the deed of sale was unconditionally dismissed in 1965 for failure to prosecute, that dismissal became a final judgment on the merits. The trial court in this later case had no legal power to re-examine or disregard that final dismissal.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text (Feliciano, **J.**, on leave; all other Division members concurred without separate opinion).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the decision of the Court of Appeals is AFFIRMED. Costs against petitioners.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court ruled entirely in favor of private respondents. The Court of Appeals' decision was affirmed, dismissing petitioners' complaint for recovery of title and possession of the disputed parcels of land. Private respondents' ownership under the 1960 Deed of Sale and resulting certificates of title stands undisturbed.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Leonora Perido, et al. v. Maria Perido, et al.**
**LEONORA PERIDO, joined by husband MANUEL PIROTE, INOCENCIA PERIDO, ALBENIO PERIDO, PAULINO PERIDO, LETIA PERIDO, joined by husband BIENVENIDO BALYAO, LETICIA PERIDO, joined by husband FELIX VILLARUZ, EUFEMIA PERIDO, CONSOLACION PERIDO, ALFREDO PERIDO, GEORGE PERIDO, AMPARO PERIDO, WILFREDO PERIDO, MARGARITA PERIDO, ROLANDO SALDE and EDUARDO SALDE, petitioners, vs. MARIA PERIDO, SOFRONIO PERIDO, JUAN A. PERIDO, GONZALO PERIDO, PACITA PERIDO, MAGDALENA PERIDO, ALICIA PERIDO, JOSEFINA PERIDO, FE PERIDO, TERESA PERIDO and LUZ PERIDO, respondents.**
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. L-28248; March 12, 1975; 63 SCRA 97
**Ponente:** Makalintal, C.J.
**Voting Breakdown:** First Division. Makalintal, C.J. (Ponente), Castro, Teehankee, Makasiar, and Esguerra, JJ., concur; Muñoz Palma, J., was on leave.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
Primary Topic Hierarchy
Civil Law → Family Code / Civil Code → Marriage & Legitimacy → Presumption of Marriage & Filiation of Children
Secondary Topic Hierarchy
1. Civil Law → Property Relations of Spouses → Conjugal Partnership of Gains → Presumption of Conjugality
2. Remedial Law → Civil Procedure → Rule 45 Appeals → Conclusiveness of Appellate Court Factual Findings
Full Text of Governing Provisions
1. Presumption of Marriage (Section 334, No. 28, Code of Civil Procedure / Rule 131, Sec. 3(aa), Rules of Court)
**Code of Civil Procedure, Sec. 334, No. 28 (Cited in Decision):**
"A presumption established by our Code of Civil Procedure is **'that a man and woman deporting themselves as husband and wife have entered into a lawful contract of marriage.'** (Sec. 334, No. 28) **Semper praesumitur pro matrimonio** — Always presume marriage."
**(Modern Counterpart: Rule 131, Section 3(aa), Rules of Court):**
"That a man and woman deporting themselves as husband and wife have entered into a lawful contract of marriage;"
2. Presumption of Conjugality of Property (Civil Code of 1889, Art. 1407 / Civil Code of the Philippines [Rep. Act No. 386], Art. 160)
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Art. 160 (Governing Law):**
"All property of the marriage is **presumed to belong to the conjugal partnership**, unless it be proved that it pertains exclusively to the husband or to the wife."
**(Modern Counterpart: Article 116, Family Code of the Philippines [Exec. Order No. 209]):**
"All property acquired during the marriage, whether the acquisition appears to have been made, contracted or registered in the name of one or both spouses, is presumed to be conjugal unless the contrary is proved."
The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision
**General Rule / Presumption of Marriage:** Persons living together in apparent matrimony are legally presumed to have entered into a lawful contract of marriage (**Semper praesumitur pro matrimonio**). Every intendment of the law leans toward legalizing matrimony because marriage is a social institution in which the public is deeply interested.
**Rebuttal Standard:** The presumption of marriage and resulting legitimacy of offspring may be overcome **only by cogent proof** on the part of those alleging illegitimacy. Recitals of civil status in certificates of title (e.g., describing a party as a "widower") or weak, uncorroborated, non-eyewitness oral testimony regarding a subsequent religious ceremony do not suffice to overcome the presumption arising from continuous cohabitation.
**Presumption of Conjugal Property:** Property acquired during the subsistence of marriage is presumed conjugal. This presumption becomes **stronger** where the certificate of title expressly recites that the registered owner is married to a designated spouse.
**Factual Trigger:** Petitioners, heirs of Lucio Perido's first marriage, sought to exclude the heirs of Lucio's second union with Marcelina Baliguat from inheriting eight parcels of land by claiming that the second set of children were illegitimate because the first wife died late (1905) and Lucio allegedly remained a widower until an alleged 1925 wedding.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
Key Parties & Roles
**Lucio Perido:** Common decedent who died in 1942.
**Benita Talorong:** First wife of Lucio Perido (died during the Spanish regime, prior to 1900).
**Marcelina Baliguat:** Second wife of Lucio Perido (died in 1943).
**Children of the First Marriage (or their surviving heirs):**
**Felix Perido** (deceased) — represented by children Inocencia, Leonora, Albinio, Paulino, Letia, Leticia, Eufemia, and grandchildren Rolando and Eduardo Salde.
**Ismael Perido** (deceased) — represented by children Consolacion, Alfredo, Wilfredo, Amparo, and grandson George Perido.
**Margarita Perido** — surviving daughter and petitioner.
**Children of the Second Marriage (or their surviving heirs - Respondents):**
**Eusebio Perido** (deceased) — represented by children Magdalena, Pacita, Alicia, Josefina, Fe, Teresa, and Luz Perido.
**Juan B. Perido** (deceased) — represented by son Juan A. Perido.
**Maria Perido, Sofronia Perido, and Gonzalo Perido** — surviving children.
How the Case Reached the Supreme Court
1. Heirs executed an extrajudicial partition on **August 15, 1960**.
2. First-marriage heirs filed a complaint on **March 8, 1962** (amended **February 22, 1963**) in the Court of First Instance of Negros Occidental (Civil Case No. 6529) to annul the partition and exclude the second-marriage heirs.
3. CFI rendered judgment on **July 31, 1965**, annulling the 1960 partition, declaring the second-marriage children legitimate, finding seven lots to be Lucio's exclusive property, and finding 11/12 of Lot 458 to be conjugal property of Lucio and Marcelina.
4. Petitioners appealed to the Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. No. 37034-R), which affirmed the CFI **in toto** and denied reconsideration.
5. Petitioners filed the instant **Petition for Review on Certiorari** under Rule 45 before the Supreme Court.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**Spanish Regime:** Lucio Perido's first wife, Benita Talorong, dies. Lucio is freed from any legal impediment to contract a second marriage.
**Circa 1900–Post-1900:** Lucio Perido and Marcelina Baliguat live together as husband and wife and begot five children: Eusebio (born 1900), Juan, Maria, Sofronia, and Gonzalo.
**1923:** Certificates of title (Exhibits B to G) for Lots Nos. 471, 506, 511, 509, 513-Part, 807, and 808 are issued in the name of Lucio Perido, described on their face as a "widower."
**1925:** Original Certificate of Title No. 21769 covering Lot No. 458 (11/12 share) is issued in the name of Lucio Perido, expressly registered as married to Marcelina Baliguat.
**1942 & 1943:** Lucio Perido dies in 1942; Marcelina Baliguat dies in 1943.
**August 15, 1960:** Children and grandchildren of both marriages execute a "Declaration of Heirship and Extra-judicial Partition" dividing Lots Nos. 458, 471, 506, 511, 509, 513-B, 807, and 808.
**March 8, 1962:** Petitioners file an action in the CFI of Negros Occidental to annul the 1960 partition and seek exclusive partition among themselves.
**July 31, 1965:** CFI annuls the 1960 partition deed due to lack of valid consent/fraud, but rules that:
The five children of the second marriage are legitimate heirs;
Lots 471, 506, 511, 509, 513-Part, 807, and 808 were Lucio's exclusive hereditary property inherited from his grandmother, ordered divided into 8 shares (1 share per child line);
11/12 of Lot No. 458 was conjugal property of Lucio and Marcelina (11/24 to Lucio, divided into 8 shares; 11/24 to Marcelina, divided into 5 shares); 1/12 belonged to Fidel Perido.
**Appellate Proceedings:** Court of Appeals affirms the trial court **in toto**. Petitioners elevate the case to the Supreme Court on certiorari.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The 1960 partition must be annulled and all properties partitioned exclusively among the heirs of the first marriage because the second-marriage children are illegitimate and have no successional rights, and the properties belonged to the first conjugal partnership.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Illegitimacy of Second-Marriage Heirs:** Benita Talorong died in 1905, not during the Spanish regime; hence, the first three children (born starting 1900) were born of an adulterous/illicit relation before Benita died. The last two were born out of wedlock and never recognized.
**Titles Show "Widower":** Certificates of title issued in 1923 describe Lucio as a "widower," proving he was not married to Marcelina at that time.
**Marriage Took Place in 1925:** Leonora Perido testified that Lucio and Marcelina were married by an Aglipayan priest only in 1925, during which flowers were taken from her garden.
**Character of Seven Lots:** Testimonies showed that Lots 471, 506, 511, 509, 513-Part, 807, and 808 were acquired during the subsistence of the first marriage with Benita.
**Character of Lot 458:** 6/12 belonged to the first conjugal partnership, and the purchase price of the remaining 5/12 came from the sale of property belonging to Lucio and his first-marriage children.
B. Respondents' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The children of the second marriage are legitimate heirs entitled to their lawful shares in the estate; the seven lots were Lucio's exclusive property, and Lot 458 was conjugal property of the second marriage.
**Specific Contentions:**
Benita Talorong died during the Spanish era, removing any impediment to Lucio's marriage to Marcelina.
Lucio and Marcelina lived as husband and wife, entitling them and their children to the legal presumption of marriage and legitimacy.
The seven parcels were inherited by Lucio from his grandmother, making them his exclusive capital.
Lot 458 is registered in the name of Lucio Perido, explicitly described as married to Marcelina Baliguat, establishing its conjugal character.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the five children of Lucio Perido with Marcelina Baliguat are legitimate children entitled to inherit from Lucio's estate based on the legal presumption of marriage.
2. **[Secondary Issue: Property Classification]** Whether or not Lots Nos. 471, 506, 511, 509, 513-Part, 807, and 808 were exclusive properties of Lucio Perido or conjugal properties of his first marriage with Benita Talorong.
3. **[Secondary Issue: Property Classification & Appellate Review]** Whether or not 11/12 of Lot No. 458 was conjugal partnership property of Lucio Perido and Marcelina Baliguat, and whether the Supreme Court may review factual findings on the appreciation of evidence in a Rule 45 petition.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Legitimacy of the Children and Presumption of Marriage
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The five children are legitimate because Lucio and Marcelina deporting themselves as husband and wife created an unrebutted presumption of lawful marriage, their cohabitation having commenced when no legal impediment existed.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"The basis of human society throughout the civilized world is that of marriage. Marriage in this jurisdiction is not only a civil contract, but it is a new relation, an institution in the maintenance of which the public is deeply interested. Consequently, every intendment of the law leans toward legalizing matrimony. Persons dwelling together in apparent matrimony are presumed, in the absence of any counter-presumption or evidence special to the case, to be in fact married. The reason is that such is the common order of society, and if the parties were not what they thus hold themselves out as being, they would be living in the constant violation of decency and of law. A presumption established by our Code of Civil Procedure is 'that a man and woman deporting themselves as husband and wife have entered into a lawful contract of marriage.' (Sec. 334, No. 28) **Semper praesumitur pro matrimonio** — Always presume marriage."
"This presumption, especially where legitimacy of the issue is involved, as in this case, may be overcome only by cogent proof on the part of those who allege the illegitimacy."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Absence of Impediment:** The Court of Appeals found that Benita Talorong died during the Spanish regime (prior to 1898/1900). This factual finding is conclusive on the Supreme Court. Consequently, Lucio had no legal impediment to marry Marcelina before their first child was born in 1900.
**Insufficiency of Recitals in Titles:** The description of Lucio as a "widower" in 1923 land titles is not conclusive proof that he was not married to Marcelina and is too weak to overcome the strong presumption that cohabiting partners are married.
**Incompetence of Oral Testimony on 1925 Marriage:** Petitioners’ witness (Leonora Perido) claimed Lucio and Marcelina only married in 1925 because church flowers were taken from her garden. The trial and appellate courts properly disregarded this testimony because Leonora was not an eyewitness to the ceremony and her claim was uncorroborated.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:**
Under Philippine law, courts must always presume that a man and woman living together as husband and wife are lawfully married (**semper praesumitur pro matrimonio**). Anyone claiming that their children are illegitimate must present clear, convincing, and cogent proof. Because the first wife died before the second union began, and because the petitioners only offered weak land-title descriptions and second-hand gossip about a 1925 wedding, the legal presumption stood firm and the children were declared legitimate.
Issue 2: Exclusive Character of the Seven Cadastral Lots
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Lots Nos. 471, 506, 511, 509, 513-Part, 807, and 808 were the exclusive properties of Lucio Perido, having been acquired by him through inheritance from his grandmother.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Then there is evidence showing that the lands were inherited by Lucio Perido from his grandmother (t.s.n., p. 21, Feb. 20, 1964). In other words, they were the exclusive properties of the late Lucio Perido which he brought into the first and second marriages. By fiat of law said properties should be divided accordingly among his legal heirs."
"The question involves appreciation of the evidence, which is within the domain of the Court of Appeals, the factual findings of which are not reviewable by this Court."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Hereditary Origin Negates Conjugality:** Testimonial evidence credited by the lower courts established that Lucio acquired these seven lots by inheritance from his grandmother. Property acquired by gratuitous title (such as inheritance) is paraphernal/exclusive capital brought into the marriage, not conjugal property of the first marriage.
**Factual Review Precluded:** Petitioners' challenge to this finding hinged purely on the credibility of their witnesses versus the defense witnesses, which is an issue of fact beyond the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Rule 45.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:**
Property inherited by a spouse belongs to that spouse alone. The lower courts found that Lucio inherited these seven lots from his grandmother, meaning they never became conjugal property of his first marriage. Because this is a question of fact that the Court of Appeals already resolved based on evidence, the Supreme Court refused to disturb it.
Issue 3: Conjugal Status of Lot No. 458 and Limits of Rule 45 Review
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The 11/12 portion of Lot No. 458 is conjugal property of Lucio Perido and Marcelina Baliguat pursuant to the statutory presumption of conjugality, reinforced by the title's express recital of marriage.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"If the law presumes a property registered in the name of only one of the spouses to be conjugal... the presumption becomes stronger when the document recites that the spouse in whose name the land is registered is married to somebody else, like in the case at bar."
"Indeed, a review of that finding would require an examination of all the evidence introduced before the trial court, a consideration of the credibility of witnesses and of the circumstances surrounding the case, their relevancy or relation to one another and to the whole, as well as an appraisal of the probabilities of the entire situation. It would thus abolish the distinction between an ordinary appeal on the one hand and review on certiorari on the other, and thus defeat the purpose for which the latter procedure has been established."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Heightened Presumption of Conjugality:** Original Certificate of Title No. 21769 was issued in 1925 in the name of Lucio Perido, expressly reciting that he was "married to Marcelina Baliguat." Under the Civil Code, property acquired during marriage is presumed conjugal; this presumption is reinforced when the title expressly names the spouse.
**Failure of Contrary Rebuttal:** Petitioners failed to produce clear proof that the funds used to purchase the lot came from the first marriage or its offspring.
**Certiorari Limits:** Evaluating whether purchase money came from another estate requires re-weighing witness credibility and evidence, which would improperly transform a Rule 45 petition into an ordinary appeal.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:**
When a title is issued to a person explicitly described as married to their spouse, the law strongly presumes that the land belongs to their conjugal partnership. To overturn this, the opposing side must present clear and convincing evidence tracing the funds to another source. Because the petitioners failed to do so and merely asked the Court to re-examine the witnesses' credibility, the Supreme Court upheld the finding that the land belonged to the second marriage.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
Verbatim Fallo
"WHEREFORE, the decision of the Court of Appeals is hereby affirmed, with costs against the petitioners."
Plain-Language Outcome
The petitioners (heirs of the first marriage) lost their petition entirely. The Supreme Court affirmed the decisions of the Court of Appeals and the Court of First Instance, declaring that the children of Lucio Perido and Marcelina Baliguat are legitimate heirs entitled to inherit, confirming that the seven lots are exclusive properties of Lucio to be divided equally among all eight children lines, and upholding that 11/12 of Lot No. 458 is the conjugal property of Lucio and Marcelina.

digest:
### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**De la Puerta v. Court of Appeals**
**Isabel de la Puerta, Petitioner, vs. The Honorable Court of Appeals and Carmelita de la Puerta, Respondents.**
**Citation:** G.R. No. 77867, February 6, 1990 (181 SCRA 861)
**Ponente:** Cruz, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** First Division (Concurring: Narvasa, Gancayco, Griño-Aquino, and Medialdea, **JJ.**) (Unanimous; no separate opinions).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
Topic Hierarchy
**Primary:** Civil Law → Succession → Legal or Intestate Succession → Right of Representation / Iron Curtain Rule (Barrier between Legitimate and Illegitimate Families)
**Secondary:** Civil Law → Family Law / Persons and Family Relations → Paternity and Filiation → Proof of Filiation of Spurious Children; Presumption of Marriage and Legitimacy
Full Text of Governing Provisions
Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 970:
"Art. 970. **Representation is a right created by fiction of law, by virtue of which the representative is raised to the place and the degree of the person represented, and acquires the rights which the latter would have if he were living or if he could have inherited.**"
Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 992:
"Art. 992. **An illegitimate child has no right to inherit ab intestato from the legitimate children and relatives of his father or mother; nor shall such children or relatives inherit in the same manner from the illegitimate child.**"
Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 255:
"Art. 255. **Children born after one hundred and eighty days following the celebration of the marriage, and before three hundred days following its dissolution or the separation of the spouses shall be presumed to be legitimate.**
Against this presumption no evidence shall be admitted other than that of the physical impossibility of the husband's having access to his wife within the first one hundred and twenty days of the three hundred which preceded the birth of the child.
This physical impossibility may be caused:
(1) By the impotence of the husband;
(2) By the fact that the husband and wife were living separately in such a way that access was not possible;
(3) By the serious illness of the husband."
Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 256:
"Art. 256. **The child shall be presumed legitimate, although the mother may have declared against its legitimacy or may have been sentenced as an adulteress.**"
Revised Rules of Court, Rule 131, Section 5(bb) **(now Section 3[aa], Rule 131)**:
"Sec. 5. **Disputable presumptions.**—The following presumptions are satisfactory if uncontradicted, but may be contradicted and overcome by other evidence:
x x x
(bb) **That a man and woman deporting themselves as husband and wife have entered into a lawful contract of marriage;**"
The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provisions
1. The "Iron Curtain" Rule (Art. 992)
An illegitimate child is absolutely barred from intestate succession (**ab intestato**) to the estate of legitimate relatives of their parents (including grandparents), whether directly or by right of representation.
2. Triggering Requirements of Representation in Succession (Art. 970)
In testamentary and intestate succession, the right of representation can only occur when the person represented:
1. Dies before the testator/decedent (predecease);
2. Is incapable of succeeding; or
3. Is disinherited.
Where an heir survives the decedent, that heir succeeds directly and in their own right at the moment of death; no right of representation arises in favor of the heir's descendants upon the heir's subsequent demise.
3. Rebuttal of Presumption of Marriage & Proof of Spurious Filiation
The disputable presumption that a cohabiting man and woman are legally married (Rule 131) is overturned by direct evidence demonstrating non-continuous cohabitation and abandonment without marital protest. Once rebutted, the presumption of legitimacy of the offspring (Arts. 255–256) collapses.
Spurious children (illegitimate non-natural children) may prove filiation using the same evidentiary modes applicable to natural children under Articles 283, 284, and 289 of the Civil Code, including open admissions in a court of record.
4. Adoption Creates No Kindred Ties with Ascendants
Adoption establishes a purely civil filiation exclusively between the adopter and the adopted child; it confers no legal or kindred relation with the adopter’s ancestors.
Factual Trigger
Carmelita de la Puerta intervened in the probate proceedings of her putative grandmother (Dominga Revuelta) claiming an allowance and successional rights as the illegitimate daughter of Vicente de la Puerta. The rule was triggered because Vicente did not predecease Dominga, and, in any event, Article 992 completely bars Carmelita, as an illegitimate (spurious) child, from inheriting from the legitimate mother/relatives of her putative father.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
Key Parties & Roles
**Dominga Revuelta:** Testatrix/decedent who died testate on July 3, 1966, leaving an estate to her three children.
**Isabel de la Puerta:** Daughter of Dominga; named executrix, legatee of the free portion, and special administratrix; petitioner opposing Carmelita’s claims.
**Vicente de la Puerta:** Son of Dominga; oppositor to Dominga’s will; married Genoveva in 1938; fathered Carmelita with Gloria Jordan; died on June 14, 1978.
**Alfredo de la Puerta:** Son of Dominga; initial oppositor who died during probate proceedings.
**Carmelita de la Puerta:** Private respondent; born out of wedlock to Vicente and Gloria Jordan; intervener claiming support and successional rights against Dominga's estate.
**Gloria Jordan:** Carmelita’s mother; lived in a common-law relationship with Vicente.
**Genoveva de la Puerta:** Legal wife of Vicente (married in 1938, separated in 1940); testified that Vicente and Gloria openly cohabited.
**Juanito Austrial:** Man claimed by petitioner to be the presumptive/legal husband of Gloria Jordan.
Procedural Posture
**Originating Action:** Probate of the will of Dominga Revuelta in the Court of First Instance (CFI) of Quezon.
**Intervention:** Carmelita intervened on November 20, 1981, filing a motion for monthly support/allowance as the acknowledged natural child of Vicente.
**Probate Court Order (November 12, 1982):** Granted Carmelita’s motion, ruling she was Vicente's natural child entitled to support from Dominga's estate.
**Court of Appeals Ruling:** Affirmed the CFI/probate court order.
**Supreme Court Vehicle:** Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 filed by Isabel de la Puerta challenging the Court of Appeals decision.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1938:** Vicente de la Puerta marries Genoveva de la Puerta.
**Circa 1940:** Vicente and Genoveva separate; they never reconcile.
**1962:** Gloria Jordan begins cohabiting openly with Vicente in his house, situated five to six houses away from Genoveva.
**December 18, 1962:** Carmelita de la Puerta is born to Gloria Jordan and Vicente.
**July 3, 1966:** Dominga Revuelta dies testate at age 92, survived by her three children: Alfredo, Vicente, and Isabel. Isabel is named executrix and recipient of the free portion.
**Probate Inception:** Isabel petitions for probate. Alfredo and Vicente oppose on grounds of the testatrix's senility and improper inclusion of their exclusive properties in the inventory. Isabel is appointed special administratrix. Alfredo subsequently dies.
**August 1, 1974:** Vicente files a petition in CFI Quezon to adopt Carmelita. Isabel opposes. The petition is granted by the trial court, but Isabel appeals to the Court of Appeals.
**September 6, 1974:** During the adoption hearing, Vicente testifies under oath in open court that Carmelita is his daughter with Gloria Jordan.
**June 14, 1978:** Vicente dies intestate while the adoption appeal is pending, causing Isabel to move for the dismissal of the adoption case.
**November 20, 1981:** Carmelita intervenes in Dominga's probate case, filing a motion for payment of a monthly allowance as Vicente’s acknowledged child.
**November 12, 1982:** Probate court grants Carmelita’s motion for support, ruling she is Vicente’s natural child.
**Appellate Stage:** Court of Appeals affirms the probate court order.
**Supreme Court Review:** Isabel petitions the Supreme Court, assailing Carmelita's status and legal right to claim support/succession from Dominga’s estate.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Isabel de la Puerta)
**Main Thesis:** Carmelita has no filiation with Vicente and zero successional or support rights against Dominga Revuelta's estate.
**Specific Contentions:**
Carmelita is not Vicente's child, but the legitimate daughter of Juanito Austrial and Gloria Jordan under Articles 255 and 256 of the Civil Code and the disputable presumption of marriage between cohabiting couples (Rule 131, Sec. 5[bb]).
Carmelita could not be a "natural child" of Vicente because Vicente was legally married to Genoveva at the time of Carmelita’s birth in 1962.
Article 278 of the Civil Code (voluntary recognition) cannot be invoked by Carmelita because she is a spurious child, not a natural child.
Carmelita has no right to receive an allowance or inheritance from Dominga's estate.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Carmelita de la Puerta)
**Main Thesis:** She is an acknowledged child of Vicente and entitled to support and her corresponding hereditary share from the estate being administered.
**Specific Contentions:**
Vicente treated her continuously as his true child from birth until his death, financing her education, signing her school report cards as parent, taking family photographs, and explicitly admitting in court under oath during the adoption proceedings that she was his daughter with Gloria Jordan.
She was Vicente's sole surviving child upon his intestate death in 1978 and had the right to step into his shoes regarding Dominga's estate.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Secondary / Preliminary Issue]** Whether or not Carmelita is presumed to be the legitimate daughter of Juanito Austrial and Gloria Jordan, or rather the recognized illegitimate (spurious) child of Vicente de la Puerta.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not the presumption of marriage between Juanito Austrial and Gloria Jordan was overturned, thereby permitting Vicente de la Puerta's open-court admission to establish Carmelita's filiation as his spurious child.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Carmelita de la Puerta may claim support and successional rights in the testate estate of her putative grandmother, Dominga Revuelta.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not an illegitimate (spurious) child can inherit by right of representation from the legitimate mother of her putative father under Articles 970 and 992 of the Civil Code.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Filiation of Carmelita de la Puerta
(a) Short Answer
**NO** to petitioner’s claim of legitimacy with Austrial; Carmelita was properly proven to be the **spurious (adulterous) child of Vicente de la Puerta.**
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements
"The so-called spurious children or illegitimate children other than natural children, commonly known as bastards, include adulterous children or those born out of wedlock to a married woman cohabiting with a man other than her husband or to a married man cohabiting with a woman other than his wife. They are entitled to support and successional rights (Art. 287, CC). But their filiation must be duly proven. (Ibid., Art. 887)"
"Article 289 of the Civil Code allows the investigation of the paternity or maternity of spurious children under the circumstances specified in Articles 283 and 284 of the Civil Code. The implication is that the rules on compulsory recognition of natural children are applicable to spurious children. Spurious children should not be in a better position than natural children. The rules on proof of filiation of natural children or the rule on voluntary and compulsory acknowledgment for natural children may be applied to spurious children."
(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi
**Overcoming Presumption of Marriage:** The disputable presumption of marriage between Juanito Austrial and Gloria Jordan was destroyed. Genoveva (Vicente's lawful wife) testified that Gloria lived openly with Vicente in the same neighborhood. Juanito did not cohabit continuously with Gloria nor protest when she consorted openly with Vicente. Isabel presented no marriage contract.
**Applicability of Civil Code Rules to Spurious Children:** While Carmelita could not be a "natural child" (as Vicente had a subsisting marriage with Genoveva in 1962), spurious children are legally permitted to establish their filiation via the same modes as natural children.
**Judicial Admission of Filiation:** Vicente categorically admitted under oath in a court record during the 1976 adoption proceedings: **"She is my daughter."** This authentic judicial testimony, combined with school records and open treatment, conclusively established Carmelita's spurious filiation.
(d) Plain-Language Explanation
The Court found that Carmelita was indeed the biological, illegitimate child of Vicente and Gloria, not of some other couple. Even though Vicente was married to someone else when Carmelita was born—making her a "spurious" or adulterous child rather than a "natural" child—spurious children can still prove their paternity through a father's sworn statements in open court. Vicente openly admitted under oath during his adoption petition that Carmelita was his daughter.
Issue 2: Successional Rights and Support from the Grandmother’s Estate
(a) Short Answer
**NO.** Carmelita has **zero right of representation and no successional or support rights** against the estate of Dominga Revuelta.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements
"In testamentary succession, the right of representation can take place only in the following cases: first, when the person represented dies before the testator; second, when the person represented is incapable of succeeding the testator; and third, when the person represented is disinherited by the testator."
"Not having predeceased Dominga Revuelta, her son Vicente had the right to inherit from her directly or in his own right. No right of representation was involved, nor could it be invoked by Carmelita upon her father's death, which came after his own mother's death."
"As a spurious child of Vicente, Carmelita is barred from inheriting from Dominga because of Article 992 of the Civil Code, which lays down the barrier between the legitimate and illegitimate families. This article provides quite clearly:
**Art. 992. An illegitimate child has no right to inherit ab intestato from the legitimate children and relatives of his father or mother; nor shall such children or relatives inherit in the same manner from the illegitimate child.**"
"Article 992 of the New Civil Code provides a barrier or iron curtain in that it prohibits absolutely a succession **ab intestato** between the illegitimate child and the legitimate children and relatives of the father or mother of said legitimate child. They may have a natural tie of blood, but this is not recognized by law for the purpose of Article 992."
"If the adopting parent should die before the adopted child, the latter cannot represent the former in the inheritance from the parents or ascendants of the adopter. The adopted child is not related to the deceased in that case, because the filiation created by fiction of law is exclusively between the adopter and the adopted. 'By adoption, the adopters can make for themselves an heir, but they cannot thus make one for their kindred.'"
(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi
**Failure of Conditions for Representation (Art. 970):** Representation requires that the person represented must predecease the testator, be incapacitated, or be disinherited. Dominga died in 1966; Vicente survived her and died 12 years later in 1978. Vicente succeeded Dominga directly at the moment of her death. Carmelita cannot represent Vicente in Dominga's estate because Vicente was alive when succession opened.
**The Iron Curtain Rule (Art. 992):** Even had Vicente predeceased Dominga, Carmelita is an illegitimate/spurious child of Vicente. Article 992 creates an absolute impassable legal barrier preventing an illegitimate child from inheriting **ab intestato** from the legitimate ascendants and relatives of their parent. Dominga was Vicente's legitimate mother; Carmelita cannot inherit from Dominga.
**Adoption Argument Ineffective:** Even assuming the adoption had been perfected before Vicente died, adoption creates a purely personal legal fiction solely between adopter and adopted. An adopted child cannot represent the adopter in the estate of the adopter’s ascendants.
**Proper Forum:** Carmelita's claims for support and inheritance pertain exclusively to the settlement of **Vicente's** intestate estate, not the probate of Dominga's will.
(d) Plain-Language Explanation
Carmelita cannot get a single centavo from her grandmother Dominga’s estate for two fatal reasons. First, representation only happens when a parent dies **before** the grandparent; here, Vicente outlived Dominga by twelve years and inherited from her directly. Second, under the "iron curtain" rule of Article 992, illegitimate children cannot inherit from the legitimate family and relatives of their parents. Carmelita's only legal remedy is to claim her inheritance as an illegitimate child in the estate proceedings of Vicente himself, not in Dominga's probate case.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
Verbatim Fallo:
"WHEREFORE, the petition is GRANTED and the appealed decision is hereby REVERSED and SET ASIDE, with costs against the private respondent. It is so ordered."
Plain-Language Outcome:
Petitioner Isabel de la Puerta prevailed. The Supreme Court reversed and set aside the Court of Appeals' and probate court's orders that granted Carmelita de la Puerta monthly allowances and succession rights from Dominga Revuelta’s estate. Carmelita was completely excluded from Dominga’s probate proceedings, with instructions that any claims for support or inheritance must be asserted in the estate settlement of her deceased father, Vicente de la Puerta.
