### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Lee v. Court of Appeals**
**Full Official Caption:** Marcelo Lee, Albina Lee-Young, Mariano Lee, Pablo Lee, Helen Lee, Catalino K. Lee, Eusebio Lee, Emma Lee, and Tiu Chuan, Petitioners, vs. Court of Appeals and Hon. Lorenzo B. Veneracion and Hon. Jaime T. Hamoy, in their capacities as Presiding Judge of Branch 47, Regional Trial Court of Manila and Branch 130, Regional Trial Court of Kalookan City, respectively, and Rita K. Lee, Leoncio Lee Tek Sheng in their personal capacities and Rosa K. Lee-Vanderlek, Melody K. Lee-Chin, Lucia K. Lee Tek Sheng, Julian K. Lee, Henry K. Lee, Martin K. Lee, Victoriano K. Lee, Natividad K. Lee-Miguel, and Thomas K. Lee, represented by Rita K. Lee, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 118387
**Promulgation Date:** October 11, 2001
**Philippine Reports:** 419 Phil. 392
**Ponente:** De Leon, Jr., **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Second Division (Bellosillo [**Chairman**], Mendoza, Quisumbing, and Buena, **JJ.**, concur). Unanimous; no separate opinions.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Special Proceedings → Rule 108 (Cancellation or Correction of Entries in the Civil Registry) → Scope of Substantial Corrections via Adversary Proceedings
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Civil Law → Family Code / Civil Code → Paternity and Filiation → Impugning Legitimacy vs. Action to Prove Non-Parentage / Prescription of Actions
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provisions:**
**Article 412, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"No entry in a civil register shall be **changed or corrected, without a judicial order**."
**Sections 3, 4, and 5, Rule 108, Revised Rules of Court:**
"SEC. 3. **Parties.** — When **cancellation or correction of an entry in the civil register is sought, the civil registrar and all persons who have or claim any interest which would be affected thereby shall be made parties** to the proceeding."
"SEC. 4. **Notice and publication.** — Upon the filing of the petition, the court shall, by an order, **fix the time and place for the hearing of the same, and cause reasonable notice thereof to be given to the persons named in the petition**. The court shall also cause the order to be **published once in a week for three (3) consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation** in the province."
"SEC. 5. **Opposition.** — The civil registrar and **any person having or claiming any interest under the entry whose cancellation or correction is sought may, within fifteen (15) days from notice of the petition, or from the last date of publication of such notice, file his opposition** thereto."
**Article 171, Family Code of the Philippines:**
"The heirs of the husband may **impugn the filiation of the child** within the period prescribed in the preceding article only in the following cases:
(1) If the husband should die before the expiration of the period fixed for bringing this action;
(2) If he should die after the filing of the complaint, without having desisted therefrom; or
(3) If the child was born after the death of the husband."
**Article 1149, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"All other actions whose periods are not fixed in this Code or in other laws must be **brought within five years from the time the right of action accrues**."
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Rule on Substantial Corrections under Rule 108 / Art. 412:** While Article 412 commands that no entry be changed or corrected without a judicial order, Rule 108 is **not restricted to harmless clerical or innocuous errors**. Substantial and controversial changes (including parentage, filiation, citizenship, and civil status) can be made under Rule 108 provided the proceeding ceases to be summary and becomes an **appropriate adversary proceeding**.
**Test for an Appropriate Adversary Proceeding:** A Rule 108 proceeding qualifies as an appropriate adversary proceeding when all procedural requirements are satisfied: (1) indispensable parties and all persons claiming an interest are impleaded (Sec. 3); (2) notice and publication once a week for three consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation are complied with (Sec. 4); (3) full opportunity is afforded to oppositors and the State to file oppositions and contest the petition (Sec. 5); and (4) a full hearing is conducted where evidence is presented, weighed, and rebutted.
**Distinction: Impugning Legitimacy vs. Proving Total Non-Parentage:** Article 171 of the Family Code (limiting the right of heirs to impugn filiation only after the father's demise) applies strictly when a husband or his heirs deny paternity of a child conceived or born by the lawful wife during wedlock. It **does not apply** where the claim is that the lawful wife **never gave birth** to the child. An action demonstrating that a child is a complete biological stranger to the mother is not an action to impugn legitimacy, but an action to establish the factual truth of non-parentage.
**Accrual of Action and Prescription (Art. 1149):** For an action under Rule 108 without a specified statutory prescription period, Article 1149 applies (5-year period). The period begins running **from the discovery of the fraud or falsification**, not from the registration of birth, because parentage cannot be acquired by prescription, nor can public registration serve to extinguish the rights of heirs kept in ignorance of falsified blood relations.
**Factual Trigger:** Lee Tek Sheng registered his eight illegitimate children by his mistress, Tiu Chuan, as the children of his lawful wife, Keh Shiok Cheng. Decades later, Keh Shiok Cheng died, and upon uncovering the hospital records showing it was biologically impossible for Keh Shiok Cheng to have given birth to these children, her legitimate children initiated Rule 108 petitions to strike her name and substitute Tiu Chuan as the true birth mother.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Lee Tek Sheng:** Common father of both sets of children; lawfully married to Keh Shiok Cheng in China (1931); maintained an illicit relationship with housemaid/mistress Tiu Chuan starting in 1948.
**Keh Shiok Cheng:** Lawful wife of Lee Tek Sheng; died on May 9, 1989.
**Tiu Chuan:** Concubine/mistress of Lee Tek Sheng; alleged true biological mother of petitioners.
**Private Respondents (Rita K. Lee, Leoncio Lee Tek Sheng, et al. [11 siblings]):** Legitimate children of Lee Tek Sheng and Keh Shiok Cheng; petitioners in the trial court proceedings.
**Petitioners (Marcelo Lee, Albina Lee-Young, Mariano Lee, Pablo Lee, Helen Lee, Catalino K. Lee, Eusebio Lee, Emma Lee, and Tiu Chuan):** Alleged biological children of Lee Tek Sheng and Tiu Chuan whose birth certificates falsely listed Keh Shiok Cheng as their mother.
**Hon. Lorenzo B. Veneracion:** Presiding Judge, RTC of Manila, Branch 47 (presiding over SP. PROC. NO. 92-63692).
**Hon. Jaime T. Hamoy:** Presiding Judge, RTC of Kalookan City, Branch 130 (presiding over SP. PROC. NO. C-1674).
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on **Certiorari** under Rule 45 (with prayer for TRO/Preliminary Injunction) assailing the October 28, 1994 Decision and December 19, 1994 Resolution of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 31786.
The CA had dismissed petitioners' Rule 65 Petition for **Certiorari** and Prohibition, thereby upholding the interlocutory orders of RTC Manila Branch 47 (February 12 and 17, 1993) and RTC Kalookan City Branch 130 (April 15, 1993) taking cognizance of and proceeding with the Rule 108 petitions.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1931:** Lee Tek Sheng and Keh Shiok Cheng are legally married in China. They subsequently have eleven (11) legitimate children (private respondents). Except for Rita K. Lee (born in China), all are born and raised in the Philippines.
**October 1948:** Lee Tek Sheng brings Tiu Chuan from China to the Philippines, introducing her to his family as a housemaid; she becomes his mistress and gives birth to eight children (petitioners).
**May 11, 1950 – 1960:** Petitioners are born. For each birth, Lee Tek Sheng registers the child's birth certificate by falsely entering his lawful wife, "Keh Shiok Cheng," as the mother instead of Tiu Chuan.
**May 9, 1989:** Keh Shiok Cheng dies. Lee Tek Sheng insists that the names of all his children—including petitioners—be listed in her newspaper obituary. This arouses the suspicion of private respondents.
**Post-May 1989:** Private respondents request the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) to investigate. The NBI uncovers hospital records from Chinese General Hospital establishing biological and physical impossibilities:
**Marcelo Lee (b. May 11, 1950):** Listed as Keh Shiok Cheng's 12th child, but hospital records reveal the mother was "Gravida I, Para I" (first pregnancy/delivery) aged 17, when Keh Shiok Cheng was already 38 years old.
**Albina Lee:** Listed as the 3rd child, but Keh Shiok Cheng's actual 3rd child was respondent Melody; mother's recorded hospital age jumped to 22.
**Mariano Lee:** Listed as the 5th child (an entry belonging to respondent Lucia); mother's age was recorded as 23, while Keh Shiok Cheng was then 40.
**Pablo Lee:** Listed as the 16th child (implying Keh Shiok Cheng would have had her first child at age 8 or 9).
**Helen Lee:** Listed as the 6th child (belonging to respondent Julian); mother's age recorded as 28 when Keh Shiok Cheng was 45.
**Catalino Lee:** Mother's age abruptly jumped from 28 to 38 within two years.
**Eusebio Lee:** Mother's registered age was 48 (hospital record: 39) with a recorded Cesarean delivery which Keh Shiok Cheng never underwent.
**December 2, 1992:** Private respondents file SP. PROC. NO. 92-63692 in RTC Manila (Branch 47, Judge Veneracion) to cancel/correct entries in the birth records of 7 petitioners (excluding Emma Lee) to delete "Keh Shiok Cheng" and substitute "Tiu Chuan."
**February 3, 1993:** Private respondents file SP. PROC. NO. C-1674 in RTC Kalookan City (Branch 130, Judge Hamoy) against Emma Lee for the same relief.
**February 12, 1993:** Judge Veneracion (RTC Manila) denies petitioners' motion to dismiss for their failure to appear at the hearing.
**February 17, 1993:** Judge Veneracion issues an order finding the petition sufficient in form and substance, setting it for hearing, and ordering publication once a week for 3 consecutive weeks, with service on the Solicitor General and respondents, and posting on the court bulletin board.
**April 15, 1993:** Judge Hamoy (RTC Kalookan) issues an order confirming that notice was published in **Media Update** once a week for 3 consecutive weeks, and copies were served upon the Solicitor General, City Prosecutor, Civil Registrar, and private respondents, thus establishing jurisdiction.
**August 1993 (approx.):** Petitioners file a Petition for **Certiorari** and Prohibition under Rule 65 with the Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. SP No. 31786) challenging the trial judges' denial of their motions to dismiss and assumption of jurisdiction.
**October 28, 1994:** The Court of Appeals dismisses the petition, ruling that Rule 108 adversarial proceedings are appropriate to establish civil status and non-parentage.
**December 19, 1994:** The Court of Appeals denies petitioners' Motion for Reconsideration.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Rule 108 is purely summary and limited to innocuous or clerical errors under Article 412 of the Civil Code; using it to alter filiation, bastardize children, or assail legitimacy is an impermissible collateral attack barred by the Family Code and barred by prescription.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Exceeding Ambit of Rule 108 / Art. 412:** Replacing "Keh Shiok Cheng" with "Tiu Chuan" amounts to bastardizing petitioners and altering substantive status; pursuant to **Ty Kong Tin**, **Go v. Civil Registrar**, and **Labayo-Rowe**, expanding Rule 108 beyond clerical errors renders the procedural rule unconstitutional under the constitutional limit on the Supreme Court's rule-making power.
**Prematurity under Article 171, Family Code:** Private respondents lack a cause of action to impugn legitimacy while the undisputed common father (Lee Tek Sheng) is still alive; heirs may only impugn filiation under narrow conditions post-mortem.
**Prescription under Article 1149, Civil Code:** Any action to correct birth certificates prescribed 5 years after the registration of the last birth in 1960. Since birth certificates are public records that serve as constructive notice to the whole world, the prescriptive period lapsed long before 1992.
**Forum Shopping:** Private respondents engaged in forum shopping by litigating the common issue of maternity across multiple fora: (1) a criminal complaint for falsification against the father and petitioners, (2) a petition to cancel the father's naturalization certificate, and (3) a petition for partition of Keh Shiok Cheng's estate.
B. Respondent's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Rule 108 is the proper mechanism because full adversarial safeguards were observed, and the action does not impugn marital legitimacy but proves that the lawful wife never gave birth to the children; the action was timely brought upon discovery of the fraud.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Propriety of Rule 108 via Valencia Doctrine:** Under **Republic v. Valencia**, substantial changes—including filiation and status—can be effected through Rule 108 as long as publication, notice, and adversarial proceedings are conducted.
**Inapplicability of Article 171:** The action is not to prove that a child born to the wife was fathered by an outsider; it is to prove that the deceased wife is biologically not the mother at all. There is no blood tie to impugn.
**Timeliness of Action:** The right of action accrued only upon discovery of the fraudulent hospital entries in 1989 following the death of Keh Shiok Cheng; parentage cannot be acquired by prescription, and public registration does not validate non-existent maternity.
**Absence of Forum Shopping:** The causes of action, rights violated, and reliefs sought in the criminal case, denaturalization case, and partition case are completely distinct from a Rule 108 special proceeding to correct civil registry entries.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not substantial errors in the civil register affecting civil status, filiation, and parentage may be corrected or changed through a petition under Rule 108 of the Revised Rules of Court.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether resort to Rule 108 of the Revised Rules of Court is improper since private respondents seek to have the entry for the name of petitioners' mother changed from "Keh Shiok Cheng" to "Tiu Chuan," in effect a declaration that petitioners were not born of the legitimate wife.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not Rule 108 of the Rules of Court can be utilized to effect substantial alterations in civil registry entries, specifically changing the recorded mother from the lawful wife to a mistress, provided an appropriate adversary proceeding is conducted.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not private respondents' petitions are barred by Article 171 of the Family Code because their common father is still alive.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether the private respondents have no cause of action to bring the cases below as Article 171 of the Family Code allows the heirs of the father to bring an action to impugn the legitimacy of his children only after his death.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not Article 171 of the Family Code bars legitimate children from filing an action to delete their deceased mother's name from the birth records of their father's illegitimate children while the father is still alive.
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not private respondents' right of action to cancel/correct entries under Rule 108 has prescribed under Article 1149 of the Civil Code.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether private respondents' cause of action had already prescribed as more than five (5) years had lapsed between the registration of the latest birth among the petitioners in 1960 and the filing of the actions in 1992 and 1993.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not the five-year prescriptive period for filing a Rule 108 petition to correct falsified birth records begins to run from the date of civil registration or from the date the fraud is discovered.
4.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not private respondents are guilty of forum shopping.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether the petitions below are part of a forum-shopping spree in view of the prior filing of a criminal complaint for falsification, a petition for denaturalization, and a petition for partition of the mother's estate.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not filing a Rule 108 petition constitutes forum shopping when a criminal falsification case, denaturalization petition, and estate partition case involving the same common parentage are pending.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Propriety of Rule 108 for Substantial Changes in Parentage
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: YES.** Rule 108 is the appropriate procedural vehicle to effect substantial and controversial changes in the civil register—including parentage and filiation—provided the requirements of an appropriate adversary proceeding are fully observed.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Provided the trial court has conducted proceedings where all relevant facts have been fully and properly developed, where opposing counsel have been given opportunity to demolish the opposite party's case, and where the evidence has been thoroughly weighed and considered, the suit or proceeding is 'appropriate.'"
"If all these procedural requirements have been followed, a petition for correction and/or cancellation of entries in the record of birth even if filed and conducted under Rule 108 of the Revised Rules of Court can no longer be described as 'summary'. There can be no doubt that when an opposition to the petition is filed either by the Civil Registrar or any person having or claiming any interest in the entries sought to be cancelled and/or corrected and the opposition is actively prosecuted, the proceedings thereon become adversary proceedings."
"We venture to say now that the above pronouncements proceed from a wrong premise, that is, the interpretation that Article 412 pertains only to clerical errors of a harmless or innocuous nature, effectively excluding from its domain, and the scope of its implementing rule, substantial changes that may affect nationality, status, filiation and the like. Why the limited scope of Article 412? Unfortunately, **Ty Kong Tin** does not satisfactorily answer this question except to opine that the procedure contemplated in Article 412 is summary in nature and cannot, therefore, cover cases involving controversial issues... The flaw in **Ty Kong Tin** lies in its theory that Article 412 contemplates a summary procedure."
"First of all, Article 412 is a substantive law... It does not provide for a specific procedure of law to be followed except to say that the corrections or changes must be effected by judicial order. As such, it cannot be gleaned therefrom that the procedure contemplated for obtaining such judicial order is summary in nature. Secondly, it is important to note that Article 412 uses both the terms 'corrected' and 'changed'... The provision neither qualifies as to the kind of entry to be changed or corrected nor does it distinguish on the basis of the effect that the correction or change may have. Hence, it is proper to conclude that all entries in the civil register may be changed or corrected under Article 412."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Rejection of the Ty Kong Tin Fallacy:** The doctrine tracing back to **Ty Kong Tin v. Republic** held that Article 412 of the Civil Code only authorized summary correction of innocuous clerical errors. The Court dismantled this premise: Article 412 is substantive law requiring a judicial order, without declaring the procedure summary. Moreover, Articles 407 and 408 explicitly mandate that civil registers record substantial matters, including births, legitimations, acknowledgments, civil status, and citizenship. Isolating Article 412 to mean only "clerical errors" violates the rule of statutory construction that a statute must be construed as a whole.
**Distinction Between Summary and Adversary Proceedings:** A special proceeding under Rule 108 is not inherently summary. Sections 3, 4, 5, and 7 require publication for three consecutive weeks, impleading of all affected interested parties, service of notice, the filing of formal oppositions, and a full trial on the merits. Once these steps are taken and an opposition is actively prosecuted, the case transforms into an **appropriate adversary proceeding**.
**Harmonization with Labayo-Rowe:** In **Labayo-Rowe**, the substantial change was disallowed not because Rule 108 was incapable of resolving substantial issues, but because that specific petitioner failed to implead indispensable parties (the father and paternal grandparents), rendering that specific proceeding summary and deficient.
**Application to the Story:** Here, both RTC Manila and RTC Kalookan scrupulously enforced Rule 108: orders were published for three consecutive weeks in newspapers of general circulation, notices were served upon the Solicitor General, the Civil Registrars, and all affected children, and oppositions/motions to dismiss were filed. Because all procedural safeguards of an adversary proceeding were met, the trial courts had full jurisdiction to try the substantial issue of maternity.
**Legislative Confirmation (R.A. No. 9048):** The Court observed that R.A. No. 9048 (enacted Feb. 8, 2001) transferred clerical and typographical errors to the administrative jurisdiction of local civil registrars, leaving substantial alterations to the judicial domain of Rule 108.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** The old rule in **Ty Kong Tin** claiming that civil registry corrections are limited strictly to simple clerical typos is fundamentally flawed because the substantive Civil Code expressly covers heavy matters like status, birth, and citizenship. Under **Republic v. Valencia**, substantial changes—even replacing a mother's name and altering filiation—can be adjudicated under Rule 108, provided the case is treated not as a summary shortcut, but as a full-blown adversary trial with newspaper publication, summons to all interested heirs, and complete presentation of evidence.
Issue 2: Applicability of Article 171 of the Family Code
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** Article 171 of the Family Code does not apply because private respondents are not impugning the marital legitimacy of a child born to their mother; they are asserting that their mother never biologically gave birth to petitioners.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Contrary to petitioners' contention that the petitions before the lower courts were actually actions to impugn legitimacy, the prayer therein is not to declare that petitioners are illegitimate children of Keh Shiok Cheng, but to establish that the former are not the latter's children. There is nothing to impugn as there is no blood relation at all between Keh Shiok Cheng and petitioners."
"Article 171 of the Family Code is not applicable to the present case. A close reading of the provision shows that it applies to instances in which the father impugns the legitimacy of his wife's child. The provision, however, presupposes that the child was the undisputed offspring of the mother. The present case alleges and shows that Hermogena [in **Babiera** / Keh Shiok Cheng here] did not give birth to petitioner. In other words, the prayer therein is not to declare that petitioner is an illegitimate child of Hermogena, but to establish that the former is not the latter's child at all."
"A careful reading of the above articles will show that they do not contemplate a situation, like in the instant case, where a child is alleged not be the child of nature or biological child of a certain couple. Rather, these articles govern a situation where a husband (or his heirs) denies as his own a child of his wife."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Scope of Family Code Articles on Impugning Legitimacy:** Articles 164, 166, 170, and 171 govern situations where a husband or his heirs deny paternity of a child conceived or born by the lawful wife during coverture. They establish strict standing rules and short prescriptive periods to prevent malicious paternity challenges.
**Presupposition of Maternity:** These provisions presuppose that the mother who delivered the child is undisputed.
**Application to the Story:** Relying on **Babiera v. Catotal** and **Benitez-Badua v. Court of Appeals**, the Court found that private respondents do not claim petitioners are adulterous or illegitimate offspring of Keh Shiok Cheng; they claim Keh Shiok Cheng never conceived, carried, or delivered petitioners at all. Because there is zero biological relationship between Keh Shiok Cheng and petitioners, there is no marital presumption of legitimacy to impugn. Private respondents, as legal heirs of Keh Shiok Cheng whose inheritance rights are impaired by simulated births, have direct standing to seek the cancellation of the false maternity entry.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Article 171 of the Family Code prevents heirs from questioning whether a child delivered by a wife was truly fathered by the husband while the father is still around to confirm or deny it. This rule has no application when the claim is that the wife was never pregnant with the child in the first place. You cannot "impugn the legitimacy" of a child with respect to a woman who never gave birth to that child.
Issue 3: Prescription of the Action under Article 1149
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** The 5-year prescriptive period under Article 1149 did not lapse because it began to run only upon private respondents' actual discovery of the falsification in 1989, not when the fraudulent births were registered.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Art. 1149. All other actions whose periods are not fixed in this Code or in other laws must be brought within five years from the time the right of action accrues."
"The right of action accrues when there exists a cause of action, which consists of three (3) elements, namely: a) a right in favor of the plaintiff by whatever means and under whatever law it arises or is created; b) an obligation on the part of the defendant to respect such right; and c) an act or omission on the part of such defendant violative of the right of the plaintiff."
"It is true that the books making up the Civil Register and all documents relating thereto are public documents and shall be **prima facie** evidence of the facts therein contained. Petitioners liken their birth records to land titles, public documents that serve as notice to the whole world. Unfortunately for the petitioners, this analogy does not hold water. Unlike a title to a parcel of land, a person's parentage cannot be acquired by prescription. One is either born of a particular mother or not. It is that simple."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Applicable Law on Prescription:** Because Rule 108 and Article 412 do not set a period of limitations, the catch-all five-year period under Article 1149 of the Civil Code applies.
**Reckoning Date of Accrual:** A cause of action requires an existing right, an obligation, and a violative act. Although the physical acts of falsification occurred decades prior (between 1950 and 1960), private respondents were completely unaware of their father's deceit. The children lived in the same compound and had no reason to suspect their father had registered the concubine's children under their mother's name.
**Discovery Rule Applied:** The suspicion arose only after Keh Shiok Cheng died on May 9, 1989, when the father insisted on publishing petitioners' names in her obituary, leading to the NBI investigation. The right of action accrued upon discovery in 1989. Since the petitions were filed in December 1992 and February 1993, less than five years had elapsed.
**Rejection of the Torrens Title Analogy:** The Court dismissed petitioners' contention that birth certificates operate as constructive notice like land titles. Parentage and biological truth cannot be acquired by prescription or adverse possession.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** You cannot acquire a mother through prescription the way you acquire land through adverse possession. The 5-year prescriptive period to correct fraudulent birth entries only started running when the legitimate children actually discovered their father's secret fraud in 1989, not when the false papers were quietly submitted to the local registrar decades earlier.
Issue 4: Forum Shopping
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** There is no forum shopping because the Rule 108 special proceedings lack identity of rights, causes of action, and reliefs with the pending criminal, denaturalization, and partition cases.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Forum shopping is present when in the two or more cases pending there is identity of parties, rights or causes of action and reliefs sought. Even a cursory examination of the pleadings filed by private respondents in their various cases against petitioners would reveal that at the very least there is no identity of rights or causes of action and reliefs prayed for."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Legal Standard for Forum Shopping:** Forum shopping requires an identity of parties, rights or causes of action, and reliefs sought across pending suits, such that a judgment in one would amount to **res judicata** in the other.
**Comparison of Pending Actions:**
**The Rule 108 Petitions:** Seek the judicial cancellation and correction of civil registry entries under the Rules of Court to reflect biological truth.
**The Criminal Complaint:** Rests on the commission of a crime under the Revised Penal Code (falsification) and seeks the penal punishment of the accused.
**The Denaturalization Petition:** Based on the commission of an immoral act by Lee Tek Sheng and aims at stripping him of Philippine citizenship and his deportation.
**The Partition Suit:** Grounded on succession rights under the Civil Code to claim an inheritance from Keh Shiok Cheng's estate.
**Conclusion:** Even if all four actions touch upon the common factual background of maternity, their legal causes of action and ultimate reliefs are entirely distinct.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Forum shopping requires the same cause of action and the same relief across different courts. Asking to fix a birth certificate (Rule 108) is completely different from sending someone to jail for falsification, deporting someone under naturalization laws, or distributing an inheritance in a partition suit, even if all cases stem from the same family lie.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.** (The decision was unanimous among the members of the Second Division).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is hereby DENIED and the assailed decision of the Court of Appeals dated October 28, 1994 is AFFIRMED.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Private respondents prevailed. The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, sustaining the orders of the Manila and Kalookan RTC judges to assume jurisdiction and proceed with the Rule 108 adversary proceedings to determine whether the name of Keh Shiok Cheng should be deleted and replaced with Tiu Chuan in the birth certificates of petitioners.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Andal v. Macaraig**
**Full Official Caption:** Mariano Andal, assisted by mother Maria Dueñas as guardian **ad litem**, and Maria Dueñas, Plaintiffs-Appellees, vs. Eduvigis Macaraig, Defendant-Appellant
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** L-2474
**Promulgation Date:** May 30, 1951
**Philippine Reports:** 89 Phil. 165
**Ponente:** Bautista Angelo, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** En Banc; Paras, **C.J.**, Feria, Pablo, Tuason, Montemayor, Reyes, and Jugo, **JJ.**, concurred. (Unanimous; no separate opinions).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Persons and Family Relations → Paternity and Filiation → Legitimacy of Children → Presumption of Legitimacy and Grounds for Rebuttal (Physical Impossibility of Access)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Remedial Law → Evidence → Conclusive and Disputable Presumptions → Presumption of Legitimacy
Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s)
**Historical Basis Cited in the Decision:**
**Article 108, Spanish Civil Code of 1889:**
"Children born after the one hundred and eighty days next following that of the celebration of marriage or **within the three hundred days next following its dissolution** or the separation of the spouses shall be **presumed to be legitimate**.
This presumption may be rebutted **only by proof that it was physically impossible for the husband to have had access to his wife during the first one hundred and twenty days of the three hundred next preceding the birth of the child**."
**Section 68, paragraph (c), Rule 123, Rules of Court (1940):**
"The issue of a wife cohabiting with the husband who is not impotent, is **indisputably presumed to be legitimate**, if not born within one hundred eighty days immediately succeeding the marriage, or after the expiration of three hundred days following its dissolution."
**Modern Counterpart Provisions (Family Code of the Philippines & 2019 Amended Rules of Evidence):**
**Article 164, Family Code of the Philippines:**
"Children conceived or born during the marriage of the parents are legitimate.
Children conceived as a result of artificial insemination of the mother with the sperm of the husband or of a donor or both are also legitimate children of the husband and his wife, provided, that both of them authorized or ratified such insemination in a written instrument executed and signed by them before the birth of the child. The instrument shall be recorded in the civil registry together with the birth certificate of the child."
**Article 166, Family Code of the Philippines:**
"Legitimacy of a child may be impugned only on the following grounds:
(1) **That it was physically impossible for the husband to have had sexual intercourse with his wife within the first 120 days of the 300 days which immediately preceded the birth of the child during which conception could have taken place**, as in cases of:
    (a) physical incapacity of the husband to have sexual intercourse with his wife;
    (b) the fact that the husband and wife were living separately in such a way that sexual intercourse was not possible; or
    (c) serious illness of the husband, which absolutely prevented sexual intercourse;
(2) That it is proved that for biological or other scientific reasons, the child could not have been that of the husband, except in the instance referred to in the second paragraph of Article 164; or
(3) That in case of children conceived through artificial insemination, the written authorization or ratification of either parent was obtained through mistake, fraud, violence, intimidation, or undue influence."
**Section 3(dd), Rule 131, Revised Rules on Evidence (as amended):**
"That a child born in lawful wedlock, there being no divorce, absolute or from bed and board, is legitimate;"
The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision
**General Rule / Provision Triggered:** A child born within 300 days following the dissolution of marriage (e.g., by the death of the husband) is presumed legitimate. This presumption can **only** be overcome by clear and convincing proof that it was **physically impossible for the husband to have had access to his wife** during the first 120 days of the 300 days next preceding the birth of the child.
**Specific Sub-Rules, Exceptions, & Doctrinal Tests:**
1. Categories of Physical Impossibility of Access (Manresa standard):
Absence during the initial period of conception;
Impotence which is patent, continuing, and incurable; and
Imprisonment, unless corrupt violation of prison regulations permitted cohabitation.
2. **Severe Illness / Tuberculosis Rule:** Severe physical weakness caused by advanced tuberculosis (even where the husband is bedridden, swollen, and can hardly move) does not establish physical impossibility of sexual intercourse.
3. **Adultery Rule:** The fact that the wife engaged in illicit sexual relations or committed adultery with another man during the period of conception cannot, by itself, overcome the presumption of legitimacy if marital cohabitation or access between the spouses was physically possible.
**Factual Trigger:** A bedridden husband dying of severe tuberculosis cohabited under the same roof with his wife during the first 120 days of the 300 days preceding the child's birth, even though the wife was simultaneously engaging in illicit sexual intercourse with the husband's brother living in the same house. The child was born 167 days after the husband's death, triggering the statutory presumption of legitimacy which the mother-in-law failed to rebut.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Mariano Andal:** Minor plaintiff-appellee; child born to Maria Dueñas on June 17, 1943; claiming title by intestate succession as the sole legitimate son of the deceased Emiliano Andal.
**Maria Dueñas:** Plaintiff-appellee; mother and guardian **ad litem** of Mariano Andal; surviving widow of Emiliano Andal.
**Emiliano Andal:** Deceased husband of Maria Dueñas and son of Eduvigis Macaraig; original owner of the disputed parcel of land by virtue of a donation **propter nuptias**; died on January 1, 1943.
**Felix Andal:** Brother of Emiliano Andal; moved into the marital home to assist with farm work; engaged in an adulterous affair with Maria Dueñas starting May 1942, eloping with her on September 10, 1942.
**Eduvigis Macaraig:** Defendant-appellant; mother of Emiliano Andal and Felix Andal; donor of the land **propter nuptias**; took possession of the land after Emiliano's death, claiming Mariano was illegitimate and that the property reverted to her as the legal heir.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Plaintiffs filed an ordinary civil action in the **Court of First Instance (CFI) of Camarines Sur** to recover ownership and possession of the land.
The CFI rendered judgment for the plaintiffs, declaring Mariano Andal the legitimate son and owner of the land.
Defendant appealed directly to the **Supreme Court on pure questions of law**.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1938:** Eduvigis Macaraig executes a donation **propter nuptias** over a parcel of land in Barrio Talacop, Calabanga, Camarines Sur, in favor of her son, Emiliano Andal, on the occasion of his marriage to Maria Dueñas. Emiliano takes possession and operates the land from 1938 until 1942.
**January 1941:** Emiliano becomes sick with pulmonary tuberculosis.
**Post-January 1941:** Felix Andal, Emiliano’s brother, moves into Emiliano and Maria's home to assist in working the farm due to Emiliano's illness.
**May 1942:** Felix Andal and Maria Dueñas commence an illicit adulterous relationship, engaging in sexual intercourse and treating each other as husband and wife while living under the same roof as Emiliano.
**August 21, 1942 – September 10, 1942:** The critical initial period of conception (falling within the first 120 days of the 300 days preceding the child's subsequent birth). Emiliano, though seriously ill, bedridden, swollen, and weak, remains living under the same roof with Maria.
**September 10, 1942:** Emiliano’s physical condition deteriorates to the point that he can hardly move or get up from bed. On the same day, Maria elopes with Felix, moving into her father’s house, where they reside until mid-1943.
**September 24, 1942:** Date of Emiliano Andal's death as initially alleged in the complaint **(Note: the proven date of death established at trial was January 1, 1943)**.
**1942:** Eduvigis Macaraig enters and takes possession of the disputed land, asserting ownership.
**January 1, 1943:** Emiliano Andal dies. Maria Dueñas does not attend his bedside or his funeral.
**June 17, 1943:** Maria Dueñas gives birth to a boy, Mariano Andal (167 days after Emiliano's death).
**Subsequent Action:** Maria Dueñas, as guardian **ad litem** for minor Mariano Andal, files suit in the CFI of Camarines Sur against Eduvigis Macaraig to recover ownership and possession.
**CFI Ruling:** CFI Camarines Sur declares Mariano the legitimate son and rightful owner of the land. Eduvigis appeals directly to the Supreme Court.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's / Appellees' Arguments (Mariano Andal & Maria Dueñas)
**Main Thesis:** Mariano Andal is the legitimate son of Emiliano Andal and therefore inherits the land acquired by Emiliano through donation **propter nuptias**.
**Specific Contentions:**
Mariano was born on June 17, 1943, within 300 days following the dissolution of the marriage caused by Emiliano’s death on January 1, 1943.
Under Article 108 of the Civil Code and Section 68(c) of Rule 123 of the Rules of Court, a child born within 300 days following marital dissolution is presumed legitimate.
Emiliano was the absolute owner of the land by donation **propter nuptias** and held continuous possession until 1942 when Eduvigis unlawfully entered the property.
B. Respondent's / Appellant's Arguments (Eduvigis Macaraig)
**Main Thesis:** Mariano Andal is not the legitimate child of Emiliano Andal, rendering Eduvigis the sole heir entitled to the land by legal reversion/succession.
**Specific Contentions:**
It was physically impossible for Emiliano to have fathered the child because he was bedridden with severe tuberculosis, unable to move or rise from bed, with swollen feet and a hoarse voice during the period of conception.
Maria Dueñas had eloped with Emiliano’s brother, Felix, and had been carrying on an active adulterous relationship with Felix since May 1942.
Maria was not with Emiliano when he died and refused even to attend his funeral.
Consequently, the presumption of legitimacy was successfully destroyed by Emiliano's physical incapacity and Maria's open adultery.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether the legal presumption of legitimacy in favor of Mariano Andal under Article 108 of the Civil Code and Section 68(c), Rule 123 of the Rules of Court was rebutted by evidence of the husband's severe, bedridden illness (tuberculosis) and the wife's concurrent adultery with the husband's brother during the period of conception.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not a husband's advanced tuberculosis and his wife's concurrent adulterous relationship with his brother are sufficient to prove the "physical impossibility of access" required to overcome the presumption of legitimacy of a child born within 300 days of the husband's death.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Overcoming the Presumption of Legitimacy via Illness and Adultery
(a) Issue & Short Answer
**NO.** The presumption of legitimacy was not overcome. Severe illness such as tuberculosis does not establish patent, incurable impotence or the physical impossibility of sexual access, and the wife's adultery does not impair the child's legitimate status where access between the spouses was possible under the marital roof during the period of conception.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement (Exact Quotes)
**"This presumption can only be rebutted by proof that it was physically impossible for the husband to have had access to his wife during the first 120 days of the 300 next preceding the birth of the child."**
**"Impossibility of access by husband to wife would include (1) absence during the initial period of conception, (2) impotence which is patent, continuing and incurable, and (3) imprisonment, unless it can be shown that cohabitation took place through corrupt violation of prison regulations."**
**"We admit that Emiliano was already suffering from tuberculosis and his condition then was so serious that he could hardly move and get up from bed, his feet were swollen and his voice hoarse. But experience shows that this does not prevent carnal intercourse. There are cases where persons suffering from this sickness can do the carnal act even in the most crucial stage because they are more inclined to sexual intercourse. As an author has said, 'the reputation of the tuberculosis towards eroticism (sexual propensity) is probably dependent more upon confinement to bed than the consequences of the disease.' (An Integrated Practice of Medicine, by Hyman, Vol. 3, p. 2202)."**
**"The fact that Maria Dueñas has committed adultery can not also overcome this presumption..."**
(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi
**Statutory Timing:** The child, Mariano Andal, was born on June 17, 1943. Emiliano Andal died on January 1, 1943. The child was born 167 days after the dissolution of the marriage, falling squarely within the statutory window of 300 days under Article 108 of the Civil Code.
**Stringent Rebuttal Standard:** Under both Article 108 of the Civil Code and Section 68(c) of Rule 123 of the Rules of Court, legitimacy is presumed unless there is affirmative proof of the physical impossibility of access during the first 120 days of the 300 days preceding the birth (specifically between August 21, 1942, and September 10, 1942).
**Application of Manresa's Threefold Test for "Impossibility of Access":**
1. **Absence:** The parties were not absent from each other. Spouses Emiliano and Maria lived together under the marital roof until September 10, 1942, which fell within the critical conception window.
2. **Impotence:** There was no evidence that Emiliano suffered from patent, continuous, and incurable impotence.
3. **Imprisonment:** Emiliano was never confined in prison.
**Medical Nature of Tuberculosis:** Although Emiliano's illness left him bedridden, swollen, and weak, medical authority (Hyman, **An Integrated Practice of Medicine**) confirms that tuberculosis does not incapacitate an individual from carnal intercourse; indeed, bed confinement often heightens sexual propensity (eroticism).
**Adultery Insufficient to Rebut:** Even if Felix and Maria engaged in illicit carnal relations within the same home beginning May 1942, concurrent access between Emiliano and Maria was not precluded. Settled doctrine dictates that the wife's adultery alone cannot defeat the presumption of legitimacy where access to the husband was physically possible.
(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation
(Plain-Language Explanation) The Supreme Court held that the law fiercely protects a child's legitimacy: if a child is born within 300 days of the husband's death, the presumption of legitimacy can only be destroyed by showing it was physically impossible for the husband to have had sexual intercourse with his wife during the conception period. Being bedridden with severe tuberculosis does not cause physical impotence, as medical science shows tuberculosis patients retain their sexual capabilities. Because the spouses lived under the same roof during the conception window, sexual access was physically possible; thus, neither the husband's illness nor the wife's concurrent adultery with the brother-in-law is sufficient to bastardize the child.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.** (The decision was unanimous, with seven Associate Justices fully concurring with the Ponente).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"Wherefore, the decision appealed from is affirmed, without pronouncement as to costs."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The plaintiffs prevailed. The Supreme Court affirmed the CFI's judgment declaring minor Mariano Andal the legitimate child of the deceased Emiliano Andal, confirming Mariano's sole ownership and right of possession over the disputed parcel of land by inheritance, and defeating Eduvigis Macaraig's claim of reversion.

### Macadangdang v. Court of Appeals
### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Title:** Macadangdang v. Court of Appeals and Mejias
**Full Official Caption:** Antonio Macadangdang, Petitioner, vs. The Honorable Court of Appeals and Elizabeth Mejias, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. L-49542; September 12, 1980; 100 SCRA 73
**Ponente:** Makasiar, J.
**Voting Breakdown:** First Division: Makasiar, J., ponente; Teehankee (Chairman), Fernandez, Guerrero, De Castro, and Melencio-Herrera, JJ., concur. (Unanimous; no separate opinions).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Civil Law → Family Law / Paternity & Filiation → Legitimacy of Children → Presumption of Legitimacy and Grounds for Impugning Legitimacy
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Evidence → Disputable / Quasi-Conclusive Presumptions → Standing to Impugn Filiation and Direct vs. Collateral Attack
Full Text of Governing Provisions
Civil Code of the Philippines (Republic Act No. 386)
**Art. 220.** In case of doubt, all presumptions favor the solidarity of the family. Thus, every intendment of law or fact leans toward the validity of marriage, the indissolubility of the marriage bonds, the **legitimacy of children**, the community of property during marriage, the authority of parents over their children, and the validity of defense for any member of the family in case of unlawful aggression.
**Art. 255. Children born after one hundred and eighty days following the celebration of the marriage, and before three hundred days following its dissolution or the separation of the spouses shall be presumed to be legitimate.**
**Against this presumption, no evidence shall be admitted other than that of the physical impossibility of the husband's having access to his wife within the first one hundred and twenty days of the three hundred which preceded the birth of the child.**
This physical impossibility may be caused:
(1) By the **impotence** of the husband;
(2) By the fact that the husband and wife were **living separately, in such a way that access was not possible**;
(3) By the **serious illness** of the husband.
**Art. 256. The child shall be presumed legitimate, although the mother may have declared against its legitimacy or may have been sentenced as an adulteress.**
**Art. 257.** Should the wife commit adultery at or about the time of the conception of the child, but there was no physical impossibility of access between her and her husband as set forth in article 255, the child is **prima facie** presumed to be illegitimate if it appears highly improbable, for ethnic reasons, that the child is that of the husband. For the purposes of this article, the wife's adultery need not be proved in a criminal case.
Revised Rules of Court (1964)
**Rule 131, Section 4. Quasi-conclusive presumptions of legitimacy —**
(a) Children born after one hundred eighty days following the celebration of the marriage, and before three hundred days following its dissolution or the separation of the spouses shall be presumed legitimate.
Against this presumption no evidence shall be admitted other than that of the physical impossibility of the husband's having access to his wife within the first one hundred and twenty days of the three hundred which preceded the birth of the child.
This physical impossibility may be caused:
[1] By the impotence of the husband;
[2] By the fact that the husband and the wife were living separately, in such a way that access was not possible;
[3] By the serious illness of the husband;
(b) The child shall be presumed legitimate although the mother may have declared against its legitimacy or may have been sentenced as an adulteress.
(c) Should the wife commit adultery at or about the time of the conception of the child, but there was no physical impossibility of access between her and her husband as set forth above, the child is presumed legitimate, unless it appears highly improbable, for ethnic reasons, that the child is that of the husband. For the purpose of the rule, the wife's adultery need not be proved in a criminal case.
**(Modern Codification Note: The Family Code of the Philippines [Executive Order No. 209], effective August 3, 1988, now governs these rules under Articles 164, 166, 167, 170, and 171).**
Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provisions
**General Rule / Provision Triggered:** Under **Art. 255 of the Civil Code** and **Rule 131, Sec. 4 of the Rules of Court**, a child born after 180 days from the celebration of marriage and before 300 days following its dissolution or separation of the spouses is conclusively presumed legitimate. The only admissible evidence to overthrow this presumption is proof **beyond reasonable doubt of the physical impossibility of access** between the husband and wife during the first 120 days of the 300 days preceding birth.
**Sub-Rules, Exceptions, and Doctrinal Tests:**
1. **Sole Grounds for Physical Impossibility:** Limited strictly to: (a) husband's impotence (physical inability to copulate, not merely sterility); (b) living separately such that access was impossible (e.g., residing in different countries/provinces with zero contact, or imprisonment without conjugal visits); or (c) serious illness precluding copulation without severe pain or causing temporary/permanent impotence.
2. **Wife's Adultery / Confession Ineffective (Art. 256):** Infidelity or a mother's express declaration against legitimacy does not overcome the presumption. Public policy and the protection of the child bar a mother from bastardizing her child to gain a personal benefit or monetary support from a paramour.
3. **Exclusive Standing / Direct Suit Requirement:** Only the husband (or exceptionally his heirs under fixed conditions) has the legal standing to impugn the child's legitimacy, and he must do so in a direct action brought for that specific purpose within statutory prescriptive periods. The mother has no right to disavow the child's legitimacy; she can only contest the identity of the child.
**Factual Trigger:** Elizabeth Mejias, a married woman whose husband lived in the same province and shared access to her parents' home where she visited, filed a direct suit against her alleged paramour (Antonio Macadangdang) to declare her child illegitimate and obtain child support, without joining her legal husband or proving that physical access to her husband was impossible during the period of conception.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Antonio Macadangdang:** Petitioner; alleged paramour whom Elizabeth sued for recognition and monthly support of minor Rolando.
**Elizabeth Mejias:** Private Respondent; married woman who engaged in an extramarital affair and sued to have her child declared the illegitimate son of petitioner.
**Crispin Anahaw:** Elizabeth's lawful husband; potent father of her first four children, who resided in the same province (at her mother's house in Samal) but was never impleaded in the action.
**Rolando Macadangdang:** Minor child born on October 30, 1967, whose legitimacy was impugned by his mother.
**Patrocinia Avila:** The baby's **yaya** who cared for Rolando after delivery.
**Procedural Posture:**
**Court of First Instance (CFI) of Davao, Branch IX (Civil Case No. 263):** On February 27, 1973, dismissed Elizabeth Mejias' amended complaint for recognition and support, citing positive provisions of the Civil Code and Rules of Court.
**Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. No. 54618-R):** On June 2, 1978, reversed the CFI, declared Rolando to be the illegitimate child of Antonio Macadangdang, and ordered the latter to pay ₱350.00 monthly support until majority. Reconsideration denied on November 6, 1978.
**Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 filed by Macadangdang on January 12, 1979, challenging the Court of Appeals' reversal.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**Pre-1967:** Elizabeth Mejias is lawfully married to Crispin Anahaw; the couple begets four children together.
**March 1967:** Elizabeth engages in an illicit sexual encounter with petitioner Antonio Macadangdang. Elizabeth claims this "incident" caused her separation from husband Crispin.
**October 30, 1967:** Elizabeth gives birth to a healthy, full-term baby boy (Rolando) at a rented house on Carpenter Street—exactly seven months (210 days) after the March 1967 sexual encounter.
**December 24, 1967:** The baby is baptized under the name "Rolando Macadangdang" without the presence, signature, or participation of petitioner.
**Post-Birth Period (Late 1967 – February 1968):** Five days after delivery, Rolando is placed in the care of a **yaya** (Patrocinia Avila). When the child is between 15 days and 2 months old, Elizabeth leaves him with the **yaya** and stays at her mother's house in Samal, Davao del Norte, where her husband Crispin and their four children reside.
**April 25, 1972:** Elizabeth files a complaint for recognition and support against petitioner Antonio in the CFI of Davao (Civil Case No. 263).
**June 30, 1972:** Antonio files his Answer praying for dismissal of the complaint.
**August 9, 1972:** The trial court conducts a pre-trial conference and issues a Pre-trial Order formalizing stipulations and agreed issues.
**October 17, 1972:** Elizabeth files an amended complaint pursuant to the pre-trial agreement.
**February 27, 1973:** CFI Davao dismisses the complaint, holding that Rolando is presumed legitimate under the law and that the wife cannot collaterally attack legitimacy without impleading her lawful husband.
**April 18, 1973:** Elizabeth appeals to the Court of Appeals.
**June 2, 1978:** The Court of Appeals reverses the CFI, declares Rolando an illegitimate son of Antonio, and awards ₱350.00 monthly child support.
**November 6, 1978:** The Court of Appeals denies Antonio's motion for reconsideration.
**January 12, 1979:** Antonio files the present Petition for Review before the Supreme Court.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Antonio Macadangdang)
**Main Thesis:** Rolando is conclusively presumed to be the legitimate child of the valid, subsisting marriage between Elizabeth Mejias and Crispin Anahaw; Elizabeth cannot bastardize her own child through an action against an alleged paramour while excluding her husband.
**Specific Contentions:**
Under Arts. 255 and 256 of the Civil Code and Rule 131, Sec. 4 of the Rules of Court, a child born during wedlock is presumed legitimate; physical impossibility of access within the first 120 days of the 300 days preceding birth was never demonstrated.
Husband Crispin Anahaw was not shown to be impotent, seriously ill, or living separately such that access was physically impossible; he lived in the very house in Samal where Elizabeth visited and stayed.
A normal full-term baby born on October 30, 1967, could not have been conceived during the March 1967 encounter (a span of only 7 months); conception had to occur around January 1967 when Elizabeth was cohabiting with her husband.
The CA's factual finding that Elizabeth separated from her husband in 1965 was contrary to evidence on record, uncorroborated, and based solely on Elizabeth's self-serving testimony.
A baptismal certificate prepared without petitioner's knowledge or consent does not establish paternity or filiation.
Filiation cannot be attacked collaterally; the right to impugn legitimacy belongs exclusively to the lawful husband in a direct suit.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Elizabeth Mejias)
**Main Thesis:** The child Rolando is the illegitimate son of Antonio Macadangdang, begotten during their illicit relationship, entitling the child to recognition and support.
**Specific Contentions:**
Arts. 255 and 256 of the Civil Code and Rule 131, Sec. 4 do not apply because she and her husband were already living separately prior to conception.
The trial court erred in holding that she could not question the child's legitimacy without joining her legal husband, Crispin Anahaw, as a party.
Antonio is the true biological father following their sexual relations in 1967, and the child carries his surname as reflected in the baptismal records.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the child Rolando is conclusively presumed the legitimate issue of the spouses Elizabeth Mejias and Crispin Anahaw under Article 255 of the Civil Code.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not a child born to a married woman seven months after an extramarital encounter is conclusively presumed the legitimate child of her lawful marriage when physical impossibility of access between the spouses during the period of conception was not proven beyond reasonable doubt.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE / PROCEDURAL]** Whether or not the wife may institute an action that would bastardize her child without giving her husband, the legally presumed father, an opportunity to be heard.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not a married mother has legal standing to collaterally attack the legitimacy of her child born in wedlock in a suit for recognition and support against an alleged paramour without impleading her lawful husband.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Conclusive / Quasi-Conclusive Presumption of Legitimacy
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The child Rolando is presumed legitimate under Article 255 of the Civil Code and Rule 131, Section 4 of the Rules of Court, because Elizabeth failed to establish physical impossibility of access between herself and her husband during the period of conception.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Against this presumption, no evidence shall be admitted other than that of the physical impossibility of the husband's having access to his wife within the first one hundred and twenty days of the three hundred which preceded the birth of the child."
"The modern rule is that, in order to overthrow the presumption of legitimacy, it must be shown beyond reasonable doubt that there was no access as could have enabled the husband to be the father of the child. Sexual intercourse is to be presumed where personal access is not disproved, unless such presumption is rebutted by evidence to the contrary; where sexual intercourse is presumed or proved, the husband must be taken to be the father of the child..."
"To defeat the presumption of legitimacy, therefore, there must be physical impossibility of access by the husband to the wife during the period of conception. The law expressly refers to physical impossibility. Hence, a circumstance which makes sexual relations improbable, cannot defeat the presumption of legitimacy; but it may be proved as a circumstance to corroborate proof of physical impossibility of access..."
"And as between the paternity by the husband and the paternity by the paramour, all the circumstances being equal, the law is inclined to follow the former; hence, the child is thus given the benefit of legitimacy."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Rejection of the CA's Factual Finding of Separation:** The Court of Appeals committed a reversible misapprehension of facts by holding that Elizabeth and her husband separated in 1965. Elizabeth's own spontaneous testimony on September 21, 1972, admitted that she separated from her husband **by reason of the March 1967 incident** with Antonio. Uncorroborated, self-serving testimony cannot sustain a finding of separation.
**Failure to Prove Physical Impossibility of Access:** Under Art. 255, the presumption can only be overcome by demonstrating physical impossibility of access due to: (1) impotence, (2) living separately in a manner that access was impossible, or (3) serious illness.
Crispin had fathered four previous children (negating impotence).
He suffered no serious illness.
The spouses lived in the same province; Crispin stayed at the mother's home in Samal where Elizabeth sent food and convalesced right after giving birth. Physical access was entirely possible.
**Gestation and Term of Child:** Rolando was born on October 30, 1967—exactly seven months (210 days) after the March 1967 encounter. Testimony established that he was a healthy, full-term baby delivered without complications or incubator care, showing he was conceived around January 1967, well before the March encounter with Antonio.
**Inefficacy of Baptismal Certificate:** Under established jurisprudence (**Paa v. Chan**; **Fortus v. Novero**), a baptismal certificate proves only the administration of the sacrament, not the veracity of statements regarding parentage, especially when prepared without the alleged father's consent.
**Adultery Does Not Defeat Legitimacy:** Under Art. 256, a mother's declaration or adultery does not destroy legitimacy because it remains scientifically and legally possible that the husband begot the child during concurrent cohabitation.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** A child born during a valid marriage is strongly shielded by law as the husband's legitimate child. To pin paternity on an outside lover, the mother must present ironclad proof that it was physically impossible for her husband to have had sexual relations with her during the time the baby was conceived. Because Elizabeth's husband was potent, healthy, and lived nearby in the family home she frequently visited, and because the baby was born full-term seven months after the affair (meaning conception took place earlier), the presumption of legitimacy remains unbroken.
Issue 2: Standing of the Mother to Impugn Legitimacy Collaterally
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The mother has no legal standing to bastardize her own child; the right to contest legitimacy belongs strictly to the husband (or his heirs) and can be raised only in a direct action where the husband is given an opportunity to be heard.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"At this juncture, it must be pointed out that only the husband can contest the legitimacy of a child born to his wife. He is the one directly confronted with the scandal and ridicule which the infidelity of his wife produces; and he should decide whether to conceal that infidelity or expose it, in view of the moral or economic interest involved..."
"The right to repudiate or contest the legitimacy of a child born in wedlock belongs only to the alleged father, who is the husband of the mother and can be exercised only by him or his heirs, within a fixed time, and in certain cases, and only in a direct suit brought for the purpose..."
"Thus the mother has no right to disavow a child because maternity is never uncertain; she can only contest the identity of the child..."
"...in general, good morals and public policy require that a mother should not be permitted to assert the illegitimacy of a child born in wedlock in order to obtain some benefit for herself..."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Exclusive Prerogative of the Husband:** Legitimacy cannot be impugned collaterally in a child support action. The right to repudiate belongs exclusively to the presumed father because he must choose whether to expose his wife's infidelity or preserve family honor.
**Public Policy Bars Mother's Disavowal:** While paternity may be questioned, maternity is never uncertain; the mother can only dispute identity (e.g., child switching). Public policy strictly prohibits a mother from bastardizing her offspring to advance her personal economic interests or shake down a wealthy paramour.
**Omission of Indispensable Party:** Elizabeth deliberately excluded her lawful husband, Crispin Anahaw, from the proceedings to protect her scheme from being contradicted, depriving the legal father of his right to defend his child's status.
**Family Solidarity Mandate:** Art. 220 mandates that all legal and factual intendments lean towards the preservation of the family, indissolubility of marriage, and the legitimacy of children.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** Under Philippine law, only the legal husband has the power to file a direct lawsuit questioning whether a child born during the marriage is really his. The mother cannot collaterally bastardize her own child in an action for financial support against her lover. Allowing a scheming mother to strip her child of legitimate status to collect money from an extramarital partner destroys family stability and violates public policy.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.** (The decision was unanimous among all five participating justices of the First Division).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, THE DECISION OF THE COURT OF APPEALS DATED JUNE 2, 1978, AND ITS RESOLUTION DATED NOVEMBER 6, 1978 ARE HEREBY REVERSED AND SET ASIDE. COSTS AGAINST PRIVATE RESPONDENT.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Petitioner Antonio Macadangdang completely prevailed. The Supreme Court reversed and set aside the Court of Appeals' decision and resolution, reinstated the CFI's dismissal of Elizabeth Mejias' complaint, freed petitioner from the monthly support obligation of ₱350.00, recognized the child Rolando as the legitimate son of spouses Elizabeth Mejias and Crispin Anahaw, and assessed costs against private respondent.
