### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Lim v. Intermediate Appellate Court**
**Full Official Caption:** Violeta Cabatbat Lim, Lim Biak Chiao, and Calasiao Bijon Factory, Petitioners, v. Intermediate Appellate Court, Consorcia Frianeza Golea, Maria Frianeza Vergara, Benedicta Frianeza Mayugba, Bonifacia Frianeza, Heirs of Domingo Frianeza namely, Decideria Q. Vda. de Frianeza, Francisco, Dona, Vilma, and Decideria, all surnamed Frianeza, Heirs of Daniel Frianeza namely, Adela V. Vda. de Frianeza in her behalf and as Guardian ad litem of Minors, Darlene, Daniel Jr., Dussel, and Daisy Glen, all surnamed Frianeza, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. L-69679; October 18, 1988; 166 SCRA 451; First Division; Griño-Aquino, **J.** (Ponente); Concurring: Narvasa, Cruz, Gancayco, and Medialdea, **JJ.** No separate opinions.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code / Civil Code of the Philippines → Filiation and Paternity → Impugning Legitimacy vs. Assertion of Non-Filiation
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Succession → Legal/Intestate Succession → Concurrence of Surviving Spouse and Collateral Relatives (Article 1001) / Right of Representation (Articles 972, 1005)
Remedial Law → Evidence → Authentication of Documents → Ancient Document Rule (Rule 132, Sec. 22 [now Sec. 21])
**Full Text of Governing Provisions:**
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 263:**
"Art. 263. **The action to impugn the legitimacy of the child shall be brought within one year from the recording of the birth in the Civil Register**, if the husband should be in the same place, or in a proper case, any of his heirs.
If the husband or his heirs are absent, the period shall be eighteen months if they should reside in the province or city where the birth took place, and two years if they are in any other place within the Philippines or abroad. If the birth was concealed, the term will be counted from the date of the discovery."
**(Note: Corresponds modernly to Articles 170 and 171 of the Family Code).**
**Rules of Court, Rule 132, Section 22 (Evidence as then cited):**
"Sec. 22. **Evidence of execution not necessary.** — **Where a private writing is more than thirty years old, is produced from a custody in which it would naturally be found if genuine, and is unblemished by any alterations or circumstances of suspicion**, no other evidence of its execution and authenticity need be given." **(Re-codified under modern Rule 132, Section 21).**
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 1001:**
"Art. 1001. **Should brothers and sisters or their children survive with the widow or widower, the latter shall be entitled to one-half of the inheritance and the brothers and sisters or their children to the other half.**"
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**Direct Action to Impugn Legitimacy vs. Collateral Contest over Filiation (Art. 263):** Article 263 strictly governs proceedings that challenge the presumed marital **legitimacy** of a child born to a married woman during wedlock. It does **not** apply to suits where legal heirs establish complete absence of biological filiation (**non-filiation** or lack of generation). A claim that a claimant is merely a foster ward (**ampon**) without formal adoption, and not the offspring of the decedent at all, is not an action to impugn legitimacy.
**Ancient Document Rule Exception (Rule 132, Sec. 22):** The rule dispenses with proof of execution and authenticity only if the writing is free from circumstances of suspicion. When surrounding official records (hospital admission logbooks, primary civil records) affirmatively contradict the document's contents, the document is clouded by suspicion, rendering the ancient document rule inapplicable.
**Intestate Shares of Collaterals and the Surviving Spouse (Art. 1001):** In the absence of legitimate or illegitimate ascendants or descendants, the surviving spouse takes one-half ($1/2$) of the decedent's net estate; surviving collateral relatives (brothers, sisters, nephews, nieces by right of representation) take the remaining one-half ($1/2$). Surviving spouses of deceased collateral relatives (widows of brothers) are excluded, as they do not inherit by right of representation.
**Factual Trigger:** The collateral relatives of the decedent, Dra. Esperanza Cabatbat, filed an action for the partition of her estate, asserting that Violeta was not the biological offspring of Esperanza, but a mere ward (**ampon**). Violeta raised Article 263 to dismiss the challenge as an untimely attack on her legitimacy, and invoked the Ancient Document Rule to uphold her 30-year-old birth entry.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Dra. Esperanza Frianeza-Cabatbat:** Deceased property owner; died without biological issue on April 23, 1977.
**Proceso Cabatbat:** Surviving spouse of Esperanza; maintained that Violeta was his and Esperanza's legitimate daughter.
**Violeta Cabatbat Lim:** Foster child claiming to be the legitimate, sole surviving daughter and compulsory heir of Esperanza.
**Lim Biak Chiao:** Husband of Violeta.
**Calasiao Bijon Factory:** A business partnership wherein Esperanza held an equity interest; occupied/possessed by Violeta and her husband.
**Consorcia Frianeza Golea, Maria Frianeza Vergara, Benedicta Frianeza Mayugba, Bonifacia Frianeza:** Surviving sisters of Esperanza; plaintiffs seeking partition.
**Heirs of Domingo Frianeza and Daniel Frianeza:** Nephews, nieces, and surviving spouses (Decideria Q. Vda. de Frianeza and Adela V. Vda. de Frianeza) representing Esperanza’s deceased brothers.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 appealing the Decision of the Intermediate Appellate Court (IAC) dated October 25, 1984, which affirmed the Decision of the Court of First Instance (CFI) of Pangasinan (Civil Case No. D-3841) holding that Violeta was not the biological child or legal heir of Esperanza.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**December 1, 1947 to June 15, 1948:** Records of the Pangasinan Provincial Hospital indicate no admission of Esperanza Frianeza-Cabatbat for obstetrics or childbirth.
**May 26, 1948:** Only one woman, Benita Lastimosa, gave birth to an illegitimate child ("Baby Girl Lastimosa") at the Pangasinan Provincial Hospital.
**June 15, 1948:** A birth certificate entry (Exhibit "5") was purportedly filed, indicating that Violeta Cabatbat was born on May 26, 1948, to Proceso Cabatbat and Esperanza Frianeza.
**May 14, 1960 & April 21, 1961:** Two Deeds of Absolute Sale were executed where Violeta, as a minor vendee, was assisted by Dra. Esperanza Cabatbat (designated as "mother") and Proceso Cabatbat (designated as "father"), respectively.
**Violeta's Schooling:** Calasiao Pilot Central School listed Proceso and Esperanza merely as her "guardians," not as parents.
**April 23, 1977:** Dra. Esperanza Frianeza-Cabatbat died intestate and without biological issue.
**April 30, 1977:** Proceso Cabatbat and Violeta Cabatbat Lim withdrew funds from the deceased's equity in the Calasiao Bijon Factory (Exhibit 29).
**Civil Case No. D-3841 (CFI Pangasinan):** Sisters and collateral heirs of Esperanza filed a complaint against Proceso Cabatbat, Violeta Cabatbat Lim, and Calasiao Bijon Factory for judicial partition of the estate.
**August 10, 1979:** The CFI of Pangasinan rendered judgment finding that Violeta was not the child by nature of Esperanza and not a compulsory heir. The court distributed the estate between the surviving spouse and the collateral heirs, ordered the return of overdrawn/withdrawn amounts, and assessed fees.
**October 25, 1984:** The Intermediate Appellate Court (AC-G.R. No. CV 67055) affirmed the trial court's decision in full, and subsequently denied a motion for reconsideration.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Violeta Cabatbat Lim, et al.)
**Main Thesis:** Violeta is the legitimate daughter and sole compulsory heir of Dra. Esperanza Cabatbat, entitled to the exclusion of collateral heirs.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Filiation Established:** Violeta's status is proven by her birth registry record of June 15, 1948 (Exhibit "5"), testimony of her father Proceso Cabatbat, and her marriage contract listing Esperanza as mother.
**Ancient Document Rule (Rule 132, Sec. 22):** The birth record (Exhibit "5") is more than thirty years old, unblemished, and produced from proper custody; hence, execution and authenticity need no independent proof.
**Bar under Civil Code Art. 263:** The collateral relatives cannot impugn Violeta's legitimacy; under Article 263, an action to impugn legitimacy is subject to strict prescriptive periods and may only be brought under specific statutory conditions by the husband or his heirs.
**Continuous Possession of Status (Exhibits 8–11):** Notarized deeds of sale from 1960 and 1961 confirm that the spouses recognized Violeta as their legitimate daughter.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Consorcia Frianeza Golea, et al.)
**Main Thesis:** Esperanza died without issue; Violeta was merely a fostered ward (**ampon**) taken in without legal adoption, possessing no hereditary rights.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Physical Impossibility & Hospital Records:** Esperanza was never admitted to the Pangasinan Provincial Hospital between December 1947 and June 1948.
**Fabricated Birth Claim:** The only female baby delivered on May 26, 1948, was "Baby Girl Lastimosa," born to Benita Lastimosa. Violeta’s birth was never recorded with the Civil Registrar General.
**Documentary Disclaimers:** Violeta was enrolled in school by Esperanza and Proceso as "guardians," not as parents.
**Inapplicability of Article 263:** The complaint does not challenge the marital legitimacy of a child born of the wife during marriage; it asserts the absolute physical fact that the decedent never gave birth to the child.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether the lower courts' finding that Violeta Cabatbat Lim was not the biological child of Esperanza Cabatbat is reviewable on certiorari.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not the factual finding of the trial court and Court of Appeals that a claimant is not the biological child of the decedent is binding upon the Supreme Court in a petition for review under Rule 45.
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether Exhibit "5" (the purported birth registry record) is admissible as an ancient document under Section 22, Rule 132 of the Rules of Court without independent proof of execution and authenticity.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not a birth registry record more than thirty years old qualifies as an ancient document when surrounding hospital admission logs and national civil registry archives show no record of the birth.
3.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether the collateral heirs’ action is barred by Article 263 of the Civil Code governing actions to impugn the legitimacy of a child.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not an action instituted by collateral relatives to claim an inheritance by asserting that the putative child was never born of the decedent is an action to impugn legitimacy governed by Article 263 of the Civil Code.
4.  **[Secondary Issue - Succession]** Whether the surviving spouses of deceased brothers of the decedent are entitled to participate in the intestate estate by right of representation under Article 1001 of the Civil Code.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not surviving spouses of deceased brothers are legal heirs entitled to participate in the collateral inheritance of the decedent.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Reviewability of Factual Findings on Biological Filiation
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** The factual findings of the CFI and IAC that Violeta was not the biological offspring of Esperanza Cabatbat are conclusive and binding upon the Supreme Court.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"Petitioners' first and fourth assignments of error raise factual issues. The finding of the trial court and the Court of Appeals that Violeta Cabatbat was not born of Esperanza Cabatbat is a factual finding based on the evidence presented at the trial, hence, it is conclusive upon Us. Well entrenched is the rule that 'factual findings of the trial court and the Court of Appeals are entitled to great respect' (Vda. de Roxas vs. IAC, 143 SCRA 77; Republic vs. IAC, 144 SCRA 705)."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Rule 45 Boundaries:** The Supreme Court's jurisdiction in petitions for review is restricted to questions of law. Factual evaluations cannot be relitigated.
**Substantial Evidentiary Foundation:** Both lower courts weighed the competing documentary and testimonial evidence (hospital registry entries, testimony of Amparo Reside, and the admission records) and concluded that Esperanza never gave birth to Violeta.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** The Supreme Court does not re-examine evidence on appeal. Because both the trial court and the Court of Appeals concluded on the basis of hospital records that Esperanza never gave birth to Violeta, that factual finding is final and binding.
Issue 2: Applicability of the Ancient Document Rule (Rule 132, Sec. 22)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** The ancient document rule does not protect a birth record surrounded by material circumstances of suspicion and directly refuted by primary public and hospital registries.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"Section 22, Rule 132 of the Rules of Court which provides that: 'Where a private writing is more than thirty years old, is produced from a custody in which it would naturally be found if genuine, and is unblemished by any alterations or circumstances of suspicion, no other evidence of its execution and authenticity need be given' does not apply to petitioners' Exhibit '5,' the supposed birth registry record of defendant Violeta Cabatbat..."
"...Furthermore, the absence of a record of the birth of petitioner Violeta Cabatbat in the Office of the Civil Registrar General, puts a cloud on the genuineness of her Exhibit 5."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Requirement of Lack of Suspicion:** The ancient document rule requires that the document be "unblemished by any alterations or circumstances of suspicion."
**Direct Evidentiary Disproof:** The hospital's Registry Book of Admissions showed that Esperanza was never admitted as an obstetrics patient at any time between December 1, 1947, and June 15, 1948.
**Hospital Live Birth Records:** On the alleged birth date (May 26, 1948), only Benita Lastimosa was admitted and gave birth to a child ("Baby Girl Lastimosa").
**Absence in Civil Registry General:** The Civil Registrar General certified that it maintained no record of Violeta's birth on May 26, 1948 or 1949, destroying the premise of reliable public custody and casting heavy suspicion over Exhibit "5".
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** A document over 30 years old cannot be presumed genuine if the facts demonstrate it is highly suspicious. Because the hospital logbooks prove the alleged mother was never admitted for childbirth and the national registry has no record of the birth, the purported birth certificate was clouded with suspicion and properly rejected.
Issue 3: Inapplicability of Civil Code Article 263 (Action to Impugn Legitimacy)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** Article 263 does not bar the collateral heirs' suit, because an action alleging that a decedent never gave birth to the claimant is not an action to impugn marital legitimacy, but a claim of non-filiation.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"Petitioners' recourse to Article 263 of the New Civil Code is not well-taken. This legal provision refers to an action to impugn legitimacy. It is inapplicable to this case because this is not an action to impugn the **legitimacy** of a child, but an action of the private respondents to claim their inheritance as legal heirs of their childless deceased aunt. They do not claim that petitioner Violeta Cabatbat Lim is an illegitimate child of the deceased, but that she is not the decedent's child at all. Being neither a legally adopted child, nor an acknowledged natural child, nor a child by legal fiction of Esperanza Cabatbat, Violeta is not a legal heir of the deceased."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Doctrinal Scope of Article 263:** Article 263 presumes a maternal-child relationship and strictly governs attacks by the husband (or his heirs) against the **legitimacy** of a child conceived or born to the wife in wedlock (e.g., alleging adultery or physical impossibility of access).
**Distinction between Non-Filiation and Illegitimacy:** The collateral relatives are not alleging that Violeta is an **adulterous or illegitimate** child of Esperanza. They assert that Esperanza had **no maternal filiation whatsoever** with Violeta.
**True Nature of Action:** The action is a claim for legal inheritance by collateral relatives asserting that their sister died childless.
**Status of Ward:** Violeta was merely a ward (**ampon**). Without a decree of judicial adoption, natural filiation, or legal fiction, she possessed no status as a compulsory heir under succession law.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** Article 263 restricts attacks on whether a child born to a married woman is the legitimate child of her husband. It does not apply where collateral relatives prove that the deceased woman never actually gave birth to the child at all. Because Violeta was merely taken in as a ward without a legal adoption, she is not an heir.
Issue 4: Legal Capacity of Widows of Deceased Brothers to Inherit by Representation (Art. 1001)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** The surviving spouses (widows) of deceased brothers are not collateral heirs and cannot participate in the intestate estate alongside the surviving sisters, nephews, and nieces.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"...affirming the appealed decision, but with modification of paragraphs 2 and 4 of the dispositive portion thereof, by excluding the widows Adela B. Vda. de Frianeza and Decideria Q. Vda. de Frianeza, who are not legal heirs of Esperanza Frianeza Cabatbat from participating with their children and the surviving sisters of the deceased in the one-fourth share of the estate pertaining to the latter under Article 1001 of the Civil Code."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Scope of Representation in the Collateral Line:** Under the Civil Code, the right of representation in the collateral line takes place only in favor of children of brothers or sisters (nephews and nieces).
**Exclusion of In-Laws:** Widows of deceased brothers are collateral relatives by affinity, not consanguinity, and have no statutory right to inherit intestate from their deceased spouse's sister.
**Recomputation:** The one-fourth ($1/4$) intestate share belonging to the collateral branch passes exclusively to the surviving sisters and the nephews and nieces who represent their deceased fathers (Daniel and Domingo).
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** In an intestate estate where brothers and sisters concur with a surviving spouse, only biological sisters, brothers, and the children of deceased siblings (nephews/nieces) inherit. Sisters-in-law (widows of deceased brothers) are not heirs under the law of intestate succession and cannot participate.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.** (Unanimous decision by the First Division).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is denied for lack of merit. The appealed decision is affirmed, but with modification of paragraphs 2 and 4 of the dispositive portion thereof, by excluding the widows Adela B. Vda. de Frianeza and Decideria Q. Vda. de Frianeza, who are not legal heirs of Esperanza Frianeza Cabatbat from participating with their children and the surviving sisters of the deceased in the one-fourth share of the estate pertaining to the latter under Article 1001 of the Civil Code.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Petitioners lost. The Supreme Court affirmed the IAC and CFI decisions ruling that Violeta Cabatbat Lim is not the daughter or heir of Dra. Esperanza Cabatbat, and must return the unauthorized funds she withdrew. The estate partition was upheld, subject only to the modification that the widows of Esperanza’s deceased brothers are excluded from sharing in the estate.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Labagala v. Santiago**
**Full Official Caption:** Ida C. Labagala, Petitioner, vs. Nicolasa T. Santiago, Amanda T. Santiago, and Hon. Court of Appeals, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 132305
**Date of Promulgation:** December 4, 2001
**Philippine Reports:** 422 Phil. 699
**Ponente:** Quisumbing, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Second Division; Bellosillo, **J.** (**Chairman**), Mendoza, and De Leon, Jr., **JJ.**, concur; Buena, **J.**, on official leave. No separate opinions.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Persons and Family Relations → Paternity and Filiation → Impugning Legitimacy vs. Asserting Non-Filiation
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Law on Sales and Donations → Essential Requisites and Simulated Sales → Annulment/Void Contracts; Proof of Filiation in Intestate Succession
Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):
**Article 263, Civil Code of the Philippines (Historical Provision governing the dispute, modern counterpart: Article 170, Family Code of the Philippines)**:
"Art. 263. **The action to impugn the legitimacy of the child shall be brought within one year from the recording of the birth in the Civil Register, if the husband should be in the same place, or in a proper case, any of his heirs.**
**If he or his heirs are absent, the period shall be eighteen months if they should reside in the Philippines; and two years if abroad. If the birth of the child has been concealed, the term shall be counted from the discovery of the fraud.**"
**Modern Equivalent — Article 170, Family Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 170. The action to impugn the legitimacy of the child shall be brought within one year from the knowledge of the birth or its recording in the civil register, if the husband or, in a proper case, any of his heirs, should reside in the municipality or city where the birth took place or was recorded.
If the husband or, in his proper case, any of his heirs, do not reside at the place of birth or where it was recorded, the period shall be two years if they should reside in the Philippines, and three years if they should reside abroad. If the birth of the child has been concealed, the term shall be counted from the discovery of the fraud."
**Article 1471, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 1471. **If the price is simulated, the sale is void, but the act may be shown to have been in reality a donation, or some other act or contract.**"
**Article 725, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 725. **Donation is an act of liberality whereby a person disposes gratuitously of a thing or right in favor of another, who accepts it.**"
**Article 741, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 741. **Minors and others who cannot enter into a contract may become donees but acceptance shall be done through their parents or legal representatives.**"
The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:
1. Rule on Impugning Legitimacy vs. Denying Parentage:
**Article 263 of the Civil Code** (and its strict prescriptive period) applies exclusively to cases where a marital child's **legitimacy** is being impugned by the husband (or his heirs in specific instances) under a presumption that the child was born in wedlock. It does **not** apply to actions where a claimant is alleged **not to be the child at all** of the putative parents, nor does it bar heirs in an ordinary recovery/property action from disproving a stranger's pretended filiation.
2. Rule on Simulated Sales and Gratuitous Transfers:
Under **Article 1471**, a contract of sale where the price is entirely simulated or unpaid is void **ab initio**. While it may be shown to be a valid donation, it must comply with all formal and substantive requirements of a donation.
3. Rule on Acceptance of Donations by Minors:
Under **Articles 725 and 741**, a donation requires valid acceptance. Where the purported donee is a minor at execution, acceptance cannot be executed by the minor herself; it must be formally accepted on her behalf by her parents or legal representative. Lacking such acceptance, no donation comes into legal existence.
4. Rule on Evidentiary Hierarchy of Pedigree:
A certified record of birth from the Local Civil Registrar is primary evidence of filiation. In contrast, a baptismal certificate is conclusive only of the administration of the sacrament on that date and does **not** prove parentage or pedigree. Open use of a family name does not establish pedigree.
**Factual Trigger:**
Upon Jose Santiago's intestate death, his surviving sisters filed an action to recover his remaining 1/3 share of real property from petitioner. Petitioner claimed title via a deed of sale for ₱150,000, or alternatively by donation or intestate succession as Jose's sole daughter; respondents proved that petitioner was born to entirely different parents per her birth certificate, that no price was ever paid, and that petitioner was a minor who never had a legal guardian or parent accept any donation on her behalf.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Jose T. Santiago:** Original registered owner of the subject property under TCT No. 64729; a college graduate; brother of respondents; died intestate on February 6, 1984, without legitimate descendants.
**Nicolasa T. Santiago & Amanda T. Santiago:** Full-blood sisters and legal intestate heirs of Jose; respondents herein; previously obtained a final judgment declaring them owners of a 2/3 **pro indiviso** share of the land.
**Ida C. Labagala (claiming to be Ida C. Santiago):** Petitioner; resided on the property; claimed to be the daughter of Jose and Esperanza Cabrigas, and holder of TCT No. 172334 issued solely in her name pursuant to a purported March 1979 deed of sale.
**Leon Labagala & Cornelia Cabrigas:** The parents appearing on the Local Civil Registrar birth certificate of petitioner; Cornelia was the sister of Jose's wife, Esperanza Cabrigas.
Procedural Posture:
**RTC Manila (Branch 54, Civil Case No. 87-41515):** Respondents filed a complaint on August 5, 1987, for recovery of title, ownership, and possession against petitioner for the remaining 1/3 share. On October 17, 1990, the RTC ruled in petitioner's favor, holding the sale was a valid donation and that petitioner was Jose's daughter based on prior ejectment cases and Jose's Income Tax Return (ITR).
**Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. CV No. 32817):** On March 4, 1997, the CA reversed the RTC, declared respondents co-owners of the 1/3 **pro indiviso** share, cancelled TCT No. 172334, and directed the issuance of a new title in respondents' names.
**Supreme Court:** Petitioner filed a Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 assailing the CA decision.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**Pre-1979:** Jose T. Santiago registered a parcel of land at No. 3075-A Rizal Avenue Extension, Sta. Cruz, Manila, in his name alone under **TCT No. 64729**. His sisters, Nicolasa and Amanda Santiago, filed **Civil Case No. 56226** (CFI Manila, Branch 6) against Jose to recover their 2/3 share, alleging fraudulent registration. During his testimony in that case, Jose explicitly testified that he had no children.
**March 1979 (Notarized March 19, 1979):** Jose purportedly executed a Deed of Sale conveying the **entire** property to petitioner Ida for a stated price of **₱150,000.00**. The deed was executed with a thumbmark (despite Jose being a college graduate who signed his name in full), falsely stated Jose was single (he had been married to Esperanza Cabrigas), stated Ida was of legal age (she was then approximately 15 years old), and stated the land was free of encumbrances (despite annotated adverse claims and **lis pendens**). Ida never paid any consideration.
**April 20, 1981:** The CFI rendered judgment in Civil Case No. 56226 in favor of Nicolasa and Amanda, adjudicating a 2/3 **pro indiviso** share to them and 1/3 to Jose, ordering the Register of Deeds of Manila to annotate their names.
**February 6, 1984:** Jose died intestate.
**1985:** Respondents instituted two successive ejectment suits against petitioner and other occupants. The first was decided in petitioner's favor; the second was dismissed.
**January 26, 1987:** Almost eight years after the alleged deed of sale was executed, petitioner registered it with the Register of Deeds of Manila, securing **TCT No. 172334** solely in her name.
**August 5, 1987:** Respondents filed a complaint for recovery of title, ownership, and possession (Civil Case No. 87-41515) before the RTC of Manila to recover Jose's 1/3 share.
**August 11, 1988 (Pre-Trial):** Petitioner's counsel admitted that petitioner possessed no birth certificate indicating that she was named "Ida Santiago."
**October 17, 1990:** The RTC ruled in favor of petitioner, holding that the unpaid deed was a valid donation and that she was Jose's daughter and sole heir.
**March 4, 1997:** The Court of Appeals reversed the RTC, finding the deed of sale void/forged, the donation invalid for lack of acceptance by a legal guardian, and petitioner's filiation disproved by her birth certificate showing Leon Labagala and Cornelia Cabrigas as her true parents.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments:
**Main Thesis:** Petitioner is the sole heir of Jose T. Santiago as his daughter, and/or the lawful owner of the property under a deed of sale that effectively operated as a valid donation.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Proof of Filiation:** She proved filiation through: (a) Jose's Income Tax Return (ITR) listing her as his daughter; (b) records and decisions in the prior 1985 ejectment cases where respondents supposedly "considered" her Jose's daughter; and (c) her baptismal certificate naming Jose and Esperanza as parents.
**Proscription Against Collateral Attack:** Respondents are barred from assailing her filiation in a collateral property action under **Article 263 of the Civil Code** and **Sayson v. CA**, which mandate that legitimacy can only be impugned in a direct action within the prescriptive periods.
**Validity of Conveyance:** The conveyance was genuine; Jose was free to place a thumbmark instead of his signature. If deemed without consideration, it operated as a valid donation, and she took title to prevent tax forfeiture.
B. Respondent's Arguments:
**Main Thesis:** Petitioner is a non-relative whose deed of sale is completely simulated and fake, and respondents are the sole intestate heirs entitled to Jose's 1/3 share.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Inapplicability of Article 263:** Article 263 applies only when impugning the **legitimacy** of a child born to a married couple, not where the child is asserted to be a total stranger and not the child of the deceased at all.
**Falsity of Pedigree:** Official Certificate of Record of Birth (Exhibit "H") proves petitioner was born to spouses Leon Labagala and Cornelia Cabrigas, as reported by Leon Labagala himself. Under evidence law, a baptismal certificate and ITR cannot rebut a civil registry birth certificate. Jose himself testified in Civil Case No. 56226 that he was childless.
**Nullity of Sale and Donation:** The deed of sale was completely simulated, forged, and lacked consideration (petitioner was an unemployed minor who paid nothing). As a donation, it was void because Jose only owned 1/3 of the property, and the required statutory acceptance by a minor’s legal representative under **Article 741** was completely absent.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not respondents may impugn petitioner's filiation in an ordinary civil action for recovery of title, ownership, and possession, or if they are barred by the prescriptive periods and direct-action requirement of Article 263 of the Civil Code.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether an action for recovery of property allows collateral challenge of a claimant's filiation where the adverse parties assert that the claimant is not the decedent's child at all.
2. **[Secondary Issue]** Whether or not petitioner adduced sufficient evidence to establish her filiation as the daughter and sole intestate heir of Jose T. Santiago.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether entries in an income tax return and a baptismal certificate prevail over an official civil registry birth certificate to prove parentage.
3. **[Secondary Issue]** Whether or not petitioner acquired lawful title to the subject property by virtue of the purported 1979 deed of sale or as an informal donation.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether an unpriced, simulated deed of sale executed in favor of a minor can be upheld as a valid donation without acceptance by the minor's legal representative.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Impugning Filiation via Recovery Action (Civil Code Art. 263)
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Respondents may challenge petitioner's filiation. Article 263 applies strictly to actions impugning the **legitimacy** of a marital child, not to cases where the person is alleged not to be the child of the putative parent at all.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"A careful reading of said chapter would reveal that it contemplates situations where a doubt exists that a child is indeed a man's child by his wife, and the husband (or, in proper cases, his heirs) denies the child's filiation. It does not refer to situations where a child is alleged not to be the child at all of a particular couple."
"Article 263 refers to an action to impugn the **legitimacy** of a child, to assert and prove that a person is not a man's child by his wife. However, the present case is not one impugning petitioner's legitimacy. Respondents are asserting not merely that petitioner is not a legitimate child of Jose, but that she is not a child of Jose at all. Moreover, the present action is one for recovery of title and possession, and thus outside the scope of Article 263 on prescriptive periods."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Textual Scope of Art. 263:** The Court analyzed the context of the Civil Code provisions on paternity and filiation. Art. 263 protects a child conceived or born within wedlock against the husband's (or his heirs') repudiation of biological paternity.
**Substantive Distinction:** There is a wide legal gulf between questioning the **legitimacy** of a child (conceding parentage by the mother during marriage, but alleging the husband is not the biological father) and alleging that the person is an outright stranger with no biological tie to either spouse.
**Inapplicability of Sayson:** In **Sayson v. CA**, the challenge involved an attack on a final adoption decree and conflicting claims over marital birth. Here, respondents directly claim petitioner is an outsider born to different parents entirely.
**Nature of Action:** Because the suit is for recovery of real property founded on intestate succession, respondents are entitled to prove that petitioner lacks statutory heirship rights.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:**
Article 263 of the Civil Code only stops a husband from arbitrarily claiming that his wife's baby is not his after a strict deadline passes. It does not prevent legal heirs in a property dispute from exposing an imposter who is not the biological child of the deceased couple at all.
Issue 2: Proof of Filiation (Succession Rights)
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Petitioner failed to prove she is Jose Santiago's daughter; her baptismal certificate and Jose's ITR are legally insufficient to overturn her official birth certificate.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"...[A] baptismal certificate is evidence only to prove the administration of the sacrament on the dates therein specified, but not the veracity of the declarations therein stated with respect to [a person's] kinsfolk. The same is conclusive only of the baptism administered, according to the rites of the Catholic Church, by the priest who baptized subject child, but it does not prove the veracity of the declarations and statements contained in the certificate concerning the relationship of the person baptized."
"A baptismal certificate, a private document, is not conclusive proof of filiation. More so are the entries made in an income tax return, which only shows that income tax has been paid and the amount thereof."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Official Civil Registry Primacy:** Respondents produced Exhibit "H" (Certificate of Record of Birth), showing that petitioner Ida was born to spouses Leon Labagala and Cornelia Cabrigas, with Leon Labagala himself supplying the entries.
**Evidentiary Defect of Baptismal Certificate:** Petitioner failed to produce any civil birth certificate naming Jose as her father. Settled doctrine (**Heirs of Pedro Cabais v. CA**) dictates that a baptismal certificate only proves the administration of church rites, not biological parentage.
**Weakness of ITR and Use of Name:** Income tax returns merely establish payment of taxes and cannot override civil records. Furthermore, continuous use of the surname "Santiago" does not establish pedigree under the law.
**Adverse Presumption and Jose's Testimony:** Petitioner was asked by the RTC to produce a civil registry record or certificate of non-record, but failed to do so without explanation, raising the legal presumption that withheld evidence would be adverse to her. This matched Jose's sworn testimony in Civil Case No. 56226 where he explicitly testified he had no children.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:**
A birth certificate in the civil registry is the gold standard for proving parentage. A baptismal certificate only proves that a priest poured water on a baby, and an income tax return only proves tax payments; neither can prove who your legal parents are when an official birth certificate states you belong to someone else.
Issue 3: Validity of the Purported Sale or Donation
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The deed of sale was completely simulated and void **ab initio**; it could not stand as a valid donation because petitioner was a minor at the time and the conveyance was never accepted by her legal representatives.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Clearly, there is no valid sale in this case. Jose did not have the right to transfer ownership of the entire property to petitioner since 2/3 thereof belonged to his sisters. Petitioner could not have given her consent to the contract, being a minor at the time. Consent of the contracting parties is among the essential requisites of a contract, including one of sale, absent which there can be no valid contract. Moreover, petitioner admittedly did not pay any centavo for the property, which makes the sale void."
"...Even assuming that the deed is genuine, it cannot be a valid donation. It lacks the acceptance of the donee required by Art. 725 of the Civil Code. Being a minor in 1979, the acceptance of the donation should have been made by her father, Leon Labagala or [her] mother Cornelia Cabrigas or her legal representative pursuant to Art. 741 of the same Code. No one of those mentioned in the law - in fact no one at all - accepted the 'donation' for Ida."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Intrinsic Defects Indicating Simulation/Forgery:** Jose was an educated college graduate who routinely signed documents, yet this deed bore a thumbmark. It purported to sell the **whole** property when Jose only owned 1/3, falsely described Jose as single, falsely described Ida as of legal age, and suppressed existing encumbrances.
**Void Sale:** Consent was non-existent because Ida was a minor (**Article 1327**), and the ₱150,000 price was completely simulated and admittedly unpaid, rendering the sale void **ab initio** under **Article 1471**.
**Failure as a Donation:** While **Article 1471** permits a simulated sale to be proven as a donation, donations are strictly formal contracts. Under **Article 725**, donation requires valid acceptance. Because Ida was a 15-year-old minor in 1979, **Article 741** explicitly required acceptance by her parents (Leon or Cornelia) or her legal representative. No such acceptance ever occurred.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:**
The deed of sale was a complete sham because the buyer was a minor who paid nothing and the seller signed with a thumbmark despite being an educated man. Even if treated as an attempted gift (donation), the law requires a parent or guardian to formally accept real property gifts on behalf of a minor, which never happened here.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is DENIED, and the decision of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. CV No. 32817 is AFFIRMED. Costs against petitioner.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Petitioner lost completely. The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' judgment ordering the Register of Deeds of Manila to cancel petitioner Ida's title (TCT No. 172334) and issue a new title recognizing Jose's surviving sisters, Nicolasa and Amanda Santiago, as lawful co-owners of his remaining 1/3 **pro indiviso** share by intestate succession.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: De Jesus v. Estate of Juan Gamboa Dizon**
**Full Official Caption:** Jinkie Christie A. De Jesus and Jacqueline A. De Jesus, Minors, represented by their mother, Carolina A. De Jesus, Petitioners, vs. The Estate of Decedent Juan Gamboa Dizon, Angelina V. Dizon, Carlos Dizon, Felipe Dizon, Juan Dizon, Jr. and Marylin Dizon and as Proper Parties: Forms Media Corp., Quad Management Corp., Filipinas Paper Sales Co., Inc. and Amity Construction & Industrial Enterprises, Inc., Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 142877
**Promulgation Date:** October 02, 2001
**Philippine Reports Citation:** 418 Phil. 768
**Ponente:** Vitug, **J.**
**Division/Voting Breakdown:** Third Division; Melo (**Chairman**), Panganiban, and Sandoval-Gutierrez, **JJ.**, concur. No separate opinions.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code → Paternity and Filiation → Legitimacy and Impugning Legitimacy → Presumption of Legitimacy / Standing to Impugn / Collateral Attack Bar
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Succession → Rights of Illegitimate Children → Proof of Filiation vs. Collateral Attack on Legitimate Status
Remedial Law → Special Proceedings / Actions → Partition vs. Direct Action to Impugn Filiation
**Full Text of Governing Statutory Provisions:**
**Family Code, Article 164, Paragraph 1:**
"Children conceived or born during the marriage of the parents are legitimate."
**Family Code, Article 166:**
"Legitimacy of a child may be impugned only on the following grounds:
(1) That it was physically impossible for the husband to have sexual intercourse with his wife within the first 120 days of the 300 days which immediately preceded the birth of the child because of:
(a) the physical incapacity of the husband to have sexual intercourse with his wife;
(b) the fact that the husband and wife were living separately in such a way that sexual intercourse was not possible; or
(c) serious illness of the husband, which absolutely prevented sexual intercourse;
(2) That it is proved that for biological or other scientific reasons, the child could not have been that of the husband, except in the instance provided in the second paragraph of Article 164; or
(3) That in case of children conceived through artificial insemination, the written authorization or ratification of either parent was obtained through mistake, fraud, violence, intimidation, or undue influence."
**Family Code, Article 167:**
"The child shall be considered legitimate although the mother may have declared against its legitimacy or may have been sentenced as an adulteress."
**Family Code, Article 170:**
"**The action to impugn the legitimacy of the child shall be brought within one year from the knowledge of the birth or its recording in the civil register, if the husband or, in a proper case, any of his heirs, should reside in the city or municipality where the birth took place or was recorded.**
**If the husband or, in his default, all of his heirs do not reside at the place of birth as defined in the first paragraph or where it was recorded, the period shall be two years if they should reside in the Philippines; and three years if abroad.** If the birth of the child has been concealed from or was unknown to the husband or his heirs, the period shall be counted from the discovery or knowledge of the birth of the child or of the fact of registration of said birth, whichever is earlier."
**Family Code, Article 171:**
"**The heirs of the husband may impugn the filiation of the child within the period prescribed in the preceding article only in the following cases:**
**(1) If the husband should die before the expiration of the period fixed for bringing his action;**
**(2) If he should die after the filing of the complaint, without having desisted therefrom; or**
**(3) If the child was born after the death of the husband.**"
**Family Code, Article 172:**
"The filiation of legitimate children is established by any of the following:
(1) The record of birth appearing in the civil register or a final judgment; or
(2) An admission of legitimate filiation in a public document or a private handwritten instrument and signed by the parent concerned.
In the absence of the foregoing evidence, the filiation shall be proved by:
(1) The open and continuous possession of the status of a legitimate child; or
(2) Any other means allowed by the Rules of Court and special laws."
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Rule on Presumption of Legitimacy (Art. 164, 166, 167):** Children born during lawful wedlock are conclusively presumed legitimate in the absence of the strict physical or biological grounds specified under Article 166. A mother's contrary assertion or admission does not overcome this statutory presumption (Art. 167).
**Exclusivity of Standing to Impugn (Arts. 170 & 171):** Only the legal husband, or in exceptional and restrictive circumstances specified under Article 171, his heirs, possess standing to contest or impugn the child’s legitimate filiation within the strictly prescribed prescriptive periods. Children themselves—or third parties claiming to be biological parents—have no standing to impugn the child's legitimate status.
**Direct Action vs. Collateral Attack:** The legal presumption of legitimacy confers an unassailable civil status that cannot be attacked collaterally (such as in an action for partition, accounting, or estate settlement); it can only be challenged directly in a suit specifically instituted for that purpose by the authorized party.
**Limits of Authentic Writing Recognition (Arts. 172 & 175):** While voluntary recognition of an illegitimate child in an authentic writing requires no judicial approval, it cannot be invoked when doing so collaterally repudiates and overrides the child’s existing legitimate status arising from a subsisting lawful wedlock.
**Factual Trigger:** Petitioners, born during the subsisting marriage of Carolina and Danilo de Jesus and registered as Danilo's legitimate children on their birth certificates, sought to enforce inheritance rights against the estate of decedent Juan G. Dizon via a complaint for partition, relying on Dizon’s notarized acknowledgment of paternity—thereby collaterally attacking their own un-impugned legitimate status.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Jinkie Christie A. De Jesus & Jacqueline A. De Jesus:** Minors claiming to be illegitimate daughters and forced heirs of decedent Juan Gamboa Dizon; born during the lawful marriage of Danilo and Carolina de Jesus.
**Carolina Aves de Jesus:** Mother of petitioners; legally married to Danilo B. de Jesus.
**Danilo B. de Jesus:** Legal husband of Carolina; registered father on the certificates of live birth of petitioners.
**Juan Gamboa Dizon:** Decedent who executed a notarized acknowledgment on June 7, 1991 claiming petitioners as his illegitimate children; died intestate on March 12, 1992.
**Estate of Juan Gamboa Dizon, Angelina V. Dizon (surviving spouse), Carlos, Felipe, Juan Jr., and Marylin Dizon (legitimate children), and affiliated corporations:** Respondents contesting petitioners' standing and capacity to claim as heirs in an action for partition.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on **Certiorari** under Rule 45 assailing the Order dated February 8, 2000 of the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Quezon City, Branch 88, which dismissed petitioners' complaint for "Partition with Inventory and Accounting" for lack of cause of action and improper forum.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**August 23, 1964:** Danilo B. de Jesus and Carolina Aves de Jesus contract marriage.
**March 1, 1979:** Petitioner Jacqueline A. de Jesus is born during the subsisting marriage of Danilo and Carolina. Her Certificate of Live Birth indicates Danilo de Jesus as the father.
**July 6, 1982:** Petitioner Jinkie Christie A. de Jesus is born during the subsisting marriage. Her Certificate of Live Birth also indicates Danilo de Jesus as the father.
**June 7, 1991:** Juan G. Dizon executes a notarized document expressly acknowledging Jacqueline and Jinkie Christie as his illegitimate children with Carolina Aves de Jesus.
**March 12, 1992:** Juan G. Dizon dies intestate, leaving substantial real property and corporate shares.
**July 1, 1993:** Petitioners, represented by their mother Carolina, file a complaint for "Partition with Inventory and Accounting" against the Dizon estate, the surviving spouse, and legitimate children in the RTC of Quezon City, Branch 88.
**September 13, 1993 & February 15, 1994:** RTC denies respondents' Motion to Dismiss and Motion for Reconsideration, which had argued that the partition suit improperly sought to alter the minors' status from legitimate to illegitimate.
**May 20, 1994:** The Court of Appeals (CA) upholds the RTC's denial of the motion to dismiss and remands the case for trial, noting that conflicting assertions must be threshed out since birth certificates contradicted the claim of illegitimacy.
**January 3, 2000:** After filing their answer, pre-trial brief, and various motions, respondents file an Omnibus Motion to Dismiss on the ground that the action was essentially one to compel recognition of illegitimate filiation, which cannot be threshed out in an action for partition, and that heirship requires a direct or special proceeding.
**February 8, 2000:** The RTC issues an Order dismissing petitioners' complaint for lack of cause of action and for being improper, ruling that the declaration of heirship must be made in a special proceeding.
**October 2, 2001:** The Supreme Court denies the Petition for Review on **Certiorari**, affirming the dismissal of the partition complaint.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The complaint for partition was proper because the notarized acknowledgment executed by Juan G. Dizon constitutes an authentic writing that legally establishes their illegitimate filiation without needing a separate action for judicial approval.
**Specific Contentions:**
Under **Divinagracia v. Bellosillo** (143 SCRA 356), voluntary recognition in an authentic writing (such as a notarized document) is a completed act of recognition; it confers the civil status of an acknowledged illegitimate child **ipso jure**.
No independent action or separate judicial proceeding is legally required to declare them heirs or recognized illegitimate children before filing a partition suit.
B. Respondent's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The complaint for partition must be dismissed because petitioners are, in law and by public record, the legitimate children of Danilo and Carolina de Jesus; an action for partition cannot serve as a collateral vehicle to impugn that legitimacy.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Divinagracia v. Bellosillo** is wholly inapplicable because it did not involve claimants attempting to impugn their own legitimate filiation established by birth in lawful wedlock.
Under **Sayson v. Court of Appeals** (205 SCRA 321), legitimacy cannot be collaterally attacked in a partition and accounting complaint; it must be timely challenged in a direct action frontally addressing the issue.
An action for partition is not the proper forum to ascertain contested paternity and filiation or to secure a declaration of heirship.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not children conceived and born during a valid marriage may, on the strength of a notarized acknowledgment of paternity by a third party, collaterally impugn their legitimate filiation in an ordinary action for partition in order to claim succession rights from the estate of said third party.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether petitioners' recognition as illegitimate children in an authentic writing by the decedent is sufficient to claim shares in his estate, where petitioners were born in lawful wedlock and their birth certificates identify the mother's husband as their father.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not minors born during a subsisting lawful marriage can establish their illegitimate filiation to a third-party decedent via a notarized document and claim inheritance through an action for partition without their legitimate status having first been successfully impugned in a direct action by the legal husband or his qualified heirs.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Impugning Legitimate Filiation Collaterally in a Partition Suit
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Children born in lawful wedlock are conclusively presumed legitimate, a status that can only be attacked directly by the legal husband (or in limited exceptions, his heirs) within strict prescriptive periods; consequently, an authentic writing executed by a third party cannot be utilized to collaterally repudiate legitimate status in an action for partition.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"There is perhaps no presumption of the law more firmly established and founded on sounder morality and more convincing reason than the presumption that children born in wedlock are legitimate."
"Quite remarkably, upon the expiration of the periods set forth in Article 170, and in proper cases Article 171, of the Family Code (which took effect on 03 August 1988), the action to impugn the legitimacy of a child would no longer be legally feasible and the status conferred by the presumption becomes fixed and unassailable."
"Succinctly, in an attempt to establish their illegitimate filiation to the late Juan G. Dizon, petitioners, in effect, would impugn their legitimate status as being children of Danilo de Jesus and Carolina Aves de Jesus. This step cannot be aptly done because the law itself establishes the legitimacy of children conceived or born during the marriage of the parents. The presumption of legitimacy fixes a civil status for the child born in wedlock, and only the father, or in exceptional instances the latter's heirs, can contest in an appropriate action the legitimacy of a child born to his wife. Thus, it is only when the legitimacy of a child has been successfully impugned that the paternity of the husband can be rejected."
"Jurisprudence is strongly settled that the paramount declaration of legitimacy by law cannot be attacked collaterally, one that can only be repudiated or contested in a direct suit specifically brought for that purpose. Indeed, a child so born in such wedlock shall be considered legitimate although the mother may have declared against its legitimacy or may have been sentenced as having been an adulteress."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Statutory Basis and Presumption of Legitimacy:** Under Article 164 of the Family Code, children conceived or born during the marriage of the parents are legitimate. Danilo and Carolina were married on August 23, 1964; Jacqueline and Jinkie were born in 1979 and 1982 during this valid marriage, and their certificates of live birth unequivocally designate Danilo de Jesus as their father.
**Conclusiveness of Presumption:** This presumption of legitimacy yields only to the strict, exclusive grounds under Article 166 (physical impossibility of access due to physical incapacity, living separately, or serious illness; biological/scientific proof; or vitiated consent in artificial insemination). None of these grounds were shown or legally invoked.
**Absolute Bar of Prescriptive Periods:** Under Article 170 (and 171 for heirs), the action to impugn legitimacy must be brought within one, two, or three years depending on the husband's residence. Once these periods expire, the status conferred by the presumption becomes fixed, conclusive, and unassailable.
**Strict Exclusivity of Standing:** Only the husband (Danilo) or, in strictly delineated instances under Article 171, his heirs, possess legal standing to contest the child's legitimacy. The mother, the children themselves, or a putative third-party biological father have no standing to destroy the child's legitimate status.
**Distinction from Divinagracia:** In **Divinagracia v. Bellosillo**, the plaintiff was an acknowledged spurious child whose legitimate filiation was never established or at issue. Here, petitioners are legally presumed legitimate children seeking to declare themselves illegitimate children of another man. The doctrine that voluntary recognition via an authentic writing dispenses with judicial action applies only when there is no existing legitimate filiation to impugn.
**Prohibition Against Collateral Attack:** A child’s legitimacy cannot be challenged collaterally as an incidental issue in an action for partition. It requires a direct action frontally addressing legitimacy brought by the party specifically designated by law. Furthermore, under Article 167, the mother's declarations or actions cannot prejudice or alter the child's legitimate status. Because their legitimate status to Danilo remains legally intact, Juan G. Dizon’s notarized acknowledgment is legally irrelevant and ineffective to confer inheritance rights.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
(Plain-Language Explanation) The Supreme Court held that children born during a valid marriage cannot claim to be someone else's illegitimate children in a partition case, even if that other man recognized them in a notarized document. The law conclusively presumes children born in wedlock to be legitimate, and this status can **only** be challenged by the legal husband (or his heirs under specific conditions) in a direct lawsuit filed within strict time limits. Because the legal husband never impugned their legitimacy, that legitimate status is permanent and unassailable; the children cannot collaterally attack their own legitimacy to claim an inheritance from another man's estate.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the foregoing disquisitions considered, the instant petition is DENIED. No costs. SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The petition was denied, and the RTC's dismissal of petitioners' complaint for partition was affirmed. Petitioners cannot claim any hereditary share in the estate of decedent Juan G. Dizon because their legal status as the legitimate children of Danilo de Jesus remains intact and cannot be collaterally attacked.
