### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Vda. de Alberto v. Court of Appeals**
**Full Official Caption: Natividad del Rosario Vda. de Alberto, in her individual capacity and as judicial guardian of the minors Antonio Alberto, Jr. and Lourdes Alberto, Petitioners, vs. The Hon. Court of Appeals and Antonio J. Alberto, Jr., assisted by his mother as his natural guardian, Andrea Jongco, Respondents.**
**Citation & Metadata:**
**Docket Number:** G.R. No. 29759
**Promulgation Date:** May 18, 1989
**Philippine Reports Citation:** 173 SCRA 488
**Ponente:** Bidin, **J.**
**Division:** Third Division
**Voting Breakdown:** Unanimous; Fernan, **C.J.**, Gutierrez, Jr., Feliciano, and Cortes, **JJ.**, concur. No separate opinions.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
Topic Hierarchy
**Primary Topic:** Civil Law → Succession → Partition and Distribution of Estate → Rescission of Partition for Preterition / Lesion → Prescription of Actions
**Secondary Topics:**
Family Law → Paternity and Filiation → Recognition of Natural Children → Period to File Action / Proof of Filiation
Remedial Law → Special Proceedings → Settlement of Estate of Deceased Persons → Character of Proceedings (**In Rem**) and Bar by Prior Judgment
Remedial Law → Civil Procedure → Jurisdiction over the Subject Matter → Estoppel by Laches / Raising Lack of Jurisdiction for the First Time on Appeal
Full Text of Governing Statutory Provisions
**Article 1100, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 1100. **The action for rescission on account of lesion shall prescribe after four years from the time the partition was made.**"
**Article 1104, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 1104. **A partition made with preterition of any of the compulsory heirs shall not be rescinded, unless it be proved that there was bad faith or fraud on the part of the other persons interested;** but the latter shall be proportionately obliged to pay to the person omitted the share which belongs to him."
**Article 1108, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 1108. **Prescription, both acquisitive and extinctive, runs against:**
**(1) Minors and other incapacitated persons who have parents, guardians or other legal representatives;**
(2) Absentees who have administrators, either appointed by them before their disappearance, or appointed by the courts;
(3) Persons living abroad, who have managers or attorneys-in-fact;
(4) Juridical persons, except the State and its subdivisions.
Persons who are disqualified from administering their property have a right to claim damages from their legal representatives, whose negligence has been the cause of prescription."
**Article 285, Civil Code of the Philippines (Historical Basis Cited in Decision):**
"Art. 285. **The action for the recognition of natural children may be brought only during the lifetime of the presumed parents, except in the following cases:**
**(1) If the father or mother died during the minority of the child, in which case the latter may file the action before the expiration of four years from the attainment of his majority;**
(2) If after the death of the father or of the mother a document should appear of which no knowledge was previously had, in which the child is expressly recognized.
In these cases, the action must be commenced within four years from the finding of the document."
**(Modern Equivalent: Article 175 in relation to Article 172, Family Code of the Philippines: "The action must be brought within the same period specified in Article 173, except when the action is based on the second paragraph of Article 172, in which case the action may be brought during the lifetime of the alleged parent.")**
Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provisions
1. **Rescission of Partition Barred by Four-Year Period:** An action seeking to set aside or rescind a judicially approved partition on the ground of fraudulent preterition of an alleged compulsory heir under **Article 1104** must be brought within **four (4) years from the approval of the agreement of partition by the probate court**, pursuant to **Article 1100**.
2. **Running of Prescription Against Represented Minors:** Under **Article 1108(1)**, minority does not stall acquisitive or extinctive prescription if the minor has a living parent, guardian, or legal representative. Consequently, an action for recognition under **Article 285(1)** where the presumed parent died during the child's minority must be commenced within **four (4) years after the death of the presumed parent** if the minor is represented by a surviving parent or guardian.
3. **In Rem** Finality of Probate Orders: A decree of final distribution in intestate proceedings binds the whole world through statutory publication; an excluded heir cannot assail the closed partition via an independent civil action once final and executed.
4. **Jurisdiction Estoppel:** A party who participates actively in trial proceedings cannot raise the trial court's lack of subject-matter jurisdiction for the first time on appeal (**Tijam v. Sibonghanoy** doctrine).
5. **Incompetence of Unsigned Birth Certificates:** A birth certificate not signed by the putative father is legally incompetent to prove paternity or involuntary recognition.
Factual Trigger
Andrea Jongco, on behalf of her minor son Antonio J. Alberto, Jr., filed an independent action on September 8, 1960 for compulsory acknowledgment and partition of the estate of Antonio C. Alberto, Sr., who died on July 3, 1949, and whose intestate estate was judicially settled and partitioned by final court approval on November 9, 1953. The action was instituted 11 years after the putative father's death and nearly 7 years after the final judicial partition, despite Andrea Jongco's presence and representation of the child throughout that period.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
Key Parties & Roles
**Antonio C. Alberto, Sr.:** Decedant/putative father who died on July 3, 1949.
**Natividad del Rosario Vda. de Alberto:** Surviving legitimate spouse of Antonio C. Alberto, Sr.; petitioner in her individual capacity and as judicial guardian of her minor legitimate children.
**Lourdes Alberto & Antonio Alberto, Jr. (Legitimate):** Legitimate minor children of Antonio C. Alberto, Sr. and Natividad del Rosario; co-petitioners.
**Antonio J. Alberto, Jr. (Respondent Alberto, Jr.):** Minor plaintiff/private respondent (born September 10, 1942), claiming to be the unacknowledged natural child of Antonio C. Alberto, Sr.
**Andrea Jongco:** Mother and natural guardian of respondent Antonio J. Alberto, Jr.; assisted him in the lawsuit.
Procedural Posture
**Originating Court:** Court of First Instance (CFI) of Manila, Branch presiding over Civil Case No. 44164 (complaint for acknowledgment and partition). The CFI dismissed the complaint on August 10, 1964.
**Intermediate Appellate Review:** The Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. No. 34750-R) reversed the CFI on August 31, 1968, declaring respondent Alberto, Jr. an acknowledged natural child entitled to a 1/5 **pro indiviso** share. The CA denied reconsideration on October 14, 1968.
**Supreme Court Vehicle:** Petition for Review on **Certiorari** under Rule 45 filed by petitioners against the CA Decision and Resolution.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1941:** Antonio C. Alberto, Sr. and Andrea Jongco allegedly cohabit as husband and wife without legal impediment to marry.
**September 10, 1942:** Antonio J. Alberto, Jr. (private respondent) is born to Andrea Jongco. Private respondent alleges Antonio, Sr. recognized him and introduced him as his child.
**Circa 1944:** Andrea Jongco and Antonio, Sr. separate. Antonio, Sr. marries petitioner Natividad del Rosario (first in a secret civil marriage in Pililla, Rizal, later solemnized religiously). Andrea learns of this marriage.
**July 3, 1949:** Antonio C. Alberto, Sr. dies intestate. Andrea Jongco stops receiving alleged support for respondent Alberto, Jr.
**July 17, 1949:** Natividad del Rosario files a petition for intestate proceedings in the CFI of Manila (Sp. Proc. No. 9092) for the settlement of the estate of Antonio C. Alberto, Sr., valued at ₱74,963.81. Respondent Alberto, Jr. is not included in the list of heirs. Notice is published pursuant to the Rules of Court.
**November 9, 1953:** The intestate court approves the project of partition and issues an order of distribution adjudicating the residue of the estate to Natividad and her legitimate children. Sp. Proc. No. 9092 is terminated.
**November 9, 1957:** The four-year prescriptive period to rescind the partition expires under Article 1100 of the Civil Code.
**September 8, 1960:** Minor Antonio J. Alberto, Jr., assisted by Andrea Jongco, files a complaint in the CFI of Manila for acknowledgment as a natural child, delivery of 1/4 (later claimed as 1/5) share in the estate, and ₱5,000 attorney's fees.
**September 21, 1960:** Petitioners file a Motion to Dismiss based on: (1) bar by prior judgment, and (2) statute of limitations/prescription. Denied by the CFI on November 11, 1960.
**August 10, 1964:** The CFI renders judgment dismissing the complaint and petitioners' counterclaim, finding Andrea's testimony incredible, tainted by laches, and contradicted by disinterested relatives.
**August 31, 1968:** The CA reverses the CFI, declares respondent Alberto, Jr. an acknowledged natural child, and awards him 1/5 **pro indiviso** of the estate subject to Natividad's usufruct.
**October 14, 1968:** The CA denies petitioners' Motion for Reconsideration.
**May 18, 1989:** The Supreme Court reverses the CA and reinstates the CFI decision.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The CFI had no jurisdiction; regardless, respondent's independent action for recognition and partition is barred by **res judicata**, extinctive prescription, and laches, and respondent failed to legally prove paternity.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Lack of Subject-Matter Jurisdiction:** The suit was filed in 1960 after R.A. No. 1401 created the Juvenile and Domestic Relations Court (JDRC) of Manila, which possessed exclusive original jurisdiction over paternity and acknowledgment. Lack of subject-matter jurisdiction cannot be waived and can be raised anytime, even on appeal.
**Bar by Prior Judgment:** Sp. Proc. No. 9092 was an **in rem** proceeding terminated by final order of distribution on November 9, 1953. That decree settled heirs and title, binding the whole world. It cannot be disturbed by an independent collateral action.
**Statute of Limitations / Prescription:**
Rescission of partition based on preterition must be brought within 4 years from court approval (Arts. 1100, 1104). The period lapsed on November 9, 1957.
Minority does not prevent prescription where the minor has a living parent/legal guardian (Art. 1108). Under Art. 285, the action for recognition must be filed within 4 years of the presumed parent's death if the minor has a representative; here, 11 years elapsed.
Actions for injury to rights prescribe in 4 years (Art. 1146) or 5 years (Art. 1149).
**Laches:** Andrea waited 16 years after learning of Antonio, Sr.'s marriage in 1944, and 11 years after his death in 1949, causing severe prejudice through witness unavailability and memory loss.
**Evaluation of Factual Evidence:** The CA misapprehended facts. Andrea's promiscuous background (5 children with 4 different men) discredits her paternity claim; the birth certificate was not signed by Antonio, Sr. and was legally incompetent under **Reyes v. Court of Appeals**.
B. Respondent's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Respondent Alberto, Jr. is entitled to recognition as a natural child and to his compulsory share because he was fraudulently omitted from the intestate proceedings without notice.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Absence of Notice:** Respondent had no knowledge or notice of Sp. Proc. No. 9092; hence, the final distribution cannot bar his rights as an omitted compulsory heir.
**Non-prescription of Partition:** An action for partition among co-heirs/co-owners does not prescribe under Art. 494.
**Tolling via Minority:** Respondent was a minor (18 years old when filing); under Art. 285(1), a minor has up to 4 years after reaching majority to sue for recognition if the parent dies during minority.
**Sufficiency of Proof:** Continuous possession of the status of a natural child was established through credible testimony of disinterested witnesses (Eufracia Cailan and Encarnacion Peralta) and corroborated by his birth and baptismal certificates.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the Court of First Instance lacked jurisdiction over the action for acknowledgment and partition due to the enactment of R.A. No. 1401 creating the Juvenile and Domestic Relations Court, and whether petitioners are barred from raising this issue for the first time on appeal.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not respondent Alberto, Jr.'s independent action for recognition and partition is barred by prior judgment (**res judicata**) due to the final order of distribution in the intestate settlement proceedings (Sp. Proc. No. 9092).
3. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not respondent Alberto, Jr.'s action for rescission of the judicial partition and compulsory acknowledgment has prescribed under Articles 1100, 1104, 1108, and 285 of the Civil Code.
4. **[Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondent's long, unexplained delay of 11 years after the father's death bars the claim under the equitable doctrine of laches.
5. **[Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the Court of Appeals erred in reversing the CFI's factual findings and holding that respondent Alberto, Jr. was sufficiently proven to be an acknowledged natural child using witness testimony and an unsigned birth certificate.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Jurisdiction of the CFI vs. JDRC Raised for the First Time on Appeal
**(a) Short Answer: NO** (to petitioners' plea). The objection cannot be entertained; petitioners are estopped by active participation, and the JDRC had already been abolished by B.P. Blg. 129.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"This Court has already ruled that the question of jurisdiction not raised in the trial court cannot be raised on appeal... Besides, a party who had voluntarily participated in the trial, like the herein petitioners, cannot later on raise the issue of the court's lack of jurisdiction..."
"Moreover, there are no more Juvenile and Domestic Relations Courts today. Under Batas Pambansa Blg. 129, the functions of the Juvenile and Domestic Relations Court have been transferred to the Regional Trial Courts..."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Estoppel by Laches in Jurisdiction:** While subject-matter jurisdiction is generally conferred by law and non-waivable, jurisprudence (**Tijam v. Sibonghanoy**, **Dalman**, **Royales**) dictates that a litigant cannot invoke a court's jurisdiction, seek affirmative relief, fully try the case, and then repudiate that same jurisdiction after receiving an adverse result.
**Statutory Reorganization:** Under B.P. Blg. 129, the separate JDRCs were abolished and their jurisdiction merged into the Regional Trial Courts. Remanding or dismissing on JDRC jurisdictional grounds would be functionally moot.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):** Petitioners actively fought the case inside the regular trial court for years without complaining. Under long-standing doctrine, you cannot treat a court's jurisdiction as a lottery where you only object after you lose, especially since the specialized domestic relations court they were pointing to no longer exists.
Issue 2: Bar by Prior Judgment (**Res Judicata** via Estate Settlement)
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The final decree of distribution in the intestate settlement is a conclusive proceeding **in rem** that binds all parties, including unnotified claimants.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"This Court has invariably ruled that insolvency proceedings and settlement of a decedent's estate are both proceedings **in rem** which are binding against the whole world. All persons having interest in the subject matter involved, whether they were notified or not, are equally bound..."
"The court acquires jurisdiction over all persons interested, through the publication of the notice prescribed... and any order that may be entered therein is binding against all of them..."
"...a final order of distribution of the estate of a deceased person vests the title to the land of the estate in the distributees; and that the only instance where a party interested in a probate proceeding may have a final liquidation set aside is when he is left out by reason of circumstances beyond his control or through mistake or inadvertence not imputable to negligence. Even then, the better practice to secure relief is reopening of the same case by proper motion within the reglementary period, instead of an independent action, the effect of which, if successful, would be, as in the instant case, for another court or judge to throw out a decision or order already final and executed and reshuffle properties long ago distributed and disposed of..."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**In Rem Effect of Intestate Decrees:** Notice by publication confers jurisdiction over all interested persons. Decrees of distribution conclude the title and status of heirs against the whole world.
**Impropriety of Independent Action:** A finalized probate distribution cannot be attacked by filing an independent civil lawsuit years later before a different branch, which would effectively nullify a final, executed order of a co-equal court.
**Proper Remedy:** The sole relief for an excluded claimant is a timely motion to reopen the original probate case within the reglementary period based on excusable mistake or fraud, not an independent collateral action.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):** Probate and intestate proceedings bind the entire world through published notice, whether a person received direct personal notice or not. Once an estate is distributed and closed by final decree, an excluded heir cannot simply file a separate lawsuit years later to unravel the partition and take properties back.
Issue 3: Prescription of Actions for Rescission and Recognition
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The four-year prescriptive period to rescind the partition expired in 1957; furthermore, because the minor had a surviving parent/representative, prescription for recognition ran from the putative father's death and expired in 1953.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Intestate proceedings were terminated as alleged in the complaint itself on November 9, 1953 so that said four years prescriptive period expired on November 9, 1957. Hence, the present action filed on September 8, 1960 and which has for one of its objects the rescission of the agreement of partition among the petitioners, as approved by the intestate court, is already barred by prescription."
"It has also been ruled by this Court that the four years period provided in Article 1100 of the Civil Code (formerly Art. 1076 of the old Civil Code) should commence to run from the approval of the agreement of partition by the Court..."
"While as a general rule the action for partition among co-owners does not prescribe so long as the co-ownership is expressly or impliedly recognized (Art. 494, Civil Code), petitioners herein had never recognized respondent as a co-owner or co-heir either expressly or impliedly. Consequently, the rule on non-prescription of action for partition of property owned in common (Art. 494) does not apply to the case at bar."
"Art. 1108. Prescription, both acquisitive and extinctive, runs against: (1) Minors and other incapacitated persons who have parents, guardians or other legal representatives..."
"However, if the minor has a guardian as in this case, prescription runs against him even during minority... In such case, the action for recognition must be instituted within four (4) years after the death of the natural father... Antonio C. Alberto, Sr., the alleged father, died on July 3, 1949. The complaint for acknowledgment and partition was filed eleven (11) years later, on September 8, 1960. Hence, prescription had set in."
"...to be entitled to the recovery of the property from the estate, Alberto, Jr. must first rescind the partition and distribution approved by the intestate proceedings, otherwise, the recovery of any property from the petitioners is not possible."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Prerequisite of Rescission:** Respondent cannot recover any estate property without first rescinding the approved partition. Under Art. 1104, an alleged preterition due to bad faith gives rise to an action for rescission, which under Art. 1100 and **Samson v. Araneta**, strictly prescribes in **4 years from judicial approval** (November 9, 1953 to November 9, 1957). The action filed in 1960 was 3 years too late.
**Inapplicability of Art. 494:** Co-ownership imprescriptibility applies only where co-ownership is admitted. Petitioners never acknowledged Alberto, Jr. as a co-heir.
**Interaction of Arts. 1108 and 285:** Although Art. 285(1) allows minors up to 4 years after reaching majority to claim filiation, **Art. 1108 explicitly enforces extinctive prescription against minors who have living parents or legal guardians**. Under **Wenzel** and **Magallanes**, when a represented minor's putative parent dies, the 4-year clock begins immediately at the parent's death (July 3, 1949) and expires 4 years later (July 3, 1953). The 1960 suit was 7 years late.
**Residual Statute of Limitations:** Even treating it as an injury to rights, the action would still be barred under Art. 1146 (4 years) or Art. 1149 (5 years).
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):** An omitted heir must rescind the existing judicial partition before claiming property, and that rescission action must be brought within four years of court approval. While minors typically have until four years after turning 21 to sue for recognition, the law creates an exception when the minor has a living parent representing them—in that case, the clock starts immediately upon the father's death. Because Andrea was present and represented her son, both the time to claim recognition and the time to break open the partition had long since expired.
Issue 4: Equitable Defense of Laches
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Respondent and his mother were guilty of unreasonable and prejudicial delay by waiting 16 years after discovering the father's marriage and 11 years after his death before taking action.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"This Court has consistently declared that laches is the failure or neglect, for an unreasonable and unexplained length of time, to do that which by exercising due diligence, could or should have been done earlier. The negligence or omission to assert a right within a reasonable time, warrants a presumption that the party entitled to assert it either has abandoned it or declined to assert it..."
"'The assertion of doubtful claims, after long delay, cannot be favored by the courts. Time inevitably tends to obliterate occurrences from the memory of witnesses, and even where the recollection appears to be entirely clear, the true clue to the solution of a case may be hopelessly lost. These considerations constitute one of the pillars of the doctrine long familiar in equity jurisprudence to the effect that laches or unreasonable delay on the part of a plaintiff in seeking to enforce a right is not only persuasive of a want of merit but may, according to the circumstances, be destructive of the right itself. **Vigilantibus non dormientibus equites subvenit**'..."
"...'The law serves those who are vigilant and diligent and not those who sleep when the law requires them to act...' The law does not encourage laches, indifference, negligence or ignorance."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Unjustified Inaction:** Andrea Jongco knew of Antonio, Sr.'s marriage in 1944 and stopped receiving support when he died in 1949. Yet she waited until 1960 to sue.
**Material Prejudice to Defense:** The 11-year delay sealed the putative father's lips by death, and key defense witnesses (such as Antonio, Sr.'s mother) grew too old and incapacitated to provide coherent testimony.
**Minority Cannot Excuse Laches Here:** Just as under Art. 1108 for prescription, a minor cannot hide behind minority to excuse laches when fully represented by an adult parent who slept on the claims.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):** Equity aids the vigilant, not those who sleep on their rights. The mother knew about the marriage in 1944 and the father's death in 1949, yet waited over a decade to sue—until the father was dead and older relatives could no longer testify clearly. This unreasonable delay destroyed the claim.
Issue 5: Sufficiency of Paternity Evidence & Exception to the Factual Review Rule
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The CA erred in overturning the trial court. An exception to the rule on finality of appellate factual findings applies because the CA and CFI contradicted each other; furthermore, an unsigned birth certificate cannot prove paternity.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"The established principle is that the factual findings of the Court of Appeals are final and may not be reviewed on appeal to this Court; except:... (6) when the findings of the Appellate Court are contrary to those of the trial court..."
"...in the case of **Reyes vs. Court of Appeals**, 135 SCRA 439 (1985), this Court, citing the cases of **Bercilles vs. GSIS**, 128 SCRA 53; **People vs. Villeza**, 127 SCRA 349; **Cid vs. Burnaman**, 24 SCRA 434; **Vudaurrazaga vs. C.A.**, 91 Phil. 492; and **Capistrano vs. Gabino**, 8 Phil. 135, ruled that a birth certificate not signed by the alleged father therein indicated, like in the instant case, is not competent evidence of paternity."
"...it is a fundamental rule that conclusions and findings of fact by the trial court are entitled to great weight on appeal and should not be disturbed unless for strong and cogent reasons because the trial court is in a better position to examine real evidence, as well as to observe the demeanor of the witnesses while testifying in the case..."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Re-examination of Facts:** The conflict between the trial court's dismissal and the CA's reversal authorizes the Supreme Court to evaluate the evidence directly.
**Credibility Findings Upheld:** Disinterested siblings (Jose, Zoilo, Pilar Alberto) established that Antonio, Sr. resided at the Alberto family home during the alleged cohabitation period. Andrea's propensity for promiscuous relationships (5 children with 4 men without marriage) made it impossible to attribute paternity reliably to Antonio, Sr.
**Incompetence of Birth Certificate:** Under established doctrine (**Reyes v. CA**), an administrative birth certificate not signed by the putative father is hearsay and lacks evidentiary competence to establish filiation or recognition.
**CA Conjecture Rebuffed:** The CA's theory that Natividad fabricated an out-of-town marriage to conceal records was purely speculative and contradicted by eyewitness testimony of the wedding sponsor.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):** The Supreme Court stepped in because the appellate court and trial court reached opposite factual conclusions. The trial court was right to reject the paternity claim: the mother had multiple children out of wedlock with several different men, the father's siblings proved he lived at home, and the child's birth certificate was never signed by the alleged father, making it legally useless to prove paternity.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.** (Unanimous decision penned by Bidin, **J.**).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the assailed decision of the Court of Appeals is hereby Reversed and the decision of the trial court is Reinstated. No costs.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court ruled completely in favor of petitioners Natividad del Rosario Vda. de Alberto and her legitimate children. The Court of Appeals' decision was reversed, the trial court's dismissal of private respondent's complaint was reinstated, and private respondent Antonio J. Alberto, Jr. was denied recognition and stripped of any share in the decedent's estate.

digest:
### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Short Title: Baluyot v. Baluyot**
**Full Official Caption:** Victoria U. Baluyut, Ma. Theresa U. Baluyut and Ma. Flordeliza U. Baluyut, all minors, represented by their mother and guardian **ad litem**, Norma Urbano, Petitioners, v. Felicidad S. Baluyut and Hon. Court of Appeals, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 33659; June 14, 1990; 186 SCRA 506; First Division; Medialdea, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Narvasa (**Chairman**), Cruz, and Gancayco, **JJ.**, concur; Griño-Aquino, **J.**, on leave.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Civil Law → Persons and Family Relations / Succession → Illegitimate Children → Proof of Filiation and Recognition → Compulsory Recognition vs. Voluntary Recognition
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Civil Law → Obligations and Contracts → Compromise → Non-Compromisable Matters (Civil Status and Future Support)
Full Text of Governing Statutory Provisions
Article 2035, Civil Code of the Philippines:
"No compromise upon the following questions shall be valid:
**(1) The civil status of persons;**
(2) The validity of a marriage or a legal separation;
(3) Any ground for legal separation;
**(4) Future support;**
(5) The jurisdiction of courts;
(6) Future legitime."
Article 278, Civil Code of the Philippines:
"Recognition shall be made in the **record of birth, a will, a statement before a court of record, or in any authentic writing**."
Article 283, Civil Code of the Philippines:
"In any of the following cases, the father is obliged to recognize the child as his natural child:
(1) In cases of rape, abduction or seduction, when the period of the offense coincides more or less with that of the conception;
**(2) When the child is in continuous possession of status of a child of the alleged father by the direct acts of the latter or of his family;**
**(3) When the child was conceived during the time when the mother cohabited with the supposed father;**
**(4) When the child has in his favor any evidence or proof that the defendant is his father.**"
Article 887, Paragraph 5, Civil Code of the Philippines:
"The following are compulsory heirs:
xxx
**(5) Illegitimate children mentioned in article 287, whether voluntary or recognized by judicial decree.**"
The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provisions
**General Rule on Illegitimate Children's Successional Rights:** Bare biological filiation does not confer successional rights under Article 887. An illegitimate (spurious/not natural) child must establish an **acknowledged** filiation, made either voluntarily under Article 278 or compulsorily under Article 283.
**Prohibition on Compromise (Art. 2035):** The civil status of persons (including the status of being an acknowledged child) and future support **cannot be the subject of a compromise agreement** or withdrawal for consideration.
**Strict Construction in Compulsory Recognition:** While **voluntary** acknowledgment under an authentic public document allows incidental recognition, an action for **compulsory recognition** must be direct, express, and strictly construed.
**Evidentiary Standard for "Continuous Possession of Status" (Art. 283[2]):** Requires positive, continuous, and convincing proof that the putative father openly treated the children as his own in societal and daily life. Secret maintenance, clandestine visits, or paying bills through third-party intermediaries fail this standard.
**Incompetence of Unsigned Birth Certificates (Art. 280, Act No. 3753):** A birth certificate bearing the putative father's name is completely incompetent to establish paternity or recognized filiation if it was **not signed by the putative father**.
**Factual Trigger:** Minor petitioners sought forced-heir shares in Enrique Baluyut's estate, presenting unsigned birth certificates, testimony of clandestine visits by Enrique to their mother, and hospital expenses paid through a conduit. Later, their guardian executed a withdrawal of their claim in exchange for financial assistance.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
Key Parties & Roles
**Victoria U. Baluyut, Ma. Theresa U. Baluyut, and Ma. Flordeliza U. Baluyut:** Minor petitioners claiming to be the acknowledged illegitimate (spurious) children of the deceased Enrique M. Baluyut.
**Norma Urbano:** Mother and guardian **ad litem** of the minor petitioners.
**Enrique M. Baluyut:** Deceased putative father whose intestate estate is under administration.
**Felicidad S. Baluyut:** Surviving legitimate widow and original administratrix of Enrique's estate.
**Milagros B. Villar:** Legitimate daughter of Enrique and Felicidad; substituted as Special Administratrix.
**Liberata Vasquez:** Key witness for petitioners who testified regarding Enrique's visits and that Enrique gave her money to pay Norma's hospital delivery bills.
How the Case Reached the Supreme Court
1. **Intestate Court (CFI Pampanga, Sp. Proc. No. 1835):** Petitioners intervened. The trial court declared petitioners as forced heirs under Art. 887(5) and awarded P150.00 monthly support **pendente lite**.
2. **Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. No. 38069-R):** Administratrix appealed. On April 22, 1971, the CA reversed the trial court, dismissed the intervention, and revoked support **pendente lite**, ruling that petitioners failed to prove recognized filiation. Reconsideration denied on May 24, 1971.
3. **Supreme Court:** Petitioners filed a Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 on June 19, 1971. During pendency, the parties filed a Joint Motion to Dismiss based on a compromise settlement.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**April 29, 1965:** Petitioners filed a petition for intervention in Sp. Proc. No. 1835 (**Intestate Estate of Deceased Enrique Baluyut**) in CFI Pampanga, alleging they were illegitimate children of Enrique and Norma Urbano, begotten while Enrique was married to Felicidad, and enjoyed continuous possession of the status of children by direct overt acts of maintenance.
**May 8, 1965:** CFI Pampanga issued an order admitting the petition for intervention over the opposition of Administratrix Felicidad.
**Trial Phase:** CFI held trial. Intervenors presented Norma Urbano, Liberata Vasquez, and unsigned birth certificates (Exhibits A, B, and C) naming Enrique Baluyut as father.
**Subsequent Trial Court Judgment:** CFI declared the minor intervenors forced heirs under Article 887(5) and ordered Felicidad to pay P150.00 monthly support out of the estate.
**February 15, 1966:** Administratrix filed a Notice of Appeal.
**May 4, 1966:** CFI treated intervenors' motion for execution as a motion for reconsideration and amended its decision, awarding P150.00 monthly support **pendente lite**.
**April 22, 1971:** Court of Appeals reversed the CFI judgment, dismissed the intervention, and set aside the alimony **pendente lite**. It held that bare filiation is insufficient and that the evidence failed the strict standard for compulsory recognition.
**June 19, 1971:** Petitioners filed the instant petition for review on certiorari before the Supreme Court.
**November 25, 1976:** Supreme Court granted petitioners' motion for continuation of support **pendente lite** effective June 1975.
**January 6, 1978:** Respondents manifested that Milagros B. Villar replaced Felicidad as Special Administratrix and deposited checks to purge potential contempt for unpaid interim support.
**February 14, 1980:** Intestate court approved petitioners' "Petition for Withdrawal of Intervention" based on a waiver of their rights in exchange for financial assistance from the administratrix.
**February 19, 1980:** Parties filed a Joint Motion to Dismiss before the Supreme Court based on that financial compromise.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Petitioners are recognized spurious children of the deceased Enrique M. Baluyut entitled to forced-heir successional rights and support.
**Specific Contentions:**
Biological filiation was proven through the credible testimony of Norma Urbano and Liberata Vasquez.
Petitioners possessed the continuous status of recognized illegitimate children because Enrique maintained them, rented a house, and provided money for hospital delivery bills.
The strict rule on compulsory recognition should be relaxed under the liberal view traced from **Javellana v. Monteclaro**.
The compromise/withdrawal of intervention in exchange for financial assistance should end the litigation via their Joint Motion to Dismiss.
B. Respondents' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Petitioners failed to establish acknowledged filiation; bare illegitimate paternity confers no successional rights under Article 887.
**Specific Contentions:**
Enrique never voluntarily recognized petitioners in an authentic writing or record of birth signed by him.
The birth certificates presented were not signed by Enrique, making them incompetent evidence of filiation under Section 5 of Act No. 3753 and Article 280 of the Civil Code.
Enrique's acts showed concealment, not recognition: he visited covertly, did not pay hospital bills directly, never presented them to society, and no neighbors corroborated any open paternal treatment.
An action for compulsory recognition requires strict adherence to legal standards and cannot rest on conjecture.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether the Joint Motion to Dismiss the petition, anchored on the petitioners' withdrawal of their intervention in exchange for financial assistance from the administratrix, can be legally granted.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** May an appellate court grant a joint motion to dismiss an action concerning the acknowledgment of illegitimate filiation and support based on a compromise settlement?
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether bare proof of biological filiation is sufficient to confer successional rights upon illegitimate (spurious) children under Article 887 of the Civil Code.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Is proof of bare biological filiation alone sufficient to vest hereditary rights in illegitimate (spurious) children in the estate of their putative father?
3. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether the evidence presented by petitioners satisfies the legal requirements for voluntary or compulsory recognition.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Do unsigned birth certificates and clandestine visits/indirect payments by a putative father establish continuous possession of the status of a recognized illegitimate child under Articles 278 and 283 of the Civil Code?
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Validity of the Joint Motion to Dismiss based on Compromise Settlement
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Acknowledgment of illegitimate children affects civil status and future support, both of which are strictly non-compromisable under Article 2035 of the Civil Code.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"The withdrawal of intervention in consideration of the financial assistance extended to petitioners by the administratrix of the estate of the deceased Enrique M. Baluyut... is in the nature of a compromise settlement of the instant petition... Considering, however, that the issue involved in this case is whether or not petitioners, Victoria, Ma. Theresa and Ma. Flordeliza, all surnamed Baluyot are the acknowledged, spurious children of the deceased, Enrique M. Baluyut, the Joint Motion to Dismiss the instant petition cannot be granted, acknowledgment, affecting as it does the civil status of persons and of future support cannot be the subject of a compromise (pars. 1 and 4, Article 2035 of the Civil Code)."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
The Court examined the nature of the withdrawal of intervention in exchange for financial assistance and classified it as an extrajudicial compromise.
Under Article 2035, paragraphs 1 and 4, the law explicitly prohibits any compromise upon the "civil status of persons" and "future support."
Citing **Advincula v. Advincula**, the Court maintained that paternity and recognition cannot be bartered away, waived, or compromised; hence, the Court refused to dismiss the petition on that ground and proceeded to resolve the merits.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** Even though the mother agreed to drop the lawsuit after the estate gave her financial help, the Supreme Court refused to dismiss the case. Under the law, a person's civil status (whether someone is legally a child of a person) and their right to future support cannot be settled through private cash bargains or compromise deals.
Issue 2: Sufficiency of Bare Biological Filiation for Successional Rights
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Bare biological filiation confers no successional rights; an illegitimate child must prove that such filiation was legally **acknowledged** by the putative parent.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"...proof of filiation of the petitioners to the late Enrique M. Baluyut is not sufficient to confer upon them any hereditary right in the estate of the deceased. What is necessary to be established by an illegitimate not natural child in order that he may be entitled to successional rights under Article 887 of the New Civil Code, is not the fact of his bare filiation but a filiation **acknowledged** by the putative parent."
"It is true that by their motion to dismiss the appellees are deemed to have admitted that the appellant is the illegitimate spurious, not natural child of the deceased Marcos Paulino. Such an admission, however, does not entitle her to inherit from her alleged putative father. **It is necessary to allege that her putative father had acknowledged and recognized her as such. Such acknowledgment is essential and is the basis of her right to inherit.**" **(Quoting Paulino v. Paulino, 113 Phil. 697)**
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
The Court traced its jurisprudence, noting that the older, liberal doctrine in **Reyes v. Zuzuarregui** (102 Phil. 346) was abandoned and reversed by **Paulino v. Paulino** (113 Phil. 697) and reaffirmed in **Republic v. Workmen's Compensation Commission** (121 Phil. 261).
Under the operative rule, the provisions governing natural children apply to spurious (illegitimate not natural) children concerning recognition.
Inheritance under Article 887(5) requires either voluntary recognition under Article 278 or compulsory judicial recognition under Article 283. Without acknowledgment, bare biological paternity produces no hereditary rights.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** Proving that a decedent is biologically your father is not enough to inherit from his estate as an illegitimate child. Philippine law requires proof that the father actually **acknowledged** or legally recognized you as his child during his lifetime, or that a valid court action for compulsory recognition was established under strict statutory grounds.
Issue 3: Sufficiency of Petitioners' Evidence for Recognition
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Petitioners failed to prove voluntary recognition because the birth certificates were unsigned by the putative father, and failed to prove compulsory recognition because clandestine support and hidden visits do not constitute continuous possession of status.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"There is no evidence as required by Article 278 which proves that the petitioners were recognized by the deceased during his lifetime as his spurious children. The petitioners' records of birth, although in the name of Enrique Baluyut, were not signed by the latter. There was no authentic writing presented nor any statement in a court of record which would prove that the petitioners were recognized by the deceased."
"'In order to prove the continuous possession of the status of a natural child, the acts must be of such a nature that they reveal, not only the conviction of paternity, but also the apparent desire to have and treat the child as such in all relations in society and in life, not accidentally, but continuously'..."
"If birth certificates, which are unsigned by the presumed father as required by section 5 of Act No. 3753 and Article 280 of the Civil Code, are incompetent evidence even to prove paternity alone, with more reason are birth certificates incompetent evidence to prove recognized filiation."
"...a distinction must be made between the two kinds of acknowledgment: (1) voluntary, and (2) compulsory. **In the former, recognition may be incidental, but in the latter, it must be direct and express.**" **(Quoting Javellana v. Monteclaro, 74 Phil. 393)**
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Absence of Voluntary Recognition (Art. 278):** Birth certificates (Exhibits A, B, C) were unsigned by Enrique. Under Section 5 of Act No. 3753 and Article 280 of the Civil Code, an unsigned birth certificate is incompetent evidence to establish paternity, much less recognized filiation. No authentic writing or statement in a court of record was presented.
**Failure of Compulsory Recognition (Art. 283):**
**Continuous Possession of Status (Art. 283[2]):** Requires acts demonstrating a desire to treat the children as his own in open society. The evidence showed Enrique visited only covertly twice a week, concealed his relationship, did not pay hospital bills personally (used Liberata as a cash courier), and produced zero neighbors from their populous neighborhood to testify to open treatment.
Enrique's acts exhibited an intent to **hide** the children from society, not to openly treat them as his own.
**Misapplication of Javellana v. Monteclaro:** Petitioners argued for a "liberal" rule. The Court clarified that **Javellana** applied liberality allowing "incidental" recognition **only to voluntary acknowledgment** in a public document. For **compulsory recognition**, the law remains strictly construed and requires direct, express, and indubitable proof.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** The petitioners failed to establish recognition. The birth certificates did not bear the father's signature, making them legally useless to prove recognition. Furthermore, keeping a mistress and children in a rented house, visiting them privately twice a week to satisfy sexual desires, and routing hospital payments through a third party to conceal one's identity proves secrecy, not the open, continuous social treatment required to claim child status.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.**
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"ACCORDINGLY, the decision appealed from is AFFIRMED. No costs.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The private respondents prevailed. The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' decision, which dismissed the petitioners' petition for intervention and revoked their monthly support **pendente lite**, ruling that petitioners are not acknowledged illegitimate children of Enrique Baluyut and have no hereditary rights in his estate.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: De la Puerta v. Court of Appeals**
**Full Official Caption:** Isabel de la Puerta, Petitioner, vs. The Honorable Court of Appeals and Carmelita de la Puerta, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 77867
**Date of Promulgation:** February 6, 1990
**Philippine Reports:** 181 SCRA 861
**Ponente:** Cruz, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** First Division (Concurring: Narvasa, Gancayco, Griño-Aquino, and Medialdea, **JJ.**) (No Separate Opinions).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Civil Law → Succession → Right of Representation → Illegitimate Children & the Barrier Rule (**Article 992**)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Family Law / Persons → Filiation & Paternity → Spurious Children → Modes of Proof of Filiation
Remedial Law → Evidence → Disputable Presumptions → Presumption of Marriage & Legitimacy
**Full Text of Governing Statutory Provisions:**
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 970:**
"Art. 970. **Representation is a right created by fiction of law**, by virtue of which the representative is raised to the place and the degree of the person represented, and acquires the rights which the latter would have if he were living or if he could have inherited."
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 992:**
"Art. 992. **An illegitimate child has no right to inherit ab intestato from the legitimate children and relatives of his father or mother**; nor shall such children or relatives inherit in the same manner from the illegitimate child."
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 255:**
"Art. 255. Children born after one hundred and eighty days following the celebration of the marriage, and before three hundred days following its dissolution or the separation of the spouses shall be presumed to be legitimate.
Against this presumption no evidence shall be admitted other than that of the **physical impossibility** of the husband's having access to his wife within the first one hundred and twenty days of the three hundred which preceded the birth of the child.
This physical impossibility may be caused:
(1) By the impotence of the husband;
(2) By the fact that the husband and wife were living separately in such a way that access was not possible;
(3) By the serious illness of the husband."
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 256:**
"Art. 256. The child shall be presumed legitimate, although the mother may have declared against its legitimacy or may have been sentenced as an adulteress."
**Rules of Court, Rule 131, Section 5(bb) (Pre-1989 Amendment):**
"Sec. 5. **Disputable presumptions.**—The following presumptions are satisfactory if uncontradicted, but may be contradicted and overcome by other evidence:
x x x
(bb) **That a man and woman deporting themselves as husband and wife have entered into a lawful contract of marriage**;"
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Rule (Right of Representation):** Under Art. 970, representation takes place only in three instances in testamentary succession: (1) death of the person represented before the testator (pre-decease); (2) incapacity; or (3) disinheritance. Where the heir survives the testator, no representation occurs because the heir succeeds in his own right and directly transmits rights upon his subsequent death.
**The Iron Curtain Doctrine / Barrier Rule (Art. 992):** An illegitimate (spurious or natural) child has an absolute impediment preventing intestate succession from the legitimate relatives of their parents. An illegitimate child cannot represent their deceased legitimate parent to inherit from their legitimate grandparent or legitimate collateral relatives.
**Proof of Filiation of Spurious Children:** Spurious/adulterous children may prove their filiation through the same modes available to natural children under Articles 283, 284, and 289, including a statement or admission in open court.
**Rebuttal of Presumption of Marriage:** The disputable presumption under Rule 131, Sec. 5(bb) that cohabiting parties are legally married fails when contradicted by credible affirmative evidence that the spouses lived separately, that a partner cohabited openly with another person, and that the alleged husband exhibited unnatural passivity.
**Factual Trigger:** Carmelita, claiming to be the acknowledged natural daughter of Vicente de la Puerta, sought support and allowances directly from the probate proceedings of the estate of Dominga Revuelta (Vicente’s mother). Because Vicente survived Dominga, Vicente inherited directly; furthermore, because Carmelita was born of Vicente's adulterous cohabitation while his legal marriage to Genoveva was subsisting, she was an illegitimate child barred by Article 992 from inheriting from Dominga's estate.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Dominga Revuelta:** Testatrix who died on July 3, 1966, leaving a will dividing her estate among her three children.
**Isabel de la Puerta:** Daughter of Dominga; executrix named in the will, instituted heir to the legitime and free portion; petitioner opposing Carmelita’s claims.
**Vicente de la Puerta:** Son of Dominga; oppositor to Dominga's will; legally married to Genoveva de la Puerta in 1938; cohabited with Gloria Jordan starting in 1962; died intestate on June 14, 1978.
**Alfredo de la Puerta:** Son of Dominga; original co-oppositor who died during probate proceedings.
**Carmelita de la Puerta:** Born December 18, 1962; alleged natural child of Vicente and Gloria Jordan; claimant of allowances and support from Dominga's estate; private respondent.
**Genoveva de la Puerta:** Legal wife of Vicente (married in 1938, separated in 1940); witness who testified regarding her separation from Vicente and his open cohabitation with Gloria.
**Gloria Jordan:** Carmelita's biological mother; cohabited with Vicente de la Puerta.
**Juanito Austrial:** Alleged common-law or legal husband of Gloria Jordan, claimed by Isabel to be Carmelita’s real father.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 appealing the Decision of the Court of Appeals, which affirmed the November 12, 1982 Order of the Court of First Instance (CFI) of Quezon sitting as a probate court in Special Proceeding for the estate of Dominga Revuelta.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1938:** Vicente de la Puerta marries Genoveva de la Puerta.
**1940:** Vicente and Genoveva separate; they never reconcile.
**1962:** Gloria Jordan begins living with Vicente de la Puerta as common-law husband and wife in a house five to six houses away from Genoveva.
**December 18, 1962:** Carmelita de la Puerta is born.
**July 3, 1966:** Dominga Revuelta dies at age 92, leaving a will dividing her properties among Alfredo, Vicente, and Isabel (giving Isabel the free portion and naming her executrix).
**Probate Filing:** Isabel petitions for the probate of Dominga’s will. Vicente and Alfredo oppose on grounds of Dominga's senility and property ownership disputes. Isabel is appointed special administratrix. Alfredo dies pendente lite.
**August 1, 1974:** Vicente files a petition in the CFI of Quezon (Branch V, Mauban) in Sp. Proc. No. 0041 to adopt Carmelita.
**September 6, 1974 / 1976:** During the adoption hearing, Vicente testifies under oath in open court that Carmelita is his daughter with Gloria Jordan. The CFI grants the adoption.
**Appeal of Adoption:** Isabel appeals the adoption decree to the Court of Appeals.
**June 14, 1978:** Vicente dies intestate without children from his legal wife Genoveva, prompting Isabel to move for the dismissal of the pending adoption appeal.
**November 20, 1981:** Carmelita, having intervened in Dominga's probate proceedings, files a motion for a monthly allowance as the acknowledged natural child of Vicente.
**November 12, 1982:** CFI Quezon (probate court) grants Carmelita's motion, ruling that she was the natural child of Vicente and entitled to support/allowance from Dominga's estate.
**Court of Appeals Ruling:** The CA affirms the probate court's order.
**Supreme Court Petition:** Isabel files a Petition for Review on Certiorari.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Isabel de la Puerta)
**Main Thesis:** Carmelita is not entitled to support or inheritance from the estate of Dominga Revuelta because she is not Vicente's natural child, but rather the legitimate child of Juanito Austrial and Gloria Jordan; even if illegitimate, she cannot claim from Dominga's estate.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Presumption of Legitimacy (Arts. 255 & 256, Civil Code):** Carmelita must be presumed the legitimate daughter of Juanito Austrial and Gloria Jordan, who deported themselves as husband and wife (Rule 131, Sec. 5[bb]).
**Legal Impossibility of Natural Child Status:** Vicente was validly married to Genoveva in 1938 and remained married until his death in 1978. Thus, Carmelita could not be a "natural child" under the Civil Code (as her parents were impeded from marrying at her conception/birth).
**Inapplicability of Art. 278:** Carmelita is a spurious child and cannot rely on Article 278 of the Civil Code to prove recognition.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Carmelita de la Puerta)
**Main Thesis:** She is the recognized child of Vicente de la Puerta and entitled to allowances and successional rights from the estate of her grandmother Dominga.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Filiation Established:** Vicente continuously treated her as his true child, paid for her education, signed her report cards, took family photos, and categorically admitted under oath in court during the adoption proceedings that she was his daughter.
**Overcoming the Presumption:** The presumption of marriage between Juanito and Gloria was demolished by Genoveva's testimony that Vicente and Gloria openly cohabited in the community since 1962.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the disputable presumption of marriage between Juanito Austrial and Gloria Jordan was rebutted, and whether Carmelita's filiation as the child of Vicente de la Puerta was sufficiently established.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether Carmelita’s filiation as the child of Vicente was duly proved despite petitioner’s invocation of the presumption of legitimacy arising from an alleged marriage between her mother and Juanito Austrial?
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Carmelita de la Puerta, as an illegitimate (spurious) child of Vicente de la Puerta, may claim support and successional rights in the probate proceedings of the estate of Dominga Revuelta.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether an illegitimate child can inherit from the estate of her legitimate grandmother by right of representation or claim support from said grandmother's estate?
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Filiation and Presumptions of Marriage and Legitimacy
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did Carmelita sufficiently prove her filiation as Vicente’s child, overcoming the presumptions of marriage and legitimacy? **YES.** The disputable presumption of marriage between Juanito and Gloria was refuted by affirmative evidence of Gloria's cohabitation with Vicente, and Vicente acknowledged Carmelita in a court of record.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
**"The presumption of marriage between Juanito and Gloria having been destroyed, it became necessary for the petitioner to submit additional proof to show that the two were legally married. She did not."**
**"The so-called spurious children or illegitimate children other than natural children, commonly known as bastards, include adulterous children or those born out of wedlock to a married woman cohabiting with a man other than her husband or to a married man cohabiting with a woman other than his wife. They are entitled to support and successional rights (Art. 287, CC). But their filiation must be duly proven. (Ibid., Art. 887)"**
**"Spurious children should not be in a better position than natural children. The rules on proof of filiation of natural children or the rule on voluntary and compulsory acknowledgment for natural children may be applied to spurious children."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Presumption of Marriage Rebutted:** Rule 131, Sec. 5(bb) is merely disputable. Genoveva (Vicente’s lawful wife) testified that Vicente and Gloria openly lived together as a couple starting in 1962 only houses away from her. Juanito Austrial never objected to Gloria leaving the home to cohabit with Vicente in the same neighborhood—conduct entirely unnatural for a lawful husband. This destroyed the presumption that Juanito and Gloria were married.
**Failure of Burden of Proof:** Once the presumption of marriage fell, the burden shifted to Isabel to present affirmative evidence (e.g., marriage contract) of Juanito and Gloria's marriage to trigger Articles 255 and 256. She failed to do so; witness Magpantay admitted he did not know if they were legally married.
**Proof of Spurious Filiation:** Spurious (adulterous) children can prove filiation using the mechanisms available to natural children under Articles 283, 284, and 289 of the Civil Code.
**Conclusive Court Admission:** Vicente de la Puerta categorically testified under oath in open court during the 1974 adoption proceedings: **"She is my daughter."** This judicial statement sufficiently proved Carmelita’s filiation as Vicente's spurious child.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language Explanation)** Isabel claimed Carmelita was the legitimate child of another couple (Juanito and Gloria). However, Vicente's own lawful wife testified that Vicente and Gloria openly lived together as common-law spouses in the neighborhood without objection from Juanito, which shattered the disputable presumption of marriage between Juanito and Gloria. Carmelita proved she was Vicente's spurious child through Vicente's explicit, sworn admission in court during her adoption case, which is a legally valid method for spurious children to prove filiation.
Issue 2: Successional Rights and Claim for Support Against Grandmother's Estate
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Can Carmelita claim support and successional rights from the estate of Dominga Revuelta? **NO.** Vicente did not predecease Dominga, meaning no representation could occur; and under Article 992 (the Iron Curtain Rule), an illegitimate child cannot inherit **ab intestato** from the legitimate relatives of her parent.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
**"In testamentary succession, the right of representation can take place only in the following cases: first, when the person represented dies before the testator; second, when the person represented is incapable of succeeding the testator; and third, when the person represented is disinherited by the testator."**
**"Not having predeceased Dominga Revuelta, her son Vicente had the right to inherit from her directly or in his own right. No right of representation was involved, nor could it be invoked by Carmelita upon her father's death, which came after his own mother's death."**
**"Article 992 of the New Civil Code provides a barrier or iron curtain in that it prohibits absolutely a succession ab intestato between the illegitimate child and the legitimate children and relatives of the father or mother of said legitimate child."**
**"If the adopting parent should die before the adopted child, the latter cannot represent the former in the inheritance from the parents or ascendants of the adopter. The adopted child is not related to the deceased in that case, because the filiation created by fiction of law is exclusively between the adopter and the adopted. 'By adoption, the adopters can make for themselves an heir, but they cannot thus make one for their kindred.'"**
**"The result is that Carmelita, as the spurious daughter of Vicente de la Puerta, has successional rights to the intestate estate of her father but not to the estate of Dominga Revuelta. Her claims for support and inheritance should therefore be filed in the proceedings for the settlement of her own father's estate and cannot be considered in the probate of Dominga Revuelta's will."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Absence of Representation Under Art. 970:** Dominga Revuelta died on July 3, 1966. Vicente de la Puerta died 12 years later on June 14, 1978. Because Vicente survived Dominga, he inherited directly in his own right at the moment of Dominga's death. There was no vacancy in Dominga's estate caused by predecease, incapacity, or disinheritance. Thus, no right of representation ever arose.
**The Iron Curtain / Barrier of Art. 992:** Even assuming Vicente had predeceased Dominga, Carmelita would still be barred. As a spurious child of Vicente, Article 992 creates an impassable barrier between the illegitimate child and the legitimate relatives of the parent. Dominga was Vicente’s legitimate mother; Carmelita, being illegitimate, is completely prohibited from inheriting **ab intestato** from Dominga.
**Inefficacy of Adoption to Breach the Barrier:** Even if the adoption decree had attained finality, an adopted child cannot represent the adopter in the inheritance of the adopter’s ascendants or kindred. Adoption creates a legal relationship strictly between adopter and adopted (**"adopters can make for themselves an heir, but they cannot thus make one for their kindred"**).
**Wrong Forum/Estate:** Carmelita’s successional rights and claims for support exist solely against the estate of her father, Vicente. Consequently, such claims must be prosecuted in the settlement of Vicente's estate, not against the estate of Dominga Revuelta.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language Explanation)** Carmelita cannot touch Dominga's estate for two independent legal reasons: First, representation only happens if the parent dies **before** the grandparent; here, Vicente outlived Dominga by 12 years, so Vicente inherited directly and representation is legally impossible. Second, even if Vicente had died first, Article 992's "Iron Curtain Rule" strictly prohibits illegitimate children from inheriting from the legitimate relatives of their parents. Carmelita’s rights are confined strictly to Vicente’s own intestate estate, so her claim in Dominga’s probate was improper.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is GRANTED and the appealed decision is hereby REVERSED and SET ASIDE, with costs against the private respondent. It is so ordered."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Isabel de la Puerta prevailed. The Supreme Court reversed and set aside the Court of Appeals' decision and the probate court's order granting Carmelita a monthly allowance/support from Dominga Revuelta’s estate. Carmelita was relegated to pursuing her claims against the estate of her father, Vicente de la Puerta.
