### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Short Recognizable Title: Grande v. Antonio**
**Full Official Caption:** Grace M. Grande, Petitioner, vs. Patricio T. Antonio, Respondent
**Citation & Metadata:**
G.R. No. 206248
Date of Promulgation: February 18, 2014
Philippine Reports Citation: 727 Phil. 448
Ponente: Velasco, Jr., **J.**
Voting Breakdown: En Banc. Concurred in by Sereno, **C.J.**, Carpio, Leonardo-De Castro, Peralta, Bersamin, Del Castillo, Abad, Villarama, Jr., Perez, Reyes, Perlas-Bernabe, and Leonen, **JJ.** On leave: Brion, **J.** No part: Mendoza, **J.** No separate opinions were filed.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code → Paternity and Filiation → Illegitimate Children → Surname of Illegitimate Children (Art. 176, as amended by R.A. 9255)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Administrative Law & Constitutional Law → Judicial Review → Subordinate Legislation → Ultra Vires Rule & Supreme Court Rule-Making / Supervisory Power over Quasi-Judicial Rules (Sec. 5[5], Art. VIII, 1987 Constitution)
Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s)
**Article 176 of Executive Order No. 209 (The Family Code of the Philippines), as amended by Republic Act No. 9255:**
"Art. 176. Illegitimate children shall use the surname and shall be under the parental authority of their mother, and shall be entitled to support in conformity with this Code. **However, illegitimate children may use the surname of their father if their filiation has been expressly recognized by their father through the record of birth appearing in the civil register, or when an admission in a public document or private handwritten instrument is made by the father.** Provided, the father has the right to institute an action before the regular courts to prove non-filiation during his lifetime. The legitime of each illegitimate child shall consist of one-half of the legitime of a legitimate child."
**Article VIII, Section 5, Paragraph 5, 1987 Philippine Constitution:**
"Sec. 5. The Supreme Court shall have the following powers:
x x x x
(5) Promulgate rules concerning the protection and enforcement of constitutional rights, pleading, practice and procedure in all courts, the admission to the practice of law, the Integrated Bar, and legal assistance to the underprivileged. Such rules shall provide a simplified and inexpensive procedure for the speedy disposition of cases, shall be uniform for all courts of the same grade, and shall not diminish, increase, or modify substantive rights. **Rules of procedure of special courts and quasi-judicial bodies shall remain effective unless disapproved by the Supreme Court.**"
The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision
**General Rule / Provision Triggered:** Under **Article 176 of the Family Code**, the default baseline rule is mandatory: **"Illegitimate children shall use the surname and shall be under the parental authority of their mother."**
**Specific Sub-Rule(s) / Doctrinal Tests:**
1. **Discretionary Right of the Child, Not the Parent:** The amendatory phrase in R.A. 9255 providing that an illegitimate child **"may use the surname of their father"** upon express recognition of filiation is permissive, not mandatory. The statutory term **"may"** operates to confer discretion exclusively upon the illegitimate child, not upon the recognizing father or the mother. A father has no legal right to compel the child to use his surname.
2. **Best Interest of the Child Standard:** Surnames are intimately bound to a child's identity; the yardstick for resolving disputes over a child's surname is the best interest of the child. The Court rejects any presumption that using the father's surname automatically serves the child's best interest.
3. **Ultra Vires Administrative Rules:** Implementing Rules and Regulations cannot expand, modify, or contradict the statute they implement. Because the statute uses permissive language ("may"), administrative provisions (such as Rules 7 and 8 of the IRR of R.A. 9255) that mandate the substitution of the father's surname ("shall") upon voluntary recognition exceed administrative authority and are null and void.
**Factual Trigger:** The respondent father, upon executing a notarized Deed of Voluntary Recognition of Paternity, petitioned the RTC to judicially alter his illegitimate sons' surnames in their birth certificates from their mother's surname ("Grande") to his own ("Antonio"). The children, who were registered under their mother's surname and lived with her, were ordered by the lower courts to adopt the father's surname against the mother's and the children's will.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Grace M. Grande (Grande):** Petitioner; biological mother of the minor children, Andre Lewis and Jerard Patrick; held custody and brought them to the United States.
**Patricio T. Antonio (Antonio):** Respondent; biological father of the children; married to another woman at the time of cohabitation with Grande; executed a notarized Deed of Voluntary Recognition of Paternity and instituted judicial proceedings to claim parental authority, custody, and impose his surname.
**Andre Lewis Grande & Jerard Patrick Grande:** Illegitimate minor children of Grande and Antonio, born February 8, 1998, and October 13, 1999, respectively.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on Certiorari under **Rule 45** challenging the July 24, 2012 Decision and March 5, 2013 Resolution of the Court of Appeals (CA) in CA-G.R. CV No. 96406.
The CA modified the September 28, 2010 Decision of the Regional Trial Court (RTC), Branch 8 of Aparri, Cagayan (SP. Proc. No. 11-4492). The RTC had granted Antonio joint parental authority, primary weekday custody, and ordered the children's surname changed to "Antonio." The CA reversed the custody transfer (awarding full custody to Grande with visitorial rights and child support to Antonio), but sustained the mandatory change of the children's surname to "Antonio."
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**Cohabitation Phase:** Grande and Antonio lived together as husband and wife without the benefit of marriage, as Antonio was legally married to another person.
**February 8, 1998 & October 13, 1999:** Andre Lewis and Jerard Patrick were born, respectively. At birth, they were not expressly recognized by Antonio in the Civil Registry and were registered under their mother's surname, "Grande."
**May 2007:** The relationship between Grande and Antonio deteriorated. Grande moved to the United States with the two minor children.
**Initiation of Suit:** Antonio filed before the RTC, Branch 8, Aparri, Cagayan, a **Petition for Judicial Approval of Recognition with Prayer to take Parental Authority, Parental Physical Custody, Correction/Change of Surname of Minors and for the Issuance of Writ of Preliminary Injunction**, appending a notarized Deed of Voluntary Recognition of Paternity.
**September 28, 2010:** The RTC ruled in Antonio's favor, judicially approving his recognition of paternity and ordering:
1. The Civil Registrar of Makati City to enter Antonio's name as father and change/annotate the children's surnames from "Grande" to "Antonio";
2. Joint parental authority;
3. Antonio primary weekday physical custody (Monday to Friday evening) and Grande weekend custody;
4. Both parties to desist from taking the children out of the country without written consent and court permission;
5. Monthly child support of ₱30,000 (70% paid by Antonio, 30% by Grande).
**November 22, 2010:** The RTC denied Grande's Motion for Reconsideration for being pro forma and lacking merit.
**July 24, 2012:** The CA partly granted Grande's appeal. It held that sole parental custody belongs to the mother under Article 176, as Antonio showed no compelling reason or maternal unfitness. However, the CA affirmed that Antonio's recognition, coupled with the "best-interest-of-the-child" standard, legally mandated that the minors adopt the surname "Antonio." Visitorial rights (twice a week) and child support allocations were also maintained.
**March 5, 2013:** The CA denied Grande's Partial Motion for Reconsideration directed against the mandatory surname change.
**Supreme Court Review:** Grande filed a Rule 45 Petition before the Supreme Court, exclusively challenging the compulsory imposition of the father's surname.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Grace M. Grande)
**Main Thesis:** Article 176 of the Family Code, as amended by R.A. 9255, is couched in permissive terms and cannot be invoked by a recognizing father to compel his illegitimate children to bear his surname without the consent of their mother.
**Specific Contentions:**
Under Article 176, the general and default statutory rule mandates the use of the mother's surname.
The statutory exception introduced by R.A. 9255 uses the word "may," which is discretionary and permissive.
The discretion to use the father's surname belongs exclusively to the children, not the father.
A father cannot use judicial recognition to override the maternal authority and custody conferred upon the mother by law.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Patricio T. Antonio)
**Main Thesis:** Judicial recognition of paternity legally entitles the father to have his surname entered as the children's surname, which aligns with the universally recognized best-interest-of-the-child principle.
**Specific Contentions:**
Having executed a notarized Deed of Voluntary Recognition of Paternity, all legal consequences flowing from paternity—including the child bearing the father's surname—must follow.
The best interest of the children is promoted when their paternity is openly reflected through their surname.
Administrative guidelines (IRR of R.A. 9255) provide for the mandatory recording and use of the father's surname upon formal recognition of filiation.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Procedural / Ancillary Issue]** Whether or not the father of recognized illegitimate children is entitled to joint parental authority and primary physical custody.
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether respondent's prayer for judicial conferment of parental authority and parental custody has legal mooring under Article 176 of the Family Code.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not an illegitimate father who recognizes his children can obtain parental authority and physical custody absent proof of the mother's unfitness.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not a father has the legal right to compel his recognized illegitimate children to use his surname under Article 176 of the Family Code, as amended by R.A. 9255.
**Faithful Court Formulation:** "The sole issue at hand is the right of a father to compel the use of his surname by his illegitimate children upon his recognition of their filiation."
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not the recognition of paternity by a father empowers the courts to compel illegitimate children to use his surname instead of their mother's surname.
3. **[Secondary / Substantive Issue]** Whether or not the provisions of the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of R.A. 9255 mandating that illegitimate children use the father's surname upon recognition are valid.
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the mandatory directives in Rules 7 and 8 of the IRR of R.A. 9255 can prevail over the permissive text of Article 176 of the Family Code.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not Rules 7 and 8 of Administrative Order No. 1, Series of 2004, are void for exceeding the scope of Article 176 of the Family Code, as amended by R.A. 9255.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Parental Authority and Custody of Illegitimate Children
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Under Article 176 of the Family Code, parental authority and sole physical custody over illegitimate children belong exclusively to the mother, unless she is proven unfit.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"Parental authority over minor children is lodged by Art. 176 on the mother; hence, respondent's prayer has no legal mooring. Since parental authority is given to the mother, then custody over the minor children also goes to the mother, unless she is shown to be unfit."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Article 176 unequivocally mandates that illegitimate children **"shall be under the parental authority of their mother."**
Voluntary recognition of paternity by the father confers rights of support and successional rights, but does not transfer or divide parental authority.
Because custody is an inherent incident of parental authority, the right of physical custody remains solely with the mother.
Antonio utterly failed to present evidence demonstrating that Grande was an unfit mother or committed any acts detrimental to the children's welfare. Therefore, the trial court gravely erred in depriving the mother of primary custody, and the CA correctly reinstated sole custody in Grande (subject to reasonable visitorial rights).
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:** (Plain-Language Explanation) The law explicitly places illegitimate children under the sole parental authority of their mother. A father's voluntary recognition of paternity does not grant him joint authority or custody; as long as the mother is fit, she retains exclusive custody of the children, and the father is only entitled to visitation rights and an obligation to provide support.
Issue 2: Compelling Illegitimate Children to Use the Father's Surname
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Under Article 176 of the Family Code, as amended by R.A. 9255, the choice to use the father's surname belongs exclusively to the illegitimate child, not to the father or mother.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"From the foregoing provisions, it is clear that the general rule is that an illegitimate child shall use the surname of his or her mother. The exception provided by RA 9255 is, in case his or her filiation is expressly recognized by the father through the record of birth appearing in the civil register or when an admission in a public document or private handwritten instrument is made by the father. In such a situation, the illegitimate child may use the surname of the father."
"Art. 176 gives illegitimate children the right to decide if they want to use the surname of their father or not. It is not the father (herein respondent) or the mother (herein petitioner) who is granted by law the right to dictate the surname of their illegitimate children."
"On its face, Art. 176, as amended, is free from ambiguity. And where there is no ambiguity, one must abide by its words. The use of the word 'may' in the provision readily shows that an acknowledged illegitimate child is under no compulsion to use the surname of his illegitimate father. The word 'may' is permissive and operates to confer discretion upon the illegitimate children."
"On the matter of children's surnames, this Court has, time and again, rebuffed the idea that the use of the father's surname serves the best interest of the minor child... Indeed, the rule regarding the use of a child's surname is second only to the rule requiring that the child be placed in the best possible situation considering his circumstances."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Verba Legis Interpretation:** Statutory construction dictates that when the law is clear, plain, and free from ambiguity, it must be given its literal meaning. Article 176 states that the illegitimate child **"shall use the surname... of their mother"** as the mandatory general rule. The exception introduced by R.A. 9255 provides that the child **"may use"** the father's surname upon express recognition. The term "may" is permissive, conferring an option and discretion exclusively upon the child.
**No Paternal Prerogative:** Neither parent has the statutory authority to impose a surname on an illegitimate child. Paternal recognition of paternity establishes filiation, but it does not entitle the father to force the child to carry his name.
**Best Interest Analysis:** The CA erred in presuming that carrying the father's surname automatically serves the child's best interest. Citing **Alfon v. Republic**, **Calderon v. Republic**, and **Republic v. Capote**, the Court emphasized that a child's name is intrinsically tied to personal identity and well-being. Prior jurisprudence allows even legitimate children to use their mother's surname where it best serves their welfare.
**Evidentiary Necessity on Remand:** Although the children (aged 13 and 15 at the time of review) submitted letters to the Supreme Court expressing their refusal to adopt the surname "Antonio," the letters were not formally offered in evidence before the trial court under Rule 132, Section 34. Consequently, they could not be accorded evidentiary weight on appeal. Remand to the trial court is required for the sole purpose of conducting an evidentiary inquiry to ascertain the children's actual choice of surname.
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:** (Plain-Language Explanation) The Family Code uses the permissive word "may" regarding the father's surname. This means using the father's surname is a right granted to the illegitimate child, not a prerogative granted to the father. Even if the father officially acknowledges paternity, he cannot compel the children or the courts to replace the mother's surname; the choice belongs entirely to the children based on their own best interests, which must be formally heard by the trial court.
Issue 3: Validity of Administrative Rules 7 and 8 of the IRR of R.A. 9255
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Rules 7 and 8 of the IRR are ultra vires, null, and void because they substitute the mandatory word "shall" for the permissive word "may," unconstitutionally expanding the statutory enactment.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Nonetheless, the hornbook rule is that an administrative issuance cannot amend a legislative act. In MCC Industrial Sales Corp. v. Ssangyong Corporation, We held:
'After all, the power of administrative officials to promulgate rules in the implementation of a statute is necessarily limited to what is found in the legislative enactment itself. The implementing rules and regulations of a law cannot extend the law or expand its coverage, as the power to amend or repeal a statute is vested in the Legislature. Thus, if a discrepancy occurs between the basic law and an implementing rule or regulation, it is the former that prevails, because the law cannot be broadened by a mere administrative issuance – an administrative agency certainly cannot amend an act of Congress.'"
"What is more, this Court has the constitutional prerogative and authority to strike down and declare as void the rules of procedure of special courts and quasi-judicial bodies when found contrary to statutes and/or the Constitution. Section 5(5), Art. VIII of the Constitution provides:
'x x x Rules of procedure of special courts and quasi-judicial bodies shall remain effective unless disapproved by the Supreme Court.'
Thus, We exercise this power in voiding the above-quoted provisions of the IRR of RA 9255 insofar as it provides the mandatory use by illegitimate children of their father's surname upon the latter's recognition of his paternity."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Administrative agencies promulgating implementing rules are strictly confined to the four corners of the legislative enactment. They lack legislative power and cannot extend, expand, or modify statutory terms.
Rules 7 and 8 of Administrative Order No. 1, Series of 2004 (issued by the Office of the Civil Registrar General), commanded that upon recognition, the illegitimate child **"shall use the surname of the father"** and directed the mandatory substitution of names in civil registry documents.
By changing the statutory "may" into an administrative "shall," the administrative body attempted to make mandatory that which Congress made discretionary.
The Supreme Court, exercising its constitutional authority under Section 5(5), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution to disapprove rules of procedure of quasi-judicial bodies, struck down and voided Rules 7 and 8 insofar as they mandated the use of the father's surname.
**(d) Plain-Language Recitation Explanation:** (Plain-Language Explanation) Administrative agencies cannot change the law through executive implementing rules. Congress made the use of the father's surname optional by using "may" in R.A. 9255; therefore, when the Civil Registrar General issued rules stating that the child "shall" use the father's surname, the agency acted beyond its powers. The Supreme Court exercised its constitutional oversight over quasi-judicial rules to strike down those administrative provisions as void.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions were discussed or filed in the decision. (The decision reflects that Associate Justice Arturo D. Brion was on leave and Associate Justice Jose Catral Mendoza took no part).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
Verbatim Fallo:
"WHEREFORE, the instant petition is PARTIALLY GRANTED. The July 24, 2012 Decision of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. CV No. 96406 is MODIFIED, the dispositive portion of which shall read:
WHEREFORE, the appeal is partly GRANTED. Accordingly, the appealed Decision of the Regional Trial Court Branch 8, Aparri Cagayan in SP Proc. Case No. 11-4492 is MODIFIED in part and shall hereinafter read as follows:
a. [Antonio] is ORDERED to deliver the minor children Jerard Patrick and Andre Lewis to the custody of their mother herein appellant, Grace Grande who by virtue hereof is hereby awarded the full or sole custody of these minor children;
b. [Antonio] shall have visitation rights at least twice a week, and may only take the children out upon the written consent of [Grande];
c. The parties are DIRECTED to give and share in support of the minor children Jerard Patrick and Andre Lewis in the amount of ₱30,000.00 per month at the rate of 70% for [Antonio] and 30% for [Grande]; and
d. The case is REMANDED to the Regional Trial Court, Branch 8 of Aparri, Cagayan for the sole purpose of determining the surname to be chosen by the children Jerard Patrick and Andre Lewis.
Rule 7 and Rule 8 of the Office of the Civil Registrar General Administrative Order No. 1, Series of 2004 are DISAPPROVED and hereby declared NULL and VOID.
SO ORDERED."
Plain-Language Outcome:
Petitioner Grace M. Grande prevailed on the issue of the children's surname. The Supreme Court reversed the CA's order compelling the minor children to adopt the father's surname ("Antonio"), confirmed the mother's sole custody (with visitorial rights and shared child support for the father), remanded the case to the RTC to formally determine the children's preferred surname, and struck down Rules 7 and 8 of the IRR of R.A. 9255 as unconstitutional/null and void.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Barcelote v. Republic**
**Full Official Caption:** In the Matter of Petition for Cancellation of Certificates of Live Birth of Yuhares Jan Barcelote Tinitigan and Avee Kynna Noelle Barcelote Tinitigan; Jonna Karla Baguio Barcelote, Petitioner, vs. Republic of the Philippines, Ricky O. Tinitigan, and Local Civil Registrar, Davao City, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:**
G.R. No. 222095
Promulgation Date: August 7, 2017
Philippine Reports Citation: 815 Phil. 664
Ponente: Carpio, **J.**
Voting Breakdown: Second Division (Peralta, Mendoza, Leonen, and Martires, **JJ.**, concur; unanimous).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code → Paternity and Filiation → Illegitimate Children → Surname, Parental Authority, and Birth Registration Requirements
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Remedial Law → Special Proceedings → Rule 108 (Cancellation and Correction of Entries in the Civil Registry) → Void Registrations under Act No. 3753
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article 176, Family Code (as amended by Republic Act No. 9255):**
"**Illegitimate children shall use the surname and shall be under the parental authority of their mother**, and shall be entitled to support in conformity with this Code. **However, illegitimate children may use the surname of their father if their filiation has been expressly recognized by their father through the record of birth appearing in the civil register, or when an admission in a public document or private handwritten instrument is made by the father.** Provided, the father has the right to institute an action before the regular courts to prove non-filiation during his lifetime. The legitime of each illegitimate child shall consist of one-half of the legitime of a legitimate child."
**Section 5, Act No. 3753 (Civil Registry Law):**
"Section 5. **Registration and Certification of Birth.** — The declaration of the physician or midwife in attendance at the birth or, in default thereof, the declaration of either parent of the newborn child, shall be sufficient for the registration of a birth in the civil register. Such declaration shall be exempt from the documentary stamp tax and shall be sent to the local civil registrar not later than thirty days after the birth, by the physician, or midwife in attendance at the birth or by either parent of the newly born child.
In such declaration, the persons above mentioned shall certify to the following facts: (a) date and hour of birth; (b) sex and nationality of infant; (c) names, citizenship, and religion of parents or, in case the father is not known, of the mother alone; (d) civil status of parents; (e) place where the infant was born; (f) and such other data may be required in the regulation to be issued.
In the case of an exposed child, the person who found the same shall report to the local civil registrar the place, date and hour of finding and other attendant circumstances.
**In case of an illegitimate child, the birth certificate shall be signed and sworn to jointly by the parents of the infant or only the mother if the father refuses.**
In the latter case, it shall not be permissible to state or reveal in the document the name of the father who refuses to acknowledge the child, or to give therein any information by which such father could be identified.
Any fetus having human features which dies after twenty four hours of existence completely disengaged from the maternal womb shall be entered in the proper registers as having been born and having died."
**Article 5, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"**Acts executed against the provisions of mandatory or prohibitory laws shall be void**, except when the law itself authorizes their validity."
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Mandatory Rule:** Illegitimate children **shall** use the surname and **shall** remain under the sole parental authority and custody of their mother. The use of the word "shall" renders maternal surname usage mandatory by default.
**Father's Surname Permissive Exception under R.A. 9255:** The word "may" confers discretion upon the child (or the mother/guardian executing an Affidavit to Use the Surname of the Father [AUSF] under the Revised IRR of R.A. 9255), not upon the putative father. The child cannot be compelled to use the father's surname.
**Mandatory Execution Formalities under Act No. 3753:** Under Section 5 (paragraph 4) of Act No. 3753 (**lex specialis** governing illegitimate births), it is mandatory that the **mother sign and swear to the birth certificate in all cases** (jointly with the father, or alone if the father refuses). A birth certificate registered unilaterally by the father without the mother's signature is void **ab initio** under Article 5 of the Civil Code.
**Factual Trigger:** A married putative father unilaterally registered two certificates of live birth for his illegitimate children before the Davao City Local Civil Registrar, designating his surname and altered first names without the knowledge, consent, or signature of the mother.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Jonna Karla Baguio Barcelote (Barcelote):** Petitioner; biological mother having sole parental authority over her two illegitimate children.
**Ricky O. Tinitigan (Tinitigan):** Respondent; biological/putative father, a married man living with his legitimate family in Davao City, who unilaterally registered the children under his surname with different given names.
**Yohan Grace Barcelote / "Avee Kynna Noelle Barcelote Tinitigan":** The elder illegitimate child born out of wedlock on June 24, 2008.
**Joshua Miguel Barcelote / "Yuhares Jan Barcelote Tinitigan":** The younger illegitimate child born out of wedlock on August 24, 2011.
**Local Civil Registrar of Davao City:** Public respondent that registered the unauthorized, unsigned birth certificates submitted by Tinitigan.
**Local Civil Registrar of Santa Cruz, Davao del Sur:** Registry that accepted petitioner's late registrations under the mother's surname.
**Republic of the Philippines:** Statutory respondent.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Origin: Petition for Cancellation of Certificates of Live Birth filed by Barcelote under **Rule 108 of the Rules of Court** before Branch 15 of the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Davao City (SPC. PROC. No. 12,007-12).
RTC Ruling (Feb. 28, 2013): Granted the petition; ordered the cancellation of the birth certificates registered in Davao City.
CA Ruling (March 5, 2015 & Dec. 3, 2015 Resolution): CA reversed the RTC and dismissed the petition for cancellation.
Elevated to the Supreme Court via a **Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45** of the Rules of Court.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**June 24, 2008:** Barcelote gives birth out of wedlock to her first child with Tinitigan (a married man) at a relative's house in Sibulan, Santa Cruz, Davao del Sur. She names her daughter **Yohan Grace Barcelote**. No hospital birth registration is made. To hide the relationship, she stays in Santa Cruz while Tinitigan visits from Davao City.
**[Date Unspecified in 2008]:** Unknown to Barcelote, Tinitigan unilaterally registers a Certificate of Live Birth with the Davao City Local Civil Registrar (Registry No. 2008-21709) naming the child **Avee Kynna Noelle Barcelote Tinitigan**, stating birth date June 4, 2008 at EUP Family Care Clinic, Agdao, Davao City, with Tinitigan as informant. Barcelote neither knew of nor signed this record.
**August 24, 2011:** Barcelote gives birth to her second child with Tinitigan, naming him **Joshua Miguel Barcelote**. Birth is again unregistered to avoid humiliation and criminal charges. Barcelote thereafter loses contact with Tinitigan and returns to Davao City.
**[Date Unspecified in 2011]:** Tinitigan unilaterally registers a second Certificate of Live Birth in Davao City (Registry No. 2011-28329) naming the child **Yuhares Jan Barcelote Tinitigan**, stating birth date August 14, 2011 at EUP Family Care Clinic, Agdao, Davao City, with Tinitigan as informant. Barcelote did not sign or consent.
**2012:** Barcelote seeks to enroll her eldest child in school, necessitating a birth certificate. Upon verifying that the National Statistics Office (NSO) had no record on file, she secures the approval of the Local Civil Registrar of Santa Cruz, Davao del Sur for the **late registration** of both children (Registry Nos. 2012-1344 and 2012-1335) under the names Yohan Grace Barcelote and Joshua Miguel Barcelote.
**Mid-2012:** Upon submitting late registrations to the NSO, Barcelote is informed that two existing birth certificates were already registered in Davao City bearing the same mother's name and corresponding birth years, but showing different child names, birth dates, birth places, and bearing the surname "Tinitigan."
**September 20, 2012:** Barcelote files an Amended Petition for Cancellation of Certificates of Live Birth under Rule 108 before the RTC of Davao City. After jurisdictional compliance, she presents evidence **ex parte**.
**February 28, 2013:** RTC Davao City grants the petition, ruling the Davao registrations legally infirm under Section 5, Act No. 3753 and Article 176 of the Family Code, and ordering both certificates cancelled.
**March 5, 2015:** CA reverses the RTC, holding that birth registration by the father certified by a midwife was valid under Act No. 3753 without need of maternal consent, and that R.A. 9255 allowed the father to recognize the children and bestow his surname.
**December 3, 2015:** CA denies Barcelote's Motion for Reconsideration.
**August 7, 2017:** Supreme Court issues Decision granting Barcelote's Rule 45 petition and ordering the Davao City birth certificates cancelled.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Jonna Karla Baguio Barcelote)
**Main Thesis:** The birth certificates registered by Tinitigan in Davao City are void **ab initio** and must be cancelled because they violate mandatory statutory provisions governing illegitimate children's surnames, maternal parental authority, and mandatory maternal signatures.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Maternal Name & Authority:** Under Article 176 of the Family Code, illegitimate children are under the sole parental authority of their mother and must use her surname. As the sole holder of parental authority, the mother's choice of names upon birth must prevail.
**Factual Falsity:** The certificates registered by Tinitigan contain false personal circumstances (wrong names, wrong birth dates, and wrong birthplaces).
**Violation of Section 5, Act No. 3753:** For illegitimate children, the law explicitly requires the birth certificate to be signed and sworn to jointly by both parents, or solely by the mother if the father refuses. Because petitioner never signed them, the certificates are void.
**Best Interests of the Child:** It is contrary to the children's welfare to carry the surname of a married father who abandoned them, exposing them to conflict with his legitimate family.
**Propriety of Rule 108 Procedure:** Even if treated alternatively, Rule 108 covers both cancellation and substantial corrections through adversary proceedings; the CA should not have dismissed the case outright.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Republic / Adopted CA Rationale)
**Main Thesis:** The Davao City registrations are valid civil registry records showing paternal recognition under R.A. 9255, and petitioner failed to establish grounds for cancellation.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Validity under Act No. 3753:** Section 5 permits birth registration upon the declaration of either parent or attending midwife; hence, registration by Tinitigan (certified by midwife Erlinda Padilla) did not require maternal consent.
**Right to Use Father's Surname:** Under Article 176 of the Family Code as amended by R.A. 9255, illegitimate children may use the father's surname once expressly recognized in the civil register, which Tinitigan accomplished by personally registering them.
**Failure of Proof:** Petitioner failed to discharge the burden of proving that the entries in the Davao certificates were false or that the late-registration entries reflected the true circumstances.
**Improper Remedy:** Cancellation was improper; petitioner should have pursued a petition for correction of entries.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Certificates of Live Birth registered unilaterally by the putative father without the mother's signature and consent, bearing the father's surname, are valid or void **ab initio**.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether the CA erred in not cancelling the certificates of live birth for Yuhares Jan Barcelote Tinitigan and Avee Kynna Noelle Barcelote Tinitigan registered by Ricky O. Tinitigan.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not a birth certificate of an illegitimate child registered unilaterally by the putative father without the signature and consent of the mother, and assigning the father's surname, is legally void and subject to cancellation under Rule 108.
2. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the petition for cancellation under Rule 108 was the proper remedy, or whether petitioner was limited to filing for correction of entries.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not the outright cancellation of an illegitimate child's birth certificate is the appropriate remedy when the certificate was executed and registered in violation of mandatory legal requirements.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Validity of the Unilaterally Registered Birth Certificates and Surname Usage
**(a) Short Answer: NO (Certificates are VOID).** Birth certificates of illegitimate children registered unilaterally by the father without the mandatory signature of the mother and imposing the father's surname violate mandatory provisions of the Family Code and Act No. 3753, rendering them void **ab initio**.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
**"The law is clear that illegitimate children shall use the surname and shall be under the parental authority of their mother. The use of the word 'shall' underscores its mandatory character. The discretion on the part of the illegitimate child to use the surname of the father is conditional upon proof of compliance with RA 9255 and its IRR."**
**"In Grande v. Antonio, we held that 'the use of the word "may" in [Article 176 of the Family Code, as amended by RA 9255] readily shows that an acknowledged illegitimate child is under no compulsion to use the surname of his illegitimate father. The word "may" is permissive and operates to confer discretion upon the illegitimate children.'"**
**"The fourth paragraph of Section 5 specifically provides that in case of an illegitimate child, the birth certificate shall be signed and sworn to jointly by the parents of the infant or only the mother if the father refuses... Lex specialis derogat generali... Thus, it is mandatory that the mother of an illegitimate child signs the birth certificate of her child in all cases, irrespective of whether the father recognizes the child as his or not."**
**"Acts executed against the provisions of mandatory or prohibitory laws shall be void... Accordingly, we declare the subject birth certificates void and order their cancellation for being registered against the mandatory provisions of the Family Code requiring the use of the mother's surname for her illegitimate children and Act No. 3753 requiring the signature of the mother in her children's birth certificates."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Mandatory Mother's Surname:** Under Article 176 of the Family Code, as amended by R.A. 9255, the baseline rule is that illegitimate children **shall** use the maternal surname. The statutory authorization for using the paternal surname employs the permissive word "may," vesting discretion exclusively in the child (exercised via an AUSF under the Revised IRR of R.A. 9255), not the father. Because no valid AUSF was executed, the children's surname must mandatorily be "Barcelote."
**Sole Maternal Parental Authority:** An illegitimate child is under the sole parental authority and custody of the mother (**Briones v. Miguel**). Custody and naming rights spring directly from this exclusive parental authority.
**Special Rule of Section 5, Act No. 3753:** While paragraph 1 of Section 5 generally permits "either parent" to report a birth, this applies only to legitimate children under the strong legal presumption of legitimacy. Conversely, paragraph 4 of Section 5 is **lex specialis** strictly governing illegitimate children, commanding that the birth certificate **"shall be signed and sworn to jointly by the parents of the infant or only the mother if the father refuses."**
**Mandatory Maternal Signature:** The mother conclusively carries the bloodline and is the only legally known parent at birth. To prevent individuals from being falsely designated, the mother's signature is indispensable in all illegitimate birth registrations, regardless of paternal recognition.
**Nullity under Article 5 of the Civil Code:** Because the mother's signature was missing on the face of the Davao City certificates, the Local Civil Registrar had no authority to register them. Under Article 5 of the Civil Code, acts executed against mandatory laws are void. Citing **Babiera v. Catotal**, unsigned and non-compliant birth certificates must be cancelled.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The Supreme Court ruled that an illegitimate father cannot unilaterally register his child's birth or impose his surname. Under Article 176 of the Family Code, illegitimate children are under the sole parental authority of their mother and must carry her surname; using the father's surname is an option belonging to the child/mother, not a right of the father. Furthermore, Section 5 of Act No. 3753 strictly requires the mother to sign the birth certificate of an illegitimate child in all instances; without her signature, the registration is completely void and must be cancelled from the civil registry.
Issue 2: Propriety of Cancellation under Rule 108
**(a) Short Answer: YES (Cancellation is the Proper Remedy).** When certificates of live birth are void **ab initio** for complete failure to comply with mandatory statutory prerequisites, cancellation under Rule 108—rather than mere correction—is the proper and necessary legal remedy.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
**"Clearly, the subject birth certificates were not executed consistent with the provisions of the law respecting the registration of birth of illegitimate children. Aside from the fact that the entry in the subject birth certificates as to the surname of the children is incorrect since it should have been that of the mother, the subject birth certificates are also incomplete as they lacked the signature of the mother."**
**"In all actions concerning children, whether undertaken by public or private social welfare institutions, courts of law, administrative authorities or legislative bodies, the best interests of the child shall be the primary consideration."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
The CA erred in holding that petitioner could only seek correction of entries rather than cancellation. Rule 108 expressly encompasses both cancellation and correction of civil registry entries.
Because the birth certificates suffered from fatal, structural nullities (lack of maternal signature and absence of legal authority by the registrar to accept them), the documents themselves are null and void under Article 5 of the Civil Code.
A totally void certificate cannot be cured by piecemeal correction; striking the entire void record down through cancellation is proper, thereby giving full legal effect to the valid late registrations executed by the mother in Santa Cruz, Davao del Sur.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Rule 108 allows parties to seek cancellation, not just corrections. Since the Davao registrations were made without the mother's signature in direct violation of mandatory law, they were completely void from the beginning. You do not merely "correct" a void document; the entire registration must be cancelled.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text** (The Decision of the Second Division was unanimous, with Peralta, Mendoza, Leonen, and Martires, **JJ.**, concurring with the **Ponente**, Carpio, **J.**).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, we GRANT the petition. We REVERSE and SET ASIDE the 5 March 2015 Decision and the 3 December 2015 Resolution of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. CV No. 03223-MIN. We REINSTATE the 28 February 2013 Decision of the Regional Trial Court of Davao City, Branch 15, in SPC. PROC. No. 12,007-12. The Civil Registrar of the Office of the Local Civil Registry of Davao City is ordered to CANCEL: (1) the Certificate of Live Birth of Avee Kynna Noelle Barcelote Tinitigan under Registry No. 2008-21709 and (2) the Certificate of Live Birth of Yuhares Jan Barcelote Tinitigan under Registry No. 2011-28329.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Petitioner Jonna Karla Baguio Barcelote prevailed completely. The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated the RTC Decision, officially ordering the Local Civil Registrar of Davao City to cancel both birth certificates registered by the putative father Ricky Tinitigan, leaving petitioner's registrations in Santa Cruz, Davao del Sur as the operative records.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Recognizable Title: Rodriguez v. Court of Appeals and Agbulos**
**Full Official Caption:** Bienvenido Rodriguez, Petitioner, v. Court of Appeals and Clarito Agbulos, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 85723
**Date of Promulgation:** June 19, 1995
**Philippine Reports Citation:** Not stated in the decision
**Ponente:** Quiason, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** First Division; Davide, Jr., Bellosillo, and Kapunan, **JJ.**, concur; Padilla, **J.**, took no part.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code / Paternity & Filiation → Illegitimate Children → Proof of Filiation and Actions for Compulsory Recognition
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Remedial Law → Special Civil Actions → Rule 65 (Certiorari) → Interlocutory Orders Exception
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Historical Landmark Rule (Civil Code of the Philippines):**
**Article 280: "When the father or the mother makes the recognition separately, he or she shall not reveal the name of the person with whom he or she had the child; neither shall he or she state any circumstance whereby the other party may be identified."**
**Article 283:**
**"In any of the following cases, the father is obliged to recognize the child as his natural child:**
**(1) In cases of rape, abduction or seduction, when the period of the offense coincides more or less with that of the conception;**
**(2) When the child is in continuous possession of status of a child of the alleged father by the direct acts of the latter or of his family;**
(3) **When the child was conceived during the time when the mother cohabited with the supposed father;**
**(4) When the child has in his favor any evidence or proof that the defendant is his father."**
**Modern Codified Equivalence (Family Code of the Philippines):**
**Article 172:**
**"The filiation of legitimate children is established by any of the following:**
**(1) The record of birth appearing in the civil register or a final judgment; or**
**(2) An admission of legitimate filiation in a public document or a private handwritten instrument and signed by the parent concerned.**
**In the absence of the foregoing evidence, the legitimate filiation shall be proved by:**
**(1) The open and continuous possession of the status of a legitimate child; or**
**(2) Any other means allowed by the Rules of Court and special laws."**
**Article 175:**
**"Illegitimate children may establish their illegitimate filiation in the same way and on the same evidence as legitimate children."**
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Rule / Provision Triggered:** The prohibition against naming the other parent under **Article 280 of the Civil Code** applies solely to **voluntary** recognition (the unilateral, separate acknowledgment executed in a public document or record of birth) and does not bar the mother from testifying on the identity of the putative father in an action for **compulsory** recognition.
**Specific Sub-Rule Highlighted:** Under **Article 283(4) of the Civil Code** (and modern **Articles 172 and 175 of the Family Code**), actions to compel recognition allow "any evidence or proof that the defendant is his father," including the direct, personal-knowledge testimony of the mother under Section 30, Rule 130 of the Rules of Court.
**Factual Trigger:** In a judicial action to compel recognition and support filed by a child against the alleged father, the defendant objected to the mother being asked to reveal the identity of the father, asserting the testimonial barrier in Article 280.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Clarito (Alarito) Agbulos:** Private respondent; illegitimate child seeking compulsory recognition and support.
**Bienvenido Rodriguez:** Petitioner; putative father who objected to the mother's testimony identifying him.
**Felicitas Agbulos Haber:** Mother of Clarito Agbulos; first witness called to identify the child's father.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on Certiorari under **Rule 45** of the Revised Rules of Court, seeking review of the November 2, 1988 Decision of the Court of Appeals in **CA-G.R. SP No. 14276**, which reversed the interlocutory order of RTC Branch 9, Baguio-Benguet.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**October 15, 1986:** Private respondent Clarito Agbulos filed a complaint for compulsory recognition and support against petitioner Bienvenido Rodriguez before the Regional Trial Court, Branch 9, Baguio-Benguet.
**Trial Phase:** At the trial, private respondent called his mother, Felicitas Agbulos Haber, as his first witness. On direct examination, counsel asked her to reveal the identity of the child's father. Counsel for petitioner raised an objection based on Article 280 of the Civil Code.
**Trial Court Action:** The RTC sustained petitioner's objection and disallowed the mother from testifying as to the putative father's identity.
**Certiorari Action (UDK 8516):** Private respondent filed a petition for review on certiorari before the Supreme Court challenging the trial court's interlocutory exclusionary order.
**March 18, 1988:** The Supreme Court referred the petition to the Court of Appeals (docketed as **CA-G.R. SP No. 14276**).
**November 2, 1988:** The Court of Appeals promulgated a decision reversing the RTC's exclusionary order, ruling that the mother's testimony on the identity of the putative father is admissible in an action for compulsory recognition.
**Present Petition:** Petitioner filed the instant Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 before the Supreme Court.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Bienvenido Rodriguez):
**Main Thesis:** The Court of Appeals erred in entertaining certiorari against an interlocutory evidentiary order and erred in reversing the exclusion of the mother's testimony.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Procedural:** The trial court's order disallowing the mother's testimony was purely interlocutory and cannot be reviewed separately via certiorari prior to final judgment.
**Substantive:** Under Article 280 of the Civil Code, a parent making a separate recognition is prohibited from revealing the name or identifying circumstances of the other parent; thus, the mother cannot testify in court to identify the father.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Clarito Agbulos):
**Main Thesis:** The mother's testimony is admissible to prove filiation in a judicial action for compulsory recognition.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Statutory Basis:** Article 283(4) of the Civil Code expressly obliges a father to recognize a child when the child has in his favor any evidence or proof of paternity.
**Evidentiary Rule:** Under Section 30, Rule 130 of the Revised Rules of Court, a witness is competent to testify on matters derived from her own personal knowledge and perception.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[Procedural Issue]:** Whether or not the Court of Appeals erred in not dismissing the petition for certiorari assailing an interlocutory order of the trial court disallowing the mother's testimony.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]:** Whether or not the prohibition under Article 280 of the Civil Code of the Philippines bars the mother of an illegitimate child from testifying as to the identity of the putative father in an action for compulsory recognition.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Reviewability of the Interlocutory Order via Certiorari
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did the Court of Appeals err in giving due course to the petition for certiorari against the interlocutory exclusionary order? **NO.** Certiorari is warranted when ordinary appeal would be inadequate and to prevent a failure of justice.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
**"As a rule, errors of judgment or of procedure, not relating to the court's jurisdiction nor involving grave abuse of discretion, are not reviewable by certiorari under Rule 65 of the Revised Rules of Court... However, there are exceptions to said rule. For instance, certiorari is justified in order to prevent irreparable damages and injury to a party, where the trial judge capriciously and whimsically exercised his judgment, or where there may be danger of failure of justice."**
**"We find that had the appellate court sanctioned the trial court's disallowance of the testimony of plaintiff's mother, private respondent would have been deprived of a speedy and adequate remedy considering the importance of said testimony and the erroneous resolution of the trial court."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
While interlocutory orders are generally not reviewable via Rule 65, the rule admits exceptions to prevent failure of justice, irreparable damage, or where the trial court exercised its judgment whimsically.
An appeal from a final judgment would be slow, inadequate, and insufficient because the excluded testimony went to the very core of the cause of action (establishing paternity).
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language Explanation):** Even though the trial court's order disallowing the mother's testimony was interlocutory, the Court of Appeals properly reviewed it via certiorari because disallowing the mother from naming the father destroyed the plaintiff's case at its inception. Waiting for a final judgment and then appealing would have been an inadequate remedy causing a failure of justice.
Issue 2: Admissibility of the Mother's Testimony Identifying the Father
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does Article 280 of the Civil Code prohibit the mother from testifying on the identity of the putative father in an action for compulsory recognition? **NO.** The statutory prohibition against naming the other parent applies solely to voluntary acknowledgment, not to judicial actions for compulsory recognition.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
**"...our conclusion that the prohibition in Article 280 against the identification of the father or mother of a child applied only in voluntary and not in compulsory recognition. This conclusion becomes abundantly clear if we consider the relative position of the progenitor of Article 280, which was Article 132 of the Spanish Civil Code of 1889, with the other provisions on the acknowledgement of natural children of the same Code."**
**"The prohibition to reveal the name or circumstance of the parent who does not intervene in the separate recognition is limited only to the very act of making such separate recognition. It does not extend to any other act or to cases allowed by law. Thus, when a recognition has been made by one parent, the name of the other parent may be revealed in an action by the child to compel such other parent to recognize him also..." (quoting Tolentino)**
**"Worth noting is the fact that no similar prohibition found in Article 280 of the Civil Code of the Philippines has been replicated in the present Family Code. This undoubtedly discloses the intention of the legislative authority to uphold the Code Commission's stand to liberalize the rule on the investigation of the paternity of illegitimate children."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Statutory History & Placement:** In the Spanish Civil Code of 1889 (Article 132) and the Civil Code of the Philippines (Article 280), the prohibition immediately followed the provisions regulating **voluntary recognition** (Articles 131 and 278, respectively, regarding acknowledgment in a birth record, will, or public document). The prohibition targeted extrajudicial acts to prevent a recognizing parent from unilaterally slandering or implicating an unconsenting third party in a public instrument.
**Compulsory Recognition Distinct:** Compulsory recognition is governed by distinct rules (Article 283, Civil Code). Paragraph 4 allows "any evidence or proof that the defendant is his father." A mother who has personal knowledge of conception and cohabitation under Section 30, Rule 130 is competent to testify on that fact in court.
**Distinction from Prior Precedents:**
In **Navarro v. Bacalla**, the Court expressly reserved ruling on whether the mother's testimony is admissible over a timely objection; **Rodriguez** resolves that question.
In **Infante v. Fiqueras**, the exclusion of the mother's testimony was anchored on Article 135 of the Spanish Civil Code and the restrictive Law of Bases of May 11, 1888, which banned paternity inquiries except for crimes or indubitable writing. Article 283 liberalized these grounds.
**Evolution into the Family Code:** Articles 276–280 of the Civil Code were repealed by the Family Code. Under Family Code Articles 172 and 175, illegitimate filiation can be proved by "any other means allowed by the Rules of Court," confirming the complete abandonment of the barrier against testimonial inquiry into paternity.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language Explanation):** Article 280 of the Civil Code was designed to stop one parent from dragging another person's name into a birth certificate or public document during a unilateral, voluntary recognition. It does not muzzle the mother on the witness stand in a lawsuit to compel the father to recognize the child; in court, the mother's direct testimony is competent personal knowledge and constitutes admissible proof of paternity.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**Padilla, J.:** Took no part.
**Other Justices:** Davide, Jr., Bellosillo, and Kapunan, **JJ.**, concurred without separate opinions.
**Conclusion:** No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
**"WHEREFORE, the Decision of the Court of Appeals is AFFIRMED. The trial court is DIRECTED to PROCEED with dispatch in the disposition of the action for compulsory recognition.**
**SO ORDERED."**
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Private respondent Clarito Agbulos prevailed. The Supreme Court affirmed the decision of the Court of Appeals, upholding the admissibility of the mother's testimony identifying the petitioner as the father, and directed the Regional Trial Court to proceed with the trial for compulsory recognition and support without delay.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Ernestina Bernabe v. Carolina Alejo**
**Full Official Caption:** Ernestina Bernabe, Petitioner, vs. Carolina Alejo as guardian ad litem for the minor Adrian Bernabe, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 140500 | January 21, 2002 | Third Division | Panganiban, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Melo (**Chairman**), Sandoval-Gutierrez, and Carpio, **JJ.**, concur; Vitug, **J.**, took no part (relationship with family).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code / Paternity & Filiation → Proof of Filiation of Illegitimate Children → Period to File Action for Recognition / Vested Rights
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Remedial Law → Civil Procedure → Rule 45 Appeals → Proper Parties / Non-Impleading of Lower Courts
**Full Text of Governing Statutory Provisions:**
**Article 285, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"ART. 285. The action for the recognition of natural children may be brought only during the lifetime of the presumed parents, except in the following cases:
(1) **If the father or mother died during the minority of the child, in which case the latter may file the action before the expiration of four years from the attainment of his majority;**
(2) If after the death of the father or of the mother a document should appear of which nothing had been heard and in which either or both parents recognize the child.
In this case, the action must be commenced within four years from the finding of the document."
**Articles 172, 173, 175, and 255, Family Code of the Philippines (Executive Order No. 209):**
"ART. 172. The filiation of legitimate children is established by any of the following:
(1) The record of birth appearing in the civil register or a final judgment; or
(2) An admission of legitimate filiation in a public document or a private handwritten instrument and signed by the parent concerned.
In the absence of the foregoing evidence, the legitimate filiation shall be proved by:
(1) The open and continuous possession of the status of a legitimate child; or
(2) Any other means allowed by the Rules of Court and special laws."
"ART. 173. The action to claim legitimacy may be brought by the child during his or her lifetime and shall be transmitted to the heirs should the child die during minority or in a state of insanity. In these cases, the heirs shall have a period of five years within which to institute the action.
The action already commenced by the child shall survive notwithstanding the death of either or both of the parties."
"ART. 175. Illegitimate children may establish their illegitimate filiation in the same way and on the same evidence as legitimate children.
**The action must be brought within the same period specified in Article 173, except when the action is based on the second paragraph of Article 172, in which case the action may be brought during the lifetime of the alleged parent.**"
"ART. 255. **This Code shall have retroactive effect insofar as it does not prejudice or impair vested or acquired rights in accordance with the Civil Code or other laws.**"
**Section 4(a), Rule 45, 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure:**
"SEC. 4. **Contents of petition.** — The petition shall be filed in eighteen (18) copies, with the original copy intended for the court being indicated as such by the petitioner, and shall (a) **state the full name of the appealing party as the petitioner and the adverse party as respondent, without impleading the lower courts or judges thereof either as petitioners or respondents;** [...]"
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Rule / Provision Triggered:** Under Article 175 in relation to Article 172 (second paragraph) of the Family Code, actions to establish illegitimate filiation based on open and continuous possession or other means must be brought **during the lifetime of the alleged parent**. However, under Article 255 of the Family Code, this retroactive procedural bar cannot prejudice or impair **vested or acquired rights**.
**Specific Sub-Rules / Doctrinal Tests Highlighted:**
1. **Substantive vs. Procedural Distinction:** A statute that creates, defines, and regulates rights is substantive, not merely adjective. The right granted by Article 285(1) of the Civil Code—giving a minor child whose putative parent died during minority a period of up to four years from reaching the age of majority to file an action for recognition—is a **substantive vested right**.
2. **Application to Spurious (Non-Natural) Children:** Although Article 285 literally mentions "natural children," its prescriptive period applies equally to spurious/adulterous children (**Divinagracia v. Rovira**; **Aruego v. CA**).
3. **Survival of Minority Rights:** An illegitimate child who was already conceived/born and still a minor when the Family Code took effect on August 3, 1988, cannot be stripped of the Article 285(1) period to sue if the putative parent dies during their minority.
**Factual Trigger:** Fiscal Ernesto Bernabe died in 1993 during the minority of his alleged illegitimate son, Adrian (born September 18, 1981). When Adrian's mother filed the recognition suit in 1994, the legitimate daughter invoked Article 175 of the Family Code to dismiss the claim because the putative father was already dead and left no written acknowledgment.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Adrian Bernabe:** Minor born on September 18, 1981; putative illegitimate son of Fiscal Ernesto A. Bernabe.
**Carolina Alejo:** Adrian's mother and guardian **ad litem**; former secretary of Fiscal Bernabe for 23 years.
**Fiscal Ernesto A. Bernabe:** Putative father; died on August 13, 1993.
**Rosalina Bernabe:** Wife of Fiscal Bernabe; died on December 3, 1993.
**Ernestina Bernabe:** Petitioner; legitimate daughter and sole surviving legal heir of Fiscal Ernesto and Rosalina Bernabe.
**Procedural Posture:**
**RTC Pasay City (Branch 109):** Granted Ernestina's Motion for Reconsideration via Order dated July 26, 1995 (reiterated October 6, 1995), dismissing the complaint under Article 175 of the Family Code.
**Court of Appeals (Special First Division):** In CA-G.R. CV No. 51919 (July 7, 1999; Resolution October 14, 1999), reversed and set aside the RTC's dismissal and remanded the case for trial on the merits under Article 285 of the Civil Code.
**Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on **Certiorari** under Rule 45 filed by Ernestina Bernabe challenging the CA decision.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**September 18, 1981:** Adrian Bernabe is born to Carolina Alejo, allegedly fathered by Fiscal Ernesto A. Bernabe out of an extramarital relationship while Carolina served as his secretary.
**August 3, 1988:** The Family Code takes effect. Adrian is seven (7) years old.
**August 13, 1993:** Fiscal Ernesto A. Bernabe dies. Adrian is eleven (11) years old (turning 12 the next month).
**December 3, 1993:** Rosalina Bernabe, wife of Fiscal Bernabe, dies, leaving their legitimate daughter, Ernestina Bernabe, as sole surviving heir in possession of the estate.
**May 16, 1994:** Carolina Alejo, as guardian **ad litem** for minor Adrian (then 12 years old), files Civil Case No. 94-0562 before the RTC of Pasay City for recognition and partition with accounting against Ernestina.
**July 26, 1995:** The RTC grants Ernestina's Motion for Reconsideration and dismisses the complaint, citing Article 175 of the Family Code and **Uyguangco v. Court of Appeals**, holding that the putative father's death barred the suit.
**October 6, 1995:** The RTC denies reconsideration, adding that absent written recognition, the suit must be filed during the putative father's lifetime.
**July 7, 1999:** The CA reverses the RTC, holding that under Article 285 of the Civil Code, Adrian has until four years after reaching majority to sue, a right not impaired by the Family Code. Reconsideration is denied on October 14, 1999.
**Appeal to the SC:** Ernestina petitions the Supreme Court under Rule 45.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's (Ernestina Bernabe) Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Adrian's action for recognition is completely barred because it was filed after the putative father's death without written acknowledgment, as required by the retroactive mandate of Article 175 of the Family Code.
**Specific Contentions:**
Article 285 of the Civil Code was supplanted and repealed by Articles 172, 173, and 175 of the Family Code.
The Family Code applies retroactively because prescriptive periods for filing actions are merely procedural, and no vested rights can attach to procedural rules.
Under Article 175, an action to establish filiation under the second paragraph of Article 172 can only be brought during the lifetime of the putative parent to prevent fraudulent post-mortem claims.
Article 285 applied only to "natural children"; Adrian was adulterous/spurious (since Fiscal Bernabe was married to Rosalina), disqualifying him from the Article 285 exception.
The petition before the SC is defective (raised as an issue, though mistakenly framed regarding impleading the CA).
B. Respondent's (Carolina Alejo / Adrian Bernabe) Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Adrian has a vested substantive right under Article 285(1) of the Civil Code to file for recognition within four years after reaching the age of majority, which cannot be impaired by the Family Code.
**Specific Contentions:**
Article 285 creates a substantive right that vested in Adrian upon his birth in 1981 prior to the enactment of the Family Code.
Under Article 255 of the Family Code, retroactive application is prohibited if it impairs vested or acquired rights.
Jurisprudence (**Divinagracia v. Rovira**; **Aruego v. CA**) has settled that the benefits and prescriptive periods of Article 285 apply equally to spurious/adulterous children.
Under the doctrine of **parens patriae**, the State must protect minors who could not legally file suit on their own during the lifetime of their putative parents.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Court of Appeals erred in ruling that respondent had four years from the attainment of majority age to file an action for recognition under Article 285 of the Civil Code, despite its alleged repeal by the Family Code.
**(Recitation-Ready Question: Does an illegitimate child born under the Civil Code whose putative father died during the child's minority retain the vested right under Article 285 of the Civil Code to file an action for recognition within four years from reaching majority, notwithstanding Article 175 of the Family Code?)**
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not respondent has a cause of action to seek recognition after the putative father's death given that the child was spurious (non-natural) and lacked written acknowledgment.
**(Recitation-Ready Question: Does the exception in Article 285 of the Civil Code allowing post-mortem filiation suits apply to spurious or adulterous children?)**
3. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the petition for review is fatally defective for failing to implead the Court of Appeals as a respondent.
**(Recitation-Ready Question: Under Rule 45 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, is an appeal defective if the Court of Appeals is omitted from the caption?)**
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Retention of Prescriptive Period under Article 285 of the Civil Code as a Vested Right
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO**, the Court of Appeals did not err. The illegitimate child retains the right to file for recognition within four years from reaching majority because it is a substantive, vested right protected from impairment under Article 255 of the Family Code.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"The right to seek recognition granted by the Civil Code to illegitimate children who were still minors at the time the Family Code took effect cannot be impaired or taken away. The minors have up to four years from attaining majority age within which to file an action for recognition."
"Applying the foregoing jurisprudence, we hold that Article 285 of the Civil Code is a substantive law, as it gives Adrian the right to file his petition for recognition within four years from attaining majority age. Therefore, the Family Code cannot impair or take Adrian's right to file an action for recognition, because that right had already vested prior to its enactment."
"To emphasize, illegitimate children who were still minors at the time the Family Code took effect and whose putative parent died during their minority are thus given the right to seek recognition (under Article 285 of the Civil Code) for a period of up to four years from attaining majority age. This vested right was not impaired or taken away by the passage of the Family Code."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Statutory Contrast:** Article 175 of the Family Code omitted the two exceptions of Article 285 of the Civil Code, requiring that actions based on open and continuous possession or other means be filed during the parent's lifetime.
**Protection of Vested Rights:** Article 255 of the Family Code explicitly provides that it shall have retroactive effect **only insofar as it does not prejudice or impair vested or acquired rights**.
**Substantive Character of Article 285:** Citing **Bustos v. Lucero** and **Fabian v. Desierto**, the Court established that a rule is substantive if it creates or defines rights, rather than merely prescribing a procedural remedy. Article 285 granted Adrian a substantive right to institute an action within four years after reaching majority.
**Distinction of Precedents: Uyguangco v. CA** does not apply because the claimant there was already of legal age when seeking recognition. In contrast, under **Aruego v. CA**, rights vested under the Civil Code cannot be extinguished by the subsequent enactment of the Family Code.
**Parens Patriae:** Adrian was 7 years old when the Family Code took effect and 12 years old when Fiscal Bernabe died. A minor cannot institute an action on his own; stripping him of the four-year window post-majority violates the State’s duty as **parens patriae**.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):**
Even though the Family Code generally requires illegitimate children to sue for recognition while the putative parent is still alive, this rule cannot retroactively strip away rights that already attached under the old Civil Code. Because Adrian was born in 1981 under the Civil Code and was still a minor when his father died in 1993, he possesses a vested substantive right under Article 285 to bring the action until four years after he turns 18.
Issue 2: Applicability of Article 285 to Spurious (Non-Natural) Children
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: YES**, the respondent has a valid cause of action. The four-year prescriptive period following majority under Article 285 of the Civil Code applies equally to spurious/adulterous children.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"A strict and literal interpretation of Article 285 has already been frowned upon by this Court in the aforesaid case of **Aruego**, which allowed minors to file a case for recognition even if their parents were disqualified from marrying each other."
"The prescriptive period for filing the action for compulsory recognition in the case of natural children, as provided for in article 285 of the Civil Code, applies to spurious children." **(Quoting Divinagracia v. Rovira)**
"Thus, under the Civil Code, natural children have superior successional rights over spurious ones. However, **Rovira** treats them as equals with respect to other rights, including the right to recognition granted by Article 285."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Rejection of Literal Construction:** Petitioner argued that because Fiscal Bernabe was married, Adrian was spurious and excluded from Article 285, which refers textually to "natural children."
**Application of Rovira Doctrine:** In **Divinagracia v. Rovira**, the Court held that while spurious children have lesser successional shares under the Civil Code, the grounds and procedural mechanisms for compulsory recognition—including the prescriptive periods in Article 285—apply to them equally.
**Reaffirmation via Aruego:** In **Aruego v. CA**, children born of an adulterous relationship whose putative father died during their minority were permitted to file recognition suits post-mortem under Article 285.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):**
Although the text of Article 285 mentions only "natural" children, established case law extends its protective deadlines to spurious or adulterous children as well. Adrian is entitled to the same procedural timeline to establish his paternity as a natural child, notwithstanding his adulterous conception.
Issue 3: Procedural Omission of the Court of Appeals in Rule 45 Petition
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO**, the petition is not defective. Under the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, lower courts should not be impleaded in Rule 45 petitions.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Under Section 4(a) of Rule 45 of the current Rules of Court, it is no longer required to implead 'the lower courts or judges x x x either as petitioners or respondents.' Under Section 3, however, the lower tribunal should still be furnished a copy of the petition. Hence, the failure of petitioner to implead the Court of Appeals as a party is not a reversible error; it is in fact the correct procedure."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Section 4(a), Rule 45 of the 1997 Rules expressly prohibits impleading the lower court or appellate court as a party.
The only requirement with respect to the CA is serving it with a copy of the petition pursuant to Section 3.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):**
Omitting the Court of Appeals from the caption of a Rule 45 petition is not an error; it is the exact requirement of the procedural rules.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the Petition is hereby DENIED and the assailed Decision and Resolution AFFIRMED. Costs against petitioner."
### "SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court ruled entirely in favor of minor Adrian Bernabe (represented by Carolina Alejo). The CA decision was affirmed, meaning the RTC's dismissal was overturned, and the case was remanded to the trial court to allow Adrian to undergo a full trial on the merits to prove his filiation and claim his share in Fiscal Bernabe's estate.
