### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Abadilla v. Tabiliran, Jr.**
**Full Official Caption:** Ma. Blyth B. Abadilla, Complainant, v. Judge Jose C. Tabiliran, Jr., Presiding Judge, 8th MCTC, Manukan and Jose Dalman, 9th Judicial Region, Manukan, Zamboanga del Norte, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:**
**Docket Number:** A.M. No. MTJ-92-716
**Date of Promulgation:** October 25, 1995
**Philippine Reports Citation:** 319 Phil. 574 (249 SCRA 447)
**Ponente: Per Curiam**
**Voting Breakdown:** En Banc. Narvasa, **C.J.**, Feliciano, Padilla, Regalado, Davide, Jr., Romero, Bellosillo, Melo, Puno, Vitug, Kapunan, Mendoza, Francisco, and Hermosisima, Jr., **JJ.**, concur; Panganiban, **J.**, took no part.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Legal & Judicial Ethics → Code of Judicial Conduct → Canon 2 (Avoiding Impropriety) & Canon 4 (Extra-Judicial Activities) → Gross Immorality, Deceitful Misrepresentation of Civil Status/Legitimation, and Corruption in Performance of **Ex-Officio** Notarial Functions / Extortion in Court Cases.
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code / Civil Code of the Philippines → Presumption of Death (Art. 390, Civil Code / Rule 131, Sec. 3[w], Rules of Court) → Requisites for Bigamous Marriage under Art. 83(2) of the Civil Code.
Civil Law → Paternity and Filiation → Legitimation → Exclusion of Adulterous/Illegitimate Children Born During an Existing Marriage (Art. 269, Civil Code / Art. 177, Family Code).
Administrative Law → Revised Administrative Code → Notarial Law (Sec. 252) → **Ex-Officio** Notarization by Judges and Accounting of Collected Fees.
**Full Text of Governing Provisions:**
**Canon 2, Code of Judicial Conduct:**
"CANON 2 — A JUDGE SHOULD AVOID IMPROPRIETY AND THE APPEARANCE OF IMPROPRIETY IN ALL ACTIVITIES."
**Article 390, Civil Code of the Philippines (Presumption of Death):**
"Art. 390. **After an absence of seven years, it being unknown whether or not the absentee still lives, he shall be presumed dead for all purposes**, except for those of succession.
The absentee shall not be presumed dead for the purpose of opening his succession till after an absence of ten years. If he disappeared after the age of seventy-five years, an absence of five years shall be sufficient in order that his succession may be opened."
**Article 269, Civil Code of the Philippines (Legitimation) / Art. 177, Family Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 269. **Only natural children can be legitimated. Children born outside of wedlock of parents who, at the time of the conception of the former, were not disqualified by any impediment to marry each other, are natural.**"
**(Family Code Equivalent)**:
"Art. 177. **Only children conceived and born outside of wedlock of parents who, at the time of the conception of the former, were not disqualified by any impediment to marry each other may be legitimated.**"
**Section 252, Notarial Law (Revised Administrative Code of the Philippines):**
"Sec. 252. **Compensation of Notaries Public.** — No fee, compensation, or reward of any sort, except such as is expressly prescribed and allowed by law, shall be collected or received for any service rendered by a notary public. Such money collected by notaries public proper shall belong to them personally. **Officers acting as notaries public ex-officio shall charge for their services the fees prescribed by law and account therefor as for Government funds.**"
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**Presumption of Death and Defense of Desertion:** A spouse cannot invoke the seven-year presumption of death under Art. 390 of the Civil Code or Rule 131, Sec. 3(w) of the Rules of Court to excuse cohabitation with another partner when seven years had not yet elapsed between the alleged desertion and the commencement of the illicit cohabitation.
**Bar to Legitimation of Adulterous Issues:** Children conceived and born while one parent is legally married to another person are adulterous/spurious issues; they cannot be legitimated by a subsequent marriage under Art. 269 of the Civil Code (or Art. 177 of the Family Code). Registering them as "legitimate" and misrepresenting their birth order by executing false affidavits constitutes deceitful conduct.
**MTC/MCTC Judges as Notaries Public Ex-Officio (A.M. No. 89-11-1303, MTC; Lapeña, Jr. v. Marcos):** Judges may act as notaries public **ex-officio** in municipalities without lawyers/notaries only if: (1) all notarial fees charged are for the account of the Government and turned over to the municipal treasurer; and (2) a certification is embedded attesting to the lack of any lawyer or notary public in the locality. Failure to turn over and account for collected fees creates a presumption of personal misappropriation.
**Preparing Pleadings and Extorting Fees in Pending Cases:** A judge who prepares an affidavit of desistance and motion to dismiss in a criminal case pending before his own sala and charges the accused a fee commits gross corruption and extortion.
**Factual Trigger:** A municipal circuit judge cohabited with another woman barely 4 years after his wife allegedly left him, fathered three children during his subsisting marriage, registered them as "legitimate," married the concubine while listing his status as "single," pocketed fees for private notarizations without remitting them to the municipal treasury, and accepted ₱500.00 from an accused to draft an affidavit of desistance in an attempted rape case pending before his own court.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Ma. Blyth B. Abadilla:** Complainant; Clerk of Court assigned to the 8th MCTC of Manukan and Jose Dalman, Zamboanga del Norte.
**Judge Jose C. Tabiliran, Jr.:** Respondent; Presiding Judge of the 8th MCTC of Manukan and Jose Dalman, Zamboanga del Norte.
**Teresita Banzuela (Teresita B. Tabiliran):** Respondent's first, legitimate, and subsisting wife.
**Priscilla Q. Baybayan:** Paramour and subsequent cohabitant of respondent; later married by him in 1986.
**Buenasol, Venus, and Saturn Tabiliran:** Illegitimate children begotten by respondent with Priscilla Baybayan between 1970 and 1975, fraudulently registered as legitimate.
**Executive Judge Jesus O. Angeles:** Investigating Judge (RTC, Dipolog City) tasked by the Supreme Court En Banc to conduct the formal investigation.
**Arcelita Salvador & Benito Sagario:** Complainant and witness in an attempted rape case pending before respondent's sala, who attested that respondent drafted an affidavit of desistance in exchange for ₱500.00.
**Ely O. Inot:** MCTC Court Aide/Interpreter who assisted respondent in processing notarizations and receiving fees.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Original Administrative Complaint filed on **September 8, 1992**, by Clerk of Court Abadilla directly with the Supreme Court, charging Respondent Judge with gross immorality, deceitful conduct, and corruption.
By Resolution dated **April 12, 1993**, the Supreme Court En Banc referred the matter to Executive Judge Jesus O. Angeles (RTC, Dipolog City) for investigation, report, and recommendation.
Investigating Judge Angeles submitted his Report and Recommendation on **August 3, 1993**, finding respondent guilty of two counts of corruption and recommending a three-month suspension. The Supreme Court reviewed the findings En Banc under its administrative disciplinary authority.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1966:** According to respondent, his first wife, Teresita Banzuela, left and abandoned their conjugal dwelling in Katipunan, Zamboanga del Norte.
**December 8, 1969:** Teresita Banzuela files an administrative complaint against respondent (**Tabiliran v. Tabiliran**, 115 SCRA 451 [1982]) for abandonment of the family home and cohabiting with a certain Leonora Pillarion. (Respondent was reprimanded therein for executing a void "Deed of Settlement of Spouses To Live Separately from Bed").
**1970:** Respondent begins publicly cohabiting with Priscilla Q. Baybayan.
**July 14, 1970:** Buenasol B. Tabiliran is born to respondent and Priscilla Baybayan.
**September 7, 1971:** Venus B. Tabiliran is born to respondent and Priscilla Baybayan.
**September 20, 1975:** Saturn B. Tabiliran is born to respondent and Priscilla Baybayan.
**May 24, 1983, May 27, 1988, & May 28, 1988:** Respondent executes separate affidavits for the delayed registration of his three children with Priscilla, falsely listing them as his "legitimate" children and attributing the delay to inadvertence or excusable negligence.
**May 23, 1986:** Respondent contracts marriage with Priscilla Baybayan before Municipal Mayor Jacinto C. Ruedas, Jr., falsely indicating his civil status as "single" on the marriage contract, while executing a joint affidavit claiming Teresita had abandoned him in 1965.
**November 12, 1991:** Respondent prepares and notarizes multiple private documents (Joint Affidavits of ages, Simultaneous Deeds of Sale) through MCTC Aide Ely O. Inot, charging sums of ₱600.00, ₱250.00, ₱150.00, and ₱50.00, retaining the fees without accounting for them or remitting them to the Municipal Treasurer.
**Undated (Prior to Sept 1992):** In an attempted rape case pending before his sala, respondent prepares an Affidavit of Desistance and a Motion to Dismiss for the private complainant, Arcelita Salvador, and extracts ₱500.00 for his services from Pitoy Oriola, brother of the accused Antonio Oriola.
**September 8, 1992:** Clerk of Court Ma. Blyth B. Abadilla formally files a verified administrative complaint charging respondent with Gross Immorality, Deceitful Conduct, and Corruption.
**April 12, 1993:** The Supreme Court En Banc refers the administrative complaint to RTC Executive Judge Jesus O. Angeles for investigation.
**August 3, 1993:** Investigating Judge Angeles submits his report recommending a 3-month suspension, finding respondent guilty of two counts of corruption, but exonerating him on gross immorality and deceitful conduct.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Complainant's Arguments (Ma. Blyth B. Abadilla)
**Main Thesis:** Respondent Judge Jose C. Tabiliran, Jr. is morally depraved, corrupt, and legally disqualified from holding judicial office due to bigamy, illicit cohabitation, falsification of public records, unauthorized private practice/pocketing of notarial fees, and extortion in pending court litigation.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Gross Immorality:** Respondent openly cohabited with Priscilla Baybayan while his lawful marriage with Teresita Banzuela was fully subsisting; he contracted a bigamous marriage on May 23, 1986, falsely entering his civil status as "single."
**Deceitful Conduct:** Respondent falsely registered his three adulterous children (Buenasol, Venus, and Saturn) as "legitimate" via false delayed-registration affidavits, knowing they were legally barred from legitimation.
**Corruption (Count 1 - Unauthorized Practice & Illegal Fees):** Respondent utilized judicial office hours to prepare and notarize private contracts and affidavits (e.g., Geromo deed of sale, age affidavits), charging excessive fees (up to ₱600.00) beyond the legal rate of ₱10.00, and retaining the proceeds for himself.
**Corruption (Count 2 - Bribery):** Respondent received a bag of squid and fish from Edna Siton, a litigant in a criminal case pending before him.
**Corruption (Count 3 - Affidavit of Desistance Extortion):** Respondent prepared an affidavit of desistance and motion to dismiss in a criminal case inside his own sala, charging and accepting ₱500.00 from the brother of the accused, Antonio Oriola.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Judge Jose C. Tabiliran, Jr.)
**Main Thesis:** The cohabitation and marriage were legal because his first wife had disappeared; the notarial fees subsidized municipal court shortages; the bribery and extortion claims are fabricated retaliations by an insubordinate clerk of court.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Defense to Immorality:** His first wife, Teresita, abandoned the conjugal home in 1966 and her whereabouts remained unknown for over 25 years. Under Art. 390 of the Civil Code, Rule 131, Sec. 3(w) of the Rules of Court, and **Jones v. Hortiguela**, she was presumed dead for all purposes without requiring a judicial declaration of absence. Entering "single" on the marriage contract was the only appropriate choice among "Single, Widow, or Divorced," and their joint affidavit fully disclosed the prior marriage.
**Defense to Deceitful Conduct:** The late registration affidavits were not fraudulent; the government midwife (Lydia Zanoria) was responsible for timely registration, and her affidavit was inadmissible hearsay because she was never presented for cross-examination.
**Defense to Corruption (Notarization):** Manukan had no commissioned notary public. Certificates from the Mayor authorized him to legalize documents. Under Canon 4, Rule 4.01 of the Code of Judicial Conduct, he acted to improve the administration of justice. The fees were lower than IBP rates and were strictly used to purchase office supplies and build an office extension due to local appropriation deficits.
**Defense to Bribery:** It was physically impossible to accept fresh seafood because he commuted 42 kilometers (1.5 hours by bus) to Katipunan, where the seafood would have spoiled.
**Defense to Corruption (Desistance Extortion):** The claim regarding the ₱500.00 fee for drafting the affidavit of desistance is a fabricated lie orchestrated by complainant Abadilla and her military husband out of malice and revenge because respondent had previously filed an administrative complaint against her for insubordination (A.M. No. P-91-597).
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not respondent Judge is guilty of gross immorality for openly cohabiting with Priscilla Baybayan and subsequently contracting marriage with her during the existence of his marriage to Teresita Banzuela.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not respondent Judge is guilty of deceitful conduct in causing the registration of his illegitimate children with Priscilla Baybayan as "legitimate" and asserting they were his second and third children.
3.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not respondent Judge is guilty of corruption for acting as an **ex-officio** notary public, collecting fees, and failing to remit the proceeds to the municipal treasury.
4.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not respondent Judge is guilty of corruption for preparing an Affidavit of Desistance and a Motion to Dismiss in a criminal case pending before his sala and collecting a ₱500.00 fee for his services.
5.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the charge of receiving bribes (a bag of fish and squid) from a party litigant was sufficiently proven.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Gross Immorality via Cohabitation and Subsequent Marriage
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Respondent lived in open concubinage with Priscilla Baybayan starting in 1970, barely four years after his wife’s alleged 1966 desertion, making the seven-year presumption of death under Art. 390 legally unavailable.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"The provisions of Sec. 3(w) of the Rules of Court and Art. 390 of the Civil Code which provide that, after an absence of seven years, it being unknown whether or not the absentee still lives, the absent spouse shall be considered dead for all purposes, except for those of succession, cannot be invoked by respondent. By respondent's own allegation, Teresita B. Tabiliran left the conjugal home in 1966. From that time on up to the time that respondent started to cohabit with Priscilla Baybayan in 1970, only four years had elapsed. Respondent had no right to presume therefore that Teresita B. Tabiliran was already dead for all purposes."
"Thus, respondent's actuation of cohabiting with Priscilla Baybayan in 1970 when his marriage to Teresita B. Tabiliran was still valid and subsisting constitutes gross immoral conduct. It makes mockery of the inviolability and sanctity of marriage as a basic social institution."
"By committing the immorality in question, respondent violated the trust reposed on his high office and utterly failed to live up to the noble ideals and strict standards of morality required of the law profession."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Investigating Judge's Error Overruled:** The Investigating Judge erred in concluding the cohabitation was cleansed by the 1986 marriage under Art. 83(2) of the Civil Code or by ratification under Art. 1395. Marital cohabitation cannot be ratified as if it were a defectively executed civil contract.
**Mathematical Failure of Presumption of Death:** Respondent claimed his wife left in 1966. However, the record proved he had already fathered Buenasol with Priscilla by July 14, 1970. This established open, illicit cohabitation beginning at least in 1969/1970—scarcely four years after the alleged disappearance. The statutory threshold of seven (7) years under Art. 390 of the Civil Code and Rule 131, Sec. 3(w) was not met.
**Judicial Contradiction on First Wife's Disappearance:** Respondent's factual assertion that Teresita had disappeared without a trace since 1966 was contradicted by Supreme Court records: she actively filed an administrative complaint against him on December 8, 1969 (**Tabiliran v. Tabiliran**, 115 SCRA 451, decided in 1982).
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** A person cannot claim their spouse is "presumed dead" to excuse having a mistress if they moved in with the mistress only four years after the spouse left. Because the law requires seven full years of unexplained absence before someone can be presumed dead, Judge Tabiliran had no legal excuse to start a new family in 1970 while his legal wife was still alive and well.
Issue 2: Deceitful Misrepresentation of Children's Legitimacy
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Respondent executed false affidavits registering his children with Priscilla as "legitimate," when as a judge, he knew that children born out of adulterous relations can never be legitimated.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"As a lawyer and a judge, respondent ought to know that, despite his subsequent marriage to Priscilla, these three children cannot be legitimated nor in any way be considered legitimate since at the time they were born, there was an existing valid marriage between respondent and his first wife, Teresita B. Tabiliran."
"Legitimation is limited to natural children and cannot include those born of adulterous relations (Ramirez vs. Gmur, 42 Phil. 855)... It is clear, therefore, that no legal provision, whether old or new, can give refuge to the deceitful actuations of the respondent."
"Thus, his statements in his affidavits marked as Exhs. 'M-4' and 'O-4' that Saturn and Venus are his third and second children respectively, are erroneous, deceitful, misleading and detrimental to his legitimate children."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Legal Impossibility of Legitimation:** Under Art. 269 of the Civil Code and Art. 177 of the Family Code, legitimation is strictly reserved for "natural" children—children conceived by parents who had no legal impediment to marry each other at the time of conception.
**Adulterous Conception:** Because respondent was legally married to Teresita Banzuela when Buenasol (1970), Venus (1971), and Saturn (1975) were conceived and born, they were spurious/adulterous children. They could never be legitimated by his subsequent 1986 marriage.
**Fraudulent Affidavits and Erased Successional Rights:** In executing delayed registration affidavits swearing these three issues were legitimate, and falsely describing Venus and Saturn as his "second" and "third" children, respondent deliberately obscured the existence and legal superiority of his two actual legitimate children with Teresita (Reynald Antonio and Jose III).
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** Under Philippine law, parents can only "legitimate" children born outside of marriage if the parents were legally free to marry each other when the child was conceived. Because Judge Tabiliran was still legally married to his first wife when these three children were born, they were legally illegitimate and could never become legitimate; by swearing they were legitimate in public birth registries, the Judge committed blatant, deliberate deceit.
Issue 3: Corruption via Notarization and Misappropriation of Notarial Fees
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** While respondent could act as an **ex-officio** notary public in a municipality without lawyers, he was strictly obligated by law to remit all collected fees to the municipal treasury; pocketing them without accounting creates a legal presumption of personal use.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Section 252 of the Notarial Law expressly provides thus: 'Sec. 252. Compensation of Notaries Public — ... Officers acting as notaries public ex-officio shall charge for their services the fees prescribed by law and account therefor as for Government funds.'"
"Respondent's failure to properly account and turn over the fees collected by him as Ex-Officio notary to the municipal government as required by law raises the presumption that he had put such fund to his personal use."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**A.M. No. 89-11-1303 Dual Conditions:** An MTC/MCTC judge can perform regular notarial work **only** when no private lawyer or notary is available, subject to two mandatory conditions: (1) all fees must be for the account of the Government and turned over to the municipal treasurer; and (2) a certification must be placed on the document attesting to the absence of a notary in the municipality.
**Unlawful Retention and Presumption of Misappropriation:** Respondent admitted charging notarial fees ranging from ₱50.00 to ₱600.00 for deeds of sale and affidavits, but failed to turn over a single centavo to the Municipal Treasurer.
**Rejection of "Office Expenses" Defense:** His defense that the money was used to buy paper, office supplies, and construct an office extension cannot exonerate him. Public funds collected under color of law cannot be disbursed at the personal whim of a judge without official accounting, audit, and appropriation.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** Even if a small-town judge is allowed to notarize documents because there are no private lawyers in town, every single peso collected belongs to the government and must be turned over to the town treasurer. Judge Tabiliran kept the money himself; claiming he used it to buy office supplies without any official receipts or accounting is an admission of illegal misappropriation of public funds.
Issue 4: Corruption via Extortion for Drafting Pleadings in a Pending Case
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Drafting an affidavit of desistance and motion to dismiss in a criminal action pending in his own court and taking ₱500.00 from the accused's brother constitutes gross corruption.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Denial, if unsubstantiated by clear and convincing evidence, is a negative and self-serving evidence which deserves no weight in law and cannot be given greater evidentiary value over the testimony of credible witnesses who testify on affirmative matters (People v. Amaguin, 229 SCRA 166)."
"It is unfortunate that respondent had failed to adhere to, and let this remind him once again of Canon 2 of the Code of Judicial Conduct, to wit: 'Canon 2 — A judge should avoid impropriety and the appearance of impropriety in all activities.'"
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Credibility of Direct Evidence:** Private complainant Arcelita Salvador and eyewitness Benito Sagario executed categorical, sworn affidavits detailing how respondent Judge himself prepared the affidavit of desistance and motion to dismiss, and then extracted ₱500.00 from Pitoy Oriola (the brother of the accused).
**Failure to Rebut or Cross-Examine:** Respondent merely offered a bare denial and an uncorroborated conspiracy theory that the charge was framed by complainant and the Iglesia Ni Cristo. Respondent failed to subpoena or confront the eyewitnesses during the investigation. Unsubstantiated negative denials cannot overcome positive, sworn testimony.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** A judge can never act as a lawyer or fixer for cases pending before his own court. Judge Tabiliran drafted an affidavit of desistance to kill an attempted rape case in his own sala and pocketed ₱500.00 from the accused; his bare denial cannot overcome the sworn testimonies of the people who watched him do it.
Issue 5: Sufficiency of Bribery Allegation Involving Fresh Seafood
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The charge was dismissed due to failure of proof, as complainant's own witness testified that the food was left anonymously at a carenderia and eaten by court staff without the Judge's knowledge.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Instead of calling the affiant himself, complainant presented the Court Interpreter Ely O. Inot, who 'confirmed that there was squid and fish contained in a plastic bag which was left in Aseniero Carenderia by a person unknown to her and some members of the Court staff. When informed by the carenderia owner that the stuff was intended for Judge Tabiliran, the latter told them to cook it, and they afterwards partook of it without the Judge who already boarded the passenger bus'... Being her witness, complainant is bound by her testimony. This particular charge is, therefore, not proved."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Complainant failed to present affiant Calixto Calunod to verify that respondent personally accepted the bag of seafood from litigant Edna Siton.
Instead, complainant presented court interpreter Ely O. Inot, whose direct testimony established that the seafood was left anonymously at an eatery, that respondent boarded a bus without touching it, and that court employees cooked and ate it themselves. Complainant was bound by the testimony of her own witness.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** The bribery charge failed because the complainant's own witness admitted on the stand that the Judge never took the bag of fish and squid; it was left at a diner and eaten by the staff after the Judge had already boarded his bus home.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.** (The decision was rendered **Per Curiam** with unanimous concurrence of all participating Justices; Panganiban, **J.**, took no part).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the Court finds respondent Judge Jose C. Tabiliran, Jr. guilty of gross immorality, deceitful conduct and corruption and, consequently, orders his dismissal from the service. Such dismissal shall carry with it cancellation of eligibility, forfeiture of leave credits and retirement benefits, and disqualification from re-employment in the government-service, all without prejudice to criminal or civil liability.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Complainant prevailed. The Supreme Court rejected the Investigating Judge's recommendation of a mere 3-month suspension, found Judge Jose C. Tabiliran, Jr. guilty of Gross Immorality, Deceitful Conduct, and Corruption, and **DISMISSED** him from the judiciary with complete forfeiture of all retirement benefits and leave credits, and perpetual disqualification from any government employment.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Lahom v. Sibulo**
**Full Official Caption:** Isabelita S. Lahom, Petitioner, vs. Jose Melvin Sibulo (previously referred to as "Dr. Melvin S. Lahom"), Respondent
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 143989; July 14, 2003; 453 Phil. 987; First Division; Vitug, **J.** (Ponente); Davide, Jr., **C.J.** (Chairman), Ynares-Santiago, Carpio, and Azcuna, **JJ.**, concurring. No separate opinions.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Persons and Family Relations → Adoption → Rescission of Adoption → Non-Retroactivity and Absence of Vested Right of Adopter to Rescind
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Remedial Law / Constitutional Law → Civil Procedure / Due Process → Concept of Vested Rights / Prescription of Cause of Action
**Full Text of Governing Statutory Provisions:**
**Section 19, Article VI, Republic Act No. 8552 (Domestic Adoption Act of 1998):**
"SEC. 19. **Grounds for Rescission of Adoption.** — Upon petition of the adoptee, with the assistance of the Department if a minor or if over eighteen (18) years of age but is incapacitated, as guardian/counsel, the adoption may be rescinded on any of the following grounds committed by the adopter(s): (a) repeated physical and verbal maltreatment by the adopter(s) despite having undergone counseling; (b) attempt on the life of the adoptee; (c) sexual assault or violence; or (d) abandonment and failure to comply with parental obligations.
**Adoption, being in the best interest of the child, shall not be subject to rescission by the adopter(s).** However, the adopter(s) may disinherit the adoptee for causes provided in Article 919 of the Civil Code."
**Section 5, Rule 100, Revised Rules of Court (Historical Procedural Rule on Prescription cited in the decision):**
"SEC. 5. **Time within which to file petition.** — A minor or other incapacitated person must file the petition for rescission or revocation of adoption within the five years following his majority, or if he was incompetent at the time of the adoption, within the five (5) years following the recovery from such incompetency.
**The adopter must also file the petition to set aside the adoption within five (5) years from the time the cause or causes giving rise to the rescission or revocation of the same took place.**"
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Rule on Rescission by Adopter:** Under Section 19 of R.A. No. 8552, adoption is strictly **not subject to rescission by the adopter(s)**. The sole legal right to petition for judicial rescission belongs exclusively to the adoptee.
**No Vested Right in Statutory Privilege:** Adoption is not an innate, fundamental, or natural right, but a mere privilege created and regulated by the State under **parens patriae**. A statutory right of action may be taken away at any time before it has been exercised. Because an unexercised cause of action subject to a prescriptive period does not constitute a present, fixed, unconditional interest, an adopter acquires no "vested right" to rescind an adoption that can survive the statutory repeal of that remedy.
**Alternative Remedy (Disinheritance):** Although an adopter can no longer rescind the adoption decree to sever the filial tie, the adopter retains the remedy of **disinheriting** the adoptee under Article 919 of the Civil Code or excluding the adoptee from the disposable free portion of the estate by will.
**Factual Trigger:** Petitioner sought to rescind a 1972 adoption decree by filing a petition in December 1999—over a year and eight months after R.A. No. 8552 took effect on March 22, 1998—invoking grounds (refusal to use surname, indifference, filing of a partition case) that had occurred years prior. The petition was confronted with the express statutory prohibition barring adopters from seeking rescission.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Dr. Diosdado Lahom & Isabelita S. Lahom:** Adopters; uncle and aunt of respondent who took him into custody when he was two years old and legally adopted him in 1972. Dr. Diosdado Lahom died prior to the rescission petition. Isabelita Lahom is the sole petitioner.
**Jose Melvin Sibulo (a.k.a. "Dr. Melvin S. Lahom"):** Adoptee; biological nephew of Isabelita Lahom; physician who allegedly refused to use the surname "Lahom," maintained cold and indifferent treatment toward his adoptive mother, and filed a partition suit against her.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petitioner filed a petition to rescind the adoption decree before RTC Naga City, Branch 22 (designated Family Court).
The RTC dismissed the petition on April 28, 2000, for lack of cause of action and prescription.
Petitioner elevated the case directly to the Supreme Court via a **Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45** of the 1997 Rules of Court on pure questions of law.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**Circa 1960s:** Dr. Diosdado Lahom and petitioner Isabelita S. Lahom, being childless, take into their care petitioner’s two-year-old nephew, Jose Melvin Sibulo, raising him as their own.
**1971:** The Lahom spouses file a petition for the legal adoption of Jose Melvin Sibulo.
**May 5, 1972:** The court issues an order granting the adoption petition. Pursuant to the order, the Civil Registrar of Naga City alters the entry to "Jose Melvin Lahom."
**1978–1990s:** Respondent obtains his medical license from the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) under the name "Jose Melvin M. Sibulo." Despite repeated pleadings from his adoptive parents, respondent continues to use "Sibulo" in his personal and professional dealings.
**Intervening Period:** Dr. Diosdado Lahom passes away. Prior to his death, he expressed a desire to revoke the adoption due to respondent's conduct, but desisted upon petitioner’s plea, requesting instead that respondent’s future share be given to charity. Respondent allegedly remains indifferent, visits petitioner only once a year, and becomes jealous of other visiting relatives.
**March 22, 1998: Republic Act No. 8552 (Domestic Adoption Act of 1998)** takes effect, explicitly deleting and abrogating the right of adopters to rescind an adoption decree.
**1999:** Respondent files **Civil Case No. 99-4463** for partition against petitioner, severely eroding their relationship.
**December 1, 1999:** Petitioner files a petition before RTC Naga City (Branch 22) to revoke and rescind the May 5, 1972 adoption decree.
**Early 2000:** Respondent files a Motion to Dismiss grounded on: (1) lack of jurisdiction; and (2) lack of cause of action under Section 19 of R.A. No. 8552. Petitioner opposes, arguing she has a vested right to rescind under Art. 348 of the Civil Code and Art. 192 of the Family Code.
**April 28, 2000:** RTC Naga City dismisses the petition, ruling that:
1. It has jurisdiction under Section 5(c) of R.A. No. 8369 as a Family Court;
2. The petition states no cause of action because Section 19 of R.A. No. 8552 deleted the adopter's right to rescind; and
3. Even if the right existed under prior law, the action had already prescribed under the 5-year bar rule of Section 5, Rule 100 of the Rules of Court.
**July 14, 2003:** The Supreme Court affirms the RTC dismissal.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The petition for revocation/rescission must proceed because the right to rescind vested under the Civil Code and Family Code prior to the enactment of R.A. No. 8552, and the new law cannot be given retroactive application to impair vested rights or divest court jurisdiction.
**Specific Contentions:**
The grounds for revocation arose and vested while Article 348 of the Civil Code and Article 192 of the Family Code were in force.
R.A. No. 8552 cannot retroactively extinguish an already-accrued vested right to rescind.
Depriving the trial court of the power to hear the revocation suit violates due process by arbitrarily extinguishing an established legal right.
B. Respondent's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The petition must be dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and failure to state a cause of action.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Lack of Jurisdiction:** The trial court lacked jurisdiction over the subject matter of an adopter-initiated rescission.
**No Cause of Action:** Under Section 19, Article VI of R.A. No. 8552, adopters are categorically prohibited from rescinding an adoption; only the adoptee has standing to bring such an action.
**Prescription (Affirmed by RTC):** Even under former laws, any purported action had prescribed under the five-year limitation in Section 5, Rule 100 of the Rules of Court, as the alleged grounds had been known to petitioner for far more than five years.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** May an adoption decreed on May 5, 1972, still be revoked or rescinded by the adopter after the effectivity of Republic Act No. 8552?
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not an adopter may judicially rescind a decree of adoption after the effectivity of R.A. No. 8552, which repealed the adopter's statutory right to rescind.
2. [Procedural / Secondary Issue] In the affirmative, has the adopter's action to rescind the adoption prescribed?
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not an action to rescind an adoption, assuming the right survived the enactment of R.A. No. 8552, is barred by the five-year prescriptive period under Rule 100 of the Rules of Court.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: May the adoption still be revoked or rescinded by the adopter after the effectivity of R.A. No. 8552?
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Section 19 of R.A. No. 8552 abrogated the right of adopters to rescind an adoption decree, and an adopter holds no vested right in a repealed statutory privilege or unexercised statutory right of action.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Jurisdiction of the court is determined by the statute in force at the time of the commencement of the action."
"It was months after the effectivity of R.A. No. 8552 that herein petitioner filed an action to revoke the decree of adoption granted in 1975. By then, the new law, had already abrogated and repealed the right of an adopter under the Civil Code and the Family Code to rescind a decree of adoption. Consistently with its earlier pronouncements, the Court should now hold that the action for rescission of the adoption decree, having been initiated by petitioner after R.A. No. 8552 had come into force, no longer could be pursued."
"The concept of 'vested right' is a consequence of the constitutional guaranty of due process that expresses a **present fixed interest** which in right reason and natural justice is protected against arbitrary state action; it includes not only legal or equitable title to the enforcement of a demand but also exemptions from new obligations created after the right has become vested. Rights are considered vested when the right to enjoyment is a present interest, absolute, unconditional, and perfect or fixed and irrefutable."
"It must also be acknowledged that a person has no vested right in statutory privileges. While adoption has often been referred to in the context of a 'right,' the privilege to adopt is itself not naturally innate or fundamental but rather a right merely created by statute. It is a privilege that is governed by the state's determination on what it may deem to be for the best interest and welfare of the child. Matters relating to adoption, including the withdrawal of the right of an adopter to nullify the adoption decree, are subject to regulation by the State. Concomitantly, a **right of action** given by statute may be taken away at anytime before it has been exercised."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Jurisdiction & Governing Law at Commencement:** The Court reiterated the doctrine settled in **Republic v. Court of Appeals** (G.R. No. 92326) and **Republic v. Miller** (G.R. No. 125932): actions are governed by the law in force **at the time the petition is filed**. Because petitioner filed her petition in December 1999, long after R.A. No. 8552 took effect on March 22, 1998, R.A. No. 8552 controls.
**Express Abrogation of Adopter's Rescission:** Section 19 of R.A. No. 8552 explicitly deleted the right of adopters to rescind an adoption, reserving that right exclusively to the adoptee. Section 26 repealed all inconsistent laws, extinguishing Article 348 of the Civil Code and Article 192 of the Family Code.
**Absence of a "Vested Right":** A vested right requires an immediate, fixed, absolute, and unconditional interest protected by due process. Adoption is purely a creature of statute—a state-conferred privilege, not an innate or fundamental right. The State, acting as **parens patriae**, has plenary authority to regulate, alter, or withdraw rights of action created by adoption statutes. Because an unexercised statutory right of action is not a vested property right, the legislature can abolish it at any time before suit is filed.
**Alternative Legal Relief:** The Court observed under **dura lex sed lex** that while the law may seem rigid, an adopter aggrieved by an ungrateful or undeserving adoptee is not left without remedy: the adopter may disinherit the adoptee pursuant to Article 919 of the Civil Code and freely exclude the adoptee from the disposable free portion of the estate by last will and testament.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
The Supreme Court held that an adopter cannot rescind an adoption after R.A. No. 8552 took effect because the new law explicitly abolished the adopter's right to rescind. Adoption is a statutory privilege rather than a constitutional or natural right, meaning the legislature can amend or withdraw it at any time. Because Mrs. Lahom did not file her case before R.A. No. 8552 became law, she had no "vested right" to sue for rescission, and her sole legal recourse against her ungrateful adopted son was testamentary disinheritance.
Issue 2: In the affirmative, has the adopter's action prescribed?
**(a) Short Answer: The issue is moot**, but the Court affirmed the RTC's reasoning that even if the right of action had survived, it would have been barred by prescription under the five-year rule of Rule 100.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Interestingly, even before the passage of the statute, an action to set aside the adoption is subject to the five-year bar rule under Rule 100 of the Rules of Court and that the adopter would lose the right to revoke the adoption decree after the lapse of that period. The exercise of the right within a prescriptive period is a condition that could not fulfill the requirements of a vested right entitled to protection."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Having ruled that R.A. No. 8552 extinguished the right of action entirely, the question of prescription became secondary/moot.
Nevertheless, the Court pointed out that under Section 5, Rule 100 of the Rules of Court, an adopter's petition to set aside an adoption had to be filed within five (5) years from the time the cause giving rise to rescission took place.
The facts set out in Mrs. Lahom's petition demonstrated that respondent's refusal to use the surname "Lahom" (practicing medicine as "Jose Melvin M. Sibulo" since 1978) and his alleged indifference had been known to petitioner for far more than five years before she filed her petition on December 1, 1999.
Consequently, the right was conditioned upon timely exercise; having lapsed, it could never be characterized as an absolute or vested right.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
Even if the old laws still applied, Mrs. Lahom waited too long to file her case. Under the Rules of Court, an adopter had to sue within five years from discovering the ground for revocation. Since she knew for decades that her adopted nephew refused to use the family surname and neglected her, any action she might once have possessed had long since prescribed.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions were filed; the decision of the First Division was unanimous.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the assailed judgment of the court **a quo** is AFFIRMED. No costs.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court affirmed the RTC Naga City's dismissal of Isabelita Lahom's petition to rescind the adoption of Jose Melvin Sibulo. The respondent prevailed; the adoption decree remains completely valid and irrevocable by the adopter, leaving disinheritance as petitioner's exclusive statutory remedy.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Republic v. Alarcon Vergara**
**Full Official Caption:** Republic of the Philippines, Petitioner, v. Hon. Concepcion S. Alarcon Vergara, in her capacity as Presiding Judge of the Regional Trial Court, Third Judicial Region, Branch 62, Angeles City, and Spouses Samuel Robert Dye, Jr. and Rosalina D. Dye, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 95551
**Date of Promulgation:** March 20, 1997
**Philippine Reports:** Not stated in the decision
**Ponente:** Romero, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Second Division (Regalado, Puno, and Torres, Jr., **JJ.**, concur; Mendoza, **J.**, concurs in the result).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code → Adoption → Qualifications and Disqualifications to Adopt → Disqualification of Aliens and Exceptions
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code → Adoption → Joint Adoption by Spouses → Mandatory Joint Adoption Rule
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article 184, Family Code (Executive Order No. 209):**
"Art. 184. The following persons may not adopt:
x x x           x x x           x x x
(3) **An alien, except:**
(a) A former Filipino citizen who seeks to adopt a relative by consanguinity;
(b) One who seeks to adopt the legitimate child of his or her Filipino spouse; or
(c) **One who is married to a Filipino citizen and seeks to adopt jointly with his or her spouse a relative by consanguinity of the latter.**
Aliens not included in the foregoing exceptions may adopt Filipino children in accordance with the rules on inter-country adoption as may be provided by law."
**Article 185, Family Code (Executive Order No. 209):**
"Art. 185. **Husband and wife must adopt jointly**, except in the following cases:
(1) When one spouse seeks to adopt his own illegitimate child;
(2) When one spouse seeks to adopt the legitimate child of the other."
**Note on Modern Statutory Development:** Republic Act No. 8552 (Domestic Adoption Act of 1998) and subsequent adoption statutes have revised these qualifications and exceptions, but under the governing Family Code provisions applied in this case, aliens were strictly barred subject only to the three enumerated exceptions.
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Disqualification of Aliens:** Under **Article 184(3)**, aliens are generally disqualified from adopting Filipino citizens.
**Strict Interpretation of Exceptions under Article 184(3)(c):** An alien married to an adopter seeking to adopt the latter's relative by consanguinity is exempt **only if married to a Filipino citizen**. Marriage to a **former** Filipino citizen (who has become a naturalized alien) does not qualify under this exception.
**Mandatory Joint Adoption:** Under **Article 185**, joint adoption by husband and wife is mandatory, subject only to two strict statutory exceptions: (1) adopting one's own illegitimate child, or (2) adopting the legitimate child of the other spouse.
**Inability of Qualified Spouse to Adopt Singly:** Even if one spouse is qualified as a former Filipino adopting a relative by consanguinity under Article 184(3)(a), that spouse cannot adopt alone if the other alien spouse is legally disqualified, because the case does not fall under the exclusive exceptions to mandatory joint adoption under Article 185.
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):**
An American citizen husband (Samuel) and his naturalized American wife (Rosalina, a former Filipino) petitioned to adopt the wife's minor siblings. Samuel was disqualified as an alien because his wife was no longer a Philippine citizen under Article 184(3)(c), and Rosalina could not adopt alone because Article 185 strictly mandates joint adoption by spouses when adopting relatives other than a spouse's legitimate child or one's own illegitimate child.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Republic of the Philippines:** Petitioner; opposed the petition for adoption on the ground of statutory disqualification under the Family Code.
**Hon. Concepcion S. Alarcon Vergara:** Respondent; Presiding Judge of RTC Angeles City, Branch 62, who granted the adoption petition.
**Samuel Robert Dye, Jr.:** Private respondent/adopter; an American citizen and member of the U.S. Air Force stationed at Clark Air Base, Pampanga.
**Rosalina D. Dye (Rosalina Due Dye):** Private respondent/adopter; Samuel's wife, a former Filipino citizen naturalized as an American citizen.
**Maricel R. Due (13 y/o) & Alvin R. Due (12 y/o):** Minors sought to be adopted; younger biological siblings of Rosalina.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 on a pure question of law filed by the Republic of the Philippines, assailing the September 10, 1990 Decision of the Regional Trial Court of Angeles City, Branch 62, in Special Proceeding No. 4203.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**June 25, 1990:** Spouses Samuel Robert Dye, Jr. (an American citizen and U.S. Air Force serviceman stationed at Clark Air Base) and Rosalina Due Dye (a naturalized American citizen and former Filipino) file a petition in the Regional Trial Court of Angeles City (Branch 62, Sp. Proc. No. 4203) to adopt Rosalina’s younger biological siblings, Maricel R. Due (13) and Alvin R. Due (12). The natural parents and both minors consent to the adoption.
**Trial Phase:** The trial court evaluates the petition. It notes that the spouses Dye are only 15 years and 3 months and 15 years and 9 months older than Maricel Due, falling short of the statutory 16-year age gap required under Article 183 of the Family Code.
**September 10, 1990:** The RTC renders its decision granting the petition and declaring Maricel and Alvin to be the adopted children of the Spouses Dye. The RTC waives the 16-year age difference rule on the rationale that a literal reading defeats the underlying philosophy of adoption statutes (promoting the child’s welfare). The RTC further finds that the spouses are physically, mentally, and financially capable and have love and affection for the minors.
**Supreme Court Review:** The Republic petitions the Supreme Court on a pure question of law, asserting that the Spouses Dye are disqualified under the Family Code.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's (Republic of the Philippines) Arguments:
**Main Thesis:** The Spouses Samuel and Rosalina Dye are statutorily disqualified from adopting the minor Filipino children under the explicit terms of the Family Code.
**Specific Contentions:**
Samuel R. Dye, Jr. is an alien and does not fall under any of the exceptions provided in Article 184(3) of the Family Code.
Specifically, under Article 184(3)(c), an alien can only adopt jointly if married to a **Filipino citizen**; here, Rosalina was already a naturalized American citizen when the petition was filed.
B. Respondent's (Spouses Dye / RTC) Arguments:
**Main Thesis:** The adoption should be sustained because it serves the best interests and welfare of the minor children, and the law must be construed liberally to advance that policy.
**Specific Contentions:**
The Spouses Dye are morally, mentally, and physically fit, financially capable, and harbor genuine love and affection for the adoptees.
A literal implementation of statutory limitations defeats the core philosophy behind adoption statutes, which is to provide homes, care, and education to less fortunate children.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  [PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE] Disqualification of Alien Spouse under Article 184(3):
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether Samuel Robert Dye, Jr., an American citizen married to a former Filipino citizen who is now a naturalized American, is qualified to adopt his wife's minor siblings under Article 184 of the Family Code.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not an alien married to a naturalized American citizen (a former Filipino) falls under the exception in Article 184(3)(c) of the Family Code allowing an alien to adopt a relative by consanguinity of his spouse.
2.  [PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE] Mandatory Joint Adoption under Article 185:
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether Rosalina D. Dye can adopt her minor brother and sister alone without her husband.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not a former Filipino citizen may adopt her biological siblings alone where her alien spouse is legally disqualified from adopting.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Disqualification of Samuel R. Dye, Jr. Under Article 184(3)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Is Samuel R. Dye, Jr. qualified to adopt Maricel and Alvin Due under Article 184(3) of the Family Code? **NO.** As an alien, he does not fall within any of the exclusive statutory exceptions, because his wife is no longer a Filipino citizen.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"As a general rule, aliens cannot adopt Filipino citizens as this is proscribed under Article 184 of the Family Code..."
"Samuel Robert Dye, Jr. who is an American and, therefore, an alien is disqualified from adopting the minors Maricel and Alvin Due because he does not fall under any of the three aforequoted exceptions laid down by the law. He is not a former Filipino citizen who seeks to adopt a relative by consanguinity. Nor does he seek to adopt his wife's legitimate child. Although he seeks to adopt with his wife her relatives by consanguinity, he is not married to a **Filipino citizen**, for Rosalina was already a naturalized American at the time the petition was filed, thus excluding him from the coverage of the exception. The law here does not provide for an alien who is married to a **former Filipino citizen** seeking to adopt jointly with his or her spouse a relative by consanguinity, as an exception to the general rule that aliens may not adopt."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Article 184(3) of the Family Code lays down an absolute general prohibition against aliens adopting Filipino children, subject only to three specific exceptions: (a) a former Filipino citizen adopting a relative by consanguinity; (b) an alien adopting the legitimate child of his/her Filipino spouse; or (c) an alien married to a Filipino citizen adopting jointly with the latter a relative by consanguinity of the Filipino spouse.
Samuel is an American citizen. Exception (a) does not apply because he is not a former Filipino. Exception (b) does not apply because the adoptees are not the children of his wife.
Exception (c) does not apply because, although the prospective adoptees are his wife's relatives by consanguinity, his wife Rosalina was no longer a **Filipino citizen**; she was a naturalized American citizen at the time the petition was filed.
The Court held that the statute cannot be extended to cover an alien married to a **former Filipino citizen** without engaging in judicial legislation.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
(Plain-Language Explanation) The Family Code strictly forbids foreigners from adopting Filipino children unless they fall squarely into one of three narrow exceptions. Under Article 184(3)(c), a foreigner can only co-adopt his spouse's relatives if his spouse is an active **Filipino citizen**. Because Samuel's wife had already become a naturalized U.S. citizen, Samuel could not use this exception, and the courts cannot rewrite the statute to include spouses of **former** Filipinos.
Issue 2: Inability of Rosalina Dye to Adopt Singly Under Article 185
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Can Rosalina Dye adopt her siblings alone under Article 184(3)(a) despite her husband's disqualification? **NO.** Joint adoption by husband and wife is mandatory under Article 185, and her situation does not fall under the two exclusive statutory exceptions permitting sole adoption.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"On her own, Rosalina Dye cannot adopt her brother and sister for the law mandates joint adoption by husband and wife, subject to exceptions. Article 29 of Presidential Decree No. 603 (Child and Youth Welfare Code) retained the Civil Code provision that husband and wife **may** jointly adopt. The Family Code amended this rule by scrapping the optional character of joint adoption and making it now mandatory."
"Although the wife in said case was qualified to adopt under Article 184, paragraph 3 (a), she being a former Filipino who seeks to adopt a relative by consanguinity, she could not jointly adopt with her husband under Article 185 because he was an alien ineligible to adopt here in the Philippines."
"Regrettably, the Court is not in a position to affirm the trial court's decision favoring adoption in the case at bar, for the law is clear and it cannot be modified without violating the proscription against judicial legislation."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
Rosalina, as a former Filipino citizen seeking to adopt her biological siblings (relatives by consanguinity), would qualify independently under Article 184(3)(a).
However, Article 185 of the Family Code explicitly eliminated the optional character of joint adoption previously recognized in the Civil Code and P.D. No. 603; joint adoption is now mandatory for married persons ("**Husband and wife must adopt jointly**").
The only exceptions allowing a single spouse to adopt alone are: (1) adopting one's own illegitimate child, or (2) adopting the legitimate child of the other spouse. Adopting a brother or sister does not fall within these exceptions.
Citing **Republic v. Court of Appeals** (227 SCRA 401), the Court reaffirmed that where one spouse is an ineligible alien and the other spouse cannot legally adopt alone due to mandatory joint adoption, the adoption petition must fail entirely.
While adoption laws are construed liberally in favor of child welfare, courts cannot disregard express statutory bars to do equity, as doing so would amount to impermissible judicial legislation.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
(Plain-Language Explanation) Even though Rosalina personally met the exception as an ex-Filipino adopting her own siblings, married individuals are legally compelled by Article 185 to adopt jointly as a couple. Since the law allows single-spouse adoption only when adopting an illegitimate child or a stepchild, Rosalina could not adopt her siblings alone; and because her alien husband was disqualified, neither of them could adopt.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**Mendoza, J.:** Concurred in the result without filing a separate written opinion.
No other separate opinions were submitted or discussed in the text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the instant petition is hereby GRANTED. The Decision of the Regional Trial Court of Angeles City in Special Proceeding No. 4203 (In the Matter of the Petition for Adoption of the minors Maricel R. Due and Alvin R. Due), dated September 10, 1990 is REVERSED AND SET ASIDE.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court ruled entirely in favor of the Republic, reversing and setting aside the trial court's decision. The petition for adoption filed by Spouses Samuel and Rosalina Dye was denied because Samuel was an ineligible alien and Rosalina could not legally adopt her siblings without her husband.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Cervantes v. Fajardo**
**Full Official Caption:** In the Matter of the Petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus of Minor Angelie Anne C. Cervantes, Nelson L. Cervantes and Zenaida Carreon Cervantes, Petitioners, vs. Gina Carreon Fajardo and Conrado Fajardo, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 79955
**Date of Promulgation:** January 27, 1989
**Philippine Reports Citation:** 251 Phil. 222 (169 SCRA 575)
**Ponente:** Padilla, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Second Division (Melencio-Herrera, **J.** [Chairperson], Paras, Sarmiento, and Regalado, **JJ.**, concur).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code / Child and Youth Welfare Code (P.D. 603) → Adoption → Effects of Adoption → Dissolution of Natural Parental Authority and Transfer of Custody
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Remedial Law → Special Proceedings → Habeas Corpus (Rule 102) → Custody of Minors → Paramount Welfare of the Child vs. Tender-Age Rule
**Full Text of Governing Constitutional / Statutory Provision(s):**
**Article 39, Presidential Decree No. 603 (Child and Youth Welfare Code):**
"Art. 39. **Effects of Adoption.** — The adoption shall:
(1) **Sever all legal ties between each parents and the adopted child**, except when the adoptive parent is the spouse of the parent of the child, in which case the relationship between said parent and the child will remain unaffected;
(2) **Vest in the adopter parental authority over the child;**
(3) Give to the adopter the right to the care and custody of the adopted child and will invest in the adopter and the adopted child the reciprocal rights and obligations of parent and child; and
(4) Confer to the adopted child the legal capacity to inherit from the adopter and for all legal intents and purposes the adopted child shall be considered the legitimate child of the adopter." **(Historical statute applied in the decision; cited alongside Art. 17, P.D. 603 and Art. 189, par. [2], Family Code).**
**Article 189, par. (2), Executive Order No. 209 (Family Code of the Philippines):**
"Art. 189. Adoption shall have the following effects:
...
(2) **The parental authority of the parents by nature over the adopted shall terminate and be vested in the adopters**, except that where a child is adopted by the spouse of the natural parent, parental authority shall be exercised jointly by both spouses;
..."
**Article 363, Civil Code of the Philippines (in relation to Art. 17, P.D. 603 and Art. 213, Family Code):**
"Art. 363. In all questions on the care, custody, education and property of children, **the latter's welfare shall be the paramount consideration. No mother shall be separated from her child under seven years of age, unless the court finds compelling reasons for such measure.**" **(Note: P.D. 603, Art. 17 set this at five [5] years of age, as cited in the decision).**
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Rule / Provision Triggered:** A decree of adoption severs and dissolves the parental authority vested in the natural parents and vests exclusive parental authority, care, and custody in the adopting parents.
**Specific Sub-Rule / Exception Highlighted:** The statutory rule that a child of tender years shall not be separated from the mother does not apply when there are **compelling reasons** to rule otherwise. In any custody dispute, the **paramount consideration is the child's moral, physical, and social welfare**, taking into account the resources, moral character, and social standing of the contending claimants.
**Factual Trigger:** Natural parents who voluntarily gave up their two-week-old infant for adoption, executed an affidavit of consent, and allowed an adoption decree to become final, subsequently extorted money from the adoptive parents and forcibly abducted the child from the adoptive home.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Minor Angelie Anne C. Cervantes (formerly Fajardo):** Minor child born out of wedlock on February 14, 1987.
**Nelson L. Cervantes and Zenaida Carreon Cervantes:** Petitioners; legally married spouses; Zenaida is the maternal aunt of the minor; legally decreed adoptive parents of the child.
**Gina Carreon (Gina Carreon Fajardo):** Respondent; natural mother of the child; jobless; living in an illicit, common-law union with a married man.
**Conrado Fajardo:** Respondent; common-law partner of Gina Carreon; legally married to another woman.
**Felisa Tansingco:** Social worker who conducted the adoption case study and testified regarding the natural mother's consent.
**Hon. Eutropio Migrino:** Executive Judge, Regional Trial Court of Pasig, who received the habeas corpus writ, conducted evidentiary hearings, and submitted a Report and Recommendation to the Supreme Court.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Original **Petition for a Writ of Habeas Corpus** filed directly with the Supreme Court by the adoptive parents (the Cervantes spouses) against the natural parents (Fajardo and Carreon) to recover physical custody of the legally adopted minor.
The Supreme Court issued the writ returnable to the Executive Judge of the RTC of Pasig to hear evidence and submit a report and recommendation.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**February 14, 1987:** Minor Angelie Anne is born out of wedlock to respondents Conrado Fajardo (a married man) and Gina Carreon (his common-law partner).
**Late February / Early March 1987 (Barely two weeks after birth):** Respondents offer the infant for adoption to Gina's sister and brother-in-law, petitioners Zenaida and Nelson Cervantes. Petitioners take actual care, charge, and custody of the child.
**March – April 1987:** Petitioners receive a letter from respondents demanding the payment of **₱150,000.00**, threatening that they will take the child back if the money is not paid. Petitioners refuse to yield to the demand.
**April 29, 1987:** Respondent Gina Carreon executes a formal **Affidavit of Consent** to the adoption of the child by petitioners.
**June 24, 1987:** Social worker Felisa Tansingco interviews Gina Carreon during the adoption case study. Gina explicitly manifests her desire to have the infant adopted by petitioners.
**August 20, 1987:** The Regional Trial Court of Rizal (Branch 67, Sp. Proc. No. 057-B) renders a **Decision granting the adoption** of the child by petitioners. The court orders the child freed from the parental authority of her natural parents and declares her, for all legal intents and purposes, the child of petitioners named Angelie Anne Cervantes.
**September 11, 1987:** While petitioners are away at work, Gina Carreon goes to petitioners' home in Angono, Rizal, tricks the minor's "yaya" under the pretext that her mother sent for the child, and forcibly takes the infant to her house in Parañaque.
**Post-Abduction:** Petitioners demand the minor's return. Gina refuses, claiming her consent was vitiated, but conveys that she will return the infant if paid **₱150,000.00**.
**October 5, 1987:** The Supreme Court issues a writ of habeas corpus returnable to the Executive Judge, RTC of Pasig.
**October 27, 1987:** Social worker Felisa Tansingco testifies before the RTC Executive Judge, confirming Gina's voluntary consent.
**December 3, 1987:** RTC Pasig Executive Judge Eutropio Migrino submits his Report and Recommendation to the Supreme Court, recommending that the petition be granted.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments (Spouses Cervantes)
**Main Thesis:** As the legally decreed adoptive parents, they possess exclusive parental authority and legal custody over the child; respondents' refusal to surrender the child constitutes unlawful detention remediable by habeas corpus.
**Specific Contentions:**
A valid, final adoption decree dissolved the natural parents' authority and vested sole parental authority and custody in them.
The natural mother voluntarily consented to the adoption via an affidavit and confirmed it during the social worker's case study interview.
Respondents' custody claim is an extortionate scheme, evidenced by their demand for ₱150,000.00 in exchange for the child.
Petitioners are legally married and financially, morally, and socially capable of raising the child, unlike respondents.
B. Respondents' Arguments (Gina Carreon and Conrado Fajardo)
**Main Thesis:** The child is under five years of age and cannot be separated from her natural mother, whose consent to the adoption was invalid.
**Specific Contentions:**
Gina Carreon had no real desire to give up the child for adoption.
The Affidavit of Consent to adoption was signed without being fully explained to her.
As the biological mother, she has a preferential right to the custody of an infant of tender age.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether the legal adoptive parents or the natural mother are entitled to the care and custody of the minor child Angelie Anne Cervantes.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether an adoptive parent who holds a final adoption decree is entitled to custody via habeas corpus over the biological mother living in an illicit relationship who attempts to reclaim the child of tender age.
2.  **[Secondary Issue]** Whether the tender-age rule (prohibiting separation of a child under five/seven years from the mother) bars awarding custody to the adoptive parents under the facts of the case.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether the tender-age prohibition applies where the biological mother is jobless and cohabits illicitly with a married man.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Entitlement to Custody and Effect of Adoption
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: YES.** The adoptive parents (petitioners) are entitled to custody because a decree of adoption completely dissolves the parental authority of the natural parents and vests it exclusively in the adopters.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"Besides, the minor has been legally adopted by petitioners with the full knowledge and consent of respondents. A decree of adoption has the effect, among others, of dissolving the authority vested in natural parents over the adopted child, except where the adopting parent is the spouse of the natural parent of the adopted, in which case, parental authority over the adopted shall be exercised jointly by both spouses. The adopting parents have the right to the care and custody of the adopted child and exercise parental authority and responsibility over him."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Application of Statutory Mandate on Adoption:** Pursuant to P.D. 603 (Arts. 17 and 39) and the Family Code (Art. 189[2]), the legal effect of a judicial decree of adoption is the total termination of natural parental authority and its vesting in the adopters.
**Factual Existence of Valid Decree:** The RTC of Rizal had already granted the adoption on August 20, 1987 in Sp. Proc. No. 057-B. Gina Carreon executed a written Affidavit of Consent and confirmed her willingness to have the child adopted during an interview with the social worker on June 24, 1987.
**Rejection of Mother's Repudiation:** The Court rejected the respondent mother's belated claim that the consent was not explained to her, noting the social worker's independent, credible testimony confirming voluntary consent.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
(Plain-Language Explanation) Once an adoption decree is finalized with proper consent, the biological parents' legal relationship with the child is completely extinguished. The adoptive parents step into their shoes with exclusive parental authority and legal custody, meaning the natural mother has no residual legal right to take the child back.
Issue 2: Paramount Welfare of the Minor vs. Tender-Age Rule
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** The tender-age rule does not prevent the separation of the child from the biological mother when compelling reasons demonstrate that the child's paramount welfare requires placing custody with the adoptive parents.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"In all cases involving the custody, care, education and property of children, the latter's welfare is paramount. The provision that no mother shall be separated from a child under five (5) years of age, will not apply where the Court finds compelling reasons to rule otherwise. In all controversies regarding the custody of minors, the foremost consideration is the moral, physical and social welfare of the child concerned, taking into account the resources and moral as well as social standing of the contending parents. Never has this Court deviated from this criterion."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Compelling Reasons Override the Tender-Age Rule:** While the law generally disfavors separating an infant from the mother, the child's moral, physical, and social welfare remains paramount. A mother can be deprived of custody for compelling reasons.
**Compelling Reasons Found in the Natural Mother's Environment:**
Conrado Fajardo is legally married to someone else; his open, illicit cohabitation with Gina Carreon cannot provide an upright and moral atmosphere for the child.
Gina Carreon had already borne another child by a different married man who abandoned her. Growing up in a household with multiple illegitimate siblings from different married men would adversely affect the minor's values and moral development.
Gina Carreon is jobless and attempted to use the child to extort ₱150,000.00 from the Cervantes spouses.
**Suitability of the Adoptive Parents:** Petitioners are legally married and demonstrate moral, physical, financial, and social capability to support and provide a stable future for the minor.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
(Plain-Language Explanation) The tender-age rule is not absolute; it yields to the paramount welfare of the child when compelling reasons exist. Because the biological mother is unemployed, lives illicitly with a married man, and attempted to sell/extort the child for ₱150,000.00, she cannot provide a wholesome environment, making the legally married, financially capable adoptive parents the rightful custodians.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim/Near-Verbatim Fallo:**
"ACCORDINGLY, and as recommended by the Executive Judge, Regional Trial Court of Pasig, Hon. Eutropio Migrino, the Petition is GRANTED. The custody and care of the minor Angelie Anne Cervantes are hereby granted to petitioners to whom they properly belong, and respondents are ordered (if they still have not) to deliver said minor to the petitioners immediately upon notice hereof. This resolution is immediately executory.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court granted the petition for habeas corpus in favor of the adoptive parents, petitioners Nelson and Zenaida Cervantes. The respondents were ordered to immediately surrender and deliver the child to the petitioners, with the ruling declared immediately executory.
