### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Sayson v. Court of Appeals**
**Full Official Caption:** Mauricio Sayson, Rosario Sayson-Malonda, Basilisa Sayson-Lirio, Remedios Sayson-Reyes, and Juana C. Bautista, Petitioners, vs. The Honorable Court of Appeals, Delia Sayson, assisted by her husband, Cirilo Cedo, Jr., Edmundo Sayson, and Doribel Sayson, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. Nos. 89224–25; January 23, 1992; Cruz, **J.**; First Division (Narvasa, **C.J.**, Griño-Aquino, and Medialdea, **JJ.**, concurring).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Succession → Intestate Succession → Right of Representation → Representation by Grandchildren vs. Adopted Children
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code & Civil Code → Adoption & Filiation → Disqualification to Adopt & Collateral Attack on Decrees and Filiation
Full Text of Governing Provisions
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 970:**
"Representation is a right created by fiction of law, by virtue of which the representative is raised to the place and the degree of the person represented, and acquires the rights which the latter would have if he were living or if he could have inherited."
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 971:**
"The representative is called to the succession by the law and not by the person represented. The representative does not succeed the person represented but the one who the person represented would have succeeded."
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 979:**
"**Legitimate children and their descendants succeed the parents and other ascendants**, without distinction as to sex or age, and even if they should come from different marriages.
**An adopted child succeeds to the property of the adopting parents in the same manner as a legitimate child.**"
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 981:**
"Should children of the deceased and descendants of other children who are dead, survive, the former shall inherit in their own right, and the latter by right of representation."
**Civil Code of the Philippines, Article 335(1) (Historical Provision applied in the dispute):**
"The following cannot adopt:
(1) Those who have legitimate, legitimated, acknowledged natural children, or natural children by legal fiction; [...]"
**(Modern Counterpart: Rep. Act No. 8552 [Domestic Adoption Act of 1998], Sec. 7 / Rep. Act No. 11642 [Administrative Adoption and Alternative Child Care Act of 2022], Sec. 21, which eliminated the pre-existing child disqualification).**
Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provisions
**General Rule on Exclusion by Direct Descendants (Art. 979):** The presence of legitimate and adopted children totally excludes collateral relatives (brothers, sisters, nephews, nieces) and ascendants (parents-in-law) from the intestate estate of the decedent parents.
**The Limited Scope of Adoptive Filiation (Art. 979, par. 2):** While an adopted child succeeds to the property of the adopting parent in the same manner as a legitimate child, the relationship created by adoption is strictly personal between the adopter and the adopted. It does not extend to the blood relatives of either party; an adopted child cannot inherit from the adopter's ascendants or collaterals by right of representation.
**Right of Representation in Direct Descending Line (Arts. 970, 971, 981):** A legitimate grandchild has the right to represent their predeceased parent in the intestate succession of the grandparents, stepping into the predeceased parent's degree and taking their per stirpes share.
**Immunity from Collateral Attack:** Neither a final decree of adoption nor a child's legitimate filiation established by a birth certificate may be attacked collaterally in an ordinary action for partition and accounting. An adoption decree or civil status of legitimacy can only be impugned in a direct, timely proceeding brought by the proper parties.
Factual Trigger (Application to the Story)
Teodoro Sayson predeceased his parents (Eleno and Rafaela) and his wife (Isabel). Following the deaths of all the parents, Teodoro’s siblings and mother-in-law sought to partition Teodoro’s and his parents' estates by asserting that Teodoro’s adopted children (Delia and Edmundo) and legitimate daughter (Doribel) had invalid legal statuses. This collateral challenge was denied, but the Court sustained the CA's exclusion of the adoptive children from the grandparents' estate because adoptive kinship does not extend to the adopter's ascendants.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
Key Parties & Roles
**Eleno and Rafaela Sayson:** Common ascendants (grandparents) who died intestate on November 10, 1952, and May 15, 1976, respectively.
**Teodoro Sayson:** Predeceased legitimate son of Eleno and Rafaela; married Isabel Bautista; died intestate on March 23, 1972.
**Isabel Bautista Sayson:** Surviving spouse of Teodoro; died intestate on March 26, 1981.
**Mauricio Sayson, Rosario Sayson-Malonda, Basilisa Sayson-Lirio, Remedios Sayson-Reyes:** Surviving legitimate children of Eleno and Rafaela; siblings of the predeceased Teodoro (Petitioners).
**Juana C. Bautista:** Surviving mother of the predeceased Isabel Bautista (Petitioner).
**Doribel Sayson:** Legitimate daughter of Teodoro and Isabel, born February 27, 1967 (Private Respondent).
**Delia Sayson and Edmundo Sayson:** Legally adopted children of Teodoro and Isabel by judicial decree dated March 9, 1967 (Private Respondents).
How the Case Reached the Supreme Court
Consolidated appeal via Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 from the February 28, 1989 Decision of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. No. 11541 (affirming RTC Albay Br. 13 in Civil Case No. 1030) and CA-G.R. No. 12364 (modifying RTC Albay Br. 12 in Civil Case No. 1042).
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**November 10, 1952:** Eleno Sayson dies intestate, leaving his wife Rafaela and five children: Mauricio, Rosario, Basilisa, Remedios, and Teodoro.
**February 27, 1967:** Doribel Sayson is born to Teodoro Sayson and Isabel Bautista.
**March 9, 1967:** The Regional Trial Court enters a final decree of adoption declaring Delia Sayson and Edmundo Sayson the legally adopted children of Teodoro Sayson and Isabel Bautista.
**March 23, 1972:** Teodoro Sayson dies intestate.
**May 15, 1976:** Rafaela Sayson dies intestate.
**March 26, 1981:** Isabel Bautista Sayson dies intestate. Her properties and those of Teodoro remain in the possession of Delia, Edmundo, and Doribel.
**April 25, 1983 (Civil Case No. 1030):** Mauricio, Rosario, Basilisa, Remedios, and Juana C. Bautista file a complaint for partition and accounting of the intestate estate of Teodoro and Isabel against Delia, Edmundo, and Doribel in the Regional Trial Court of Albay, Branch 13.
**July 11, 1983 (Civil Case No. 1042):** Delia, Edmundo, and Doribel file a complaint for partition and accounting of the intestate estate of grandparents Eleno and Rafaela against Mauricio, Rosario, Basilisa, and Remedios in RTC Albay, Branch 12, invoking their right of representation for Teodoro’s 1/5 share.
**May 26, 1986:** RTC Albay Branch 12 (Judge Rafael P. Santelices) decides Civil Case No. 1042 in favor of Delia, Edmundo, and Doribel, declaring Delia and Edmundo legally adopted and Doribel a legitimate daughter, ruling that all three are entitled to inherit from Eleno and Rafaela by right of representation.
**September 30, 1986:** RTC Albay Branch 13 (Judge Jose S. Sañez) dismisses Civil Case No. 1030, holding that Delia, Edmundo, and Doribel are the exclusive legitimate heirs of Teodoro and Isabel, totally excluding petitioners from the estate.
**February 28, 1989:** The Court of Appeals resolves the consolidated appeals:
**Civil Case No. 1030 (CA-G.R. No. 11541):** Affirmed in full.
**Civil Case No. 1042 (CA-G.R. No. 12364):** Modified by disqualifying adopted children Delia and Edmundo from inheriting from the estate of the grandparents Eleno and Rafaela, but affirmed in allowing Doribel to inherit by representation.
**Petition to SC:** Petitioners elevate the CA's decision to the Supreme Court on certiorari.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioners' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Petitioners (Teodoro’s siblings and mother-in-law) are the lawful heirs to the estates of Teodoro, Isabel, Eleno, and Rafaela, to the complete exclusion of Delia, Edmundo, and Doribel.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Invalidity of Adoption:** Delia and Edmundo were never legally adopted because Doribel had already been born on February 27, 1967, prior to the adoption decree of March 9, 1967. Under Article 335(1) of the Civil Code, having a child completely disqualified Teodoro and Isabel from adopting.
**Illegitimacy of Doribel:** Doribel is not the legitimate child of Teodoro and Isabel, but was born to a woman named Edita Abila, who manifested in a guardianship proceeding that she was Doribel's natural mother.
**Exclusion from Inheriting Grandparents' Estate:** Neither adopted children nor spurious claimants can represent Teodoro in the estate of Eleno and Rafaela.
B. Private Respondents' Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Delia, Edmundo, and Doribel are the exclusive compulsory heirs of Teodoro and Isabel, and are entitled by right of representation to Teodoro's portion of Eleno and Rafaela's estate.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Conclusiveness of Status:** Delia and Edmundo's adoption is backed by a final and executory decree from 1967; Doribel’s legitimacy is established by her official birth certificate.
**Impermissible Collateral Attack:** The adoption decree and Doribel's legitimate filiation cannot be questioned collaterally inside an ordinary action for partition.
**Right of Representation:** As children of the predeceased Teodoro, they succeed to his rights in his parents' succession under the Civil Code.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the validity of the 1967 adoption decree of Delia and Edmundo Sayson, as well as the legitimate filiation of Doribel Sayson, can be collaterally attacked in an action for partition and accounting.
2.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not Delia, Edmundo, and Doribel Sayson are the exclusive intestate heirs to the estate of the deceased spouses Teodoro Sayson and Isabel Bautista, to the exclusion of Teodoro's siblings and Isabel's mother.
3.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not an adopted child (Delia and Edmundo) and a legitimate grandchild (Doribel) have the right to inherit from the intestate estate of their adopting parents' parents (Eleno and Rafaela Sayson) by right of representation.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Permissibility of Collateral Attack on Adoption Decree and Filiation
(a) Issue & Short Answer
Can the validity of an adoption decree and the legitimacy of a child be attacked collaterally in an action for partition? **NO.** Judgments of adoption that have attained finality and the legitimate civil status of a child cannot be challenged collaterally, but only through timely direct proceedings brought by the proper parties.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements
"The settled rule is that a finding that the requisite jurisdictional facts exists, whether erroneous or not, **cannot be questioned in a collateral proceeding**, for a presumption arises in such cases where the validity of the judgment is thus attacked that the necessary jurisdictional facts were proven..."
"[A] mere error cannot affect the jurisdiction, and the determination must stand until reversed on appeal, and hence **cannot be collaterally attacked**. If this were not the rule, the status of adopted children would always be uncertain, since the evidence might not be the same at all investigations, and might be regarded with different effect by different tribunals, and the adoption might be held by one court to have been valid, while another court would hold it to have been of no avail."
"The presumption of legitimacy in the Civil Code . . . does not have this purely evidential character. It serves a more fundamental purpose. It actually fixes a civil status for the child born in wedlock, and that civil status **cannot be attacked collaterally**. The legitimacy of the child **can be impugned only in a direct action brought for that purpose**, by the proper parties, and within the period limited by law."
(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi
**Laches and Timeliness on Adoption:** The adoption decree was issued on March 9, 1967, and became final and executory long before the present 1983 lawsuits. Petitioners never appealed or moved to revoke it at the time of its rendition, even though petitioner Mauricio Sayson claimed he had personal knowledge of Doribel's birth 10 days prior to the decree.
**No Collateral Attack on Final Adoption:** Under **Santos v. Aranzanso**, once a court renders an adoption order, all jurisdictional facts are presumed established. Such determination cannot be undermined in an independent action for partition.
**Self-Contradictory Posture:** The petitioners argued that the adoption was void because Doribel was already born, while simultaneously arguing that Doribel was not the couple's child at all.
**Evidentiary Weight of Birth Certificate:** Doribel’s birth certificate serves as prima facie evidence of filiation under Art. 265 of the Civil Code and Art. 172 of the Family Code. Under **Legaspi v. Court of Appeals**, public documents cannot be overcome by unoffered hearsay affidavits (such as the unpresented affidavit of Edita Abila) or the biased, self-serving testimony of an interested relative (Mauricio).
**Filiation Must Be Directly Impugned:** Legitimacy establishes a substantive civil status; it cannot be raised defensively or as an incidental issue in an action for partition.
(d) Plain-Language Explanation
The Supreme Court ruled that you cannot try to cancel someone's adoption or claim that a child is illegitimate as a side argument in an inheritance dispute. If you want to challenge an adoption or someone's birth legitimacy, you must file a direct court action specifically for that purpose within the strict deadlines provided by law. Because the petitioners waited more than 15 years and merely brought up these claims inside a partition case, their attacks were completely barred.
Issue 2: Exclusive Heirship Over the Estate of Teodoro Sayson and Isabel Bautista
(a) Issue & Short Answer
Are Doribel (as legitimate daughter) and Delia and Edmundo (as legally adopted children) the exclusive heirs of Teodoro and Isabel Sayson, completely excluding collateral relatives and ascendants? **YES.** Direct descendants (both legitimate and adopted) exclude collateral relatives (brothers/sisters) and surviving parents-in-law under Article 979 of the Civil Code.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements
"Art. 979. Legitimate children and their descendants succeed the parents and other ascendants, without distinction as to sex or age, and even if they should come from different marriages.
An adopted child succeeds to the property of the adopting parents in the same manner as a legitimate child."
"The philosophy underlying this article is that a person's love descends first to his children and grandchildren before it ascends to his parents and thereafter spreads among his collateral relatives. It is also supposed that one of his purposes in acquiring properties is to leave them eventually to his children as a token of his love for them and as a provision for their continued care even after he is gone from this earth."
(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi
**Application of Art. 979:** The law explicitly dictates that an adopted child succeeds to the adopting parents' property in exactly the same manner as a legitimate child.
**Total Exclusion:** In intestate succession, descendants stand first in the order of succession. The presence of children—whether legitimate or legally adopted—completely bars collateral relatives (the brothers and sisters, Mauricio et al.) and ascendants (Isabel’s mother, Juana Bautista) from inheriting.
**Underlying Philosophy:** Succession law is designed on the natural premise that love first descends to children, then ascends to parents, and only lastly spreads horizontally to collaterals. Consequently, Delia, Edmundo, and Doribel are the sole, exclusive heirs to the estate left by Teodoro and Isabel.
(d) Plain-Language Explanation
Under Philippine law, children (both biological legitimate children and legally adopted children) are primary compulsory heirs who wipe out any inheritance claims by the deceased’s brothers, sisters, or parents-in-law. Because Teodoro and Isabel left behind a legitimate daughter and two legally adopted children, these three take the entire estate of their parents, leaving absolutely nothing for Teodoro’s siblings or Isabel's mother.
Issue 3: Right of Representation in the Grandparents' Intestate Estate
(a) Issue & Short Answer
Do adopted children and a legitimate grandchild have the right of representation in the intestate estate of the deceased grandparents? **PARTIALLY MERITORIOUS.** The legitimate grandchild (Doribel) has the right of representation to step into her predeceased father's share, but the adopted children (Delia and Edmundo) do not, because adoption creates no legal relationship between the adopted child and the adopter's ascendants.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements
"Art. 970. Representation is a right created by fiction of law, by virtue of which the representative is raised to the place and the degree of the person represented, and acquires the rights which the latter would have if he were living or if he could have inherited."
"Art. 971. The representative is called to the succession by the law and not by the person represented. The representative does not succeed the person represented but the one who the person represented would have succeeded."
"There is no question that as the legitimate daughter of Teodoro and thus the granddaughter of Eleno and Rafaela, Doribel has a right to represent her deceased father in the distribution of the intestate estate of her grandparents. Under Article 981, quoted above, she is entitled to the share her father would have directly inherited had he survived, which shall be equal to the shares of her grandparents' other children."
"While it is true that the adopted child shall be deemed to be a legitimate child and have the same right as the latter, these rights do not include the right of representation. The relationship created by the adoption is between only the adopting parents and the adopted child and does not extend to the blood relatives of either party."
(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi
**Application of Arts. 970, 971, and 981 to Doribel:** When Teodoro predeceased his mother Rafaela, his right to inherit a child’s share in his parents' (Eleno and Rafaela) estate passed by operation of law to his legitimate descending line. Doribel, being his legitimate daughter, inherits per stirpes from her grandparents Eleno and Rafaela by fiction of law (right of representation).
**Disqualification of Adopted Children:** Under settled jurisprudence (**Teotico v. Del Val**), the legal ties generated by adoption are strictly bilateral and personal: they link only the adopter to the adopted. Adoption does not introduce the adopted child into the broader bloodline or family tree of the adopter.
**Grandparents are Legal Strangers to the Adopted:** To Eleno and Rafaela Sayson, Delia and Edmundo were legal strangers. Therefore, Delia and Edmundo cannot use the right of representation to reach into the grandparents' estate, as they are not "descendants" of Eleno and Rafaela under Article 979 and Article 981.
(d) Plain-Language Explanation
A legitimate grandchild can step into the shoes of her dead father to claim his share of the grandparents' estate by what the law calls the "right of representation." Doribel, being a legitimate daughter, gets her father's full 1/5 share of the grandparents' estate. However, her adopted siblings, Delia and Edmundo, cannot do this; the legal effect of an adoption only links the adoptive children to their adoptive parents, not to their adoptive grandparents or aunts and uncles.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions were filed or discussed in the decision; the decision was unanimous among the four sitting Justices of the First Division.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is DENIED, and the challenged decision of the Court of Appeals is AFFIRMED in toto, with costs against the petitioners."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court ruled completely against the petitioners (the siblings and mother-in-law). The Court affirmed that:
1.  Delia, Edmundo, and Doribel are the sole, exclusive heirs to the estate of their parents, Teodoro and Isabel;
2.  Doribel alone has the right of representation to inherit Teodoro's portion from the estate of the grandparents, Eleno and Rafaela; and
3.  Delia and Edmundo, being adopted, are disqualified from participating in the grandparents' estate.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Republic v. Court of Appeals and Bobiles**
**Full Official Caption:** Republic of the Philippines, Petitioner, v. Court of Appeals and Zenaida C. Bobiles, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 92326 (Note: header mentions 92326 / typographical 93226 in prompt title; official docket is G.R. No. 92326)
**Date of Promulgation:** January 24, 1992
**Philippine Reports Citation:** 282 Phil. 450 (Not expressly stated in the decision)
**Ponente:** Regalado, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Second Division; Melencio-Herrera, Paras, Padilla, and Nocon, **JJ.**, concur. Unanimous; no separate opinions.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code & Child and Youth Welfare Code → Adoption → Retroactivity of Laws and Mandatory Joint Adoption
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Remedial Law → Civil Procedure → Jurisdiction & Pleadings → Non-Joinder of Parties / Adherence to Form vs. Substantial Justice
Full Text of Governing Statutory Provisions
**Article 246, Executive Order No. 209 (The Family Code of the Philippines):**
"This Code shall have retroactive effect insofar as it **does not prejudice or impair vested or acquired rights** in accordance with the Civil Code or other laws."
**Article 185, Executive Order No. 209 (The Family Code of the Philippines):**
"**Husband and wife must jointly adopt**, except in the following cases:
(1) When one spouse seeks to adopt his own illegitimate child; or
(2) When one spouse seeks to adopt the legitimate child of the other."
**Presidential Decree No. 603 (The Child and Youth Welfare Code) [Historical Basis Governing When Filed]:**
Under the governing provisions of P.D. No. 603, an adoption proceeding could be instituted by **either spouse alone** (with the other spouse's consent) or **jointly by both spouses**.
The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision
**General Rule / Provision Triggered:** Under Article 246 of the Family Code, retroactive application of new provisions (such as the mandatory joint adoption requirement under Article 185) is barred when it impairs or prejudices **vested or acquired rights**. Furthermore, jurisdiction is substantive and determined by the statute in force at the time the action is commenced.
**Specific Sub-Rules / Exceptions / Doctrinal Tests:**
1.  **Rule on Vested Right:** A vested right is one whose existence, effectivity, and extent do not depend upon events foreign to the will of the holder; it constitutes a present fixed interest protected against arbitrary State action. An individual who validly files a petition for sole adoption under a statute permitting it secures a vested right to have that petition proceed to final adjudication under the governing law at filing.
2.  **Retroactivity of Remedial/Procedural Statutes:** Procedural laws are generally retroactive to pending actions, but they **will not be applied to defeat procedural steps completed before their enactment**, nor to invalidate proceedings properly begun.
3.  **Adherence of Jurisdiction:** Jurisdiction, once attached pursuant to the law in force at commencement, cannot be ousted by subsequent statutory amendments.
4.  **Substantial Compliance in Adoption:** Technical defects in pleadings and the formal joinder of parties yield to substantial justice and the best interests of the child. Where a non-party spouse executes an authenticated affidavit of consent declaring a mutual desire to adopt, submits it with the petition, and confirms it in open court testimony, he is deemed a co-petitioner in substance.
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):** Zenaida Bobiles filed a petition to adopt Jason Condat on February 2, 1988 under P.D. No. 603 (which allowed sole adoption). The trial court granted the adoption before August 3, 1988, when the Family Code took effect making joint adoption mandatory under Article 185. The Republic challenged the decree on appeal, claiming the Family Code retroactively applied to nullify the petition for non-joinder of the husband.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Republic of the Philippines (Petitioner):** Represented by the Solicitor General; opposed the adoption decree on appeal, asserting retroactive application of the Family Code.
**Zenaida Corteza Bobiles (Private Respondent / Adopting Mother):** Filed the petition for adoption under P.D. No. 603 in the RTC of Legaspi City.
**Dioscoro Bobiles (Husband):** Resided in Chicago, Illinois; executed an authenticated Affidavit of Consent annexed to the petition and testified in court in support of the adoption.
**Jason Condat (Minor Child to be Adopted):** Six years old at the time of petition; reared and cared for by the Bobiles spouses since he was four months old.
**Salvador Condat:** Natural father of the minor child who consented to the adoption.
**Court of Appeals (Public Respondent):** Affirmed the RTC adoption decree **in toto**.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on **Certiorari** under Rule 45 filed by the Republic, assailing the February 20, 1990 Decision of the Court of Appeals (affirming **in toto** the March 20, 1988 Decision of RTC Legaspi City, Branch 2, in Sp. Proc. No. 1386).
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**Infancy of Jason Condat:** At the age of four (4) months, Jason Condat was taken in, continuously reared, and cared for by spouses Dioscoro and Zenaida Bobiles.
**October 17, 1987:** Dioscoro Bobiles executed an "Affidavit of Consent" in Chicago, Illinois (duly authenticated by the Philippine Consulate General), stating that he and his wife mutually desired to adopt Jason, that they were filing the petition together, and giving his lawful consent.
**February 2, 1988:** Zenaida Corteza Bobiles filed a petition for adoption of minor Jason Condat (then 6 years old) before the Regional Trial Court of Legaspi City (Sp. Proc. No. 1386), attaching Dioscoro's Affidavit of Consent as Annex "B". At the time, P.D. No. 603 was the governing law.
**February 15, 1988:** The RTC found the petition sufficient in form and substance and issued an order setting it for hearing on March 28, 1988. The order was published, posted, and served on the OSG, the Assistant Provincial Fiscal, the child’s natural father, and the DSWD social worker. Nobody opposed the petition.
**March 28, 1988:** Hearing held. Jurisdictional facts established. Testimonies were received from Zenaida Bobiles, her husband Dioscoro Bobiles, and Ma. Luz Salameno of the DSWD (who unqualifiedly recommended approval). Sworn written consent from the children of the adopters and the natural parents was established.
**March 20, 1988 [Date as stated in decision]:** The RTC rendered judgment granting the adoption, declaring Jason Condat the child of spouses Dioscoro and Zenaida Bobiles to all intents and purposes, and changing his surname to "Bobiles."
**August 3, 1988:** Executive Order No. 209 (The Family Code of the Philippines) took effect while the case was pending on appeal.
**February 20, 1990:** The Court of Appeals affirmed the RTC decision **in toto**.
**Subsequent Event:** The Republic filed the instant Petition for Review on **Certiorari** before the Supreme Court.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Republic of the Philippines)
**Main Thesis:** The petition for adoption must be dismissed outright because it was filed solely by Zenaida Bobiles without joining her husband, violating mandatory Article 185 of the Family Code, which applies retroactively. In the alternative, the decree should benefit only Zenaida Bobiles.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Retroactivity under Art. 246:** The Family Code must be applied retroactively because Zenaida Bobiles acquired no vested right to adopt the child by the mere filing of her petition.
**Mandatory Joint Adoption:** Article 185 mandates joint adoption by husband and wife; non-compliance is a fatal/jurisdictional defect warranting outright dismissal.
**Alternative Modification:** Even if the Family Code does not apply retroactively, the CA erred in granting adoption in favor of **both** spouses since Dioscoro Bobiles was not named as a petitioner in the caption/pleading.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Zenaida C. Bobiles)
**Note: Specific written counter-arguments of private respondent are not elaborately detailed in the text beyond defending the rulings below, but were embodied in the adopted CA decision:**
The petition complied with the law in force at filing (P.D. No. 603).
The husband fully consented, executed an authenticated affidavit of consent made an integral part of the petition, and testified in court.
The welfare and best interest of the child govern adoption proceedings and should not be defeated by technicalities.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the Court of Appeals erred in ruling that Article 185 of the Family Code (requiring mandatory joint adoption by spouses) cannot be applied retroactively to divest the trial court of jurisdiction or mandate the outright dismissal of an adoption petition filed prior to its effectivity.
**(Recitation-Ready Question: Does the mandatory joint adoption requirement of the Family Code apply retroactively to invalidate a petition filed solely by one spouse under prior law?)**
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the Court of Appeals erred in affirming the trial court's adoption decree in favor of **both** spouses Dioscoro and Zenaida Bobiles, even though the husband was not formally named as a co-petitioner in the title of the petition.
**(Recitation-Ready Question: May an adoption decree be validly rendered in favor of both spouses where the husband was omitted from the title of the petition but submitted an authenticated affidavit of consent and testified in open court?)**
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Retroactivity of Article 185 of the Family Code
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** The Court of Appeals did not err. The Family Code cannot be retroactively applied to impair the vested right of private respondent or oust the jurisdiction of the trial court validly acquired under P.D. No. 603.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"A vested right is one whose existence, effectivity and extent does not depend upon events foreign to the will of the holder. The term expresses the concept of present fixed interest which in right reason and natural justice should be protected against arbitrary State action, or an innately just and imperative right which enlightened free society, sensitive to inherent and irrefragable individual rights, cannot deny. Vested rights include not only legal or equitable title to the enforcement of a demand, but also an exemption from new obligations created after the right has vested."
"When private respondent filed her petition in Special Proceeding No. 1386, the trial court acquired jurisdiction thereover in accordance with the governing law. Jurisdiction being a matter of substantive law, the established rule is that the jurisdiction of the court is determined by the statute in force at the time of the commencement of the action."
"Procedural statutes are ordinarily accorded a retrospective construction in the sense that they may be applied to pending actions and proceedings, as well as to future actions. However, they will not be so applied as to defeat procedural steps completed before their enactment."
"As long as the petition for adoption was sufficient in form and substance in accordance with the law in governance at the time it was filed, the court acquires jurisdiction and retains it until it fully disposes of the case... Such jurisdiction of a court, whether in criminal or civil cases, once it attaches cannot be ousted by subsequent happenings or events, although of a character which would have prevented jurisdiction from attaching in the first instance."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Application of Article 246 (Vested Rights):** Under Article 246 of the Family Code, retroactive application is prohibited if it impairs vested or acquired rights. Under P.D. No. 603 (governing at the time of filing on February 2, 1988), Zenaida Bobiles had an explicit, unconditional right to file solely. Once filed, her right to proceed to final adjudication under that law became vested and could not be prejudiced by the Family Code taking effect on August 3, 1988.
**Jurisdiction is Substantive and Fixed at Commencement:** Jurisdiction is governed by the statute in force when the action begins. When the RTC took cognizance of the petition under P.D. No. 603, its jurisdiction attached. It cannot be ousted by a subsequent statute.
**Limits of Procedural Retroactivity:** While procedural statutes can apply to pending cases, they cannot defeat procedural steps completed prior to enactment. Since the petition was already filed, heard, and decided by the RTC before the Family Code took effect, the new procedural requirement of joint filing cannot invalidate completed proceedings.
**Non-Joinder is Not a Dismissal Ground:** Under procedural rules, non-joinder of parties is not even a ground for outright dismissal.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language Explanation)** The Supreme Court ruled that laws cannot apply retroactively if they destroy vested rights or divest a court of jurisdiction it already validly acquired. When Mrs. Bobiles filed her adoption petition under P.D. No. 603, the law allowed her to file alone, and the trial court properly acquired jurisdiction. Because the trial court had already heard and granted the adoption before the Family Code took effect, the Republic cannot use the Family Code's new joint adoption rule to nullify the completed proceedings retroactively.
Issue 2: Validity of Decree in Favor of Both Spouses (Omission in Caption)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** The Court of Appeals did not err. The adoption decree in favor of both spouses is valid because the husband substantially complied with all statutory requirements and became a party in substance.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"The foregoing declarations, and his subsequent confirmatory testimony in open court, are sufficient to make him a co-petitioner. Under the circumstances then obtaining, and by reason of his foreign residence, he must have yielded to the legal advice that an affidavit of consent on his part sufficed to make him a party to the petition... Punctiliousness in language and pedantry in the formal requirements should yield to and be eschewed in the higher considerations of substantial justice. The future of an innocent child must not be compromised by arbitrary insistence of rigid adherence to procedural rules on the form of pleadings."
"It is a settled rule therein that adoption statutes, as well as matters of procedure leading up to adoption, should be liberally construed to carry out the beneficent purposes of the adoption institution and to protect the adopted child in the rights and privileges coming to it as a result of the adoption."
"In determining whether or not to set aside the decree of adoption the interests and welfare of the child are of primary and paramount consideration."
"Adoption statutes, being humane and salutary, hold the interests and welfare of the child to be of paramount consideration. They are designed to provide homes, parental care and education for unfortunate, needy or orphaned children and give them the protection of society and family in the person of the adopted..."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Substantial Compliance of the Husband:** Although not formally named in the title, Dioscoro Bobiles executed an authenticated Affidavit of Consent annexed to and made an integral part of the petition. In it, he stated that he and his wife mutually desired to adopt Jason, that they were filing the petition together, and that he loved the child as his own. He also testified in open court. This effectively made him a co-petitioner.
**Rejection of Technical Pedantry:** Technical rules of pleading are not stringently applied in adoption proceedings. As long as the petition contains the essential facts and shows substantial compliance, formal defects in the caption are not fatal.
**Paramount Interest of the Child:** The overriding objective of adoption law is the child’s best interest. Jason had lived with the spouses since he was four months old, the natural parents consented, the adopters' biological children consented, the DSWD recommended approval, and trial custody was dispensed with. Defeating the child’s legal status over a caption defect violates the humane intent of the statute.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language Explanation)** The Court held that form must yield to substance when protecting the welfare of a child. Even though the husband was not listed as a petitioner in the caption, he attached an authenticated affidavit stating that he and his wife were adopting the boy together and testified in support of the petition in court. Because adoption statutes must be liberally construed to serve the child's best interests, his active participation made him a co-petitioner in substance, justifying the decree in favor of both spouses.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text. (The decision of the Second Division was unanimous, penned by Regalado, **J.**, with Melencio-Herrera, Paras, Padilla, and Nocon, **JJ.**, concurring).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the instant petition is hereby DENIED.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The petition of the Republic was denied, and the Court of Appeals' decision affirming the trial court's adoption decree was upheld. Jason Condat remains legally adopted by both spouses Dioscoro and Zenaida Bobiles, with all statutory rights and the surname "Bobiles."

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Landingin v. Republic**
**Full Official Caption:** Diwata Ramos Landingin, Petitioner, vs. Republic of the Philippines, Respondent
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 164948
**Date of Promulgation:** June 27, 2006
**Philippine Reports:** 526 Phil. 365
**Ponente:** Callejo, Sr., **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** First Division; Panganiban, **C.J.** (Chairperson), Ynares-Santiago, Austria-Martinez, and Chico-Nazario, **JJ.**, concur. No separate opinions filed.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code & Special Laws → Republic Act No. 8552 (Domestic Adoption Act of 1998) → Necessary Consents for Adoption → Biological Parents and Adopter's Children
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Remedial Law → Evidence → Rule 132 (Authentication of Foreign Notarized Documents & Formal Offer of Evidence)
Civil Law → Family Code & Special Laws → R.A. No. 8552 → Qualifications of Adopter → Financial Capacity and Requirement of Personal Ability to Support
**Full Text of Governing Statutory Provisions:**
**Section 9, Republic Act No. 8552 (Domestic Adoption Act of 1998):**
"SEC. 9. **Whose Consent is Necessary to the Adoption.** — After being properly counseled and informed of his/her right to give or withhold his/her approval of the adoption, the **written consent** of the following to the adoption is hereby required:
(a) The adoptee, if ten (10) years of age or over;
(b) **The biological parent(s) of the child, if known, or the legal guardian, or the proper government instrumentality which has legal custody of the child;**
(c) **The legitimate and adopted sons/daughters, ten (10) years of age or over, of the adopter(s)** and adoptee, if any;
(d) The illegitimate sons/daughters, ten (10) years of age or over, of the adopter, if living with said adopter and the latter’s spouse, if any;
(e) The spouse, if any, of the person adopting or to be adopted."
**Section 2, Act No. 2103:**
"SEC. 2. An instrument or document acknowledged and authenticated in a foreign country shall be considered authentic if the acknowledgment and authentication are made in accordance with the following requirements:
(a) The acknowledgment shall be made before (1) an ambassador, minister, secretary of legation, **chargé d'affaires**, consul, vice-consul, or consular agent of the Republic of the Philippines, acting within the country or place to which he is accredited, or (2) a notary public or officer duly authorized by law of the country to take acknowledgments of instruments or documents in the place where the act is done.
(b) The person taking the acknowledgment shall certify that the person acknowledging the instrument or document is known to him, and that he is the same person who executed it, and acknowledged that the same is his free act and deed. The certificate shall be under his official seal, if he is by law required to keep a seal, and if not, his certificate shall so state. **In case the acknowledgment is made before a notary public or an officer mentioned in subdivision (2) of the preceding paragraph, the certificate of the notary public or the officer taking the acknowledgment shall be authenticated by an ambassador, minister, secretary of legation, chargé d'affaires, consul, vice-consul, or consular agent of the Republic of the Philippines, acting within the country or place to which he is accredited.** The officer making the authentication shall certify under his official seal that the person who took the acknowledgment was at the time duly authorized to act as notary public or that he was duly exercising the functions of the office by virtue of which he assumed to act, and that as such he had authority under the law to take acknowledgment of instruments or documents in the place where the acknowledgment was taken, and that his signature and seal, if any, are genuine."
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provisions:**
**General Rule on Consent:** Under Section 9, R.A. No. 8552, the written consent of known biological parents and the legitimate children (aged 10 or older) of the adopter is **mandatory and indispensable** to the validity of an adoption decree.
**Sub-Rule on Biological Parent's Consent and Abandonment:** The biological parent's consent can only be dispensed with if said parent has **abandoned** the child or cannot be found, in which case the written consent of the **legal guardian** or proper government instrumentality is mandatory. Abandonment means conduct showing a settled purpose to forgo all parental duties, neglect, and absolute refusal to perform obligations of love and support at the time of adoption. Merely leaving a child with relatives due to financial constraints or sending periodic/minimal support while keeping open parental consultation lines does **not** constitute legal abandonment.
**Sub-Rule on Foreign Affidavits of Consent:** An affidavit of consent executed abroad before a foreign notary public (under Act No. 2103, Sec. 2) must be **duly authenticated by a Philippine diplomatic or consular officer** in that country. Without consular authentication or independent proof of due execution and genuineness under Rule 132, the document is an unauthenticated private document, legally inadmissible.
**Sub-Rule on Financial Capacity:** Financial capacity is **personal to the prospective adopter**. The adopter cannot cure financial inadequacy by relying on prospective, unproven voluntary commitments of support from siblings or adult children.
**Factual Trigger:** A paternal aunt residing in Guam sought to adopt her deceased brother's three minor children without submitting the biological mother's written consent (alleging abandonment), presenting an unauthenticated Guam notarized consent from her own adult children, and demonstrating an income derived solely from a part-time waitress job supplemented by promised backing from relatives.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Diwata Ramos Landingin:** Petitioner; paternal aunt of the minors; 57-year-old widow; naturalized US citizen residing in Guam; employed as a part-time restaurant server.
**Manuel Ramos:** Petitioner’s deceased brother; biological father of the minors (died May 19, 1990).
**Amelia Ramos:** Surviving biological mother of the minors; relocated to Italy as a domestic worker in November 1990, entered a second union, and sent minimal financial support.
**Elaine Dizon Ramos, Elma Dizon Ramos, Eugene Dizon Ramos:** Proposed adoptees; minor children of Manuel and Amelia Ramos (born August 31, 1986, September 7, 1987, and August 5, 1989, respectively).
**Maria Taruc Ramos:** Paternal grandmother of the minors who took custody after Manuel died; died on November 23, 2000.
**Ann, Errol, Dennis, and Ricfel Branitley Landingin:** Petitioner's adult legitimate children who executed an unauthenticated Affidavit of Consent in Guam.
**Elizabeth Pagbilao:** Social Welfare Officer II, DSWD Field Office III, Tarlac; author of the Child Study Report.
**Republic of the Philippines:** Respondent, represented by the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG).
**Procedural Posture:**
Petitioner filed a petition for adoption before the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Tarlac City, Branch 63 (Civil Case No. 2733).
The RTC granted the petition.
The Republic, through the OSG, appealed to the Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. CV No. 77826).
The CA reversed and set aside the RTC Decision.
The CA denied petitioner's Motion for Reconsideration.
Petitioner filed the present **Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45** before the Supreme Court.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**August 31, 1986; September 7, 1987; August 5, 1989:** Elaine, Elma, and Eugene Ramos are born to spouses Manuel Ramos and Amelia Ramos.
**May 19, 1990:** Manuel Ramos dies. The minors are placed in the custody and care of their paternal grandmother, Maria Taruc Ramos.
**November 20, 1990:** Impelled by financial constraints and her parents' medical needs, Amelia leaves for Italy to work as a domestic worker. She leaves her children with her mother-in-law, Maria. In Italy, Amelia later lives with Jun Tayag and bears another son (John Mario). She remits financial support through her parents, a portion of which (₱3,000 to ₱5,000 monthly) reaches the children.
**November 23, 2000:** Maria Taruc Ramos passes away. A paternal cousin and his family act as temporary guardians of the children in Tarlac, while petitioner, her children, and other relatives abroad continue financial support.
**January 16, 2002:** In Guam, USA, petitioner's adult children (Ann, Errol, Dennis, and Ricfel Branitley) execute a joint Affidavit of Consent to the adoption, notarized by a Guam notary public. It is **not** authenticated by the Philippine Consulate.
**February 4, 2002:** Petitioner files a Petition for Adoption of the three minors before the RTC of Tarlac City, Branch 63.
**March 5, 2002:** The RTC orders the DSWD to conduct a home and child study report and sets initial hearing for April 4, 2002.
**May 2002:** Amelia Ramos returns to the Philippines on a three-week vacation with her son John Mario. Elizabeth Pagbilao of the DSWD interviews Amelia regarding the adoption.
**May 24, 2002:** Pagbilao submits her Child Study Report recommending approval of the adoption, noting Amelia’s verbal conformity. However, petitioner never calls Pagbilao as a witness, does not present Amelia's written consent, and fails to formally offer Pagbilao's Report into evidence.
**November 23, 2002:** The RTC renders a Decision granting the adoption petition and dispensing with trial custody.
**December 2, 2002:** The OSG files a Notice of Appeal to the CA.
**April 29, 2004:** The CA renders its Decision reversing and setting aside the RTC decision due to: (1) lack of written consent from the biological mother; (2) inadmissibility of the unauthenticated Affidavit of Consent of petitioner’s children; and (3) petitioner’s lack of personal financial stability.
**August 12, 2004:** The CA denies petitioner's Motion for Reconsideration.
**September 7, 2004:** Petitioner files the instant Rule 45 petition before the Supreme Court.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The CA erred in reversing the adoption decree; statutory consent requirements were sufficiently satisfied or excused by abandonment, and petitioner is financially capable with familial backing.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Abandonment by Mother Excuses Consent:** Amelia Ramos abandoned the children for 12 years after her husband died in 1990 by relocating to Italy, remarrying, starting a new family, and ceasing communications. Paternal relatives, not Amelia, raised and supported the minors.
**Mother Consented Factually:** Amelia returned to the country during the trial and verbally consented to the adoption during an interview with DSWD worker Pagbilao, as confirmed in the Child Study Report.
**Sufficiency of Children's Consent:** The children executed an Affidavit of Consent notarized in Guam, and the eldest adoptee (Elaine) confirmed the family's assent during her testimony.
**Financial Capacity Proven:** Petitioner has worked in Guam for 14 years, owns a house, earns $5.15 per hour plus monthly tips of around $1,000, has savings, and has written and committed financial backing from her gainfully employed adult children and her brother Mariano Ramos.
B. Respondent's Arguments (Republic / OSG)
**Main Thesis:** The petition for adoption fails on indispensable statutory requirements under R.A. No. 8552 and the Rules of Court.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Absence of Biological Mother's Consent:** Section 9 of R.A. No. 8552 explicitly demands the written consent of the biological mother. Abandonment was not proven because Amelia sent support, consulted with her children on serious matters, and only left due to economic necessity. Even if abandoned, the written consent of a legal guardian was required and missing.
**Inadmissibility of Petitioner's Children's Consent:** The Affidavit of Consent executed by petitioner's children was notarized in Guam but was not authenticated by a Philippine consular official pursuant to Act No. 2103, Section 2; thus, it is legally inadmissible.
**Lack of Financial Capacity:** Under the Guam Home Study Report, petitioner works only part-time as a waitress, has "limited income," amortizes a home mortgage, and is of advanced age (57). Support obligations are personal to the adopter and cannot legally rest upon third-party relatives whose commitments are legally unenforceable.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the petition for adoption may be granted without the written consent of the biological mother, Amelia Ramos, under Section 9 of R.A. No. 8552.
**Faithful Phrasing:** "[W]hether the petitioner is entitled to adopt the minors without the written consent of their biological mother, Amelia Ramos[.]"
2.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the joint Affidavit of Consent executed in Guam by petitioner's legitimate children is admissible and complies with the legal consent requirement.
**Faithful Phrasing:** "[W]hether or not the affidavit of consent purportedly executed by the petitioner-adopter's children sufficiently complies with the law[.]"
3.  **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not petitioner established that she has the financial capacity to support the proposed adoptees under the law.
**Faithful Phrasing:** "[W]hether or not petitioner is financially capable of supporting the adoptees."
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Necessity of the Biological Mother's Written Consent
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The written consent of the biological mother is an indispensable statutory requirement, and abandonment was not established to dispense with it.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"[T]he discretion to approve adoption proceedings is not to be anchored solely on best interests of the child but likewise, with due regard to the natural rights of the parents over the child."
"Clearly, the written consent of the biological parents is indispensable for the validity of a decree of adoption. Indeed, the natural right of a parent to his child requires that his consent must be obtained before his parental rights and duties may be terminated and re-established in adoptive parents."
"Ordinarily, abandonment by a parent to justify the adoption of his child without his consent, is a conduct which evinces a settled purpose to forego all parental duties. The term means neglect and refusal to perform the filial and legal obligations of love and support. If a parent withholds presence, love, care, the opportunity to display filial affection, and neglects to lend support and maintenance, the parent, in effect, abandons the child. Merely permitting the child to remain for a time undisturbed in the care of others is not such an abandonment. To dispense with the requirement of consent, the abandonment must be shown to have existed at the time of adoption."
"It would thus be against the spirit of the law if financial consideration were to be the paramount consideration in deciding whether to deprive a person of parental authority over his/her children."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Statutory Rule:** Section 9(b) of R.A. No. 8552 explicitly mandates the written consent of known biological parents. Its purpose is to protect natural parental relations from unwarranted third-party interference.
**Application to Amelia Ramos:** Pagbilao's DSWD report showed that Amelia visited the Philippines in May 2002 and was personally interviewed. Petitioner inexplicably failed to secure her written consent or present her as a trial witness.
**Rebuttal of Abandonment Theory:** Abandonment requires a settled intention to completely sever parental duties. Amelia left for Italy out of financial distress to support her parents and children, placed the children safely with her mother-in-law, remitted monthly support of ₱3,000–₱5,000, and remained available for consultation on serious problems (as testified to by eldest daughter Elaine). Emotional abandonment was not proven.
**Guardianship Requirement:** Even assuming **arguendo** that abandonment occurred, Section 9 mandates that the written consent of the **legal guardian** or proper government agency must be obtained. Petitioner presented neither.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** Under Philippine law, courts cannot sever a mother's parental rights without her express written consent. A mother who leaves her children with loving relatives to work abroad due to extreme poverty, and continues to send small remittances while giving parental advice, has not legally "abandoned" her children. Because petitioner never obtained the mother’s or a legal guardian’s written consent, the adoption cannot legally proceed.
Issue 2: Validity and Admissibility of the Adopter's Children's Consent Executed Abroad
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The Affidavit of Consent is inadmissible because it was notarized in Guam without Philippine consular authentication and was never formally offered in evidence.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Section 34, Rule 132 of the Rules of Court provides that the Court shall consider no evidence which has not been formally offered. The purpose for which the evidence is offered must be specified. The offer of evidence is necessary because it is the duty of the Court to rest its findings of fact and its judgment only and strictly upon the evidence offered by the parties. Unless and until admitted by the court in evidence for the purpose or purposes for which such document is offered, the same is merely a scrap of paper barren of probative weight."
"As the alleged written consent of petitioner's legitimate children did not comply with the afore-cited law [Section 2 of Act No. 2103], the same can at best be treated by the Rules as a private document whose authenticity must be proved either by anyone who saw the document executed or written; or by evidence of the genuineness of the signature or handwriting of the makers. Since, in the instant case, no further proof was introduced by petitioner to authenticate the written consent of her legitimate children, the same is inadmissible in evidence."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Authentication Requirements for Foreign Documents:** Under Act No. 2103, Section 2, a document notarized before a foreign notary public must be authenticated by a Philippine diplomatic or consular officer accredited to that place.
**Defective Proof:** The joint consent of petitioner’s children was notarized in Guam, USA, but bore no consular authentication. Lacking this, it degraded into a mere private document under Rule 132, requiring independent evidence of execution and signature genuineness. Petitioner offered zero witness testimony or proof of genuineness.
**Fatal Procedural Bar:** Furthermore, petitioner failed to formally offer the Affidavit of Consent and the DSWD Home Study Report in evidence under Rule 132, Section 34. Unoffered documents are mere "scraps of paper" without probative weight.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** A consent form signed and notarized in a foreign country (like Guam) cannot simply be filed in a Philippine court; it must be authenticated by a Philippine consulate official, or someone must testify in court to verify the signatures. Because petitioner failed to have the Guam document authenticated, failed to prove its authenticity with witnesses, and failed to formally offer it as evidence, the consent of her adult children was completely inadmissible.
Issue 3: Adopter's Personal Financial Capability
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Financial capacity is personal to the adopter, and petitioner’s part-time earnings and advanced age failed to demonstrate an independent ability to support three minors.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Since the primary consideration in adoption is the best interest of the child, it follows that the financial capacity of prospective parents should also be carefully evaluated and considered. Certainly, the adopter should be in a position to support the would-be adopted child or children, in keeping with the means of the family."
"While petitioner claims that she has the financial support and backing of her children and siblings, the OSG is correct in stating that the ability to support the adoptees is personal to the adopter, as adoption only creates a legal relation between the former and the latter. Moreover, the records do not prove nor support petitioner's allegation that her siblings and her children are financially able and that they are willing to support the minors herein."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Evaluation of Capacity:** The Guam Home Study Report showed petitioner was 57 years old, working only part-time as a waitress earning minimum wage ($5.15/hour plus tips), and still amortizing a home loan. The report acknowledged her income was "limited" and could hinder the proceedings.
**Support is Strictly Personal:** The legal relationship of adoption is strictly confined to the adopter and adoptee. Consequently, the duty of support cannot be offloaded to third persons. Petitioner cannot legally anchor her qualification on promises of support from siblings or adult children.
**Failure of Proof:** Even if third-party support were legally relevant, petitioner presented no concrete evidence establishing that her siblings or adult children possessed the financial means or binding legal willingness to support the minors in the US.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** To adopt children, the prospective adopter must personally possess the financial ability to provide for them. The legal obligation to support belongs exclusively to the adopter, not her siblings or adult children. Because petitioner was 57 years old, worked only part-time as a waitress, had a pending mortgage, and offered no concrete proof of reliable outside support, she failed to prove she could adequately provide for three growing children in the United States.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions were filed or discussed in the decision.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, premises considered, the petition is hereby DENIED.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' Decision, thereby completely dismissing Diwata Ramos Landingin's petition to adopt her nieces and nephew. However, the Court explicitly noted that petitioner is not precluded from curing the procedural and substantive defects and filing a new petition for adoption in the future.
