### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Bagcat-Gullas v. Gullas**
**Full Official Caption:** Nena Bagcat-Gullas, Petitioner, vs. Joselito F. Gullas, Joie Marie F. Gullas Yu, and John Vincent F. Gullas, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 264146
**Date of Promulgation:** August 7, 2023
**Philippine Reports Citation:** Not stated in the decision
**Ponente:** Singh, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Third Division; Caguioa (**Chairperson**), Inting, Gaerlan, and Dimaampao, **JJ.**, concur. No separate opinions.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:**
Civil Law → Family Code & Special Laws → Domestic Adoption (R.A. No. 8552) → Consent Requirements & Indispensable Parties → Jurisdiction over Adopter's Legitimate Children Over 10 Years Old
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:**
Remedial Law → Civil Procedure → Rule 45 (Questions of Fact vs. Law) → Exceptions to the Doctrine of Immutability of Judgments (Void Judgments for Lack of Jurisdiction)
Full Text of Governing Statutory / Procedural Provision(s):
**Section 9, Republic Act No. 8552 (Domestic Adoption Act of 1998):**
**SECTION 9. Whose Consent is Necessary to the Adoption.** — After being properly counseled and informed of his/her right to give or withhold his/her approval of the adoption, the written consent of the following to the adoption is hereby required:
(a) The adoptee, if ten (10) years of age or over;
(b) The biological parent(s) of the child, if known, or the legal guardian, or the proper government instrumentality which has legal custody of the child;
**(c) The legitimate and adopted sons/daughters, ten (10)-years of age or over, of the adopter(s) and adoptee, if any;**
(d) The illegitimate sons/daughters, ten (10) years of age of over, of the adopter if living with said adopter and the latter's spouse, if any; and
(e) The spouse, if any, of the person adopting or to be adopted.
The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:
**General Rule / Provision Triggered:** Under **Section 9(c) of R.A. No. 8552**, the written consent of the legitimate children aged 10 years or older of the adopter is an indispensable statutory requirement for a petition for adoption to validly prosper.
**Specific Sub-Rules / Doctrinal Tests Highlighted by This Case:**
1. **Indispensable Parties in Adoption Proceedings:** The legitimate children of the adopter are **indispensable parties**. Because an adoption decree materially affects their future legitimes, care, and family relations, their presence is mandatory.
2. **Defective Jurisdiction via Constructive Notice:** In adoption cases, constructive notice by publication does **not** suffice to vest the trial court with jurisdiction over the adopter’s legitimate children. **Personal service of summons** upon them is mandatory to protect substantive statutory rights.
3. **Void Judgment Exception to Immutability:** The absence of an indispensable party and lack of personal summons deprives the trial court of jurisdiction. A judgment rendered without jurisdiction is void **ab initio**, produces no binding effect, never attains finality, and is a recognized exception to the **doctrine of immutability of judgments**.
4. **Rule 45 Factual Review Bar:** The Supreme Court is not a trier of facts; questioning the authenticity and genuineness of an alleged notarial Affidavit of Consent presents a pure question of fact outside the scope of a Rule 45 petition.
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):** Petitioners secured a decree of adoption over a minor child without personally impleading or serving summons on the husband's adult legitimate children, relying instead on newspaper publication and a spurious, non-registered "Affidavit of Consent." When the legitimate children discovered the proceedings, the trial court and the appellate court properly vacated the finality of the adoption decree because the judgment was rendered void for want of personal jurisdiction over indispensable parties.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Nena Bagcat-Gullas (Petitioner):** Adopter; co-petitioner in the underlying petition for adoption; wife of Jose R. Gullas.
**Jose R. Gullas (Jose):** Co-adopter; husband of Nena; biological father of the respondents.
**Joselito F. Gullas, Joie Marie F. Gullas Yu, and John Vincent F. Gullas (Respondents):** Legitimate adult children of co-adopter Jose R. Gullas whose statutory consent was required.
**Jo Anne Maria Ariraya (Jo Anne):** Minor child sought to be adopted.
**Settie Asiah Ariraya (Settie):** Biological mother of Jo Anne who abandoned her.
**Atty. Jaime O. Gonzales:** Notary public whose notarial register revealed that the alleged "Affidavit of Consent" was falsified/non-genuine.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on **Certiorari** under **Rule 45** of the Rules of Court filed by petitioner Nena Bagcat-Gullas assailing the Court of Appeals' Decision (dated June 22, 2021) and Resolution (dated September 6, 2022) in CA-G.R. SP No. 12402, which affirmed the RTC Orders setting aside the final adoption decree as null and void for lack of jurisdiction over indispensable parties.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**May 5, 2016:** Nena Bagcat-Gullas and her husband, Jose R. Gullas, file a **Petition for Adoption and Correction of Entries in the Birth Record** of minor Jo Anne Maria Ariraya before the RTC, Branch 24, Cebu City (docketed as SP Proc. No. R-CEB-16-02302-SP).
**October 24, 2017:** The RTC issues an Order finding the petition sufficient in form and substance, setting it for hearing on December 1, 2017, ordering publication once a week for three consecutive weeks in a Cebu newspaper of general circulation, directing notice to government agencies (OSG, Local Civil Registrar, DSWD), and ordering a social case study. No personal summons is directed to Jose’s legitimate children.
**December 1, 2017:** The petition is read thrice in open court during hearing. No person registers an objection or opposition.
**May 18, 2018:** The RTC renders a Decision granting the Petition for Adoption.
**June 6, 2018:** Wee Lim and Salas Law Firm files an **Entry of Appearance** on behalf of Jose’s legitimate children (respondents Joselito, Joie Marie, and John Vincent).
**June 8, 2018:** The RTC rules that respondents' Entry of Appearance is without basis because they are not parties of record.
**July 16, 2018:** The RTC issues a Certificate of Finality stating that the May 18, 2018 Adoption Decision became final and executory on July 4, 2018.
**July 17, 2018:** Respondents file a Motion for Reconsideration of the June 8, 2018 Order, arguing that as legitimate children over 10 years of age, their consent is mandatory and they are indispensable parties/real parties in interest.
**August 20, 2018:** Bagcat-Gullas and Jose file an opposition (**Comment Ad Cautelam**), asserting respondents are not indispensable parties and had already executed an **Affidavit of Consent**.
**October 3, 2018:** The RTC grants respondents' Motion for Reconsideration and Formal Entry of Appearance. It vacates its May 18, 2018 Decision, sets aside the July 16, 2018 Certificate of Finality, reinstates the case in the docket, and directs that summons be formally served upon respondents as indispensable parties.
**November 21, 2018:** The RTC denies Bagcat-Gullas and Jose's Motion for Reconsideration, reiterating that the rule on immutability does not shield a void judgment rendered without service of summons on indispensable parties.
**Subsequent CA Proceedings:** Bagcat-Gullas and Jose file a Petition for **Certiorari** with an injunctive prayer before the CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 12402).
**June 22, 2021:** The CA denies the Petition for **Certiorari**. It inspects Atty. Gonzales's notarial register and finds that the entry corresponding to the alleged Affidavit of Consent actually recorded an **Affidavit of Loss** of an SSS ID by one Jovito Aquiles Remulta, demonstrating the consent document was not genuine. It concludes the adoption decree was void for lack of jurisdiction.
**September 6, 2022:** The CA denies Bagcat-Gullas’s Motion for Reconsideration. Bagcat-Gullas files the present Rule 45 petition before the Supreme Court.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments (Nena Bagcat-Gullas):
**Main Thesis:** The RTC's May 18, 2018 Decision granting adoption had already become final and executory under the doctrine of immutability of judgments; the respondents are not indispensable parties, and their consent was in fact executed via an Affidavit of Consent.
**Specific Contentions:**
The trial court complied with the publication requirement in a proceeding **in rem**, which binds the whole world.
The respondents executed an Affidavit of Consent signifying their knowledge of and assent to the adoption; thus, intervention was unnecessary.
The CA erred in evaluating and determining that the Affidavit of Consent was not genuine.
The RTC lacked authority to vacate a decision after the issuance of a Certificate of Finality.
B. Respondents' Arguments (Joselito, Joie Marie, and John Vincent Gullas):
**Main Thesis:** The adoption decree and Certificate of Finality are null and void **ab initio** for lack of jurisdiction over indispensable parties whose substantive rights are directly impacted.
**Specific Contentions:**
Under Section 9(c) of R.A. No. 8552, the written consent of the adopter's legitimate children over 10 years of age is mandatory.
As legitimate children whose successional legitimes and family harmony are directly altered, they are indispensable parties entitled to personal service of summons; constructive notice via publication is legally insufficient.
The purported Affidavit of Consent is spurious and non-existent in the notary public's register.
A void judgment never acquires finality; therefore, the doctrine of immutability of judgments does not apply.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not the Court of Appeals committed reversible error in finding that the Affidavit of Consent allegedly executed by respondents was not genuine, and whether such an inquiry can be properly reviewed under a Rule 45 petition.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not the Supreme Court under Rule 45 can review the CA’s factual determination that the respondents’ Affidavit of Consent was not genuine.
2. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not the legitimate children of an adopter are indispensable parties entitled to personal service of summons in an adoption proceeding, the absence of which renders the judgment void and unshielded by the doctrine of immutability of judgments.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not an adoption decree that attained a Certificate of Finality is void and exempt from the rule on immutability of judgments when the adopter’s legitimate children over 10 years of age were neither impleaded nor personally served with summons.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Review of Factual Determination Regarding the Affidavit of Consent
(a) Issue & Short Answer:
Did the CA err in ruling that the Affidavit of Consent was not genuine, and may this factual issue be re-examined under Rule 45?
**NO.** The issue is purely factual, and the Supreme Court is not a trier of facts under Rule 45.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:
"It must be emphasized that when an issue invites a review of the evidence presented, the question posed is one of fact. It is a settled rule that the Court is not a trier of facts. The function of the Court in petitions for review on **certiorari** under Rule 45 of the Rules of Court is limited to reviewing errors of law that may have been committed by the lower courts. As a matter of sound practice and procedure, the Court defers and accords finality to the factual findings of trial courts. To do otherwise would defeat the very essence of Rule 45 and would convert the Court into a trier of facts, which is not its intended purpose under the law. On this ground alone, therefore, the Petition ought to be denied."
(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:
**Nature of Rule 45 Review:** Petitions for review on **certiorari** under Rule 45 are strictly confined to questions of law.
**Factual Issue Raised:** Evaluating whether the signatures on the Affidavit of Consent were genuine or whether the notarial register entry of Atty. Gonzales pertained to an unrelated Affidavit of Loss requires examining the weight and credibility of documentary evidence.
**Deference to Lower Court Findings:** The CA found that Entry No. 95 in the Notarial Register of Atty. Gonzales corresponded to an **Affidavit of Loss** of an SSS ID by one Jovito Aquiles Remulta, not the respondents' alleged consent. The Supreme Court accords finality to this factual determination.
(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:
The Supreme Court refused to re-investigate whether the respondents truly signed the consent form because that is a factual question. Under Rule 45, the Court only resolves pure questions of law, so it accepted the CA’s finding that the supposed consent affidavit was fake.
Issue 2: Indispensable Party Status of Adopter's Legitimate Children and Non-applicability of Immutability of Judgments
(a) Issue & Short Answer:
Are legitimate children over 10 years old indispensable parties entitled to personal service of summons, such that its omission renders the final adoption decree void?
**YES.** Under Section 9(c) of R.A. No. 8552, legitimate children over 10 years of age are indispensable parties; without personal summons served upon them, the trial court never acquired jurisdiction, rendering the adoption decree void and wholly exempt from the doctrine of immutability of judgments.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:
"The consent of the adopter's other children is necessary as it ensures harmony among the prospective siblings. It also sufficiently puts the other children on notice that they will have to share their parent's love and care, as well as their future legitimes, with another person." **(Quoting Castro v. Gregorio)**
"For the adoption to be valid, petitioners' consent was required by Republic Act No. 8552. Personal service of summons should have been effected on the spouse and all legitimate children to ensure that their substantive rights are protected. It is not enough to rely on constructive notice as in this case. Surreptitious use of procedural technicalities cannot be privileged over substantive statutory rights. Since the trial court failed to personally serve notice on Rosario and Joanne of the proceedings, it never validly acquired jurisdiction." **(Quoting Castro v. Gregorio)**
"The respondents' interest is material as an adoption decree not only affects the rights of the adoptee vis-à-vis the adopter, but also the rights of the other children of the adopter, Jose in this case. Further, it is not enough to rely on constructive notice. The respondents, as children of Jose, should have been personally served summons by the trial court. Without impleading the respondents, and absent service of summons upon them, the judgment rendered by the RTC is void."
"In this case, the rule on immutability of judgments does not apply because the judgment is void. The respondents, being the legitimate children of one of the adopters, Jose, are without a doubt, indispensable parties. The absence of an indispensable party renders all subsequent actions of the court null and void, as such the court has no authority to act not only as to the absent party but also as to those present."
(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:
**Statutory Mandate of Consent:** Section 9(c) of R.A. No. 8552 explicitly requires the written consent of the adopter's legitimate children who are at least 10 years of age. All three respondents were indisputably over 10 years old.
**Substantive Rights at Stake:** Citing **Castro v. Gregorio**, the Court emphasized that adoption directly reduces the future legitimes of existing legitimate children and alters family harmony. Consequently, their interest is substantial and material.
**Constructive Notice Insufficient:** General publication in an adoption case does not cure the failure to personally serve summons on the adopter's legitimate children. Personal service is required to confer jurisdiction over their persons and to protect their substantive statutory rights.
**Void Judgment Exception to Immutability:** While final judgments are generally immutable under **People v. Layag**, a void judgment produces no legal effect, never attains finality, and divests no rights. Because the RTC lacked jurisdiction due to the total omission of indispensable parties, its May 18, 2018 Decision was void **ab initio**, and the RTC acted correctly in setting aside both the decision and its Certificate of Finality.
**Note on Subsequent Legislation (R.A. No. 11642):** The Court noted that under the **Domestic Administrative Adoption and Alternative Child Care Act** (R.A. No. 11642), domestic adoption is now an administrative proceeding under the National Authority for Child Care (NACC), and pending judicial petitions may potentially be withdrawn under its transitory clause.
(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:
An adopter's legitimate children who are at least 10 years old have a direct legal stake in an adoption because the new child will share in their parent's inheritance and care. Because of this, they are indispensable parties who must be personally served with summons; mere newspaper publication will not do. Because the Gullas children were never served with summons, the trial court never acquired jurisdiction, rendering the adoption decree completely void and preventing it from ever becoming final or immutable.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.**
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
**WHEREFORE,** the Petition for Review on **Certiorari** is **DENIED**. The Decision, dated June 22, 2021, and the Resolution, dated September 6, 2022, of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 12402 are **AFFIRMED**.
**SO ORDERED.**
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Petitioner Nena Bagcat-Gullas lost the appeal. The Supreme Court affirmed the CA and RTC rulings, confirming that the May 18, 2018 adoption decree and its Certificate of Finality are null and void for failure to personally serve summons on Jose Gullas's legitimate children, who must be properly brought into the proceedings as indispensable parties.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Gan v. Reyes**
**Full Official Caption:** AUGUSTUS CAEZAR R. GAN, Petitioner, vs. HON. ANTONIO C. REYES, in his capacity as Presiding Judge of RTC-Br. 61, Baguio City, ALBERT G. TOLENTINO, in his capacity as RTC Sheriff of Baguio City, and FRANCHESKA JOY C. PONDEVIDA, assisted by BERNADETTE C. PONDEVIDA, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 145527; May 28, 2002; Second Division; Bellosillo, **J.** (Ponente); Mendoza, Quisumbing, De Leon, Jr., and Corona, **JJ.**, concur.
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Civil Procedure → Execution, Satisfaction, and Effect of Judgments (Rule 39) → Judgments Not Stayed by Appeal → Immediate Execution of Support Judgments
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Civil Law → Family Code → Support → Support **Pendente Lite** / Illegitimate Children
**Full Text of Governing Provision:**
**Rule 39, Section 4, 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure:**
**"Sec. 4. Judgments not stayed by appeal. — Judgments in actions for injunction, receivership, accounting and support, and such other judgments as are now or may hereafter be declared to be immediately executory, shall be enforceable after their rendition and shall not be stayed by an appeal taken therefrom, unless otherwise ordered by the trial court. On appeal, the appellate court in its discretion may make an order suspending, modifying, restoring or granting the injunction, receivership, accounting, or award of support.**
**The stay of execution shall be upon such terms as to bond or otherwise as may be considered proper for the security or protection of the adverse party."**
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Rule / Provision Triggered:** Under the plain language of **Section 4, Rule 39 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure**, judgments in actions for support are **immediately executory upon rendition** and **cannot be stayed by an appeal**, unless otherwise ordered by the trial court.
**Exception to General Execution Rules:** This constitutes an express statutory exception to the standard rule that an appeal stays execution and that execution pending appeal under Section 2, Rule 39 requires a showing of "good reasons." No special or extraordinary reasons are required to execute a support judgment immediately.
**Factual Trigger:** The trial court issued a writ of execution to enforce an award of child support and alimony **pendente lite** while the main decision was on appeal. Petitioner challenged the writ, contending it lacked the "good reasons" required for execution pending appeal and violated procedural due process because he received the motion two weeks after the scheduled hearing.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Augustus Caezar R. Gan:** Petitioner; putative father who denied paternity and sought to block execution of the support order.
**Francheska Joy S. Pondevida:** Private respondent; minor child (3 years old at complaint's filing) seeking recognition and support.
**Bernadette C. Pondevida:** Mother of Francheska Joy, acting as her legal guardian/representative.
**Hon. Antonio C. Reyes:** Public respondent; Presiding Judge of the Regional Trial Court (RTC), Branch 61, Baguio City.
**Albert G. Tolentino:** Public respondent; RTC Sheriff of Baguio City tasked with enforcing the writ of execution.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 assailing the August 31, 2000 Decision and subsequent Resolution of the Court of Appeals (CA) in CA-G.R. SP No. 59147, which dismissed petitioner's Rule 65 petition for certiorari and prohibition challenging the RTC's writ of execution.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**Pre-Litigation Demand:** Bernadette C. Pondevida sent a demand letter to Augustus Caezar R. Gan demanding financial support for their three-year-old child, Francheska Joy, so she could attend school. Gan replied, denying paternity.
**Complaint Filed:** Bernadette filed a complaint in RTC-Br. 61, Baguio City (Civil Case No. 4234-R) on behalf of Francheska Joy for recognition and support with a prayer for support **pendente lite**.
**Motion to Dismiss:** Gan moved to dismiss the complaint for failure to state a cause of action, pointing out that Francheska's birth certificate listed her father as "UNKNOWN." The RTC denied the motion.
**Default Order:** Gan failed to file his Answer within the reglementary period. On **January 19, 2000**, private respondent moved to declare Gan in default. Gan filed a **Motion to Admit Answer** more than **90 days** past the reglementary deadline. The RTC declared Gan in default and denied his subsequent motion for reconsideration, proceeding to receive evidence **ex parte**.
**May 12, 2000 (RTC Judgment):** The RTC rendered a Decision ordering Gan to:
1. Recognize Francheska Joy as his illegitimate child;
2. Pay regular monthly support of **₱20,000.00**, beginning April 15, 2000;
3. Pay accumulated arrears of **₱20,000.00 per month** from the date Francheska was born;
4. Pay ₱50,000.00 as attorney's fees and ₱25,000.00 for litigation expenses; and
5. Pay **₱20,000.00 per month** starting May 15, 2000 as alimony **pendente lite** should he pursue further remedies.
**Writ of Execution:** Private respondent moved for execution. The RTC granted the motion, citing the child's immediate need for schooling, and issued the writ.
**Levy:** Sheriff Albert Tolentino levied upon a Honda City sedan (Plate No. UMT 884) found in Gan's Caloocan City warehouse (later determined to be registered to A.B. Leasing & Fin. Corp. and leased to G & G Trading).
**Parallel Actions:**
Gan appealed the RTC Decision on the merits to the Court of Appeals.
On **June 9, 2000**, Gan simultaneously filed a Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition (Rule 65) with the CA, attacking the issuance of the writ of execution.
**August 31, 2000 (CA Decision):** The CA dismissed Gan’s Rule 65 petition, holding that under Rule 39, Section 4, support judgments are immediately executory and not stayed by appeal; that procedural technicalities regarding notice yielded to substantial justice; and that his excuse for the late answer was not excusable negligence.
**Supreme Court Petition:** After the CA denied his motion for reconsideration, Gan elevated the case to the Supreme Court.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's (Augustus Caezar R. Gan) Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The writ of execution was issued with grave abuse of discretion because judgments pending appeal cannot be executed without "good reasons," and the writ was issued without compliance with notice and hearing rules.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Requirement of Good Reasons:** Judgments for support that have not attained finality require extraordinary or good reasons before advance execution can issue.
**Denial of Due Process:** The writ was void because he received a copy of the motion for immediate execution two weeks **after** the scheduled hearing date.
**Meritorious Defense / Order of Default:** The judgment proceeded from an invalid default order. He should be allowed to present the defense of adultery against the child's mother to disprove paternity and disentitle the child to support.
**DNA Testing:** Petitioner offered to submit himself and the mother to Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) testing to resolve the paternity issue objectively.
B. Respondents' (Francheska Joy Pondevida, Judge Reyes, et al.) Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Under express procedural rules, judgments for support are immediately executory as an exception to the general rule on appeals, and procedural defects must yield to the paramount welfare of the child.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Rule 39, Section 4 Governs:** Support judgments are enforceable immediately upon rendition and are not stayed by the perfection of an appeal.
**Substantial Justice over Technicality:** Any delayed receipt of the motion for execution does not invalidate the writ, as child support addresses immediate and irreplaceable subsistence and schooling needs.
**Default and Dilatory Tactics:** Petitioner failed to answer for over 90 days without excusable negligence, surrendered a vehicle he did not own, and reneged on his formal undertaking to deposit support **pendente lite** with the CA.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether a judgment directing the payment of support is immediately executory pending appeal without the necessity of demonstrating independent "good reasons."
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether under the rules a judgment for support which is subject of an appeal cannot be executed absent any good reason for its immediate execution.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether an appealed judgment for child support is immediately executory under Rule 39, Section 4 without requiring a demonstration of "good reasons."
2. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether the writ of execution was rendered void due to the petitioner receiving notice of the motion for execution two weeks after the scheduled hearing.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether the writ of execution should be annulled on the ground that petitioner was not notified of its issuance prior to the hearing.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether the delayed receipt of a copy of the motion for immediate execution of a support judgment violates due process so as to invalidate the resulting writ of execution.
3. **[Substantive / Secondary Issue]** Whether the Supreme Court, in reviewing the validity of the writ of execution, should set aside the default order and pass upon petitioner's defense of adultery or his offer to submit to DNA testing.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** Whether the Supreme Court should dwell on petitioner's arguments concerning the validity of the judgment by default and his insistence to undergo DNA testing to settle paternity.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether the Court in a certiorari proceeding assailing execution may delve into the merits of the default order and substantive paternity defenses while the main case is pending appeal in the CA.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Immediate Execution of Support Judgments Pending Appeal
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO (to petitioner's contention) / YES (to immediate execution).** An appealed judgment for support is immediately executory upon rendition under Section 4, Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, and requires no independent showing of "good reasons."
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
**"Section 4, Rule 39, of the Rules of Court clearly states that, unless ordered by the trial court, judgments in actions for support are immediately executory and cannot be stayed by an appeal. This is an exception to the general rule which provides that the taking of an appeal stays the execution of the judgment and that advance executions will only be allowed if there are urgent reasons therefor. The aforesaid provision peremptorily calls for immediate execution of all judgments for support and makes no distinction between those which are the subject of an appeal and those which are not."**
**"Petitioner is reminded that to the plain words of a legal provision we should make no further explanation. Absoluta sententia expositore non indiget. Indeed, the interpretation which petitioner attempts to foist upon us would only lead to absurdity, its acceptance negating the plain meaning of the provision subject of the petition."**
**"The money and property adjudged for support and education should and must be given presently and without delay because if it had to wait the final judgment, the children may in the meantime have suffered because of lack of food or have missed and lost years in school because of lack of funds. One cannot delay the payment of such funds for support and education for the reason that if paid long afterwards, however much the accumulated amount, its payment cannot cure the evil and repair the damage caused." (Quoting De Leon v. Soriano, 95 Phil. 806)**
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Plain Meaning of Rule 39, Section 4:** The rule explicitly categorizes judgments in actions for support (alongside injunction, receivership, and accounting) as immediately executory and immune from being stayed by an appeal, unless the trial court orders otherwise.
**Distinction from Discretionary Execution:** Petitioner mistakenly conflated discretionary execution under Section 2, Rule 39 (which requires "good reasons") with Section 4, Rule 39. Section 4 provides a statutory mandate that applies automatically by operation of law without requiring distinct exceptional circumstances.
**Human and Social Rationale:** Support cannot await the ultimate finality of appellate review. Delaying basic support for food, shelter, and education inflicts irreparable harm; a child cannot later "eat voraciously" to compensate for years of starvation, nor attend multiple schools at once to make up for lost years of schooling.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** Under Rule 39, Section 4, child support judgments are an express exception to the rule that an appeal pauses execution. Because children need food and education daily, support judgments are immediately enforceable as soon as they are rendered, and a prevailing child does not have to prove "good reasons" to receive court-ordered support while the parent appeals.
Issue 2: Validity of Writ Despite Delayed Notice of Hearing
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** The writ of execution was not invalidated by the late delivery of the motion, as technical rules yield to substantial justice and the child's paramount welfare, especially where the debtor engaged in dilatory tactics.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
**"We are not intimating that in every case the right to notice of hearing can be disregarded. That is not so. It appears in this case that there has been too much temporizing in the execution of the writ which must not be allowed to thwart the constitutional mandate for speedy disposition of cases. As has been said, a technicality should be an aid to justice and not its great hindrance and chief enemy."**
**"Truly, if the writ of execution would be voided on this ground alone, then procedural rules which were primarily drafted to protect parties in the realm of constitutional guarantees would acquire a new sanctity at the expense of equity and justice."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Dilatory Conduct of Petitioner:** Petitioner repeatedly attempted to stall execution. He surrendered a car leased to a third-party corporation to feign compliance, and failed to deposit a single centavo with the CA despite filing a formal **Motion for Leave to Deposit in Court Support Pendente Lite**.
**Subordination of Form to Substance:** While notice of hearing is an essential safeguard, mechanical application of procedural rules cannot be used as an instrument of evasion to starve a minor dependent. Elevating strict notice rules above the child’s subsistence needs would pervert procedural safeguards into tools of injustice.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** While notice is generally mandatory, the Court will not nullify an execution order for child support on a technicality where the obligor has deliberately stalled proceedings and evaded payment. Procedural rules exist to promote justice, not to permit a parent to avoid supporting an infant child through procedural maneuvering.
Issue 3: Review of Default Judgment, Adultery Defense, and DNA Testing
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** The Supreme Court declined to address the default order, the defense of adultery, or the DNA testing demand, because doing so would impermissibly pre-empt the Court of Appeals' review of the pending main appeal.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
**"Lastly, we note that no useful purpose would be served if we dwell on petitioner's arguments concerning the validity of the judgment by default and his insistence that he be subjected, together with private respondent Bernadette C. Pondevida to DNA testing to settle the issue of paternity. The futility of his arguments is very apparent. It is not for us at this instance to review or revise the Decision rendered by the trial court for to do so would pre-empt the decision which may be rendered by the Court of Appeals in the main case for support."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Hierarchy of Review and Preemption:** The default order and the substantive determination of paternity are issues properly before the Court of Appeals in petitioner's ordinary appeal of the RTC Decision. Ruling on them within an interlocutory certiorari petition challenging the writ of execution would usurp the CA's appellate jurisdiction.
**Logical Incoherence of the Adultery Defense:** The Court parenthetically noted the absurdity of petitioner raising "adultery" as a defense, given that petitioner and the mother were never married to each other.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:** In a petition questioning only the writ of execution, the Supreme Court will not rule on the merits of the trial court’s default order or examine paternity defenses (like adultery or DNA testing). Those substantive issues belong strictly to the main appeal pending before the Court of Appeals.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
**"WHEREFORE, finding no reversible error in the Decision sought to be reviewed, the instant petition is DENIED. The 31 August 2000 Decision of the Court of Appeals dismissing the Petition for Certiorari instituted by petitioner Augustus Caezar C. Gan and upholding the validity of the 2 June 2000 Writ of Execution issued by the Regional Trial Court – Br. 61, Baguio City, in Civil Case No. 4234-R, is AFFIRMED. Costs against petitioner.**
**SO ORDERED."**
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Augustus Caezar R. Gan lost the petition. The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals, sustaining the validity of the RTC's writ of execution. The monthly child support and arrears ordered by the trial court in favor of minor Francheska Joy Pondevida remain immediately enforceable against Gan despite his pending appeal. Costs were assessed against him.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Spouses Lim v. Cheryl Lim**
**Full Official Caption: Spouses Prudencio and Filomena Lim, Petitioners, vs. Ma. Cheryl S. Lim, for herself and on behalf of her minor children Lester Edward S. Lim, Candice Grace S. Lim, and Mariano S. Lim, III, Respondents.**
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 163209
**Promulgation Date:** October 30, 2009
**Philippine Reports Citation:** 619 Phil. 694
**Ponente:** Carpio, **J.**
**Division / Voting Breakdown:** Third Division; Quisumbing, Chico-Nazario, Peralta, and Abad, **JJ.**, concurred. (No separate opinions).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Civil Law → Family Code (Executive Order No. 209) → Title VIII: Support → Order of Support & Ascendant’s Concurrent Liability (Articles 195 & 199)
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Civil Law → Family Code → Title VIII: Support → Options in Fulfilling Support & Moral Obstacles (Article 204)
**Full Text of Governing Statutory Provisions:**
**Article 195, Family Code:**
"Subject to the provisions of the succeeding articles, the following are obliged to support each other to the whole extent set forth in the preceding article:
(1) The spouses;
(2) **Legitimate ascendants and descendants;**
(3) Parents and their legitimate children and the legitimate and illegitimate children of the latter;
(4) Parents and their illegitimate children and the legitimate and illegitimate children of the latter; and
(5) Legitimate brothers and sisters, whether of the full or half-blood."
**Article 199, Family Code:**
"Whenever two or more persons are obliged to give support, the liability shall devolve upon the following persons in the order herein provided:
(1) The spouse;
(2) The descendants in the nearest degree;
(3) **The ascendants in the nearest degree;** and
(4) The brothers and sisters."
**Article 204, Family Code:**
"The person obliged to give support shall have the option to fulfill the obligation either by paying the allowance fixed, or by receiving and maintaining in the family dwelling the person who has a right to receive support. **The latter alternative cannot be availed of in case there is a moral or legal obstacle thereto.**"
**The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision:**
**General Rule on Ascendant Support (Arts. 195 & 199):** The statutory obligation of ascendants (grandparents) to provide support to descendants (grandchildren) is subsidiary to the parents' duty. However, when the parents (ascendants in the nearest degree) are incapable of providing **sufficient** support to meet the children's basic needs, a concurrent, partial liability directly shifts down the hierarchy of Article 199 to the grandparents.
**Limitation to Direct Descendants:** The ascendants’ concurrent liability extends **only** to their blood descendants (grandchildren). It does not extend to an in-law (daughter-in-law), whose right to support arises solely from the marital bond with her husband.
**Exception to Alternative Option under Article 204:** An obligor's statutory option to fulfill support by maintaining the obligee in the family dwelling is unavailable if there exists a **moral or legal obstacle**. A spouse/parent’s steadfast insistence on past spousal infidelity within that dwelling constitutes a sufficient moral impediment precluding forced cohabitation.
**Factual Trigger (Application to the Story):** The father (Edward) earned only ₱6,000.00 per month, while the mother (Cheryl) had no steady income, rendering them incapable of sufficiently supporting their three minor school-bound children whose adjudged monthly needs totaled ₱40,000.00. This inability triggered the concurrent liability of the paternal grandparents (Spouses Prudencio and Filomena Lim) under Article 199, but their attempt to satisfy it by bringing the family back into their residence failed because Cheryl caught Edward committing adultery in that exact house.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Spouses Prudencio and Filomena Lim (Petitioners):** Paternal grandparents of the minor respondents; parents of Edward Lim.
**Ma. Cheryl S. Lim (Respondent Cheryl):** Wife of Edward Lim; mother of the three minor children.
**Lester Edward, Candice Grace, and Mariano III, all surnamed Lim (Minor Respondents):** Legitimate children of Cheryl and Edward; grandchildren of petitioners.
**Edward Lim (Edward):** Cheryl's husband and father of the children; son of petitioners; earning ₱6,000.00 monthly from the family business.
**Chua Giak & Mariano Lim:** Edward's ailing grandmother and her husband, who originally resided with the family in Forbes Park.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, assailing the April 28, 2003 Decision and April 12, 2004 Resolution of the Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. CV No. 54406), which affirmed the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Makati City, Branch 140.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**1979:** Cheryl married Edward Lim. They bore three children: Lester Edward, Candice Grace, and Mariano III. The family lived in the home of Edward’s parents (petitioners) in Forbes Park, Makati City, together with Edward’s ailing grandmother, Chua Giak, and her husband Mariano Lim. Family expenses were paid by the family business, which gave Edward a monthly salary of ₱6,000.00. Cheryl had no steady income.
**October 14, 1990:** Cheryl abandoned the Forbes Park home, taking her minor children, after catching Edward in a "very compromising situation" with Chua Giak’s in-house midwife. Cheryl subsequently filed criminal charges against Edward for concubinage, physical injuries, and grave threats (which the investigating prosecutor later dismissed). Edward filed an action for declaration of nullity of marriage (Civil Case No. 99-1852).
**Complaint for Support (RTC Makati, Branch 140):** Cheryl, for herself and the children, sued Edward, petitioners, Chua Giak, and Mariano for support.
**June 28, 1991:** The trial court ordered Edward to provide monthly support **pendente lite** of ₱6,000.00.
**January 31, 1996 (RTC Decision):** The trial court ordered Edward and petitioners to "jointly" provide ₱40,000.00 monthly support to Cheryl and the children—₱6,000.00 from Edward and ₱34,000.00 from petitioners (with Chua Giak subsidiarily liable).
**Order on Reconsideration (RTC):** The trial court denied petitioners' motion for reconsideration but amended the dispositive portion, clarifying that petitioners were liable for ₱34,000.00 because of Edward’s "inability... to give sufficient support."
**April 28, 2003 (CA Decision):** The Court of Appeals affirmed the RTC, invoking Article 195 and Article 200, paragraph 3 of the Family Code.
**April 12, 2004:** The CA denied petitioners' motion for reconsideration. Petitioners filed a Rule 45 petition before the Supreme Court.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Petitioners (grandparents) are not concurrently liable to provide legal support to respondents because the primary duty belongs to the parents, whose parental authority has neither been suspended nor terminated; alternatively, if liable, they should be permitted to maintain respondents in their Forbes Park residence under Article 204.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Title IX (Parental Authority) Governs:** Under Title IX of the Family Code (specifically Articles 214 and 216), ascendants' liability to support is activated only upon default, termination, or suspension of parental authority. Because Edward and Cheryl both exercised parental authority over the children when the suit was filed, the obligation remained exclusively with them.
**Standard of Financial Capacity:** While Edward’s income is insufficient, the law itself accommodates this under Article 194 by stating that support is conditioned on "the financial capacity of the family."
**Article 204 Alternative Option:** Under Article 204 of the Family Code, petitioners are entitled to fulfill any support obligation by receiving and maintaining respondents at their Makati residence.
B. Respondent's Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The grandparents are liable under the Family Code to provide necessary support because the father’s means are grossly insufficient to support the children.
**Specific Contentions:**
**Applicability of Order of Support:** Under Articles 195 and 199 of the Family Code, the duty to support extends to ascendants when the relatives of the nearest degree (the parents) are unable to satisfy the claims for support.
**(Defense to Article 204 alternative option not expressly stated as formal brief arguments in the decision, but sustained by Cheryl’s factual refusal to return to the scene of marital infidelity).**
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1.  **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether petitioners (grandparents) are concurrently liable with the father (Edward) to provide legal support to respondents.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not grandparents can be held concurrently liable to support their grandchildren when the parents are unable to provide sufficient support, despite the fact that parental authority has not been suspended or terminated.
2.  **[Secondary Issue]** Whether petitioners can fulfill their obligation by exercising the alternative option under Article 204 of the Family Code to maintain respondents in their family residence.
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not grandparents ordered to pay support can invoke the Article 204 option to house their daughter-in-law and grandchildren in the family dwelling despite the wife's moral objection arising from her husband's prior infidelity in that home.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Grandparents' Concurrent Liability for Support and its Scope
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: PARTIALLY MERITORIOUS.** Petitioners are concurrently liable to support their **grandchildren**, but **not** their daughter-in-law (Cheryl).
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"Neither the text of the law nor the teaching of jurisprudence supports this severe constriction of the scope of familial obligation to give support. In the first place, the governing text are the relevant provisions in Title VIII of the Civil Code, as amended, on Support, not the provisions in Title IX on Parental Authority."
"Also, while parental authority under Title IX (and the correlative parental rights) pertains to parents, passing to ascendants only upon its termination or suspension, the obligation to provide legal support passes on to ascendants not only upon default of the parents but also for the latters inability to provide sufficient support."
"This inability of Edward and Cheryl to sufficiently provide for their children shifts a portion of their obligation to the ascendants in the nearest degree, both in the paternal (petitioners) and maternal lines, following the ordering in Article 199. To hold otherwise, and thus subscribe to petitioners' theory, is to sanction the anomalous scenario of tolerating extreme material deprivation of children because of parental inability to give adequate support even if ascendants one degree removed are more than able to fill the void."
"However, petitioners' partial concurrent obligation extends only to their **descendants** as this word is commonly understood to refer to relatives by blood of lower degree. As petitioners' grandchildren by blood, only respondents Lester Edward, Candice Grace and Mariano III belong to this category. Indeed, Cheryl's right to receive support from the Lim family extends only to her husband Edward, arising from their marital bond."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Title VIII (Support) Controls Over Title IX (Parental Authority):** Petitioners conflated parental authority with the duty of support. While parental authority terminates upon emancipation, the general familial obligation to support can last throughout the obligee’s lifetime. Parental rights transfer to ascendants only upon suspension or termination of parental authority, but the legal **obligation to support** shifts to ascendants under Article 199 not only upon total default, but also upon the parents' **inability to provide sufficient support**.
**Application to the Facts:** The mother (Cheryl) had no steady income, and the father (Edward) earned only ₱6,000.00 per month, which was undeniably insufficient to support three school-bound children. This inadequacy triggered the concurrent liability of the paternal ascendants (petitioners) to shoulder the deficiency up to the required level.
**Daughter-in-Law Excluded:** The term "descendants" in Article 199(2) applies strictly to blood relatives of a lower degree. Cheryl is an in-law, not a blood descendant. Her right to support is enforceable exclusively against her husband (Edward) by virtue of their marriage; in-laws are legal strangers to the mutual obligation of support between spouses.
**Remand for Apportionment:** Because the trial court awarded a lump sum of ₱40,000.00 without segregating Cheryl's individual share from that of the three children, the case had to be remanded to the RTC to compute the exact portion allocated solely to the grandchildren.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):** Grandparents cannot escape the duty to support their grandchildren by claiming that the parents still have parental authority. The obligation to provide support is governed by the rules on Support (Title VIII), not Parental Authority (Title IX); thus, whenever parents cannot earn enough to meet their children's basic living and schooling needs, the law automatically requires capable grandparents to step in and cover the deficit. However, grandparents are only obligated to support blood descendants, meaning they cannot be forced to pay for the living expenses of their daughter-in-law.
Issue 2: Availability of the Alternative Option under Article 204
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** Petitioners cannot invoke the Article 204 alternative option to maintain the obligees in their Forbes Park home because a moral obstacle exists.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncement:**
"The application of Article 204 which provides that —
'The person obliged to give support shall have the option to fulfill the obligation either by paying the allowance fixed, or by receiving and maintaining in the family dwelling the person who has a right to receive support. **The latter alternative cannot be availed of in case there is a moral or legal obstacle thereto.**'
is subject to its exception clause. Here, the persons entitled to receive support are petitioners' grandchildren and daughter-in-law. Granting petitioners the option in Article 204 will secure to the grandchildren a well-provided future; however, it will also force Cheryl to return to the house which, for her, is the scene of her husband's infidelity. While not rising to the level of a **legal** obstacle, as indeed, Cheryl's charge against Edward for concubinage did not prosper for insufficient evidence, her steadfast insistence on its occurrence amounts to a **moral** impediment bringing the case within the ambit of the exception clause of Article 204, precluding its application."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Application of Article 204 Exception Clause:** While Article 204 grants the obligor the choice to either pay an allowance or maintain the obligee in the family dwelling, this choice is expressly withheld when there is a legal or moral obstacle.
**Presence of a Moral Impediment:** Compelling the grandchildren to live in the Forbes Park home would necessarily force their mother, Cheryl, to reside in the very house where she discovered her husband's infidelity. Even though her criminal concubinage complaint was dismissed by the prosecutor for insufficiency of evidence, her steadfast insistence on the occurrence of the marital betrayal created an untenable domestic environment that constitutes a valid **moral impediment**.
**(d) (Plain-Language Explanation):** Although an obligor normally has the right under Article 204 to fulfill support by housing the dependent rather than paying cash, this right disappears when a moral or legal obstacle exists. Forcing the mother to move back into the house where she caught her husband in a compromising situation with the in-house midwife is a clear moral obstacle, meaning the grandparents must pay the monthly cash allowance instead.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
"No separate opinions discussed in the provided text."
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, we DENY the petition. We AFFIRM the Decision of the Court of Appeals, dated 28 April 2003, and its Resolution dated 12 April 2004 with the MODIFICATION that petitioners Prudencio and Filomena Lim are liable to provide support only to respondents Lester Edward, Candice Grace and Mariano III, all surnamed Lim. We REMAND the case to the Regional Trial Court of Makati City, Branch 140, for further proceedings consistent with this ruling.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court affirmed the liability of the paternal grandparents (Spouses Lim) to provide financial support to their minor grandchildren due to the parents' inability to sufficiently do so, and denied their request to house them in lieu of payment. However, the Court modified the judgment by totally relieving the grandparents from supporting their daughter-in-law (Cheryl) and remanded the case to the RTC to calculate and deduct Cheryl’s individual share from the monthly support award.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Lim-Lua v. Lua**
**Full Official Caption:** Susan Lim-Lua, Petitioner, vs. Danilo Y. Lua, Respondent
**Citation & Metadata:**
**Docket Nos.:** G.R. Nos. 175279–80
**Date of Promulgation:** June 5, 2013
**Philippine Reports:** 710 Phil. 211
**Ponente:** Villarama, Jr., **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** First Division; Sereno, **C.J.** (Chairperson), Leonardo-De Castro, Bersamin, and Reyes, **JJ.**, concur (Unanimous).
### 2. Syllabus Topic Grouping, Codal Provision, & Rule Matrix
Topic Hierarchy
**Primary Topic Hierarchy:** Civil Law → Family Code → Title VIII: Support → Support **Pendente Lite** → Crediting/Deduction of Direct Expenses Against Support Arrears
**Secondary Topic Hierarchy:** Remedial Law → Special Civil Actions → Rule 71: Contempt → Indirect Contempt (Non-compliance with Support Orders)
Full Text of Governing Provisions
**Article 194, Family Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 194. Support comprises **everything indispensable for sustenance, dwelling, clothing, medical attendance, education and transportation**, in keeping with the financial capacity of the family.
The education of the person entitled to be supported referred to in the preceding paragraph shall include his schooling or training for some profession, trade or vocation, even beyond the age of majority. Transportation shall include expenses in going to and from school, or to and from place of work."
**Articles 201 and 203, Family Code of the Philippines:**
"Art. 201. The amount of support, in the cases referred to in Articles 195 and 196, shall be in proportion to the **resources or means of the giver and to the necessities of the recipient**."
"Art. 203. The obligation to give support shall be **demandable from the time the person who has a right to receive the same needs it for maintenance, but it shall not be paid except from the date of judicial or extrajudicial demand**.
Payment shall be made within the first five days of each corresponding month or when the recipient dies, his heirs shall not be obligated to return that which he had received in advance."
**Sections 2 and 3, Rule on Provisional Orders (A.M. No. 02-11-12-SC):**
"Sec. 2. **Spousal Support.**–In determining support for the spouses, the court may be guided by the following rules:
(a) In the absence of adequate provisions in a written agreement between the spouses, the spouses may be supported from the properties of the absolute community or the conjugal partnership.
(b) The court may award support to either spouse in such amount and for such period of time as the court may deem just and reasonable based on their standard of living during the marriage.
(c) The court may likewise consider the following factors: (1) whether the spouse seeking support is the custodian of a child whose circumstances make it appropriate for that spouse not to seek outside employment; (2) the time necessary to acquire sufficient education and training to enable the spouse seeking support to find appropriate employment, and that spouse’s future earning capacity; (3) the duration of the marriage; (4) the comparative financial resources of the spouses, including their comparative earning abilities in the labor market; (5) the needs and obligations of each spouse; (6) the contribution of each spouse to the marriage, including services rendered in home-making, child care, education, and career building of the other spouse; (7) the age and health of the spouses; (8) the physical and emotional conditions of the spouses; (9) the ability of the supporting spouse to give support, taking into account that spouse’s earning capacity, earned and unearned income, assets, and standard of living; and (10) any other factor the court may deem just and equitable.
(d) The Family Court may direct the deduction of the provisional support from the salary of the spouse.
Sec. 3. **Child Support.**– The common children of the spouses shall be supported from the properties of the absolute community or the conjugal partnership.
Subject to the sound discretion of the court, either parent or both may be ordered to give an amount necessary for the support, maintenance, and education of the child. It shall be in proportion to the resources or means of the giver and to the necessities of the recipient.
In determining the amount of provisional support, the court may likewise consider the following factors: (1) the financial resources of the custodial and non-custodial parent and those of the child; (2) the physical and emotional health of the child and his or her special needs and aptitudes; (3) the standard of living the child has been accustomed to; (4) the non-monetary contributions that the parents will make toward the care and well-being of the child.
The Family Court may direct the deduction of the provisional support from the salary of the parent."
The Controlling Rule & Sub-Rules Mapped to the Provision
1. **General Rule on Support Pendente Lite Arrears:** A spouse ordered to pay support **pendente lite** must remit the fixed periodic amount directly to the recipient/custodial spouse. Voluntarily procured items or unilateral monetary advances directly to the children cannot be offset or dictated by the obligor as satisfaction of court-ordered support.
2. **Equitable Exception for Offsetting/Deductions:** Direct expenses and advances voluntarily paid by the supporting spouse may only be credited against accrued support **pendente lite** arrears under "special considerations of an equitable nature... when that can be done without injustice to [the payee-spouse]," and **strictly limited to expenses covering basic needs and sustenance** (e.g., medical, dental, groceries, and dry goods/clothing) that the decree intended to cover. Luxury items, automobiles, vehicle maintenance, and leisure travel bear no relation to the decree and cannot be deducted.
3. **Indirect Contempt Test:** Indirect contempt requires a willful disregard, disobedience, or defiance of a lawful court order done for an illegitimate or improper purpose. Where an obligor's non-payment or deferral is anchored on a good-faith belief that he was entitled to an equitable offset of substantial provisions already lavished directly on the family, contumacious intent is negated.
Factual Trigger
After being ordered to pay accrued monthly support **pendente lite** under an executory judgment, the husband unilaterally deducted **₱3,428,813.80**—representing the costs of two luxury automobiles, car maintenance, travel expenses, and personal cash advances given directly to their children—wiping out the wife's accrued spousal support and leaving a nominal cash balance of only ₱162,651.90. This triggered disputes over what expenditures are legally deductible from support arrears and whether the husband's non-remittance constituted indirect contempt.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Susan Lim-Lua:** Petitioner; full-time housewife suffering from scoliosis and eye problems; plaintiff in the nullity of marriage case seeking spousal and child support **pendente lite**.
**Danilo Y. Lua:** Respondent; wealthy businessman husband of Susan; father of their two common children (Angelli Suzanne and Daniel Ryan); obligor of support **pendente lite**.
**Angelli Suzanne Lua & Daniel Ryan Lua:** The adult/common children of Susan and Danilo who received substantial direct gifts, cars, and credit card privileges from Danilo.
**Judge Raphael B. Yrastorza, Sr.:** Presiding Judge, Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Cebu City, Branch 14.
**How the Case Reached the Supreme Court:**
Petition for Review on Certiorari under **Rule 45** of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure, assailing the CA Decision dated April 20, 2006 and Resolution dated October 26, 2006 in consolidated cases CA-G.R. SP No. 01154 and CA-G.R. SP No. 01315.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
**September 3, 2003:** Susan Lim-Lua filed a complaint for declaration of nullity of marriage against Danilo Y. Lua (Civil Case No. CEB-29346, RTC Cebu City, Branch 14), with an application for support **pendente lite** of **₱500,000.00/month** for herself and two children, citing Danilo's substantial earnings.
**March 31, 2004:** RTC Cebu City (Branch 14) granted support **pendente lite**, ordering Danilo to pay **₱250,000.00/month** effective April 2004, plus **₱1,750,000.00** as retroactive support (7 months from September 2003 to March 2004), **excluding** ₱135,000.00 for Susan's required eye operations.
**May 13, 2004:** RTC declared the March 31, 2004 Order final and executory, striking Danilo’s motion for reconsideration as a mere scrap of paper for violating the 3-day notice rule (Rule 15, Sec. 4) and ordered him to show cause why he should not be held in contempt. Danilo's second motion for reconsideration was denied.
**April 12, 2005:** Acting on Danilo's Rule 65 petition (**CA-G.R. SP No. 84740**), the CA nullified the RTC orders, reducing monthly support **pendente lite** to **₱115,000.00** beginning April 2005, and ordered Danilo to pay arrears from September 2003 to March 2005 at ₱115,000.00/month, **"less than the amount supposedly given by petitioner to the private respondent as her and their two (2) children monthly support."** Neither party appealed; this judgment became **final and executory**.
**June 28, 2005:** Danilo filed a "Compliance" in the RTC attaching a check for **₱162,651.90**. He computed total support due (September 2003 to July 2005) at ₱2,645,000.00, but unilaterally deducted **₱2,482,348.16** for:
Two car purchases (Volkswagen Beetle for Angelli [₱1,350,000.00] and BMW 316i for Daniel Ryan [₱613,472.86]);
Car maintenance (Angelli: ₱51,232.50; Daniel: ₱118,960.52);
Credit card purchases by Daniel Ryan (₱348,682.28).
**September 27, 2005:** The RTC rejected Danilo's unilateral deductions and granted Susan’s motion for a writ of execution for the full support in arrears.
**November 25, 2005:** RTC denied Danilo’s motion for reconsideration (and his motion for inhibition), holding that a second motion for reconsideration was prohibited, and ordered execution for accumulated arrears.
**Subsequent CA Proceedings:**
Susan filed a **Petition for Contempt of Court with Damages** (**CA-G.R. SP No. 01154**).
Danilo filed a **Petition for Certiorari** (**CA-G.R. SP No. 01315**) challenging the RTC's refusal to allow deductions, asserting an additional **₱946,465.64** in advances (grand total: **₱3,428,813.80**).
**April 20, 2006:** The CA consolidated both cases and rendered judgment:
1. Dismissing Susan’s contempt petition (CA-G.R. SP No. 01154);
2. Granting Danilo’s certiorari petition (CA-G.R. SP No. 01315);
3. Authorizing the full deduction of **₱3,428,813.80** from support arrears;
4. Directing Danilo to resume paying ₱115,000.00/month starting from the time payment was deferred, subject to said deductions; and
5. Issuing a permanent writ of preliminary injunction against the RTC orders.
**October 26, 2006:** CA denied Susan’s motion for reconsideration. Susan elevated the matter to the Supreme Court.
### 5. Exhaustive Party Arguments Matrix
A. Petitioner's (Susan Lim-Lua) Arguments
**Main Thesis:** The CA gravely erred in failing to hold Danilo in indirect contempt for deliberately refusing to pay executory support, and in permitting the deduction of luxury cars and unrelated advances totaling ₱3,428,813.80 from accrued support arrears.
**Specific Contentions:**
The purchase prices and maintenance of the two cars (Volkswagen Beetle and BMW 316i) are not indispensable for sustenance or in keeping the family alive under Article 194 of the Family Code.
In the final April 12, 2005 decision in CA-G.R. SP No. 84740, the CA had already taken into account the fact that Danilo provided cars and credit cards when it fixed monthly support **pendente lite** at ₱115,000.00. That base amount was specifically calculated for household maintenance and miscellaneous food/needs, **excluding** her ₱135,000.00 eye operation.
Crediting Danilo's unilateral gifts completely deprives her of spousal maintenance and leaves her without funds for medical therapy and sustenance.
Danilo's defiance of the executory support orders was willful, malicious, and contumacious.
B. Respondent's (Danilo Y. Lua) Arguments
**Main Thesis:** Disallowing the deductions would constitute unjust enrichment and compel him to pay twice; his temporary suspension of payments was done in good faith pending judicial clarification.
**Specific Contentions:**
Since Susan and the children shared the same residence, groceries and dry goods bought by the children on his credit cards (₱594,151.58) benefited Susan directly.
As upper-class individuals who never commuted or ate at **carinderias**, personal vehicles (and their upkeep) were indispensable to the children's day-to-day living, education, and transportation in accordance with the family's social standing under Article 194.
The dispositive portion of the April 12, 2005 CA decision explicitly commanded the deduction of amounts given to the children and wife as monthly support.
Susan maintained a boutique in Ayala Center Cebu and a money-lending business, and thus failed to contribute her share to child support, while the children had since finished school and earned salaries.
He acted without contumacious intent, having faithfully provided substantial financial support and seeking only a definitive judicial resolution on allowable offsets.
### 6. Complete Inventory of Issues Found by the Supreme Court
1. **[PRIMARY SYLLABUS ISSUE]** Whether or not expenses already incurred by the respondent—specifically the purchase price and maintenance of two luxury vehicles, travel expenses, and personal cash advances to the children—may be deducted from the total support **pendente lite** in arrears owing to petitioner and the children.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** "The main issue is whether certain expenses already incurred by the respondent may be deducted from the total support in arrears owing to petitioner and her children pursuant to the Decision dated April 12, 2005 in CA-G.R. SP No. 84740."
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not a husband obligated to pay court-ordered support **pendente lite** may credit the cost of luxury vehicles, car maintenance, travel expenses, and direct cash advances to his children against his accrued support arrears.
2. **[Procedural / Secondary Issue]** Whether or not respondent Danilo Y. Lua is guilty of indirect contempt of court for deferring or refusing to pay the support **pendente lite** in arrears.
**Faithful Court Phrasing:** "THE HONORABLE COURT ERRED IN NOT FINDING RESPONDENT GUILTY OF INDIRECT CONTEMPT."
**Recitation-Ready Question:** Whether or not an obligor's non-remittance of support **pendente lite** constitutes indirect contempt when anchored on a good-faith belief that he was legally entitled to offset direct expenditures incurred for the family.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Deductions from Support **Pendente Lite** in Arrears
**(a) Short Answer: PARTIALLY MERITORIOUS.** The Supreme Court held that only basic sustenance and medical/dental expenses totaling **₱648,102.29** may be deducted from the support arrears; the costs of two luxury automobiles, car upkeep, leisure travel, and personal cash advances cannot be credited.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"In the absence of some finding of consent by the mother, most courts refuse to allow a husband to dictate how he will meet the requirements for support payments when the mode of payment is fixed by a decree of court. Thus he will not be credited for payments made when he unnecessarily interposed himself as a volunteer and made payments direct to the children of his own accord." **(Quoting Bradford v. Futrell, 225 Md. 512, citing Openshaw v. Openshaw)**
"The general rule is to the effect that when a father is required by a divorce decree to pay to the mother money for the support of their dependent children and the unpaid and accrued installments become judgments in her favor, he cannot, as a matter of law, claim credit on account of payments voluntarily made directly to the children... However, special considerations of an equitable nature may justify a court in crediting such payments on his indebtedness to the mother, when that can be done without injustice to her." **(Quoting Martin, Jr. v. Martin, 59 Wn.2d 468)**
"Here, the CA should not have allowed all the expenses incurred by respondent to be credited against the accrued support pendente lite. As earlier mentioned, the monthly support pendente lite granted by the trial court was intended primarily for food, household expenses such as salaries of drivers and house helpers, and also petitioner’s scoliosis therapy sessions. Hence, the value of two expensive cars bought by respondent for his children plus their maintenance cost, travel expenses of petitioner and Angelli, purchases through credit card of items other than groceries and dry goods (clothing) should have been disallowed, as these bear no relation to the judgment awarding support pendente lite."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
**Nature and Scope of the Decree:** Support **pendente lite** is provisional and fixed according to the resources of the giver and the necessities of the recipient (Arts. 194, 201, Family Code; Rule on Provisional Orders). The final CA Decision in CA-G.R. SP No. 84740 fixed monthly support at ₱115,000.00 specifically to cover daily sustenance, household help, drivers, and scoliosis therapy.
**Disallowance of Luxury/Independent Expenditures:** The appellate court erred in treating all voluntary paternal expenditures as deductible advances. The ₱1.96M spent buying a Volkswagen Beetle and BMW 316i, along with subsequent repair bills, leisure travel, and pocket money, bore zero relation to the purpose of the court decree. Allowing an obligor father to volunteer such gifts and then offset them against support would allow him to dictate the terms of the decree and usurp the custodial mother's management of family allowances.
**Protection of Spousal Support:** The husband had completely ignored spousal support. Deducting millions in gifts made to the children wiped out the funds explicitly earmarked for the wife’s sustenance and medical treatments, resulting in manifest injustice.
**Authorized Equitable Offsets:** Under equitable principles, credits are permitted only for items that genuinely satisfied the basic living necessities contemplated by the judgment. Consequently, the Supreme Court recomputed and allowed **only** the following deductions:
1. Medical expenses of Susan Lim-Lua: ₱42,450.71
2. Dental expenses of Daniel Ryan: ₱11,500.00
3. Credit card purchases of Angelli (Groceries and Dry Goods): ₱365,282.20
4. Credit card purchases of Daniel Ryan (Groceries and Dry Goods): ₱228,869.38
**Total Permissible Deductions: ₱648,102.29** (disallowing the remaining ₱2,780,711.51 of Danilo's claimed ₱3,428,813.80).
**Forum for Modification:** Allegations that Susan now operates commercial boutiques or that the adult children are now gainfully employed cannot be resolved on certiorari before the Supreme Court. Decrees of support never become final and are subject to future modification upon proof of altered needs and capacities submitted directly to the trial court (**Advincula v. Advincula**).
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** A spouse ordered by a court to pay monthly support cannot unilaterally buy luxury cars or give extravagant gifts directly to the children and then deduct those costs from the back support he owes his wife. Support is meant for basic food, shelter, and medical needs under the managing spouse's household budget. Permitting an obligor to credit luxury gifts against his support arrears would let him control the family's finances in defiance of the court order and starve the wife of her legal maintenance. Only genuine expenses for basic necessities (such as groceries, medicine, and dental care) can be equitably deducted.
Issue 2: Indirect Contempt
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Danilo Y. Lua is not guilty of indirect contempt, as his deferral of cash payments was made under a good-faith belief that he was entitled to an equitable offset and was devoid of contumacious intent.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Contempt of court is defined as a disobedience to the court by acting in opposition to its authority, justice, and dignity. It signifies not only a willful disregard or disobedience of the court’s order, but such conduct which tends to bring the authority of the court and the administration of law into disrepute or, in some manner, to impede the due administration of justice."
"To constitute contempt, the act must be done willfully and for an illegitimate or improper purpose. The good faith, or lack of it, of the alleged contemnor should be considered."
**(c) Step-by-Step Ratio Decidendi:**
While support **pendente lite** is immediately executory and Danilo suspended direct payments, the presence of willful defiance for an improper purpose was absent.
Danilo had consistently lavished financial support upon his children, paying for their complete education and living needs well beyond basic standards.
His failure to remit the full cash balance arose from an honest, good-faith reliance on the wording of the executory CA decision in CA-G.R. SP No. 84740 (which directed payment of arrears **less** amounts given to the wife and children). Seeking judicial clarification on the deductible amounts was not contumacious.
**(d) Plain-Language Explanation:** For a party to be held in indirect contempt, there must be a willful, bad-faith intent to defy the authority of the court. Danilo did not abandon his family—he continually spent massive sums directly on their education and needs, and genuinely believed the previous court ruling allowed him to credit those expenses against the arrears. Because he acted in good faith seeking legal clarification, he cannot be punished for contempt.
8. Separate Opinions Summary
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.** (The decision was unanimous, with Sereno, **C.J.**, Leonardo-De Castro, Bersamin, and Reyes, **JJ.**, concurring with the Ponente, Villarama, Jr., **J.**).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
Verbatim Fallo
"WHEREFORE, the petition is PARTLY GRANTED. The Decision dated April 20, 2006 of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP Nos. 01154 and 01315 is hereby MODIFIED to read as follows:
'WHEREFORE, judgment is hereby rendered:
a) DISMISSING, for lack of merit, the case of Petition for Contempt of Court with Damages filed by Susan Lim Lua against Danilo Y. Lua with docket no. SP. CA-G.R. No. 01154;
b) GRANTING IN PART Danilo Y. Lua’s Petition for Certiorari docketed as SP. CA-G.R. No. 01315. Consequently, the assailed Orders dated 27 September 2005 and 25 November 2005 of the Regional Trial Court, Branch 14, Cebu City issued in Civil Case No. CEB-29346 entitled "Susan Lim Lua versus Danilo Y. Lua," are hereby NULLIFIED and SET ASIDE, and instead a new one is entered:
ORDERING the deduction of the amount of Php 648,102.29 from the support pendente lite in arrears of Danilo Y. Lua to his wife, Susan Lim Lua and their two (2) children;
ORDERING Danilo Y. Lua to resume payment of his monthly support of PhP115,000.00 pesos starting from the time payment of this amount was deferred by him subject to the deduction aforementioned.
DIRECTING the immediate execution of this judgment.
SO ORDERED.'
No pronouncement as to costs.
SO ORDERED."
Plain-Language Outcome
Susan Lim-Lua partially prevailed. The Supreme Court affirmed the dismissal of the indirect contempt charge against Danilo, but radically reduced his allowable deductions from support arrears from **₱3,428,813.80** down to **₱648,102.29** (disallowing the cost of the two vehicles, repairs, and pocket money). Danilo was ordered to immediately pay the remaining balance of the accrued support **pendente lite** and resume paying the ₱115,000.00 monthly support without further delay.
