**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether Tan can be considered a Philippine citizen qualified to register as a voter on October 26, 2009, when she took the Oath of Allegiance only on November 30, 2009.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Retroactivity of R.A. No. 9225 and Meaning of "Reacquire" vs. "Retain"
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Section 2 and Section 3 of R.A. No. 9225 do not operate retroactively; a natural-born Filipino who naturalized abroad prior to the Act only reacquires Philippine citizenship from the exact moment they take the statutory Oath of Allegiance, leaving any intervening acts undertaken as an alien legally defective.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**On Plain Meaning / Verba Legis:**
"The plain meaning rule or **verba legis** is the most basic of all statutory construction principles. When the words or language of a statute is clear, there may be no need to interpret it in a manner different from what the word plainly implies. This rule is premised on the presumption that the legislature know the meaning of the words, to have used words advisedly, and to have expressed its intent by use of such words as are found in the statute."
**On the Whole Act Rule (Harmonious Holistic Construction):**
"The law must not be read in truncated parts; its provisions must be read in relation to the whole law. It is a cardinal rule in statutory construction that a statute's clauses and phrases must not be taken as detached and isolated expressions, but the whole and every part thereof must be considered in fixing the meaning of any of its parts in order to produce a harmonious whole. Every part of the statute must be interpreted with reference to the context, **i.e.**, that every part of the statute must be considered together with other parts of the statute and kept subservient to the general intent of the whole enactment."
**On Judicial Legislation:**
"To go beyond what the law says and interpret it in its ordinary and plain meaning would be tantamount to judicial legislation."
**On the Presumption Against Retroactivity:**
"Finally, it is a well-settled rule that statutes are to be construed as having only a prospective operation, unless the legislature intended to give them a retroactive effect. We must bear in mind that a law is a rule established to guide our actions without no binding effect until it is enacted. It has no application to past times but only to future time, and that is why it is said that the law looks to the future only and has no retroactive effect unless the legislator may have formally given that effect to some legal provisions."
**On the Presumption Against Absurdity:**
"Moreover, to consider that the reacquisition of Philippine citizenship retroacts to the date it was lost would result in an absurd scenario where a Filipino would still be considered a Philippine citizen when in fact he had already renounced his citizenship. We are not about to give a statute a meaning that would lead to absurdity as it is our duty to construe statutes in such a way to avoid such consequences."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court found the language of R.A. No. 9225 plain, clear, and unambiguous. It declined petitioner's invitation to expand the statute beyond its ordinary textual meaning, holding that doing so would constitute judicial legislation.
2. Intrinsic Aids Examined (Whole Act Rule):
The Court rejected reading Section 2 in isolation. It harmonized Section 2 ("deemed not to have lost") with the structural architecture of Section 3.
Section 3 splits natural-born citizens into two distinct legal classes:
Class 1 (Paragraph 1): Those who naturalized abroad **prior** to R.A. No. 9225 are deemed to have **"reacquired"** Philippine citizenship **upon taking the oath**.
Class 2 (Paragraph 2): Those who naturalize abroad **"after"** the effectivity of the Act shall **"retain"** their citizenship **upon taking the oath**.
Reading the statute holistically demonstrates that the phrase "deemed not to have lost" in Section 2 applies only to those who naturalized **after** the Act became effective (Class 2). For those who naturalized prior to the Act (Class 1, like Tan), they had already definitively lost their citizenship under C.A. No. 63 and could only "reacquire" it starting from the date of the oath.
3. **Extrinsic Aids Examined:** The historical statutory baseline under Commonwealth Act No. 63 was evaluated. C.A. No. 63 operated as the governing law when Tan acquired U.S. citizenship on January 19, 1993, under which both naturalization in a foreign country and express renunciation irrevocably extinguished Philippine citizenship. Tan was bound by the legal consequence of that historical act.
4. Statutory Presumptions & Policies Applied:
**Presumption of Prospectivity (Lex prospicit, non respicit):** Absent an express statutory mandate by Congress directing retroactivity, R.A. No. 9225 operates only prospectively from its enactment and from the individual compliance date (the oath).
**Presumption Against Absurdity:** Reading Section 2 retroactively leads to the absurd scenario where the law treats an individual as a continuous Filipino citizen during the very period they had sworn a solemn naturalization oath abjuring all fidelity to the Philippines and professing exclusive allegiance to a foreign state.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court repudiated Tan's contention that "reacquire" and "retain" were used casually or interchangeably by Congress. Applying the **verba legis** principle, the Court held that the legislature is presumed to know the difference between the words and used them advisedly. "Reacquisition" presupposes an interrupted state of citizenship, requiring an affirmative, conditional act (the oath) to restore political status prospectively.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation: (Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
The Supreme Court held that R.A. No. 9225 uses "reacquire" for Filipinos naturalized abroad before 2003, and "retain" only for those naturalized after 2003. Because Tan naturalized in 1993, she completely lost her Philippine citizenship under C.A. No. 63 and remained an alien until she took her oath of allegiance on November 30, 2009. Under the plain meaning and whole-act rules, the law operates prospectively; it cannot magically retroact to make her a Filipino on October 26, 2009, when she filed her voter's registration.
Issue 2: Validity of Voter Registration Prior to Taking the R.A. No. 9225 Oath
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Tan was not a Filipino citizen on October 26, 2009, the date she registered as a voter; therefore, her registration was void **ab initio** and could not be cured retroactively.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Without any doubt, only Filipino citizens are qualified to vote and may be included in the permanent list of voters. Thus, to be registered a voter in the Philippines, the registrant must be a citizen at the time he or she filed the application."
"[O]nce Philippine citizenship is renounced because of naturalization in a foreign country, we cannot consider one a Filipino citizen unless and until his or her allegiance to the Republic of the Philippines is reaffirmed. Simply stated, right after a Filipino renounces allegiance to our country, he or she is to be considered a foreigner."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Constitutional & Statutory Baseline:** Article V, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution and Section 9 of R.A. No. 8189 explicitly restrict suffrage and voter registration to "citizens of the Philippines."
2. **Application of Temporal Rule:** Citizenship is an indispensable qualification that must be possessed **at the very time** the voter application is filed.
3. **Operative Facts Applied:** On October 26, 2009, Tan was exclusively an American citizen. Her subsequent oath on November 30, 2009, operated purely prospectively. Since she was an alien when she registered, her registration was void and incapable of being "cured" retroactively.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation: (Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
Suffrage is strictly conditional upon possessing Philippine citizenship at the exact moment of registration. Because Tan was legally an alien on the day she filed her voter application, the subsequent oath under R.A. No. 9225 could not cure the defect, making her inclusion in the voter's list illegal and warranting her exclusion.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.** (The Third Division decision was unanimous, with all four participating Associate Justices concurring).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
**WHEREFORE**, premises considered, the petition for review on **certiorari** is **DENIED** and the 20 April 2010 Decision and the 1 October 2010 Resolution of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 112815 is **AFFIRMED in toto**.
**SO ORDERED.**
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Respondent Vincent "Bingbong" Crisologo prevailed. The Supreme Court sustained the Court of Appeals and the MeTC, ordering Vivenne K. Tan permanently excluded from the voter's list of Precinct 0853-A, Barangay Sto. Domingo, Quezon City. Henceforth, R.A. No. 9225 must be applied prospectively: former Filipinos who naturalized abroad prior to the Act only regain their citizenship from the moment they take the Section 3 oath, and any civic act (such as voter registration) performed prior to that oath is void for lack of citizenship.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Yu Cong Eng v. Trinidad**
**Full Official Caption:** Yu Cong Eng, et al., Petitioners, v. W. Trinidad, Collector of Internal Revenue, et al. (The Fiscal of the City of Manila, and Honorable Pedro Concepcion, Judge of First Instance of Manila), Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 20479
**Date of Promulgation:** February 6, 1925
**Phil. Reports Citation:** 47 Phil. 385
**Ponente:** Malcolm, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** En Banc. Malcolm, **J.**, ponente, joined by Avanceña, Villamor, Ostrand, and Romualdez, **JJ.**; Johnson, Acting **C.J.**, took no part; Street, **J.**, dissented; Johns, **J.**, dissented.
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
**Primary StatCon Classification:**
Presumptions in Aid of Construction → Presumption of Constitutionality → Duty to Construe Statute to Avoid Unconstitutionality (**Ut res magis valeat quam pereat**) → Restrictive Construction of Broad Phrasing to Avoid Confiscatory/Oppressive Invalidation.
**The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim):**
Act No. 2972 (The Chinese Bookkeeping Law):
"SECTION 1. It shall be unlawful for any person, company, partnership or corporation engaged in commerce, industry or any other activity for the purpose of profit in the Philippine Islands, in accordance with existing law, **to keep its account books in any language other than English, Spanish or any local dialect**."
"SEC. 2. Any person violating the provisions of this Act shall, upon conviction, be punished by a fine of not more than ten thousand pesos, or by imprisonment for not more than two years or both."
"SEC. 3. This Act shall take effect on November first, nineteen hundred and twenty-one." (Amended by Act No. 2998 to take effect on January 1, 1923).
**Historical / Amendment Tracking:**
Prior administrative trigger: Bureau of Internal Revenue Circular Letter dated October 8, 1914 (attempting to require merchants subject to percentage tax to keep daily sales records in English or Spanish; invalidated in **Young v. Rafferty** [1916], 33 Phil. 556, for lack of statutory authority).
Enacted Text: Act No. 2972, approved February 21, 1921. Effective date deferred to January 1, 1923 by Act No. 2998. Enforcement suspended until February 1923.
**StatCon Diagnostic Profile:**
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Latent Ambiguity arising from broad phrasing. The statutory term "its account books" does not explicitly denote whether it covers **all** books of a commercial enterprise, a **duplicate set** of books, or **only such books and records as are strictly necessary for governmental tax assessment and inspection**. Furthermore, literal application to all books would extinguish the right of non-English/Spanish-speaking alien merchants to do business, creating an unconstitutional deprivation of liberty and property.
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?: YES.** The Court explicitly ruled that the phrase "its account books" is ambiguous and susceptible of two or more constructions, holding that judicial construction was mandatory because a literal application would render the Act unconstitutional.
**Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed:**
Presumption of Constitutionality ("To doubt is to sustain").
Canon of Constitutional Avoidance: Where a statute is susceptible of two constructions—one that maintains it and one that destroys it—the court must adopt the construction that upholds the law, even if not the most natural or obvious.
Purposive Construction / Contextual Harmonization (**Ratio Legis**): Interpreting a fiscal statute by reference to the mischief to be remedied, legislative history, and the underlying taxation framework.
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** BIR agents inspected the commercial books of Chinese merchant Yu Cong Eng, found them kept exclusively in Chinese characters, seized them, and filed a criminal information charging him under Act No. 2972 with failing to keep his account books in English, Spanish, or a local dialect.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Yu Cong Eng, et al. (Petitioners):** Chinese merchants residing and operating commercial enterprises in the Philippine Islands, suing on their own behalf and on behalf of approximately 12,000 Chinese merchants similarly situated.
**W. Trinidad (Collector of Internal Revenue) & Juan Posadas (Successor Collector) (Respondents):** Heads of the Bureau of Internal Revenue charged with tax collection and enforcing commercial recordkeeping laws.
**City Fiscals Revilla, Guevara, and Felix (Respondents):** Public prosecutors of the City of Manila who initiated the criminal prosecution.
**Hon. Pedro Concepcion (Respondent):** Judge of the Court of First Instance of Manila who received the information and issued the warrant of arrest against Yu Cong Eng.
**Procedural History & Vehicle:**
**Origin:** Information filed by the City Fiscal against Yu Cong Eng in Criminal Case No. 25551, Court of First Instance of Manila, followed by the issuance of a warrant of arrest and his arrest.
**Apex Vehicle:** Petitioners filed an original petition for Prohibition and Injunction directly before the Supreme Court of the Philippine Islands.
**Preliminary Pleadings:** Respondents interposed a demurrer challenging the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction and defending constitutionality. The Supreme Court overruled the demurrer. Respondents answered; petitioners demurred to the answer. Evidence was taken before a commissioner.
**Supreme Court Ruling:** Overruled jurisdictional objections due to exceptional public interest affecting 12,000 merchants; rejected petitioners' challenge of total facial unconstitutionality; adopted a saving, restrictive construction limiting the law's reach to tax-related records; dissolved the preliminary injunction and denied the petition.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **October 8, 1914:** The Collector of Internal Revenue issues a circular letter requiring merchants subject to the percentage tax to keep records of daily sales in English or Spanish.
2. **February 14, 1916:** The Supreme Court in **Young v. Rafferty** (33 Phil. 556) invalidates the BIR circular, ruling that the Collector lacked delegated authority to designate the language of accounting entries, leaving any such mandate to the Legislature.
3. **October 16, 1920:** The Governor-General sends an executive message recommending legislation requiring business houses to keep books in English, Spanish, or a local dialect to prevent wholesale tax frauds. Representative Urgello introduces the bill in the House of Representatives with an explanatory note focusing on tax verification difficulties and costs.
4. **February 21, 1921:** The Philippine Legislature passes Act No. 2972 (the Chinese Bookkeeping Law), punishing the keeping of account books in any language other than English, Spanish, or a local dialect.
5. **1921–1923:** The effective date is deferred to January 1, 1923 (via Act No. 2998). Following diplomatic protests from China, executive concerns from the War Department, and legislative hearings where the BIR reported millions in lost revenues, enforcement is held in abeyance until the Legislature adjourns in February 1923 without repealing the Act.
6. **March 2, 1923:** BIR agents inspect the premises and accounting records of Chinese merchant Yu Cong Eng in Manila. Finding the books kept solely in Chinese, agents seize the books.
7. **March 7, 1923:** Manila City Fiscal causes an information to be filed against Yu Cong Eng in CFI Manila (Crim. Case No. 25551) for violating Act No. 2972. Judge Pedro Concepcion issues a warrant of arrest, and Yu Cong Eng is arrested.
8. **March 1923:** Yu Cong Eng, on behalf of himself and ~12,000 Chinese merchants handling 60% of Philippine internal commerce, files an original petition for prohibition and injunction before the Supreme Court, attacking Act No. 2972 as unconstitutional class legislation violating due process, equal protection, and treaties.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
A. Petitioners' Interpretation
**Core Reading:** The phrase "keep its account books" in Section 1 is an absolute, unqualified command that **all** internal and commercial accounting books must be maintained exclusively in English, Spanish, or a local dialect. Because over 90% of Chinese merchants do not read, write, or comprehend these languages and cannot secure bookkeepers, the law makes it impossible for them to know their own financial standing or conduct lawful commerce.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Plain Meaning / Verba Legis:** The statute contains no exceptions; "account books" means all commercial books known to the law (e.g., Code of Commerce).
**Strict Construction of Penal Statutes:** Penal statutes affecting life and liberty must be construed strictly against the State and cannot be judicially rewritten.
**Substantive Due Process and Equal Protection:** The law functions as destructive, discriminatory class legislation depriving alien merchants of lawful livelihoods without due process (**Yick Wo v. Hopkins**; **Meyer v. Nebraska**; **The King v. Lau Kiu**).
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Literal enforcement creates oppressive commercial paralysis, subjects thousands of small merchants to financial ruin or extortion by third-party bookkeepers, and drives Chinese traders out of Philippine commerce.
B. Respondents' Interpretation
**Core Reading:** The law prohibits maintaining accounting records exclusively in an incomprehensible tongue; alternatively, it permits merchants to keep their native Chinese books provided they maintain an auxiliary, translated, or duplicate set in English, Spanish, or a local dialect for government inspection.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Police Power and Inherent Taxing Power:** Absolute legislative prerogative to prevent fraud, ensure revenue collection, and regulate commerce (**Lawton v. Steele**; **M'Culloch v. Maryland**).
**Presumption of Constitutionality:** Legislative enactments must be presumed valid until proven unconstitutional beyond a rational doubt.
**Contemporaneous/Executive Purpose:** The measure is directly tied to the enforcement of the sales and income tax systems.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** The Chinese handle 60% of domestic business, generating the bulk of percentage and sales taxes. BIR auditors cannot read Chinese, leading to annual revenue losses of millions of pesos; the State's existence depends on its ability to audit business records.
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
1. **[Procedural Issue]** Whether the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to entertain an original petition for prohibition and injunction to determine the constitutionality of a penal statute at the inception of a criminal prosecution.
**Recit-Ready Question:** Does the Supreme Court have jurisdiction in an original action for prohibition to test the constitutionality of Act No. 2972 prior to trial in the Court of First Instance?
2. **[Constitutional / Formal Issue]** Whether Act No. 2972 is unconstitutional on the ground that its subject is not expressed in its title.
**Recit-Ready Question:** Does Act No. 2972 violate the constitutional title-subject requirement when its title refers generally to the language in which account books shall be kept and penalties for violation?
3. **[PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]** Whether the phrase "its account books" in Section 1 of Act No. 2972 must be given a literal meaning prohibiting all accounts in foreign languages, or be restrictively construed to mean only such books and records as are necessary for governmental inspection for taxation purposes.
**Court Formulation:** "Does the phrase 'its account books' mean that all the account books of the person, company, partnership, or corporation must be kept exclusively in English, Spanish, or any local dialect? ... Or does the phrase 'its account books' mean that the persons, company, partnership, or corporation shall keep duplicate sets of account books... Or does the phrase 'its account books' mean that the person, company, partnership, or corporation must keep such account books as are necessary for taxation purposes?"
**Recit-Ready Question:** Whether the phrase "its account books" in Section 1 of Act No. 2972 applies to all commercial books of a merchant or, under the rule of constitutional avoidance, must be restrictively construed to apply only to sales books and records necessary for taxation purposes.
4. **[Substantive / Constitutional Issue]** Whether Act No. 2972, as restrictively construed to cover only records necessary for taxation, violates the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses of the Jones Law and the Fourteenth Amendment.
**Recit-Ready Question:** Does Act No. 2972, when construed as requiring only tax-related records to be kept in English, Spanish, or a local dialect while leaving merchants free to keep commercial books in Chinese, constitute an unconstitutional deprivation of liberty and property?
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Jurisdiction to Entertain Original Prohibition Challenging a Penal Law
(a) **Issue & Short Answer: YES.** While appellate courts generally refrain from meddling with pending criminal prosecutions, the Court may entertain original prohibition where a new statute affects widespread property rights of thousands of individuals and threatens a multiplicity of suits.
(b) **Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Yet occasionally, under a recently enacted statute affecting numerous persons and extensive property rights, liable to give rise to a multiplicity of actions and numerous prosecutions, it is proper, right at the threshold of a prosecution, to have the validity of a given law determined in the interest of the accused and of the public, so as to permit of the orderly administration of justice."
(c) **Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
**Threshold Gate:** General jurisdictional bar versus equitable exception in extraordinary circumstances.
**Analysis:** Code of Civil Procedure Section 516 grants concurrent original jurisdiction over CFIs exceeding jurisdiction. Enforcing an unconstitutional statute causes irreparable injury to property rights and breeds thousands of separate prosecutions.
**Factual Application:** With 12,000 Chinese merchants handling 60% of Philippine business facing prosecution under a newly effective, unconstrued statute, extraordinary public interest warrants relaxing the general rule requiring a prior trial court constitutional ruling.
(d) **(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation):** The Court exercised extraordinary jurisdiction because allowing 12,000 merchants to be prosecuted individually under an unclarified statute would cause severe commercial chaos and judicial backlog, justifying immediate apex review.
Issue 2: Validity of Title Under Title-Subject Requirement
(a) **Issue & Short Answer: NO (the statute is NOT void).** Act No. 2972 sufficiently expresses its subject in its title, as the constitutional title requirement is satisfied when the title reasonably informs the legislature and the public of the scope of the enactment.
(b) **Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"A faint effort has been made by the petitioners to have the court declare Act No. 2972 void because the subject thereof is not expressed in its title. But legislation should not be embarrassed by such strict construction as is urged by counsel. No distinguishable variance between the title of the law and the body of the law can be discovered after microscopic examination. The law is brief in its terms, and neither the Legislature nor the public need be misled by the title."
(c) **Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
**Threshold Gate:** Strict versus reasonable construction of constitutional title requirements.
**Analysis:** The title read: **"An Act to provide in what language account books shall be kept, and to establish penalties for its violation."** The body contains three short sections prescribing authorized languages and penalties.
**Conclusion:** There is zero variance between title and text; hyper-technical construction should not be used to embarrass legislation.
(d) **(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation):** The title clearly gave notice that the law governed the languages allowed for account books and set penalties, which is precisely what the body of the statute did.
Issue 3: Meaning and Scope of "Its Account Books" [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]
(a) **Issue & Short Answer: RESTRICTIVELY CONSTRUED.** The phrase "its account books" does not mean all internal commercial books, nor does it require duplicate commercial sets; rather, under the duty of constitutional avoidance, it is restricted to mean only those sales books, records, and returns required for taxation purposes.
(b) **Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**Ambiguity Finding:**
"The law, in speaking of any person, company, partnership, or corporation, makes use of the expression 'its account books.' Does the phrase 'its account books' mean that all the account books... must be kept exclusively in English, Spanish, or any local dialect? ... Or does the phrase 'its account books' mean that the persons... shall keep duplicate sets... Or does the phrase 'its account books' mean that the person... must keep such account books as are necessary for taxation purposes? This latter interpretation occurs to us as a reasonable one and as best safeguarding the rights of the accused... The interrogatories above made at least lead to the deduction that the law is more or less ambiguous and that it will bear two or more constructions."
**Canon of Constitutional Avoidance:**
"It may be said to be an elementary, a fundamental, and a universal rule of construction, applied when considering constitutional questions, that when a law is susceptible of two constructions one of which will maintain and the other destroy it, the courts will always adopt the former. Whenever a law can be so construed as to uphold it, it will be so construed although the construction which is adopted does not appear to be as natural as another construction."
**Presumption of Constitutionality:**
"...every possible presumption is in favor of the validity of an act of Congress until overcome beyond rational doubt."
**Definitive Statutory Holding:**
"We construe Act No. 2972 as meaning that any person, company, partnership, or corporation, engaged in commerce, industry, or any other activity for the purpose of profit in the Philippine Islands, shall keep its account books, consisting of sales books and other records and returns required for taxation purposes by regulations of the Bureau of Internal Revenue, in effect when this action was begun, in English, Spanish, or a local dialect."
(c) **Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court explicitly recognized that a literal reading prohibiting all accounts in Chinese would render the statute unconstitutional and void. Finding latent ambiguity in the phrase "its account books," the Court rejected literalism to avoid striking down the statute.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court examined the phrase "its account books" alongside the broader commercial legal framework, observing that the statute failed to specify **which** books were mandated (unlike the Code of Commerce, which explicitly mandates inventories, daybooks, ledgers, and letter copiers).
3. Extrinsic Aids Examined:
**Prior Judicial History: Young v. Rafferty** established that administrative tax authorities needed sales records to prevent fraud, but required legislative authority to set language requirements.
**Legislative History & Executive Messages:** The Governor-General's 1920 message, Representative Urgello's explanatory note, and legislative committee hearings proved that Act No. 2972 was designed strictly as a **fiscal measure** to prevent sales tax and income tax evasion caused by unintelligible books.
4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** Applied the presumption of constitutionality (**to doubt is to sustain**) and the rule that courts must harmonize a statute with higher organic law (**In re Guariña**). The Court also balanced the State's paramount power of taxation against arbitrary deprivation of private property.
5. Rejection of Alternative Constructions:
**Literal/Total Prohibition:** Rejected because depriving Chinese merchants of the ability to maintain internal books in their native tongue would be oppressive and unconstitutional.
**Duplicate Full Accounting Sets:** Rejected as commercially burdensome, ineffective against fraud, and promoting dangerous discrepancies.
**Adopted Saving Construction:** Restricting "account books" to sales books and tax returns required by BIR regulations fulfills the fiscal legislative purpose without destroying the merchant's business.
(d) **(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation):** The Court held that the phrase "its account books" does not mean every single private business ledger a merchant owns, but only the specific sales books and records needed by tax collectors to assess taxes. By narrowing the phrase this way, the Court prevented the law from being struck down as unconstitutional, allowing merchants to keep their private ledgers in Chinese so long as their tax and sales records were kept in English, Spanish, or a local dialect.
Issue 4: Constitutionality of the Act as Restrictively Construed
(a) **Issue & Short Answer: YES (it is CONSTITUTIONAL).** As narrowed to encompass only books and records necessary for taxation, the Act is a reasonable and valid exercise of the police power and the taxing power, and does not violate the Fourteenth Amendment or the Jones Law.
(b) **Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Under such a construction as is above indicated, the Chinese will not be singled out as a special subject for discriminating and hostile legislation. There will be no arbitrary deprivation of liberty or arbitrary spoliation of property. There will be no unjust and illegal discrimination between persons in similar circumstances... The law is not intended for the convenience of the trader or the protection of the creditors, but has relation to the public welfare, to the power of taxation, to the right of the government to exist."
(c) **Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
**Police & Taxing Power Scope:** The State has sovereign authority to prevent fraud, cheating, and evasion in revenue collection (**Lawton v. Steele**; **M'Culloch v. Maryland**).
**Equal Protection Review:** The law applies equally to all merchants of all nationalities who engage in commercial business in the Philippines. It does not unconstitutionally single out the Chinese.
**Proportionality:** Requiring basic sales entries and tax returns in an official language or local dialect is a minimally burdensome requirement reasonably adapted to revenue verification, whereas an absolute ban on Chinese bookkeeping would have been oppressive.
(d) **(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation):** Once narrowed to tax records, the law is a constitutional exercise of tax and police powers because every merchant, regardless of nationality, must provide intelligible sales data to the government to ensure fair taxation.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
**Dissenting Opinion of Street, J.:**
**Interpretative Divergence:** Vehemently criticized the majority for engaging in "an illegitimate process of judicial amendment under the guise of interpretation."
**Critique of Majority's Tool:** Emphasized that the majority openly conceded that the law as written was dead and unconstitutional, yet salvaged it by writing in entirely new limiting language: `"(consisting of sales books and other records and returns required for taxation purposes by regulations of the Bureau of Internal Revenue, in effect when this action was begun)"`.
**Doctrinal Stance:** Argued that no canon of construction allows a court to deduce an administrative tax delegation from a broad penal prohibition. The statute is arbitrary and void under **Meyer v. Nebraska** and **King v. Lau Kiu**; the Court was bound to strike it down completely: **"In addition to smashing the law the court should have removed the debris."**
**Dissenting Opinion of Johns, J.:**
**Interpretative Divergence:** Grounded dissent on the **Strict Construction of Penal Statutes** and the **Plain Meaning Rule (Verba Legis)**.
**Canons & Authorities Invoked:** Extensively cited Sutherland on Statutory Construction (§§ 363, 366, 520, 521, 531). Argued that Act No. 2972 is a penal statute expressed in plain, simple, and unambiguous English.
**Critique of Majority's Tool:** Where statutory language is plain, legislative intent cannot be imagined or remodeled: **"If a statute is plain, certain and unambiguous... interpretation is needless."** Sutherland forbids judicial addition to cure omissions or avoid unconstitutionality.
**The "Two Holes" Dilemma:** Argued that the majority's construction constitutes blatant judicial legislation that creates an unworkable penal law: if the statute now means "account books for taxation purposes only," the statute fails to define what those books are or delegate the power to define them, leaving an accused without fair notice of what specific act constitutes a crime. The law should have been declared void under **Meyer v. Nebraska**.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"We construe Act No. 2972 as meaning that any person, company, partnership, or corporation, engaged in commerce, industry, or any other activity for the purpose of profit in the Philippine Islands, shall keep its account books, consisting of sales books and other records and returns required for taxation purposes by regulations of the Bureau of Internal Revenue, in effect when this action was begun, in English, Spanish, or a local dialect. Agreeable to such construction, we hold Act No. 2972 valid and constitutional.
The temporary injunction heretofore issued is dissolved although under the construction given to the law it may well be doubted if the Government will care to proceed with the criminal prosecution. If the Government should not dismiss the information, this question may be raised by demurrer in the lower court.
Petition denied without costs."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Chinese merchants lost their bid to have the Chinese Bookkeeping Law struck down as facially unconstitutional, but secured a narrowing interpretation. The Supreme Court upheld Act No. 2972 by judicially restricting its scope: merchants are legally prohibited from keeping **sales and tax-inspection records** in Chinese, but remain free to maintain their general internal commercial account books in Chinese or any other language. The temporary injunction was dissolved, leaving the trial court to determine whether the pending criminal information against Yu Cong Eng could stand under the narrowed construction.

The dispute turns on whether the generic word **"gambling"** in Section 458(a)(1)(v) of R.A. No. 7160 encompasses **all** gambling without distinction (including state-authorized casinos operated by PAGCOR under P.D. A secondary defect is an alleged implied repeal/modification of P.D. No. 1869 by the blanket repealing clause in Section 534(f) of R.A. No. 7160. **Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. While the Court observed that the text is **"clear and unmistakable"** when read properly, it actively deployed established rules of statutory hermeneutics (**noscitur a sociis**, statutory harmonization, and rules on implied repeals) to resolve the clash between the local police power delegated under R.A. **Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether Ordinance Nos. 3353 and 3375-93 enacted by the Sangguniang Panlungsod of Cagayan de Oro City are ultra vires and invalid for contravening a national statute.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Scope of "Gambling" under Section 458(a)(1)(v) of R.A. No. 7160
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
**Issue 1:** Does Section 458(a)(1)(v) of the Local Government Code authorize the city to suppress all gambling, including casinos authorized by national law?
**Short Answer: NO.** Under the rule of **noscitur a sociis**, the word **"gambling"** is qualified by the accompanying phrase **"and other prohibited games of chance,"** restricting the local government's power of suppression exclusively to **illegal** gambling.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"Under the rule of **noscitur a sociis**, a word or phrase should be interpreted in relation to, or given the same meaning of, words with which it is associated. Accordingly, we conclude that since the word 'gambling' is associated with 'and **other** prohibited games of chance,' the word should be read as referring to only illegal gambling which, like the **other** prohibited games of chance, must be prevented or suppressed."
"We begin by observing that under Sec. 458 of the Local Government Code, local government units are authorized to prevent or suppress, among others, 'gambling and **other** prohibited games of chance.' Obviously, this provision excludes games of chance which are not prohibited but are in fact permitted by law. The petitioners are less than accurate in claiming that the Code could have excluded such games of chance but did not. In fact it does. The language of the section is clear and unmistakable."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court observed that the text itself is clear, but because petitioners invoked competing canons (**ubi lex non distinguit** and liberal construction under Sec. 5), the Court applied grammatical and contextual hermeneutics.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined (Associated Words):** The Court evaluated the internal syntax of Section 458(a)(1)(v). The presence of the adjective/connector **"other"** in the phrase **"and other prohibited games of chance"** acts as a grammatical link showing that the preceding word **"gambling"** belongs to the same genus—that is, games that are **prohibited**. By application of **noscitur a sociis**, legal forms of gambling authorized by statute are excluded.
3. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies (Absurdity):** The Court observed that if **"shall ... prevent [and] suppress"** applied to **all** gambling without distinction, local governments would have a mandatory duty to suppress all state-sanctioned lotteries, horse races, and sweepstakes across the country. This reading produces an unacceptable absurdity that frustrates national revenue collection.
4. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court rejected the petitioners' invocation of **Ubi lex non distinguit, nec nos distinguere debemos**. The statute **does** make a distinction: by adding **"and other prohibited games of chance,"** Congress specifically qualified the preceding generic term.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation):** The Supreme Court held that the word "gambling" in the Local Government Code cannot be read in isolation to mean all betting activities. Because the statute says "gambling and **other prohibited** games of chance," the rule of **noscitur a sociis** dictates that "gambling" takes its meaning from the surrounding words—meaning it only covers **prohibited** (unlawful) gambling, leaving state-authorized games like PAGCOR's casinos outside the city's power to ban.
Issue 2: Implied Repeal / Modification of P.D. No. 1869 by R.A. No. 7160
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
**Issue 2:** Did the Local Government Code of 1991 impliedly repeal or modify **pro tanto** P.D. No. 1869?
**Short Answer: NO.** Implied repeals are strictly disfavored, and general laws (R.A. No. 7160) do not abrogate prior special laws (P.D. No. 1869) unless an irreconcilable conflict clearly indicates that legislative intent.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"Furthermore, it is a familiar rule that implied repeals are not lightly presumed in the absence of a clear and unmistakable showing of such intention."
"The cases relating to the subject of repeal by implication all proceed on the assumption that if the act of later date clearly reveals an intention on the part of the lawmaking power to abrogate the prior law, this intention must be given effect; but there must always be a sufficient revelation of this intention, and it has become an unbending rule of statutory construction that the intention to repeal a former law will not be imputed to the Legislature when it appears that the two statutes, or provisions, with reference to which the question arises bear to each other the relation of general to special." **(Quoting Lichauco & Co. v. Apostol, 44 Phil. 138).**
"It is a canon of legal hermeneutics that instead of pitting one statute against another in an inevitably destructive confrontation, courts must exert every effort to reconcile them, remembering that both laws deserve a becoming respect as the handiwork of a coordinate branch of the government. On the assumption of a conflict between P.D. 1869 and the Code, the proper action is not to uphold one and annul the other but to give effect to both by harmonizing them if possible."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Intrinsic Aids Examined (Expressio Unius / Sectional Context):** The Court examined the comprehensive repealing clause in Section 534 of R.A. No. 7160. Paragraphs (a) through (e) explicitly, specifically, and painstakingly enumerated dozens of statutes, decrees, and codal sections being repealed or modified. Crucially, **P.D. No. 1869 was not listed**. The petitioners relied entirely on the blanket, catch-all paragraph (f), which cannot overcome the specific omission.
2. **Extrinsic Aids Examined (Subsequent Legislative Acts):** The Court pointed out that after enacting R.A. No. 7160, Congress enacted R.A. No. 7309 (creating the DOJ Board of Claims) and R.A. No. 7648 (addressing the national power crisis), both of which expressly designated PAGCOR earnings as funding sources. This confirms that Congress considered P.D. No. 1869 active and operative, not repealed or crippled.
3. **Harmonization Canon Applied:** Applying the rule that coordinate statutes must be harmonized (**ut res magis valeat quam pereat**), the Court held that the Local Government Code gives LGUs general police power to suppress illegal gambling, while P.D. No. 1869 operates as a specific, carved-out exception for state-regulated casinos.
4. **Rejection of "Modification Pro Tanto" Argument:** Petitioners argued they were not claiming complete repeal, only "modification **pro tanto**" subjecting PAGCOR to local consent. The Court dismissed this as "playing with words," because empowering each LGU to veto PAGCOR would effectively reduce the corporation to a "toothless tiger or a white elephant," nullifying the national mandate.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation):** The Supreme Court ruled that the general repealing clause of the Local Government Code did not repeal PAGCOR's charter because implied repeals are never presumed, especially when a general law clashes with an earlier special law. Instead of declaring a conflict, the Court harmonized both statutes by holding that local governments must suppress illegal gambling, while PAGCOR's state-authorized casinos stand as a lawful, special statutory exception.
Issue 3: Validity of Cagayan de Oro City Ordinance Nos. 3353 and 3375-93
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
**Issue 3:** Are Ordinance Nos. 3353 and 3375-93 valid and enforceable?
**Short Answer: NO.** The ordinances directly contravene a valid national statute (P.D. No. 1869) and are therefore **ultra vires**, null, and void.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"The tests of a valid ordinance are well established. A long line of decisions has held that to be valid, an ordinance must conform to the following substantive requirements:
1) It must not contravene the constitution or any statute.
2) It must not be unfair or oppressive.
3) It must not be partial or discriminatory.
4) It must not prohibit but may regulate trade.
5) It must be general and consistent with public policy.
6) It must not be unreasonable."
"Municipal governments are only agents of the national government. Local councils exercise only delegated legislative powers conferred on them by Congress as the national lawmaking body. The delegate cannot be superior to the principal or exercise powers higher than those of the latter. It is a heresy to suggest that the local government units can undo the acts of Congress, from which they have derived their power in the first place, and negate by mere ordinance the mandate of the statute."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Substantive Test Applied:** The first and foundational requirement of a valid ordinance is that it cannot contravene any existing statute.
2. **Delegated vs. Plenary Power:** Local governments derive their entire existence and authority from the national legislature. Under the established doctrine governing municipal corporations, an agent cannot veto or overturn the will of its principal.
3. **Statutory Subordination:** Because P.D. No. 1869 carries the force and effect of a national statute, any municipal ordinance that criminalizes, prohibits, or frustrates its implementation is an impermissible act in excess of delegated power (**ultra vires**).
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation):** The Supreme Court held that local city ordinances must yield to national statutes. Because PAGCOR was authorized by a national law (P.D. No. 1869) to run casinos, the City Council had no legal authority to enact local measures barring casinos, rendering the ordinances invalid for violating the cardinal rule that a local ordinance cannot contravene a national statute.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
**Concurring Opinion of Padilla, J.:**
**Interpretive Stance:** Concurred fully in the majority's legal conclusion that municipal ordinances cannot modify or repeal P.D. No. 1869.
**Moral / Policy Divergence:** Stressed that while gambling may be legally authorized, what is legal is not always moral. Emphasized that gambling erodes the moral fabric of the Filipino character (drawing an analogy to prostitution). Urged the national government and PAGCOR to re-evaluate imposing casinos upon unwilling communities, reminding the political branches that the legislative authorization of gambling is an act of state policy for which they remain solely accountable to the people.
**Concurring Opinion of Davide, Jr., J.:**
**Procedural Divergence (Hierarchy of Courts):** Noted that Pryce's petition in the Court of Appeals was in reality an action for declaratory relief disguised as a petition for prohibition, over which the CA lacked original jurisdiction. Even if treated as prohibition, it violated the hierarchy of courts and should have been filed with the Regional Trial Court of Cagayan de Oro City.
**StatCon Harmonization Alternative:** Concurred that the ordinances could not repeal P.D. No. 1869. Disagreed, however, with the Court of Appeals' holding that the ordinances were completely **unconstitutional**; rather, under proper statutory harmonization, the ordinances should simply be interpreted and construed as **inapplicable to PAGCOR**, while remaining otherwise intact.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
**WHEREFORE**, the petition is DENIED and the challenged decision of the respondent Court of Appeals is AFFIRMED, with costs against the petitioners.
**It is so ordered.**
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The City of Cagayan de Oro and Mayor Magtajas lost the case; Ordinance Nos. 3353 and 3375-93 were declared null, void, and unenforceable; and PAGCOR's statutory right to open and operate its casino at the Pryce Plaza Hotel was legally sustained. LGUs have no statutory power to prohibit state-authorized gambling entities created by national law.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Philippine Basketball Association v. Court of Appeals**
**Full Official Caption:** Philippine Basketball Association, Petitioner, v. Court of Appeals, Court of Tax Appeals, and Commissioner of Internal Revenue, Respondents
**Citation & Metadata:**
G.R. No. 119122
Promulgation Date: August 8, 2000
Ponente: Purisima, **J.**
Voting Breakdown: Third Division; Panganiban and Gonzaga-Reyes, **JJ.**, concur; Melo and Vitug, **JJ.**, concur in the result.
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
Primary StatCon Classification:
Intrinsic Aids → Associated Words → **Ejusdem Generis** → Scope of general catch-all clauses following specific enumerations.
Extrinsic Aids → Legislative History / Sequential Enactments → Tracking statutory cross-references to discern national vs. local taxing jurisdiction.
Plain Meaning Rule / **Verba Legis** → Broad statutory definition of "gross receipts" without room for extended interpretation.
Executive Construction → Limits of Administrative Deference → Non-estoppel of the State due to erroneous administrative rulings.
The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim):
**Section 13, Presidential Decree No. 231 (The Local Tax Code of 1973):**
"SECTION 13. **Amusement tax on admission.** — The province shall impose a tax on admission to be collected from the proprietors, lessees, or operators of theaters, cinematographs, concert halls, circuses and **other places of amusement** . . ."
**Section 268, National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC), as amended by P.D. No. 1456 and P.D. No. 1959 (Sec. 44):**
"Sec. 268. **Amusement taxes.** — There shall be collected from the proprietor, lessee or operator of cockpits, cabarets, night or day clubs, boxing exhibitions, **professional basketball games**, Jai-Alai, race tracks and bowling alleys, a tax equivalent to:
xxx xxx xxx
'4. **Fifteen per centum in the case of professional basketball games as envisioned in Presidential Decree No. 871. Provided, however. That the tax herein shall be in lieu of all other percentage taxes of whatever nature and description**;
xxx xxx xxx
of their gross receipts, irrespective of whether or not any amount is charged or paid for admission. **For the purpose of the amusement tax, the term gross receipts' embraces all the receipts of the proprietor, lessee or operator of the amusement place**. Said gross receipts also include income from television, radio and motion picture rights, if any. (A person or entity or association conducting any activity subject to the tax herein imposed shall be similarly liable for said tax with respect to such portion of the receipts derived by him or it.)
The taxes imposed herein shall be payable at the end of each quarter and it shall be the duty of the proprietor, lessee, or operator concerned, as well as any party liable, within twenty days after the end of each quarter, to make a true and complete return of the amount of the gross receipts derived during the preceding quarter and pay the tax due thereon. If the tax is not paid within the time prescribed above, the amount of the tax shall be increased **by twenty-five per centum**, the increment to be part of the tax.
In case of willful neglect to file the return within the period prescribed herein, or in case a false or fraudulent return is willfully made, there shall be added to the tax or to the deficiency tax, in case any payment has been made on the basis of the return before the discovery of the falsity or fraud, a surcharge of **fifty per centum** of its amount..."
Historical / Amendment Tracking:
**P.D. No. 231 (June 28, 1973):** Local Tax Code authorized provinces to levy amusement taxes on admission fees for "theaters, cinematographs, concert halls, circuses and other places of amusement."
**P.D. No. 871 (January 6, 1976):** Section 8 placed the PBA under Games and Amusements Board regulation and set an amusement tax of 5% of gross receipts from admission tickets.
**P.D. No. 1456 (June 11, 1978):** Amended NIRC Section 268; increased the national amusement tax on professional basketball games as envisioned in P.D. No. 871 to 10% and codified that "gross receipts" embraces all receipts, including television/radio/motion picture rights.
**P.D. No. 1959 (1984):** Further amended Section 268; increased the national amusement tax rate on professional basketball games to 15%, explicitly providing that it is in lieu of all other percentage taxes.
**Modern Successor Tracking:** Republic Act No. 7160 (Local Government Code of 1991), Section 140 retained local amusement taxes on theaters, cinemas, concert halls, and circuses without listing professional basketball; Republic Act No. 8424 (NIRC of 1997), Section 125 retained the 15% national amusement tax on professional basketball games.
StatCon Diagnostic Profile:
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Latent Ambiguity / Conflict Between Provisions (whether the catch-all phrase **"and other places of amusement"** in the Local Tax Code encompasses professional basketball, divesting the national government of taxing jurisdiction) combined with an alleged defect of overbreadth regarding whether **"all the receipts"** in the definition of "gross receipts" includes venue advertising and streamer spaces.
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes, for reconciling the general catch-all clause of the Local Tax Code with the specific national tax codal provisions via **ejusdem generis** and legislative history; but No (**Verba Legis** applied) regarding the definition of "gross receipts," which the Court held was clear and plain on its face.
**Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed:**
**Ejusdem Generis** ("where general words follow an enumeration of persons or things, by words of a particular and specific meaning, such general words are not to be construed in their widest extent, but are to be held as applying only to persons or things of the same kind or class as those specifically mentioned").
Plain Meaning Rule / **Verba Legis** ("The law being clear, there is no need for an extended interpretation").
Doctrine of Non-Estoppel of the State ("erroneous application and enforcement of the law by public officers do not preclude subsequent correct application of the statute, and that the Government is never estopped by mistake or error on the part of its agents").
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The Commissioner of Internal Revenue issued an assessment letter on June 21, 1989, assessing the Philippine Basketball Association for P5,864,260.84 in deficiency national amusement taxes, surcharges, and interest for taxable year 1987, prompting the PBA to claim that taxing jurisdiction belonged solely to local governments under P.D. No. 231 and prior BIR rulings.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
Key Parties & Roles:
**Philippine Basketball Association (PBA):** Petitioner; professional basketball league operating games and commercial concessions.
**Commissioner of Internal Revenue (CIR):** Public Respondent; national tax authority assessing deficiency amusement taxes under the NIRC.
**Court of Tax Appeals (CTA):** Public Respondent; specialized tax court that affirmed the CIR’s deficiency assessment.
**Court of Appeals (CA):** Public Respondent; appellate court that affirmed the CTA’s decision.
**Vintage Enterprises, Inc. (VEI):** Third-party commercial partner granted advertising, broadcast, and streamer spaces by the PBA.
Procedural History & Vehicle:
1. **BIR Assessment (June 21, 1989):** CIR issued an assessment to PBA for 1987 deficiency amusement tax (P5,864,260.84, including 75% surcharge and 20% interest).
2. **Administrative Protest (July 18, 1989):** PBA protested the assessment; CIR denied the protest on November 6, 1989.
3. **Petition for Review before the CTA (January 8, 1990):** PBA contested the CIR's denial in C.T.A. Case No. 4419. On December 24, 1993, the CTA dismissed the petition and ordered payment. Reconsideration was denied on April 8, 1994.
4. **Petition for Review before the CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 34095):** PBA appealed. On November 21, 1994, the CA affirmed the CTA. Reconsideration was denied on January 31, 1995.
5. **Supreme Court Review (Rule 45):** PBA filed the instant petition for review on certiorari. The Supreme Court affirmed the CA and CTA decisions in toto.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **June 28, 1973:** P.D. No. 231 (Local Tax Code) took effect, granting provinces the power under Section 13 to levy amusement taxes on admissions to theaters, cinematographs, concert halls, circuses, and "other places of amusement."
2. **January 6, 1976:** P.D. No. 871 was enacted, regulating professional basketball through the Games and Amusements Board and fixing a 5% amusement tax on PBA admission tickets.
3. **June 11, 1978:** P.D. No. 1456 amended Section 268 of the NIRC, explicitly increasing the national amusement tax on professional basketball games to 10% and defining gross receipts as embracing "all the receipts."
4. **1984:** P.D. No. 1959 further amended Section 268 of the NIRC, raising the national amusement tax on professional basketball games to 15%, payable in lieu of all other percentage taxes.
5. **1986–1988:** The BIR issued administrative issuances, notably BIR Ruling No. 231-86 and BIR Revenue Memorandum Circular No. 8-88, expressing the view that jurisdiction to levy amusement taxes on admission tickets to places of amusement had been transferred to local governments under P.D. No. 231.
6. **Taxable Year 1987:** PBA derived gross receipts of P19,970,928.00 from admissions and the cession of advertising and streamer spaces to Vintage Enterprises, Inc. (VEI), paying only P602,063.35 in amusement taxes.
7. **June 21, 1989:** The CIR issued an assessment against PBA for deficiency amusement tax of P2,393,575.85, a 75% surcharge of P1,795,181.89, and 20% interest of P1,675,503.10, totaling P5,864,260.84.
8. **July 18, 1989:** PBA filed an administrative protest with the CIR, contending that amusement taxes were local taxes and that streamer/advertising income was not subject to amusement tax.
9. **November 6, 1989:** The CIR denied PBA's protest.
10. **January 8, 1990:** PBA elevated the case to the CTA (C.T.A. Case No. 4419).
11. **December 24, 1993:** The CTA dismissed the petition and ordered the PBA to pay the assessed deficiency plus 20% annual delinquency interest from July 22, 1989.
12. **April 8, 1994:** The CTA denied PBA's motion for reconsideration.
13. **November 21, 1994:** The CA affirmed the CTA in CA-G.R. SP No. 34095. Reconsideration was denied on January 31, 1995.
14. **August 8, 2000:** The Supreme Court denied the PBA's Rule 45 petition.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
| Dimension | Petitioner's Interpretation (PBA) | Respondent's Interpretation (CIR / Government) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Core Reading of Sec. 13, P.D. 231 vs. Sec. 268, NIRC** | The power to levy amusement taxes was transferred wholesale to local governments. The catch-all phrase "other places of amusement" in Sec. 13 of the Local Tax Code encompasses basketball stadiums. Section 268 was modified by P.D. 231. | The province's taxing power is confined to places of artistic entertainment. Professional basketball is specifically governed by Sec. 268 of the NIRC, as amended by P.D. 1959, making it a national percentage tax to the exclusion of local taxes. |
| **Canons & Maxims Invoked** | Contemporaneous Executive Construction (relying on BIR Ruling No. 231-86 and BIR RMC No. 8-88); Non-retroactivity of administrative revocations. | **Ejusdem Generis**; Legislative Intent through Historical StatCon Analysis; Non-Estoppel of the Government by mistakes of public officers. |
| **Gross Receipts Scope (Advertising/Streamers)** | Income derived from ceding advertising and streamer spaces to VEI is non-admission revenue, not part of the amusement taxable base. | **Verba Legis** / Plain Meaning Rule: The statutory phrase "embraces all the receipts" is expansive and covers all inflows, including advertising and broadcast rights. |
| **Policy / Consequence Argument** | Double taxation and administrative injustice result if the taxpayer relies on the BIR's own rulings only to be assessed retroactively with severe surcharges. | The state cannot be deprived of statutory revenues due to mistaken administrative opinions; tax laws must be applied as drafted by the legislature. |
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
### 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]
**Faithful Court Formulation:** "Is the amusement tax on admission tickets to PBA games a national or local tax? Otherwise put, who between the national government and local government should petitioner pay amusement taxes?"
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the phrase **"and other places of amusement"** in Section 13 of the Local Tax Code includes professional basketball games under the principle of **ejusdem generis**, or whether such games remain exclusively subject to national amusement tax under Section 268 of the NIRC as amended.

**Faithful Court Formulation:** "Is the cession of advertising and streamer spaces to Vintage Enterprises, Inc. (VEI) subject to the payment of amusement tax?"
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the statutory definition in Section 268 of the NIRC stating that the term **"gross receipts' embraces all the receipts of the proprietor, lessee or operator of the amusement place"** plainly includes revenues derived from the cession of venue advertising and streamer spaces under the **verba legis** rule.
3. [Procedural Issue]
**Faithful Court Formulation:** "If ever petitioner is liable for the payment of deficiency amusement tax, is it liable to pay a seventy-five percent (75%) surcharge on the deficiency amount due?"
**Recit-Ready Question:** Whether the petitioner can raise the defense of good faith reliance on administrative rulings to avoid surcharges for the first time on appeal before the Supreme Court.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: National vs. Local Taxing Jurisdiction over Professional Basketball Games
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
Is the amusement tax on admission tickets to PBA games a national or local tax?
**NATIONAL TAX.** Under the doctrine of **ejusdem generis** and sequential legislative history, professional basketball games are not "other places of amusement" under the Local Tax Code, but are specifically subject to national amusement tax under Section 268 of the NIRC.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**On Ejusdem Generis:**
"Under the principle of **ejusdem generis**, where general words follow an enumeration of persons or things, by words of a particular and specific meaning, such general words are not to be construed in their widest extent, but are to be held as applying only to persons or things of the same kind or class as those specifically mentioned."
**On Distinguishing Classes of Entertainment:**
"Thus, in determining the meaning of the phrase 'other places of amusement', one must refer to the prior enumeration of theaters, cinematographs, concert halls and circuses with artistic expression as their common characteristic. Professional basketball games do not fall under the same category as theaters, cinematographs, concert halls and circuses as the latter basically belong to artistic forms of entertainment while the former caters to sports and gaming."
**On Legislative Intent via Historical Analysis:**
"A historical analysis of pertinent laws does reveal the legislative intent to place professional basketball games within the ambit of a national tax... With the reference to PD 871 by PD 1456 and PD 1959, there is a recognition under the laws of this country that the amusement tax on professional basketball games is a national, and not a local, tax."
**On Non-Estoppel of the Government:**
"It bears stressing that the government can never be in estoppel, particularly in matters involving taxes. It is a well-known rule that erroneous application and enforcement of the law by public officers do not preclude subsequent correct application of the statute, and that the Government is never estopped by mistake or error on the part of its agents."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court found that Section 13 of the Local Tax Code and Section 268 of the NIRC were clear in their respective spheres and did not confer concurrent or local jurisdiction over basketball.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined (Ejusdem Generis):** The Court examined the specific enumeration in Section 13 of P.D. 231: **"theaters, cinematographs, concert halls, circuses."** The genus running through the specific words is **artistic expression**. The general words **"and other places of amusement"** must be restricted to that same class. Professional basketball involves **sports and gaming**, excluding it from Section 13.
3. Extrinsic Aids Examined (Legislative History): The Court mapped the legislative progression:
P.D. 231 (1973) created the local taxing power over artistic venues.
P.D. 871 (1976) specifically regulated the PBA and set a 5% amusement tax.
P.D. 1456 (1978) amended NIRC Section 268, raising the rate to 10% on basketball games as envisioned in P.D. 871.
P.D. 1959 (1984) further amended Section 268, raising the rate to 15% and explicitly commanding that it was **"in lieu of all other percentage taxes of whatever nature and description."**
Modern statutes (NIRC Sec. 125 vs. Local Government Code Sec. 140) affirmed this sustained legislative design.
4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies (Sovereignty and Non-Estoppel):** The Court dismissed petitioner's reliance on BIR Ruling No. 231-86 and BIR RMC No. 8-88. An administrative officer’s erroneous reading cannot amend the statute or estop the State from collecting taxes properly imposed by law.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** Petitioner’s attempt to absorb sports arenas into the general words of the Local Tax Code ignored both the contextual genus of Section 13 and the clear, specific national amendments in P.D. 1456 and P.D. 1959.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
Under the rule of **ejusdem generis**, general catch-all phrases like "other places of amusement" take their meaning from the specific list preceding them—which, in the Local Tax Code, consists only of artistic performances (theaters, concerts, circuses). Because professional basketball is sports and gaming rather than artistic entertainment, and because subsequent presidential decrees specifically classified it under the Tax Code as subject to a 15% national tax in lieu of all others, jurisdiction belongs exclusively to the national government via the BIR.
Issue 2: Taxability of Streamer and Advertising Spaces under "Gross Receipts"
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
Is the cession of advertising and streamer spaces to VEI subject to the payment of amusement tax?
**YES.** Under the plain meaning rule (**verba legis**), the statutory definition of "gross receipts" embraces all receipts without exception.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**On Plain Meaning / Verba Legis:**
"The foregoing definition of gross receipts is broad enough to embrace the cession of advertising and streamer spaces as the same embraces all the receipts of the proprietor, lessee or operator of the amusement place. The law being clear, there is no need for an extended interpretation."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court applied the threshold rule: where the statute is clear, plain, and unambiguous, there is no room for judicial interpretation.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined (Codal Definition):** Section 268 explicitly legislates its own definition: **"the term 'gross receipts' embraces all the receipts of the proprietor, lessee or operator of the amusement place."** The statute also expressly states that gross receipts include television, radio, and motion picture rights, showing legislative intent to reach non-admission revenues generated within the venue.
3. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** Tax statutes defining their own terms must be applied strictly according to their statutory definitions without carving out judicial exemptions.
4. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The PBA’s argument that "gross receipts" should be limited to gate admissions contradicts the statutory command that the tax applies **"irrespective of whether or not any amount is charged or paid for admission"** and encompasses **"all the receipts."**
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
When the Tax Code itself explicitly defines "gross receipts" as embracing **all** receipts derived by the operator irrespective of admission fees, courts must apply the literal meaning (**verba legis**). Income from leasing banner and streamer spaces inside the basketball stadium falls squarely within "all receipts" and is subject to national amusement tax.
Issue 3: Propriety of Surcharge and Interest Assessments
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
Is petitioner liable to pay a seventy-five percent (75%) surcharge on the deficiency amount due?
**YES (PROCEDURALLY BARRED).** The issue cannot be considered because petitioner failed to raise its good-faith reliance defense before the lower courts.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**On Issues Raised for the First Time on Appeal:**
"This issue must necessarily fail as the same has never been posed as an issue before the respondent court. Issues not raised in the court a quo cannot be raised for the first time on appeal."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Procedural Bar:** The Court refused to evaluate whether petitioner's good faith reliance on BIR issuances excused it from the statutory surcharge under Section 268.
2. **Appellate Review Rule:** Points of law, issues, or defenses not pleaded or ventilated before the CTA or CA cannot be opened for review under Rule 45.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
The Supreme Court did not reach the substantive interpretation of the surcharge provision because the PBA raised its argument of "good faith reliance on BIR issuances" for the first time on appeal, violating the rule that courts will not review questions not brought before the court **a quo**.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
**Associate Justices Melo and Vitug:** Concurred "in the result" without issuing separate written opinions.
**No separate opinions discussing alternative statutory construction canons are set forth in the text.**
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the Petition is DENIED, and the Decisions of the Court of Appeals and Court of Tax Appeals dated November 21, 1994 and December 24, 1993, respectively AFFIRMED. No pronouncement as to costs.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The CIR prevailed entirely. The Philippine Basketball Association was ordered to pay P5,864,260.84 in deficiency national amusement taxes, surcharges, and interest for 1987, plus 20% annual delinquency interest. The ruling solidifies the doctrine that professional basketball is exclusively subject to national amusement tax under the NIRC and that its taxable gross receipts encompass all commercial arena revenues, including advertising spaces.
