### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Amadora v. Court of Appeals**
**Full Official Caption:** JOSE S. AMADORA, LORETA A. AMADORA, JOSE A. AMADORA JR., NORMA A. YLAYA, PANTALEON A. AMADORA, JOSE A. AMADORA III, LUCY A. AMADORA, ROSALINDA A. AMADORA, PERFECTO A. AMADORA, SERREC A. AMADORA, VICENTE A. AMADORA and MARIA TISCALINA A. AMADORA, **petitioners**, vs. HONORABLE COURT OF APPEALS, COLEGIO DE SAN JOSE-RECOLETOS, VICTOR LLUCH, SERGIO P. DAMASO JR., CELESTINO DICON, ANIANO ABELLANA, PABLITO DAFFON thru his parents and natural guardians, MR. and MRS. NICANOR GUMBAN, and ROLANDO VALENCIA, thru his guardian, A. FRANCISCO ALONSO, **respondents**.
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** L-47745
**Promulgation Date:** April 15, 1988
**Reporter Citation:** 160 SCRA 315
**Ponente:** Cruz, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown (En Banc):**
**Concurring without separate opinion:** Yap, Narvasa, Paras, Feliciano, Gancayco, Bidin, Sarmiento, Cortes, and Griño-Aquino, **JJ.**
**Concurring and Dissenting Opinion:** Melencio-Herrera, **J.**
**Concurring Opinion:** Gutierrez, Jr., **J.**
**Took No Part:** Fernan, Padilla, and Teehankee, **C.J.**
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
**Primary StatCon Classification:**
Intrinsic Aids & Syntactical Canons → Grammatical Modification & Distribution → **Reddendo Singula Singulis** / Doctrine of Last Antecedent → Qualifying effect of "of establishments of arts and trades" on "teachers" vs. "heads"; Scope and temporal duration of statutory "custody."
**The Contested Statutory Text (Verbatim):**
**Article 2180, Paragraph 7, Civil Code of the Philippines:**
"Lastly, **teachers or heads of establishments of arts and trades** shall be liable for damages caused by their **pupils and students or apprentices so long as they remain in their custody**."
**Historical / Amendment Tracking:**
**Prior Codal Provision (Article 1903, Spanish Civil Code of 1889):**
"Lastly, teachers or heads of establishments of arts and trades shall be liable for damages caused by their pupils and students or apprentices, respectively, so long as they remain under their custody." (**"Son, por último, responsables los maestros o directores de artes y oficios por los perjuicios causados por sus alumnos o aprendices, mientras permanezcan bajo su custodia."**) Derived from European continental equivalents referring to **"preceptores y artesanos"**.
**Re-codified / Subsequent Development (Family Code of the Philippines, Executive Order No. 209 [effective August 3, 1988, enacted shortly after this decision]):** Articles 218 and 219 explicitly vested substitute parental authority and direct, primary, and solidary liability over minor children upon the school, its administrators, and teachers.
**StatCon Diagnostic Profile:**
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Syntactical Ambiguity / Grammatical Antecedence and Latent Ambiguity (whether the prepositional phrase **"of establishments of arts and trades"** modifies both **"teachers"** and **"heads"**, or strictly **"heads"**; and whether **"in their custody"** requires boarding/living status or co-extensiveness strictly with active semester class schedules).
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?: YES.** Construction was essential to resolve the conflicting **obiter dicta** established in **Exconde v. Capuno** and **Mercado v. Court of Appeals** versus the doctrine established in **Palisoc v. Brillantes**, and to determine the syntactical distribution of the subjects and direct objects in Paragraph 7 of Article 2180.
**Controlling Canons / Maxims Deployed:**
**Reddendo singula singulis** (referring each to each / distributing respective terms).
Doctrine of the Last Antecedent / Restrictive Adjectival Qualification (qualifying phrases modify only the immediate proximate antecedent unless legislative intent requires otherwise).
Principle of **Culpa in vigilando** / **In loco parentis**.
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** A graduating academic high school student was fatally shot by a classmate inside the school auditorium after classes had formally ended for the semester, but before commencement exercises, prompting an action for vicarious damages against an academic school, its administrators, and teachers under an article historically interpreted as limited to technical/vocational trade schools.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Litigants:**
**The Victim & Petitioners:** Alfredo Amadora (17-year-old graduating high school student, deceased), represented by his parents, Jose S. Amadora and Loreta A. Amadora, and his siblings.
**The Tortfeasor Student:** Pablito Daffon (classmate of Alfredo who discharged the fatal firearm).
**The Student Companions / Gun Possessors:** Jose Gumban (student from whom Dean Damaso had confiscated an unlicensed pistol six days prior) and Rolando Valencia, along with their parents/guardians.
**The Institutional & School Administration Respondents:**
**Colegio de San Jose-Recoletos:** An academic institution of learning where the shooting occurred.
**Victor Lluch:** Rector of the school.
**Sergio P. Damaso, Jr.:** Dean of boys (who confiscated and returned an unlicensed pistol to Jose Gumban on April 7, 1972).
**Celestino Dicon:** Physics teacher of Alfredo Amadora.
**Aniano Abellana:** High school principal.
**Procedural History & Vehicle:**
**Criminal Action:** Pablito Daffon was tried and convicted of homicide through reckless imprudence.
**Civil Action (Court of First Instance of Cebu):** Petitioners filed a civil suit for damages under Article 2180 against Colegio de San Jose-Recoletos, its rector, principal, dean of boys, physics teacher, Daffon, and two other students (complaint against the students was dropped). The CFI held the school and school officials solidarily liable for P294,984.00.
**Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. No. 50419-R):** The CA reversed the CFI, absolving all defendants on the grounds that: (1) Article 2180 applies strictly to schools of arts and trades, not academic institutions; (2) the semester had already ended, terminating "custody"; (3) the fatal gun was not positively identified; and (4) defendants observed due diligence.
**Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on **Certiorari** under Rule 45. The Supreme Court affirmed the reversal/dismissal of liability, but categorically overturned the CA’s statutory construction of Article 2180.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **April 7, 1972:** Sergio Damaso, Jr., Dean of Boys at Colegio de San Jose-Recoletos, confiscated an unlicensed pistol from student Jose Gumban. Damaso returned the firearm to Gumban later that day without filing a report with the principal or initiating disciplinary proceedings.
2. **April 13, 1972:** Although fourth-year high school classes had formally ended, Alfredo Amadora went to the school auditorium to submit his physics report/experiment, a prerequisite for graduation scheduled for April 16, 1972. While in the auditorium, classmate Pablito Daffon discharged a gun, mortally wounding Alfredo (aged 17). Gumban was present with Daffon.
3. **April 16, 1972:** Scheduled commencement exercises of Colegio de San Jose-Recoletos.
4. **Subsequent Criminal Proceedings:** Daffon was prosecuted and convicted of homicide through reckless imprudence.
5. **Civil Litigation:** Alfredo’s parents and siblings instituted an action under Article 2180 of the Civil Code against the school, Rector Victor Lluch, Principal Aniano Abellana, Dean Sergio Damaso, Jr., and Physics Teacher Celestino Dicon.
6. **Trial Court Ruling:** The CFI of Cebu rendered judgment holding the school, Rector, Principal, Dean of Boys, and Physics Teacher jointly and severally liable to plaintiffs for P294,984.00.
7. **Appellate Ruling:** The Court of Appeals reversed the CFI judgment **in toto**, ruling that under **Exconde** and **Mercado**, Article 2180 applies exclusively to vocational/trade schools, and that the student was no longer in the school's custody since classes had ended.
8. **Supreme Court Petition:** Petitioners elevated the case to the Supreme Court under Rule 45 to determine the statutory scope of Article 2180.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
A. Petitioner's Interpretation
**Core Reading:**
1. Article 2180, paragraph 7 applies to academic schools and their teachers/administrators, not merely schools of arts and trades.
2. "Custody" does not end on the final day of formal classes; it encompasses the period where a graduating student is within the school campus to complete graduation prerequisites (e.g., submitting physics experiments/reports).
3. The Dean of Boys and school authorities are directly liable due to gross negligence in returning a confiscated firearm to a companion of the shooter on campus.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Distinction Rejection / In Loco Parentis:** Parents surrender custody and disciplinary authority to school officials whenever a child is on campus for school-related requirements; **culpa in vigilando** applies equally regardless of institutional classification.
**Adoption of Justice J.B.L. Reyes's Exconde Dissent / Palisoc Clarification:** The qualifying words "of arts and trades" qualify only "heads of establishments," leaving "teachers" broadly applicable to all schools.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Relieving academic schools and their faculties from supervisory tort liability while penalizing trade schools creates an irrational double standard, depriving parents of legal protection when students are placed under school authority.
B. Respondent's Interpretation
**Core Reading:**
1. Article 2180, paragraph 7 restricts vicarious liability strictly to "establishments of arts and trades." As Colegio de San Jose-Recoletos is purely an academic institution, neither it nor its staff fall under the statute.
2. The statutory phrase "so long as they remain in their custody" requires that the semester be actively in session and that students be under immediate boarding/classroom control. Because the school term had closed, custody had reverted to the parents.
3. Under Article 2180, the school entity itself is not imposable with direct liability; liability is restricted to teachers or heads.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Stare Decisis / Plain Meaning (Verba Legis):** Reliance on **Exconde v. Capuno** and **Mercado v. Court of Appeals**, holding that academic schools are excluded from the codal text.
**Strict Construction of Vicarious Liability:** Statutory exceptions to the general rule of personal fault must be strictly construed.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Expanding "custody" to post-semester activities or holding academic administrators liable would subject educational institutions to unbearable open-ended liability for acts of students outside the classroom setting.
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE] Scope of Institutions and Persons Covered:
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether Article 2180 of the Civil Code covers establishments which are technically not schools of arts and trades, and whether its coverage applies to academic institutions and teachers in general.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does the qualifying phrase "of establishments of arts and trades" in Article 2180, paragraph 7 modify both "teachers" and "heads," or does the canon **reddendo singula singulis** restrict trade schools to "heads" while extending "teachers" to all educational institutions (academic and technical alike)?
2. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE] Meaning and Temporal Scope of "In Their Custody":
**Faithful Court Formulation:** When an offending student is supposed to be "in its custody," and whether such responsibility is co-extensive with the period when the student is actually undergoing studies during the school term.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does the statutory clause "so long as they remain in their custody" mandate that the student board in the school or commit the tort during the active class semester, or does it encompass any instance where the student is within school premises for a legitimate student objective?
3. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE & Substantive Issue] Allocation of Direct Liability (School vs. Teacher):
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the school itself is directly liable under Article 2180, paragraph 7, and which specific school authority qualifies as the "teacher" or "head" subject to statutory vicarious liability.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does Article 2180, paragraph 7 impose direct vicarious liability upon the educational institution itself or its administrative superiors, or is direct liability confined exclusively to the specific "teacher-in-charge"?
4. [Substantive Issue] Defense of Due Diligence and Causation:
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the private respondents successfully established the defense of due diligence of a good father of a family under the last paragraph of Article 2180, and whether the Dean of Boys' prior confiscation and return of a firearm constituted actionable negligence for the fatal shooting.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
ISSUE 1: Scope of Institutions Covered by Article 2180, Paragraph 7
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does Article 2180 apply to academic institutions and their teachers, or is it restricted strictly to schools of arts and trades?
**YES (it applies to all schools).** Following the canon **reddendo singula singulis**, "teachers" applies broadly to pupils and students in all institutions (academic and non-academic), while the phrase "heads of establishments of arts and trades" applies exclusively to apprentices in technical/vocational institutions.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"After an exhaustive examination of the problem, the Court has come to the conclusion that the provision in question should apply to **all** schools, academic as well as non-academic. Where the school is academic rather than technical or vocational in nature, responsibility for the tort committed by the student will attach to the teacher in charge of such student, following the first part of the provision. This is the general rule. In the case of establishments of arts and trades, it is the head thereof, and only he, who shall be held liable as an exception to the general rule. In other words, teachers in general shall be liable for the acts of their students except where the school is technical in nature, in which case it is the head thereof who shall be answerable. Following the canon of **reddendo singula singulis** 'teachers' should apply to the words 'pupils and students' and 'heads of establishments of arts and trades' to the word 'apprentices.'"
"'...In my opinion, in the phrase "teachers or heads of establishments of arts and trades" used in Art. 1903 of the old Civil Code, the words "arts and trades" does not qualify "teachers" but only "heads of establishments." The phrase is only an updated version of the equivalent terms "preceptores y artesanos" used in the Italian and French Civil Codes.' **(quoting J.B.L. Reyes, J., dissenting in Exconde v. Capuno)**"
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court discarded the restrictive **obiter dicta** of **Exconde** and **Mercado**, finding that the syntax of the provision required formal statutory construction.
2. Intrinsic Aids Examined (Syntactical Canons):
**Doctrine of the Last Antecedent:** The adjectival qualifying phrase **"of establishments of arts and trades"** qualifies only its proximate antecedent **"heads"**, and does not reach back across the disjunctive "or" to qualify **"teachers"**.
**Reddendo Singula Singulis:** The subjects and objects are distributed respectively: "teachers" corresponds to "pupils and students"; "heads of establishments of arts and trades" corresponds to "apprentices."
3. Extrinsic Aids Examined:
**Historical & Comparative Law Origins:** The Court reviewed European civil law antecedents (French and Italian Civil Codes) which paired **"preceptores"** (teachers) with students, and **"artesanos"** (artisans/masters) with apprentices.
**Historical Institutional Roles:** Historically, the head of an arts and trades school acted as an artisan-master exercising direct personal tutelage over live-in apprentices, whereas academic school heads exercised remote, purely administrative functions over independent teachers.
4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies (Presumption Against Absurdity & Discrimination):** The Court held it irrational to demand high vigilance from trade school instructors while immunizing academic teachers from **culpa in vigilando**, as the degree of required student oversight is identical.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The prior pronouncements in **Exconde** and **Mercado** excluding academic institutions were declared **dicta** and officially overturned.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
The Supreme Court applied the rule of **reddendo singula singulis** to distribute the subjects to their corresponding terms: academic "teachers" watch over "pupils and students," while "heads of establishments of arts and trades" watch over "apprentices." The qualifying words "of arts and trades" only attach to "heads," so academic schools and their teachers fall squarely within the coverage of Article 2180.
ISSUE 2: Meaning and Temporal Scope of "In Their Custody"
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does "custody" require the student to board at school or commit the tort during formal classroom hours within the active semester?
**NO.** "Custody" does not mean boarding or physical detention, nor is it strictly co-terminous with the active semester; it exists whenever the student is within school premises for any legitimate school purpose or student objective.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"From a reading of the provision under examination, it is clear that while the custody requirement, to repeat **Palisoc v. Brillantes**, does not mean that the student must be boarding with the school authorities, it does signify that the student should be within the control and under the influence of the school authorities at the time of the occurrence of the injury. This does not necessarily mean that such custody be co-terminous with the semester, beginning with the start of classes and ending upon the close thereof... In the view of the Court, the student is in the custody of the school authorities as long as he is under the control and influence of the school and within its premises, whether the semester has not yet begun or has already ended."
"As long as it can be shown that the student is in the school premises in pursuance of a legitimate student objective, in the exercise of a legitimate student right, and even in the enjoyment of a legitimate student right, and even in the enjoyment of a legitimate student privilege, the responsibility of the school authorities over the student continues."
"Custody does not connote immediate and actual physical control but refers more to the influence exerted on the child and the discipline instilled in him as a result of such influence."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** Rejecting the rigid literal interpretation that custody terminates on the last official day of lectures.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** Harmonized "custody" with the protective and disciplinary rationale underlying substitute parental authority (**in loco parentis**) in the Civil Code framework.
3. **Extrinsic Aids (Jurisprudential Evolution):** Reaffirmed **Palisoc v. Brillantes**, confirming that the living-in/boarding requirement stated in **Mercado** was obsolete and repudiated.
4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** Presumption against an interpretation producing absurdity: a student registering early or completing graduation requirements is fully amenable to school rules; it would be illogical to treat them as discipline-free strangers the moment formal lectures cease.
5. **Application to Facts:** Alfredo Amadora was lawfully inside the auditorium to submit his physics experiment for graduation; therefore, he was legally in the custody of the school authorities.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
"Custody" under Article 2180 does not mean living in a school dormitory or being confined to a classroom desk during semester dates. It means being subject to school discipline and authority within school grounds for any valid student purpose—even after regular classes end or while merely enjoying campus life with peers.
ISSUE 3: Allocation of Direct Vicarious Liability (School vs. Teacher-in-Charge)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Can the school entity itself or general administrative officers (Rector, Principal, Dean of Boys) be held directly liable under Article 2180, paragraph 7?
**NO.** Under the plain text of Article 2180, paragraph 7, direct vicarious liability attaches exclusively to the specific "teacher-in-charge" (in academic schools) or the head (in trade schools); the school itself can only be pursued under **respondeat superior** (Article 2180, paragraph 5) as an employer.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"In any event, it should be noted that the liability imposed by this article is supposed to fall directly on the teacher or the head of the school of arts and trades and not on the school itself. If at all, the school, whatever its nature, may be held to answer for the acts of its teachers or even of the head thereof under the general principle of **respondeat superior**, but then it may exculpate itself from liability by proof that it had exercised the diligence of a **bonus paterfamilias**."
"The rector, the high school principal and the dean of boys cannot be held liable because none of them was the teacher-in-charge as previously defined. Each of them was exercising only a general authority over the student body and not the direct control and influence exerted by the teacher placed in charge of particular classes or sections and thus immediately involved in its discipline."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate / Verba Legis:** The text explicitly states: **"teachers or heads... shall be liable"**; it does **not** state that the "school" or "institution" is liable.
2. **Literal Allocation:** The statute names specific individuals because liability is founded upon direct personal **culpa in vigilando** over students.
3. **Harmonization with Paragraph 5 (Respondeat Superior):** The school entity is implicated only secondarily as an **employer** of the negligent teacher under paragraph 5, which allows the school to be exonerated if it proves diligence in selection and supervision (**bonus paterfamilias**).
4. **Definition of "Teacher-in-Charge":** The "teacher" contemplated by law is the designated teacher-in-charge of the particular class, section, or activity. General administrators (rector, principal, dean) possess only macro-administrative oversight and are not "teachers-in-charge." Respondent Dicon was merely the physics teacher, not the teacher-in-charge of the killer (Daffon).
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
Article 2180 singles out the individual teacher or shop head, not the school corporation, because liability rests on the personal failure to supervise students. An academic school can only be sued as an employer under the separate employer-employee liability clause, and administrators like principals and deans are not the specific "teachers-in-charge" of the offending student.
ISSUE 4: Exoneration via Due Diligence and Causal Connection
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Were any of the named respondents liable for damages resulting from Alfredo Amadora’s death?
**NO.** The designated teacher-in-charge was never identified or impleaded; Physics Teacher Dicon was not negligent; the Dean of Boys' prior return of a confiscated weapon was not causally proven to be the fatal instrument; and the school demonstrated adequate protective regulations and security.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"The responsibility treated of in this article shall cease when the persons herein mentioned prove that they observed all the diligence of a good father of a family to prevent damages."
"While this was clearly negligence on his part, for which he deserves sanctions from the school, it does not necessarily link him to the shooting of Amadora as it has not been shown that the confiscated and returned pistol was the gun that killed the petitioners' son."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Statutory Exculpation Clause:** The final paragraph of Article 2180 expressly provides that vicarious liability ceases upon proof of the diligence of a good father of a family (**bonus paterfamilias**).
2. **Failure of Identification:** The records failed to establish who the teacher-in-charge of Pablito Daffon was. Dicon was not shown to be Daffon’s teacher-in-charge, was not scheduled to report on that day, and did not condone rule infractions.
3. **Break in Proximate Causation:** Although Dean Damaso committed an administrative infraction by returning an unlicensed firearm to student Gumban days earlier, petitioners failed to present evidence that this specific pistol was the weapon Daffon used to shoot Amadora.
4. **Institutional Diligence:** Colegio de San Jose-Recoletos showed it maintained established safety rules and an adequate security force to enforce discipline, satisfying employer due diligence.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
Even though academic teachers are legally covered by Article 2180, plaintiffs failed to sue the specific teacher supervising the shooter. The physics teacher was not at fault, and while the dean was careless in returning a gun days earlier, there was no proof that gun was the murder weapon. Hence, statutory defenses and failure of proof blocked civil recovery.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
**Concurring and Dissenting Opinion of Melencio-Herrera, J.:**
**StatCon Divergence:** Dissented from the majority's restrictive construction of "teacher" as solely the "teacher-in-charge."
**Canons / Intrinsic Harmony Invoked:** Harmonized Article 2180 with Article 349 (which vests substitute parental authority broadly in "teachers and professors") and Article 352. Argued that restricting liability to a "teacher-in-charge" of a class undercuts the broad protective purpose of **in loco parentis**.
**Vicarious Liability Analysis:** Maintained that the protective custody of school heads and teachers is mandatorily substituted for that of parents under **Palisoc**, and schools should be readily held accountable as employers whenever teachers or administrators breach substitute parental obligations.
**Concurring Opinion of Gutierrez, Jr., J.:**
**StatCon Critique / Plea for Legislative Action:** Concurred in the outcome but urged the complete statutory repeal or amendment of Article 2180, paragraph 7.
**Obsolete Text / Cessante Ratione Legis:** Characterized the provision as an antiquated "relic of the past" founded on an extinct social model of artisan masters and live-in apprentices. Argued that modern college/high school students are not compliant children, and subjecting teachers to a presumption of negligence (**culpa in vigilando**) for adult or violent students is profoundly unjust. Emphasized that the Court cannot legislate, and ordinary quasi-delict principles (Article 2176) should govern.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
**"WHEREFORE, the petition is DENIED, without any pronouncement as to costs. It is so ordered."**
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals' dismissal of the civil suit against Colegio de San Jose-Recoletos, its administrators, and its faculty, completely denying monetary damages to the Amadora family. While the decision established the groundbreaking statutory doctrine that Article 2180 governs **all** schools (academic and trade alike) and that "custody" extends to legitimate presence on campus outside formal class dates, the respondents were absolved because the true teacher-in-charge was never identified, no actionable negligence was causally proven against the impleaded staff, and the school proved due diligence.

Davide, Jr., **C.J.**, Bellosillo, Melo, Puno, Vitug, Kapunan, Mendoza, Panganiban, Quisumbing, Pardo, Buena, De Leon, Jr., Sandoval-Gutierrez, and Carpio, **JJ.**, concurred. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown Primary StatCon Classification: **Statutory Construction Area:** Intrinsic & Extrinsic Aids / Implication & Omission in Statutes / Repeals **Specific Canons / Principles Applied:** 1. Legislative Intent through Legislative History and Deliberations (Extrinsic Aid) ### 2. Doctrine of Necessary Implication (Ex necessitate legis) 3. Presumption Against Implied Repeals / Express Mention in Repealing Clause 4. Principle of Omission (Casus omissus pro omisso habendus est) 5. No. 7160 include the salaries and benefits of extension class teachers, and whether the omission of scholarship grants therein precludes funding college scholarships from the Special Education Fund (SEF). The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim): Republic Act No. 7160 (Local Government Code of 1991) **SEC. 100. Meeting and Quorum; Budget.** — xxx xxx xxx (c) The annual school board budget shall give priority to the following: (1) Construction, repair, and maintenance of school buildings and other facilities of public elementary and secondary schools; (2) **Establishment and maintenance of extension classes** where necessary; and (3) Sports activities at the division, district, municipal, and barangay levels. **SEC. 272. Application of Proceeds of the Additional One Percent SEF Tax.** — The proceeds from the additional one percent (1%) tax on real property accruing to the SEF shall be automatically released to the local school boards: **Provided,** That, in case of provinces, the proceeds shall be divided equally between the provincial and municipal school boards: **Provided, however,** That the proceeds shall be allocated for the **operation and maintenance of public schools**, construction and repair of school buildings, facilities and equipment, educational research, purchase of books and periodicals, and sports development as determined and approved by the local school board. **SEC. 534. Repealing Clause.** — xxx (c) The provisions of . . . **Sections 3, a (3) and b (2) of Republic Act No. 5447**, regarding the Special Education Fund . . . are hereby repealed and rendered of no force and effect. Historical / Amendment Tracking: Republic Act No. 5447 (Special Education Fund Act of 1968), Section 1: **SEC. 1. Declaration of Policy; Coverage of the Fund.** — ...the SEF may be expended exclusively for the following activities of the DECS — (a) the **organization and operation of such number of extension classes** as may be needed to accommodate all children of school age desiring to enter Grade I, **including the creation of positions of classroom teachers, head teachers and principals for such extension classes** x x x; xxx xxx xxx (c) the **payment and adjustment of salaries of public school teachers** under and by virtue of Republic Act Numbered Five Thousand One Hundred Sixty-Eight and all the benefits in favor of public school teachers provided under Republic Act Numbered Four Thousand Six Hundred Seventy; xxx xxx xxx (j) the **granting of government scholarships to poor but deserving students under Republic Act Numbered Four Thousand Ninety**; and (k) the promotion of physical education, such as athletic meets. StatCon Diagnostic Profile: **The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Latent Ambiguity / Legislative Omission. Sections 100(c) and 272 of R.A. No. 7160 provide for "operation and maintenance of public schools" and "establishment and maintenance of extension classes" without explicitly repeating the detailed list found in Section 1 of R.A. No. 5447 (which expressly itemized teacher salaries/positions and college scholarship grants). **Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. Because the statute enumerated broad operational priorities without detailing the specific allowable line-item expenditures (e.g., personnel costs vs. structural maintenance) and omitted specific items previously authorized by R.A. No. 5447, judicial interpretation was required to ascertain legislative intent. **Controlling Canons / Maxims Deployed:** 1. **Legislative Intent:** "It is a basic precept in statutory construction that the intent of the legislature is the controlling factor in the interpretation of a statute." 2. **Ex necessitate legis (Doctrine of Necessary Implication):** "Every statute is understood, by implication, to contain all such provisions as may be necessary to effectuate its object and purpose... Verily, the services and the corresponding compensation of these teachers are necessary and indispensable to the establishment and maintenance of extension classes." 3. **Presumption Against Implied Repeal:** The legislature is presumed to know existing laws; the express repeal of only Section 3 of R.A. No. 5447 leaves Section 1 provisions that are not inconsistent with R.A. No. 7160 in force. 4. **Casus omissus pro omisso habendus est:** "A person, object, or thing omitted from an enumeration in a statute must be held to have been omitted intentionally. It is not for this Court to supply such grant of scholarship where the legislature has omitted it." **Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The Provincial Auditor of Cebu issued Notices of Suspension disallowing the Provincial Government's use of its SEF to pay the salaries of extension class public school teachers and to finance college scholarship grants, asserting that R.A. No. 7160 repealed prior authorizations under R.A. No. 5447. 3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture **Key Parties & Roles:** **Petitioner:** Commission on Audit (COA) of the Province of Cebu, represented by Provincial Auditor Roy L. Ursal, tasked with auditing provincial public expenditures. **Respondent:** Province of Cebu, represented by Governor Pablo P. Garcia (acting as Chairman of the Provincial School Board), which appointed non-plantilla teachers for extension classes and funded college scholarship grants from the SEF. **Implementing/Referenced Agencies:** Department of Education, Culture and Sports (DECS); Provincial and Municipal School Boards. **Procedural History & Vehicle:** 1. **Notices of Suspension:** Issued by petitioner COA against the Province of Cebu for January–June 1998 expenditures from the SEF for teachers' salaries and scholarship grants. 2. **Trial Court:** Respondent Province filed a Petition for Declaratory Relief (Civil Case No. CEB-24422) before the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Cebu City, Branch 20. On December 13, 1999, the RTC rendered a decision declaring both teachers' compensation and scholarship grants authorized expenditures of the SEF, and declared pages 36 and 37 of COA’s Annual Audit Report for 1999 null and void. 3. **Supreme Court:** Direct Petition for Review on a pure question of law filed by COA. The Supreme Court affirmed the RTC decision with modification: salaries of extension class teachers are chargeable to the SEF, but college scholarship grants are not. ### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard 1. **January 1, 1969:** R.A. No. 5447 takes effect, creating the SEF and expressly dedicating it under Section 1 to activities including the organization of extension classes, creation of teacher positions, payment of teacher salaries, and granting of scholarships under R.A. No. 4090. 2. **January 1, 1992:** R.A. No. 7160 (Local Government Code of 1991) takes effect. Under Sections 100(c) and 272, SEF proceeds are allocated to the "operation and maintenance of public schools" and "establishment and maintenance of extension classes," while Section 534(c) expressly repeals Sections 3, a(3), and b(2) of R.A. No. 5447. 3. **1998:** Pablo P. Garcia, Governor of Cebu and Chairman of the Provincial School Board, appoints classroom teachers lacking DECS plantilla items to handle extension classes to accommodate public school students. 4. **January to June 1998:** The Province pays the salaries and personnel-related benefits of these extension class teachers, as well as college scholarship grants for poor and deserving students, out of the provincial SEF. 5. **Post-June 1998 Audit:** Provincial Auditor Roy L. Ursal conducts an audit of the Province's accounts and determines that teacher salaries and college scholarship grants are not lawful charges against the SEF under the Local Government Code. 6. **1998–1999:** COA issues Notices of Suspension to the Province of Cebu. COA also reflects these findings in pages 36 and 37 of the Annual Audit Report on the Province of Cebu for 1999. 7. **Declaratory Relief Action:** Confronted by the suspensions, the Province files a Petition for Declaratory Relief (Civil Case No. CEB-24422) in RTC Cebu, Branch 20. 8. **December 13, 1999:** The RTC renders judgment in favor of the Province, declaring both the personnel benefits and scholarship grants validly chargeable to the SEF, and voiding the audit findings. 9. **Direct Appeal:** Petitioner COA elevates the case to the Supreme Court on a pure question of law. 5. **Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the expenses for college scholarship grants may be charged to the Special Education Fund (SEF) of the local government unit concerned.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does the omission of "granting of government scholarships" from Sections 100(c) and 272 of R.A. No. 7160—which otherwise substantially reproduced Section 1 of R.A. No. 5447—prohibit charging college scholarships to the SEF under the principle of **casus omissus pro omisso habendus est**?
3. [Procedural Issue]
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the petition for declaratory relief was proper considering that the COA had already issued Notices of Suspension.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does the issuance of audit Notices of Suspension constitute a breach or violation that bars an action for declaratory relief under Section 1, Rule 63 of the Rules of Court?
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Salaries and Benefits of Extension Class Teachers
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The salaries and personnel-related benefits of teachers appointed by local school boards strictly in connection with the establishment and maintenance of extension classes are lawful charges against the SEF under the doctrine of necessary implication and clear legislative intent.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"It is a basic precept in statutory construction that the intent of the legislature is the controlling factor in the interpretation of a statute."
"Undoubtedly, the aforecited exchange of views clearly demonstrates that the legislature intended the SEF to answer for the compensation of teachers handling extension classes."
"The legislature is presumed to know the existing laws, such that whenever it intends to repeal a particular or specific provision of law, it does so expressly. The failure to add a specific repealing clause particularly mentioning the statute to be repealed indicates that the intent was not to repeal any existing law on the matter, unless an irreconcilable inconsistency and repugnancy exists in the terms of the new and the old laws. Hence, the provisions allocating funds for the salaries of teachers under Section 1, of R.A. No. 5447, which are not inconsistent with Sections 272 and 100 (c) of the Local Government Code, remain in force and effect."
"Even under the doctrine of necessary implication, the allocation of the SEF for the establishment and maintenance of extension classes logically implies the hiring of teachers who should, as a matter of course be compensated for their services. Every statute is understood, by implication, to contain all such provisions as may be necessary to effectuate its object and purpose, or to make effective rights, powers, privileges or jurisdiction which it grants, including all such collateral and subsidiary consequences as may be fairly and logically inferred from its terms. **Ex necessitate legis**. Verily, the services and the corresponding compensation of these teachers are necessary and indispensable to the establishment and maintenance of extension classes."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court rejected petitioner's rigid invocation of **expressio unius est exclusio alterius**, finding that the phrase "establishment and maintenance of extension classes" could not be read in a vacuum without ascertaining legislative intent.
2. Extrinsic Aids Examined (Deliberations):
**Senate (July 30, 1990):** Senator Pimentel clarified to Senator Guingona that the transfer of the elementary school system covered "payment of salaries, emoluments, allowances et cetera."
**House of Representatives (August 16, 1990):** Representative De Pedro explained to Representative Raymundo that regarding the maintenance of extension classes, "the school boards may provide out of its own funds, for additional teachers or other requirements if the national government cannot provide funding therefor."
3. **Repeal Analysis & Presumptions:** The Court examined Section 534(c) of R.A. No. 7160 and found that it only expressly repealed Section 3 of R.A. No. 5447 (taxes on Virginia-type cigarettes). Because implied repeals are disfavored, Section 1 of R.A. No. 5447 (authorizing payment of teachers for extension classes) remained valid since it was entirely consistent with Section 100(c) and Section 272.
4. **Intrinsic Aid / Doctrine of Necessary Implication (**Ex necessitate legis**):** Setting up an extension class is physically and functionally impossible without an instructor. The power to establish and maintain classes necessarily and indispensable includes the authority to hire and compensate teachers.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction & Limitation:** Petitioner's contention that "maintenance" refers exclusively to structural upkeep of buildings was rejected as contrary to legislative intent. However, the Court circumscribed the ruling: not **every** kind of personnel-related benefit is chargeable to the SEF, but **only** those of teachers appointed in connection with extension classes needed to accommodate school-age children seeking basic education.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation: (Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
The Supreme Court held that the authority under the Local Government Code to "establish and maintain extension classes" using the Special Education Fund inherently includes paying the teachers hired for those classes. Under the doctrine of necessary implication (**ex necessitate legis**), a school cannot operate classes without teachers, and the legislative transcripts confirm that Congress explicitly intended for local school boards to fund supplementary teachers where the national government cannot.
Issue 2: College Scholarship Grants
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** College scholarship grants are not authorized expenditures under the SEF because Congress intentionally omitted them from the priorities listed in the Local Government Code.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"With respect, however, to college scholarship grants, a reading of the pertinent laws of the Local Government Code reveals that said grants are not among the projects for which the proceeds of the SEF may be appropriated. It should be noted that Sections 100 (c) and 272 of the Local Government Code substantially reproduced Section 1, of R.A. No. 5447. But, unlike payment of salaries of teachers which falls within the ambit of 'establishment and maintenance of extension classes' and 'operation and maintenance of public schools,' the 'granting of government scholarship to poor but deserving students' was omitted in Sections 100 (c) and 272 of the Local Government Code. **Casus omissus pro omisso habendus est**. A person, object, or thing omitted from an enumeration in a statute must be held to have been omitted intentionally. It is not for this Court to supply such grant of scholarship where the legislature has omitted it."
"In the same vein, however noble the intention of the province in extending said scholarship to deserving students, we cannot apply the doctrine of necessary implication inasmuch as the grant of scholarship is neither necessary nor indispensable to the operation and maintenance of public schools. Instead, such scholarship grants may be charged to the General Funds of the province."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Comparative Statutory Analysis:** The Court compared Section 1 of R.A. No. 5447 with Sections 100(c) and 272 of R.A. No. 7160. While R.A. No. 7160 substantially reproduced the old statute's operational categories, it conspicuously left out Section 1(j) of R.A. No. 5447 ("granting of government scholarships to poor but deserving students").
2. **Application of Casus Omissus:** Under the maxim **casus omissus pro omisso habendus est**, an omission from an enumeration must be treated as intentional by the legislature. The judiciary has no power to supply an omitted item.
3. **Inapplicability of Necessary Implication:** Unlike teachers—who are indispensable to maintaining a classroom—college scholarships are neither necessary nor indispensable to the "operation and maintenance of public schools."
4. **Harmonization:** While the SEF cannot be used, the Court clarified that the Province may still legally fund college scholarships by charging them against its General Funds.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation: (Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
College scholarships cannot be funded by the SEF because, while Congress copied most of the old SEF activities into the Local Government Code, it deliberately dropped the provision on scholarships. Under the principle of **casus omissus**, an item omitted from a statutory list must be deemed intentionally excluded by lawmakers, and unlike hiring teachers, college scholarships are not indispensable to running basic public schools.
Issue 3: Propriety of Declaratory Relief Post-Notice of Suspension
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The petition for declaratory relief was proper because resolving the statutory interpretation of the SEF was indispensable to guide future transactions and remove administrative uncertainty.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"As held in **Shell Company of the Philippines, Ltd. v. Municipality of Sipocot**, any breach of the statute subject of the controversy will not affect the case; the action for declaratory relief will prosper because the applicability of the statute in question to future transactions still remains to be resolved. Absent a definite ruling in the instant case for declaratory relief, doubts as to the disposition of the SEF will persist. Hence, the trial court did not err in giving due course to the petition for declaratory relief filed by the province of Cebu."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Procedural Rule:** Section 1, Rule 63 requires an action for declaratory relief to be filed before any breach or violation.
2. **Evaluation of COA's Argument:** COA contended that its Notices of Suspension constituted an antecedent breach.
3. **Application of Jurisprudential Exception:** Citing **Shell Company of the Philippines, Ltd. v. Municipality of Sipocot**, the Court affirmed that when the ongoing applicability of a statute to continuous, recurrent, and future public fiscal transactions is unsettled, an action for declaratory relief will lie to avoid recurring statutory doubt.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation: (Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
Even though COA had already issued audit suspensions, declaratory relief remained procedurally valid because the provincial government needed an authoritative legal interpretation of the Local Government Code to determine how it could legally budget and spend its Special Education Fund in future fiscal years.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text. (The decision is unanimous).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, in view of all the foregoing, the Decision of the Regional Trial Court of Cebu City, Branch 20, in Civil Case No. CEB-24422, is AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. The salaries and personnel-related benefits of the teachers appointed by the provincial school board of Cebu in connection with the establishment and maintenance of extension classes, are declared chargeable against the Special Education Fund of the province. However, the expenses incurred by the provincial government for the college scholarship grants should not be charged against the Special Education Fund, but against the General Funds of the province of Cebu.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Province of Cebu partially prevailed: the Supreme Court upheld its use of the Special Education Fund to pay the salaries and benefits of extension class teachers, but disallowed charging college scholarship grants to the SEF, ordering that college scholarships instead be drawn from the Province's General Funds. Henceforth, local school boards may only charge personnel costs to the SEF if the teachers are hired specifically for extension classes to accommodate basic education students.

### STATUTORY CONSTRUCTION CASE BRIEFER
### 1. CASE HEADER & CITATION BLOCK
**Concise Recognizable Title: Spouses Delfino v. St. James Hospital, Inc.**
**Full Official Caption:** SPS. NEREO & NIEVA DELFINO, Petitioners, v. ST. JAMES HOSPITAL, INC., and THE HONORABLE RONALDO ZAMORA, EXECUTIVE SECRETARY, OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:**
G.R. No. 166735
Promulgation Date: November 23, 2007 (Resolution on Motion for Reconsideration; original Decision promulgated September 5, 2006)
538 SCRA 367 / Phil. Reports citation pending
Ponente: Chico-Nazario, **J.**
Voting Breakdown: Special Third Division; Unanimous (Ynares-Santiago, **J.** [Chairperson], Quisumbing, Austria-Martinez, Chico-Nazario, and Reyes, **JJ.**, concurring). No separate opinions.
### 2. STATCON DIAGNOSTIC MATRIX & GOVERNING PROVISION BREAKDOWN
Primary StatCon Classification
**Statutory Construction Area:** Intrinsic Aids / Canons of Restrictive Interpretation & Amendment by Omission
**Specific Canon / Principle / Rule Applied:** Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius; Casus Omissus Pro Omisso Habendus Est; Prospective Application of Statutes / Non-Retroactivity (**Lex Retro Non Agit**)
**Specific Latin Maxim: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius** (the express mention of one thing in a law means the exclusion of others not expressly mentioned); **Casus omissus** (a thing omitted must be considered to have been omitted intentionally)
**Specific Sub-Issue:** Whether the broad term "institutional" within a residential zone regulation allows hospitals, where the zoning ordinance specifically created a separate "institutional zone" and deleted hospitals from the enumeration of permitted residential uses.
The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim)
1. 1991 Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP) / Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance of the Municipality of Santa Rosa, Laguna:
**Article VI, Section 2, Paragraph 1:**
**[Residential Zone Use Regulations]**
"...retained uses that are commercial and **institutional** as well as recreational in character and those for the maintenance of ecological balance..."
**(Note: As construed alongside the restrictive enumeration of allowable uses under the same Section).**
**Article VI, Section 4. USE REGULATIONS IN INSTITUTIONAL ZONE:**
"In the Institutional Zone, only the following shall be allowed:
1. Government center to move all national, regional, or local offices in the area;
2. School;
    2.1. Public/Private Elementary schools.
    2.2. Municipal/Barangay/Private high schools
3. **Health facilities;**
    **3.1. Emergency hospital**
    **3.2 Health centers**
    **3.3. Multi-purpose clinics**
    **3.4 Day-care centers**
4. Religious Facilities such as churches, chapels and other places of worships.
5. Scientific, cultural and academic centers and research facilities."
**Article X, Section 1. EXISTING NON-CONFORMING USES AND BUILDINGS:**
"The lawful uses of any building, structure or land at the point of adoption or amendment of this Ordinance may be continued, although such does not conform with the provisions of this Ordinance.
1. That **no non-conforming use shall be enlarged or increased or extended to occupy a greater area or land that has already been occupied by such use at the time of the adoption of this Ordinance**, or moved in whole or in part to any other portion of the lot parcel of land where such non-conforming use exist at the time of the adoption of this Ordinance."
Historical / Amendment Tracking
**1981 Zoning Ordinance of Santa Rosa, Laguna:** Expressly allowed within a residential zone uses such as schools, religious facilities/places of worship, clinics, and hospitals ("hospital with not more than ten capacity"), as well as parks, playgrounds, and recreation centers under letters (h) and (k).
**1991 Zoning Ordinance:** Transferred schools, religious facilities, and health facilities (hospitals/clinics) out of the residential zone and placed them into an entirely separate, newly created "Institutional Zone" (Art. VI, Sec. 4). "Hospital" was completely deleted from the enumeration of permitted uses under the Residential Zone (Art. VI, Sec. 2).
**1999 Santa Rosa Zoning Ordinance:** Enacted subsequently; sought to be invoked by respondent for the first time on Motion for Reconsideration before the Supreme Court.
StatCon Diagnostic Profile
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Latent Ambiguity / Conflict Between General Terms and Specific Enumerations. Respondent and the lower tribunals seized upon the general descriptive word "institutional" in Section 2, Article VI to subsume hospitals within permitted residential uses, despite the affirmative omission of "hospitals" from the residential list and its express relocation to Section 4 (Institutional Zone).
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. Construction was necessary to harmonize the general descriptive word "institutional" with the explicit, restrictive enumeration of allowed uses, and to determine the legal effect of the transfer of health facilities from residential to institutional zones across successive municipal ordinances.
**Controlling Canons / Maxims Deployed:**
1. Expressio unius est exclusio alterius
2. Casus omissus
3. Non-retroactivity / Cause of action governed by the law in force at the time it arose
4. Bar against changing theory / raising new issues for the first time on motion for reconsideration
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** In 1994, St. James Hospital, Inc. applied for an expansion permit with the Housing and Land Use Regulatory Board (HLURB) to convert its existing facility into a four-storey, 40-bed capacity hospital within the residential Mariquita Pueblo Subdivision, prompting neighboring residents (Sps. Delfino) to challenge the expansion as a prohibited enlargement of a non-conforming use under the 1991 Zoning Ordinance.
### 3. CAST OF CHARACTERS & PROCEDURAL POSTURE
Key Parties & Roles
**Spouses Nereo & Nieva Delfino (Petitioners):** Residents of Mariquita Pueblo Subdivision, Santa Rosa, Laguna, who opposed the expansion of St. James Hospital on the ground that it violated the 1991 Zoning Ordinance.
**St. James Hospital, Inc. (Private Respondent):** Owner/operator of a medical facility inside Mariquita Pueblo Subdivision seeking a building permit to expand into a four-storey, 40-bed institution.
**Executive Secretary Ronaldo Zamora / Office of the President (Public Respondent):** Executive appellate authority that reversed the HLURB zoning denial, ruling that "institutional" uses permitted hospitals within residential zones.
**Housing and Land Use Regulatory Board (HLURB):** The administrative agency that originally evaluated the 1994 permit application.
Procedural History & Vehicle
1. **Administrative Tier (HLURB & Office of the President):** St. James Hospital applied in 1994 with the HLURB to expand. The dispute reached the Office of the President (OP). The OP ruled in favor of the hospital, giving expansive meaning to the word "institutional" in Sec. 2, Art. VI of the 1991 Ordinance.
2. **Court of Appeals (CA):** Affirmed the OP decision, holding that the term "institutional" under Sec. 2, Art. VI encompassed hospitals.
3. **Supreme Court (Petition for Review under Rule 45 - September 5, 2006 Decision):** The Supreme Court **reversed** the CA and OP, holding that under **expressio unius est exclusio alterius** and **casus omissus**, the 1991 Ordinance excluded hospitals from residential zones, rendering St. James Hospital a non-conforming structure whose enlargement was barred by Section 1, Article X.
4. **Current Vehicle (Motion for Reconsideration):** Respondent St. James Hospital filed an MR assailing the September 5, 2006 Decision, re-arguing the legislative history of the 1991 Ordinance and invoking for the first time the 1999 Zoning Ordinance. The Supreme Court **denied** the Motion for Reconsideration.
### 4. CHRONOLOGICAL FACTS STORYBOARD
1. **1981:** The Municipality of Santa Rosa, Laguna enacts its 1981 Zoning Ordinance. Under this ordinance, residential zones allow residential dwellings as well as schools, places of worship, clinics, and "hospitals with not more than ten capacity."
2. **1991:** Santa Rosa enacts its 1991 Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP) / Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance. The new ordinance restructures municipal classifications:
Section 2, Article VI regulates Residential Zones, retaining commercial, institutional, and recreational descriptors, but strictly enumerating allowable uses without listing hospitals.
Section 4, Article VI establishes an entirely separate "Institutional Zone" expressly covering "Health facilities," including emergency hospitals, clinics, and health centers.
Section 1, Article X provides that existing non-conforming uses may continue, but prohibits any non-conforming use from being enlarged, increased, or extended.
3. **1994:** St. James Hospital, Inc. applies to the HLURB for an expansion permit to upgrade its facility inside Mariquita Pueblo Subdivision into a four-storey, 40-bed medical hospital.
4. **Administrative & Appellate Litigation:** Sps. Delfino oppose the application. The HLURB proceedings lead to an appeal to the Office of the President. The OP rules that the hospital is an allowed "institutional" use in a residential zone.
5. Court of Appeals Review: The CA affirms the OP's broad construction of "institutional."
6. **September 5, 2006:** The Supreme Court (Third Division) renders a Decision granting the Delfinos' petition, reversing the CA, declaring the hospital a non-conforming structure under the 1991 Ordinance, and invalidating its expansion under Section 1, Article X.
7. **Post-Decision Motion for Reconsideration:** St. James Hospital files an MR arguing: (a) the legislative history of the 1991 Ordinance shows institutional uses remained authorized in residential zones; and (b) the case must now be governed by a subsequent 1999 Zoning Ordinance, raised for the first time before the SC.
### 5. COMPETING INTERPRETATIONS MATRIX (THE CLASH OF CANONS)
A. Private Respondent’s Interpretation (St. James Hospital, Inc.)
**Core Reading:** The phrase "commercial and institutional" in Sec. 2, Par. 1 of the 1991 Zoning Ordinance acts as an umbrella clause. The omission of specific words like "hospitals," "parks," and "playgrounds" from the detailed list did not mean they were banned; they were subsumed under the broad categories of "institutional" and "recreational" uses. Consequently, the hospital is a conforming use, rendering the non-conforming expansion ban of Art. X inapplicable. Additionally, the dispute should be governed by the 1999 Zoning Ordinance.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Legislative History:** Comparing the 1981 and 1991 ordinances reveals an intent to retain broad categories rather than prohibit established public-welfare activities.
**Generalia Verba Sunt Generaliter Intelligenda:** Broad, generic words ("institutional") should be given their natural, comprehensive scope.
**Subsequent Enactment Rule:** The latest zoning ordinance (1999) supervenes prior zoning restrictions.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Reading the exclusion literally leads to absurdity, as it would ban even parks and playgrounds from residential subdivisions merely because they were not explicitly re-listed.
B. Petitioners' Interpretation (Sps. Delfino) & Adopted Court Doctrine
**Core Reading:** Sec. 2, Art. VI of the 1991 Ordinance sets forth an exhaustive and restrictive list of permitted uses in residential zones. Any general reference to "institutional" is cabined and restricted by the express enumeration that follows it. Because health facilities/hospitals were expressly excised from the residential classification and transferred into a newly created "Institutional Zone" under Sec. 4, Art. VI, their omission from the residential zone was deliberate. St. James Hospital is therefore an existing non-conforming use that cannot legally be expanded under Sec. 1, Art. X.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Expressio unius est exclusio alterius:** Express mention of permitted uses excludes all omitted uses.
**Casus omissus pro omisso habendus est:** An omission in a revised or amendatory enactment is presumed to be intentional.
**Rule of Non-Retroactivity / Law at Time Cause of Action Arose:** The legality of an administrative permit application is governed strictly by the law in effect at the time of the application (1994 / 1991 Ordinance).
**Procedural Due Process Rule on New Theories:** A party cannot raise an entirely new statutory defense (the 1999 Ordinance) for the first time in a Motion for Reconsideration before the court of last resort.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Allowing high-capacity commercial-institutional hospitals inside quiet residential subdivisions destroys zoning boundaries and flouts the municipal council's explicit scheme of segregating high-density health facilities into designated institutional zones.
### 6. INVENTORY OF ISSUES
### 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the term "institutional" in Section 2, Article VI of the 1991 Zoning Ordinance must be given an expansive definition to include hospitals, or whether it is strictly limited by the explicit enumeration in that section construed alongside the creation of a separate "Institutional Zone" under Section 4.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Under the maxims of **expressio unius est exclusio alterius** and **casus omissus**, did the transfer of "health facilities/hospitals" to an independent "Institutional Zone" in the 1991 Zoning Ordinance, coupled with its omission from the residential enumeration, intentionally prohibit hospital construction and expansion in residential zones notwithstanding general references to "institutional" uses?

**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the legality of the hospital's expansion application should be decided under the 1991 Zoning Ordinance in force at the time of application, or under the subsequent 1999 Zoning Ordinance belatedly submitted on Motion for Reconsideration.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Can an applicant invoke a newer zoning ordinance enacted during the pendency of the dispute if that law was never pleaded before lower tribunals and was raised for the first time in a Motion for Reconsideration before the Supreme Court?
### 7. DEEP-DIVE VERDICT, TOOL ANALYSIS, & RATIO DECIDENDI
Issue 1: Scope of "Institutional" and Exclusion of Hospitals from Residential Zones
(a) Issue & Short Answer
**NO.** The term "institutional" in Section 2, Article VI cannot be broadly interpreted to permit hospitals within residential zones because the specific statutory enumeration governs general terminology, and the intentional omission of hospitals from residential zones renders them non-conforming uses subject to the expansion ban of Article X, Section 1.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements
**"Moreover, both the Office of the President and the appellate court failed to consider that any meaning or interpretation to be given to the term 'institutional' as used in Section 2, Article VI must be correspondingly limited by the explicit enumeration of allowable uses contained in the same section. Whatever meaning the legislative body had intended in employing the word 'institutional' must be discerned in light of the restrictive enumeration in the said article."**
**"Under the legal maxim expressio unius est exclusio alterius, the express mention of one thing in a law, means the exclusion of others not expressly mentioned. Thus, in interpreting the whole of Section 2, Article VI, it must be understood that in expressly enumerating the allowable uses within a residential zone, those not included in the enumeration are deemed excluded."**
**"Furthermore, according to the rule of casus omissus in statutory construction, a thing omitted must be considered to have been omitted intentionally. Therefore, with the omission of the phrase 'hospital with not more than ten capacity' in the new Zoning Ordinance, and the corresponding transfer of said allowable usage to another zone classification, the only logical conclusion is that the legislative body had intended that said use be removed from those allowed within a residential zone."**
**"That no non-conforming use shall be enlarged or increased or extended to occupy a greater area or land that has already been occupied by such use at the time of the adoption of this Ordinance... Hence, we accordingly resolve that the expansion of the St. James Hospital into a four-storey, forty-bed capacity medical institution within the Mariquita Pueblo Subdivision as prohibited under the provisions of the 1991 Zoning Ordinance."**
(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court rejected the lower tribunals' broad semantic construction of the word "institutional." It held that the text must be examined intrinsically in relation to its surrounding sub-clauses and the comprehensive zoning scheme.
2. Intrinsic Aids Examined (Contextual Harmonization & Expressio Unius):
The Court juxtaposed Section 2 (Residential Zone) against Section 4 (Institutional Zone) of Article VI.
While Section 2 mentions "institutional" as a general descriptor, it provides an exhaustive, restrictive itemization of permissible activities.
Section 4 explicitly carves out an exclusive "Institutional Zone" and specifically itemizes "Health facilities" ("Emergency hospital," "Health centers," "Multi-purpose clinics").
Under **expressio unius est exclusio alterius**, the explicit listing of specific residential structures excludes hospitals. The general word "institutional" cannot be blown up to swallow the specific items excluded.
3. Extrinsic Aids / Legislative Evolution Tracking (Casus Omissus):
Under the prior 1981 Ordinance, hospitals of up to 10 beds were expressly permitted in residential zones.
In the 1991 revision, the Sangguniang Bayan removed the clause "hospital with not more than ten capacity" from the residential list and simultaneously established a standalone Institutional Zone.
Under the rule of **casus omissus**, an omission made in an amendatory or superseding text must be treated as intentional. The council intentionally eliminated hospitals from residential zones.
4. Statutory Application to Non-Conforming Uses:
Because hospitals became unauthorized in residential zones in 1991, St. James Hospital was relegated to the status of an "existing non-conforming use" under Article X, Section 1.
Section 1(1) of Article X explicitly dictates that **"no non-conforming use shall be enlarged or increased or extended to occupy a greater area."**
Therefore, expanding the structure into a 4-storey, 40-bed hospital was an illegal expansion of a non-conforming structure.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court dismissed respondent’s argument that "institutional" served as an open-ended catch-all, pointing out that such an interpretation rendered Section 4 (the dedicated Institutional Zone) completely superfluous.
(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**: Even though the zoning law generally mentions "institutional" uses in residential areas, that general word is strictly limited by the specific list that follows it; because the town council purposely deleted "hospitals" from the residential list in 1991 and created a brand-new "Institutional Zone" specifically for medical facilities, the omission of hospitals from residential zones was deliberate (**casus omissus** / **expressio unius**). As a result, the hospital became a "non-conforming" building which, by express statutory mandate, cannot be enlarged or expanded.
Issue 2: Governing Law at the Time Cause of Action Arose vs. Belated Invocation of Subsequent Enactment
(a) Issue & Short Answer
**NO.** The case cannot be decided under the 1999 Zoning Ordinance. The controversy is governed by the 1991 Ordinance in effect when the cause of action accrued in 1994; furthermore, a new statute cannot be raised as a defense for the first time on a motion for reconsideration before the Supreme Court.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements
**"It is a well-settled rule that the law in force at the time of the occurrence of the cause of action is the applicable law notwithstanding its subsequent amendment or repeal."**
**"Hence, in resolving the instant case, the zoning ordinance to be used in interpreting the legality or illegality of said expansion is that which was in full force and effect at the time of the application for expansion which is the 1991 Zoning Ordinance, regardless of its subsequent amendment or repeal by the passage of the 1999 Zoning Ordinance."**
**"Points of law, theories, issues and arguments not adequately brought to the attention of the trial court need not be, and ordinarily will not be, considered by a reviewing court as they cannot be raised for the first time on appeal because this would be offensive to the basic rules of fair play, justice and due process. This rule holds even more true when the points of law, theories, issues and arguments are belatedly raised for the first time in the motion for reconsideration of this Court's decision."**
(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning
1. **Threshold Gate:** Private respondent sought to moot the 1991 statutory analysis by introducing an extrinsic post-enactment development—the 1999 Santa Rosa Zoning Ordinance.
2. Temporal Rule of Statutory Applicability:
The operative legal trigger occurred in 1994 when St. James Hospital applied for its expansion permit.
Rights and legal duties crystallize under the statutory framework existing at the time the cause of action accrues. Subsequent repeal or amendment does not retroactively sanitize an act that was prohibited when performed.
3. Procedural Bar on New Statutory Theories:
The 1999 Ordinance was enacted years before the case reached the SC in 2005, yet respondent litigated throughout on the basis of the 1991 text.
Raising a new statutory regime on a Motion for Reconsideration before the Supreme Court violates basic fair play and due process.
4. **Rejection of Respondent's Stance:** The Court declined to examine the substantive merits of the 1999 Ordinance within this petition, preserving the integrity of appellate review.
(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**: A lawsuit over a permit is governed by the law in effect when the permit was applied for (1994 under the 1991 Ordinance), not by an amended ordinance passed years later. Furthermore, a litigant cannot sit on a new ordinance and bring it up for the very first time in a Motion for Reconsideration before the Supreme Court.
### 8. SEPARATE OPINIONS ON STATUTORY CONSTRUCTION
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.** (The Resolution was unanimous).
### 9. OVERALL VERDICT (DISPOSITIVE PORTION / FALLO)
Verbatim Fallo:
**"ACCORDINGLY, the Motion for Reconsideration of respondent St. James Hospital, Inc., is hereby DENIED. However, this is without prejudice to respondent St. James Hospital, Inc.'s reapplication for expansion in accordance with the requirements under zoning ordinances now in effect.**
**SO ORDERED."**
Plain-Language Outcome:
The Supreme Court maintained its original ruling in favor of Petitioners Sps. Delfino: the planned four-storey, 40-bed expansion of St. James Hospital remains illegal and prohibited under the 1991 Zoning Ordinance as an impermissible enlargement of a non-conforming use. However, the denial is without prejudice to the hospital filing a fresh application under whatever new zoning ordinances are currently in effect.

Administrative investigations shall be conducted by at least two members of the Medical Board with one legal officer sitting during the investigation, otherwise the proceedings shall be considered void. The existing rules of evidence shall be observed during all administrative investigations. **The Board may disapprove applications for examination or registration**, reprimand erring physicians, or suspend or revoke registration certificates, if the respondents are found guilty after due investigation." **Historical / Amendment Tracking:** **Pre-Amendment R.A. No. 2382 (1959):** Created the Board of Medical Examiners under the Civil Service Commissioner. **R.A. No. 4224 (June 19, 1965):** Amended Sections 20 and 22, explicitly empowering the Board to investigate applicants and "disapprove applications for examination or registration," and restricting oath administration strictly to those "who qualified in the examinations." **StatCon Diagnostic Profile:** **The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Latent tension created by an isolated literal reading of the mandatory term "shall" and the three negative exclusionary grounds in Section 20, versus the overarching prerequisite phrases ("satisfactorily complied," "satisfactorily passed," "qualified") and regulatory powers in Sections 8, 9, 20, and 22. **Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. The Court explicitly ruled that the appellate court erred by isolating Section 20, holding that statutory construction requires harmonizing every part of an enactment with every other part to ascertain legislative intent from the whole text. **Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed:** Construction of the statute as a whole (**Ex visceribus actus** / **Ut res magis valeat quam pereat**); the imperative command of "shall" is conditioned and circumscribed by statutory qualifications and prerequisites established across the entire Act. **Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The Board of Medicine withheld the oath-taking and registration of examinees from Fatima College of Medicine after discovering an unprecedented, statistically anomalous clustering of 100% and 99% scores in Biochemistry and Obstetrics-Gynecology, prompting the examinees to demand immediate registration via **mandamus**. 3.
