### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Vda. de Urbano v. Government Service Insurance System**
**Full Official Caption:** Purificacion M. Vda. de Urbano, Pedro De Castro, Aurelio I. Arrienda, Arnel U. Arrienda, Albert U. Arrienda, Alice A. Pedron, and Marilyn C. Bilog, Petitioners, v. Government Service Insurance System (GSIS), Feliciano Belmonte, Jr., Zacarias Beltran, Jr., Marcial Secoquian, and Crispina Dela Cruz, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:**
G.R. No. 137904
Date of Promulgation: October 19, 2001
Ponente: Puno, **J.**
Voting Breakdown: First Division; Davide, Jr., **C.J.**, Kapunan, and Pardo, **JJ.**, concur; Ynares-Santiago, **J.**, took no part.
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
**Primary StatCon Classification:**
Statutory Construction Area: Intrinsic/Extrinsic Aids & Harmonization of Related Acts
Specific Canon / Principle / Rule Applied: Doctrine of **In Pari Materia** / Legislative Declaration of Prior Meaning / Rational & Equitable Construction / Contextual Harmonization with Declared National Policy
Specific Latin Maxim: **In pari materia**; **Qui haeret in litera, haeret in cortice** ("He who considers merely the letter of an instrument goes but skin deep, i.e., sticks to the bark")
Specific Sub-Issue: Construction of audit/disposal exception clauses covering "merchandise/inventory held for sale in the regular course of business" in light of subsequent administrative circulars and contemporaneous national privatization/divestment policies.
**The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim):**
**Commission on Audit (COA) Circular No. 86-264 (October 16, 1986)**
"3.0 Modes of Disposal
3.1. Public Auction
As a rule, public auction or bidding shall be the primary mode of disposal of assets.
3.2. Sale thru Negotiation
Disposal thru this mode, which is a sale without public bidding, shall be resorted to only in case of failure of public auction.
...
5.0 Exceptions and Effectivity
This Circular shall **not apply to sales of merchandise/inventory held for sale in the regular course of business**."
**Commission on Audit (COA) Circular No. 89-296 (January 27, 1989)**
### "III. DEFINITION AND SCOPE:
These audit guidelines shall be observed and adhered to in the divestment or disposal of property and other assets of all government entities/instrumentalities, whether national, local or corporate, including the subsidiaries thereof but **shall not apply to the disposal of merchandise or inventory held for sale in the regular course of business nor to the disposal by government financial institutions of foreclosed assets or collaterals acquired in the regular course of business** and not transferred to the National Government under Proclamation No. 50..."
**Presidential Decree No. 1445 (Government Auditing Code of the Philippines)**
"SECTION 79. Destruction or sale of unserviceable property. — When government property has become **unserviceable for any cause, or is no longer needed**, it shall, upon application of the officer accountable therefor, be inspected by the head of the agency or his duly authorized representative in the presence of the auditor concerned and, if found to be valueless or unsalable, it may be destroyed in their presence. If found to be valuable, **it may be sold at public auction to the highest bidder** under the supervision of the proper committee on award or similar body... In the event that the public auction fails, the property may be sold at a private sale at such price as may be fixed by the same committee or body concerned and approved by the Commission."
**Presidential Decree No. 1146 (Revised Government Service Insurance Act of 1977)**
"Sec. 35. Powers and Functions of the System. — The System shall have the following powers and functions specified in this Act and the usual general corporate powers:
...
(d) **To acquire, utilize or dispose of, in any manner recognized by law, real or personal properties** in the Philippines or elsewhere necessary to carry out the purposes of this Act."
**Historical / Amendment Tracking:**
**COA Circular No. 86-264** (operative in 1987–1988 when the disputed sale took place) expressly excepted only **"sales of merchandise/inventory held for sale in the regular course of business."**
**COA Circular No. 89-296** (promulgated subsequently in 1989) expanded/clarified the exception to read: **"disposal of merchandise or inventory held for sale in the regular course of business nor to the disposal by government financial institutions of foreclosed assets or collaterals acquired in the regular course of business..."**
**P.D. 1146, Section 36** was amended by **P.D. 1981** (July 19, 1985), adding paragraph (f) empowering the Board: **"The provisions of any law to the contrary notwithstanding, to compromise or release, in whole or in part, any claim or settled liability to the System, regardless of the amount involved, under such terms and conditions as it may impose for the best interest of the System..."**
**StatCon Diagnostic Profile:**
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Patent/Latent Ambiguity and Perceived Inter-Circular Conflict—whether the phrase **"merchandise/inventory held for sale in the regular course of business"** in Circular No. 86-264 included acquired foreclosed collaterals of government financial institutions, or whether the mandatory public auction requirement barred a direct negotiated private sale.
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. The Court engaged in active construction because COA Circular No. 86-264, standing alone, did not explicitly enumerate "foreclosed assets," necessitating the application of **in pari materia** alongside subsequent circulars, government economic recovery decrees, and the organic charter of the GSIS.
**Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed:** The Doctrine of **In Pari Materia**; the principle that subsequent acts serve as a legislative/administrative declaration of the meaning of earlier acts; and **qui haeret in litera, haeret in cortice** (rational/equitable construction over literal adherence).
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The GSIS sold a foreclosed residential property via a negotiated sale to a third party (a non-member) for spot cash without first conducting a public auction, prompting the original foreclosed mortgagors to demand the annulment of the deed of sale under Section 79 of P.D. 1445 and COA Circular No. 86-264.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Purificacion M. Vda. de Urbano, Pedro De Castro, Aurelio I. Arrienda, et al. (Petitioners):** Former owners/mortgagors of the subject property whose mortgage was foreclosed; remained in physical possession without paying rent; repeatedly failed to meet GSIS cash terms for repurchase.
**Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) and its Officers (Feliciano Belmonte, Jr., Zacarias Beltran, Jr., Marcial Secoquian) (Respondents):** Foreclosing mortgagee; governmental succor/financial institution administering social security and housing loan funds.
**Crispina Dela Cruz (Private Respondent):** Third-party buyer (non-GSIS member) who bought the acquired foreclosed asset from GSIS via negotiated sale for P267,000.00 cash.
**Commission on Audit (COA):** Constitutional auditing body whose administrative divestment circulars (Nos. 86-264 and 89-296) were the subject of conflicting interpretations.
**Procedural History & Vehicle:**
**Trial Court (RTC of Quezon City, Branch 102):** Petitioners filed a Complaint for Annulment of Contract, Reconveyance, and Damages against GSIS and Dela Cruz. The RTC dismissed the complaint.
**Appellate Court (Court of Appeals, Former 11th Division):** In CA-G.R. CV No. 43339 (penned by Velasco, Jr., **J.**), the CA affirmed the RTC dismissal on October 30, 1998, and denied reconsideration on March 4, 1999. It held that no perfected contract to resell to petitioners existed and that GSIS did not violate disposal rules.
**Supreme Court (Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45):** Petitioners challenged the CA's affirmance. The Supreme Court denied the petition and affirmed the CA in full.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **1971:** Petitioners mortgaged their 200-square-meter property in Quezon City to GSIS to secure a P47,000.00 housing loan.
2. **October 28, 1983:** Following loan default, GSIS foreclosed the mortgage and bought the property at public auction as the highest bidder for P154,896.00.
3. **September 26–28, 1984:** Arnel Arrienda and Purificacion Vda. de Urbano wrote to GSIS expressing their intent to redeem the property and asking for redemption procedures.
4. **October 16, 1984:** GSIS notified petitioners that they must pay the full redemption price of P154,896.00 in cash on or before the redemption expiry date (November 18, 1984), otherwise the property would be auctioned.
5. **November 16, 1984:** The Board passed Resolution No. 929 approving the sale of the property to petitioner Urbano for P174,572.62 in cash within 60 days of notice; petitioners failed to pay.
6. **November 18, 1984:** The statutory 1-year redemption period lapsed without redemption.
7. **January–February 1985:** Petitioners requested a "re-mortgage through repurchase." GSIS denied this because the Acquired Assets Department (AAD) lacked competence to grant real estate/housing loans.
8. **July 6, 1985:** Following intercession by Ismael Mathay, Jr., the GSIS Board adopted Resolution No. 593 granting petitioner Aurelio Arrienda another 60 days from notice to purchase the property for P174,572.62 in cash. Notice was sent on August 2, 1985.
9. **August 21, 1985:** GSIS consolidated title due to the expiration of the redemption period; TCT No. 167532 was cancelled and TCT No. 33418 was issued in GSIS's name.
10. **September 5, 1985:** Respondent Crispina Dela Cruz began negotiations with GSIS to buy the property for P250,000.00 spot cash.
11. **October 4, 1985:** Petitioner Arnel Arrienda counter-offered to buy the property with P50,000.00 down and the remainder in 5-year monthly installments, enclosing a P10,000.00 cashier's check.
12. **October 10, 1985:** By Resolution No. 881, the Board declined petitioners' installment counter-offer.
13. **December 12, 1985:** By Resolution No. 1022, the Board denied petitioners' motion for reconsideration, returned their P10,000.00 check, and directed that Dela Cruz's offer be entertained upon posting of a 10% forfeitable deposit.
14. **January 16, 1986:** By Resolution No. 36, the Board denied a further loan restructuring plea from Aurelio Arrienda.
15. **January 20, 1987:** Petitioner Urbano sought to re-acquire the property under GSIS's "Operation Pabahay." This was denied on March 3, 1987, because Dela Cruz's cash offer was pending and Urbano was an 81-year-old non-member lacking a certificate of award.
16. **August 11, 1987:** The Board passed Resolution No. 342 approving the absolute sale to Dela Cruz for P267,000.00 cash (the market value).
17. **August 12, 1987:** GSIS demanded P58,500.00 in back rentals for 45 months of unpaid occupancy from petitioners.
18. **January 20–21, 1988:** GSIS executed a Deed of Absolute Sale to Dela Cruz; TCT No. 374292 was issued in her name.
19. **September 1987 – January 1988:** Petitioners protested the sale and demanded an administrative investigation, which proved unsatisfactory to them.
20. **Subsequent Action:** Petitioners filed suit in RTC Quezon City for annulment of sale, reconveyance, and damages.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
A. Petitioners' Interpretation
**Core Reading:** Under Section 79 of P.D. 1445 and COA Circular No. 86-264, GSIS is legally prohibited from disposing of real property via private negotiated sale without first conducting a public auction and suffering a failed bidding. Negotiated sale to an outsider (non-GSIS member) is illegal.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Verba Legis / Plain Meaning:** COA Circular No. 86-264 mandatorily prescribes that "public auction or bidding shall be the primary mode of disposal" and negotiated sale is permissible "only in case of failure of public auction."
**Strict Construction of Exceptions:** Exception 5.0 of Circular No. 86-264 only exempts "merchandise/inventory held for sale"; real estate acquired via foreclosure cannot be deemed ordinary merchandise.
**Administrative Promissory Estoppel / Precedent:** Citing **Maharlika Publishing Corp. v. Tagle**, representations made in Board Resolutions that the property "shall be sold thru public bidding" created a binding obligation on GSIS to hold an auction.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Allowing direct negotiated sales to private non-members invites administrative favoritism, deprives members of succor, and breaches state audit safeguards.
B. Respondents' Interpretation
**Core Reading:** Foreclosed collaterals acquired by a government financial institution in its lending operations do not fall under Section 79 of P.D. 1445 (which governs unserviceable/useless office property), but rather constitute ordinary inventory held for sale in the regular course of business, exempt from compulsory public auction under COA Circular No. 86-264 as illuminated by COA Circular No. 89-296.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**In Pari Materia:** COA Circular No. 86-264 and COA Circular No. 89-296 cover the exact same subject matter (disposal of GOCC assets) and must be read together as a uniform system.
**Subsequent Act as Legislative Declaration of Prior Meaning:** The explicit mention of "foreclosed assets or collaterals acquired in the regular course of business" in Circular No. 89-296 merely clarifies the original legislative/administrative intent of Circular No. 86-264's "merchandise/inventory" exemption.
**Harmonization with National Policy / Ratio Legis:** P.D. 2029, P.D. 2030, LOI 1520, and Proclamation No. 50 mandate wide operational flexibility and rapid divestment of non-performing assets by GOCCs.
**P.D. 1146 (GSIS Charter) as amended by P.D. 1981:** Section 35(d) broadly authorizes GSIS to dispose of real property "in any manner recognized by law" to preserve actuarial solvency, without limiting sales exclusively to GSIS members.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Forcing public bidding on all acquired banking/lending collateral paralyzes the financial viability and liquidity of the System, jeopardizing the actuarial solvency of the common fund.
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
1. **[Substantive Issue]** Whether the petitioners possessed a legally enforceable right to repurchase the foreclosed property after the expiration of the statutory redemption period.
2. **[PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]** Whether the phrase **"sales of merchandise/inventory held for sale in the regular course of business"** in Section 5.0 of COA Circular No. 86-264 exempts foreclosed assets and collaterals acquired by the GSIS from the mandatory requirement of public auction, when construed **in pari materia** with COA Circular No. 89-296, P.D. 2029, P.D. 2030, and Proclamation No. 50.
**Faithful Court Formulation:** "The pivotal question is whether the subject property is covered by COA Circular 86-264 or falls under the exception in its paragraph 5 above."
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether foreclosed collaterals held by GSIS fall within the exception of "merchandise/inventory held for sale in the regular course of business" under COA Circular No. 86-264 when interpreted **in pari materia** with the clarifying text of subsequent COA Circular No. 89-296 and governing state economic recovery policies.
3. **[PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]** Whether Section 79 of Presidential Decree No. 1445 (Government Auditing Code) applies to the sale of foreclosed real estate assets held by the GSIS.
**Faithful Court Formulation:** "Section 79 of P.D. 1445 does not apply to the case at bar as this provision covers unserviceable government property and not acquired assets like the subject property."
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the phrase "unserviceable for any cause, or is no longer needed" in Section 79 of P.D. No. 1445 encompasses usable, acquired real properties foreclosed by government financial institutions to maintain actuarial solvency.
4. **[Substantive Issue]** Whether the GSIS acted in bad faith or violated the petitioners' constitutional right to information by negotiating the cash sale with respondent Dela Cruz without notifying petitioners.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Right to Repurchase Foreclosed Property Post-Redemption
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Did petitioners retain a right to repurchase the foreclosed property? **NO.** Repurchase after the redemption period has expired is not a matter of right but rests purely on the discretion of the owner-buyer; the GSIS charter gave the Board full discretion to accept or reject repurchase offers to protect its actuarial solvency.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"The right to redeem becomes functus officio on the date of its expiry, and its exercise after the period is not really one of redemption but a repurchase. Distinction must be made because redemption is by force of law; the purchaser at public auction is bound to accept redemption. **Repurchase however of foreclosed property, after redemption period, imposes no such obligation.** After expiry, the purchaser may or may not re-sell the property but no law will compel him to do so." (Quoting **Natino v. IAC**)
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** Sections 35 and 36 of P.D. 1146, as amended by P.D. 1981, are clear. The Board is vested with discretion to fix terms and conditions of financial accommodations and to dispose of property to maintain the actuarial solvency of the fund.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** The "Whereas" clauses of P.D. 1981 expressly emphasize the dual purpose of responsiveness to members and assuring the "actuarial solvency of the Fund administered by the GSIS."
3. **Statutory Scope:** The power in Section 35(d) to dispose of real property contains no restriction or qualification that GSIS may sell exclusively to GSIS members.
4. **Rejection of Losing Argument:** The Court rejected the application of **Maharlika Publishing Corp. v. Tagle**. Unlike in **Maharlika**, where the GSIS accepted an offer by suspending bidding to negotiate, the GSIS here gave petitioners two 60-day extensions to pay in cash, which petitioners failed to do. Petitioners' subsequent counter-proposals for installment purchases were outrightly rejected. No binding contract was ever perfected under Article 1319 of the Civil Code.
**(d) Plain-Language StatCon Explanation:**
Once the 1-year redemption period expired, GSIS became the absolute owner of the house. Repurchasing it was not an automatic legal right, and GSIS was entitled to reject petitioners' installment proposals to protect the financial health of the pension fund.
Issue 2: Construction of COA Circular No. 86-264 and COA Circular No. 89-296 (**In Pari Materia**)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does the exception in COA Circular No. 86-264 cover foreclosed collaterals, allowing GSIS to dispose of them through a negotiated sale without public auction? **YES.** Construed **in pari materia** with subsequent COA Circular No. 89-296 and national economic decrees, the term "merchandise/inventory held for sale in the regular course of business" includes foreclosed collaterals acquired by government financial institutions.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"The correct rule of interpretation is, that if divers (sic) statutes relate to the same thing, they ought all to be taken into consideration in construing any one of them, and it is an established rule of law, that all acts in pari materia are to be taken together, as if they were one law... If a thing contained in a subsequent statute, be within the reason of a former statute, it shall be taken to be within the meaning of that statute... and if it can be gathered from a subsequent statute in pari materia, what meaning the Legislature attached to the words of a former statute, they will amount to a legislative declaration of its meaning, and will govern the construction of the first statute." (Quoting **The United States v. Freeman**)
"It is a familiar canon of construction that a thing which is within the intention of the makers of a statute is as much within the statute as if it were within the letter; and a thing which is within the letter of the statute is not within the statute unless it be within the intention of the makers... Such a construction ought to be put upon a statute as will best answer the intention which the makers had in view, for **qui haret in litera, haret in cortice**." (Quoting **Riggs v. Palmer**)
"Statutes in **pari materia** should be read and construed together because enactments of the same legislature on the same subject are supposed to form part of one uniform system; later statutes are supplementary or complimentary (sic) to the earlier enactments..." (Quoting **Agpalo, Statutory Construction**)
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** A literal, narrow reading of COA Circular No. 86-264's exception ("sales of merchandise/inventory") would restrict exemptions to retail commodities, excluding real estate assets and conflicting with broad corporate management. The Court looked past the literal letter (**qui haeret in litera, haeret in cortice**) to determine true administrative intent.
2. **Intrinsic Aids / In Pari Materia Harmonization:** The Court placed COA Circular No. 86-264 alongside COA Circular No. 89-296. The 1989 circular explicitly exempted the "disposal by government financial institutions of foreclosed assets or collaterals acquired in the regular course of business." Under the doctrine that subsequent acts serve as a declaration of the meaning attached to former acts, Circular No. 89-296 clarified what Circular No. 86-264 intended all along.
3. **Extrinsic Aids & Broader Statutory Context:** The Court reviewed state policies embodied in P.D. No. 2029 (operational flexibility for GOCCs), LOI No. 1520, P.D. No. 2030 (orderly, rapid disposition of non-performing assets to recover substantial cash returns), and Proclamation No. 50 (asset privatization and disposition of non-performing assets). These statutes established an overarching national policy to afford GOCCs flexibility to divest non-performing assets rapidly.
4. **Statutory Presumption:** Statutes and administrative regulations relating to the same subject matter must be construed as a consistent, harmonious system. The exception in Circular No. 86-264 had to be interpreted liberally to accommodate this national policy.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court rejected petitioners' argument that a negotiated sale was void without prior failed biddings. GSIS's internal policy requiring two failed biddings before negotiated sales was only adopted in 1991 (PPG 1991), years after the 1987–1988 sale to Dela Cruz. Prior to 1991, the Board held full discretion.
**(d) Plain-Language StatCon Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**: Even though COA Circular No. 86-264 literally exempted only "merchandise/inventory," the Supreme Court read it alongside the later 1989 COA circular and state privatization laws. Because GSIS operates as a financial institution that forecloses properties in its ordinary business, these acquired houses represent banking inventory; hence, GSIS was legally authorized to sell the property directly through negotiation without holding a public auction first.
Issue 3: Inapplicability of Section 79 of P.D. 1445
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Does Section 79 of P.D. No. 1445 require GSIS to sell the foreclosed property at a public auction? **NO.** Section 79 applies strictly to property that is "unserviceable" or "no longer needed," neither of which describes usable foreclosed loan collaterals held for financial recovery.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"Section 79 of P.D. 1445 does not apply to the case at bar as this provision applies only to unserviceable property... That the subject property is not 'unserviceable' or useless is rather obvious. Petitioners are precisely fighting tooth and nail to claim the subject property as they are still using it as their family home. It still serves its purpose well. Neither is it 'no longer needed' by the GSIS. As a financial institution extending housing loans, the disposition of foreclosed properties — such as the subject property — at a price beneficial to the GSIS helps maintain the actuarial solvency of the GSIS fund."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate / Verba Legis:** The Court examined the express words of the statute: "unserviceable for any cause, or is no longer needed."
2. **Plain Meaning Application:** "Unserviceable" means broken down, worn out, or useless. A habitable residential home used by petitioners is plainly serviceable.
3. **Contextual Meaning of "No Longer Needed":** The acquired asset is not redundant government equipment. It is an investment asset held by a financial institution to recoup lost loan capital. Thus, it remains actively needed by GSIS to maintain actuarial solvency.
4. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** Petitioners erroneously attempted to stretch a provision meant for condemning and disposing of dilapidated government office supplies/equipment to the portfolio management of a state financing and lending institution.
**(d) Plain-Language StatCon Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**: Section 79 of the Government Auditing Code governs the disposal of worn-out or useless government items (like junk vehicles or obsolete equipment). It does not apply to a good, habitable house that the GSIS foreclosed and needs to sell to recoup its money and protect its investment funds.
Issue 4: Imputation of Bad Faith & Right to Information
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:** Was GSIS in bad faith for conducting unannounced cash negotiations with Dela Cruz? **NO.** The sale of an acquired housing asset is a private commercial transaction rather than a matter of public concern under **Valmonte v. Belmonte, Jr.**
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"The negotiation and subsequent sale of the subject property by the GSIS to private respondent dela Cruz was by no stretch of the imagination imbued with public interest as it was a purely private transaction. Petitioners cannot therefore demand that it be informed of such negotiation and sale more so since they no longer had any interest on the subject property upon failure to comply with GSIS' terms for repurchase..."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** Analysis of the scope of the constitutional right to information under **Valmonte v. Belmonte, Jr.**
2. **Distinction of Precedent:** In **Valmonte**, the information sought involved clean housing loans granted to members of the defunct Batasang Pambansa, which involved public funds and policy. Here, the transaction was an ordinary private sale of a single acquired asset.
3. **Lack of Legal Standing/Interest:** Petitioners had already lost their legal rights to the property upon expiration of the redemption period and the lapse of multiple grace periods granted by the Board.
**(d) Plain-Language StatCon Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**: The GSIS did not act deceitfully when it negotiated with a cash buyer without telling the former owners. Because the former owners' legal rights had expired and the sale was a routine business transaction, it was not a matter of public concern that GSIS was required to disclose to them.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.**
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Dispositive Portion:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is DENIED and the impugned decision and resolution of the Court of Appeals are AFFIRMED. No costs.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Petitioners lost their bid to annul the sale of their former home. Respondent GSIS acted strictly within its legal powers when it sold the foreclosed property to private respondent Crispina Dela Cruz for cash via a negotiated sale, without prior public auction, because acquired loan collaterals held by government financial institutions are legally exempt from public bidding requirements under statutory principles of **in pari materia** and declared national privatization policy.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Calingin v. Court of Appeals**
**Full Official Caption:** GOV. ANTONIO CALINGIN, **Petitioner**, versus COURT OF APPEALS, Special 17th Division, EXECUTIVE SECRETARY RENATO S. DE VILLA, DEPT. OF INTERIOR & LOCAL GOVERNMENT SECRETARY JOEY LINA, UNDERSECRETARY EDUARDO R. SOLIMAN, JR., DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR & LOCAL GOVERNMENT, REGIONAL OFFICE NO. 10, DIRECTOR RODOLFO Z. RAZUL, **Respondents**.
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 154616
**Date of Promulgation:** July 12, 2004
**Phil Reports / SCRA Citation:** 479 Phil. 154 / 434 SCRA 173
**Ponente:** Quisumbing, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Second Division (Unanimous: Puno, **J.** [Chairman], Austria-Martinez, Callejo, Sr., and Tinga, **JJ.**, concur). No separate concurring or dissenting opinions filed.
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
**Primary StatCon Classification:**
Conflict of Laws / Inconsistent Statutes → Special Statute vs. General Statute → **Lex specialis derogat legi generali** / Later Statute Prevails Over Prior Inconsistent Statute (**Lex posterior derogat priori**) → Disciplinary Procedures and Finality of Decisions in Administrative Cases Involving Elective Local Officials.
**The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim):**
1. Section 67, Chapter 4, Republic Act No. 7160 (Local Government Code of 1991):
"SEC. 67. **Administrative Appeals.** — Decisions in administrative cases may, within thirty (30) days from receipt thereof, be appealed to the following:
(a) The **sangguniang panlalawigan**, in the case of decisions of the **sangguniang panlungsod** of component cities and the **sangguniang bayan**; and
(b) The Office of the President, in the case of decisions of the **sangguniang panlalawigan** and the **sangguniang panlungsod** of highly urbanized cities and independent component cities.
**Decisions of the Office of the President shall be final and executory.**"
2. Section 15, Chapter 3, Book VII, Executive Order No. 292 (Administrative Code of 1987):
"SEC. 15. **Finality of Order.** — The decision of the agency shall become final and executory fifteen (15) days after the receipt of a copy thereof by the party adversely affected unless within that period an administrative appeal or judicial review, if proper, has been perfected. **One motion for reconsideration may be filed, which shall suspend the running of the said period.**"
3. Section 68, Republic Act No. 7160 (Local Government Code of 1991):
"SEC. 68. **Execution Pending Appeal.** — **An appeal shall not prevent a decision from becoming final or executory.** The respondent shall be considered as having been placed under preventive suspension during the pendency of an appeal in the event he wins such appeal. In the event the appeal results in an exoneration, he shall be paid his salary and such other emoluments during the pendency of the appeal."
**Historical / Amendment Tracking:**
**Prior/General Law:** E.O. No. 292 (Administrative Code of 1987), signed July 25, 1987.
**Subsequent/Special Law:** R.A. No. 7160 (Local Government Code of 1991), enacted October 10, 1991, which comprehensively codified local governance and disciplinary proceedings against elective local officials.
**StatCon Diagnostic Profile:**
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Conflict Between Provisions across distinct statutes (whether Section 15, Book VII of the 1987 Administrative Code allowing a motion for reconsideration to stay execution governs disciplinary orders of the Office of the President against a Governor, or whether Section 67 in relation to Section 68 of the 1991 Local Government Code renders the Office of the President's decision immediately final, executory, and unstayed by a motion for reconsideration or appeal).
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. The Court engaged in statutory reconciliation and prioritization between two overlapping statutes, applying the established rules on **lex specialis** and **lex posterior**.
**Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed: Lex specialis derogat legi generali** (a special statute governs over a general statute); **Lex posterior derogat priori** (a later statute repeals or modifies inconsistent earlier laws).
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) issued a Memorandum immediately executing a 90-day suspension order rendered by the Office of the President against Governor Antonio Calingin during an election period, prompting the Governor to challenge the order's executory status because he had a pending motion for reconsideration under the Administrative Code.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Gov. Antonio Calingin:** Petitioner; incumbent Governor of Misamis Oriental who was ordered suspended for 90 days.
**Vice Governor Danilo P. Lagbas, et al.:** Complainants in the original administrative case against Gov. Calingin.
**Executive Secretary Renato S. De Villa:** Public Respondent; signed and approved the Office of the President's suspension resolution by authority of the President.
**DILG Secretary Jose "Joey" D. Lina, Jr. & Undersecretary Eduardo R. Soliman, Jr.:** Public Respondents; authorized and issued the DILG implementing memorandum enforcing the 90-day suspension.
**DILG Regional Office No. 10 & Director Rodolfo Z. Razul:** Public Respondents; regional implementing arm tasked with serving and executing the suspension order.
**Commission on Elections (COMELEC):** Constitutional agency that issued COMELEC Resolution No. 3992 exempting Calingin's suspension from the election ban under Section 1(a) of COMELEC Resolution No. 3401.
**Procedural History & Vehicle:**
**Administrative Level:** The Office of the President (O.P. Case No. 00-1-9220 / DILG ADM Case No. P-16-99) issued a Resolution on March 22, 2001, suspending Gov. Calingin for 90 days.
**COMELEC Exemption:** On April 24, 2001, COMELEC promulgated Resolution No. 3992 granting an exemption to the election ban against moving/suspending public officials.
**DILG Enforcement:** On April 30, 2001, DILG Undersecretary Soliman issued an implementing Memorandum. Gov. Calingin filed a Motion for Reconsideration before the Office of the President on May 3, 2001.
**Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. SP No. 64583):** On May 7, 2001, Calingin filed a Petition for Prohibition with a prayer for TRO/status quo ante order. The CA dismissed the petition on May 11, 2001, and denied reconsideration on July 1, 2002.
**Supreme Court:** Calingin filed the instant Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45. The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals in full.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **March 22, 2001:** The Office of the President, through Executive Secretary Renato S. De Villa, approves and signs a Resolution in O.P. Case No. 00-1-9220 (**Vice Governor Danilo P. Lagbas, et al. v. Governor Antonio P. Calingin**) imposing a 90-day suspension on petitioner Gov. Calingin. On the same date, the Senior Deputy Executive Secretary requests the COMELEC for authority/exemption to implement the suspension order during the election ban period.
2. **April 24, 2001:** COMELEC promulgates Resolution No. 3992 granting an exemption to the election ban on the movement and suspension of public officers (pursuant to COMELEC Resolution No. 3401).
3. **April 30, 2001:** Undersecretary Eduardo R. Soliman, Jr., by authority of DILG Secretary Jose D. Lina, Jr., issues a Memorandum directing the enforcement and implementation of the 90-day suspension against petitioner.
4. **May 3, 2001:** Petitioner files a Motion for Reconsideration of the suspension resolution before the Office of the President.
5. **May 7, 2001:** Petitioner files a Petition for Prohibition with prayer for a TRO and/or status quo ante order before the Court of Appeals to enjoin the DILG from executing the suspension order, arguing that the decision was not yet final and executory due to his pending motion for reconsideration, and that the COMELEC exemption was invalid.
6. **May 11, 2001:** The Court of Appeals dismisses the petition for prohibition.
7. **July 1, 2002:** The Court of Appeals denies petitioner's Motion for Reconsideration.
8. **July 12, 2004:** The Supreme Court renders judgment denying the petition for review and affirming the Court of Appeals.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
A. Petitioner's Interpretation (Gov. Antonio Calingin):
**Core Reading:**
1. Under Section 15, Chapter 3, Book VII of the 1987 Administrative Code, decisions of the Office of the President in the exercise of its **original** jurisdiction become final and executory only after 15 days, and the timely filing of a motion for reconsideration suspends that period;
2. Section 67 of the Local Government Code (R.A. No. 7160)—declaring decisions of the Office of the President final and executory—applies solely to administrative **appeals** originating from local legislative councils (**sanggunians**), not to original administrative complaints against provincial governors.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Strict/Literal Reading of Section Titles and Structural Placement:** The heading and structure of Section 67 is explicitly titled **"Administrative Appeals"**; thus, the final sentence ("Decisions of the Office of the President shall be final and executory") cannot be extended to original disciplinary actions.
**General Administrative Law Application:** In the absence of an explicit provision in the LGC governing original jurisdiction of the OP, the Administrative Code of 1987 operates as the governing procedural charter.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Executing a suspension during the pendency of a motion for reconsideration deprives the elective official of due process and an opportunity to have the administrative body correct its own errors before penalization.
B. Respondent's Interpretation (Executive Secretary, DILG, et al.):
**Core Reading:** Disciplinary proceedings against local elective officials are governed exclusively by the Local Government Code of 1991 (Sections 67 and 68). Decisions of the Office of the President rendered under this statutory regime are immediately executory and final; neither a motion for reconsideration nor an appeal prevents the immediate execution of the decision.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Special Law Over General Law (Lex specialis derogat legi generali):** The Local Government Code specially governs disciplinary actions against elective local officials and prevails over the general Administrative Code of 1987.
**Later Statute Prevails (Lex posterior derogat priori):** The LGC (enacted 1991) is a subsequent statute that modifies or repeals inconsistent provisions of the Administrative Code (enacted 1987).
**Statutory Harmonization & Immediate Execution:** Under Section 68 of the LGC and Section 12, Rule 43 of the Rules of Court, an appeal or further review does not stay the execution of administrative decisions involving local elective officials.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Elective local officials face disciplinary systems intended by Congress to be prompt, preventing suspended officials from using procedural delays to stay in office during their limited political terms.
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
### 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the decision of the Office of the President suspending a provincial governor was already final and executory, notwithstanding a pending motion for reconsideration under Section 15, Book VII of the Administrative Code of 1987, in light of Section 67 and Section 68 of the Local Government Code of 1991.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the general rule under Section 15, Book VII of the Administrative Code of 1987 (where a motion for reconsideration stays execution) yields to Sections 67 and 68 of the Local Government Code of 1991 under the **lex specialis** and **lex posterior** doctrines, thereby rendering decisions of the Office of the President immediately executory.

**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the exemption from the election ban in the movement of any public officer granted by COMELEC in its Resolution No. 3992 was valid.
**Recit-Ready Question:** Whether the COMELEC exemption granted via Resolution No. 3992 was legally defective because the request submitted to it included a draft resolution alongside the approved decision and formal pleadings.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Finality and Immediate Execution of Office of the President Decisions under the Local Government Code
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
**Issue 1:** Was the decision of the Office of the President already final and executory despite the filing of a motion for reconsideration?
**Short Answer: YES.** Under the doctrines of **lex specialis** and **lex posterior**, the Local Government Code of 1991 governs disciplinary actions against elective local officials to the exclusion of the 1987 Administrative Code; hence, decisions of the Office of the President are immediately executory and cannot be stayed by a motion for reconsideration.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**"In Lapid v. Court of Appeals, we held that it is a principle of statutory construction that where there are two statutes that apply to a particular case, that which was specially intended for the said case must prevail."**
**"The case on hand involves a disciplinary action against an elective local official. Thus, the Local Government Code is the applicable law and must prevail over the Administrative Code which is of general application."**
**"Further, the Local Government Code of 1991 was enacted much later than the Administrative Code of 1987. In statutory construction, all laws or parts thereof which are inconsistent with the later law are repealed or modified accordingly."**
**"In sum, the decisions of the Office of the President are final and executory. No motion for reconsideration is allowed by law but the parties may appeal the decision to the Court of Appeals. The appeal, however, does not stay the execution of the decision. Thus, the DILG Secretary may validly move for its immediate execution."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning (The Tool Deep-Dive):**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court confronted an apparent statutory conflict between Section 15, Book VII of the Administrative Code (which allows a motion for reconsideration that suspends execution) and Sections 67 and 68 of the Local Government Code (which provide that decisions of the Office of the President are final, executory, and unstayed). Statutory construction was necessary to resolve which statutory scheme controlled.
2. Intrinsic Aids & Harmonization:
The Court examined the nature and subject matter of both statutes. While the Administrative Code governs executive branch agencies broadly, the Local Government Code specifically regulates local governments and the administrative discipline of elective local officials.
The Court integrated Section 68 of the LGC (providing that an appeal shall not prevent a decision from becoming final or executory) with Section 12, Rule 43 of the Rules of Court (an appeal shall not stay the award, judgment, final order, or resolution unless the appellate court directs otherwise).
3. Extrinsic Aids & Canons Applied:
**Lex specialis derogat legi generali:** Relying on the precedent in **Lapid v. Court of Appeals** (citing **Corona v. Court of Appeals** and **Zaldivia v. Reyes**), the Court ruled that where two statutes apply to a case, the specific statute intended for the precise situation governs over a statute of general application.
**Lex posterior derogat priori:** The Court applied the canon that a later enactment prevails over a prior inconsistent law. Because the Local Government Code was enacted in 1991, it modified or repealed inconsistent provisions of the 1987 Administrative Code regarding disciplinary proceedings of local elective officials.
4. **Statutory Policy & Execution Scheme:** The Court reaffirmed the doctrine in **Lapid** that decisions of the Office of the President under the Local Government Code are immediately executory even pending appeal because the governing special statute expressly commands them to be so.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** Petitioner's attempt to restrict Section 67's finality clause strictly to administrative **appeals** from lower sanggunians, and relegate original jurisdiction cases against governors to the general Administrative Code, was rejected. The Court ruled that disciplinary actions against elective local officials are comprehensively governed by the LGC, which contains no statutory authorization for a stay of execution via a motion for reconsideration before the OP.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** The Supreme Court ruled that a governor facing disciplinary suspension cannot invoke the general Administrative Code to delay his suspension through a motion for reconsideration, because the Local Government Code is both a **special law** and a **subsequent law** governing elective local officials. Under the Local Government Code, decisions of the Office of the President are immediately executory, meaning the DILG has full legal authority to enforce the suspension at once without waiting for a motion for reconsideration or an appeal to resolve.
Issue 2: Validity of the COMELEC Exemption Resolution (No. 3992)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
**Issue 2:** Was the exemption from the election ban in the movement of any public officer granted by COMELEC valid?
**Short Answer: YES.** The suspension resolution of the Office of the President was already approved and signed prior to the grant of exemption, and the administrative submission complied with all regulatory evidentiary requirements.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**"A perusal of the records, however, reveals that the Resolution in O.P. Case No. 00-1-9220 was approved and signed on March 22, 2001 by Executive Secretary Renato de Villa by the authority of the President. Hence, the approval was before the promulgation of COMELEC Resolution No. 3992 on April 24, 2001."**
**"Moreover, COMELEC Resolution No. 3529 — which may be applied by analogy and in relation to Sec. 2 of COMELEC Resolution No. 3401 — merely requires the request to be in writing indicating the office and place from which the officer is removed, and the reason for said movement, and submitted together with the formal complaint executed under oath and containing the specific charges and the answer to said complaint."**
**"There being a proper basis for its grant of exemption, COMELEC Resolution No. 3992 is valid."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning (The Tool Deep-Dive):**
1. **Factual Verification:** The Court verified that the suspension was not an unsigned "draft" as alleged by petitioner; it had been approved and signed by Executive Secretary De Villa by presidential authority on March 22, 2001, prior to the COMELEC exemption on April 24, 2001.
2. **Administrative Rule Application by Analogy:** The Court harmonized Section 2 of COMELEC Resolution No. 3401 with COMELEC Resolution No. 3529, determining that the rules merely require a written request stating reasons, accompanied by sworn complaints and answers.
3. **Substantial Compliance:** The inclusion of a draft resolution alongside the affidavits, complaint, and answers did not invalidate the request; all substantive requirements to support administrative action during the election period were satisfied.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** The Court held that the COMELEC's election-ban exemption was fully valid because the Office of the President had officially signed and promulgated the suspension order before the COMELEC acted. The mere fact that supporting paperwork submitted to COMELEC included a draft version alongside the final pleadings and affidavits did not vitiate compliance with administrative election regulations.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the instant petition for review on certiorari is DENIED. The assailed Court of Appeals' resolutions dated May 11, 2002 and July 1, 2002 in CA-G.R. SP No. 64583 are hereby AFFIRMED.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Petitioner Gov. Antonio Calingin lost. The Court of Appeals' dismissal of his petition for prohibition was affirmed, confirming that the DILG validly enforced the 90-day suspension order immediately. Under the Local Government Code of 1991, disciplinary orders of the Office of the President against local elective officials are immediately executory and are not stayed by a motion for reconsideration or an appeal.

**Official Citation:** 628 Phil. 181; 106 O.G. No. 51, 7184 (December 20, 2010)
**Ponente:** Carpio, J.
**Voting Breakdown:** Second Division (Carpio, **ponente**; Brion, Del Castillo, Abad, and Perez, JJ., concurring). Unanimous. No separate concurring or dissenting opinions.
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
**Primary StatCon Classification:**
**Statutory Construction Area:** Statute Construction & Harmonization → General Law vs. Special Law → Presumption Against Implied Repeal → Statutory Provisos & Permissive Words
**Specific Canons / Principles Applied: Lex specialis derogat generali** (a special law governs over a general law regardless of passage date); Presumption against implied repeal; Plain meaning of statutory provisos limiting general rights; Permissive nature of the word "may."
**Specific Latin Maxims: Generalia specialibus non derogant** / Special law controls general law; **Verba legis non est recedendum**.
**Specific Sub-Issue:** Whether the permissive option of a married woman to use or not use her husband's surname under Article 370 of the Civil Code authorizes her to revert at will to her maiden name in a replacement passport under Section 5(d) of Republic Act No. 8239 while the marriage subsists.
**The Contested Statutory / Administrative Texts (Verbatim):**
1. Article 370, Title XIII, Civil Code of the Philippines (Republic Act No. 386):
"ART. 370. A married woman **may** use:
(1) Her maiden first name and surname and add her husband's surname, or
(2) Her maiden first name and her husband's surname, or
(3) Her husband's full name, but prefixing a word indicating that she is his wife, such as 'Mrs.'"
2. Section 5(d), Republic Act No. 8239 (The Philippine Passport Act of 1996):
"Sec. 5. **Requirements for the Issuance of Passport**. -- No passport shall be issued to an applicant unless the Secretary or his duly authorized representative is satisfied that the applicant is a Filipino citizen who has complied with the following requirements: x x x
(d) In case of a woman who is married, separated, divorced or widowed or whose marriage has been annulled or declared by court as void, a copy of the certificate of marriage, court decree of separation, divorce or annulment or certificate of death of the deceased spouse duly issued and authenticated by the Office of the Civil Registrar General: **Provided, That in case of a divorce decree, annulment or declaration of marriage as void, the woman applicant may revert to the use of her maiden name: Provided, further, That such divorce is recognized under existing laws of the Philippines;** x x x"
3. Section 1, Article 12, Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of RA 8239:
"The passport can be amended **only** in the following cases:
a) Amendment of woman's name due to marriage;
b) Amendment of woman's name due to death of spouse, annulment of marriage or divorce initiated by a foreign spouse; or
c) Change of surname of a child who is legitimated by virtue of a subsequent marriage of his parents."
**Historical / Amendment Tracking:**
Article 370 of the Civil Code was enacted on June 18, 1949 (taking effect in 1950) as a general statute governing names and surnames.
Republic Act No. 8239 was enacted on November 22, 1996 as a special law comprehensively regulating the requirements, issuance, and amendment of Philippine passports.
**StatCon Diagnostic Profile:**
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Alleged conflict between provisions and implied repeal. Petitioner asserted that Section 5(d) of RA 8239 and its IRR conflicted with, and unlawfully curtailed, the permissive right granted to married women under Article 370 of the Civil Code to use their maiden name at will.
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. While the texts of both statutes are individually clear, construction was required to resolve the apparent repugnancy between the permissive choice of surname under the Civil Code and the restrictive conditions for passport replacement/reversion under RA 8239.
**Controlling Canons / Maxims Deployed:**
**Special law prevails over general law:** "[T]o the extent of any necessary repugnancy between a general and a special law or provision, the latter will control the former without regard to the respective dates of passage."
**Presumption against implied repeal:** Implied repeals are disfavored; laws in **pari materia** must be harmonized and reconciled so that each provision remains operative.
**Construction of statutory provisos:** A proviso operates to qualify, restrict, or limit the general application of the enacting clause or surrounding laws.
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** Maria Virginia V. Remo, an applicant seeking renewal of her expiring Philippine passport (which bore her married surname "Rallonza"), requested to revert to her maiden surname ("Remo") despite her marriage still subsisting, leading the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) to reject the application under Section 5(d) of RA 8239.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Maria Virginia V. Remo (Petitioner):** Married Filipino citizen whose expiring passport carried her husband's surname ("Rallonza"); sought administrative and judicial clearance to revert to her maiden name in her renewed passport while remaining married.
**Francisco R. Rallonza:** Petitioner's husband; the marriage remained valid and subsisting.
**Atty. Manuel Joseph R. Bretaña III:** Legal counsel for petitioner who submitted the formal written request to the DFA.
**Honorable Secretary of Foreign Affairs / Department of Foreign Affairs (Public Respondent):** The executive department mandated under RA 8239 to regulate and issue passports; represented by Assistant Secretary Belen F. Anota and subsequently defended by the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG).
**Office of the President (OP):** The executive appellate body that affirmed the DFA’s denial of petitioner’s request.
**Procedural History & Vehicle:**
**Administrative Phase (DFA):** Petitioner applied at the DFA Chicago Consular Office for renewal of her passport with a request to revert to her maiden surname. The Chicago office denied the request. Counsel Bretaña appealed directly to DFA Secretary Domingo Siazon. On August 28, 2000, DFA Assistant Secretary Belen F. Anota formally denied the request. Petitioner's motion for reconsideration was denied on October 13, 2000.
**Administrative Phase (Office of the President):** On November 15, 2000, petitioner appealed to the OP. On July 27, 2004, the OP dismissed the appeal, ruling that Section 5(d) of RA 8239 exclusively limits reversion to cases of divorce, annulment, or nullity, and that RA 8239, as a special law, governs over the Civil Code. Reconsideration was denied on October 28, 2004.
**Appellate Phase (Court of Appeals):** Petitioner filed a Rule 43 Petition for Review with the CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 87710). On May 27, 2005, the CA denied the petition, holding that there was no conflict between the provisions and that RA 8239 specifically limits the instances of maiden-name reversion in passports. Reconsideration was denied on August 2, 2005.
**Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45. The Supreme Court denied the petition and affirmed the CA.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **Prior to October 27, 2000:** Petitioner Maria Virginia V. Remo held a Philippine passport expiring on October 27, 2000. Having married Francisco R. Rallonza, she previously elected to secure her passport under the name: "Rallonza" as surname, "Maria Virginia" as given name, and "Remo" as middle name.
2. **Renewal Application (Chicago):** Before the passport's expiration, petitioner applied for a replacement passport at the DFA Consular Office in Chicago, Illinois, U.S.A., requesting to drop "Rallonza" and resume her maiden name and surname ("Maria Virginia V. Remo"), notwithstanding that her marriage to Rallonza was intact and subsisting.
3. **Chicago Denial & Legal Representation:** The Chicago consular office denied the request. Petitioner engaged Atty. Manuel Joseph R. Bretaña III, who wrote a formal letter to DFA Secretary Domingo Siazon urging approval of the reversion based on the general right under the Civil Code.
4. **August 28, 2000 (DFA Formal Denial):** DFA Assistant Secretary Belen F. Anota formally denied the request, clarifying that while using a husband's surname is not mandatory, the use of a maiden name is permitted on renewal only if the married name was never used in previous applications, and under the IRR of RA 8239, reversion after adopting the married surname is limited strictly to annulment, divorce, or death of the husband.
5. **October 13, 2000:** DFA denied petitioner's motion for reconsideration.
6. **November 15, 2000 – July 27, 2004 (OP Proceedings):** Petitioner appealed to the Office of the President (O.P. Case No. 001-A-9344). On July 27, 2004, the OP dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 5(d) of RA 8239 offers no leeway other than allowing reversion upon divorce, annulment, or nullity of marriage, and as a special law, it overrides the general provisions of the Civil Code.
7. **October 28, 2004:** The OP denied reconsideration.
8. **May 27, 2005 – August 2, 2005 (Court of Appeals):** The CA denied petitioner’s Rule 43 petition, ruling that RA 8239 explicitly restricts the right of reversion for passport purposes. The CA denied reconsideration on August 2, 2005.
9. **March 5, 2010 (Supreme Court Decision):** The Supreme Court rendered its final decision denying the Rule 45 petition.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
A. Petitioner's Interpretation (Maria Virginia V. Remo)
**Core Reading:** Under Article 370 of the Civil Code, the use of a husband's surname is purely optional ("may"). A married woman never loses her maiden name upon marriage; she changes only her civil status. Therefore, she possesses the continuous right to resume her maiden name in her replacement passport at any time. Any statutory provision or administrative regulation (such as Section 5(d) of RA 8239 and its IRR) that prevents her from resuming her maiden name while married conflicts with and operates as an impermissible restriction or implied repeal of Article 370.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Permissive construction of "may":** "May" denotes discretion and freedom of choice, not a mandatory imposition.
**Precedent Application: Yasin v. Shari'a District Court** (holding that a woman does not change her name upon marriage, only her status, and use of the husband's name is not obligatory).
**Principle of Descent:** Surnames indicate biological lineage and descent, which a woman retains throughout life.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Forcing a woman to continue bearing her husband's surname in an official identity document infringes on her personal liberty, forces an unwanted name upon her, and creates an unauthorized distinction not intended by the substantive law of names.
B. Respondent's Interpretation (Secretary of Foreign Affairs / OSG)
**Core Reading:** While a married woman has the initial option under Article 370 to use her maiden name or married name, once she voluntarily elects to use her husband's surname in her passport, Section 5(d) of RA 8239 limits the instances when she may revert to her maiden name in a replacement passport. Such reversion is exclusively permitted upon severance of the marriage ties (divorce, annulment, declaration of nullity, or death).
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Lex specialis derogat generali:** A special law governing passports (RA 8239) prevails over a general law on surnames (Civil Code), regardless of the dates of passage.
**Plain Meaning of Provisos:** The proviso in Section 5(d) explicitly qualifies and restricts the instances of maiden name reversion.
**Executive/Administrative Construction:** Great weight must be accorded to the implementing rules of the DFA tasked with maintaining passport integrity.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Passports are official State-issued documents of identity and nationality imbued with public interest. Allowing married individuals to alternate surnames at will in replacement passports compromises the integrity, reliability, and security of travel records, creating international confusion and facilitating fraudulent identity shifts.
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
### 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether petitioner, who originally used her husband's surname in her expired passport, can revert to the use of her maiden name in the replacement passport, despite the subsistence of her marriage.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the permissive word "may" in Article 370 of the Civil Code gives a married woman an unrestricted right to revert to her maiden surname in a replacement passport, or whether the restrictive proviso in Section 5(d) of RA 8239 controls as a special law that limits reversion exclusively to cases where the marriage tie is severed.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Lichauco & Company, Inc. v. Apostol**
**Full Official Caption:** LICHAUCO & COMPANY, INC., petitioner, vs. SILVERIO APOSTOL, as Director of Agriculture, and RAFAEL CORPUS, as Secretary of Agriculture and Natural Resources, respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:**
G.R. No. 19628
Promulgated: December 4, 1922
Ponente: Street, **J.**
Voting Breakdown: En Banc (5–3). Concurring: Malcolm, Avanceña, Villamor, and Ostrand, **JJ.** Dissenting: Johns, **J.**, joined by Araullo, **C.J.**, and Romualdez, **J.**
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
**Primary StatCon Classification:**
**Statutory Construction Area:** Repeals by Implication & Harmonization of Statutes
**Specific Canon / Principle / Rule Applied:** Presumption Against Implied Repeals; **Generalibus specialia derogant** (General statutes do not repeal prior special statutes without clear repugnancy); Harmonization of Statutes **In Pari Materia**
**Specific Latin Maxim: In pari materia**; **Generalia specialibus non derogant** (embodied in: "the general must yield to the particular")
**Specific Sub-Issue:** Whether a general amendatory statute with a mandatory proviso ("shall in all cases permit") impliedly repeals a pre-existing special emergency quarantine statute conferring authority to prohibit animal imports from disease-infected foreign ports.
**The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim):**
**First paragraph of Section 1762, Act No. 2711 (Administrative Code of 1917), as amended by Act No. 3052 (approved March 14, 1922):**
"SEC. 1762. **Bringing of animals imported from foreign countries into the Philippine Islands.** — It shall be unlawful for any person or corporation to import, bring or introduce live cattle into the Philippine Islands from any foreign country. The Director of Agriculture may, with the approval of the head of the department first had, authorize the importation, bringing or introduction of various classes of thoroughbred cattle from foreign countries for breeding the same to the native cattle of these Islands, and such as may be necessary for the improvement of the breed, not to exceed five hundred head per annum: **<ins>Provided, however, That the Director of Agriculture shall in all cases permit the importation, bringing or introduction of draft cattle and bovine cattle for the manufacture of serum:</ins> Provided, further,** That all live cattle from foreign countries the importation, bringing or introduction of which into the Islands is authorized by this Act, shall be submitted to regulations issued by the Director of Agriculture, with the approval of the head of the department, prior to authorizing its transfer to other provinces."
**Section 1770, Act No. 2711 (Administrative Code of 1917):**
"**<ins>SEC. 1770. Prohibition against bringing of animals from infected foreign countries.</ins>** — When the Department Head shall by general order declare that a dangerous communicable animal disease prevails in any foreign country, port, or place and that there is danger of spreading such disease by the importation of domestic animals therefrom, **<ins>it shall be unlawful for any person knowingly to ship or bring into the Philippine Islands any such animal, animal effects, parts, or products from such place, unless the importation thereof shall be authorized under the regulation of the Bureau of Agriculture.</ins>**"
**Historical / Amendment Tracking:**
**Prior Version (Section 1762, Act No. 2711 [1917]):**
"SEC. 1762. **Bringing of diseased animal into Islands forbidden.** — Except upon permission of the Director of Agriculture, with the approval of the head of Department first had, it shall be unlawful for any person knowingly to ship or otherwise bring into the Philippine Islands any animal suffering from, infected with, or dead of any dangerous communicable disease, or any effects pertaining to such animal which are liable to introduce such disease into the Philippine Islands."
**Amendatory Act (Act No. 3052 [1922]):** Retitled the section to **"Bringing of animals imported from foreign countries into the Philippine Islands,"** prohibited importation of live cattle generally, set an exception for up to 500 breeding thoroughbreds, and appended the mandatory proviso: **"Provided, however, That the Director of Agriculture shall in all cases permit the importation, bringing or introduction of draft cattle and bovine cattle for the manufacture of serum[.]"** It contained no repealing clause.
**StatCon Diagnostic Profile:**
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Apparent Conflict Between Provisions / Claimed Repeal by Implication (The absolute phrasing of **"shall in all cases permit"** in amended Section 1762 seemed irreconcilable with the discretionary embargo power under Section 1770 over infected foreign countries).
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?: YES.** Construction was essential to determine whether the later affirmative enactment in Act No. 3052 operated as an implied repeal of Section 1770 or whether both provisions could be harmonized **in pari materia**.
**Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed:** Presumption against implied repeals; Harmonization **in pari materia**; Rule that a general statute does not repeal a prior special statute; General provisions must yield to specific emergency exceptions (**Generalia specialibus non derogant**).
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The Director of Agriculture refused to issue an unrestricted import permit for 300 to 400 carabaos from Pnom-Pehn, French Indo-China (a rinderpest-infected territory), imposing Administrative Order No. 21 requiring immunization prior to embarkation, which the importer challenged as contrary to the mandatory command of Act No. 3052.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Petitioner:** Lichauco & Company, Inc., a domestic corporation engaged in importing carabaos and draft cattle.
**Respondents:** Silverio Apostol (Acting Director of Agriculture) and Rafael Corpus (Secretary of Agriculture and Natural Resources), the executive officials charged with enforcing animal quarantine laws.
**Procedural History & Vehicle:**
**Vehicle:** Original Petition for Writs of Mandamus and Injunction filed directly in the Supreme Court.
**Initial Action:** The Supreme Court issued an order to show cause and a temporary restraining order on September 21, 1922.
**Action of the Executive / Respondents:** The Attorney-General filed a return in the nature of a demurrer to the petition, asserting that Department Order No. 6 and Administrative Order No. 21 were lawful exercises of authority under Section 1770.
**Supreme Court Disposition:** Sustained the demurrer; dissolved the temporary restraining order; dismissed the petition conditionally upon failure to amend within five days.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **March 14, 1922:** The Philippine Legislature approves Act No. 3052, amending Section 1762 of the Administrative Code, inserting a proviso directing that the Director of Agriculture **"shall in all cases permit the importation, bringing or introduction of draft cattle and bovine cattle for the manufacture of serum."**
2. **July 28, 1922:** The Secretary of Agriculture and Natural Resources issues **Department Order No. 6**, declaring that rinderpest prevails in Hong Kong, French Indo-China, and British India, and prohibiting the importation of cattle, carabaos, and pigs therefrom under Section 1770 of the Administrative Code, unless authorized under Bureau regulations.
3. **July 29, 1922:** The Director of Agriculture promulgates **Administrative Order No. 21**, prohibiting the importation of livestock from the specified infected territories, but allowing entry of animals immunized against rinderpest if the importer secures a written permit prior to placing the order.
4. **August 31, 1922:** Acting Director Silverio Apostol responds to the application of Faustino Lichauco (for petitioner) to import 300 to 400 carabaos from Pnom-Pehn, French Indo-China, granting permission only on strict conditions: (a) simultaneous immunization before shipment via virulent blood and serum, and a subsequent injection of virulent blood alone; and (b) certification by a French government veterinarian, with embarkation barred until 10 days post-second injection.
5. **September 1922:** Petitioner files an original petition for **mandamus** and **injunction** in the Supreme Court to compel an unconditional permit, arguing Act No. 3052 gives it an absolute right to import draft cattle. On September 21, 1922, the Supreme Court issues a temporary restraining order against the respondents.
6. **October 7, 1922:** The Attorney-General files a demurrer on behalf of respondents, arguing Section 1770 remains in full force and justifies the pre-embarkation immunization requirement.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
A. Petitioner's Interpretation
**Core Reading:** The phrase **"shall in all cases permit"** in Section 1762 (as amended by Act No. 3052) confers an absolute, non-discretionary right to import draft cattle and bovine cattle for serum. Consequently, Act No. 3052 impliedly repealed Section 1770 insofar as draft and serum cattle are concerned. Administrative Order No. 21 is **ultra vires** because quarantine powers attach only upon actual arrival in Philippine ports, not prior to foreign embarkation.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked: Verba legis** / Plain Meaning Rule (mandatory nature of "shall"); Doctrine of Implied Repeal (a subsequent inconsistent act repeals prior inconsistent legislation); Territoriality Principle (statutes have no extraterritorial operation, precluding regulations on foreign soil prior to embarkation).
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Requiring immunization at the foreign port under foreign veterinarians, coupled with follow-up virulent tests in the Philippines, imposes severe financial burdens and risks killing whole herds.
B. Respondent's Interpretation
**Core Reading:** Section 1770 is a special emergency statute empowering the Department Head to embargo domestic animals from foreign countries plagued by dangerous communicable diseases (rinderpest). Act No. 3052 is a general law governing standard cattle importation and breed improvement. Section 1770 stands as a special qualification or exception to Section 1762.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:** Presumption against implied repeals; Construction **in pari materia**; **Generalia specialibus non derogant** (a general act does not repeal a particular enactment); Executive discretion in administrative quarantine execution.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Striking down Section 1770 for draft animals would completely destroy animal quarantine in the Philippines, exposing the entire domestic agricultural industry to devastation from foreign epidemics.
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
### 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether Section 1770 of the Administrative Code has been repealed by implication by Act No. 3052, amendatory to Section 1762, in so far as it relates to draft animals and bovine cattle for the manufacture of serum.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the mandatory proviso in Section 1762, as amended by Act No. 3052, providing that the Director of Agriculture **"shall in all cases permit"** the importation of draft and serum cattle, impliedly repealed Section 1770's special quarantine embargo powers over infected foreign ports under the rule of **generalia specialibus non derogant**.
