digest:
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the requirement of Administrative Order No. 21, imposing immunization at the port of embarkation before shipment, is unreasonable or beyond the regulative authority of the Director of Agriculture under Section 1770.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the administrative power under Section 1770 to authorize importation under regulations permits the Director of Agriculture to impose pre-embarkation immunization as a prospective condition precedent to entering Philippine ports.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Implied Repeal of Section 1770 by Act No. 3052 (Amended Section 1762)
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
**NO.** Section 1770 remains in full force; it is a special emergency quarantine provision that acts as an exception to the general import rules of Section 1762, and repeals by implication are disfavored.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**"We are of the opinion that the contention of the petitioner is untenable, for the reason that section 1762, as amended, is obviously of a general nature, while section 1770 deals with a particular contingency not made the subject of legislation in section 1762. Section 1770 is therefore not to be considered as inconsistent with section 1762, as amended; on the other hand, it must be treated as a special qualification of section 1762."**
**"In our opinion section 1762, as amended, and section 1770 must be construed in pari materia as harmonious parts of the law dealing with animal quarantine; and section 1762, as amended, can be given effect only in so far as it is not restricted by section 1770. Here, as always, the general must yield to the particular."**
**"'Wherever there is a particular enactment and a general enactment in the same statute, and the latter, taken in its most comprehensive sense, would overrule the former, the particular enactment must be operative, and the general enactment must be taken to affect only the other parts of the statute to which it may properly apply.' (Sir John Romilly, Master of the Rolls, in Pretty vs. Solly...)"**
**"It is well settled that repeals by implication are not to be favored. And where two statutes cover, in whole or in part, the same matter, and are not absolutely irreconcilable, the duty of the court — no purpose to repeal being clearly expressed or indicated — is, if possible, to give effect to both."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court acknowledged that if amended Section 1762 were read in isolation, its literal words would grant unrestricted entry; however, statutory construction is necessary because an apparent conflict exists with Section 1770.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court harmonized the two sections **in pari materia**. Section 1762 governs the ongoing, general subject of importing cattle at any time from anywhere for agricultural and breeding purposes. Section 1770 is a specific emergency provision addressing a unique contingency: foreign countries officially declared to be infected with dangerous communicable animal diseases. Section 1770 serves as a continuing special exception/qualification to the general rule.
3. **Extrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court analyzed extensive US and common law precedents on implied repeal (**Pretty v. Solly**, **Rodgers v. United States**, **Ex Parte United States**, **Frost v. Wenie**, and Chas. C. Moore's treatise in **Federal Statutes Annotated**), affirming the rule that broad general statutes lack the power to abrogate prior specific emergency enactments without plain, unavoidable repugnancy.
4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** Presumption against implied repeals; presumption against absurdity and public detriment. The Court reasoned by analogy: if Congress repealed Chinese exclusion laws, it could never be construed as abolishing the power to enforce quarantine against ports stricken with cholera or bubonic plague.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court rejected petitioner's argument that "shall in all cases permit" admits no exceptions. The Legislature could not possibly have intended to disable the Philippine government from protecting the domestic cattle industry from rinderpest epidemics. Words of qualification must be read into the general enactment rather than destroying the special one.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** The Court ruled that amended Section 1762 is a general law governing ordinary cattle imports, while Section 1770 is a special quarantine law designed for emergency outbreaks in specific infected countries. Because repeals by implication are disfavored, the phrase "shall in all cases permit" applies only to normal importations and must yield to the government’s special emergency power to exclude diseased animals under Section 1770.
Issue 2: Validity of Pre-Embarkation Immunization Under Section 1770
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
**YES.** The requirement of pre-embarkation immunization under Administrative Order No. 21 is a valid exercise of administrative regulatory power under Section 1770.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**"About the principal fact that rinderpest exists in the regions referred to in Department Order No. 6, there is, and can be no dispute; and when the Department Head declared that the disease prevails in those regions and that there is danger of spreading it by the importation of cattle and carabao into this country, he was acting upon a matter within his province, and we are not disposed to review the conclusion."**
**"This contention, in our opinion, reflects a mistaken point of view with reference to the effect of the regulations; and the answer is to be found in the consideration that the regulation in question has prospective reference to the condition of the cattle upon their arrival here. In other words, the prior immunization of the cattle is made a condition precedent to the right to bring them in; as much as to say, that only animals conforming to the required type will be admitted."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court addressed whether the executive exceeded statutory boundaries by imposing requirements taking place outside the territorial limits of the Philippines.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** Section 1770 expressly makes it unlawful to ship or bring domestic animals from infected ports **"unless the importation thereof shall be authorized under the regulation of the Bureau of Agriculture."** The statute vests broad authority to specify the terms under which an import is permissible.
3. **Extrinsic Aids Examined:** General principles of administrative quarantine discretion and police power.
4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** Presumption of validity of executive regulations enacted within statutory authority to preserve public welfare.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court rejected the argument that regulations cannot require foreign acts. Pre-embarkation immunization is merely a condition precedent defining the physical state (immunity) of animals eligible to enter Philippine jurisdiction, not an extraterritorial command.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** The Court held that requiring cattle to be immunized before leaving Indo-China is not an unlawful extraterritorial rule, but a valid administrative condition precedent ensuring that animals arriving at Philippine ports are safe and disease-free. The Director of Agriculture has full statutory authority under Section 1770 to define the safety standards cattle must meet before they are allowed into the country.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
**Dissenting Opinion of Justice Johns (joined by Araullo, C.J., and Romualdez, J.):**
**Interpretative Divergence:** Justice Johns argued that Act No. 3052 is a complete, later substitute that specifically, positively, and unconditionally stripped the executive of discretion regarding draft cattle: **"the Director of Agriculture shall in all cases permit the importation."**
**StatCon Canons Invoked by Dissent:**
1. **Verba Legis / Plain Meaning:** The legal definition of "importation" means bringing goods into port with intent to land; thus, the Director has a non-discretionary duty to permit the physical entry of such cattle.
2. **Direct Repugnancy and Later Enactment:** Relying on **Lewis' Sutherland Statutory Construction** and **Gorham v. Luckett**, the dissent stressed that when a later act affirmatively grants limited, specific instructions that contradict prior broad grants of power, the later act prevails and constructively repeals the former.
3. **Interdependence of Codal Provisions:** The dissent maintained that Section 1770 was not an independent special act, but was completely dependent on Section 1762 within the same code. When Section 1762 was rewritten to mandate permits "in all cases" for draft animals, it completely removed the statutory foundation upon which Section 1770 could operate as to those specific animals.
4. **Subordination of Administrative Rules:** Subordinate administrative orders cannot nullify an express, mandatory act of the Legislature.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"Upon the whole we are of the opinion that the petition does not show sufficient ground for granting the writs of **mandamus** and injunction. The demurrer interposed thereto by the respondents in their return to the order to show cause, dated October 7, 1922, is therefore sustained, and the temporary restraining order heretofore promulgated in this cause, dated September 21, 1922, is dissolved; and unless within five days after notification hereof the petitioner shall so amend his petition as to show a sufficient cause of action, an order absolute will be entered, dismissing the same, with costs. So ordered."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The respondents (Director and Secretary of Agriculture) prevailed. The Supreme Court sustained their demurrer and dissolved the temporary restraining order, establishing that Section 1770 remains in full effect as a special exception to Act No. 3052, meaning the government may lawfully prohibit or place pre-embarkation immunization conditions on the importation of cattle from countries infected with rinderpest.

**Citation & Metadata:**
**Docket Number:** G.R. No. 156117
**Date of Promulgation:** May 26, 2005
**Official Repositories:** 498 Phil. 227 (also 459 SCRA 183)
**Ponente:** Chico-Nazario, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Second Division: Puno, **Acting C.J.** (Chairman), Austria-Martinez, and Callejo, Sr., **JJ.**, concur; Tinga, **J.**, out of the country. No separate concurring or dissenting opinions were registered.
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
Primary StatCon Classification
**Statutory Construction Area:** Statute vs. Statute Conflict (General Law vs. Special Law) & Mandatory vs. Directory Procedural Requirements / Provisos.
**Specific Canon / Principle / Rule Applied:**
1. **Generalia specialibus non derogant** (a general law does not derogate from a special law; a special statute governing a particular subject prevails over a general statute).
2. Mandatory Construction of Due Process / Notice Clauses (Publication Proviso Subordinated to Constitutional Due Process).
3. Inter-statute Harmonization & Suppletory Application of Procedural Rules (**Casus Omissus** in Special Procedure supplied by General Rules of Procedure).
**Specific Latin Maxim: Generalia specialibus non derogant**.
**Specific Sub-Issue:** Whether the 30-year extraordinary prescription under Articles 1113 and 1137 of the Civil Code can override the specific requirement of open, continuous, exclusive, and notorious possession since June 12, 1945 under Section 48(b) of the Public Land Act (C.A. No. 141, as amended by P.D. No. 1073) for the judicial confirmation of imperfect title to public agricultural lands; and whether the proviso in Section 23(1) of P.D. No. 1529 makes newspaper publication merely directory.
The Contested Statutory Text (Verbatim)
1. Section 48(b), Commonwealth Act No. 141 (The Public Land Act), as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1073:
"SEC. 48. The following-described citizens of the Philippines, occupying lands of the public domain or claiming to own any such lands or an interest therein, but whose titles have not been perfected or completed, may apply to the Court of First Instance of the province where the land is located for confirmation of their claims and the issuance of a certificate of title thereafter, under the Land Registration Act, to wit:
(a) [Repealed by Presidential Decree No. 1073].
(b) Those who by themselves or through their predecessors-in-interest have been in open, continuous, exclusive, and notorious possession and occupation of agricultural lands of the public domain, under a bona fide claim of acquisition of ownership, **<ins>since June 12, 1945, or earlier</ins>**, immediately preceding the filing of the applications for confirmation of title, except when prevented by war or force majeure. These shall be conclusively presumed to have performed all the conditions essential to a Government grant and shall be entitled to a certificate of title under the provisions of this chapter."
2. Articles 1113 and 1137, Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines):
"ART. 1113. All things which are within the commerce of men are susceptible of prescription, unless otherwise provided. Property of the State or any of its subdivisions not patrimonial in character shall not be the object of prescription."
"ART. 1137. Ownership and other real rights over immovables also prescribe through **<ins>uninterrupted adverse possession thereof for thirty years</ins>**, without need of title or of good faith."
3. Section 23(1), Presidential Decree No. 1529 (Property Registration Decree):
"SEC. 23. **Notice of initial hearing, publication, etc.** — The court shall, within five days from filing of the application, issue an order setting the date and hour of the initial hearing which shall not be earlier than forty-five days nor later than ninety days from the date of the order.
The public shall be given notice of the initial hearing of the application for land registration by means of (1) publication; (2) mailing; and (3) posting.
1. By publication. —
Upon receipt of the order of the court setting the time for initial hearing, the Commissioner of Land Registration shall cause a notice of initial hearing to be **<ins>published once in the Official Gazette and once in a newspaper of general circulation</ins>** in the Philippines: **<ins>Provided, however, that the publication in the Official Gazette shall be sufficient to confer jurisdiction upon the court</ins>**. Said notice shall be addressed to all persons appearing to have an interest in the land involved including the adjoining owners so far as known, and 'to all whom it may concern.' Said notice shall also require all persons concerned to appear in court at a certain date and time to show cause why the prayer of said application shall not be granted."
4. Section 18, Presidential Decree No. 1529:
"SEC. 18. **Application covering two or more parcels.** — An application may include two or more parcels of land **<ins>belonging to the applicant/s</ins>** provided they are situated within the same province or city. The court may at any time order an application to be amended by striking out one or more of the parcels or by a severance of the application."
Historical / Amendment Tracking
**C.A. No. 141, Section 48(b) (Original Text):** Required possession "for at least thirty years immediately preceding the filing of the application."
**P.D. No. 1073 (Promulgated January 25, 1977):** Amended Section 48(b) by replacing the 30-year rolling period with the definitive historical cut-off date: **"since June 12, 1945, or earlier."**
StatCon Diagnostic Profile
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:**
1. **Conflict Between Provisions:** Conflict between the 30-year general acquisitive prescription clause of the Civil Code (Arts. 1113 & 1137) invoked through Sec. 14(4) of P.D. No. 1529, and the specific requirement of possession since June 12, 1945 under Sec. 48(b) of C.A. No. 141 (as amended by P.D. No. 1073).
2. **Internal Inconsistency / Statutory Tension:** Tension between the mandatory command in Sec. 23(1) of P.D. No. 1529 requiring publication in **both** the Official Gazette and a newspaper of general circulation, and its immediately following proviso stating that **"publication in the Official Gazette shall be sufficient to confer jurisdiction upon the court."**
3. **Legislative Silence / Procedural Gap:** Silence of P.D. No. 1529 on whether two applicants separately claiming two distinct, individually owned parcels can join their claims in a single petition.
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. The Court engaged in statutory construction to harmonize the procedural gap via suppletory application of the Rules of Court; to read down the **jurisdictional proviso** of Section 23(1) of P.D. No. 1529 in light of constitutional due process; and to resolve the conflict between the Civil Code and the Public Land Act through the canon of special laws prevailing over general laws.
**Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed:**
1. **Generalia specialibus non derogant** (General laws do not derogate from special laws; special laws prevail over general laws).
2. Mandatory construction of **in rem** statutory publication requirements over conflicting statutory provisos to preserve constitutional due process.
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** Two brothers jointly filed a single application for registration of two individually owned lots which had only been classified as alienable and disposable on June 25, 1963, publishing the notice in a newspaper **three months after** the initial hearing had already occurred and an order of special default had already been entered.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
Key Parties & Roles
**Petitioner:** Republic of the Philippines (represented by the Office of the Solicitor General), opposing the registration on the grounds of lack of adverse possession since June 12, 1945, invalid muniments of title, inalienability of the public domain, and jurisdictional defect due to misjoinder.
**Respondents:** Jeremias Herbieto (applicant claiming fee simple ownership over Lot No. 8422) and David Herbieto (applicant claiming fee simple ownership over Lot No. 8423).
**Predecessors-in-Interest:** Spouses Gregorio Herbieto and Isabel Owatan (parents of respondents, who allegedly possessed the lots since 1950 and executed a deed of sale in 1976).
**Enforcing / Administering Agencies:**
**Community Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO), DENR:** Issued certification on June 23, 1963/Forestry Administrative Order No. 4-1063 classifying the land as alienable and disposable only on June 25, 1963.
**Land Registration Authority (LRA):** Directed to issue decrees of registration.
Procedural History & Vehicle
**Originating Body:** Municipal Trial Court (MTC) of Consolacion, Cebu (LRC Case No. N-75). On December 21, 1999, the MTC confirmed respondents' title. On February 2, 2000, it declared the decision final and executory.
**Appellate Court:** Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. CV No. 67625). On November 22, 2002, the CA affirmed the MTC, holding that the lots became alienable in 1963 and respondents acquired them via 30-year extraordinary prescription under Civil Code Articles 1113 and 1137 in relation to Section 14(4) of P.D. No. 1529.
**Judicial Vehicle to Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on **Certiorari** under Rule 45 filed by the Republic. The Supreme Court **reversed** the CA and MTC, declaring all lower court proceedings **null and void**.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **June 25, 1963:** The Subject Lots (Lots No. 8422 and 8423, located in Cabangahan, Consolacion, Cebu) are officially classified as alienable and disposable public land pursuant to Forestry Administrative Order No. 4-1063 (LC Map No. 2545, Project No. 28). Prior thereto, they formed part of the inalienable public domain.
2. **June 25, 1976:** Spouses Gregorio Herbieto and Isabel Owatan execute a "Deed of Definite Sale" conveying Lot No. 8422 to their son Jeremias Herbieto, and Lot No. 8423 to their son David Herbieto, for the sum of ₱1,000.00. The parents claimed to have possessed and cultivated the lots since 1950.
3. **1994:** Assessment of Real Property (ARP) No. 941800301831 is issued in the name of Jeremias for Lot No. 8422, and ARP No. 941800301833 is issued in the name of David for Lot No. 8423.
4. **September 23, 1998:** Jeremias and David Herbieto file a single, joint application for original registration of title to Lots No. 8422 and 8423 before the MTC of Consolacion, Cebu. They do not claim co-ownership, but separate individual ownership over each distinct parcel.
5. **December 11, 1998:** The Republic files its formal Opposition to the application, citing failure to prove the required period of open, continuous, and adverse possession; insufficient muniments of title; and the public character of the land.
6. **April 29, 1999:** The MTC issues an order setting the initial hearing of the application on September 3, 1999, at 8:30 a.m.
7. **July 27, 1999:** Notice of Initial Hearing is posted on the subject lots and the municipal bulletin board. Adjoining owners are mailed notices.
8. **August 2, 1999:** Notice of Initial Hearing is published in the Official Gazette (officially released August 10, 1999).
9. **September 3, 1999:** The MTC holds the initial hearing, issues an Order of Special Default against the whole world (except the Republic), and delegates the reception of evidence to the Clerk of Court.
10. **December 19, 1999:** The Notice of Initial Hearing is published in **The Freeman Banat News**—**more than three months after the initial hearing had already occurred and the order of special default had been entered.**
11. **December 21, 1999:** The MTC renders Judgment confirming title in fee simple to Jeremias over Lot No. 8422 and to David over Lot No. 8423.
12. **February 2, 2000:** The MTC issues an Order declaring its December 21, 1999 Judgment final and executory and directing the LRA to issue the registration decrees.
13. **November 22, 2002:** The Court of Appeals affirms the MTC Judgment, applying extraordinary acquisitive prescription of 30 years under the Civil Code (1963 to 1998 = 35 years).
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
| Interpretative Parameter | Petitioner (Republic of the Philippines) | Respondent (Herbieto Brothers) / Court of Appeals |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Governing Law on Possession** | **C.A. No. 141, Sec. 48(b) (as amended by P.D. 1073)** governs exclusively. Possession must be shown **since June 12, 1945, or earlier**. Possessory acts prior to alienability date (June 25, 1963) are legally void. | **Civil Code, Arts. 1113 & 1137 in relation to P.D. 1529, Sec. 14(4)** governs. Title was acquired by **30-year extraordinary prescription** running from the 1963 alienability date to the 1998 application (35 years). |
| **Canons / Maxims Invoked** | Special Law Precedence; Plain Meaning (**Verba Legis**); Non-alienable public lands cannot be subject to prescription (**Regalian Doctrine**). | Liberal Construction; Broad application of "any other manner provided by law" (P.D. 1529, Sec. 14[4]); Acquisitive prescription under the Civil Code. |
| **Consequence / Policy Argument** | Public lands cannot be acquired without explicit statutory authorization; ignoring the June 12, 1945 cut-off circumvents P.D. No. 1073 and destabilizes public land administration. | Possession for 35 years of alienable land satisfies the 30-year rule, fulfilling the equitable objective of quieting title and recognizing long-term agricultural cultivation. |
| **Joinder of Non-Co-Owners** | **Mandatory statutory limitation:** P.D. 1529 strictly limits multiple applicants to co-owners, and multiple lots to the same owner; breach deprives court of jurisdiction. | **Not expressly argued by respondents.** Treated as a single joint application over adjoining familial parcels. |
| **Publication Requirement (Sec. 23[1], P.D. 1529)** | **Not raised by petitioner; raised motu proprio by Supreme Court:** Both Official Gazette and newspaper publication are jurisdictional and mandatory. | The statutory text of Section 23(1) contains an express proviso: **"Provided, however, that the publication in the Official Gazette shall be sufficient to confer jurisdiction upon the court."** |
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
1. **[PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]** Whether the procedural defect of filing a single application for two distinct parcels of land by two separate, individual non-co-owners constitutes a jurisdictional defect under P.D. No. 1529 that renders the proceedings void, or merely a misjoinder of causes of action and parties governed suppletorily by the Rules of Court.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does the absence of an express provision in P.D. No. 1529 allowing non-co-owners to file a joint registration application create a jurisdictional bar, or does Section 34 mandate the suppletory application of the Rules of Court to treat the defect as a non-fatal misjoinder?
2. **[PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE / Constitutional Due Process]** Whether the proviso in Section 23(1) of P.D. No. 1529—declaring that **"publication in the Official Gazette shall be sufficient to confer jurisdiction upon the court"**—dispenses with the mandatory requirement of publishing the Notice of Initial Hearing in a newspaper of general circulation prior to the hearing.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the statutory proviso in Section 23(1) of P.D. No. 1529 can be interpreted literally to confer **in rem** jurisdiction despite the publication in a newspaper of general circulation taking place three months **after** the initial hearing had terminated.
3. **[PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]** Whether an applicant seeking judicial confirmation of title to public agricultural land alienable since June 25, 1963 may bypass the June 12, 1945 possession requirement of Section 48(b) of C.A. No. 141 by invoking 30-year extraordinary acquisitive prescription under Articles 1113 and 1137 of the Civil Code through Section 14(4) of P.D. No. 1529 under the maxim **generalia specialibus non derogant**.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does the Civil Code's general 30-year acquisitive prescription regime yield to the specific June 12, 1945 possessory requirement of Section 48(b) of the Public Land Act under the canon **generalia specialibus non derogant** when seeking registration of alienable public land?
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
ISSUE 1: Misjoinder of Causes of Action and Parties Under P.D. 1529
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The joint application by non-co-owners for separate parcels does not deprive the court of jurisdiction; pursuant to Section 34 of P.D. No. 1529, the Rules of Court apply suppletorily, and misjoinder of causes of action or parties is not a ground for dismissal or lack of jurisdiction.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"The Property Registration Decree recognizes and expressly allows the following situations: (1) the filing of a single application by several applicants for as long as they are co-owners of the parcel of land sought to be registered; and (2) the filing of a single application for registration of several parcels of land provided that the same are located within the same province. The Property Registration Decree is silent, however, as to the present situation wherein two applicants filed a single application for two parcels of land, but are seeking the separate and individual registration of the parcels of land in their respective names."
"Since the Property Registration Decree failed to provide for such a situation, then this Court refers to the Rules of Court to determine the proper course of action. Section 34 of the Property Registration Decree itself provides that, '[t]he Rules of Court shall, insofar as not inconsistent with the provisions of this Decree, be applicable to land registration and cadastral cases by analogy or in a suppletory character and whenever practicable and convenient.'"
"Misjoinder of causes of action and parties do not involve a question of jurisdiction of the court to hear and proceed with the case. They are not even accepted grounds for dismissal thereof."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate / Gap Identification:** P.D. No. 1529 expressly regulates co-owners filing for one parcel (Sec. 14) and one applicant filing for multiple parcels in the same province (Sec. 18), but exhibits a legislative gap (**casus omissus**) regarding multiple separate owners filing for separate parcels in one application.
2. **Intrinsic Aids / Harmonization:** The Court analyzed Section 34 of P.D. No. 1529, which explicitly incorporates the Rules of Court by analogy or suppletorily when not inconsistent with the Decree.
3. **Application of Suppletory Law:** Under Rule 2, Section 6 and Rule 3, Section 11 of the Rules of Court, misjoinder of causes of action and misjoinder of parties are never grounds for dismissal nor do they impair subject-matter jurisdiction.
4. **Rejection of Losing Argument:** The Court distinguished **Director of Lands v. Court of Appeals** (102 SCRA 370). The defect here was purely procedural and subject to a motion for severance, not a statutory violation that ousts the MTC of judicial power.
**(d) Plain-Language StatCon Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** When a specialized registration statute does not specifically address a procedural anomaly (such as two brothers filing one petition for two distinct properties), the statute's own suppletory clause directs the court to use the general Rules of Court. Under these general rules, joining claims or parties that should have been filed separately is just a misjoinder to be separated upon motion, not a fatal mistake that strips the court of its authority to hear the case.
ISSUE 2: Late Publication in a Newspaper of General Circulation and the Proviso of Section 23(1)
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The MTC lacked jurisdiction because publication in a newspaper of general circulation is mandatory and must precede the initial hearing; publication three months after the hearing is legally void and cannot be cured by the proviso in Section 23(1).
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Even as this Court concedes that the aforequoted Section 23(1) of the Property Registration Decree expressly provides that publication in the Official Gazette shall be sufficient to confer jurisdiction upon the land registration court, it still affirms its declaration in **Director of Lands v. Court of Appeals** that publication in a newspaper of general circulation is mandatory for the land registration court to validly confirm and register the title of the applicant or applicants."
"The reason is due process and the reality that the Official Gazette is not as widely read and circulated as newspaper and is oftentimes delayed in its circulation, such that the notices published therein may not reach the interested parties on time, if at all... In sum, the all encompassing in rem nature of land registration cases, the consequences of default orders issued against the whole world and the objective of disseminating the notice in as wide a manner as possible demand a mandatory construction of the requirements for publication, mailing and posting."
"The late publication of the Notice of Initial Hearing in the newspaper of general circulation is tantamount to no publication at all, having the same ultimate result. Owing to such defect in the publication of the Notice, the MTC failed to constructively seize the Subject Lots and to acquire jurisdiction over respondents' application for registration thereof."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** Confronted with an express statutory proviso (**"Provided, however, that the publication in the Official Gazette shall be sufficient to confer jurisdiction upon the court"**), the Court refused a literal interpretation that would nullify the concurrent newspaper publication requirement.
2. **Constitutional & Intrinsic Context:** Land registration is an **in rem** proceeding resulting in judgments binding against the entire world. Constitutional due process requires constructive seizure through broad public notice.
3. **Statutory Purpose / Teleological Interpretation:** The legislative objective in prescribing three distinct forms of notice (publication, mailing, posting) is wide dissemination. Reading the proviso literally would render newspaper publication an empty, optional formality.
4. **Mandatory vs. Directory Construction:** The Court held that newspaper publication is mandatory, strictly indispensable, and must take place **prior** to the initial hearing.
5. **Factual Application:** Because **The Freeman Banat News** publication occurred on December 19, 1999—over three months after the September 3, 1999 hearing and special default order—it was a legal nullity, leaving the court without **in rem** jurisdiction.
**(d) Plain-Language StatCon Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** Even though the statute includes a sentence saying Official Gazette publication is enough to confer jurisdiction, the Court construed the entire notice section strictly in light of the constitutional guarantee of due process. Because land registration cuts off property rights against the whole world, publishing the notice in a local newspaper **after** the court hearing has already been held is equivalent to no notice at all, rendering everything the trial court did completely void.
ISSUE 3: C.A. No. 141 (Public Land Act) vs. Civil Code Acquisitive Prescription (**Generalia Specialibus Non Derogant**)
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Respondents cannot acquire title to public agricultural lands under the 30-year extraordinary prescription rule of the Civil Code; Section 48(b) of C.A. No. 141 is a special law that controls over the general Civil Code under the maxim **generalia specialibus non derogant**, requiring adverse possession since June 12, 1945 or earlier.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal Pronouncements:**
"Not being members of any national cultural minorities, respondents may only be entitled to judicial confirmation or legalization of their imperfect or incomplete title under Section 48(b) of the Public Land Act, as amended. Section 48(b), as amended, now requires adverse possession of the land since 12 June 1945 or earlier. In the present Petition, the Subject Lots became alienable and disposable only on 25 June 1963. Any period of possession prior to the date when the Subject Lots were classified as alienable and disposable is inconsequential and should be excluded from the computation of the period of possession; such possession can never ripen into ownership and unless the land had been classified as alienable and disposable, the rules on confirmation of imperfect title shall not apply thereto."
"The Court of Appeals overlooked the difference between the Property Registration Decree and the Public Land Act. Under the Property Registration Decree, there already exists a title which is confirmed by the court; while under the Public Land Act, the presumption always is that the land applied for pertains to the State, and that the occupants and possessors only claim an interest in the same by virtue of their imperfect title or continuous, open, and notorious possession."
"Moreover, provisions of the Civil Code on prescription of ownership and other real rights apply in general to all types of land, while the Public Land Act specifically governs lands of the public domain. Relative to one another, the Public Land Act may be considered a special law that must take precedence over the Civil Code, a general law. It is an established rule of statutory construction that between a general law and a special law, the special law prevails – **Generalia specialibus non derogant**."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate & Doctrinal Subjugation:** The CA applied Civil Code Arts. 1113 and 1137 (30-year acquisitive prescription) via Sec. 14(4) of P.D. No. 1529 ("in any other manner provided by law"). The Supreme Court rejected this path, holding that public lands are exclusively governed by the Public Land Act (C.A. No. 141).
2. **Canon Applied (Generalia Specialibus Non Derogant):** The Civil Code is a general law applicable to property and prescription broadly; C.A. No. 141 is a special law governing the alienability and disposition of the public domain. Under **generalia specialibus non derogant**, the special law prevails and cannot be diluted by general prescription provisions.
3. **Temporal Threshold Analysis:** Section 48(b) of C.A. No. 141, as amended by P.D. No. 1073, sets a strict, fixed baseline: possession must be open, continuous, exclusive, and notorious **since June 12, 1945, or earlier**.
4. **Regalian Doctrine / Legal Impossibility of Adverse Possession:** Land of the public domain not yet classified as alienable and disposable cannot be possessed adversely in the concept of an owner. The Subject Lots were only classified as alienable on June 25, 1963. Any prior possession is excluded as a matter of law.
5. **Rejection of 30-Year Prescription Theory:** Counting possession only from June 25, 1963, respondents could not possibly satisfy the June 12, 1945 statutory requirement of C.A. No. 141. They cannot escape this clear requirement by seeking refuge in the 30-year Civil Code acquisitive prescription.
**(d) Plain-Language StatCon Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** Under the rule **generalia specialibus non derogant**, a specific statute governing public land (the Public Land Act) always overrules a general statute governing ordinary property contracts and prescription (the Civil Code). Because the Public Land Act expressly demands continuous possession dating all the way back to June 12, 1945, an applicant trying to obtain public land cannot rely on the Civil Code’s shorter 30-year prescription rule to bypass the clear command of the special public land law.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.**
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
Verbatim Fallo:
"WHEREFORE, based on the foregoing, the instant Petition is GRANTED. The Decision of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. CV No. 67625, dated 22 November 2002, is REVERSED. The Judgment of the MTC of Consolacion, Cebu in LRC Case No. N-75, dated 21 December 1999, and its Order, dated 02 February 2000 are declared NULL AND VOID. Respondents' application for registration is DISMISSED.
SO ORDERED."
Plain-Language Outcome:
The Republic prevailed completely. The Supreme Court nullified the judgments of the Court of Appeals and the Municipal Trial Court and dismissed the registration application of the Herbieto brothers because: (1) the trial court never acquired jurisdiction due to publishing the notice in a newspaper after the hearing took place, and (2) public agricultural lands can only be acquired upon affirmative proof of possession dating back to June 12, 1945 or earlier under the Public Land Act, which special rule entirely overrides the general 30-year prescription period found in the Civil Code.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Goldenway Merchandising Corporation v. Equitable PCI Bank**
**Full Official Caption: Goldenway Merchandising Corporation, Petitioner, v. Equitable PCI Bank, Respondent**
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 195540
**Date of Promulgation:** March 13, 2013
**Official Citation:** 706 Phil. 427 (2013)
**Ponente:** Villarama, Jr., **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** First Division: Sereno, **C.J.** (Chairperson), Leonardo-De Castro, Bersamin, and Reyes, **JJ.**, concur. Unanimous; no separate concurring or dissenting opinions.
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
**Primary StatCon Classification:**
**Statute Application & Temporal Scope** → Prospective Application vs. Retroactivity → Express Saving Clause / Non-Retroactivity Provision → Scope of Foreclosure Governed by Amending Law
**Extrinsic Aids** → Legislative History & Deliberations → Senate Deliberations / Sponsorship Speeches → Reasonable Classification under Equal Protection
**Conflict of Laws / Intrinsic Repealing Clause** → Express Non Obstante Clause ("Notwithstanding Act 3135") → Amendment of Prior General Redemption Period
**Statutory Presumptions** → Presumption of Constitutionality (**Presumptio pro constitutione**) → Police Power Subordination of Contractual Rights
**The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim):**
**Section 47 of Republic Act No. 8791 (The General Banking Law of 2000):**
"SECTION 47. **Foreclosure of Real Estate Mortgage.** — In the event of foreclosure, whether judicially or extrajudicially, of any mortgage on real estate which is security for any loan or other credit accommodation granted, the mortgagor or debtor whose real property has been sold for the full or partial payment of his obligation shall have the right within one year after the sale of the real estate, to redeem the property by paying the amount due under the mortgage deed, with interest thereon at the rate specified in the mortgage, and all the costs and expenses incurred by the bank or institution from the sale and custody of said property less the income derived therefrom. However, the purchaser at the auction sale concerned whether in a judicial or extrajudicial foreclosure shall have the right to enter upon and take possession of such property immediately after the date of the confirmation of the auction sale and administer the same in accordance with law. Any petition in court to enjoin or restrain the conduct of foreclosure proceedings instituted pursuant to this provision shall be given due course only upon the filing by the petitioner of a bond in an amount fixed by the court conditioned that he will pay all the damages which the bank may suffer by the enjoining or the restraint of the foreclosure proceeding.
**Notwithstanding Act 3135, juridical persons** whose property is being sold pursuant to an extrajudicial foreclosure, shall have the right to redeem the property in accordance with this provision **until, but not after, the registration of the certificate of foreclosure sale** with the applicable Register of Deeds **which in no case shall be more than three (3) months after foreclosure, whichever is earlier**. **Owners of property that has been sold in a foreclosure sale prior to the effectivity of this Act shall retain their redemption rights until their expiration.**"
**Section 6 of Act No. 3135 (as amended by Act No. 4118):**
"SEC. 6. In all cases in which an extrajudicial sale is made under the special power herein before referred to, the debtor, his successors-in-interest or any judicial creditor or judgment creditor of said debtor, or any person having a lien on the property subsequent to the mortgage or deed of trust under which the property is sold, may redeem the same at any time **within the term of one year from and after the date of the sale**; and such redemption shall be governed by the provisions of sections four hundred and sixty-four to four hundred and sixty-six, inclusive, of the Code of Civil Procedure, in so far as these are not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act."
**Historical / Amendment Tracking:**
**Prior Rule (Act No. 3135, § 6, enacted March 6, 1924, as amended by Act No. 4118):** All extrajudicially foreclosed mortgagors (natural and juridical) possessed a uniform right to redeem within one (1) year from the registration of the certificate of sale.
**Modern Rule (R.A. No. 8791, § 47, enacted June 13, 2000):** Introduced a non obstante clause (**"Notwithstanding Act 3135"**) bifurcating redemption rules. Juridical mortgagors whose property is extrajudicially foreclosed by banks may redeem only until the registration of the certificate of sale, capped at three (3) months after the foreclosure sale, whichever is earlier. Properties sold in foreclosure **prior** to June 13, 2000 were grandfathered under the old rules.
**StatCon Diagnostic Profile:**
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Plain Meaning coupled with an alleged conflict between an earlier specific statute (Act No. 3135) and a later banking statute (R.A. No. 8791), alongside an alleged constitutional invalidity (impairment of contractual obligations and equal protection violation).
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes, primarily to determine the temporal reach (retroactive vs. prospective application) of Section 47's grandfather clause, examine legislative intent via Senate deliberations, and resolve the claimed conflict between Act No. 3135 and Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791.
**Controlling Canons / Maxims Deployed:**
**Presumption of Constitutionality** (Every statute is presumed valid; nullity requires clear and unequivocal breach beyond reasonable doubt).
**Non-retroactivity rule / Prospective operation** governed by express transition text ("Owners of property that has been sold in a foreclosure sale prior to the effectivity of this Act shall retain their redemption rights...").
**Express legislative exception / Non obstante clause** ("Notwithstanding Act 3135").
**Extrinsic Aid: Legislative History & Deliberations** (Records of the Senate Second Reading and Sponsorship Speeches).
**Subordination of contract non-impairment to State Police Power**.
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** A corporate mortgagor executed a real estate mortgage in 1985 expressly invoking Act No. 3135. Following an extrajudicial foreclosure sale conducted in December 2000 (after R.A. No. 8791 took effect) and registration of the sale certificate in February 2001, the bank rejected the mortgagor's March 2001 redemption attempt, triggering a specific performance suit questioning which statutory redemption window governed.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Goldenway Merchandising Corporation (Petitioner):** A juridical corporate entity that obtained a ₱2,000,000.00 loan in 1985 secured by a real estate mortgage, claiming a vested 1-year statutory redemption period under Act No. 3135.
**Equitable PCI Bank (Respondent):** Mortgagee commercial bank that extrajudicially foreclosed the properties in December 2000, registered the certificate of sale on February 16, 2001, consolidated title, and rejected petitioner's post-registration redemption tender pursuant to Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791.
**Chan Guan Pue:** Alleged President of Goldenway who orally instructed counsel to effect redemption.
**Atty. Judy Ann Abat-Vera:** Counsel for petitioner who attempted to tender a ₱3,500,000.00 redemption check without board authorization.
**Register of Deeds (Province of Bulacan / Valenzuela):** Public recording office that inscribed the Certificate of Sale and subsequently consolidated title in favor of the bank on March 9, 2001.
**Procedural History & Vehicle:**
**Trial Court (RTC Valenzuela City, Branch 171, Civil Case No. 295-V-01):** Petitioner filed a Complaint for Specific Performance and Damages to compel redemption. On January 8, 2007, the RTC dismissed the complaint, ruling that: (1) the constitutional attack was not properly raised during pre-trial/trial; (2) redemption was attempted out of time under Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791; and (3) petitioner's counsel lacked corporate board authority to effect redemption.
**Appellate Court (Court of Appeals, CA-G.R. CV No. 91120):** Petitioner appealed. On November 19, 2010, the CA affirmed the RTC, holding that Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791 plainly applies to foreclosures conducted when the law was already in effect, deliberately shortened redemption for juridical entities, and was not shown to be unconstitutional. CA denied reconsideration on January 31, 2011.
**Supreme Court (G.R. No. 195540):** Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45. The Supreme Court affirmed the CA in full.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **November 29, 1985:** Goldenway Merchandising Corporation executed a Real Estate Mortgage in favor of Equitable PCI Bank over three parcels of land in Valenzuela covered by TCT Nos. T-152630, T-151655, and T-214528 to secure a ₱2,000,000.00 loan. The mortgage deed stipulated that in the event of default, the bank could foreclose judicially under the Rules of Court or extrajudicially pursuant to Act No. 3135, as amended.
2. **June 13, 2000:** Republic Act No. 8791 (The General Banking Law of 2000) took effect. Section 47 introduced a specific shortened redemption period for juridical persons whose properties are extrajudicially foreclosed by banks: until registration of the certificate of sale, or three (3) months from foreclosure, whichever is earlier.
3. **December 13, 2000:** Following Goldenway's default, Equitable PCI Bank extrajudicially foreclosed the mortgage. At the public auction, the bank was declared the highest bidder for ₱3,500,000.00.
4. **January 26, 2001:** The Certificate of Sale was issued to Equitable PCI Bank.
5. **February 16, 2001:** The Certificate of Sale was registered and inscribed on TCT Nos. T-152630, T-151655, and T-214528 in the Registry of Deeds.
6. **March 8, 2001:** Petitioner's counsel sent a letter offering to redeem the foreclosed properties and tendering a check for ₱3,500,000.00.
7. **March 9, 2001:** The Register of Deeds consolidated title to the properties in favor of Equitable PCI Bank, issuing new certificates of title in its name.
8. **March 12, 2001:** Petitioner's counsel met with respondent's legal counsel to reiterate its redemption offer, but the bank refused on the ground that the right of redemption had already expired upon registration of the certificate of sale under Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791.
9. **December 7, 2001:** Petitioner filed a complaint for specific performance and damages against respondent bank in the RTC of Valenzuela City, arguing that the 1-year redemption period under Act No. 3135 governed and that applying Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791 violated the non-impairment and equal protection clauses of the Constitution.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
A. Petitioner's Interpretation (Goldenway Merchandising Corp.):
**Core Reading:** The 1-year redemption period under Section 6 of Act No. 3135 governs the mortgage. Because the mortgage was executed in 1985, Act No. 3135 was incorporated as part and parcel of the contract, conferring a vested substantive right of redemption upon execution that cannot be altered by a subsequent statute.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Lex Retro Non Agit / Rule Against Retroactivity:** Laws operate prospectively unless retroactive intent is expressly declared; R.A. No. 8791 cannot apply to a 1985 contract.
**Generalia Specialibus Non Derogant:** Act No. 3135 is a special law specifically governing real estate mortgage foreclosures, whereas R.A. No. 8791 is a general law governing the banking industry; hence, Act No. 3135 must prevail regardless of enactment dates.
**Vested Rights & Liberal Construction of Redemption:** Citing **Co v. PNB**, **Rural Bank of Davao City v. CA**, and **Sulit v. CA**, courts must aid rather than defeat the mortgagor's right of redemption.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Applying Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791 impairs contractual obligations, alters the parties' original intent, and unconstitutionally discriminates against juridical persons by denying them equal protection.
B. Respondent's Interpretation (Equitable PCI Bank):
**Core Reading:** Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791 controls all extrajudicial foreclosures conducted after its effectivity. For juridical mortgagors, the redemption right is cut off upon the registration of the certificate of sale, or after three months from foreclosure, whichever is earlier.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Verba Legis / Plain Meaning Rule:** Section 47 plainly provides that juridical persons may redeem only "until, but not after, the registration of the certificate of foreclosure sale... whichever is earlier."
**Express Non Obstante Clause:** The statutory phrase **"Notwithstanding Act 3135"** explicitly supersedes and amends the prior 1-year redemption period under Act No. 3135 for bank foreclosures involving juridical persons.
**Express Transition / Grandfather Clause:** The statute expressly confines the old redemption period to foreclosures completed **prior** to its effectivity.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** The right of redemption is a statutory privilege subject to reasonable time limits and state police power. The classification serves the public interest of stabilizing the banking system, reducing uncertainty over corporate commercial collateral, and preventing non-performing banking assets from being tied up.
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
### 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791 applies to a real estate mortgage executed in 1985 prior to its enactment, when the foreclosure sale occurred after the law took effect.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does the application of Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791 to a foreclosure conducted after its effectivity constitute an impermissible retroactive application to a pre-existing 1985 mortgage contract, in light of the statute's express saving clause?

**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791 infringes the equal protection clause of the Constitution by distinguishing between natural and juridical persons.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791 violate the equal protection clause by granting natural mortgagors a one-year redemption period while restricting juridical mortgagors to a maximum of three months or until registration of the certificate of sale?
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
ISSUE 1: Prospective Application of Section 47, R.A. No. 8791 to Pre-Existing Mortgages
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: YES.** Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791 applies prospectively to all foreclosure sales conducted after its June 13, 2000 effectivity, and applying it to a foreclosure held in December 2000 does not constitute an impermissible retroactive application.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"Section 47 did not divest juridical persons of the right to redeem their foreclosed properties but only modified the time for the exercise of such right by reducing the one-year period originally provided in Act No. 3135. The new redemption period commences from the date of foreclosure sale, and expires upon registration of the certificate of sale or three months after foreclosure, whichever is earlier. There is likewise no retroactive application of the new redemption period because Section 47 exempts from its operation those properties foreclosed prior to its effectivity and whose owners shall retain their redemption rights under Act No. 3135."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate & Plain Meaning:** The Court examined the plain text of Section 47, Paragraph 2, specifically its non obstante opening (**"Notwithstanding Act 3135..."**) and its concluding grandfather clause.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined (Express Saving Clause):** The second sentence of Section 47, paragraph 2, expressly defines the law's temporal applicability: **"Owners of property that has been sold in a foreclosure sale prior to the effectivity of this Act shall retain their redemption rights until their expiration."** Under the principle of plain expression, the legislature specifically marked the event governing the applicability of the old law: the **date of the foreclosure sale**, not the date of mortgage execution.
3. **Harmonization with Prior Law (Conflict Resolution):** By using the non obstante phrase **"Notwithstanding Act 3135,"** Congress explicitly signaled an amendment and carve-out from Act No. 3135. Petitioner's general vs. special law argument (**generalia specialibus non derogant**) fails because Section 47 is an express, subsequent modification explicitly overriding Act No. 3135 for bank foreclosures of corporate mortgagors.
4. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court rejected petitioner's premise that a mortgagor acquires a vested, unchangeable redemption period on the day the mortgage contract is signed. The right of redemption in extrajudicial foreclosures is purely statutory and procedural, triggered only upon default and the occurrence of an actual foreclosure sale. Since the foreclosure took place on December 13, 2000—months after R.A. No. 8791 took effect—the new law applied fully and prospectively to that sale.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** R.A. No. 8791 did not act retroactively because the statute expressly preserved the 1-year redemption period only for properties foreclosed **before** its effectivity; since Goldenway's property was foreclosed in December 2000—after the law took effect—the operative event occurred under the new law, and the express phrase "Notwithstanding Act 3135" supplanted the old one-year rule for corporations.
ISSUE 2: Constitutionality Under the Non-Impairment Clause
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** Section 47 does not violate the constitutional non-impairment clause because the statutory right of redemption is subordinate to the State's police power to regulate the banking industry for public welfare.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"When confronted with a constitutional question, it is elementary that every court must approach it with grave care and considerable caution bearing in mind that every statute is presumed valid and every reasonable doubt should be resolved in favor of its constitutionality. For a law to be nullified, it must be shown that there is a clear and unequivocal breach of the Constitution. The ground for nullity must be clear and beyond reasonable doubt."
"The right of redemption being statutory, it must be exercised in the manner prescribed by the statute, and within the prescribed time limit, to make it effective. Furthermore, as with other individual rights to contract and to property, it has to give way to police power exercised for public welfare."
"Settled is the rule that the non-impairment clause of the Constitution must yield to the loftier purposes targeted by the Government. The right granted by this provision must submit to the demands and necessities of the State's power of regulation. Such authority to regulate businesses extends to the banking industry which, as this Court has time and again emphasized, is undeniably imbued with public interest."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Presumption of Constitutionality:** The Court applied the foundational presumption **presumptio pro constitutione**—statutes enjoy a presumption of validity, and nullification requires proof beyond reasonable doubt.
2. **Nature of the Right Examined:** The right of redemption is not an inherent natural right or an untouchable immutable contract term, but a purely statutory privilege. As a creature of statute, its terms, duration, and exercise are defined by the prevailing statute at the time of the sale.
3. **Police Power Superiority over Contracts:** Freedom of contract is never absolute. The non-impairment clause (**Art. III, Sec. 10**) is universally limited by the State's inherent police power. Contracts entered into by private parties are deemed subject to future regulatory modifications enacted for general welfare and economic stability.
4. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** Petitioner's reliance on **Co v. PNB** was misplaced; Section 47 did not abolish redemption for corporations, but merely re-calibrated the procedural timeframe to eliminate extended asset-freezes in banks. Contractual rights must yield to police power enactments protecting the liquidity of the banking system.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** The constitutional bar against impairing contracts must always yield to the State's superior police power to regulate businesses imbued with public interest, such as banking; because redemption is purely a creature of law, the legislature is fully empowered to shorten the statutory redemption timeframe without violating the Constitution.
ISSUE 3: Constitutionality Under the Equal Protection Clause & Legislative Intent
**(a) Issue & Short Answer: NO.** Section 47 does not violate the equal protection clause because the differential treatment between natural and juridical persons is based on a reasonable and real classification germane to the legislative purpose.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"The equal protection clause is directed principally against undue favor and individual or class privilege. It is not intended to prohibit legislation which is limited to the object to which it is directed or by the territory in which it is to operate. It does not require absolute equality, but merely that all persons be treated alike under like conditions both as to privileges conferred and liabilities imposed. Equal protection permits of reasonable classification."
"The difference in the treatment of juridical persons and natural persons was based on the nature of the properties foreclosed – whether these are used as residence, for which the more liberal one-year redemption period is retained, or used for industrial or commercial purposes, in which case a shorter term is deemed necessary to reduce the period of uncertainty in the ownership of property and enable mortgagee-banks to dispose sooner of these acquired assets."
"It cannot therefore be disputed that the said provision amending the redemption period in Act 3135 was based on a reasonable classification and germane to the purpose of the law."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Standards for Reasonable Classification:** The Court recalled the four classic requirements of valid classification: (1) it must rest on substantial distinctions; (2) it must be germane to the purpose of the law; (3) it must not be limited to existing conditions only; and (4) it must apply equally to all members of the same class.
2. Extrinsic Aids Examined (Legislative History & Deliberations):
The Court reviewed the records of the Eleventh Congress regarding consolidated House Bill No. 6814 and Senate Bill No. 1519.
The Court explicitly quoted the Senate Second Reading deliberations of September 14, 1999 (Record of the Senate, Vol. I, No. 22, p. 569), where Senator Franklin Drilon proposed distinguishing residential properties from commercial/industrial properties, pointing out that an extended 1-year freeze on commercial properties **"can tie up a lot of assets."**
The Court also examined the Sponsorship Speech of Senator Raul S. Roco (March 17, 1999), underscoring that R.A. No. 8791 was crafted in the wake of the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis to reform banking laws and maintain solvency and liquidity by curbing non-performing, frozen assets.
3. **Substantial Distinction:** Natural persons generally mortgage properties for personal or residential shelter (demanding higher social protection and longer redemption leniency), whereas juridical corporate mortgagors utilize properties for commercial or industrial pursuits.
4. **Germane to Purpose:** Shortening the redemption period for corporate mortgagors frees up commercial assets, prevents banks from holding illiquid, unproductive properties for extended durations, and accelerates asset disposition, directly achieving the statute's goal of banking solvency.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** The legislative history of R.A. No. 8791 demonstrates that Congress deliberately distinguished corporate mortgagors from individual homeowners because commercial properties held by corporations tie up vital bank assets; this real and substantial economic distinction fulfills the requirements of a valid classification under the equal protection guarantee.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.**
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Dispositive Portion:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition for review on certiorari is DENIED for lack of merit. The Decision dated November 19, 2010 and Resolution dated January 31, 2011 of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. CV No. 91120 are hereby AFFIRMED.
With costs against the petitioner.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** Equitable PCI Bank prevailed. The Supreme Court upheld the CA and RTC rulings dismissing Goldenway's complaint, confirming that Goldenway's redemption right was cut off upon the registration of the certificate of sale on February 16, 2001. Under Section 47 of R.A. No. 8791, banks foreclosing extrajudicially against juridical entities are governed strictly by the shortened redemption period (expiring upon registration or within three months, whichever comes first), rendering any subsequent redemption tender legally ineffective.
