### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Philippine Registered Electrical Practitioners, Inc. v. Francia**
**Full Official Caption:** Philippine Registered Electrical Practitioners, Inc. (PREPI), represented by Ben Rosete, Herminio S. Ramirez, Casiano Paulino, Nonato Villanueva, Jr., Renato Ame, Mario Blas, Samuel Bravo, Amor Cruz, Francisco Duller, Benito Español, Pablo Fernandez, Wilfredo Gorricho, Graciano Lapid, Luisito Magana, Fernando Malabanan, Martin Martinez, Edgardo Merida, Arnel Palilio, Gaudioso Seura, Zenon Tubio, Mariano Yape, and Nilo Montalban, Petitioners, v. Julio Francia, Jr., in his capacity as Commissioner of Professional Regulation Commission, Mederico T. Cortez, in his capacity as Chairman of the Board of Electrical Engineering, and Honorable Rebecca Salvador, Judge of the Regional Trial Court of Manila, Branch 1, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 87134, January 20, 2000; Second Division; Quisumbing, **J.** (Ponente); Concurred in by Bellosillo (**Chairman**), Mendoza, Buena, and De Leon, Jr., **JJ.** (Unanimous Resolution).
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
**Primary StatCon Classification:**
Statutory Construction Area → Intrinsic Aids / Statutory Meaning of Permissive vs. Mandatory Words → Plain Meaning of the Term "May" (Directory vs. Mandatory) → Scope of Administrative Regulatory Power vs. Limitation to Ocular Inspections.
**The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim):**
**Section 6(a), Presidential Decree No. 223:**
"The various Boards shall retain the following powers, functions and responsibilities:
a) To look from time to time into the conditions affecting the practice of the profession or occupation under their respective jurisdictions and whenever necessary, **adopt such measures as may be deemed proper for the enhancement of the profession or occupation and/or the maintenance of high professional, ethical and technical standards**...
For said purposes, the members of a Board **may** personally or through subordinate employees of the Commission conduct ocular inspection or visit industrial, mechanical, electrical or chemical plants or works, hospitals, clinics and other engineering works..."
**Section 3, paragraph 3, Republic Act No. 184:**
"The Board shall exercise the powers conferred upon it by this Act, shall from time to time, look into conditions affecting the practice of electrical engineering in the Philippines and, whenever necessary, recommend to the Secretary of Public Works and Communications (now Professional Regulation Commission) the **adoption of such measures as may be deemed proper for the maintenance of good ethics and standards in the practice of electrical engineering in the Philippines** and thus safeguard public welfare, life, health and property."
**Historical / Amendment Tracking:**
**Governing Statutes at Dispute:** Republic Act No. 184 (Electrical Engineering Law) and Presidential Decree No. 223 (Creating the Professional Regulation Commission).
**Supervening Administrative/Executive Issuances:**
Executive Order No. 266 (issued July 25, 1995 by President Fidel V. Ramos), institutionalizing the Continuing Professional Education (CPE) Programs of Various Professional Regulatory Boards as a mandatory requirement for license renewal across all professions.
PRC Resolution No. 507, Series of 1997 ("Standardized Guidelines and Procedures for the Implementation of the Continuing Professional Education [CPE] Programs for all Professions"), which explicitly repealed all prior circulars and resolutions on CPE, including the challenged BEE Resolution No. 1, Series of 1986.
**StatCon Diagnostic Profile:**
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Patent/Structural Restriction Claim. Petitioner argued that the second sentence of Section 6(a) of P.D. No. 223 restricted the broad grant of authority ("adopt such measures...") found in the first sentence solely to the power of visitation and ocular inspection.
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes, regarding the operative force and linguistic meaning of the auxiliary verb "may" in Section 6(a) of P.D. No. 223. The Court resolved this by adhering to the plain, directory character of the word.
**Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed:** The rule on permissive versus mandatory statutory terms (**"may"** denotes discretion/directory power, not a restrictive or mandatory mandate).
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The Board of Electrical Engineering (BEE) issued Resolution No. 1, Series of 1986 (approved by PRC), requiring all registered electrical engineers and master electricians to earn mandatory Continuing Professional Education (CPE) credits as a condition precedent to the triennial renewal of their professional licenses.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Philippine Registered Electrical Practitioners, Inc. (PREPI):** An association of professional electrical engineers, associate electrical engineers, assistant electrical engineers, and master electricians, appearing through its officers/members as petitioners challenging the CPE rules.
**Julio Francia, Jr.:** Commissioner of the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC), who approved BEE Resolution No. 1.
**Mederico T. Cortez:** Chairman of the Board of Electrical Engineering (BEE), which drafted and promulgated the assailed resolution.
**Hon. Rebecca Salvador:** Presiding Judge, Regional Trial Court of Manila, Branch 1, who upheld the validity of the regulation and dismissed PREPI's action.
**Procedural History & Vehicle:**
**RTC of Manila, Branch 1:** PREPI filed a petition for declaratory relief and/or prohibition with a prayer for preliminary injunction on July 6, 1988, challenging BEE Resolution No. 1, Series of 1986. After issuing a TRO, the trial court dismissed the petition for lack of merit, ruling that the resolution was a valid exercise of regulatory powers under Sec. 3 of R.A. No. 184 and Sec. 6 of P.D. No. 223.
**Supreme Court:** Direct appeal by certiorari on pure questions of law under Rule 45. The Supreme Court affirmed the statutory authority of the BEE and PRC, but ultimately denied the petition for being moot and academic due to supervening issuances (E.O. No. 266 and PRC Res. No. 507, S. 1997).
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **February 10, 1986:** The Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) approves Resolution No. 1, Series of 1986, promulgated by the Board of Electrical Engineering (BEE). The resolution adopts guidelines implementing the Continuing Professional Education (CPE) Program, requiring registered master electricians (100 credit units) and electrical engineers (200 credit units) to comply every three years as a condition precedent to license renewal, effective January 1, 1988.
2. **July 6, 1988:** Petitioner PREPI files an action for declaratory relief and/or prohibition before the Regional Trial Court of Manila, Branch 1, assailing the constitutionality and statutory basis of Resolution No. 1, Series of 1986.
3. **July 13, 1988:** The RTC issues a temporary restraining order (TRO) against respondents.
4. **Trial Court Judgment:** After hearing, the RTC dismisses PREPI's petition for lack of merit, finding that all reasonable doubts favor the validity of the regulation, which correctly implemented Sec. 3 of R.A. No. 184 and Sec. 6 of P.D. No. 223.
5. **Direct Appeal:** PREPI elevates the dispute directly to the Supreme Court on pure questions of law.
6. **July 25, 1995 (Supervening Event):** President Fidel V. Ramos issues Executive Order No. 266, mandating the institutionalization of CPE for all PRB-regulated professions as a mandatory requirement for license renewal.
7. **August 4, 1997 (Supervening Event):** The PRC issues Resolution No. 507, Series of 1997, standardizing CPE programs across all professions and expressly repealing all prior conflicting issuances, including BEE Resolution No. 1, Series of 1986.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
A. Petitioner's (PREPI) Interpretation
**Core Reading:** Under Section 6(a) of P.D. No. 223, the BEE's powers are strictly confined to visitation and ocular inspections of industrial/electrical plants to safeguard workers' remuneration and welfare. It has no statutory authority to mandate CPE credits as an unauthorized condition for license renewal.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:** Strict construction of delegated administrative powers; expressio unius / restrictive construction of regulatory penalties (license non-renewal amounts to uncodified suspension/revocation without notice and hearing, contrary to Sec. 32 of R.A. 184).
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Licenses are vested property rights. Imposing an extra-statutory CPE pre-requisite arbitrarily impairs livelihoods, causes bureaucratic red tape, and invidiously discriminates against electrical engineers vis-à-vis unregulated professions.
B. Respondent's (PRC, BEE, Solicitor General) Interpretation
**Core Reading:** Section 3 of R.A. No. 184 and Section 6(a) of P.D. No. 223 confer broad, comprehensive police-power authority on the Board to adopt any and all measures necessary for the maintenance of high ethical, technical, and professional standards. The clause mentioning ocular inspections is merely an illustrative, directory enforcement mechanism.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:** Broad construction of administrative regulatory mandates designed to protect public safety; plain meaning of the permissive auxiliary verb "may."
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** The practice of engineering involves vital public welfare and safety. Administrative bodies must possess flexible authority to implement continuing education to keep practitioners updated on modern technology.
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
### 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the Board of Electrical Engineering, in light of the provisions of R.A. No. 184 and Section 6(a) of P.D. No. 223, had the authority to issue Resolution No. 1, Series of 1986, or whether its authority is limited strictly to conducting ocular inspections.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the phrase **"the members of a Board may... conduct ocular inspection"** in Section 6(a) of P.D. No. 223 restricts the Board's regulatory mandate to visitation powers alone, or whether the permissive term "may" indicates that ocular inspection is merely directory and not the exclusive method to maintain professional standards.

### MASTER STATUTORY CONSTRUCTION BENCH BRIEF ### 1. CASE HEADER & CITATION BLOCK **Concise Recognizable Title: Subido v. Sandiganbayan** **Full Official Caption:** Bayani Subido, Jr. and Rene Parina, Petitioners, vs. The Honorable Sandiganbayan and The People of the Philippines, Respondents **Citation & Metadata:** **G.R. No.:** 122641 **Date of Promulgation:** January 20, 1997 **SCRA Citation:** 266 SCRA 379 **Ponente:** Davide, Jr., **J.** **Voting Breakdown:** Third Division (Concurring: Narvasa, **C.J.**, Melo, Francisco, and Panganiban, **JJ.**). No separate concurring or dissenting opinions. ### 2. STATCON DIAGNOSTIC MATRIX & GOVERNING PROVISION BREAKDOWN Primary StatCon Classification **Statutory Construction Area:** Prospective vs. Retroactive Operation of Statutes → Nature and Classification of Statutes (Penal vs. Procedural/Curative Laws) → Plain Meaning / **Verba Legis** **Specific Canon / Principle / Rule Applied:** Procedural and curative statutes apply retroactively to pending actions and accrued causes of action because no party has a vested right in rules of procedure; **Verba legis** threshold regarding temporal jurisdiction triggers ("at the time of the commission of the offense"). **Specific Latin Maxim: Verba legis non est recedendum** (from the words of the statute there should be no departure). **Specific Sub-Issue:** Whether Republic Act No. 7975 (amending Presidential Decree No. 1606) is a penal statute strictly construed against the State and applied prospectively, or a procedural/curative statute applicable retroactively; and whether the jurisdictional benchmark of government position/salary grade is determined at the time of the commission of the offense or at the time of filing the Information. The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim) Section 2 of Republic Act No. 7975 (amending Section 4 of P.D. No. 1606): "Sec. 2. Section 4 of [P.D. No. 1606] is hereby further amended to read as follows: 'Sec. 4. **Jurisdiction.** — The Sandiganbayan shall exercise original jurisdiction in all cases involving: a. Violations of Republic Act No. 3019, as amended, otherwise known as the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, Republic Act No. 1379, and Chapter II, Section 2, Title VII of the Revised Penal Code, where one or more of the principal accused are officials occupying the following positions in the government, whether in a permanent, acting or interim capacity, **at the time of the commission of the offense**: (1) Officials of the executive branch occupying the positions of regional director and higher, otherwise classified as grade 27 and higher, of the Compensation and Position Classification Act of 1989 (Republic Act No. 6758), specifically including: x x x (5) All other national and local officials classified as Grade "27" and higher under the Compensation and Position Classification Act of 1989. b. Other offenses or felonies committed by the public officials and employees mentioned in subsection (a) of this section in relation to their office. ### c. Civil and criminal cases filed pursuant to and in connection with Executive Order Nos. 1, 2, 14 and 14-A. In cases **where none of the principal accused are occupying positions corresponding to salary grade "27" or higher**, as prescribed in said Republic Act No. 6758, or PNP officers occupying the rank of superintendent or higher, or their equivalent, exclusive jurisdiction thereof shall be vested in the proper Regional Trial Court, Metropolitan Trial Court, Municipal Trial Court, and Municipal Circuit Trial Court, as the case may be, pursuant to their respective jurisdiction as provided in Batas Pambansa Blg. 129.'" Section 7 of Republic Act No. 7975: "Sec. 7. Upon the effectivity of this Act, all criminal cases in which trial has not begun in the Sandiganbayan shall be referred to the proper courts." Historical / Amendment Tracking Predecessor Text: Section 4 of P.D. No. 1606, as amended by Executive Order No. 184 (applicable at the time the offense was committed on June 25, 1992): "Sec. 4. **Jurisdiction.** — The Sandiganbayan shall exercise: (a) Exclusive appellate jurisdiction in all cases involving: (1) violations of Republic Act No. 3019, as amended, otherwise known as the Anti-Graft and practices Act, Republic Act No. 1379, and Chapter II, Section 2, Title VII of the Revised Penal Code; (2) other offenses or felonies committed by public officers and employees in relation to their office, including those employed in government-owned or controlled corporations, whether simple or complexed with other crimes, **where the penalty prescribed by law is higher than prision correccional or imprisonment for six (6) years, or a fine of P6,000.00**: **PROVIDED, HOWEVER**, that offenses or felonies mentioned in this paragraph where the penalty prescribed by law does not exceed **prision correccional** or imprisonment of six (6) years or a fine of P6,000.00 shall be tried by the proper Regional Trial Court, Metropolitan Trial Court, Municipal Trial Court and Municipal Circuit Trial Court." Intervening Enactment Text: R.A. No. 7975 (effective May 16, 1995): Restructured jurisdiction based on Salary Grade 27 (R.A. No. 6758) and specified that the threshold applies to officials occupying specified positions **"at the time of the commission of the offense."** StatCon Diagnostic Profile **The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Latent Ambiguity arising from the temporal confluence of an amendment: specifically, whether the Salary Grade 27 threshold applies to the accused's status at the time of the commission of the offense versus at the time of the filing of the Information, and whether a statute allocating judicial jurisdiction qualifies as a "penal law" subject to the rule of prospectivity and strict construction against the State. **Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes, as to classifying the statute (penal vs. procedural/curative) to govern its temporal application; but strictly barred (**Verba Legis**) as to the temporal reckoning point of public office, where the plain language of the statute expressly dictates the rule. **Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed:** 1. **Verba legis non est recedendum** (Plain Meaning Rule): The text explicitly pinpoints the reckoning period as "at the time of the commission of the offense." 2. Procedural/Curative Exception to Non-Retroactivity: Statutes regulating court jurisdiction and judicial procedure are procedural and remedial, operating retroactively to actions accrued or pending, absent impairment of vested rights. 3. Definition of Penal Laws: Statutes reallocating jurisdiction do not define offenses or impose penalties, and are therefore non-penal. **Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The filing of an Arbitrary Detention Information against a former BID Commissioner (separated from service before the law took effect) and a Special Agent (Salary Grade below 27) after R.A. No. 7975 took effect, prompting a Motion to Quash asserting lack of Sandiganbayan jurisdiction. ### 3. CAST OF CHARACTERS & PROCEDURAL POSTURE Key Parties & Roles **Bayani Subido, Jr.:** Petitioner; former Commissioner of the Bureau of Immigration and Deportation (BID), classified higher than Salary Grade 27 during his incumbency; separated from government service on February 28, 1995. **Rene Parina:** Petitioner; BID Special Agent, occupying a rank below Salary Grade 27; charged as a co-conspirator. **James J. Maksimuk:** Private complainant; alien subject to BID deportation proceedings who was arrested and detained for 43 days prior to the finality of his deportation order. **The Honorable Sandiganbayan:** Respondent special anti-graft court whose jurisdiction was contested. **The People of the Philippines:** Public respondent, represented by the Office of the Special Prosecutor/Ombudsman. Procedural History & Vehicle 1. **Filing of Charge:** On July 28, 1995, an Information for Arbitrary Detention (Art. 124, RPC) was filed before the Sandiganbayan (Criminal Case No. 22825) against Subido and Parina for acts committed on or about June 25, 1992. 2. **Motion to Quash:** On August 28, 1995, petitioners moved to quash the Information, alleging lack of jurisdiction under R.A. No. 7975, arguing that Subido was already a private person at the time of filing, Parina was below SG 27, and penal laws must be strictly construed and applied prospectively. 3. **Supplement to Motion to Quash:** On October 9, 1995, petitioners filed a supplement raising vagueness and administrative discretion over alien bail under Memorandum Order No. 04-92. 4. **Sandiganbayan Resolutions:** On October 25, 1995, the Sandiganbayan denied the Motion to Quash and its Supplement. On November 10, 1995, it denied reconsideration and entered a plea of "not guilty" for both accused upon their refusal to plead. 5. **Supreme Court Petition:** Petitioners filed a Petition for **Certiorari** under Rule 65 before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition and affirmed the Sandiganbayan. ### 4. CHRONOLOGICAL FACTS STORYBOARD **June 6, 1991:** The BID issues a Decision ordering the deportation of James J. Maksimuk. Maksimuk timely files a Motion for Reconsideration. **June 25, 1992:** While Maksimuk's Motion for Reconsideration remains pending and unresolved, Commissioner Bayani Subido, Jr. and Special Agent Rene Parina cause the issuance and execution of a warrant of arrest against him. **June 25 – August 1992:** Maksimuk is unlawfully detained for a total of forty-three (43) days pursuant to the warrant. **February 28, 1995:** Subido is separated from government service, reverting to the status of a private individual. **May 16, 1995:** Republic Act No. 7975 takes effect, amending Section 4 of P.D. No. 1606 by restructuring Sandiganbayan jurisdiction, introducing the Salary Grade 27 threshold, and reserving cases where none of the principal accused hold SG 27 or higher to the regular trial courts. **July 17, 1995:** An Information charging Subido and Parina with Arbitrary Detention under Article 124(3) of the RPC is signed by the prosecutor. **July 28, 1995:** The Information is officially filed with the Sandiganbayan, docketed as Criminal Case No. 22825. **August 28, 1995:** Petitioners file their Motion to Quash on jurisdictional and non-retroactivity grounds. **October 25, 1995:** Sandiganbayan denies the Motion to Quash. **November 10, 1995:** Sandiganbayan denies reconsideration, enters a not-guilty plea, and schedules pre-trial. ### 5. COMPETING INTERPRETATIONS MATRIX (THE CLASH OF CANONS) | Analytical Element | Petitioner's Interpretation | Respondent's Interpretation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Core Reading** | The Sandiganbayan lacks jurisdiction. Under R.A. No. 7975, jurisdiction must be determined at the time of the filing of the Information. Since Subido was already a private citizen and Parina held a position below SG 27, the case belongs to the RTC. | The Sandiganbayan maintains jurisdiction. Jurisdiction is fixed by the position held by the public official **at the time of the commission of the crime**, not at the time of filing the Information. | | **Canons & Maxims Invoked** | **1. Rule of Prospectivity of Penal Laws:** Penal laws apply prospectively unless favorable to the accused.
**2. Strict Construction of Penal Statutes:** Penal statutes must be strictly construed against the State and liberally in favor of the accused.
**3. Beneficial Curative Relief:** R.A. No. 7975 was enacted to relieve low-ranking officers from traveling to Manila, requiring trial before local courts. | **1. Verba Legis (Plain Meaning): Section 4(a) expressly states "at the time of the commission of the offense."
2. Nature of Statute: R.A. No. 7975 is a procedural/curative statute, not a penal law, and applies retroactively to pending actions.
3. Joinder of Co-Conspirators:** Jurisdiction over a principal accused holding a position above SG 27 extends to lower-ranking co-conspirators. | | **Policy / Consequence Argument** | Subjecting a former official (now private citizen) and a low-ranking agent to the Sandiganbayan violates constitutional rights against retroactive penal enforcement and causes oppressive litigation costs. | An accused cannot divest a court of jurisdiction by merely resigning or retiring before charges are filed; procedural statutes immediately govern pending and future filings without impairing vested rights. | ### 6. INVENTORY OF STATUTORY CONSTRUCTION & SUBSTANTIVE ISSUES ### 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE] **Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether Republic Act No. 7975 is a penal law that cannot be applied retroactively if prejudicial to the accused, or a procedural and curative statute that applies to offenses committed prior to its effectivity. **Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does R.A. No. 7975 constitute a "penal law" subject to strict prospective construction, or is it a procedural and curative statute governing court jurisdiction that applies retroactively to offenses committed prior to its enactment?

digest:
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the Sandiganbayan has jurisdiction over a co-accused holding a salary grade below "27" who is charged as a co-conspirator with an official occupying a position higher than salary grade "27."
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does the Sandiganbayan acquire jurisdiction over a low-ranking public employee (below SG 27) when charged as a co-conspirator with a principal official whose rank exceeds SG 27?
### 7. DEEP-DIVE VERDICT, TOOL ANALYSIS, & RATIO DECIDENDI PER ISSUE
ISSUE 1: Classification and Temporal Operation of R.A. No. 7975 (Penal vs. Procedural/Curative)
(a) Issue & Short Answer
**Issue:** Whether R.A. No. 7975 is a penal law that cannot be applied retroactively.
**Short Answer: NO.** R.A. No. 7975 is not a penal statute but a procedural and curative enactment regulating court jurisdiction, which validly operates retroactively because no person possesses a vested right in procedural rules.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements
"Finally, the petitioners' invocation of the prohibition against the retroactivity of penal laws is misplaced. Simply put, R.A. No. 7975 is not a penal law. Penal laws or statutes are those acts of the Legislature which prohibit certain acts and establish penalties for their violation; or those that define crimes, treat of their nature, and provide for their punishment."
"R.A. No. 7975, in further amending P.D. No. 1606 as regards the Sandiganbayan's jurisdiction, mode of appeal, and other procedural matters, is clearly a procedural law, **i.e.**, one which prescribes rules and forms of procedure of enforcing rights or obtaining redress for their invasion, or those which refer to rules of procedure by which courts applying laws of all kinds can properly administer justice."
"All told, as a procedural and curative statute, R.A. No. 7975 may validly be given retroactive effect, there being no impairment of contractual or vested rights."
(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court rejected the applicability of the penal non-retroactivity doctrine by examining the legal definition and nature of the statute.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court examined the title, subject matter, and operative sections of R.A. No. 7975 ("An Act to Strengthen the Functional and Structural Organization of the Sandiganbayan..."). It determined that the statute deals purely with court jurisdiction, methods of appeal, and the administration of justice.
3. **Extrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court referenced standard statutory construction authorities (Agpalo, Statutory Construction) and classic jurisprudence defining penal statutes (**Lorenzo v. Posadas**; **Hernandez v. Albano**) versus remedial/procedural statutes.
4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** Procedural statutes are presumed to apply to all actions accrued, pending, or future. A party has no vested right in a particular forum or procedural mechanism. Because R.A. No. 7975 does not alter the definition of Arbitrary Detention or increase its penalty, it impairs no substantive or constitutional rights.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The petitioners' attempt to characterize jurisdictional statutes as "penal" merely because they are applied in criminal proceedings was rejected as legally unsound.
(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
R.A. No. 7975 is not a penal law because it does not define any crime or prescribe any punishment; rather, it is a procedural statute that simply regulates the jurisdiction of the Sandiganbayan. Because litigants have no vested right in rules of procedure or specific courts, procedural and curative statutes apply retroactively to pending and accrued cases without violating the rules against non-retroactivity.
ISSUE 2: Reckoning Point for Sandiganbayan Jurisdiction (Time of Commission vs. Time of Filing)
(a) Issue & Short Answer
**Issue:** Whether public official status and salary grade are determined at the time of the commission of the crime or at the time of filing the Information.
**Short Answer: YES (Time of Commission).** Under the express and plain language of Section 4(a) of P.D. No. 1606, as amended by R.A. No. 7975, jurisdiction is determined exclusively by the position occupied by the accused **at the time of the commission of the offense**.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements
"The petitioners overlook the fact that for purposes of §4 of P.D. No. 1606, as amended, the reckoning point is the time **of the commission of the crime**. This is plain from the last clause of the opening sentence of paragraph (a), §4 of P.D. No. 1606, as further amended by R.A. No. 7975."
"Petitioner Subido never denied the respondents' claim that as 'commissioner of Immigration and Deportation [now Bureau of Immigration] at the time of the commission of the crime [he was] classified as having a position even higher than grade 27.' ... There can, therefore, be no doubt that the Sandiganbayan had jurisdiction over the crime allegedly committed by Subido."
(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning
1. **Threshold Gate:** Application of the **Verba Legis** / Plain Meaning Rule. The statutory language admits of no ambiguity; the text explicitly provides the exact temporal benchmark.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court isolated the opening clause of Section 4(a): **"where one or more of the principal accused are officials occupying the following positions in the government... at the time of the commission of the offense."**
3. **Extrinsic Aids Examined:** None required, as the text was clear and unambiguous.
4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** Public policy prevents public officers from evading the jurisdiction of the Sandiganbayan by simply resigning, retiring, or being separated from service before an Information can be filed.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The petitioners' theory that Subido's status as a "private person" at the time of the filing of the Information divested the Sandiganbayan of jurisdiction directly contradicts the verbatim text of the statute.
(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
The plain text of R.A. No. 7975 explicitly states that the accused's position and salary grade must be measured "at the time of the commission of the offense." Consequently, Subido's subsequent retirement or separation from service before the Information was filed did not strip the Sandiganbayan of jurisdiction, since he held the rank of Commissioner (above Salary Grade 27) when the arbitrary detention was committed.
ISSUE 3: Sandiganbayan Jurisdiction Over Co-Conspirators Holding Ranks Below Salary Grade 27
(a) Issue & Short Answer
**Issue:** Does the Sandiganbayan retain jurisdiction over a public employee holding a position below Salary Grade 27 when charged as a co-conspirator with an official holding a position above Salary Grade 27?
**Short Answer: YES.** Under the qualifying proviso of Section 4 of P.D. No. 1606, as amended by R.A. No. 7975, jurisdiction is transferred to the regular trial courts only where **none** of the principal accused occupy a position corresponding to Salary Grade 27 or higher.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements
"That petitioner Parina held a position with a salary grade of less than '27' at the time of the commission of the alleged arbitrary detention is of no moment. He is prosecuted as a co-conspirator of petitioner Subido, a principal accused, who held a position higher than grade '27.' The following provision of §4 of P.D. No. 1606, as amended by R.A. No. 7975, then applies:
'In cases **where none of the principal accused are occupying the positions corresponding** to salary grade "27" or higher, as prescribed in the said Republic Act No. 6758 . . . exclusive jurisdiction therefor shall be vested in the proper Regional Trial Court...'"
(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning
1. Threshold Gate: Literal construction of the negative quantifier "where none of the principal accused are occupying..."
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court analyzed the exclusionary clause in Section 4. The phrase "where none of the principal accused" means that if **at least one** principal accused holds Salary Grade 27 or higher, the exception does not apply, and Sandiganbayan jurisdiction remains intact over all co-principals and co-conspirators.
3. **Extrinsic Aids Examined:** Analysis of prior jurisprudence (**Aguinaldo v. Domagas**; **Sanchez v. Demetriou**; **Republic v. Asuncion**) establishing that offenses committed in relation to office by public servants fall under Sandiganbayan authority.
4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** Presumption against splitting of jurisdiction. Trying co-conspirators in separate forums (e.g., Subido in the Sandiganbayan and Parina in the RTC) for the identical conspiratorial act risks conflicting decisions and impairs judicial economy.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** Parina's contention that his low salary grade automatically entitled him to trial before the regular trial courts fails because his co-accused and alleged co-conspirator was a principal official holding an office above SG 27.
(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
The statute explicitly states that the regular courts take over only when **none** of the principal accused hold Salary Grade 27 or higher. Because Parina was indicted as a co-conspirator alongside Subido—who occupied an office classified well above Salary Grade 27—the Sandiganbayan validly retained jurisdiction over both accused.
### 8. SEPARATE OPINIONS ON STATUTORY CONSTRUCTION
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.** (The decision of the Third Division was unanimous).
### 9. OVERALL VERDICT (DISPOSITIVE PORTION / FALLO)
Verbatim Fallo:
"WHEREFORE, the instant petition is DISMISSED, and the questioned resolution and orders of the respondent Sandiganbayan are AFFIRMED.
Costs against the petitioners.
SO ORDERED."
Plain-Language Outcome:
The Supreme Court ruled entirely in favor of the prosecution and affirmed the Sandiganbayan's denial of the Motion to Quash. The Sandiganbayan properly retained jurisdiction to try both the former Immigration Commissioner and the Special Agent for Arbitrary Detention, cementing the doctrines that: (1) jurisdiction is determined by official rank at the time the offense was committed, not when the Information is filed; (2) jurisdictional amendments are procedural/curative, not penal, and apply retroactively; and (3) a low-ranking officer is triable before the Sandiganbayan if indicted as a co-conspirator with an official holding Salary Grade 27 or higher.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block **Concise Recognizable Title: Zulueta v. Asia Brewery, Inc.** **Full Official Caption:** Perla S. Zulueta, Petitioner, v. Asia Brewery, Inc., Respondent. **Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 138137; March 8, 2001; 354 SCRA 100; Third Division; Panganiban, **J.**, Ponente; Concurred in by Melo (**Chairman**), Vitug, Gonzaga-Reyes, and Sandoval-Gutierrez, **JJ.** Separate Opinions: None. 2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown Primary StatCon Classification **Statutory Construction Area:** Prospective vs. Retroactive Operation of Statutes → Remedial / Procedural Statutes Exception → **Lex Prospicit, Non Respicit** (Exception: Remedial Laws) → Retroactive Applicability to Pending Proceedings Without Impairment of Vested Rights. **Secondary StatCon Principles Applied:** 1. **Ubi lex non distinguit, nec nos distinguere debemus** (Where the law does not distinguish, the courts must not distinguish) → Applied to the Certification against Forum Shopping requiring the petitioner’s signature without distinction between natural and juridical persons. 2. Plain Meaning / Mandatory vs. Directory Words → Mandatory requirement of written explanation for non-personal service under Section 11, Rule 13 of the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure. Contested Statutory / Codal Text (Verbatim) **Article 4, Civil Code of the Philippines:** "Laws shall have **no retroactive effect**, **unless the contrary is provided**." **Section 4, Rule 65, 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure (as amended, effective July 1, 1997):** "SEC. 4. **Where and when to file.** — The petition shall be filed **not later than sixty (60) days** from notice of the judgment, order or resolution. In case a motion for reconsideration or new trial is timely filed, whether such motion is required or not, the sixty (60) day period shall be counted from notice of the denial of said motion." **Supreme Court Circular No. 28-91 / Section 5, Rule 7, 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure:** "SEC. 5. **Certification against forum shopping.** — The **plaintiff or principal party** shall certify under oath in the complaint or other initiatory pleading asserting a claim for relief, or in a sworn certification annexed thereto and simultaneously filed therewith: (a) that he has not theretofore commenced any action or filed any claim involving the same issues in any court, tribunal or quasi-judicial agency and, to the best of his knowledge, no such other action or claim is pending therein..." **Section 11, Rule 13, 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure:** "SEC. 11. **Priorities in modes of service and filing.** — Whenever practicable, the service and filing of pleadings and other papers shall be done personally. Except with respect to papers emanating from the court, a resort to other modes must be accompanied by a **written explanation** why the service or filing was not done personally. A violation of this Rule may be cause to consider the paper as **not filed**." **Section 1, Rule 31, 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure:** "SEC. 1. **Consolidation.** — When actions involving a **common question of law or fact** are pending before the court, it may order a joint hearing or trial of any or all the matters in issue in the actions; it may order all the actions consolidated; and it may make such orders concerning proceedings therein as may tend to avoid unnecessary costs or delay." StatCon Diagnostic Profile **The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Conflict between the statutory presumption of non-retroactivity under Article 4 of the Civil Code and the retroactive reach of procedural changes under the 1997 Rules of Civil Procedure over pending actions. Latent ambiguity regarding the meaning of "petitioner" in corporate forum shopping certifications (whether retained counsel qualifies as an authorized corporate agent under Circular No. 28-91). Scope of mandatory enforcement regarding the "written explanation" requirement under Section 11, Rule 13 when inter-city postal service is self-evident. **Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. The Court applied settled statutory doctrines governing exceptions to statutory non-retroactivity, interpreted corporate representation under the plain terms of Circular No. 28-91 via **ubi lex non distinguit**, and enforced the strict statutory mandate of Section 11, Rule 13. **Controlling Canons / Maxims Deployed:** **Nova constitutio futuris formam imponere debet, non praeteritis** / Remedial statutes exception (procedural laws operate retrospectively to pending actions because no one has a vested right in procedural rules). **Ubi lex non distinguit, nec nos distinguere debemus** (Where the law does not distinguish between natural and juridical persons, courts must not make distinctions). Plain Meaning / Mandatory Statutory Command (Absence of statutory written explanation converts discretionary striking into mandatory exclusion). **Factual Interpretive Trigger:** Respondent Asia Brewery, Inc. filed a Petition for Certiorari before the Court of Appeals challenging trial court consolidation orders 90 days after receipt of the denial order (invoking pre-1997 jurisprudence), with the non-forum shopping certification executed only by its retained counsel and omitting the mandatory Section 11, Rule 13 written explanation for service by registered mail. 3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture **Key Parties & Roles:** **Perla S. Zulueta (Petitioner):** Commercial beer dealer and operator of an outlet selling Asia Brewery products; plaintiff in the prior Iloilo breach of contract case; defendant in the subsequent Makati collection case. **Asia Brewery, Inc. (Respondent):** Domestic brewing and distribution corporation; defendant in the Iloilo case; plaintiff in the subsequent Makati collection case. **RTC of Iloilo City, Branch 22:** Forum where the first action for breach of contract, specific performance, and damages (Civil Case No. 20341) was lodged. **RTC of Makati City, Branch 66 / Branch 142:** Branch 66 (Judge Eriberto U. Rosario) originally handled Civil Case No. 94-2110; Branch 142 (Judge Jose Parentala Jr.) ordered the consolidation of the Makati case with the Iloilo case. **Court of Appeals (CA):** Nullified and set aside the consolidation orders, holding there was no commonality of facts or law. **Procedural History & Judicial Path:** 1. **RTC Makati, Branch 142:** Issued Orders dated February 13, 1997, and May 19, 1997, consolidating the Makati case with the earlier Iloilo case. 2. **Court of Appeals (CA-G.R. SP No. 45020):** Respondent filed a Rule 65 petition on August 21, 1997. The CA gave it due course and, on August 4, 1998, granted certiorari, annulling the consolidation orders. 3. **Supreme Court:** Petitioner filed a Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45. The Supreme Court reversed and set aside the CA Decision, reinstating the trial court's consolidation orders. ### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard 1. **March 30, 1992:** Petitioner Perla S. Zulueta files Civil Case No. 20341 in the RTC of Iloilo, Branch 22, against Asia Brewery, Inc., alleging breach of their Dealership Agreement and praying for specific performance and damages. 2. **July 7, 1994:** While the Iloilo case is pending, Asia Brewery files Civil Case No. 94-2110 before the RTC of Makati, Branch 66, demanding payment of ₱463,107.75 representing unpaid beer shipments delivered to Zulueta. 3. **Pleadings in Makati RTC:** Zulueta moves to dismiss the Makati case on the grounds of splitting causes of action and violation of the rule against multiplicity of suits. Judge Eriberto U. Rosario denies the motion, but subsequently inhibits himself upon Zulueta's motion. The case is re-raffled to Branch 142, presided by Judge Jose Parentala Jr. 4. **January 3, 1997:** Zulueta files a Motion for Consolidation before RTC Makati, Branch 142, seeking to transfer and merge the Makati case with the pending Iloilo case. 5. **February 13, 1997:** Judge Parentala issues an Order granting consolidation. Asia Brewery files a Motion for Reconsideration. 6. **May 19, 1997:** RTC Makati denies Asia Brewery's Motion for Reconsideration. Asia Brewery receives notice of this denial on **May 23, 1997**. 7. **July 1, 1997:** The 1997 Revised Rules of Civil Procedure take effect, explicitly establishing in Rule 65, Section 4 a uniform 60-day reglementary period for petitions for certiorari. 8. **August 21, 1997:** Ninety (90) days after receipt of the May 19 Order, Asia Brewery files its Rule 65 Petition for Certiorari before the CA (CA-G.R. SP No. 45020). The petition is certified against forum shopping solely by Asia Brewery’s outside retained counsel, and is served on Zulueta’s counsel via registered mail without an attached written explanation. 9. **August 4, 1998:** The CA grants Asia Brewery’s petition, holding that the collection case and the breach of contract action share no common issue of law or fact, thereby annulling the consolidation orders. 10. **February 23, 1999:** The CA denies Zulueta’s Motion for Reconsideration. Zulueta elevates the matter to the Supreme Court. 5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons) | Dimension | Petitioner's Interpretation (Perla S. Zulueta) | Respondent's Interpretation (Asia Brewery, Inc.) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Issue 1A: Retroactivity of 60-Day Period (Rule 65)** | **Core Reading:** The 60-day period under the 1997 Rules applies retroactively to pending actions as a remedial law. Respondent had only until July 22, 1997 (21 days post-effectivity).

**Canons/Maxims:** Exception to Art. 4, Civil Code; procedural statutes apply immediately to pending undetermined actions; no vested right in procedural periods.

**Policy Argument:** Permitting parties to exploit obsolete jurisprudential timeframes destroys uniform practice and subverts court administration. | **Core Reading:** The 60-day period cannot apply retroactively because the order was received prior to July 1, 1997; the prevailing pre-1997 90-day period controls.

**Canons/Maxims: Lex prospicit, non respicit** (Art. 4, Civil Code); non-impairment of accrued procedural rights.

**Policy Argument:** Retroactive truncation of an existing 90-day period offends due process and causes forfeiture of the remedy. | | **Issue 1B: Signatory to Forum Shopping Certification** | **Core Reading:** "Petitioner" under Circular No. 28-91 encompasses juridical entities, requiring execution by an authorized officer, not outside counsel.

**Canons/Maxims: Ubi lex non distinguit, nec nos distinguere debemus**; strict adherence to anti-forum shopping mandates.

**Policy Argument:** Allowing retained counsel to sign enables corporate parties to easily evade forum-shopping prohibitions. | **Core Reading:** A corporation acts through agents; outside retained counsel has personal knowledge of pending cases and acts as an agent.

**Canons/Maxims:** Doctrine of substantial compliance; agency law principles.

**Policy Argument:** Rigidity undermines corporate access to courts where counsel is actively handling the litigation. | | **Issue 1C: Written Explanation for Non-Personal Service** | **Core Reading:** Section 11, Rule 13 admits of no exception; written explanation is mandatory even if geographical distance is manifest.

**Canons/Maxims:** Plain Meaning Rule / **Verba Legis**; mandatory vs. directory statutory terms.

**Policy Argument:** Discretion to waive becomes arbitrary without uniform textual enforcement. | **Core Reading:** Explanation is superfluous when counsel is based in Makati and adverse party is in Iloilo City.

**Canons/Maxims:** Substantial compliance; **lex non cogit ad impossibilia** / statutory rationality.

**Policy Argument:** Dismissing an action for failure to state the obvious elevates technicality over substantive justice. | | **Issue 2: Consolidation of Related Actions** | **Core Reading:** The collection claim arose directly from the Dealership Agreement under scrutiny in Iloilo; both cases turn on common contractual facts.

**Canons/Maxims:** Rule 31, Section 1 plain meaning; avoidance of multiplicity of suits.

**Policy Argument:** Prevents bifurcated, conflicting judgments regarding reciprocal obligations under the same contract. | **Core Reading:** The collection case stands independently of any contractual breach; the delivery of beer products creates a distinct debt.

**Canons/Maxims:** Strict distinction of causes of action; autonomy of independent debt collection.

**Policy Argument:** Consolidating a simple collection case with an intricate damages suit causes prejudicial delay. | 6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE] Retroactive Applicability of the 60-Day Reglementary Period under Rule 65: **Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the 60-day period prescribed under Section 4, Rule 65 of the 1997 Revised Rules of Civil Procedure applies retroactively to govern an original petition for certiorari assailing an interlocutory order received prior to the effectivity of said Rules. **Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does the remedial exception to Article 4 of the Civil Code permit the retroactive application of the 60-day period under Rule 65 to cut short a pre-existing 90-day period for actions undetermined upon its effectivity, absent any vested procedural right? 2. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE] Scope of Signatory Requirement under Circular No. 28-91 via Ubi Lex Non Distinguit: **Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether a certification against forum shopping signed merely by retained outside counsel complies with Supreme Court Circular No. 28-91 and the Rules of Court when the party is a corporation. **Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does the maxim **ubi lex non distinguit, nec nos distinguere debemus** bar retained counsel from signing the certification against forum shopping on behalf of a corporate litigant where the rule makes no distinction between natural and juridical entities? 3. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE] Mandatory Character of Written Explanation under Section 11, Rule 13: **Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether Section 11, Rule 13 requires a written explanation for non-personal service even when the geographic disparity between the parties' locations is evident. **Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Is the requirement of a written explanation under Section 11, Rule 13 mandatory such that its omission compels the appellate court to consider the petition as not filed, notwithstanding obvious geographic distance? 4. [Substantive / Procedural Issue] Propriety of Consolidation under Section 1, Rule 31: **Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the Makati RTC correctly ordered the consolidation of the collection suit with the prior breach of contract suit in Iloilo City. **Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does a collection action for goods delivered arise out of the overarching distributorship agreement so as to constitute a common question of fact warranting consolidation under Rule 31, Section 1? ### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue Issue 1: Retroactivity of the 60-Day Certiorari Period under Rule 65 **(a) Short Answer: YES.** Procedural laws are retroactive in nature and govern actions pending and undetermined at the time of their effectivity, as there are no vested rights in rules of procedure. **(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:** "It is true that under the Civil Code of the Philippines, '(l)aws shall have no retroactive effect, unless the contrary is provided.' But there are settled exceptions to this general rule, such as when the statute is CURATIVE or REMEDIAL in nature or when it CREATES NEW RIGHTS." "On the other hand, remedial or procedural laws, i.e., those statutes relating to remedies or modes of procedure, which do not create new or take away vested rights, but only operate in furtherance of the remedy or confirmation of such rights, ordinarily do not come within the legal meaning of a retrospective law, nor within the general rule against the retrospective operation of statutes." "Thus, procedural laws may operate retroactively as to pending proceedings even without express provision to that effect. Accordingly, rules of procedure can apply to cases pending at the time of their enactment. In fact, statutes regulating the procedure of the courts will be applied on actions undetermined at the time of their effectivity." "It is a well-established doctrine that rules of procedure may be modified at any time to become effective at once, so long as the change does not affect vested rights. Moreover, it is equally axiomatic that there are no vested rights to rules of procedure." **(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:** 1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court directly addressed the clash between the statutory presumption of prospective operation under Article 4 of the Civil Code and the temporal reach of procedural amendments. 2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court analyzed the intrinsic remedial nature of Section 4, Rule 65. Because it regulates only the remedy and mode of procedure without impairing substantive obligations, it is excluded from the general ban on retroactive operation. 3. **Extrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court relied on established procedural jurisprudence (**Frivaldo v. Comelec**, **Hosana v. Diomano**, **MRCA, Inc. v. CA**) holding that procedural amendments apply immediately to pending, undetermined disputes. 4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** The Court enforced the absolute presumption that litigants hold no vested private property rights in rules of procedure. The prior 90-day period was not a vested right but a discretionary jurisprudential guideline. 5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court rejected Asia Brewery’s reliance on the non-retroactivity doctrine, holding that since respondent still had 21 days remaining between the July 1, 1997 effectivity of the Rules and the expiration of the 60-day period on July 22, 1997, its right of action was not foreclosed without due process. **(d) Plain-Language StatCon Explanation:** **(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** Changes to procedural rules apply immediately to pending court cases because no one owns a vested legal right in judicial timelines. Because Asia Brewery had 21 days left under the new 60-day rule to file its petition after the 1997 Rules took effect, applying the new period retroactively was valid and its petition was filed out of time. Issue 2: Signatory to Forum Shopping Certification under Circular No. 28-91 **(a) Short Answer: YES.** The certification against forum shopping must be executed by the party or an authorized corporate officer, not by outside retained counsel, pursuant to the rule that where the law makes no distinction, none should be made. **(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:** "The requirement that the petitioner should sign the certificate of non-forum shopping applies even to corporations, considering that the mandatory directives of the Circular and the Rules of Court make no distinction between natural and juridical persons." "Verily, the signatory in the Certification of the Petition before the CA should not have been respondent's retained counsel, who would not know whether there were other similar cases of the corporation. Otherwise, this requirement would easily be circumvented by the signature of every counsel representing corporate parties." **(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:** 1. **Threshold Gate:** Circular No. 28-91 and Rule 7, Section 5 plainly command the "petitioner" to verify the absence of other pending litigations. 2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** Deploying the canon **ubi lex non distinguit, nec nos distinguere debemus**, the Court noted that the text uses "petitioner" generally, without distinguishing between natural and corporate litigants. 3. **Extrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court distinguished **Robern Development Corp. v. Quitain**, where the signatory was an in-house regional legal counsel acting as an organic corporate officer with personal knowledge of local suits. 4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** The Court applied the anti-circumvention policy: allowing outside retained counsel to verify certifications would defeat the statutory objective of preventing forum shopping, as retained counsel cannot reliably certify the nationwide litigation footprint of a corporation. 5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court rejected the argument that retained counsel is an authorized corporate agent under general principles of agency, ruling that outside counsel lacks the institutional standing required by the text of the rule. **(d) Plain-Language StatCon Explanation:** **(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** The anti-forum shopping rule commands the litigant itself to execute the certification and makes no special exception for corporations. An outside retained lawyer cannot sign on behalf of a corporation because doing so bypasses the rule's safeguard that an actual company officer verify that no other cases exist. Issue 3: Mandatory Character of Written Explanation under Section 11, Rule 13 **(a) Short Answer: YES.** Section 11, Rule 13 imposes an indispensable requirement of a written explanation for non-personal service, the omission of which renders the striking of the pleading mandatory. **(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:** "Under Section 11, Rule 13 of the 1997 Rules, personal service of petitions and other pleadings is the general rule, while a resort to other modes of service and filing is the exception." "Where recourse is made to the exception, a written explanation why the service and the filing were not done personally is indispensable, even when such explanation by its nature is acceptable and manifest. Where no explanation is offered to justify the resort to other modes, the discretionary power of the court to expunge the pleading becomes mandatory." **(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:** 1. **Threshold Gate:** The text of Section 11, Rule 13 sets personal service as the rule and other modes as exceptions requiring an accompanying written explanation. 2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** The clause providing that a violation "may be cause to consider the paper as not filed" was evaluated alongside the indispensable nature of the written explanation. 3. **Extrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court applied the controlling precedent of **Solar Team Entertainment, Inc. v. Ricafort**, establishing that the court's discretion to excuse service defects is extinguished when no written explanation is tendered at all. 4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** The Court enforced the policy favoring personal service as an instrument to curb frivolous delays and ensure verifiable receipt of pleadings. 5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court explicitly rejected Asia Brewery’s defense that the geographic distance between Makati and Iloilo was manifest, holding that obviousness cannot substitute for the written explanation required by the text. **(d) Plain-Language StatCon Explanation:** **(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** When a party serves a pleading by registered mail instead of personal delivery, the rule strictly requires a written explanation explaining why. Even if the parties are in different cities, failing to provide this written explanation leaves the court with no choice but to treat the petition as not filed. Issue 4: Propriety of Consolidation under Section 1, Rule 31 **(a) Short Answer: YES.** Rule 31, Section 1 authorizes consolidation when cases share common questions of law or fact, and an action to collect on goods delivered under a disputed dealership contract is an incident that must be consolidated with the earlier breach of contract action. **(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:** "Two cases involving the same parties and affecting closely related subject matters must be ordered consolidated and jointly tried in court, where the earlier case was filed." "The consolidation of cases is proper when they involve the resolution of common questions of law or facts." "When two or more cases involve the same parties and affect closely related subject matters, they must be consolidated and jointly tried, in order to serve the best interests of the parties and to settle expeditiously the issues involved. Consolidation, when appropriate, also contributes to the declogging of court dockets." **(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:** 1. **Threshold Gate:** Rule 31, Section 1 establishes a single substantive standard: the presence of a "common question of law or fact." 2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court examined the phrase "common question of law or fact" in relation to the operational facts of both suits. 3. **Extrinsic Aids Examined:** Relying on **Active Wood Products Co. v. CA** and **Syndicated Media Access Corp. v. CA**, the Court held that cases involving identical parties and inextricably linked transactions should be merged in the court where the first action was commenced. 4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** The Court applied the presumption in favor of avoiding multiplicity of suits, preventing contradictory rulings, and advancing docket declogging. 5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court rejected the CA’s view that the collection suit was wholly independent, finding that the alleged debt and the dealer's refusal to pay were direct outgrowths of the Dealership Agreement being litigated in Iloilo. **(d) Plain-Language StatCon Explanation:** **(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** Under the Rules of Court, cases with common facts and parties should be consolidated to avoid duplicate trials and conflicting rulings. Because the unpaid beer deliveries arose directly out of the contested distributorship agreement, the debt collection case had to be consolidated with the earlier breach of contract case in Iloilo. 8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction **No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.** 9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo) **Verbatim Fallo:** "WHEREFORE, the Petition is hereby GRANTED and the assailed Decision REVERSED and SET ASIDE. The Orders of the Makati RTC (Br. 142) dated February 13, 1997 and May 19, 1997 are hereby REINSTATED. No costs. SO ORDERED." **Plain-Language Outcome:** Petitioner Perla S. Zulueta prevailed completely. The Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated the trial court’s orders consolidating Asia Brewery’s Makati collection case into Zulueta’s earlier-filed Iloilo breach of contract action. The Court confirmed that Asia Brewery’s CA petition was defective and tardy because procedural amendments apply retroactively, corporate forum-shopping certifications cannot be signed by retained counsel alone, and written explanations for postal service are mandatory.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block **Concise Recognizable Title: Mecano v. Commission on Audit** **Full Official Caption:** Antonio A. Mecano, Petitioner, v. Commission on Audit, Respondent **Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 103982 Promulgated: December 11, 1992 Secondary Citation: 216 SCRA 500 Ponente: Campos, Jr., **J.** Voting Breakdown: En Banc; Narvasa, **C.J.**, Cruz, Feliciano, Padilla, Bidin, Griño-Aquino, Regalado, Davide, Jr., Romero, Nocon, Bellosillo, and Melo, **JJ.**, concurred; Gutierrez, Jr., **J.**, concurred in the result. No separate written opinions. 2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown **Primary StatCon Classification:** Repeals by Implication → Presumption Against Implied Repeal → Two Categories of Implied Repeal (Irreconcilable Inconsistency vs. Total Revision/Codification) → General Repealing Clause vs. Express Repeal **The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim):** **Section 27, Book VII (Final Provisions), Executive Order No. 292 (Administrative Code of 1987):** "Sec. 27. **Repealing Clause.** — **All laws, decrees, orders, rules and regulations, or portions thereof, inconsistent with this Code are hereby repealed or modified accordingly.**" **Section 699, Revised Administrative Code of 1917 (Act No. 2711), as amended by Republic Act No. 1232:** "Sec. 699. **Allowances in case of injury, death, or sickness incurred in performance of duty.** — When a person in the service of the national government of a province, city, municipality or municipal district is so injured in the performance of duty as thereby to receive some actual physical hurt or wound, the proper Head of Department may direct that absence during any period of disability thereby occasioned shall be on full pay, though not more than six months, and in such case he may in his discretion also authorize the payment of the medical attendance, necessary transportation, subsistence and hospital fees of the injured person. Absence in the case contemplated shall be charged first against vacation leave, if any there be. x x x           x x x           x x x **In case of sickness caused by or connected directly with the performance of some act in the line of duty, the Department head may in his discretion authorize the payment of the necessary hospital fees.**" **Article 173, Title II, Book IV of the Labor Code (Presidential Decree No. 442), as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1921:** "x x x The payment of compensation under this Title **shall not bar the recovery of benefits as provided for in Section 699 of the Revised Administrative Code** . . . whose benefits are administered by the system (meaning SSS or GSIS) or by other agencies of the government." **Historical / Amendment Tracking:** **Historical Text:** Section 699 of Act No. 2711 (Revised Administrative Code of 1917), as amended by Republic Act No. 1232 (enacted June 7, 1955). **Intervening Enactment:** Executive Order No. 292 (Administrative Code of 1987), signed July 25, 1987, which took effect in 1989 and omitted Section 699 without an express repealing clause targeting Act No. 2711 by name or number. **StatCon Diagnostic Profile:** **The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Alleged Implied Repeal / Conflict Between Provisions / Omission in Subsequent Codification (whether the omission of an old administrative welfare provision in a new administrative code, paired with a general repealing clause and a codifying preamble, effects an implied repeal). **Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. The repealing clause (Section 27, Book VII, E.O. No. 292) is a general repealing clause lacking express designation of the acts repealed; hence, judicial construction was required to ascertain whether an implied repeal occurred by irreconcilable inconsistency or complete revision/substitution. **Controlling Canons / Maxims Deployed:** **Presumption against implied repeals** (**Interpretatio fienda est ut res magis valeat quam pereat** / laws are presumed enacted with full knowledge of existing law). Express repeal requires naming the specific statute by number or title; an omnibus clause repealing inconsistent acts is merely a general repealing clause creating a presumption against repeal absent irreconcilable repugnancy. Two categories of implied repeal: (1) Irreconcilable inconsistency, and (2) Total revision or codification intended as an exhaustive substitute. Construction of statutes **in pari materia** through executive and administrative opinions. **Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The Commission on Audit (COA) rejected an NBI Director's claim for P40,831.00 in service-connected hospitalization expenses on the ground that Section 699 of the 1917 Revised Administrative Code was completely abrogated when the Administrative Code of 1987 took effect without restating or re-enacting it. 3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture **Key Parties & Roles:** **Antonio A. Mecano:** Petitioner; Director II of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), who incurred P40,831.00 in medical and hospital expenses due to service-connected cholecystitis. **Commission on Audit (COA) / Chairman Eufemio C. Gerarda Galang (Chief, Legal Evaluation Division, NBI) and DOJ Committee on Physical Examination (both found the illness service-connected). **Procedural History & Vehicle:** 1. **Administrative Claim:** Mecano submitted his claim for reimbursement under Section 699 of the Revised Administrative Code of 1917 to the NBI Director on May 11, 1990. 2. **DOJ Transmission & 1st COA Action:** Favorably indorsed by the NBI and DOJ Committee on Physical Examination; returned on November 21, 1990 by Undersecretary Bello following COA's 5th Indorsement (September 19, 1990) asserting repeal. 3. **Re-submission via DOJ Opinion No. 73, S. 1991:** Secretary Drilon formally ruled that E.O. No. 292 did not repeal Section 699 and forwarded the claim to COA on July 2, 1991. 4. **Final COA Denial:** In a 7th Indorsement dated January 16, 1992, COA Chairman Eufemio C. Domingo denied the claim, asserting that the omission of Section 699 in the Administrative Code of 1987 constituted an implied repeal. 5. **Supreme Court Review:** Direct petition for **certiorari** under Rule 65 (and Section 2, Rule 64) to annul COA's 7th Indorsement. The Supreme Court granted the petition and reversed the COA. ### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard 1. **March 26, 1990 – April 7, 1990:** Petitioner Antonio A. Mecano, Director II of the NBI, was hospitalized for cholecystitis, incurring P40,831.00 in medical and hospitalization expenses. 2. **May 11, 1990:** Mecano submitted a memorandum to NBI Director Alfredo S. Bello III returned the claim to Director Lim (4th Indorsement) in light of COA’s adverse stance. 7. **April 26, 1991:** Secretary of Justice Franklin M. Drilon issued DOJ Opinion No. 73, S. 1991, concluding that the Administrative Code of 1987 did not repeal the 1917 RAC in its entirety, and specifically left Section 699 in full force. 8. **May 10, 1991:** Director Lim transmitted Mecano’s claim back to Undersecretary Bello (5th Indorsement) with DOJ Opinion No. 73. 9. **July 2, 1991:** Secretary Drilon issued a 6th Indorsement to COA Chairman Eufemio C. Domingo, recommending payment of the claim. 10. **January 16, 1992:** COA Chairman Domingo issued the assailed 7th Indorsement denying Mecano's claim solely because Section 699 was omitted from E.O. No. 292, suggesting instead that Mecano file with the Employees' Compensation Commission (ECC). 11. **February 7, 1992:** Undersecretary Eduardo Montenegro returned the denied claim to Director Lim (9th Indorsement), advising Mecano to elevate the controversy to the Supreme Court. 12. **March 1992:** Mecano filed the instant petition for **certiorari** before the Supreme Court. 5. Any section omitted from the 1987 Code (such as Sec. 699) is repealed. | | **Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked** | 1. **Presumption Against Implied Repeal:** Repeals by implication are disfavored.

**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether recovery under Section 699 of the Revised Administrative Code is barred by the availability of compensation under the Employees' Compensation Program under P.D. No. 626.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether Article 173 of the Labor Code (as amended by P.D. 1921) permits simultaneous or independent recovery of medical benefits under Section 699 of the 1917 RAC alongside State Insurance Fund benefits administered by the ECC.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Repeal of Section 699 by the Administrative Code of 1987
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** The Administrative Code of 1987 did not repeal Section 699 of the 1917 Revised Administrative Code because Section 27, Book VII of the 1987 Code is merely a general repealing clause, there is no irreconcilable inconsistency between the two statutes, and the 1987 Code was never intended to completely cover the entire field of the 1917 Code as an exhaustive substitute.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**On Express vs. Implied Repeal:**
"The question of whether a particular law has been repealed or not by a subsequent law is a matter of legislative intent. The lawmakers may expressly repeal a law by incorporating therein a repealing provision which expressly and specifically cites the particular law or laws, and portions thereof, that are intended to be repealed... A declaration in a statute, usually in its repealing clause, that a particular and specific law, identified by its number or title, is repealed is an express repeal; all others are implied repeals."
**On the Nature of General Repealing Clauses:**
"Sec. 27. **Repealing Clause.** — All laws, decrees, orders, rules and regulations, or portions thereof, inconsistent with this Code are hereby repealed or modified accordingly... It is certainly not an express repealing clause because it fails to identify or designate the act or acts that are intended to be repealed... The failure to add a specific repealing clause indicates that the intent was not to repeal any existing law, unless an irreconcilable inconsistency and repugnancy exist in the terms of the new and old laws."
**On the Two Categories of Implied Repeal:**
"There are two categories of repeal by implication. The first is where provisions in the two acts on the same subject matter are in an irreconcilable conflict, the later act to the extent of the conflict constitutes an implied repeal of the earlier one. The second is if the later act covers the whole subject of the earlier one and is clearly intended as a substitute, it will operate to repeal the earlier law."
**On the Presumption Against Implied Repeals:**
"Repeals by implication are not favored, and will not be decreed unless it is manifest that the legislature so intended. As laws are presumed to be passed with deliberation with full knowledge of all existing ones on the subject, it is but reasonable to conclude that in passing a statute it was not intended to interfere with or abrogate any former law relating to some matter, unless the repugnancy between the two is not only irreconcilable, but also clear and convincing..."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The text of Section 27, Book VII of E.O. 292 is not an express repeal because it does not identify Act No. 2711 by title or number; it is an omnibus general repealing clause. Hence, an implied repeal cannot be assumed—it must be judicially tested under the two recognized categories of implied repeal.
2. **First Category Analysis (Irreconcilable Inconsistency):** Implied repeal by inconsistency requires that two statutes cover the exact same subject matter and be so utterly repugnant that both cannot stand together. Comparing the two Codes, Section 699 has no counterpart in the 1987 Code; therefore, no direct textual clash exists. One statute can be enforced without nullifying the other.
3. **Second Category Analysis (Revision / Substitution of the Whole Subject Matter):** An implied repeal by revision occurs only where the subsequent statute covers the entire subject matter of the prior act and is plainly intended to be a complete, perfect, and exhaustive substitute. The Court found that the 1987 Code did not attempt to cover the entire field of the 1917 Code. Omitted subjects in the 1987 Code include notaries public, the leave law, the public bonding law, military reservations, and sickness benefits under Section 699.
4. **Intrinsic Aids Examined (Whereas Clauses):** COA pointed to the preamble of E.O. 292, which stated an intent to incorporate principles and rules of governance in a "unified document." The Court held that this intrinsic aid merely signaled an intent to unify the structural, organizational, functional, and procedural aspects of government, not to abolish substantive rights and specialized administrative welfare mechanisms.
5. **Extrinsic Aids Examined (DOJ Executive Construction):** The Court credited DOJ Opinion No. 73, S. 1991 (Secretary Franklin Drilon), holding that opinions of the Secretary of Justice are material intrinsic/extrinsic aids in construing statutes **in pari materia**. The Court rejected COA's claim of unreviewable administrative discretion (**Sison v. Pangramuyen**), noting that administrative statutory interpretations are fully reviewable when based on an error of law.
6. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** The Court enforced the steadfast presumption against implied repeals: the legislature is presumed to know existing law and does not intend to abrogate prior statutes sub silentio. A statute is construed as cumulative and a continuation of prior law unless an intention to abrogate is clear and manifest.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** Section 699 of the 1917 Revised Administrative Code remains good law because the 1987 Administrative Code used only a generic repealing clause and did not intend to wipe out everything in the old code. Because the 1987 Code only restructured government administration and left out substantive subjects like leaves, notaries, and service-sickness benefits, the old provisions continue to operate side-by-side with the new Code.
Issue 2: Effect of the Employees' Compensation Program (P.D. 626 / Labor Code)
**(a) Short Answer: NO.** Recovery under Section 699 is not barred by the Employees' Compensation Program, because Article 173 of the Labor Code explicitly preserves Section 699 benefits alongside Title II compensation.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**On Statutory Harmony with the Labor Code:**
"Regarding respondent's contention that recovery under this subject section shall bar the recovery of benefits under the Employees' Compensation Program, the same cannot be upheld. The second sentence of Article 173, Chapter II, Title II (dealing on Employees' Compensation and State Insurance Fund), Book IV of the Labor Code, as amended by P.D. 1921, expressly provides that 'the payment of compensation under this Title shall not bar the recovery of benefits as provided for in Section 699 of the Revised Administrative Code . . . whose benefits are administered by the system (meaning SSS or GSIS) or by other agencies of the government.'"
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Plain Text Rule (Verba Legis):** The Court evaluated the explicit text of Article 173 of the Labor Code, as amended by P.D. No. 1921.
2. **Harmonization of Statutes (In Pari Materia):** Rather than reading P.D. 626 as an exclusive remedy that pre-empted or rendered redundant Section 699 of the 1917 RAC, the Court applied the text of P.D. 1921, which unambiguously commanded that compensation under the Labor Code's State Insurance Fund shall not bar simultaneous or separate recovery under Section 699 of the 1917 RAC.
3. **Rejection of COA's "Unjust Double Recovery" Argument:** COA’s policy argument—that allowing Section 699 benefits alongside ECC benefits was unfair to the Government—was flatly overridden by the positive command of the statute.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** COA cannot bar an employee from claiming under Section 699 on the ground that the employee could instead file with the ECC, because Article 173 of the Labor Code expressly declares that receiving ECC benefits does not prevent a government employee from also recovering medical allowances under Section 699.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text. (Justice Gutierrez, Jr. concurred in the result without a separate written opinion).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, premises considered, the Court resolves to GRANT the petition; respondent is hereby ordered to give due course to petitioner's claim for benefits. No costs.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Petitioner Antonio A. Mecano prevailed completely. The Supreme Court set aside COA's 7th Indorsement and directed the Commission on Audit to process and pay Mecano's P40,831.00 claim for medical reimbursement. The ruling established that Section 699 of the Revised Administrative Code of 1917 survived the enactment of the Administrative Code of 1987 and remains an effective, enforceable remedy for work-connected sickness and injury of public officers.
