### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Berces, Sr. v. Guingona, Jr.**
**Full Official Caption:** Achilles C. Berces, Sr., Petitioner, v. Hon. Executive Secretary Teofisto T. Guingona, Jr., Chief Presidential Legal Counsel Antonio Carpio, and Mayor Naomi C. Corral of Tiwi, Albay, Respondents.
**Citation & Metadata:**
**Docket No.:** G.R. No. 112099
**Date of Promulgation:** February 21, 1995
**Collection Citations:** 241 SCRA 539; Phil. Reports (unlisted in text)
**Ponente:** Quiason, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** En Banc. Narvasa, **C.J.**, Feliciano, Padilla, Bidin, Regalado, Davide, Jr., Romero, Bellosillo, Melo, Puno, Vitug, Kapunan, Mendoza, and Francisco, **JJ.**, concurred. (Unanimous; no separate concurring or dissenting opinions filed).
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
**Primary StatCon Classification:**
Repeals & Statute Harmonization → Implied Repeal → Presumption Against Implied Repeal (**Presumptio contra repeal tacitum**) → General Repealing Clauses / Harmonization of Prior Administrative Regulations with Subsequent Statutes.
Statutory Language Interpretation → Mandatory vs. Directory Words → Construction of the Auxiliary Imperative "Shall."
**The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim):**
**Section 68, Republic Act No. 7160 (Local Government Code of 1991):**
"Sec. 68. **Execution Pending Appeal.** — An appeal <ins>**shall not prevent a decision from becoming final or executory**</ins>. The respondent shall be considered as having been placed under preventive suspension during the pendency of an appeal in the events he wins such appeal. In the event the appeal results in an exoneration, he shall be paid his salary and such other emoluments during the pendency of the appeal."
**Section 6, Administrative Order No. 18 (February 12, 1987):**
"Sec. 6 Except as otherwise provided by special laws, the execution of the decision/resolution/order appealed from is stayed upon filing of the appeal within the period prescribed herein. <ins>**However, in all cases, at any time during the pendency of the appeal, the Office of the President may direct or stay the execution of the decision/resolution/order appealed from upon such terms and conditions as it may deem just and reasonable**</ins>."
**Section 530 (f) [Repealing Clause], Republic Act No. 7160:**
"All general and special laws, acts, city charters, decrees, executive orders, administrative regulations, part or parts thereof, <ins>**which are incosistent with any of the provisions of this Code, are hereby repealed or modified accordingly**</ins>."
**Historical / Amendment Tracking:**
**Prior Administrative Rule:** Administrative Order No. 18, issued by President Corazon C. Aquino on February 12, 1987 ("Prescribing the Rules and Regulations Governing Appeals to the Office of the President").
**Subsequent Codification:** Republic Act No. 7160, enacted on October 10, 1991, effective January 1, 1992 (cited in petition as January 1, 1991).
**StatCon Diagnostic Profile:**
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Alleged conflict between provisions (repugnancy between Section 68 of R.A. No. 7160 and Section 6 of A.O. No. 18), paired with the meaning of the imperative verb "shall" in Section 68 (whether directory or mandatory).
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. The Court held that Section 68 is not an absolute prohibition against stays: **"As worded, there is room to construe said provision as giving discretion to the reviewing officials to stay the execution of the appealed decision."**
**Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed:**
Implied repeals are disfavored (**implied repeal predicates the intended repeal upon the condition that a substantial conflict must be found between the new and prior laws; the two laws must be absolutely incompatible**).
Harmonious construction (**statutes in pari materia must be read together and reconciled if possible**).
Construction of "shall" as directory or mandatory depending on legislative intent, context, and consequences.
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The Office of the President issued an interlocutory stay of execution suspending two decisions of the **Sangguniang Panlalawigan** of Albay which had ordered the suspension of a municipal mayor pending her administrative appeal.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Achilles C. Berces, Sr.:** Petitioner; former municipal councilor of Tiwi, Albay (1988–1992); complainant in two administrative cases before the provincial board.
**Naomi C. Corral:** Private Respondent; incumbent Municipal Mayor of Tiwi, Albay.
**Hon. Teofisto T. Guingona, Jr. & Antonio Carpio:** Public Respondents; Executive Secretary and Chief Presidential Legal Counsel, respectively, representing the Office of the President.
**Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Albay:** Local legislative/adjudicative body that found Mayor Corral administratively liable and ordered her suspension from office.
**Procedural History & Vehicle:**
**Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Albay:** Rendered decisions on July 1, 1993 (Adm. Case No. 02-92) and July 5, 1993 (Adm. Case No. 05-92), imposing consecutive suspensions of two months and three months on Mayor Corral.
**Office of the President (OP):** Mayor Corral filed an administrative appeal under Section 67(b) of R.A. No. 7160 and petitioned for a stay of execution. On July 28, 1993, the OP granted the stay of execution pursuant to Section 6 of A.O. No. 18. Petitioner’s motion for reconsideration was denied on September 13, 1993 (erroneously dated September 13, 1990 in the decision text).
**Supreme Court:** Petitioner filed a petition for certiorari and prohibition under Rule 65 with a prayer for mandatory preliminary injunction, challenging the OP stay orders as ultra vires and issued with grave abuse of discretion.
**Supreme Court Disposition:** The Court affirmed the OP's construction, rejected petitioner's theory of implied repeal, and dismissed the petition.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **Filing of Administrative Cases:** Petitioner Achilles C. Berces, Sr. instituted two administrative complaints before the **Sangguniang Panlalawigan** of Albay against Mayor Naomi C. Corral:
**Administrative Case No. 02-92:** For abuse of authority and/or oppression, arising from the mayor's non-payment of petitioner's accrued leave benefits amounting to ₱36,779.02 earned as a municipal councilor (1988–1992).
**Administrative Case No. 05-92:** For dishonesty and abuse of authority, stemming from the municipal installation, operation, maintenance, and payment of a water pipeline servicing the mayor's private residence and medical clinic.
2. July 1 & 5, 1993: The Sangguniang Panlalawigan disposed of both cases:
Adm. Case No. 02-92: Ordered Mayor Corral to pay petitioner ₱36,779.02 plus legal interest, and suspended her from office for two (2) months.
Adm. Case No. 05-92: Ordered Mayor Corral suspended from office for three (3) months (to run consecutively after the first suspension) and directed reimbursement of half the municipal water and electric bills from July to December 1992.
3. **July 1993:** Mayor Corral appealed both decisions to the Office of the President pursuant to Section 67(b) of R.A. No. 7160, simultaneously praying for an interlocutory stay of execution.
4. **July 28, 1993:** The Office of the President issued an Order staying the execution of the suspensions, citing Section 68 of R.A. No. 7160 and Section 6 of A.O. No. 18, finding that a stay was **“just and reasonable to prevent undue prejudice to public interest.”**
5. **September 13, 1993:** The Office of the President denied petitioner's Motion for Reconsideration.
6. **Filing of Certiorari:** Petitioner elevated the matter directly to the Supreme Court under Rule 65.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
A. Petitioner's Interpretation
**Core Reading:** Section 68 of R.A. No. 7160 categorically mandates that an appeal **"shall not prevent a decision from becoming final or executory."** The use of "shall" is mandatory, precluding any appellate authority from issuing a stay. Furthermore, Section 6 of A.O. No. 18 (which authorizes presidential stays) is inconsistent with Section 68 and was consequently repealed by the general repealing clause of Section 530 (f) [534 (f)] of R.A. No. 7160.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Express Repealing Clause Theory:** Section 530 (f) invalidates all inconsistent prior administrative regulations.
**Mandatory Construction of "Shall":** Imperative terms require immediate, non-discretionary enforcement of decisions pending review.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Allowing administrative stays frustrates the legislative intent of the Local Government Code to hold errant local officials immediately accountable upon an adverse finding by the local sanggunian.
B. Respondent's Interpretation
**Core Reading:** Section 68 does not deprive the appellate authority of its discretionary power to grant a stay. Section 6 of A.O. No. 18 remains valid; it gives the Office of the President express discretion during the pendency of an appeal to direct or stay execution on terms deemed just and reasonable.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Presumption Against Implied Repeal:** A general repealing clause does not work an express repeal; irreconcilable inconsistency must be demonstrated.
**Harmonization / Reading Laws Together:** Statutes and administrative regulations should be reconciled so both have operative effect.
**Directory Construction of "Shall":** Auxiliary verbs are construed in light of context and consequences.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Abruptly removing an incumbent mayor from office disrupts public service; execution pending appeal causes undue prejudice to public interest if the official is subsequently exonerated.
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
### 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether Section 68 of R.A. No. 7160 repealed Section 6 of Administrative Order No. 18 dated February 12, 1987, via the general repealing clause of the Local Government Code.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Did the general repealing clause of Section 530(f) of R.A. No. 7160 effect an implied repeal of Section 6 of A.O. No. 18, stripping the Office of the President of its authority to stay decisions suspending local elective officials pending appeal?

digest:
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the word "shall" in the clause "an appeal shall not prevent a decision from becoming final or executory" under Section 68 of R.A. No. 7160 is mandatory or directory.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Does the phrase "shall not prevent" in Section 68 of R.A. No. 7160 mandate automatic, unstoppable execution of a **sanggunian** suspension order, or is it directory, preserving the appellate body's discretion to grant a stay?
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Implied Repeal of Section 6, A.O. No. 18 by Section 68, R.A. No. 7160
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
Did Section 68 of R.A. No. 7160 repeal Section 6 of Administrative Order No. 18?
**NO.** The general repealing clause does not identify the specific regulation to be repealed, and no irreconcilable repugnancy exists between the two provisions; they must be harmonized and read together.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**"The aforementioned clause is not an express repeal of Section 6 of Administrative Order No. 18 because it failed to identify or designate the laws or executive orders that are intended to be repealed..."**
**"If there is any repeal of Administrative Order No. 18 by R.A. No. 7160, it is through implication though such kind of repeal is not favored... There is even a presumption against implied repeal."**
**"An implied repeal predicates the intended repeal upon the condition that a substantial conflict must be found between the new and prior laws. In the absence of an express repeal, a subsequent law cannot be construed as repealing a prior law unless an irreconcible inconsistency and repugnancy exists in the terms of the new and old laws... The two laws must be absolutely incompatible... There must be such a repugnancy between the laws that they cannot be made to stand together..."**
**"We find that the provisions of Section 68 of R.A. No. 7160 and Section 6 of Administrative Order No. 18 are not irreconcillably inconsistent and repugnant and the two laws must in fact be read together."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** A general repealing clause (e.g., Section 530 [f]) that purports to repeal all laws or regulations "inconsistent with" the Code is not an express repeal because it lacks specific identification of the targets of repeal.
2. **Statutory Presumptions:** Repeals by implication are disfavored in law. The legal presumption is always against an implied repeal.
3. **Standard for Implied Repeal:** Implied repeal requires the presence of an irreconcilable inconsistency, absolute incompatibility, and such mutual repugnancy that the two legal rules cannot stand together.
4. **Harmonization:** Section 68 of R.A. No. 7160 and Section 6 of A.O. No. 18 are not repugnant. Section 68 sets the baseline rule that filing an appeal does not **per se** intercept the executory nature of the decision, whereas Section 6 of A.O. No. 18 provides an administrative mechanism allowing the appellate tribunal (the OP), upon motion, to order an interlocutory stay when just and reasonable.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** Petitioner's premise that Section 530(f) wiped away the President's stay powers fails because the legislature provided no explicit, direct language expressing an intent to strip reviewing officials of procedural control over execution pending appeal.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** A standard clause repealing all "inconsistent laws" is never an express repeal; it requires the court to determine whether true incompatibility exists. Because Section 68 of the Local Government Code merely establishes that an appeal does not automatically stop execution, it can easily co-exist with an administrative rule that gives the President discretion to order a temporary stay when the public interest demands it.
Issue 2: Mandatory vs. Directory Construction of "Shall" in Section 68, R.A. No. 7160
**(a) Issue & Short Answer:**
Is the word "shall" in Section 68 of R.A. No. 7160 mandatory so as to deprive reviewing officials of the discretion to grant a stay of execution?
**NO.** The term "shall" is construed as directory in this context, leaving reviewing officials with the procedural discretion to issue a stay pending appeal.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
**"The first sentence of Section 68 merely provides that an 'appeal shall not prevent a decision from becoming final or executory.' As worded, there is room to construe said provision as giving discretion to the reviewing officials to stay the execution of the appealed decision. There is nothing to infer therefrom that the reviewing officials are deprived of the authority to order a stay of the appealed order."**
**"The execution of decisions pending appeal is procedural and in the absence of a clear legislative intent to remove from the reviewing officials the authority to order a stay of execution, such authority can [be] provided in the rules and regulations governing the appeals of elective officials in administrative cases."**
**"The term 'shall' may be read either as mandatory or directory depending upon a consideration of the entire provisions in which it is found, its object and the consequences that would follow from construing it one way or the other... In the case at bench, there is no basis to justify the construction of the word as mandatory."**
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The auxiliary verb "shall" does not have an exclusive, unbending mandatory character in statutory construction.
2. **Intrinsic Context & Legislative Intent:** Determining whether "shall" is mandatory or directory requires analyzing the entire provision, the subject matter, the statutory object, and the consequences of the competing readings.
3. **Procedural Character of the Rule:** Execution of judgments pending appeal is inherently procedural. Unless Congress uses direct, unambiguous language depriving appellate bodies of power, procedural authority to regulate execution remains with the reviewing tribunal under applicable regulations.
4. **Evaluation of Consequences:** Reading "shall" as mandatory would force the immediate suspension of local chief executives regardless of the merits of their appeal or the disruption to the public, causing irreparable harm if the executive is later exonerated.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** Construing "shall" as an absolute, mandatory prohibition against stays creates an unnecessary conflict with administrative appellate procedures and undermines the orderly administration of local governance.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:**
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** The word "shall" in statutory interpretation is not always an ironclad command; it may be read as directory depending on the statute's purpose and the real-world consequences of its enforcement. Here, "shall not prevent" means only that an appeal does not automatically halt the penalty on its own, leaving the Office of the President full procedural leeway to grant a stay to keep municipal operations running smoothly.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text. (The decision was unanimous).
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Dispositive Portion:**
**WHEREFORE**, the petition is **DISMISSED**.
**SO ORDERED**.
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, ruling in favor of respondents Mayor Corral and the Office of the President. The administrative orders issued by the Office of the President staying the mayor's suspension pending appeal were affirmed as valid exercises of procedural discretion, establishing that Section 68 of R.A. No. 7160 does not disable appellate authorities from staying execution pending appeal.

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Erectors, Inc. v. NLRC**
**Full Official Caption: Erectors, Inc., Petitioner, v. National Labor Relations Commission, Hon. Julio Andres, Jr. and Florencio Burgos, Respondents.**
**Citation & Metadata:**
**G.R. No.:** 104215
**Date of Promulgation:** May 8, 1996
**SCRA Citation:** 256 SCRA 629
**Ponente:** Puno, **J.**
**Voting Breakdown:** Second Division; Regalado, Romero, Mendoza, and Torres, Jr., **JJ.**, concurred. (Unanimous; no separate concurring or dissenting opinions).
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
**Primary StatCon Classification:**
Prospective vs. Retroactive Operation of Statutes → General Rule on Prospective Application → **Lex prospicit, non respicit** → Non-retroactivity of jurisdictional statutes creating administrative agencies vs. Curative statutes exception.
Ancillary Maxim/Doctrine: **Jurisdiction over the subject matter is determined by the law in force at the time of the commencement of the action.**
**The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim):**
**Section 4(a), Executive Order No. 797 (Reorganizing the Ministry of Labor and Employment, Creating the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration, and for Other Purposes; promulgated May 1, 1982):**
"Section 4. (a) The governing Board of the Administration (POEA) shall have the following functions: ... The Administration shall have **original and exclusive jurisdiction over all cases, including money claims, involving employer-employee relations arising out of or by virtue of any law or contract involving Filipino workers for overseas employment, including seamen.**"
**Article 15(b), Labor Code of the Philippines, as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1691 (promulgated May 1, 1980):**
"(b) The regional offices of the Ministry of Labor shall have the **original and exclusive jurisdiction over all matters or cases involving employer-employee relations including money claims, arising out of or by virtue of any law or contracts involving Filipino workers for overseas employment except seamen**: Provided that the Bureau of Employment Services may, in the case of the National Capital Region, exercise such power, whenever the Minister of Labor deems it appropriate. The decisions of the regional offices or the Bureau of Employment Services if so authorized by the Minister of Labor as provided in this Article, shall be appealable to the National Labor Relations Commission upon the same grounds provided in Article 223 hereof. The decisions of the National Labor Relations Commission shall be final and inappealable."
**Article 4, Civil Code of the Philippines (Underlying Rule of Interpretation):**
"Laws shall have no retroactive effect, unless the contrary is provided."
**Historical / Amendment Tracking:**
**Prior Regime (P.D. No. 1412, effective June 9, 1978):** Vested original and exclusive jurisdiction over overseas contract workers' claims (except seamen) in the Bureau of Employment Services (BES).
**Interim Regime (P.D. No. 1391, May 29, 1978 & P.D. No. 1691, May 1, 1980):** Integrated Labor Arbiters into Regional Offices and vested original and exclusive jurisdiction over overseas employer-employee money claims in the Regional Offices / Labor Arbiters.
**Challenged Enactment (E.O. No. 797, effective May 1, 1982):** Created the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration (POEA) and transferred original and exclusive jurisdiction over overseas worker claims to the POEA.
**StatCon Diagnostic Profile:**
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Legislative Silence / Scope of Temporal Reach. E.O. No. 797 contained no express clause divesting existing tribunals of, or retroactively transferring, pending cases; petitioner asserted an implied retroactive divestment of jurisdiction by operation of law on the theory that E.O. No. 797 was a curative statute.
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. While the grant of jurisdiction to POEA in E.O. No. 797 was textually explicit, its silence on pending actions required the application of the statutory presumption of prospectivity and the legal definition of curative statutes.
**Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed:**
**Lex prospicit, non respicit** (Laws look forward, not backward; statutes are to be construed as operating only prospectively unless the legislative intent for retroactivity is express or necessarily implied).
Rule on Curative Statutes: A statute is curative only if enacted to cure defects in prior law or validate void proceedings/acts for lack of conformity with legal requisites.
Principle of Adherence to Jurisdiction: Jurisdiction is conferred by the statute in force at the time of the commencement of the action and is not ousted by subsequent legislation absent express retroactive terms.
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The overseas worker filed a money claim before the Labor Arbiter on March 31, 1982. One month later, on May 1, 1982, E.O. No. 797 took effect, transferring jurisdiction over overseas employment money claims to the newly created POEA, prompting the employer to argue that the Labor Arbiter lost jurisdiction mid-proceeding.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
**Key Parties & Roles:**
**Erectors, Inc. (Petitioner):** The recruitment and construction contractor firm that deployed Burgos to Saudi Arabia under an altered, lower-paying contract.
**Florencio Burgos (Private Respondent):** The overseas contract worker hired initially as a service contract driver but subsequently made to sign a contract as helper/laborer at reduced pay.
**Hon. Julio Andres, Jr. (Public Respondent):** The Labor Arbiter of the Ministry/Department of Labor and Employment who took cognizance of the case, conducted hearings, and rendered the judgment against Petitioner.
**National Labor Relations Commission [NLRC] (Public Respondent):** The labor appellate body that affirmed the Labor Arbiter’s jurisdiction and decision.
**Philippine Overseas Employment Administration [POEA]:** The agency established under E.O. No. 797 whose newly created jurisdiction was invoked by petitioner to divest the Labor Arbiter.
**Procedural History & Vehicle:**
**Initiatory Filing (March 31, 1982):** Burgos filed a complaint with the Labor Arbiter (NLRC-NCR) for underpayment of wages, non-payment of overtime pay, and contractual bonus.
**Statutory Interruption (May 1, 1982):** E.O. No. 797 took effect while the case was at the conciliation stage.
**Labor Arbiter Decision (September 23, 1983):** Labor Arbiter Andres proceeded to hear and decide the case on the merits, awarding Burgos US$2,496.00 in allowance differentials and a US$1,000.00 contractual bonus.
**NLRC Appeal (July 17, 1991):** The NLRC dismissed petitioner's appeal, ruling that jurisdiction accrued under P.D. 1391 and P.D. 1691 which were in effect at the time of filing.
**Supreme Court Petition:** Special civil action for **certiorari** under Rule 65 filed by Erectors, Inc. The Supreme Court **DISMISSED** the petition, affirming the NLRC and the Labor Arbiter.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **September 1979:** Petitioner Erectors, Inc. recruits Florencio Burgos to work as a service contract driver in Saudi Arabia for 12 months with a monthly salary of US$165.00, monthly allowance of US$165.00, and a contractual bonus of US$1,000.00 if he renewed/extended without taking home leave. The contract was approved by the Ministry of Labor and Employment on September 20, 1979.
2. **December 14, 1979:** Prior to deployment, petitioner informs Burgos that the driver position is no longer available and causes him to sign a substitute contract as helper/laborer at a reduced monthly salary of US$105.00 and monthly allowance of US$105.00. This second contract was never submitted to the Ministry for approval.
3. **December 18, 1979 – August 1981:** Burgos departs for Saudi Arabia, works on the Buraidah Sports Complex project as a helper/laborer, renews his contract after one year (wages raised to US$231.00 total), and foregoes home leave.
4. **August 24, 1981:** Burgos returns to the Philippines and demands payment from petitioner under the first approved contract (salary/allowance differential plus the US$1,000.00 bonus). Petitioner denies the claim.
5. **March 31, 1982:** Burgos files a formal complaint with the Labor Arbiter against petitioner for underpayment of wages, non-payment of overtime pay, and contractual bonus.
6. **May 1, 1982:** E.O. No. 797 takes effect, creating the POEA and clothing it with original and exclusive jurisdiction over money claims of overseas contract workers.
7. **September 23, 1983:** The Labor Arbiter rejects petitioner's jurisdictional objection and enters judgment ordering petitioner to pay US$2,496.00 in differentials and US$1,000.00 in bonus.
8. **July 17, 1991:** Respondent NLRC resolves petitioner's appeal by affirming the Arbiter, holding that jurisdiction was lawfully fixed at the time the complaint was commenced under P.D. 1691 and P.D. 1391.
9. **Certiorari to the Supreme Court:** Petitioner challenges the judgment on the ground that the Labor Arbiter acted without jurisdiction due to the retroactive divestiture worked by E.O. No. 797.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
A. Petitioner's Interpretation (Erectors, Inc.):
**Core Reading:** Section 4(a) of E.O. No. 797, by conferring "original and exclusive jurisdiction" over overseas worker money claims to the POEA, instantly ousted the Labor Arbiter of jurisdiction over all pending, undecided overseas employment disputes filed prior to May 1, 1982.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Curative Statute Doctrine:** Relied on **Briad Agro Development Corp. v. Dela Cerna** (179 SCRA 269), asserting that jurisdictional amendments regulating labor money claims are curative and must operate retroactively to reach pending actions.
**Immediate Application of Procedural/Jurisdictional Laws:** Laws affecting jurisdiction are procedural and take immediate effect on pending proceedings.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Allowing Labor Arbiters to continue deciding overseas contract worker claims post-May 1, 1982 violates the executive policy centralizing all overseas recruitment regulation and adjudication under the POEA.
B. Respondent's Interpretation (Burgos / NLRC):
**Core Reading:** Section 4(a) of E.O. No. 797 applies purely prospectively to claims initiated on or after May 1, 1982. Jurisdiction acquired by the Labor Arbiter on March 31, 1982 remained undisturbed.
**Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked:**
**Lex prospicit, non respicit / Rule on Prospectivity:** Laws operate prospectively unless retroactivity is expressly provided or necessarily implied.
**Rule on Adherence of Jurisdiction:** Subject-matter jurisdiction is determined by the law in force at the time of the commencement of the action.
**Inapplicability of Curative Doctrine:** E.O. 797 was not enacted to cure legal defects or validate void proceedings, but to reorganize administrative functions.
**Policy / Consequence Argument:** Retroactive application would disrupt ongoing litigations, nullify proceedings lawfully commenced, and penalize workers who sought redress under the precise laws in force when their actions were brought.
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
### 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE]
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether Executive Order No. 797 divested the Labor Arbiter of authority to hear and decide the overseas worker money claim filed prior to its effectivity, by virtue of it being a curative statute entitled to retroactive operation.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether Section 4(a) of E.O. No. 797 operates retroactively as a curative statute to divest a Labor Arbiter of subject-matter jurisdiction over an overseas worker's money claim lawfully commenced prior to the order's effectivity.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
(a) Issue & Short Answer:
**Issue 1:** Did E.O. No. 797 retroactively divest the Labor Arbiter of jurisdiction over private respondent's complaint filed prior to its effectivity?
**Short Answer: NO.** E.O. No. 797 is an administrative reorganizational statute, not a curative statute; hence, under the doctrine of prospectivity (**lex prospicit, non respicit**) and the established principle that subject-matter jurisdiction is determined by the statute in force at the time an action is commenced, the Labor Arbiter retained full jurisdiction to hear and decide the pending suit.
(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:
"The rule is that jurisdiction over the subject matter is determined by the law in force at the time of the commencement of the action."
"E.O. No. 797 did not divest the Labor Arbiter's authority to hear and decide the case filed by private respondent prior to its effectivity. Laws should only be applied prospectively unless the legislative intent to give them retroactive effect is expressly declared or is necessarily implied from the language used. We fail to perceive in the language of E.O. No. 797 an intention to give it retroactive effect."
"A curative statute is enacted to cure defects in a prior law or to validate legal proceedings, instruments or acts of public authorities which would otherwise be void for want of conformity with certain existing legal requirements."
"The law at bar, E.O. No. 797, is not a curative statute. It was not intended to remedy any defect in the law. It created the POEA to assume the functions of the Overseas Employment Development Board, the National Seamen Board and the overseas employment functions of the Bureau of Employment Services. ... The rule on prospectivity of laws should therefore apply to E.O. No. 797. It should not affect jurisdiction over cases filed prior to its effectivity."
(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court tested the text of E.O. No. 797 against the baseline statutory presumption of prospectivity codified in Article 4 of the Civil Code. Finding neither an express declaration nor a necessary implication of retroactivity in the text, the Court held that the statute applies purely prospectively.
2. **Intrinsic Aids Examined:** The Court analyzed the text, title, and structure of E.O. No. 797. The statute was explicitly enacted to create the POEA and reallocate executive and adjudicative responsibilities (merging the functions of the Overseas Employment Development Board, National Seamen Board, and Bureau of Employment Services). The words contain no jurisdictional transfer clause or transition provision ordering the dismissal or physical transfer of cases already pending before Labor Arbiters.
3. Extrinsic Aids / Precedent Harmonization:
**Distinction from Briad Agro Development Corp. v. Dela Cerna:** In **Briad**, E.O. No. 111 and R.A. No. 6715 were properly categorized as curative statutes. E.O. 111 cured a jurisdictional deficit by granting concurrent jurisdiction, and R.A. 6715 cured the resultant statutory overlap by delineating monetary thresholds ($P5,000.00$). They were intended to fix flaws in prior enactments. By contrast, E.O. No. 797 did not cure any structural defect or validate flawed proceedings; it merely accomplished an administrative reorganization.
**Application of Philippine-Singapore Ports Corp. v. NLRC:** The Court reaffirmed **Philippine-Singapore Ports Corp.**, holding that subsequent shifts in statutory jurisdiction over overseas workers (from BES under P.D. 1412, to Regional Offices/Arbiters under P.D. 1691/1391, to POEA under E.O. 797) do not retroactively unseat jurisdiction once attached at the time of commencement.
4. **Statutory Presumptions & Policies:** Presumption against retroactivity (**lex prospicit, non respicit**). Subject-matter jurisdiction is an immutable statutory grant anchored at the moment the initiatory pleading is docketed. Statutory amendments will not be presumed to oust a court or tribunal of jurisdiction over pending cases unless the legislature commands it in unequivocal, unmistakable language.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** Petitioner’s invocation of **Briad** was rejected because **Briad** represents a narrow exception reserved exclusively for genuine curative legislation. To treat every statute reorganizing administrative agency jurisdiction as "curative" would obliterate the general rule of prospectivity and undermine stability in administrative adjudications.
(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation:
**(Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)**
The Supreme Court ruled that a tribunal’s jurisdiction over a case is permanently fixed by the law in force on the exact date the complaint is filed. Because Florencio Burgos filed his complaint on March 31, 1982—when P.D. 1691 and P.D. 1391 authorized the Labor Arbiter to hear overseas employment claims—the subsequent enactment of E.O. No. 797 on May 1, 1982 did not take that case away. E.O. No. 797 is an administrative reorganizing law, not a "curative statute," and under the presumption of prospectivity, it cannot be read retroactively to strip an existing tribunal of a case already before it without express statutory words to that effect.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"IN VIEW WHEREOF, the Petition is DISMISSED. Costs against petitioner.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:**
Petitioner Erectors, Inc. lost completely. The Supreme Court affirmed the NLRC and sustained the Labor Arbiter’s award of wage differentials and bonus to Burgos. The ruling confirms that E.O. No. 797 cannot be applied retroactively to divest Labor Arbiters of jurisdiction over overseas employment money claims commenced prior to May 1, 1982.

citation: Recitation Title: City Government of San Pablo v. Reyes
subject: Statutory Construction
category: Statutory Construction | General Topic
digest:
**Full Official Caption:** City Government of San Pablo, Laguna, City Treasurer of San Pablo, Laguna, and The Sangguniang Panglunsod of San Pablo, Laguna, Petitioners, v. Honorable Bienvenido V. Reyes, in his capacity as Presiding Judge, Regional Trial Court, Branch 29, San Pablo City, and The Manila Electric Company, Respondents. **Citation & Metadata:** G.R. No. 127708 March 25, 1999 (364 Phil. 842 / 305 SCRA 353) Ponente: Gonzaga-Reyes, **J.** Voting Breakdown: Third Division (Romero, Vitug, Panganiban, and Purisima, **JJ.**, concur). Unanimous; no separate opinions. 2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown Primary StatCon Classification **Statutory Construction Area:** Implied Repeals & Intrinsic Aids **Specific Canon / Principle / Rule Applied:** General Law vs. Prior Special Franchises; Express Withdrawal of Exemptions; Presumption Against Implied Repeals Rebutted by Manifest Intent; Strict Construction of Tax Exemptions **Specific Latin Maxim: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius** (The express mention of one person, thing, act, or consequence excludes all others) **Specific Sub-Issue:** Whether the broad authorization to levy franchise taxes "notwithstanding any exemption granted by any law or other special law" (Sec. 137) coupled with an express blanket withdrawal of exemptions (Sec. 193) under the Local Government Code of 1991 (R.A. No. 7160) impliedly repealed or altered the "in lieu of all taxes" exemption clauses in private electric franchises (Act No. 3648, R.A. No. 2340, P.D. No. 551). The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim) 1. Republic Act No. 7160 (Local Government Code of 1991) **Sec. 137. Franchise Tax.** — **Notwithstanding any exemption granted by any law or other special law**, the province may impose a tax on business enjoying a franchise, at a rate not exceeding fifty percent 50% of one percent 1% of the gross annual receipts for the preceding calendar year based on the incoming receipts, or realized, within its territorial jurisdiction... **Sec. 151. Scope of Taxing Powers.** — Except as otherwise provided in this Code, the city, may levy the taxes, fees, and charges which the province or municipality may impose... **Sec. 193. Withdrawal of Tax Exemption Privileges.** — **Unless otherwise provided in this Code, tax exemptions or incentives granted to, or presently enjoyed by all persons, whether natural or juridical, including government-owned or controlled corporations, except local water districts, cooperatives duly registered under R.A. 6938, non-stock and non-profit hospitals and educational institutions, are hereby withdrawn upon the effectivity of this Code.** **Sec. 534 (f). Repealing Clause.** — **All general and special law, acts, city charters, decrees, executive orders, proclamation and administrative regulations, or part or parts thereof which are inconsistent with any of the provisions of this code are hereby repealed or modified accordingly.** 2. Act No. 3648 (Escudero Legislative Franchise, transferred to MERALCO via R.A. No. 2340), Section 10 "...In consideration of the franchise and rights hereby granted, the grantee shall pay unto the municipal treasury of each municipality in which it is supplying electric current to the public under this franchise, a tax equal to two percentum of the gross earnings from electric current sold or supplied under this franchise in each said municipality. Said tax shall be due and payable quarterly and **shall be in lieu of any and all taxes of any kind nature or description levied, established or collected by any authority whatsoever, municipal, provincial or insular, now or in the future**, on its poles, wires, insulator, switches, transformers, and structures, installations, conductors, and accessories placed in and over and under all public property, including public streets and highways, provincial roads, bridges and public squares, and on its franchise, rights, privileges, receipts, revenues and profits from which taxes the grantee is hereby expressly exempted." 3. Presidential Decree No. 551, Section 1 "Sec. 1. Any provision of law or local ordinance to the contrary notwithstanding, the franchise tax payable by all grantees of franchise to generate, distribute and sell electric current for light, heat and power shall be two percent (2%) of their gross receipts received from the sale of electric current and from transactions incident to the generation, distribution and sale of electric current. Such franchise tax shall be payable to the Commissioner of Internal Revenue of his duly authorized representative on or before the twentieth day of the month following the end of each calendar quarter or month as may be provided in the respective franchise or pertinent municipal regulation and **shall, any provision of the Local Tax Code or any other law to the contrary notwithstanding, be in lieu of all taxes and assessments of whatever nature imposed by any national or local authority on earnings, receipts, income and privilege of generation, distribution and sale of electric current.**" StatCon Diagnostic Profile **The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:** Apparent Conflict Between Provisions / Implied Repeal. The general subsequent enactment (LGC of 1991, Secs. 137 & 193) conflicted with prior special legislative charters and decrees granting electric franchise holders an "in lieu of all taxes" tax exemption. **Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. While the repealing clause of the LGC (Sec. 534[f]) was general and non-specific—preventing an immediate finding of express repeal—the Court conducted an in-depth statutory reconciliation to discern whether Congress intended to effect an implied repeal of special franchise exemptions. **Controlling Canon / Maxim Deployed: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius**; Presumption against implied repeals overturned by clear and manifest legislative intent (**lex posterior generalis non derogat priori speciali** yield to categorical, all-encompassing statutory withdrawals); Constitutional canon favoring municipal taxing power under Article X, Section 5 of the 1987 Constitution. **Factual Interpretive Trigger:** The City Treasurer of San Pablo levied a local franchise tax under Section 2.09 of Ordinance No. 56 against MERALCO, prompting MERALCO to pay ₱1,857,711.67 under protest and sue for a declaratory judgment of invalidity and a tax refund, arguing that its franchise charter exempted it from local franchise taxation. 3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture Key Parties & Roles **Petitioners:** City Government of San Pablo, Laguna; City Treasurer of San Pablo; and Sangguniang Panglunsod of San Pablo City (Local government taxing authorities asserting delegated/constitutional power to levy local franchise taxes). **Private Respondent:** Manila Electric Company (MERALCO) (Public utility holding a legislative electric distribution franchise initially granted under Act No. 3648, transferred via R.A. No. 2340, claiming exemption under the "in lieu of all taxes" clause). **Public Respondent:** Hon. Bienvenido V. Reyes, Presiding Judge, Regional Trial Court (RTC) of San Pablo City, Branch 29 (Rendered the judgment nullifying the local tax and ordering a refund). Procedural History & Vehicle 1. **Local Action:** On October 5, 1992, the Sangguniang Panglunsod enacted Ordinance No. 56 (Revenue Code of San Pablo City), imposing a 0.5% franchise tax under Sec. 2.09. 2. **Payment Under Protest & Trial Court Action:** MERALCO paid ₱1,857,711.67 under protest from 1994 to 1996 and instituted Civil Case No. SP-4359(96) before the RTC Branch 29, San Pablo City, seeking the nullification of Sec. 2.09 of Ordinance No. 56 and a full refund. 3. **RTC Ruling:** The RTC declared Section 2.09 void as applied to MERALCO and ordered the City to refund ₱1,857,711.67 plus subsequent amounts paid, finding no express or implied repeal of MERALCO’s tax exemption under Act No. 3648, R.A. No. 2340, and P.D. No. 551 by the LGC. 4. **Supreme Court Vehicle:** Petitioners filed a direct Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 raising pure questions of law. The Supreme Court **REVERSED** the RTC. ### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard 1. **November 1929:** Act No. 3648 was approved, granting the Escudero Electric Service Company a 50-year legislative franchise to operate an electric light and power system in San Pablo and neighboring municipalities, featuring a 2% gross earnings tax "in lieu of any and all taxes... now or in the future" (Sec. 10). 2. **June 1959:** Republic Act No. 2340 approved the transfer of Escudero’s legislative franchise to MERALCO under the same terms and privileges. 3. **September 11, 1974:** Presidential Decree No. 551 was promulgated, standardizing franchise taxes for electric utilities at 2% of gross receipts payable to the BIR, which "shall, any provision of the Local Tax Code or any other law to the contrary notwithstanding, be in lieu of all taxes and assessments of whatever nature imposed by any national or local authority." 4. **January 1, 1992:** Republic Act No. 7160 (The Local Government Code of 1991) took effect, establishing Sec. 137 (authorizing provinces/cities to levy franchise taxes "notwithstanding any exemption granted by any law or other special law") and Sec. 193 (withdrawing all tax exemptions enjoyed by all persons, natural or juridical, except local water districts, cooperatives, and non-stock, non-profit hospitals and educational institutions). 5. **October 5, 1992:** The Sangguniang Panglunsod of San Pablo enacted Ordinance No. 56 (effective October 30, 1992), embodying Section 2.09, which levied a 0.5% franchise tax on gross annual receipts realized within the city. 6. **1994–1996:** Pursuant to formal demand letters from the City Treasurer, MERALCO paid the assessed franchise tax under protest, totaling ₱1,857,711.67. 7. **Post-Payment:** MERALCO initiated Civil Case No. SP-4359(96) in the RTC of San Pablo City to invalidate the ordinance and demand a tax refund. 8. **Trial Court Judgment:** RTC San Pablo City Branch 29 held for MERALCO, finding that the LGC neither expressly nor impliedly repealed the "in lieu of all taxes" provisions of Act No. 3648, R.A. No. 2340, and P.D. No. 551, and ruled that taxing MERALCO impaired the contract between it and the State. 9. **January 10, 1996:** The RTC denied the City's Motion for Reconsideration, precipitating the Petition for Review on Certiorari before the Supreme Court. 5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons) | Interpretive Element | Petitioner's Interpretation (City of San Pablo) | Respondent's Interpretation (MERALCO) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Core Reading of the Contested Texts** | Sections 137 and 193 of the LGC operate as an express and categorical general withdrawal of all pre-existing franchise tax exemptions. Section 534(f) repeals all inconsistent special and general laws. | The "in lieu of all taxes" clause in Act No. 3648, R.A. No. 2340, and P.D. No. 551 constitutes a special law and a private contract/commutative tax that cannot be impliedly repealed by a later general law (LGC). | | **Canons, Aids, & Maxims Invoked** | - **Expressio unius est exclusio alterius** (Sec. 193 enumerates all exceptions; non-included entities are withdrawn).
- Presumption against implied repeals yields to manifest and all-encompassing legislative intent.
- Article X, Section 5, 1987 Constitution: Fiscal doubts resolved in favor of local autonomy.
- Administrative interpretation: BLGF/DOF 3rd Indorsement (Feb. 15, 1994).
- Doctrine in **Mactan Cebu International Airport Authority v. Marcos**. | - **Lex posterior generalis non derogat priori speciali** (A general later statute does not repeal an earlier special statute).
- Presumption against implied repeals.
- Commutative tax doctrine (**Cagayan Electric Power** line).
- Constitutional Non-Impairment Clause (charter is an inviolable contract with the State). | | **Policy / Consequence Argument** | Failure to withdraw exemptions erodes local tax bases, frustrates constitutional and statutory local autonomy, and prevents local governments from becoming self-reliant communities. | Subjecting MERALCO to local franchise taxes imposes double taxation, violates vested rights under its franchise contract, and ignores the special nature of public utility charters. | 6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues ### 1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE] **Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the City of San Pablo may impose a local franchise tax pursuant to the LGC upon the Manila Electric Company which pays a tax equal to two percent of its gross receipts "in lieu of" all taxes and assessments of whatever nature imposed by any national or local authority on savings or income; specifically, whether R.A. No. 7160 impliedly repealed the MERALCO franchise tax exemption. **Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Did the general withdrawal of tax exemptions under Section 193 and the non-obstante clause of Section 137 of the Local Government Code impliedly repeal the special "in lieu of all taxes" exemption provisions granted to MERALCO under Act No. 3648, R.A. No. 2340, and P.D. No. 551 pursuant to the maxim **expressio unius est exclusio alterius**?

### 1. Case Header & Citation Block
**Concise Recognizable Title: Juan v. People**
**Full Official Caption:** Rogelio Juan, Pedro De Jesus, Delfin Carreon, and Antonio Galguerra, Petitioners, vs. People of the Philippines, Respondent.
**Citation & Metadata:**
G.R. No. 132378
Promulgated: January 18, 2000
379 Phil. 125 / 322 SCRA 125
Ponente: Panganiban, **J.**
Voting Breakdown: Third Division (Melo [**Chairman**], Vitug, Purisima, and Gonzaga-Reyes, **JJ.**, concur). Unanimous; no separate concurring or dissenting opinions.
2. StatCon Diagnostic Matrix & Governing Provision Breakdown
Primary StatCon Classification
**Issue 1 (Jurisdiction):** Harmonization of Statutes → General Law vs. Special Law (**Generalia specialibus non derogant** / Special Law as Exception to General Law) → Exception Clause Construction → Jurisdiction over Election Offenses.
**Issue 2 (Preventive Suspension):** Statutes in Pari Materia / Complementary Statutes → Legislative Expansion via Amendment (**Batas Pambansa Blg. 195**) → Broad Statutory Meaning of Fraud upon Government Property → Application of R.A. No. 3019 to Omnibus Election Code Violations.
The Contested Statutory / Constitutional Text (Verbatim)
1. Section 13, Republic Act No. 3019 (Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act), as amended by Batas Pambansa Blg. 195:
"Sec. 13. **Suspension and loss of benefits.** — Any incumbent public officer against whom any criminal prosecution under a valid information under this Act or under Title 7, Book II of the Revised Penal Code **or for any offense involving fraud upon government or public funds or property whether as a simple or as a complex offense and in whatever stage of execution and mode of participation**, is pending in court, shall be suspended from office. Should he be convicted by final judgment, he shall lose all retirement or gratuity benefits under any law, but if he is acquitted, he shall be entitled to reinstatement, and to the salaries and benefits which he failed to receive during suspension, unless in the meantime administrative proceedings have been filed against him.
In the event that such convicted officer, who may have already been separated from the service, has already received such benefits he shall be liable to restitute the same to the government."
2. Section 261(o), Batas Pambansa Blg. 881 (Omnibus Election Code of the Philippines):
"Sec. 261. **Prohibited Acts.** — The following shall be guilty of an election offense:
(o) **Use of public funds, money deposited in trust, equipment, facilities owned or controlled by the government for an election campaign.** — Any person who uses under any guise whatsoever, directly or indirectly, (1) public funds or money deposited with or held in trust by, public financing institutions or by government offices, banks, or agencies; (2) any printing press, radio, or television station or audio-visual equipment operated by the Government or by its divisions, sub-divisions, agencies or instrumentalities, including government-owned or controlled corporations, or by the Armed Forces of the Philippines; or (3) **any equipment, vehicle, facility, apparatus or paraphernalia owned by the government or by its political subdivisions, agencies, including government-owned or controlled corporations, or by the Armed Forces of the Philippines for any election campaign or for any partisan political activity**."
3. Section 32, Batas Pambansa Blg. 129, as amended by Section 2 of Republic Act No. 7691:
"Sec. 32. **Jurisdiction of Metropolitan Trial Courts, Municipal Trial Courts and Municipal Circuit Trial Courts in Criminal Cases.** — **Except in cases falling within the exclusive original jurisdiction of the Regional Trial Courts and of the Sandiganbayan**, the Metropolitan Trial Courts, Municipal Trial Courts, and Municipal Circuit Trial Courts shall exercise:
(1) Exclusive original jurisdiction over all violations of city or municipal ordinances, committed within their respective territorial jurisdiction; and
(2) Exclusive original jurisdiction over all offenses punishable with imprisonment not exceeding six (6) years irrespective of the amount of fine, and regardless of other imposable accessory or other penalties, including the civil liability arising from such offenses or predicated thereon, irrespective of kind, nature, value or amount thereof; **Provided, however**, that in offenses involving damage to property through criminal negligence, they shall have exclusive original jurisdiction thereof."
4. Section 268, Batas Pambansa Blg. 881 (Omnibus Election Code of the Philippines):
"Sec. 268. **Jurisdiction of courts.** — **The regional trial court shall have the exclusive jurisdiction to try and decide any criminal action or proceeding for violation of this Code, except those relating to the offense of failure to register or failure to vote**, which shall be under the jurisdiction of the metropolitan or municipal trial courts. From the decision of the courts, appeal will lie as in other criminal cases."
Historical / Amendment Tracking
**Historical Text of Section 13, R.A. No. 3019 (Prior to B.P. Blg. 195):**
"Sec. 13. **Suspension and loss of benefits.** — Any public officer against whom any criminal prosecution under a valid information **under this Act or under the provisions of the Revised Penal Code on bribery** is pending in court shall be suspended from office..."
**Amendment by B.P. Blg. 195:**
The legislature deliberately broadened the reach of mandatory preventive suspension by adding: **"or under Title 7, Book II of the Revised Penal Code or for any offense involving fraud upon government or public funds or property whether as a simple or as a complex offense and in whatever stage of execution and mode of participation."**
StatCon Diagnostic Profile
**The Linguistic / Interpretive Defect:**
1. **Apparent Conflict / Jurisdictional Overlap:** Alleged clash between R.A. No. 7691 (conferring jurisdiction on first-level courts for offenses punishable by not more than six years) and Section 268 of the Omnibus Election Code (vesting exclusive jurisdiction over election offenses in the RTC).
2. **Scope / Categorization Ambiguity:** Whether the catch-all clause in Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019 (**"any offense involving fraud upon government or public funds or property"**) applies solely to traditional anti-graft crimes or extends to election offenses under Section 261(o) of the Omnibus Election Code.
**Was Statutory Construction Legally Permissible?:** Yes. Harmonization of complementary statutes (**in pari materia**) was necessary to determine if an election offense involving misapplication of government property constitutes "fraud upon government... property" within the meaning of R.A. No. 3019. Furthermore, statutory construction was required to resolve the apparent overlap between general jurisdictional thresholds (R.A. No. 7691) and specialized jurisdictional grants (B.P. Blg. 881).
**Controlling Canons / Maxims Deployed:**
**Generalia specialibus non derogant** (A general law does not derogate from a special law; a special law is an exception to a general statute).
**Statutes in Pari Materia / Complementary Reading** ("Every law must be read together with the provisions of any other complementing law, unless both are otherwise irreconcilable").
**Legislative Intent via Amendatory Expansion** (Legislative history tracking changes made by amendatory enactments to ascertain expanded statutory coverage).
**Substantial Compliance Doctrine** (Procedural rules interpreted liberally when underlying constitutional due process is satisfied).
**Factual Interpretive Trigger:** Barangay officials were criminally charged with an election offense for using government communications gear and a government tricycle in their campaign. Private complainants sought their preventive suspension under Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019, prompting the accused to claim that an election offense is outside the scope of the Anti-Graft Law and beyond the jurisdiction of the RTC under R.A. No. 7691.
3. Cast of Characters & Procedural Posture
Key Parties & Roles
**Rogelio Juan:** Petitioner; incumbent Barangay Chairman of Barangay Talipapa, Novaliches, Quezon City; accused of unlawfully using a government-owned VHF radio transceiver for his political campaign.
**Pedro De Jesus:** Petitioner; incumbent Barangay Kagawad of Barangay Talipapa; co-accused with Juan regarding the VHF radio transceiver.
**Delfin Carreon & Antonio Galguerra:** Petitioners; incumbent Barangay Kagawads of Barangay Talipapa; accused of unlawfully using a government-owned tricycle for their election campaigns.
**People of the Philippines:** Respondent; represented by the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) and prosecuted at the trial level through the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) prosecutor.
**Rodolfo Cayubit & Ricardo Galguerra:** Witnesses/private complainants who initiated the "Motion for Removal from Office."
**Atty. Leonides S. Bernabe, Jr.:** Counsel representing private complainants.
**Hon. Lucas P. Bersamin:** Presiding Judge, Regional Trial Court of Quezon City, Branch 96 (trial court judge who ordered the 60-day preventive suspension).
Procedural History & Vehicle
1. Regional Trial Court (Branch 96, Quezon City):
Criminal Case Nos. Q-96-64564 to 66 were filed charging petitioners with violation of Section 261(o) of B.P. Blg. 881.
Private complainants filed a "Motion for Removal from Office." The COMELEC prosecutor filed a Manifestation and Comment conforming to and adopting the motion.
On April 3, 1997, Judge Bersamin issued an Order directing the immediate preventive suspension of all petitioners from office for sixty (60) days.
2. Court of Appeals (Special Ninth Division):
Petitioners filed a Petition for Certiorari under Rule 65 (CA-G.R. SP No. 43903) alleging lack of jurisdiction, improper application of Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019, and violation of Rule 15 procedural notice rules.
On October 14, 1997, the CA dismissed the petition, ruling that preventive suspension under Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019 is mandatory upon the filing of a valid information. On January 26, 1998, the CA denied reconsideration.
3. **Supreme Court:** Petition for Review on Certiorari under Rule 45 filed by petitioners. The Supreme Court denied the petition and affirmed the Court of Appeals.
### 4. Chronological Facts Storyboard
1. **May 1996:** Petitioners Rogelio Juan (Barangay Chairman), Pedro de Jesus, Delfin Carreon, and Antonio Galguerra (Barangay Kagawads), all incumbent public officers of Barangay Talipapa, Novaliches, Quezon City, allegedly deploy barangay-owned property to advance their election campaign activities. Specifically, Juan and De Jesus use a barangay VHF radio transceiver, while Carreon and Galguerra use a barangay-owned tricycle.
2. **1996:** Separate Informations are filed before the RTC of Quezon City, Branch 96, docketed as Criminal Case Nos. Q-96-64564 to 66, indicting petitioners for violating Section 261(o) of the Omnibus Election Code.
3. **December 5, 1996:** Rodolfo Cayubit and Ricardo Galguerra, through Atty. Leonides S. Bernabe, Jr., file a "Motion for Removal from Office" before the RTC.
4. **December 6, 1996:** The motion is officially received by the RTC.
5. **Oppositions and Comments Filed:** Petitioners oppose the motion, arguing that private complainants have no legal standing, that no private damages were claimed, that the public prosecutor did not sign or conform to the motion, and that it failed to comply with the mandatory 3-day notice and hearing requirements of Rule 15 of the Rules of Court.
6. **Subsequent Conformance by COMELEC Prosecutor:** The COMELEC prosecutor files a "Manifestation and Comment" stating that he formally "conforms" to and adopts the private complainants' motion, submitting it for court resolution.
7. **February 28, 1997:** A "Supplement to Motion for Removal from Office" is filed, to which petitioners again file written opposition and a comprehensive six-page Memorandum challenging the applicability of R.A. No. 3019 and Section 60 of the Local Government Code.
8. **April 3, 1997:** The RTC issues an Order placing all accused under immediate preventive suspension from office for sixty (60) days.
9. **October 14, 1997:** The Court of Appeals dismisses petitioners' Rule 65 Certiorari Petition, affirming the RTC's suspension order.
10. **January 26, 1998:** The Court of Appeals denies petitioners' Motion for Reconsideration, precipitating the Rule 45 petition to the Supreme Court.
5. Competing Interpretations Matrix (The Clash of Canons)
A. Petitioners' Interpretation
**Issue 1 (Jurisdiction):** R.A. No. 7691 expanded the exclusive original jurisdiction of first-level courts (MeTC/MTC) to cover all offenses punishable by imprisonment not exceeding six years. Since election offenses under Section 261(o) carry a maximum penalty of six years, jurisdiction was divested from the RTC. R.A. No. 7691, being a later enactment, supersedes prior jurisdictional statutes.
**Issue 2 (Preventive Suspension):** Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019 applies **only** to violations of R.A. No. 3019 or Title 7, Book II of the Revised Penal Code (Crimes Committed by Public Officers). Violations of the Omnibus Election Code are purely election offenses, not graft offenses, and do not fall within the ambit of "fraud upon government or public funds or property." Hence, the RTC had no power to order suspension in an election case.
**Issue 3 (Procedural Requirements):** Sections 4 and 5 of Rule 15 are mandatory. A motion lacking a notice of hearing is a "useless piece of paper" (**Del Castillo v. Aguinaldo**). Subsequent adoption by the public prosecutor cannot breathe life into a void, non-existent motion.
B. Respondent's (The People's) Interpretation
**Issue 1 (Jurisdiction):** The opening clause of Section 32 of B.P. Blg. 129 expressly retains the exclusive jurisdiction of the RTC where specific statutes so provide (**"Except in cases falling within the exclusive original jurisdiction of the Regional Trial Courts..."**). Section 268 of B.P. Blg. 881 is a special law specifically lodging jurisdiction over election offenses in the RTC; general jurisdictional changes under R.A. No. 7691 did not repeal it (**Generalia specialibus non derogant**).
**Issue 2 (Preventive Suspension):** Following its amendment by B.P. Blg. 195, Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019 covers **any** offense involving fraud upon government property. The unauthorized use of government equipment by incumbent officers for personal campaign advantage constitutes fraud against the government. Statutes must be read together complementarily.
**Issue 3 (Procedural Requirements):** Procedural rules must yield to substantial justice where their purpose has been achieved. The prosecutor's adoption cured any defect of standing, and the filing of written oppositions and memoranda satisfied due process.
6. Inventory of Statutory Construction & Substantive Issues
1. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE] Jurisdiction Over Election Offenses:
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the Regional Trial Court has jurisdiction to hear and decide criminal cases for violation of the Omnibus Election Code punishable by imprisonment not exceeding six years, in light of Section 32 of B.P. Blg. 129, as amended by R.A. No. 7691.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the general jurisdictional grant to first-level courts under R.A. No. 7691 repealed Section 268 of the Omnibus Election Code under the exception clause of Section 32 of B.P. Blg. 129, or whether the specialized grant of jurisdiction over election offenses to the RTC governs under the principle of **generalia specialibus non derogant**.
2. [PRIMARY STATCON ISSUE] Scope of Mandatory Preventive Suspension under Section 13, R.A. No. 3019:
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019 confers authority upon the trial court to order the preventive suspension of public officials charged with an election offense under Section 261(o) of the Omnibus Election Code.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the phrase **"any offense involving fraud upon government or public funds or property"** in Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019, as amended by B.P. Blg. 195, encompasses an election offense under Section 261(o) of B.P. Blg. 881 involving the unauthorized use of government equipment by incumbent public officers.
3. [Procedural Issue] Notice Requirements and Pre-Suspension Hearing:
**Faithful Court Formulation:** Whether the trial court committed reversible error in acting upon a motion for removal from office that originally lacked a notice of hearing, and in ordering preventive suspension without conducting a separate oral pre-suspension hearing.
**Recit-Ready StatCon Question:** Whether the adoption of a defective motion by the public prosecutor and the consideration of multiple responsive pleadings satisfy procedural due process and the requirement for a pre-suspension hearing under Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019.
### 7. Deep-Dive Verdict, Tool Analysis, & Ratio Decidendi per Issue
Issue 1: Jurisdiction over Election Offenses (R.A. No. 7691 vs. Section 268, Omnibus Election Code)
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** The Regional Trial Court possesses exclusive original jurisdiction over violations of the Omnibus Election Code pursuant to Section 268 thereof, which constitutes an express exception preserved by the opening clause of Section 32 of B.P. Blg. 129, as amended by R.A. No. 7691.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"It is evident from Section 32, BP 129, as amended by Section 2 of RA 7691, that the jurisdiction of first-level courts... does not cover those criminal cases which by specific provision of law are cognizable by regional trial courts."
"...[B]y virtue of the exception provided for in the opening sentence of Section 32, the exclusive original jurisdiction of Metropolitan Trial Courts, Municipal Trial Courts, and Municipal Circuit Trial Courts does not cover criminal cases which by specific provisions of law fall within the exclusive original jurisdiction of Regional Trial Courts and of the Sandiganbayan, regardless of the penalty prescribed therefor."
"Such law would be a special law and must be construed as an exception to the general law on jurisdiction of courts, namely, the Judiciary Act of 1948, as amended, and the Judiciary Reorganization Act of 1980. R.A. 7691 can by no means be considered as a special law on jurisdiction; it is merely an amendatory law intended to amend specific sections of the Judiciary Reorganization Act of 1980. Hence, R.A. No. 7691 does not have the effect of repealing laws vesting upon Regional Trial Courts or the Sandiganbayan exclusive original jurisdiction to hear and decide the cases therein specified. That Congress never intended that RA 7691 should repeal such special provisions is indubitably evident from the fact that it did not touch at all the opening sentence of Section 32 of B.P. Blg. 129 providing for the exception."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate & Plain Text:** The Court analyzed the introductory saving clause of Section 32 of B.P. Blg. 129: **"Except in cases falling within the exclusive original jurisdiction of the Regional Trial Courts..."** The presence of this explicit exception bars any plain-meaning assumption that **all** offenses under six years belong to first-level courts.
2. **Intrinsic Aids / Harmonization:** The phrase **"Except in cases..."** deliberately conditions and limits the subsequent general grant in paragraph (2) of Section 32.
3. **Extrinsic Aids & Nature of the Statutes:** Following the doctrine in **COMELEC v. Noynay** and **Morales v. Court of Appeals**, the Court treated Section 268 of the Omnibus Election Code as a special law governing a specialized subject matter (election offenses), whereas B.P. Blg. 129 and R.A. No. 7691 are general laws on judicial structure.
4. **Statutory Presumptions:** The Court invoked the presumption against implied repeals. Congress did not intend R.A. No. 7691 to dismantle specific jurisdictional grants, as demonstrated by its intentional preservation of the exception clause in Section 32.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** Petitioners' argument—that the six-year penalty ceiling mechanically controls—was rejected because it impermissibly ignored the opening exception clause of Section 32.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation: (Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** R.A. No. 7691 is a general law amending court jurisdiction, but it explicitly maintained the opening phrase in Section 32 of B.P. Blg. 129 that excludes cases specifically reserved by special statutes for the RTC. Because Section 268 of the Omnibus Election Code specifically vests exclusive jurisdiction over election offenses in the RTC, that special provision operates as an exception to the general six-year jurisdictional threshold of municipal trial courts.
Issue 2: Applicability of Preventive Suspension under Section 13, R.A. No. 3019 to Section 261(o) of the Omnibus Election Code
**(a) Short Answer: YES.** Incumbent public officers charged with the unauthorized and unlawful use of government property under Section 261(o) of the Omnibus Election Code commit acts constituting fraud against the government, triggering mandatory preventive suspension under the expanded terms of Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"Interestingly, prior to its amendment by BP 195, the said provision had applied to public officers who, under a valid information, were charged with violations of RA 3019 or with offenses covered by the Revised Penal Code provision on bribery. The amendatory law expanded the scope of the provision; now public officers may likewise be suspended from office if, under a valid information, they are charged with an offense falling under Title 7 of Book II of the Revised Penal Code, or with any other form of fraud involving government funds or property."
"True, the cases against petitioners involve violations of the Election Code; however, the charges are not unidimensional. Every law must be read together with the provisions of any other complementing law, unless both are otherwise irreconcilable."
"It must be emphasized that petitioners were incumbent public officers charged with the unauthorized and unlawful use of government property in their custody, in the pursuit of personal interests. The crime being imputed to them is akin to that committed by public officers as laid down in the Revised Penal Code. Certainly, petitioners' acts constitute fraud against the government; thus, the present case is covered by Section 13 of RA 3019."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Threshold Gate:** The Court rejected petitioners' rigid classification that an offense must be exclusively categorized as an "election offense" or a "graft offense."
2. **Legislative History / Amendatory Tracking (B.P. Blg. 195):** The Court evaluated the historical text of Section 13. Before amendment, suspension applied strictly to R.A. No. 3019 charges and bribery. By enacting B.P. Blg. 195, the legislature intentionally added the phrase **"or for any offense involving fraud upon government or public funds or property."** This expansion removed the statutory limitation confining suspension strictly to graft or bribery cases.
3. **Statutes in Pari Materia / Complementary Construction:** The Court held that statutes are not unidimensional and must be read together complementarily unless irreconcilable. Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019 complements penal provisions in other codes where the underlying factual conduct involves misuse of public assets.
4. **Statutory Policy & Purpose:** The Court anchored its construction on the constitutional maxim that "public office is a public trust." The statutory purpose of preventive suspension is prophylactic—to prevent an incumbent official from tampering with evidence, intimidating witnesses, or committing further malfeasance while holding public office.
5. **Rejection of Losing Construction:** The Court refused to permit public officials to escape preventive suspension simply because their fraudulent misapplication of public equipment was codified in the Election Code rather than the Revised Penal Code or R.A. No. 3019.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation: (Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** When the legislature enacted B.P. Blg. 195, it deliberately broadened Section 13 of R.A. No. 3019 to mandate suspension for **any** crime involving fraud upon government property, not just traditional graft offenses. Because the barangay officials were charged with unlawfully using government-owned communication gear and vehicles for their personal political campaigns, their conduct constituted fraud against the government, directly subjecting them to mandatory preventive suspension.
Issue 3: Procedural Defects in Motion and Lack of Separate Pre-Suspension Hearing
**(a) Short Answer: NO (Procedural Objections Dismissed).** While the private motion initially suffered from formal defects, the formal adoption thereof by the COMELEC prosecutor cured the standing defect, and the filing and consideration of comprehensive written memoranda satisfied both the notice requirements of Rule 15 and the pre-suspension hearing mandate of Section 13, R.A. No. 3019.
**(b) Verbatim Doctrinal & Canons Pronouncements:**
"Considering the circumstances of the present Petition, however, we believe that the requirements of procedural due process were substantially complied with, and that such compliance justifies a liberal interpretation of the above-mentioned rules."
"In his 'Manifestation on Comment of the Accused,' the COMELEC prosecutor adopted the assailed Motion as well as the February 28, 1997 'Supplement to Motion for Removal from Office.' This action should be considered to have thus cured the procedural defect pointed out by petitioners. More important, however, is the fact that the trial court heard petitioners and considered their arguments."
"In the case at bar, while there was no pre-suspension hearing held to determine the validity of the Informations that had been filed against petitioners, we believe that the numerous pleadings filed for and against them have achieved the goal of this procedure. The right to due process is satisfied not just by an oral hearing but by the filing and the consideration by the court of the parties' pleadings, memoranda and other position papers."
**(c) Step-by-Step Interpretative Reasoning:**
1. **Rule of Procedure vs. Substantial Due Process:** While acknowledging the strict doctrine that litigated motions without notice of hearing are generally **pro forma**, the Court held that procedural rules must be interpreted liberally where their underlying objective—notice and opportunity to be heard—is fully accomplished.
2. **Curing of Standing:** The private complainants' lack of independent personality to move for removal in a public prosecution was cured when the authorized COMELEC prosecutor expressly conformed to and adopted the motion on the record.
3. **Functional Equivalence of Pre-Suspension Hearing:** Under **Socrates v. Sandiganbayan**, a pre-suspension hearing is required to determine the validity of the information. The Court ruled that this requirement does not dictate an exclusively oral hearing; the submission of extensive memoranda and written oppositions addressing the validity of the charge functionally satisfies due process.
**(d) Plain-Language "Recit-Ready" Explanation: (Plain-Language StatCon Explanation)** Procedural rules requiring notice and pre-suspension hearings are designed to ensure fair play, not to act as empty technical hurdles. Because the public prosecutor formally adopted the motion and the petitioners were granted full opportunity to argue their defenses through comprehensive written briefs, the constitutional and statutory requirements of due process were completely satisfied.
8. Separate Opinions on Statutory Construction
**No separate opinions discussed in the provided text.**
9. Overall Verdict (Dispositive Portion / Fallo)
**Verbatim Fallo:**
"WHEREFORE, the petition is hereby DENIED and the assailed Decision of the Court of Appeals AFFIRMED. Costs against petitioners.
SO ORDERED."
**Plain-Language Outcome:** The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Appeals and the Regional Trial Court. Petitioners (the Barangay Chairman and Kagawads) remained validly suspended from public office for sixty (60) days. The decision establishes that the Regional Trial Courts retain exclusive jurisdiction over criminal violations of the Omnibus Election Code, and that any incumbent public officer indicted for unlawfully using government equipment or property is subject to mandatory preventive suspension under Section 13 of the Anti-Graft Law.
